A diplomatic rank for an envoy authorised to act for a state; Renault received the title in recognition of his services in 1903.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Advancements in precision metrology and spectroscopy
sections.body: The 1907 presentation highlighted a major gain in precision from measuring lengths through light interference. It described accuracy approaching one-fiftieth of a wavelength, roughly one hundred-thousandth of a millimetre, and compared this favourably with microscopes available at the time. The measurement came from changes in the interference pattern, expressed in fractions of the light’s wavelength. Astronomical applications included measuring the apparent sizes of Jupiter’s satellites. For closely spaced spectral features such as those in the Zeeman effect, Michelson showed how an interferometer or an echelon grating could resolve details that ordinary spectroscopy missed. These were alternative optical approaches, not necessarily two components used together. The work linked instrument design with measurable improvements in both laboratory physics and astronomy.

sections.heading: Michelson's optical inventions and light velocity investigations
sections.body: Michelson’s early optical work included precise measurements of light’s speed. With Morley, he used interference to test for the effect expected from Earth’s motion through a supposed stationary light-carrying medium. The experiment did not detect that expected effect; it was not a test of every possible inertial frame. He also measured the existing metre standard in wavelengths of cadmium light and developed the echelon spectroscope. His career continued after the 1907 award. During the First World War he worked on naval instruments, including a rangefinder. In 1920 his astronomical interferometry helped determine the diameter of Betelgeuse, while Studies in Optics appeared in 1927. These later achievements extended the precision-measurement programme for which he had already been honoured.

terms.definition: A measuring instrument based on light interference laws used to determine lengths, angles, and small distances with extreme accuracy.
An optical instrument designed to distinguish very closely spaced wavelengths, making fine details within a spectrum observable.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Michelson and Morley (1887): On the Relative Motion of the Earth and the Luminiferous Ether

sections.heading: Methods for measuring radioactive radiation intensity
sections.body: Electrical measurements made radioactive changes visible when ordinary balances and spectroscopes could not detect them. Rutherford developed precise ways to compare radiation intensity and distinguish alpha from beta radiation. Research on radioactive gases also revealed a sequence of changes: an emanation transformed into further radioactive substances, some of which formed thin deposits on nearby surfaces. Rutherford and Frederick Soddy interpreted such observations through their disintegration theory in 1902. The changes occurred within atoms, rather than merely rearranging atoms into different molecules. A radioactive substance could therefore generate another substance with different properties, which might itself undergo further transformation. Their account also described a characteristic rate of change for each member of a sequence. This gave investigators a way to identify and organise short-lived products that were otherwise difficult to isolate through ordinary chemical methods.

sections.heading: Research on radioactive rays and thorium emanation
sections.body: Rutherford continued his research on uranium radiation after moving to McGill University, studying it in the Macdonald Laboratory. With R. B. Owens, he investigated the radioactive emanation from thorium. This gas was later understood as an isotope of radon and called thoron. Frederick Soddy joined him at McGill in 1900, and their collaboration developed the account of radioactivity as atomic transformation. Experimental observations helped place newly identified radioactive substances within sequences of decay. After Rutherford moved to Manchester, he worked with Hans Geiger on detecting individual alpha particles and counting those emitted by radium. Counting individual events added a different kind of measurement to studies of overall radiation intensity and helped investigators connect the properties of radioactive materials with the particles they emitted.

terms.definition: A theory proposing that radioactivity results from changes within the atom itself, causing elements to break into radiation and new atoms.
A historical term for a radioactive gas released by a material; thorium’s emanation was later called thoron.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of Eucken's philosophical method and works
sections.body: Eucken examined philosophical concepts in relation to the periods that produced them. In his 1878 study of contemporary fundamental ideas, he traced the development of such alternatives as immanence and transcendence, or monism and dualism. The 1908 presentation praised this attention to both intellectual history and present concerns. His survey of major thinkers followed different conceptions of human life from Plato onwards. Other works developed his own account of spiritual existence: The Struggle for a Spiritual Content of Life and Life’s Basis and Life’s Ideal connected historical investigation with philosophical argument. His books of 1908 included The Meaning and Value of Life and an introduction to the philosophy of spiritual life. Across this programme he treated philosophy as continuing inquiry, revising and expanding earlier works rather than presenting one permanently finished system.

sections.heading: Eucken's philosophical development and key publications
sections.body: As an idealist philosopher, Eucken constructed a flexible system through various writings that underwent numerous revisions over several decades. His academic background included studying philology, history, and philosophy at the universities of Berlin and Göttingen, eventually producing a dissertation regarding Aristotelian language. Throughout his career, he authored significant texts such as The Problem of Human Life as Viewed by the Great Thinkers from Plato to the Present Time and The Struggle for a Spiritual Content of Life. Additionally, his 1907 essay, Philosophie der Geschichte, contributed to the series Contemporary Civilization. He revised his books over several decades, and some appeared in more than twelve editions.

terms.definition: The study of how ideas develop and change within different historical settings.
A philosophical outlook giving mind, ideas or spirit a fundamental role in understanding reality; Eucken emphasised spiritual life.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of bacteria-destroying and poison immunity
sections.body: The presentation distinguished resistance to microbes from resistance to the poisons they release. Mechnikov studied cells that engulf foreign material, including observations in small aquatic animals. Ehrlich's work addressed another aspect of defense: specific substances in body fluids that act against toxins. Anti-diphtheria serum illustrated how antitoxins could be transferred into an animal or patient to neutralize diphtheria toxin. Investigators also studied the body's own production of antibodies following exposure to particular substances. These were complementary lines of inquiry. Neutralizing a toxin was a different process from a cell taking up a microbe, even when both could contribute to protection during an infection.

sections.heading: Ehrlich's research on aniline dyes and chemotherapy
sections.body: Ehrlich used aniline dyes to study tissues and classified them as acidic, basic or neutral. His 1882 staining method for the tuberculosis bacterium became the basis for later refinements. His interest in selective chemical affinities also shaped a wider search for substances that could attack pathogens. With collaborators he investigated trypan red and arsenic-containing compounds. This research career extended beyond the immunity work recognized in 1908: subsequent testing with Hata led to Salvarsan for syphilis. The staining, immunity and chemotherapy projects were related by an interest in why particular chemicals bind to particular biological targets, but they were distinct investigations.

sections.heading: Mechnikov's experimental observations of cellular defense
sections.body: While working in Messina, Mechnikov used tangerine tree thorns to test defensive mechanisms in starfish larvae. He observed mobile cells surrounding these foreign objects, Knowing that leucocytes leave blood vessels during inflammation, he proposed that they might engulf and digest invading bacteria. He later validated this process by observing phagocytes attacking fungal spores in Daphnia and noting that less virulent anthrax strains were susceptible to such cellular attacks. His research eventually led to the publication of his 1901 treatise regarding immunity in infectious diseases.

terms.definition: A form of protection where the organism produces elements that act specifically against the toxic products released by bacteria.
Ehrlich’s historical model in which cell receptors bind toxins and released binding material can act as antibodies; it was later revised.
A cell that engulfs and digests foreign material or microbes; Mechnikov investigated its role in defense against infection.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Peace advocacy and international organizational development
sections.body: Arnoldson contributed to the Swedish Peace and Arbitration Association as its editor and secretary. He authored works such as The Hope of the Centuries, which details the expansion of peace ideals in international relations. Bajer established the Danish Peace Society and served on the council for the Interparliamentary Union. His efforts were instrumental in founding a Nordic Interparliamentary Union. Additionally, Bajer utilized various articles and pamphlets to address diverse issues within the peace movement while maintaining connections with international figures like Frédéric Passy.

sections.heading: Arnoldson's legislative efforts and peace publications
sections.body: As a Swedish parliamentarian from 1882 to 1887, Arnoldson introduced legislation to expand the franchise and pursued antimilitaristic policies. He drafted a resolution investigating guaranteed neutrality for Sweden and campaigned for a popular petition favoring arbitration agreements with foreign nations. His literary contributions included the historical essay Is World Peace Possible? and the pacifist history The Hope of the Centuries. Additionally, he served as secretary for the Swedish Peace and Arbitration Association and edited various journals, including Tiden and Fredsvännen, to promote peace information.

sections.heading: Bajer's proposals for neutrality and international arbitration
sections.body: Bajer utilized his military background to highlight strategic risks regarding Nordic water routes, proposing a Scandinavian neutrality modeled after Switzerland and Belgium. He advocated for arbitration as a replacement for war, successfully guiding a 1888 Danish Parliament proposal to establish agreements with Sweden and Norway. To centralize pacifist information, he proposed creating a permanent bureau in Bern, which later functioned as a clearinghouse. His organizational efforts included founding the Society for Promotion of Danish Neutrality and serving as the first president of the International Peace Bureau's governing board.

terms.definition: A continuing commitment to remain outside wars between other states, which Arnoldson wanted Sweden to declare and have guaranteed.
The right to vote in elections; Arnoldson supported legislation that would extend it to more people.
A mechanism Bajer believed could satisfactorily supplant war when settling differences among nations through formal, agreed-upon procedures.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The mechanism of Lippmann's color photography method
sections.body: Lippmann described his color-photography process in 1891. A glass plate carried a light-sensitive gelatin emulsion backed by mercury, which served as a mirror. Light entering through the glass crossed the emulsion and reflected back from the mercury. The incident and reflected waves produced a stationary pattern of bright and dark planes. Successive bright planes were separated by half the wavelength within the material. Development left layers of silver corresponding to this pattern. When the finished plate was illuminated, reflections from these layers interfered with one another, reproducing colors associated with their spacing. The principle resembled the interference colors of a soap film. The colors therefore depended on the structure recorded inside the emulsion rather than on adding colored pigments.

sections.heading: Scientific developments in physics and instrumentation
sections.body: Lippmann conducted research on electrical and capillary phenomena while studying in Heidelberg, which resulted in the creation of a highly sensitive capillary electrometer. His scientific contributions extended to astronomy through the invention of the coelostat, a device designed to immobilize images of stars for photography. In 1895, he developed a technique using photographic registration to remove the personal equation from time measurements and studied ways to reduce irregularities in pendulum clocks by comparing oscillation periods. Beyond his color photography theory, which he communicated to the Academy of Sciences in 1891, his work involved improving standard instruments across various physics branches, including thermodynamics, optics, and photochemistry.

terms.definition: Stationary patterns produced when waves traveling in opposite directions overlap; in this process they recorded alternating bright and dark planes in the emulsion.
A specialized device used in astronomy to immobilize the image of a star and its surrounding stars for photography.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Measuring acid strength through reaction rates
sections.body: Ostwald compared acids and bases by measuring the rates of reactions they promoted. He then related these results to Arrhenius’s account of ions in aqueous solutions. Conductivity measurements supplied an independent way to investigate dissociation and the concentrations of hydrogen and hydroxyl ions. The agreement between electrical and reaction-rate measurements supported an explanation of why different acids and bases produced different effects. In the reactions studied, the relevant ions acted as catalysts. Ostwald broadened these investigations into a systematic account of catalysis as a question of reaction speed. This helped separate two issues: where a reaction’s equilibrium lies and how quickly it approaches that equilibrium. A suitable catalyst could greatly shorten the time needed without determining a new equilibrium composition.

sections.heading: Foundations of classical physical chemistry and scientific publishing
sections.body: Ostwald established himself as a founder of classical physical chemistry through extensive experimental investigations beginning in 1875. His early research addressed chemical affinity, electrochemistry and the dynamics of reactions. Beyond his laboratory work, he significantly shaped the field through organized scientific communication. He launched the journal Zeitschrift für physikalische Chemie in 1887, continuing as editor after the Nobel award and completing one hundred volumes by 1922. His educational contributions included several major textbooks, such as the 1884 Lehrbuch der Allgemeinen Chemie and the 1893 Hand- und Hilfsbuch zur Ausführung physikalisch-chemischer Messungen. Additionally, he organized professional scientific communities by founding the Deutsche Elektrochemische Gesellschaft in 1894, which later expanded into the Deutsche Bunsen-Gesellschaft für angewandte physikalische Chemie.

terms.definition: Acceleration of a chemical reaction by a substance that participates in the process but is regenerated overall.
The study of chemical substances and reactions through physical measurements and principles, including energy, equilibrium and reaction rates.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Swedish Academy presentation of the 1909 Nobel Prize
sections.body: During the 1909 ceremony, President Claes Annerstedt highlighted how Lagerlöf's writing captures the inner life of nature and the spiritual movements of the peasantry. He noted her ability to extract secrets from saints’ stories and folk legends by perceiving the invisible world beneath the visible. Her work includes realistic depictions of peasant life, such as Tösen från Stormyrtorpet, which features themes of unselfish love. Additionally, her achievement is evident in Jerusalem, a work tracing the pilgrimage of Dalekarlia people to the Holy Land. Annerstedt emphasized that her style maintains a purity of diction and musical beauty derived from her native language. He also referenced the Swedish Academy's previous recognition of her importance through a Gold Medal awarded five years prior.

sections.heading: Evolution of Lagerlöf's Literary Works and Travels
sections.body: Following a literary competition win in 1890, Lagerlöf published Gösta Berlings Saga in 1891. Although initially unnoticed, a Danish translation brought critical acclaim to the book. Supported by the Swedish Academy and royal family in 1895, she transitioned from teaching to full-time writing. Her travels led to Antikrists mirakler, a novel set in Sicily, and Jerusalem, which depicted Swedish peasants emigrating to the Holy Land after her 1900 visit. She also produced Nils Holgerssons underbara resa genom Sverige as an elementary school primer. After the 1909 award, her publications in the 1920s included the historical trilogy consisting of Löwensköldska Ringen, Charlotte Löwensköld, and Anna Svärd, alongside her Mårbacka reminiscences.

terms.definition: An imaginative quality that gives literary form to spiritual experience, folk belief and worlds beyond ordinary observation.
A set of three connected literary works that develop a shared story, family history or group of themes.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Thyroid physiology and surgical advancements
sections.body: Kocher’s observations showed that surviving an operation did not guarantee lasting health. Patients whose thyroid glands had been completely removed could later develop muscular weakness, swelling, anaemia and severe deterioration. The condition was called cachexia strumipriva. His 1883 account helped establish the importance of retaining functioning thyroid tissue in the surgical practice of that period. Earlier animal experiments by J. M. Schiff had raised related questions, but clinical follow-up made the gland’s role especially clear. The work connected surgery with physiology: the thyroid performed an essential function, rather than being an expendable swelling. It also improved understanding of illnesses associated with reduced or abnormal thyroid activity. The historical advance combined safer operations with recognition of complications that might emerge after apparently successful healing.

sections.heading: Surgical advancements in abdominal and orthopedic procedures
sections.body: Beyond thyroid research, Kocher contributed to several surgical fields through experimental and anatomical studies. His method for reducing shoulder dislocations was widely adopted in his time. In abdominal surgery, he developed procedures for removing stones from the lower bile duct and improved access to the duodenum by mobilising it. His investigations also addressed trauma, including the effects of small-calibre projectiles and the mechanisms of gunshot wounds. For rectal excision, he extended an approach involving removal of the coccyx by also removing part of the sacrum. His writings on surgical infection accompanied strong support for antiseptic wound treatment. These examples illustrate the breadth of his surgical programme and its close connection between anatomical investigation and improvements in operative technique.

terms.definition: A historical term for severe illness following loss of thyroid function after complete removal, including weakness, swelling, anaemia and mental deterioration.
The control or stopping of bleeding. Kocher experimentally investigated twisting arteries as one method of achieving it.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Contributions to international law and parliamentary arbitration
sections.body: Beernaert chaired the commission tasked with proposing armament restrictions during the first Hague Conference. He also held honorary leadership roles in legal associations, including the International Law Association. Meanwhile, d’Estournelles de Constant established the Groupe parlementaire de l’arbitrage international in 1903. His advocacy helped bring about arbitration treaties between France and other nations. Additionally, he promoted peace by organizing reciprocal visits between various national parliamentary groups to strengthen international cooperation.

sections.heading: Diplomatic methods for advancing international arbitration
sections.body: D’Estournelles de Constant utilized parliamentary exchanges to promote peace, founding a cross-party group in 1903 that organized visits between foreign legislators. These missions helped establish the Franco-German Association and supported the Entente Cordiale. He also established the Association for International Conciliation in 1905 to foster global understanding. His legal efforts included strengthening arbitration language within Article 27 of Convention I and influencing President Theodore Roosevelt to submit a United States-Mexico dispute to the Hague Tribunal. He remained active in the Permanent Court of Arbitration and the Interparliamentary Union.

sections.heading: Beernaert's contributions to maritime law and international arbitration
sections.body: Beernaert drove efforts to unify international maritime law through initiatives in 1885 and 1888, though these early proposals were not adopted. After the 1909 Nobel award, he chaired a Brussels conference where 1910 conventions regarding sea collisions and assistance were signed by various nations. His arbitration work included representing Mexico during its 1902 dispute with the United States, marking the first case presented to the Permanent Court of Arbitration. Additionally, he led commissions at the Hague conferences focused on arms limitation and the codification of land warfare.

terms.definition: An agreement under which states commit specified disputes to an agreed arbitration process for decision.
An association of legislators around a shared policy interest; d’Estournelles’s group included members of different parties and both parliamentary houses.
An institution providing a framework for arbitration, including the 1902 dispute in which Beernaert represented Mexico before an appointed tribunal.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Paul Henri d'Estournelles de Constant — biography

sections.heading: Improvements in electrical wave transmission
sections.body: Early wireless transmitters produced trains of oscillations whose amplitude fell rapidly. The weak response at a distant receiver left it vulnerable to interference from other stations. Braun changed the transmitter’s circuit arrangement to produce stronger oscillations with less damping. A receiver tuned to the corresponding frequency could then respond more strongly through resonance while being less affected by other frequencies. The 1909 presentation identified this improvement as crucial to extending wireless communication over long distances. Its importance lay in combining usable signal strength with better selectivity, rather than simply generating electrical waves.

sections.heading: Ferdinand Braun's electrical and wireless telegraphy advancements
sections.body: Braun studied vibrations in rods and strings before concentrating on electricity. He investigated departures from Ohm’s law and relationships between heat and the electrical behaviour of reversible cells. His experimental instruments included an electrometer and a cathode-ray oscillograph constructed in 1897. In 1898 he began wireless experiments, initially trying to send Morse signals through water using high-frequency currents. He subsequently introduced a closed oscillating circuit into wireless transmission. A 1901 brochure described work on wireless telegraphy through water and air. His successful reception of directed messages using inclined antennas followed in 1902, so it was a later development.

sections.heading: Advancements in wireless telegraphy and signal transmission
sections.body: Marconi’s experiments at Pontecchio led to a wireless telegraphy patent in 1896. In 1897 he demonstrated signals over twelve miles to the Italian government, followed by communication across the English Channel in 1899. His 1900 tuning patent sought more selective transmission and reception. The Nobel biography recounts his 1901 transatlantic experiment between Cornwall and Newfoundland, followed by a commercial transatlantic service in 1907. Patents for a magnetic detector and a directional aerial accompanied these developments. Much later, after the Nobel award, his short-wave research contributed to a microwave telephone link between Vatican City and Castel Gandolfo in 1932.

terms.definition: Oscillations whose amplitude decreases over time as energy is lost. Reducing damping lets a train of oscillations persist longer.
An electrical circuit in which charge and current vary repeatedly, enabling the generation of oscillations used in a radio transmitter.
Wireless communication that adjusts transmitting and receiving circuits to compatible frequencies, strengthening the desired signal and reducing interference.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Advancements in alicyclic compound research and industrial application
sections.body: Wallach began systematic terpene research in 1884, developing methods to identify and separate substances in essential oils. An early survey reduced many supposedly different names to eight distinct terpenes then recognised; additional compounds were identified later. The result did not mean that only eight terpenes exist. He also investigated how ordinary reagents could change one compound into another, so that analysis itself did not create a misleading result. His programme extended to related alcohols, ketones and larger terpene compounds. These methods helped manufacturers characterise raw materials and detect adulteration. The 1910 presentation cited growth in Germany’s essential-oil preparations from twelve million marks in 1885 to forty-five or fifty million, crediting research and trained chemists with contributions to that industry.

sections.heading: Chemical characterization of diverse hydrocarbon structures
sections.body: Wallach compared substances in the C10H16 group using familiar reagents such as hydrogen chloride and hydrogen bromide. The many existing names did not always correspond to different chemical identities. Careful reactions and characterisation let him distinguish genuinely different structures while showing that some differently named samples represented the same compound. His 1909 book Terpene und Campher collected his extensive terpene and camphor research in a volume dedicated to his students. Other investigations ranged beyond that field, including conversion of chloral into dichloroacetic acid and studies of amide chlorides, imide chlorides and amidines. The biography emphasises carefully performed experiments as central to this approach. In a field crowded with names and mixtures, comparable chemical evidence made a more reliable classification possible.

terms.definition: Organic compounds containing carbon rings that are not aromatic; many of the terpene structures investigated by Wallach belong to this group.
The existence of compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of their atoms, giving them potentially different properties.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Principles of novella composition and lyrical poetry
sections.body: Heyse developed an account of novella writing that placed a consequential human fate at the centre of the story. The 1910 presentation praised his ability to combine careful construction with narrative freedom. It illustrated his range with Andrea Delfin, set against a Venetian background; Bild der Mutter; and the troubadour story Marion. The speaker’s description of these works as morally profound or artistically masterful expresses the Academy’s critical judgement. Heyse also wrote lyric poetry and verse narratives, including Salamander in terza rima, and plays such as Kolberg and Hadrian. His tastes did not simply follow literary fashion: he admired some of Ibsen’s earlier plays while disliking Ghosts and later symbolic dramas. His translations of writers including Manzoni and Leopardi extended his engagement with Italian literature to German readers.

sections.heading: Philological research and scholarly publications
sections.body: Heyse began with classical philology in Berlin before turning to Romance philology under Friedrich Diez in Bonn. His doctorate, completed in 1852, examined refrains in Provençal poetry. A grant from the Prussian Ministry of Culture then enabled him to study manuscripts in Italian libraries; he published the results as Romanische Inedita in 1856. His later scholarship included five volumes combining translations and studies of Italian poets from the mid-eighteenth century onwards, published between 1889 and 1905. He also translated José Caveda y Nava’s history of Spanish architecture. Literary work and scholarly networks supported one another in his career. In 1854, on Emanuel Geibel’s recommendation, King Maximilian II of Bavaria offered him a paid position in Munich that included attending the king’s weekly gatherings of poets and scholars.

terms.definition: A prose fiction form between a short story and a novel; Heyse emphasised concentrated construction around a significant human fate.
A field of linguistic study focused on the development and analysis of languages derived from Latin.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Advancements in protein and nucleic acid chemistry
sections.body: Kossel extended earlier investigations by Drechsel and his students into the substances obtained when proteins break down. He developed analytical methods that helped determine the quantities of these components within proteins. He also studied protamines, relatively simple proteins obtained from fish milt, and identified histones as another important group of cellular proteins. The 1910 presentation described histones as intermediate in character between protamines and ordinary proteins; this was a chemical classification, not a description of their position inside a cell. His research also examined the combination of proteins with nucleic acids. These phosphorus-containing substances included purine and pyrimidine components together with sugars or related materials. Determining what these complex mixtures contained was a necessary step toward explaining the chemistry of cells.

sections.heading: Chemical investigations into cell nucleus components
sections.body: During his research on fish-roe, Kossel studied protamines and hexone bases. In 1896, he discovered histidine and developed a classical method for the quantitative separation of hexone bases. His laboratory work also involved studying how proteins transform into peptone and investigating arginase, an enzyme that hydrolyses arginine into urea and ornithine, alongside his pupil H. D. Dakin. He further explored agmatine in herring roe by devising a specific preparation method. These chemical studies were documented in significant publications such as Investigations into the nucleins and their cleavage products. Through his leadership in various institutes, he also worked to establish independent chairs for physiology and medical chemistry within German universities.

terms.definition: The study of the chemical substances and processes of living tissues and cells.
A historical name for a group of basic protein breakdown products that Kossel investigated and developed methods to separate quantitatively.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: How the Bureau operated around 1910
sections.body: The 1910 presentation described the practical work behind an international peace network. The Bureau in Bern maintained records and a library, circulated information, prepared questions for annual congresses and helped carry out their decisions. Its associated society gave it a legal structure under Swiss law that allowed it to receive legacies. Publications were a substantial part of its work: a regular bulletin reported movement news and new literature, while a yearbook collected information about international affairs, institutions and individuals. The speech also mentioned an affiliated office in Washington, established in 1894. Its finances were modest. Interest on capital of about 40,000 francs, government grants and private donations provided roughly 8,000 francs annually at the time. Much of that income went towards publication. These figures describe the Bureau’s position when it received the award.

sections.heading: Bureau activities and institutional objectives
sections.body: The Bureau served as the coordinating office of the International Union of Peace Societies. Founded following the 1891 congress in Rome, it connected organisations seeking peaceful settlement of international disputes. Its early programme included arbitration, bilateral peace agreements, a permanent international court and institutions through which governments could cooperate. Arranging congresses and circulating publications gave these proposals a continuing organisational base. The Bureau also worked with the Interparliamentary Union to reach politicians as well as wider public opinion. The Nobel history presents these efforts as part of the background to later international institutions, including the League of Nations. That history also records the limits of its resources: before the prize, annual funds were generally about 8,000–9,000 francs. Its contribution lay in sustained coordination and advocacy across national borders.

terms.definition: A gathering where peace organisations discussed common proposals and coordinated activities; the Bureau prepared agendas and followed up decisions.
The association of peace organisations for which the Bureau acted as a central office and executive body.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
International Peace Bureau: foundation, congresses and coordination before the 1910 award

sections.heading: Mechanisms of molecular attraction and corresponding states
sections.body: Van der Waals’s equation addressed departures from simple gas behaviour by allowing for the space molecules occupy and their attraction to one another. Both effects become important as a gas is compressed. Treating a liquid and its vapour through the same molecular account helped explain their continuity near the critical state. His broader idea of corresponding states compared substances after scaling their properties by critical quantities. This supplied an organising model for experiments rather than an exact prediction for every liquid under all conditions. He also extended his investigations from pure substances to mixtures. The 1910 presentation connected his theoretical work with refrigeration and low-temperature research, including Kamerlingh Onnes’s liquefaction of helium in 1908. Its significance lay in making molecular interactions part of a quantitative description linking gases with liquids.

sections.heading: Development of the Law of Corresponding States
sections.body: Van der Waals expanded his research by enunciating the Law of Corresponding States in 1880. Within his model, expressing pressure, volume and temperature relative to their critical values gives different substances a common form of equation. By utilizing these critical constants, specific variables within the equation disappear. This theoretical framework provided a guide for experimentalists, eventually assisting J. Dewar in the 1898 liquefaction of hydrogen and H. Kamerlingh Onnes in the 1908 liquefaction of helium. Additionally, his work included a thermodynamic theory of capillarity introduced in 1893, which proposed that density changes gradually at the liquid-vapour boundary layer. He also published a treatise on the theory of binary solutions in the Archives Néerlandaises.

terms.definition: The limiting condition at which the distinction between a liquid and its vapour disappears.
Pressure, volume and temperature expressed relative to their respective critical values, allowing comparisons between substances in corresponding-states theory.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Johannes Diderik van der Waals — biography

sections.heading: Chemical investigation of radioactive elements
sections.body: Measurements of uranium and thorium compounds suggested that their activity depended on how much radioactive element they contained. Pitchblende was unexpectedly more active, pointing to additional constituents. The Curies repeatedly separated large quantities of the mineral and tracked the activity of the resulting fractions, obtaining compounds associated with polonium and radium. Establishing radium's chemical identity required further measurements: Marie Curie reported an atomic weight of 226.45, and in 1910 she and André Debierne obtained radium as a metal. The chemistry award recognized this investigation of the elements and their compounds. The presentation also described the growing field of radioactivity research and the medical uses then being explored. Its account belongs to the early development of those applications.

sections.heading: Chemical methods for radium isolation and characterization
sections.body: The 1911 chemistry prize recognized research into radioactivity through specific chemical processes. Curie developed techniques to separate radium from radioactive residues, producing enough material to permit detailed study of its properties and therapeutic uses. Her written works, including the 1910 Traité de radioactivité, documented these scientific investigations. Beyond element isolation, her methods enabled the characterization of substances for medical applications. Her later academic leadership included directing the Curie Laboratory at the Radium Institute. These chemical advancements provided the foundation for understanding radioactive elements, moving beyond initial observations of spontaneous radiation to the systematic study of their specific chemical behaviors and potential for alleviating suffering.

terms.definition: A measure of an element’s atomic mass relative to a reference; Curie used such measurements to characterize radium chemically.
A 1910 scientific publication by Curie that documented her research and findings regarding the nature of radioactivity.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Marie Curie — 1911 Nobel lecture: isolation of metallic radium with André Debierne

sections.heading: Literary characteristics and early published works
sections.body: Maeterlinck's writing displays a singular, mystical talent that deviates from traditional literary forms. His early publication, the verse collection Serres chaudes, contains tormented poems contrasting with his meditative nature. In the 1889 drama La Princesse Maleine, he utilized deliberate monotony and repetition to create an impression of duration within a somber, fairy-tale setting. His later compositions, such as Pelléas et Mélisande and Alladine et Palomides, explore the fatal power of love constrained by external circumstances. Through works like Aglavaine et Sélysette, he employs a symbolic style to reflect profound realities beyond the tangible world. Additionally, his philosophical writing, including Le Trésor des humbles, examines spiritual life and figures such as the mystic Ruysbrock.

sections.heading: Evolution of Maeterlinck’s literary themes and prose
sections.body: Maeterlinck's early dramas, including L'Intruse, Les Aveugles and Pelléas et Mélisande, often used limited action and an atmosphere of uncertainty, fatalism and death. L'Oiseau bleu introduced a different, fairy-tale optimism. He also explored mystical ideas in prose works such as Le Trésor des Humbles and La Sagesse et la destinée. His writing about nature included bees and flowers. Books about termites and ants belonged to his later career, after the 1911 award, as did the Belgian title of count granted in 1932. The biography therefore covers a longer and more varied career than the dramatic achievement for which the Nobel citation particularly honored him.

terms.definition: A literary method used by Maeterlinck to perceive reflections of a profound, secret reality beyond the tangible, physical world.
A predominant genre in Maeterlinck's writing characterized by themes of mysticism, fatalism, and a lack of traditional action.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mathematical formulation of eye dioptrics
sections.body: Gullstrand addressed complex challenges regarding how light refracts through the eye's varying layers. He focused on the difficulty of charting light passage through a medium where the refractive index changes from layer to layer. His research investigated the laws governing lens shape changes required for clear images at different ranges, as well as how these curvature changes influence refractive power. Additionally, he clarified the role of the eye's diaphragm and other previously inaccurate interpretations. By formulating a fundamental equation, he established general laws for optical image formation. This work provided a reliable basis for studying both normal and abnormal ocular conditions, transforming the theoretical understanding of how the eye functions as an optical instrument.

sections.heading: Development of ophthalmic diagnostic instruments and optical theories
sections.body: Gullstrand developed several significant scientific works through self-taught expertise in geometric and physiological optics. His 1890 thesis, Bidrag till astigmatismens teori, established a foundation for his later research into monochromatic aberrations and the true optical image. Beyond theoretical calculations regarding heterogeneous media and the human crystalline lens, he created practical diagnostic tools. These included a reflex-free ophthalmoscope and methods for focal illumination using the slit lamp, both introduced in 1911. His investigations also extended to the photographic illustration of eye muscle disabilities and corneal refractions. After the 1911 award, further research involved calculating optical systems with non-spherical surfaces and exploring higher-order laws of optical systems, contributing to the advancement of ophthalmic dioptrics and the design of refracting surfaces for optical instruments.

terms.definition: The study of how light refracts through the eye's complex structures to form images on the retina.
An instrument that directs a narrow beam of light into the eye so its structures can be examined in detail.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Developments in international private law and peace organization
sections.body: Asser instigated Dutch-led conferences at The Hague during 1893, 1894, 1900, and 1904 to establish uniformity in international private law. These sessions resulted in seven conventions regarding family law and civil procedure, with Norway subscribing to five. Asser suggested nations appoint permanent commissions to facilitate the codification of international civil law. Simultaneously, Fried utilized his monthly periodical, Die Friedenswarte, to engage university faculties. He advocated for replacing international anarchy with organized bureaus to address the underlying causes of war through structured international relations.

sections.heading: Development of international private law codification
sections.body: Asser utilized international conferences to establish common legal solutions for participating nations. Presiding over meetings in 1893 and 1894, he helped create a treaty effective in 1899 that standardized procedures for civil trials. His leadership continued through 1900 and 1904, producing treaties regarding marriage, divorce, and guardianship of minors. Beyond these conferences, he co-founded the Revue de droit international et de législation comparée in 1869 and served as a member of the Permanent Court of Arbitration during its first case involving the United States and Mexico.

sections.heading: Alfred Fried's journalistic and organizational peace efforts
sections.body: Fried used journalism to advocate an organized international order. He edited the Monthly Peace Correspondence and launched Die Waffen Nieder! with Bertha von Suttner as editor. Die Friedenswarte replaced that journal in 1899 and addressed an intellectual readership. His Annuaire de la vie internationale reflected his interest in international cooperation, including the Pan-American movement and Hague conferences. He combined publishing with organizational work: he was a member of the Bern Peace Bureau and secretary-general of an international association of journalists for peace. He also helped establish the Society for International Understanding in 1911. His argument increasingly emphasized economic cooperation and political organization as foundations for peace, alongside campaigns directed against war.

terms.definition: Rules for private disputes that cross national borders, including which courts and national laws should govern a case.
Organizing legal rules into a systematic written form; Asser sought agreed rules for private legal matters crossing national borders.
A condition of disorder between states that Fried identified as a primary cause of war, necessitating substitution through international order.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental methods for studying heat radiation
sections.body: Investigating black-body radiation presented significant challenges because no perfectly black body exists in nature to reflect no light or allow no transmission. In 1895, Wien and Lummer established principles for constructing a functional substitute using a hollow body whose walls were at one temperature, with a small opening. Radiation leaving the opening closely approximated black-body radiation. This apparatus allowed researchers like Lummer, Pringsheim, and Kurlbaum to substantiate the Stefan-Boltzmann law regarding heat quantity and temperature. Furthermore, Wien’s displacement law enabled scientists to calculate temperatures for various sources, including the sun and fixed stars, by identifying the wavelength of peak radiation intensity. These advancements built upon earlier spectrum analysis developments initiated by Bunsen and Kirchhoff.

sections.heading: Experimental investigations into light diffraction and cathode rays
sections.body: Wien’s early experiments concerned diffraction of light at metal surfaces and the influence of materials on light. At the Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt, he worked with Holborn on measuring high temperatures using thermoelements. Alongside his radiation studies, he investigated electrical discharges and the deflection of charged particles in electric and magnetic fields. These methods contributed to the later development of mass spectrography, which distinguished atoms and isotopes by their masses. His work on canal rays also continued after the 1911 Nobel award. In 1912 he showed how collisions with residual gas could cause the particles to lose and regain electric charge. In 1918 he examined how their emitted light faded, connecting experimental measurements with the duration of excited atomic states.

terms.definition: At thermal equilibrium, a material’s ability to emit radiation at a given wavelength matches its ability to absorb radiation at that wavelength.
Streams of positively charged ions produced in a gas-discharge tube, studied through their motion and interactions with surrounding gas.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Advancements in organic chemical synthesis methods
sections.body: Grignard’s reagent was prepared by reacting magnesium with an organic compound containing chlorine, bromine or iodine in ether. The resulting organomagnesium compound could react with other organic substances to form new carbon–carbon bonds. Sabatier’s separate method used finely divided metals to catalyse hydrogenation. The presentation described first reducing a metal oxide with hydrogen at about 300°C, then lowering the temperature and introducing the organic vapour with hydrogen. The first stage prepared the catalyst; the second modified the organic compound. Both methods widened the practical options for synthesis, although they performed different chemical tasks.

sections.heading: Grignard's academic career and chemical research
sections.body: After studying at the University of Lyons, Grignard worked with Louis Bouveault before beginning a long association with Philippe Barbier. His 1901 thesis, Sur les Combinaisons organomagnésiennes mixtes, earned him a doctorate. Beyond his magnesium-based reagent, he investigated the cracking of hydrocarbons using aluminium chloride and studied fulvene synthesis. He also explored the constitution of unsaturated compounds through quantitative ozonization and ketone splitting. His extensive research included preparing various substances like nitriles and terpenes, eventually resulting in approximately 170 published works.

sections.heading: Sabatier's chemical theory and catalytic advancements
sections.body: After studying sulphur thermochemistry and nitrogen oxides, Sabatier investigated catalysis by proposing that temporary intermediate compounds formed during reactions. He showed that catalysts could favour particular reactions and that particular substances could poison them, reducing their effectiveness. He also investigated supports that enhanced catalytic activity. Research into hydration and dehydration compared the reactions possible with different catalysts. His work on finely divided metals helped establish methods later important to oil hydrogenation, margarine production and synthetic methanol. His book La Catalyse en Chimie Organique was first published in 1913, after the Nobel award, and brought together his account of catalysis.

terms.definition: The artificial production of organic compounds, specifically derivatives that use carbon as their basic element.
An organic-chemistry reference work initiated by Grignard late in his career and completed by collaborators after his death in 1935.
A concept within Sabatier's chemical theory describing temporary structures formed during the catalytic process.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Realism and diverse dramatic genres in Hauptmann's work
sections.body: In the presentation, Hans Hildebrand praised Hauptmann’s ability to create individual characters rather than representatives of a single opinion. He argued that the difficult living conditions in the realistic plays could encourage audiences to imagine social improvement. Hauptmann also wrote fairy-tale dramas, including Hanneles Himmelfahrt, with its contrast between earthly suffering and heavenly consolation, and the popular Die versunkene Glocke. The speech treated the 1910 novel Emanuel Quint as another example of sustained imaginative investigation. Its earlier sketch, Der Apostel, had appeared in 1892. Hildebrand acknowledged divided opinion about the novel but admired its portrayal of an unusual religious inner life. Historical drama, comedy and poems embedded in plays further demonstrated the range the committee was recognising.

sections.heading: Evolution of literary styles and thematic influences
sections.body: Following Before Dawn, Hauptmann wrote works including The Weavers, The Beaver Coat and The Rats, while also exploring symbolic drama in The Assumption of Hannele and The Sunken Bell. His pre-award range already included adaptations of older literature: Der arme Heinrich, published in 1902, drew on a medieval German romance. Greek Spring appeared in 1908. Classical interests continued after the 1912 Nobel award, including a later cycle based on the house of Atreus; its final two parts were published posthumously in 1948. The Heretic of Soana, dated 1918, and the autobiographical volumes published in 1937 and 1949 also belong to the later career. They expand the picture of his writing but cannot explain a committee decision made in 1912.

terms.definition: Fairy-tale dramas: plays using fantastic or legendary elements. Hauptmann applied the term to work beyond his naturalistic social dramas.
A movement in Germany characterized by the use of observation and determinism within creative dramatic and prose works.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Techniques for vascular suturing and tissue preservation
sections.body: Carrel’s suturing method used three holding stitches to spread the cut end of a vessel into a triangular opening. Fine stitches could then join the edges while keeping the channel open. The 1912 presentation particularly emphasised reduced narrowing at the join, alongside protection against bleeding and embolism. He also investigated how vessel segments might be stored before experimental transplantation. The speech reported that some cold-storage preparations remained usable months later, whereas boiled or chemically sterilised segments did not. These were findings from the experimental programme of the time. Applying and refining the suturing method allowed him to reconnect the circulation of organs removed from an animal or substituted from another animal. Experiments included kidneys, spleens, thyroid tissue and limbs. Restoring circulation was a crucial technical achievement, distinct from solving the longer-term biological problems of transplantation.

sections.heading: Experimental surgical advancements and organ preservation techniques
sections.body: Carrel’s research at the Rockefeller Institute centred on experimental surgery, tissue transplantation and organ preservation. He had published a method of joining blood-vessel ends in 1902, developed experimental organ-transplantation methods by 1908 and investigated storing vessels in the cold before later use. These techniques formed part of the work recognised in 1912. His career continued in other directions after the award. During the First World War he helped develop the Carrel–Dakin method for treating wounds. In 1935 he collaborated with Charles Lindbergh on apparatus intended to support organs outside the body under sterile conditions. Lindbergh solved the mechanical problems involved. This later work extended the investigation of organs maintained separately from an intact animal. The biography also records experimental heart-valve operations with surgeon Théodore Tuffier and tissue-culture work with Montrose Burrows.

terms.definition: A reduction in the internal channel of a blood vessel; avoiding it at a surgical join was a central aim of Carrel’s technique.
A specific surgical technique used for connecting the two ends of blood vessels together.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Diplomatic efforts and Pan-American institutional development
sections.body: The presentation delivered in 1913 described Root’s application of legal training to diplomacy. His government service included administering affairs in Cuba and the Philippines after the Spanish-American War. A South American tour in 1906 sought closer regional relations. He also proposed a headquarters for the Pan-American organisation and secured Andrew Carnegie’s support for its construction; the source’s editorial note corrects the speech’s claim that he founded the bureau itself. His negotiations with Japan addressed an immigration dispute without providing a final settlement. After leaving the cabinet, he advocated arbitration and opposed preferential Panama Canal tolls for American vessels, supporting the British interpretation of the treaty. The committee presented these actions as efforts to apply legal commitments to international disputes.

sections.heading: Diplomatic developments and international legal institutions
sections.body: As Secretary of State, Root helped reform the consular service and negotiated the Gentlemen’s Agreement concerning Japanese emigration to America. He sponsored the 1907 Central American Peace Conference, which created a court for disputes among the participating states. He also pursued reciprocal arbitration treaties and worked with Lord Bryce on mechanisms for resolving American–Canadian disagreements. At the 1907 Hague conference he instructed American delegates to support an international court. His involvement continued after the Nobel award: in 1920 he served on the committee preparing plans for the Permanent Court of International Justice. That later work extended an existing programme of international legal cooperation. It should be distinguished from both his earlier cabinet service and the particular achievements available to the original prize decision.

terms.definition: A diplomatic effort aimed at strengthening relations and cooperation between the countries of North and South America.
An agreed procedure in which states submit a dispute to an impartial tribunal for a decision.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Advancements in acetylene gas regulation and storage
sections.body: Commercial production from calcium carbide made acetylene available as a bright lighting fuel in the 1890s. Its storage posed a serious difficulty: simply compressing the gas could be dangerous. Claude and Hess’s discovery that acetone could hold large quantities of dissolved acetylene helped make practical storage possible. Dalén addressed a different problem, controlling how little fuel a navigation light could use. His mechanism opened and closed the gas supply quickly enough to produce distinct, brief flashes. The 1912 presentation reported several thousand flashes from a litre of gas, compared with about fifty using the petroleum-gas apparatus it described. A small pilot flame ignited the successive releases. Flashing made the beacon conspicuous while limiting fuel use. Combined with suitable gas accumulators and other automatic controls, the equipment supported lights on remote coasts and buoys where regular attendance was difficult.

sections.heading: Engineering developments for acetylene storage and gas regulation
sections.body: Dalén’s engineering combined fuel storage with automatic control. After technical study in Gothenburg and Switzerland, he worked on turbines, pumps and other machinery before concentrating on acetylene systems. His company acquired rights to dissolved-acetylene technology in 1901. He developed a storage cylinder filled with a porous material, historically made using asbestos and diatomaceous earth, to reduce the hazards of handling the gas. Other inventions maintained the gas–air mixture for incandescent mantles and automatically replaced broken mantles. He became managing director of the reorganised AGA company in 1909. An acetylene-cylinder explosion in 1912 cost him his sight, but he continued engineering work. His later projects extended beyond navigation lighting to a heat-retaining cooking stove; this later invention was separate from the automatic regulators recognised by the Nobel award.

terms.definition: A gaseous hydrocarbon that produces an extremely bright and white light when burnt for use in maritime lighting.
A lighting component heated by burning gas until it glows; Dalén developed controls for its fuel mixture and replacement.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Expansion of valence and development of inorganic stereochemistry
sections.body: Werner reconsidered how an atom could bind other atoms or groups around it. His historical distinction between primary and secondary valences helped explain compounds containing coordinated water or ammonia that older representations had struggled to organise. Coordination number described the number of surrounding attachments, while spatial geometry explained why compounds with similar composition could differ. For many six-coordinate complexes, an octahedral arrangement predicted distinct possible forms. Experimental preparation and separation of such forms tested the proposal. Some complexes, including cobalt compounds, could occur as mirror-image forms with different optical behaviour. This extended stereochemical reasoning beyond the carbon compounds in which it had become established. The achievement was therefore both conceptual and experimental: a spatial model generated predictions that chemists could investigate through new compounds.

sections.heading: Development of coordination theory and spatial atomic arrangements
sections.body: Werner’s early research with Arthur Hantzsch examined spatial arrangements in nitrogen compounds. He then developed a broader account of chemical affinity and, in 1893, proposed a geometrical description of inorganic complexes. A central atom could be surrounded by a definite number of attached atoms or groups. Coordination number six often corresponded to an octahedral arrangement. Werner and his collaborators spent the following years preparing compounds and comparing their possible configurations. The separation of optically active mirror-image forms provided particularly strong tests of the spatial theory. He also investigated coordination number four, for which tetrahedral and square arrangements were possible. His work turned the description of inorganic compounds from a list of constituents into questions about attachment, geometry and experimentally distinguishable forms.

terms.definition: Compounds with the same connectivity but different arrangements in space; Werner used such differences to test coordination geometry.
The number of atoms directly attached to a central atom in a coordination complex.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The Swedish Academy's recognition of idealistic poetry
sections.body: The Academy's presentation interpreted Tagore's poetry as fulfilling the idealistic direction it associated with Nobel's will. A significant factor in this decision was the 1912 collection Gitanjali: Song Offerings, which featured religious poems recast into English. This work demonstrated a rhythmically balanced style and an austere taste in word choice. The author also presented The Gardener, Lyrics of Love and Life in 1913, which recast earlier inspirations to explore themes of youthful love and longing. Additionally, his versatility appeared in prose stories titled Glimpses of Bengal Life, alongside poetic collections like The Crescent Moon and lectures such as Sâdhanâ: The Realisation of Life. These works utilized a borrowed tongue to harmonize original ideas with new forms.

sections.heading: Literary works and educational ideals
sections.body: Tagore tried educational ideas drawn from the Upanishads at his experimental school in Shantiniketan. His writing already ranged widely before the Nobel award, from the poetry collections Manasi and Sonar Tari to plays including Raja and Dakghar and the novel Gora. His English collections were selective recreations rather than straightforward equivalents of individual Bengali books: even Gitanjali: Song Offerings included poems drawn from more than its Bengali namesake. His subsequent career continued this diversity. Balaka and Ghare-Baire both appeared in 1916, after the prize. He also wrote musical and dance dramas, essays, travel diaries and autobiographies, composed music for his songs, and made drawings and paintings. The biography connects his management of the family estates with his growing interest in social reform.

terms.definition: The ideal direction in literature invoked by the Academy when explaining its interpretation of Nobel's will and its selection of Tagore.
Religious principles from the Upanishads used by Tagore to guide his experimental educational methods at Shantiniketan.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental mechanisms of anaphylactic hypersensitivity
sections.body: In 1902, Richet and Portier published initial research regarding toxin sensitivity. Building upon earlier observations with Héricourt involving toxic eel blood-serum in dogs, Richet expanded his studies through the 1912 monograph L’Anaphylaxie. His experiments utilized various animal and vegetable protein toxins. By injecting small, non-reactive doses subcutaneously and repeating the process after two or three weeks, he demonstrated that subsequent weak doses triggered violent toxic symptoms. This regular hypersensitivity differs from sporadic cases seen in diphtheria immunization. Furthermore, Richet showed that this reaction is transferable between animals via blood serum injection. He established that anaphylaxis functions with a specific incubation period and specificity to the previously used toxin, mirroring certain characteristics of immunity while producing an opposite physiological result.

sections.heading: Physiological research and experimental findings in Paris
sections.body: Richet’s laboratory in Paris investigated normal physiology alongside disease. Between 1885 and 1895, he studied temperature regulation, including shivering and the increased breathing that helps some animals avoid overheating when they cannot rely on sweating. His experimental interests also included the protective effects of blood from immunized animals. He attempted serum treatment for tuberculosis and investigated dietary approaches in tuberculous dogs; these were parts of his wider therapeutic experimentation, distinct from the discovery honoured in 1913. His anaphylaxis studies pursued a different outcome of prior exposure: increased sensitivity. Later experiments showed that sensitivity could also be transferred through serum, linking the reaction to components carried in blood. Much of his laboratory’s work appeared in a six-volume series published between 1890 and 1911.

terms.definition: A severe systemic allergic reaction; Richet’s experiments showed how prior exposure could make a later dose dangerously effective.
The processes by which an organism controls its body temperature, including changing heat production and heat loss.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of international documentation and arbitration records
sections.body: La Fontaine contributed to the organization of peaceful internationalism through significant administrative efforts and documentary research. With Paul Otlet, he founded the International Institute of Bibliography in 1895 and the Central Office of International Associations twelve years later. His literary work included a major documentary project titled Pasicrisie internationale: Histoire documentaire des arbitrages internationaux, 1794-1900, which examined arbitration cases spanning over a century. Beyond these institutions, he participated in the 1899 Peace Congress in Oslo and worked within the Interparliamentary Union to promote solutions for international relations through governmental channels. His involvement in various peace conferences focused on the practical organization of movements and the framing of international law.

sections.heading: Development of international documentation and classification systems
sections.body: La Fontaine utilized a Belgian government subsidy to implement a methodology for universal classification. This systematic approach enabled the production of specialized reference works, including bibliographies focused on peace and the social sciences. Through his work at the Institute, he established the Union of International Associations in 1907 alongside Paul Otlet. He directed the Union as secretary-general. Its publications included The Yearbook of International Organizations, first issued in 1909. This institution functioned as a global center for researching and promoting nongovernmental organizations by compiling directories, meeting calendars, and various proceedings. Across his teaching career, his academic role also involved lecturing on subjects such as disarmament, world federation, and the evolution of judicial structures to educate others on international law.

terms.definition: An organization composed of parliamentarians from different nations discussing international law, peace, and the arbitration of international disputes.
A systematic methodology used to organize information and produce reference works regarding peace and the social sciences.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Union of International Associations: Henri La Fontaine et Paul Otlet, 1979

sections.heading: Experimental investigations into low temperature matter properties
sections.body: Beginning his laboratory work in the early 1880s, Kamerlingh Onnes designed and improved specialized physical apparatus for studying deviations from Van der Waals' gas laws. His research focused on how molecular structure and temperature influence gas properties. By determining helium isotherms, he achieved the first successful liquefaction of helium in 1908, overcoming previous failed attempts by researchers like Travers and Jacquerod. He constructed cold baths using liquid helium to reach temperatures between 4.3 and 1.15 Kelvin from absolute zero. These experiments on electrical conduction resistance at helium temperatures provided essential data for the theory of electrons, demonstrating that physical phenomena change significantly near absolute zero compared to higher temperatures.

sections.heading: Scientific foundations of low-temperature research
sections.body: Kamerlingh Onnes developed his investigations into matter at low temperatures by applying the kinetic theory of liquids to Van der Waals’ law of corresponding states. His research program involved reorganizing the Physical Laboratory at Leyden to establish a cryogenic facility for verifying these theories across various temperatures. This laboratory environment supported diverse studies, including the resistance of metals and observations regarding magnetism, fluorescence, and the Hall effect. Through his motto, knowledge through measurement, he emphasized quantitative research in physics. His experimental work enabled the liquefaction of helium in 1908, followed by further cooling toward absolute zero. This specialized laboratory also functioned as a training school for glass-blowers and instrument-makers to support such complex physical investigations.

terms.definition: A curve showing how a substance’s pressure and volume are related while its temperature remains constant.
A laboratory equipped to create and measure very low temperatures and investigate the behaviour of materials under those conditions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Methods for improving atomic weight determination accuracy
sections.body: Richards improved atomic weight measurements by addressing several sources of error, such as hygroscopic moisture, gas occlusion in metal oxides, and impurities from laboratory vessels. To mitigate errors related to free ions, he utilized smaller substance quantities, ranging from 5 to 20 grams, within highly dissociated, dilute solutions. He developed a specialized bottling apparatus to expel moisture and weigh substances in an absolutely dry atmosphere. Additionally, Richards adapted an earlier concept to construct a nephelometer. This device uses scattered light to perform quantitative assessments of tiny, suspended precipitates that are otherwise difficult to measure gravimetrically. His work included redetermining thirty atomic weights, including fundamental elements like oxygen, sodium, and chlorine, often through methods applied by his trained pupils.

sections.heading: Experimental techniques for atomic weight determination
sections.body: Beyond refining mass measurements, Richards created a new technique to determine halide ratios and developed a nephelometer. His research addressed how occluded moisture in solids and gases creates insidious effects during analysis. He also investigated atomic and molecular volume, formulating a hypothesis regarding compressible atoms through measurements of various element and compound compressibilities. To aid thermometer standardization, he introduced using transition temperatures of pure hydrated salts as fixed points. Furthermore, his guidance contributed to the development of adiabatic calorimetry fundamentals. By 1912 he had also redetermined the atomic weights of more than thirty important elements with high accuracy.

terms.definition: An instrument that measures light scattered by fine particles suspended in a liquid, helping detect material difficult to weigh directly.
Measurement of heat changes while minimizing heat transfer between the experimental system and its surroundings.

sections.heading: Development of clinical otological investigation methods
sections.body: After reporting his observations in 1905, Bárány developed methods for testing vestibular responses. He explained the caloric reaction through changes in the density of endolymph, the fluid in the semicircular canals: cooling made it tend to sink, while warming made it tend to rise. These movements produced differing sensations of rotation and involuntary eye movements. He also adapted Ewald’s experimental pressure method into a clinical fistula test and developed a pointing test. The latter examined how a person’s attempt to point could deviate during vestibular disturbance, with the response changing according to head position. By comparing reported sensations with observable movements, clinicians gained practical ways to investigate the function of the inner ear and its connections with movement and balance.

sections.heading: Neurological research during wartime service
sections.body: While serving as a civilian surgeon for the Austrian army, Bárány treated soldiers suffering from head injuries. This clinical experience allowed him to investigate the connections between the cerebellum, the muscular apparatus, and the vestibular apparatus. His scientific investigations built upon existing theories from researchers such as Flourens, Purkinje, Mach, and Breuer. Following his 1914 Nobel Prize, professional friction with colleagues in Vienna regarding his citations led him to relocate to Sweden. There, he accepted a position as Principal and Professor at an Otological Institute in Uppsala. His later medical interests expanded to include the study of causes related to muscular rheumatism.

terms.definition: A vestibular response to warming or cooling the ear, which can produce vertigo and involuntary eye movements and is used to investigate balance function.
An anatomical structure within the inner ear that Bárány studied to understand its relationship with balance and neurological functions.

sections.heading: Theoretical development of space-lattice theory
sections.body: Von Laue connected two ideas: crystals contain a regular three-dimensional arrangement of atoms, and X-rays were suspected to be waves with very short wavelengths. Atomic spacing seemed appropriate for producing diffraction, much as a grating does with visible light. He developed a mathematical account of the interference expected from this arrangement. Photographic patterns from crystals showed distinct intensity maxima consistent with that account, while absorption tests established that the radiation forming them was X-radiation. The observations supplied evidence of wave behaviour; they did not exclude the quantum description of radiation developed in other experiments. The discovery also made the crystal and the radiation mutually informative: diffraction could reveal properties of X-rays and provide evidence about atomic arrangements inside solid materials.

sections.heading: Mathematical formulation and experimental verification of X-ray diffraction
sections.body: Von Laue’s work on waves developed before the crystal experiment. His 1903 doctorate under Planck concerned interference in plane-parallel plates, and he later investigated the thermodynamics of radiation and light’s coherence. While teaching in Munich, he proposed that a crystal’s periodic structure could diffract X-rays. Colleagues raised objections, but Walter Friedrich and Paul Knipping tested the idea and obtained the predicted kind of pattern after initial unsuccessful attempts. Von Laue supplied its mathematical interpretation, and the discovery was published in 1912. He became professor in Zurich that year and moved to Frankfurt in 1914. His career continued well beyond the Nobel award, including investigations of superconductivity in Berlin and later work in Göttingen.

terms.definition: A regular, repeating three-dimensional array used to describe the arrangement of a crystal’s constituent units.
The reinforcement or cancellation produced when waves overlap, creating patterns that depend on their relative phases.

sections.heading: Chemical structure and components of chlorophyll
sections.body: Willstätter developed methods for preparing and analysing plant pigments. He showed that chlorophyll was an ester that could be split with alkali, releasing the alcohol phytol and a magnesium-containing coloured component called chlorophyllin. An enzyme in leaves could also alter the pigment. This helped explain why certain crystalline preparations then called chlorophyll were not unchanged leaf pigment: they were laboratory products lacking phytol. The distinction concerned those preparations, rather than a general rule that crystallisation removes phytol.
