He also separated two related chlorophyll pigments, one blue-green and the other yellow-green. His wider pigment programme included preparing carotenoids in pure form and investigating the red and blue anthocyanin pigments of flowers and fruit. Purification and chemical comparison made these substances experimentally distinguishable.

sections.heading: Chemical investigations into plant alkaloids and pigments
sections.body: Willstätter’s early work on alkaloids such as atropine and cocaine helped develop methods for studying more complicated natural substances. Investigations of quinone-related dyes followed. He moved to Zurich in 1905, then to a research laboratory in Berlin in 1912. There, with collaborators, he completed important chlorophyll studies, related work on haemoglobin and investigations of anthocyanins, the pigments of flowers and fruit. These plant-pigment studies were recognised in 1915. His broader chemical work also included synthesising cyclooctatetraene and attempting to produce cyclobutadiene. Research after the award examined enzymes and ways of concentrating them by adsorption, using materials such as metal hydroxides and gels. That programme expanded biochemical investigation, although the methods described in the biography did not yield crystallised enzymes.

terms.definition: An alcohol released when chlorophyll is chemically split; it forms a substantial part of the natural pigment’s molecular structure.
A method used to concentrate enzymes by attaching them to the surface of substances like metal hydroxides or silicic acids.

sections.heading: Academic foundations and musical criticism
sections.body: Rolland’s scholarship and literary writing developed alongside one another. His two doctoral theses of 1895 investigated the origins of modern opera and the decline of Italian painting in the sixteenth century. He taught music history at the École Normale and the Sorbonne while also publishing criticism. Collections including Musicians of Today and Musicians of Former Days brought those articles to a wider readership. Biographies of Beethoven and Handel combined historical study with interpretation of musical achievement. His dramatic writing, including Théâtre de la révolution, accompanied an ambition to make theatre accessible beyond exclusive circles. The Nobel account treated these interests as connected: music, drama and fiction could each contribute to exploring people’s lives, moral choices and search for meaning.

sections.heading: Musical scholarship and musicological development
sections.body: Rolland’s historical training at the École normale supérieure combined critical study of sources with attention to individual psychology. While preparing his opera thesis, he and Clotilde Bréal explored archives in Rome, Florence, Bologna, Venice and Padua, copying excerpts from little-known Italian operas. His later teaching connected musical history with wider historical and sociological questions. He continued transcribing material from French and other European libraries to prepare lectures, using piano readings and concert performances to make unfamiliar works audible. In 1900 he organised an international congress on musical history and subsequently helped found the Revue d’histoire et de critique musicale with other scholars. This work treated musical scholarship as both archival investigation and an effort to bring historical music before listeners.

terms.definition: In this account of Rolland, a commitment to human experience and sympathy, connecting artistic creation with moral questions and the pursuit of truth.
The scholarly study of music, including its history, forms, sources and relationships with society.

sources.title: Bibliothèque nationale de France: Rolland’s musical and literary development through 1914 (French excerpt)

sections.heading: Mathematical simplification of X-ray reflection
sections.body: Lawrence Bragg treated crystal diffraction as reflection from successive parallel planes through a regular lattice. This simplified the relation between the X-ray wavelength, the spacing of those planes and the reflection angle. William Bragg helped develop the experimental method, using characteristic radiation from metal targets in an X-ray tube. Palladium and rhodium supplied shorter wavelengths useful for investigating more complicated arrangements. Measurements on alkali halide salts revealed two interpenetrating cubic arrangements, one for each constituent. These findings showed that such crystals were extended repeating structures, rather than assemblies of separate salt molecules. The researchers also investigated diamond, obtaining evidence for the tetrahedral arrangement around carbon.

sections.heading: Systematic Analysis of Crystal Structure
sections.body: In 1913–1914, William Bragg and his son Lawrence developed X-rays into a practical instrument for analysing crystal structure. Their work built on the diffraction discovery of von Laue and his collaborators and helped establish X-ray crystallography as a research field. William’s subsequent wartime work addressed a different measurement problem: detecting and measuring underwater sound to locate submarines. His career took him from a mathematics and physics professorship in Adelaide to Leeds in 1909 and University College London in 1915. He later became Fullerian Professor of Chemistry at the Royal Institution. These later activities extended his career beyond the crystal investigations recognised by the joint award.

sections.heading: Scientific publications and academic career of Lawrence Bragg
sections.body: Lawrence Bragg began investigating von Laue’s diffraction results in autumn 1912 and published his first paper on the subject that November. He became a Fellow and lecturer at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1914. His work with his father during 1912–1914 was summarised in their book X-rays and Crystal Structure in 1915. After the award, Lawrence applied sound-ranging methods during the First World War. He became professor of physics at Manchester in 1919, later directed the National Physical Laboratory and then held the Cavendish professorship at Cambridge. In subsequent decades, his interests included applying X-ray methods to protein structures. That later research belonged to the field’s development after the original prize-winning investigations.

terms.definition: A repeating spatial arrangement used to describe a crystal’s structure.
The study of crystal structures using the patterns produced when X-rays are diffracted by them.
Locating a source of sound through measurements of the sound it produces.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Evolution of Swedish poetic and prose forms
sections.body: The 1916 announcement presented Heidenstam as a force in Swedish literature’s move away from dominant realist conventions. It praised the colour, rhythm and imaginative freedom of his first poetry collection, Pilgrimage: The Wander Years, published in 1888. Its later account traced a shift from sensuous enjoyment towards more troubled inward experience. Hans Alienus, which mixes prose with verse, follows an uprooted devotee of beauty; Poems, published in 1895, offered further explorations of inner life. Historical narratives widened this range. The Charles XII stories in Karolinerna and the medieval family epic Folkunga Trädet gave national history an imaginative form. The announcement read his later poetry, including New Poems, through gravity, sadness and reflection on human life. This is the Academy’s interpretation of his development, rather than a claim that every work followed one uniform progression.

sections.heading: Evolution of Heidenstam's poetic themes and historical prose
sections.body: The Swedish biographical dictionary describes the conversational verse of Heidenstam’s 1888 debut as indebted to Heine and Byron. The collection itself moved beyond the pale idealism of his youthful writing to celebrate sensory pleasure; Moguls kungaring exemplified that outlook. Endymion, published in 1889, explored the encroachment of Western civilisation on the East through an unsuccessful revolt. His later engagement with Sweden’s past used both historical accounts and literary responses. Karolinerna drew extensively on Anders Fryxell’s narratives, while Strindberg supplied a partly oppositional stimulus. The essay Om svenskarnas lynne examined national character through highly personal observations. In 1899, the cycle Ett folk brought historical and social concerns into contemporary politics. Its Medborgarsång advocated voting rights without restrictions based on wealth. These examples show changing uses of historical imagination, from idealised distant worlds to Swedish identity and political participation.

terms.definition: A group of Swedish poets led by Heidenstam who utilized imagination and new forms to move beyond realistic literary traditions.
Narrative writing that draws on earlier events and societies; Heidenstam combined historical sources with imaginative treatment.

sources.title: Swedish National Archives: Heidenstam’s literary career from his 1888 debut to the 1916 award (Swedish excerpt)

sections.heading: Evolution of Karl Gjellerup's literary and philosophical focus
sections.body: Gjellerup completed his theology degree in 1878 and published An Idealist under a pseudonym that year. In his autobiographical account, he traced a movement from German idealism towards the evolutionary outlook of Heredity and Morals, which won a university gold medal in 1881. His interests later shifted again towards Kant and Schopenhauer. Travel also widened his artistic practice: in Rome in 1883 he studied watercolour, and he subsequently explored pastel and oil painting. His literary work included the tragedy Brynhild, published in 1884, and plays written during his years at Hellerup, including Wuthhorn. He wrote about Wagner’s Ring and translated divine songs from the Edda. After settling in Dresden, German increasingly became his literary medium. Works from this period included The Pilgrim Kamanita and The Golden Bough, connecting his changing philosophical interests with poetic fiction.

sections.heading: Evolution of Pontoppidan’s literary focus and novelistic style
sections.body: After studying at the Polytechnical College in Copenhagen, Pontoppidan transitioned from writing about nature and folk life to focusing on human subjects. His early publications included smaller tales such as Fra hytterne. Seeking a broader style for complex themes, he adopted the novel, which he regarded as having gained a standing comparable to drama and ancient epic during the nineteenth century. Through his trilogy, comprising Det forjaettede land, Lykke-Per, and De dødes rige, he attempted to provide a continuous depiction of contemporary Denmark. These works utilize descriptions of human fates and minds to reflect the era's religious, social, and political struggles. His extensive bibliography also includes various personal works like Ung elskov and several volumes of memoirs published later in his life.

terms.definition: An approach that explains life through natural processes; Gjellerup associated his early evolutionary work with this outlook.
An extended work of prose fiction, allowing sustained development of characters, settings and connected events.

sections.heading: Expansion of the International Prisoners-of-War Agency
sections.body: The First World War expanded the ICRC's operations far beyond its small prewar organization. It established the International Prisoners-of-War Agency on 21 August 1914 to restore contact between separated family members. By the end of that year, about 1,200 people worked for the ICRC, mainly in the Agency; around 3,000 worked for the Agency over the course of the war. Its fourteen national sections developed as different countries entered the conflict. Alongside information work, the committee sought exchanges of seriously ill or wounded prisoners. With Swiss support and permission from France and Germany, convoys crossed Switzerland between Konstanz and Lyon in both directions. The ICRC also pressed belligerents to respect the revised 1906 Geneva Convention, including its provisions for returning detained medical personnel.

sections.heading: Founding principles and the 1864 Geneva Convention
sections.body: The committee originated from a five-member group of Swiss citizens established in February 1863 by the Geneva Public Welfare Society. This group investigated concepts from Henri Dunant’s book, Un Souvenir de Solferino, regarding combatant care. Following an October 1863 conference involving sixteen nations, the organization promoted voluntary units to assist wartime casualties and adopted a specific international emblem. Under Gustave Moynier's organizational leadership, the committee facilitated a 1864 diplomatic meeting in Geneva. This resulted in the Convention for the Amelioration of the Condition of the Wounded and Sick in Armed Forces in the Field. Signed by twelve states, this treaty established protections for medical equipment and personnel while officially adopting the red cross on a white background as a neutral identifier.

terms.definition: A specialized division established in 1914 to restore communication between families and manage prisoner information during wartime.
An international treaty providing neutrality for medical personnel and equipment while establishing an official emblem to identify humanitarian care.

sources.title: ICRC: the International Committee of the Red Cross in the First World War
International Committee of the Red Cross: founding and the 1864 Geneva Convention

sections.heading: Discovery of characteristic X-radiation series
sections.body: Barkla distinguished two kinds of secondary X-rays: radiation scattered without changing its character, and characteristic radiation associated with the irradiated element. Electron emission accompanied these processes but was a different kind of radiation. Within the characteristic X-rays, he identified the K and L series. For a given element, the K radiation was more penetrating. He followed the K series from calcium to cerium and the L series from silver to bismuth, comparing their absorption by materials such as aluminium. These measurements supported the conclusion that elements have their own characteristic X-ray spectra. The announcement contrasted the regular progression of these spectra with the repeating patterns of chemical properties in the periodic table. This made the radiation a tool for investigating differences between atoms.

sections.heading: Experimental findings on X-ray polarization and secondary emission
sections.body: Barkla’s investigations into Röntgen radiation revealed that secondary emission consists of two distinct types: scattered X-rays that remain unchanged and a specific fluorescent radiation unique to each substance. Through his experimental work, he identified the polarization of X-rays, demonstrating that X-radiation behaves similarly to ordinary light. His research also explored the absorption and photographic action of these rays, alongside the relationship between characteristic X-radiation and accompanying corpuscular radiation. He also investigated how to interpret these experimental properties of X-radiation. Much of this scientific progress was documented through his various papers published primarily within the Transactions and Proceedings of the Royal Society, contributing to the broader understanding of elemental line spectra.

terms.definition: Two families of characteristic X-rays named by Barkla; for a given element, the K radiation is harder and more penetrating than the L radiation.
A preferred orientation in a wave’s oscillations; Barkla’s experiments showed this property in X-rays and helped connect them with ordinary light.

sections.heading: Experimental principles of ammonia synthesis
sections.body: Haber and van Oordt began systematic experiments on ammonia synthesis in 1904, showing that nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia reach chemical equilibrium. Higher pressure favours ammonia formation because the reaction reduces the number of gas molecules. Lower temperature also improves the equilibrium yield, but practical synthesis requires a catalyst and sufficient heat. In a 1913 paper, Haber and Le Rossignol described equipment operating near 500°C and at roughly 150–200 atmospheres. With iron as a catalyst, their apparatus produced about 250 grams of ammonia per hour per litre of contact volume; uranium and osmium gave larger outputs. The design circulated gases under pressure and recovered heat from the reaction. These laboratory results supported the subsequent development of industrial manufacture at BASF under Carl Bosch.

sections.heading: Experimental requirements for ammonia synthesis
sections.body: Achieving the spontaneous combination of nitrogen and hydrogen requires strict conditions and specialized equipment to overcome unfavorable equilibrium. While electrical discharges can induce this reaction, they consume alarming amounts of energy. Success depends on integrating experimental results with thermodynamic considerations. By calculating outcomes at specific pressures and temperatures, scientists can predict how maximum ammonia content relates to gas pressure and temperature decreases. Specifically, a mixture containing three parts hydrogen to one part nitrogen yields the highest ammonia concentration. Although high-pressure laboratory synthesis is possible using modified pressure ovens, such as those used by Hempel for nitrogen absorption, achieving results at red heat remains difficult because catalysts produce only trace amounts of ammonia under normal pressure.

terms.definition: A state in which forward and reverse reactions balance. Changing pressure or temperature can alter the proportions of substances present.
The study of heat, work and energy, used here to calculate how pressure and temperature constrain the attainable ammonia concentration.

sections.heading: Development of the elementary quanta theory
sections.body: Planck’s radiation formula contained constants with implications beyond the immediate spectrum. It allowed an accurate estimate of the number of molecules in a mole, while introducing the constant now written as h. An energy element was obtained by multiplying h by frequency: higher-frequency oscillations corresponded to larger elements. This differed from treating exchanged energy as continuously divisible. Later work extended quantum ideas to other problems. Einstein applied them to the photoelectric effect and specific heat, while Bohr, Sommerfeld and others used quantum conditions to investigate atomic spectra. The award presentation treated these developments as evidence of the importance of Planck’s starting point. They were contributions by several researchers, rather than discoveries all made in Planck’s original derivation.

sections.heading: Planck's early research and academic career
sections.body: Planck’s early work concerned thermodynamics, influenced by Kirchhoff’s teaching and Clausius’s publications. He investigated entropy, thermoelectricity and dilute solutions while pursuing an academic career in Munich, Kiel and Berlin. His book Thermodynamik appeared in 1897, before his decisive radiation work. The problem was to account for the measured distribution of black-body radiation at different temperatures. In 1900 he introduced discrete energy elements into his derivation: the energy assigned to material resonators was counted in multiples of h times their frequency. This provided a radiation law consistent with experiment. His later book Theorie der Wärmestrahlung (1906) presented his work on thermal radiation. Subsequent quantum developments, including Einstein’s treatment of the photoelectric effect, went beyond the original black-body problem.

terms.definition: The constant h relating a quantum’s energy to its frequency; it sets a characteristic scale for quantum phenomena.
The distribution of thermal radiation across frequencies from an ideal absorber and emitter at a given temperature.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Thematic structure and stylistic elements of Olympian Spring
sections.body: Harald Hjärne’s presentation described Olympischer Frühling as a distinctive imaginative world rather than an imitation of ancient Greek poetry or Goethe’s Faust. Its gods, heroes and oracles serve Spitteler’s own account of suffering, hope and the struggle between free will and necessity. Hjärne specifically rejected the charge that the poem depended on obscure scholarly references. Although epic in scope, it advances through dramatic monologues and dialogues. Its tones range from solemn passages to playful episodes, while its descriptions of nature evoke the poet’s native Alps. The verse uses iambic six-foot lines with alternating masculine and feminine rhymes. The presentation also stressed the work’s delayed reception: its revised 1909 version brought greater popularity in Switzerland and Germany.

sections.heading: Development and publication of Olympian Spring
sections.body: Olympischer Frühling first appeared in four volumes: Die Auffahrt, Hera die Braut, Die Hohe Zeit, and Ende und Wende. In his autobiographical account, Spitteler recalled that the first two attracted little attention. He credited the musician Felix Weingartner with changing that reception through a 1904 pamphlet introducing the epic and Prometheus to German readers. He also acknowledged J. V. Widmann’s earlier advocacy in Switzerland. A revised five-volume version of the epic appeared in 1909 and had gone through several editions by 1920, when the delayed 1919 Nobel award was presented. Spitteler’s other writing included Glockenlieder, the novel Imago and recollections of his childhood. His account shows how publication, revision and critical advocacy each contributed to the work’s public reception.

terms.definition: A writer’s own imaginative system of gods, heroes and stories, used to express ideas and experiences rather than simply retell inherited myths.
A short, separately published written work, used here to introduce and champion an author’s books.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of bacteriolysis and complement fixation
sections.body: Bordet distinguished a relatively heat-resistant specific antibody from a more heat-sensitive component already present in normal serum. The latter, called alexin or complement, cooperated with antibody in the bacterial destruction he studied. This explained a particular serum mechanism, rather than every form of immunity. In 1900 he observed that a suitable combination of antigen and specific antibody could use up complement activity. Work with Gengou extended the observation to laboratory testing. If a patient’s serum reacted with known microbial material, complement could become unavailable for a subsequent test reaction. This offered an indirect way of looking for a specific antibody response. Complement did not simply vanish as matter, and the method did not establish that every antibody or immune response behaved identically.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of antimicrobic sera and bacterial cultivation
sections.body: Bordet’s serum studies connected specific recognition with other protective components in blood. In 1898 he investigated haemolytic sera, which could break down foreign red blood cells, and found an analogy with serum-mediated destruction of bacteria. The comparison extended his inquiry beyond a single organism or infection. With Gengou, he cultivated the bacterium responsible for whooping cough in 1906, helping establish its role in the disease. His broader investigations also concerned blood coagulation and reactions associated with anaphylaxis. He brought his immunological work together in Traité de l’Immunité dans les Maladies Infectieuses; its second edition appeared in 1939, well after the Nobel award. The combined work linked experimental studies of serum with bacteriology and the development of laboratory methods.

terms.definition: The binding and consumption of complement activity during an antigen–antibody reaction, leaving less available for a subsequent indicator reaction in a laboratory test.
An older name for complement, the serum components that can cooperate with antibodies and also participate in other immune defence pathways.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Implementation of domestic reforms and international peace objectives
sections.body: Before his presidency, Wilson published Congressional Government, examining the relationship between legislative and executive powers in the American Constitution. As president, he pursued reforms outlined in The New Freedom, including changes to banking and tariffs and measures against monopolies and fraudulent advertising. During the First World War, he mobilised national resources and helped direct public messaging. At the Versailles negotiations, he secured agreement to the Covenant of the League of Nations, although other elements of his proposed peace settlement met resistance. His party lost control of Congress in the 1918 elections. The Senate subsequently refused to approve American membership in the League. Establishing an international organisation and securing his own country’s participation proved to be different political challenges.

sections.heading: The Inquiry and the Fourteen Points Program
sections.body: To develop his 1918 peace proposals, Wilson drew on The Inquiry, a group of approximately 150 social and political scientists organised under Edward M. House. Its secret research analysed global economic, social and political conditions, producing nearly 2,000 documents and at least 1,200 maps. The Fourteen Points called for an end to secret treaties, reduced armaments, freedom of the seas and fewer economic barriers. They also addressed territorial settlements and the political claims of populations living under imperial rule. Wilson hoped the proposals would weaken the Central Powers’ resolve. During the Versailles negotiations, British and French leaders resisted many provisions. His proposal for an organisation providing collective security nevertheless became part of the treaty settlement.

terms.definition: A set of presidential reforms involving tariff changes, banking revisions, and the regulation of monopolies and unfair business practices.
A research group of about 150 specialists, organised under Edward M. House, whose documents and maps informed Wilson’s peace proposals.

sources.title: US National Archives: Wilson’s Fourteen Points — 8 January 1918 address and historical context

sections.heading: Researching canal rays and spectral line splitting
sections.body: Building upon Goldstein's discovery of canal rays, Stark investigated how these positively charged atoms behave within discharge tubes. In 1902, he predicted that moving particles would become luminous, a theory he confirmed in 1905 using hydrogen. He observed that light from approaching rays shifts toward the violet end of the spectrum, demonstrating a terrestrial Doppler effect. Furthermore, his 1913 investigations into hydrogen passing through strong electric fields revealed that spectral lines decompose into several components with specific polarization conditions. This splitting occurs due to the intense electric field rather than atomic motion. By measuring these changes across various substances, Stark showed that electric fields alter atomic optical dynamics differently than magnetic fields, contributing to the modern understanding of internal atomic structure.

sections.heading: Scientific research areas and publications
sections.body: Stark’s research covered electrical currents in gases, spectroscopy and chemical bonding. His book Die Elektrizität in Gasen appeared in 1902, followed by works on radiation, spectra and atomic structure. He also founded the Jahrbuch der Radioaktivität und Elektronik and edited it from 1904 to 1913. The Nobel biography credits him with more than 300 scientific papers across his career, rather than presenting that number as a pre-1919 total. His investigations continued after the prize, which enabled him to establish a private laboratory. In his later years he studied light deflection in a non-uniform electric field. These later interests belong to his wider biography; the award itself recognised the Doppler effect in canal rays and spectral splitting in electric fields.

terms.definition: A type of ray discovered in discharge tubes containing rarefied gas, composed of positively charged atoms moving at high velocity.
The study of spectra to identify substances or investigate their properties, including how atomic radiation changes under different conditions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Connecting temperature changes to chemical affinity
sections.body: Thermochemical measurements showed how reaction heat changed with temperature, but did not by themselves determine where a reaction would reach equilibrium. Nernst’s heat theorem supplied a low-temperature condition linking this missing information with thermal data. His team’s experiments used strong cooling, including liquid hydrogen, to study heat capacities as they fell towards very small values. The theorem proposed that the temperature dependence of chemical affinity also became very small near absolute zero. Combining that limiting behaviour with measured reaction heat and heat capacities made further equilibrium calculations possible. Galvanic cells offered a practical check because their voltages were connected to the chemical work available. The achievement joined low-temperature investigation with the prediction of reactions under other conditions, rather than merely measuring how much heat one experiment released.

sections.heading: Early electrochemical theories and industrial applications
sections.body: Nernst’s early electrochemical research drew on Arrhenius’s theory of ions in solution. In 1889 he modelled galvanic cells using a proposed pressure of dissolution that drove ions from an electrode into solution, opposed by the solution’s osmotic pressure. He also derived conditions for precipitation from saturated solutions. These were attempts to connect measurable electrical and chemical behaviour quantitatively. His heat theorem later supplied calculations useful to industrial questions such as ammonia synthesis. With students in Berlin, he measured heat capacities at low temperatures and vapour densities at high temperatures, considering the results in relation to quantum theory. His practical interests included the Nernst lamp, which used a ceramic element. Theory, measurement and technological applications were therefore closely connected throughout his work.

terms.definition: The thermodynamic driving force of a reaction. At equilibrium, there is no net driving force favouring further change in either direction.
A force assumed by Nernst to drive ions from electrodes into solution, opposing the osmotic pressure of dissolved ions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The Academy’s reading of Growth of the Soil
sections.body: The 1920 presentation read Growth of the Soil as an epic of sustained agricultural work. It contrasted scattered activity with the concentrated effort of settlers clearing land and establishing farms. In this interpretation, labour gave lives a common direction and the pioneer’s struggle acquired a heroic scale. These are claims about the novel’s values, rather than evidence that farming necessarily unites people or produces uninterrupted progress. The speech also stressed the variety of its characters: some persevere at their work, while others become confused by selfish ambitions. It praised Hamsun’s restrained style, humour and attention to both attractive and troubling aspects of human behaviour. The Academy’s account thus connected the novel’s subject with its artistic form, presenting the ordinary work of cultivating land as material for an expansive literary narrative.

sections.heading: Evolution of Hamsun's Literary Themes and Style
sections.body: Hamsun’s pre-award writing moved across several settings and forms. His account of American life, published in 1889, grew from time spent travelling and working there and was largely satirical. Hunger followed in 1890, while Pan appeared in 1894. The Nobel biography describes these early novels through their alienated central figures and opposition to established society. It identifies a different emphasis in works such as the plays Game of Life and Sunset and the novel A Wanderer Plays on Muted Strings: resignation about ageing and lost youth. Children of the Age and Segelfoss Town developed broader social criticism. In the biography’s interpretation, the preference for life close to the land reached its clearest expression in Growth of the Soil in 1917. This account describes a recurring literary outlook across his work, rather than a single theme shared by every book.

terms.definition: A large-scale narrative that gives its characters’ struggles an expansive or heroic significance; the Academy applied the term to this novel.
An idealisation of simpler ways of life in contrast with modern civilisation; here it describes the biography’s reading of Hamsun’s writing.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Quantifying oxygen diffusion and capillary recruitment
sections.body: Krogh measured how gases diffuse through tissues and used the geometry of the muscle capillary network to calculate oxygen differences between blood and surrounding tissue. Assuming the full network carried blood produced a surprising result: calculated tissue oxygen tension remained close to capillary values even during work. He reconciled this with lower values in resting muscle by proposing that the distance between blood-filled capillaries changes with demand. In his account, activity brought more capillaries into use, enlarging the surface through which oxygen could diffuse. He then observed organs microscopically while preserving their blood supply. In the frog's tongue, previously unseen capillaries began carrying blood after stimulation and later disappeared from view. These observations supported the regulating mechanism celebrated by the award.

sections.heading: Techniques for measuring blood flow and gas exchange
sections.body: Krogh utilized specialized techniques to investigate how respiratory gases interact within the blood. Working with Christian Bohr and K. A. Hasselbalch, he demonstrated how carbon dioxide tension affects the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve. To determine general blood flow, Krogh and J. Lindhard adopted an idea from A. Bornstein to develop a nitrous oxide method. His research also explored the diffusion capacity of animal tissues, leading him to conclude that muscular activity increases the available diffusion surface by opening previously closed capillaries. Additionally, his studies on grasshopper tracheal tubes showed that gas diffusion alone can account for oxygen uptake. These investigations into blood flow and gas transport provided essential insights into how organisms manage varying oxygen demands during physical exertion.

terms.definition: Krogh's historical account of regulation through changes in the number of capillaries carrying blood and the surface available for oxygen diffusion.
A graph showing how much oxygen hemoglobin holds at different oxygen pressures; the collaborators investigated how carbon dioxide changes this relationship.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Diplomatic contributions to international arbitration and legal institutions
sections.body: During the 1899 Hague Peace Conference, Bourgeois chaired the Third Commission, focusing on international arbitration. Working alongside British and American delegation chairmen, he helped secure the proposal to create a Permanent Court of Arbitration, eventually serving as a member of this court starting in 1903. At the 1907 Hague conference, he led the First Commission, addressing boards of inquiry and the pacific settlement of disputes. His published works, including Pour la Société des Nations and Le Pacte de 1919 et la Société des Nations, documented his peace efforts. In 1918, he headed a commission that drafted an official proposal for a League of Nations, later serving as the inaugural president of the Council of the League of Nations.

sections.heading: Bourgeois’s later explanation of the League
sections.body: Unable to travel because of ill health, Bourgeois sent a written Nobel communication in December 1922. He treated the League of Nations as a reason for renewed confidence after the devastation of the First World War. His account connected it with the Hague conferences and the 1919 Covenant, arguing that international cooperation required practical institutions as well as ideals. He also stressed public understanding: people should know both the League’s purposes and the limits imposed by state sovereignty. His discussion of international law emphasised increasingly precise obligations set out in conventions. These were his hopes and arguments for the institution, not a demonstration that future war had become impossible. The communication also referred to his proposal for intellectual cooperation, adopted by the League Assembly in September 1921, after the year of his award.

terms.definition: An international institution established following the 1899 Hague Peace Conference to facilitate the peaceful settlement of global disputes.
Rules and obligations governing relations between states and other international actors; Bourgeois emphasised their expression in binding conventions.

sources.title: Léon Bourgeois: The Reasons for the League of Nations — written communication, December 1922

sections.heading: Metrological advancements through nickel steel research
sections.body: Guillaume’s work at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures combined precision measurement with systematic investigation of alloys. He tested expansion, elasticity, hardness, ageing and stability. The discovery of invar, a nickel–iron alloy with very small thermal expansion, addressed a central problem: a measuring standard changes length as its temperature changes. Invar wires became especially useful for surveying baselines, and the material found applications in scientific instruments. Other nickel steels also had practical uses, including replacing costly platinum in incandescent-lamp manufacture. The 1920 presentation connected the wider alloy programme with improvements in watchmaking and praised its contribution to contemporary theories of solid materials. The value of the research lay both in identifying unusual properties and in determining how reliably those properties could support measurements and manufactured devices.

sections.heading: Expansion coefficients and alloy development at the Bureau
sections.body: During his tenure at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, Guillaume conducted investigations regarding mercury-in-glass thermometer corrections and the thermal expansion of length standards. He utilized a contact method to determine the volume of one kilogram of water and contributed to initial work on the International Metre. Beyond invar, he identified elinvar, an alloy featuring a nearly zero thermoelastic coefficient that maintains a nearly constant Young’s modulus over a useful temperature range. This material enabled the creation of elinvar hair springs for compensating balances in chronometers. His systematic research into nickel-iron alloys also supported rapid geodetic baseline measurements and the production of precision instruments like thermostats and astronomical clock pendulums. His findings were documented in various technical treatises, including studies on thermometry and nickel-steel applications.

terms.definition: The science of measurement, including standards and methods for making results accurate and comparable.
A nickel–iron alloy whose stiffness changes very little with temperature over a useful operating range.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The Law of Shifting in Radioactive Decay
sections.body: Radioactive changes could be related to the charge of the atomic nucleus. Emission of an alpha particle lowers that charge by two units, so the product has an atomic number two smaller. In beta-minus decay, emission of an electron accompanies an increase of one unit in nuclear charge and atomic number. These rules explained how a sequence of transformations could return to the same chemical element with a different mass. After one alpha decay and two beta-minus decays, the nuclear charge has returned to its original value while roughly four mass units have been lost. The products therefore occupy the same place in the periodic system but are different isotopes. Beta changes can also connect different elements with nearly the same atomic mass.

sections.heading: Research on radioactive decay and displacement law
sections.body: During his tenure at McGill University, Soddy collaborated with Ernest Rutherford to publish papers regarding atomic disintegration and the formation of new kinds of matter. Their joint investigations included studying the gaseous emanation of radium. Later, while working with William Ramsay at University College, London, they utilized spectroscopic means to demonstrate that helium production occurs during the radioactive decay of radium bromide. While lecturing at the University of Glasgow, Soddy developed the Displacement Law. This principle describes how an element changes to one with an atomic number two smaller following the emission of an alpha-particle. His chemical research into radioactive materials eventually led to his formulation of isotopes in 1913, defining elements that possess different atomic weights but remain chemically indistinguishable.

terms.definition: Forms of the same element with the same atomic number but different masses, occupying the same place in the periodic table.
A rule relating radioactive emission to a change in chemical identity; an alpha decay lowers the atomic number by two.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary development and stylistic refinement
sections.body: In his presentation speech, E. A. Karlfeldt described France’s long preparation before the success of Le Crime de Sylvestre Bonnard. Although his early literary output was limited, his reading and intellectual development were extensive. At fifteen, France dedicated an essay about Saint Radegund to his parents; the speech notes that the work was later lost. His father’s bookshop exposed him to collectors, editions and literary conversation, a world that also entered his fiction. Karlfeldt particularly praised the clarity of France’s prose. He borrowed an image France had used for a fictional character’s voice—speaking crystal—to describe that style. The speech also discussed Thaïs (1890), set amid the encounter between Hellenic culture and Christianity, and France’s continuing imaginative interest in saints and legends.

sections.heading: Literary styles and classical influences
sections.body: France practiced a style rooted in French classicism, drawing inspiration from the eighteenth-century traditions of Fénélon and Voltaire. His writing often featured enlightened hedonism and urbane scepticism, themes explicitly presented in his 1895 aphorisms, Le Jardin d’Épicure. As a critic for Le Temps, he utilized subjective reviews influenced by Renan's scepticism. His historical fiction explored the transition from paganism to Christianity through works such as Balthazar and Thaïs. He also engaged with contemporary subjects and social issues, moving away from Zola's naturalism toward complex character studies. This versatility extended to autobiographical novels like Le Livre de mon ami and large-scale tableaux of eighteenth-century life, notably La Rôtisserie de la Reine Pédauque, which showcased his ability to blend irony with historical insight.

terms.definition: Someone with a strong interest in books, especially their collecting, editions and physical or literary qualities.
A brief, memorable statement expressing an observation or idea; France used this form in Le Jardin d’Épicure.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Branting's political development and international security efforts
sections.body: Branting’s political ideas developed through contact with socialists including Paul Lafargue and Eduard Bernstein. He helped build Sweden’s Social Democratic Labour Party, founded in 1889, and argued that parliamentary activity should work alongside organized labour. He campaigned for expanded voting rights and supported a peaceful resolution of the Swedish–Norwegian crisis in 1905. Internationally, he helped bring Sweden into the League of Nations and chaired the Assembly’s disarmament committee in 1920–21. His work continued after the Nobel award: he participated in the Greek–Italian dispute of 1923, served as rapporteur on the Mosul dispute in 1924, and helped draft proposals for compulsory arbitration in the Geneva Protocol. These later activities illustrate the continuation of his approach, rather than events for which the 1921 prize could already have rewarded him.

sections.heading: Management of the Inter-Parliamentary Union
sections.body: During his leadership, Christian Lange maintained the Inter-Parliamentary Union despite significant financial hardships caused by the First World War. When German authorities impounded funds in Brussels and parliamentary groups ceased contributions, Lange secured loans from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace to sustain operations. He managed expenses through rigorous cost-cutting and personally handled essential correspondence. He convened the Union’s Council in Geneva in 1919; the Council then arranged the first postwar conference in 1921. Beyond this role, he served as a technical delegate at the 1907 Hague Peace Conference and acted as a special correspondent for the Carnegie Endowment from 1916, continuing after the award until 1929. He also provided orientations for various League of Nations committees regarding disarmament and political questions.

terms.definition: A procedure in which states submit a dispute to an agreed decision-maker instead of attempting to settle it by force.
An organization comprising active parliamentarians from national legislative bodies working to promote international intercourse and substitute adjudication for force.

sections.heading: Kinetic theory and the photoelectric law
sections.body: Beyond his work on light, Einstein developed a kinetic theory during the early 1900s to explain Brownian movement. This classical mechanics-based approach describes the properties of suspensions, specifically how solid particles behave within liquids in colloidal solutions. Regarding the photoelectric effect, Einstein applied quantum theory to explain how energy from a light quantum transfers to an electron. He proposed that if a quantum possesses enough energy to detach an electron from a metal surface, the remaining energy becomes kinetic energy for that electron. This explains why the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons depends on light frequency rather than intensity. His quantitative law also provided a way to calculate ionization potential in gas molecules and helped explain Stokes’ rule regarding the frequency changes observed during photo-luminescence processes like fluorescence.

sections.heading: Einstein's investigations into radiation and statistical mechanics
sections.body: Einstein used statistical reasoning to connect microscopic behaviour with observable effects. His 1905 account of Brownian motion treated suspended particles as buffeted by moving molecules; it belonged to classical statistical mechanics. In other work, he investigated thermal radiation at low density, helping develop the quantum description of light. He also studied atomic transition probabilities and applied general relativity to cosmology. His wider programme continued beyond the 1921 award. In the 1920s he developed a quantum account of a monatomic gas and pursued attempts to construct unified field theories, work he continued after moving to the United States. These investigations show how his methods ranged across classical physics, quantum theory and relativity without making them interchangeable explanations of the same phenomenon.

terms.definition: Irregular motion of small particles suspended in a fluid, caused by collisions with the fluid’s moving molecules.
The use of probabilities to relate the behaviour of many microscopic constituents to a system’s macroscopic properties, such as temperature and pressure.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The Whole-Number Rule and Isotopic Mixtures
sections.body: Aston’s measurements helped explain why an element could have a fractional atomic weight even when its individual isotopes had masses close to whole numbers. Chlorine, for example, combined isotopes with masses near 35 and 37; their mixture produced an average near 35.46. The 1922 presentation described evidence from more than thirty elements and treated the whole-number pattern as an important clue to nuclear structure. On the historical scale that assigned oxygen-16 a mass of 16, ordinary hydrogen stood noticeably above one, at about 1.008. Its single-proton nucleus differed from the more complex nuclei under discussion. The pattern was approximate, not an exact law that made every isotope an integer. Aston’s increasingly precise instruments later measured smaller departures from it.

sections.heading: Development of electromagnetic focusing in mass spectrography
sections.body: Before the First World War, Aston worked with J. J. Thomson on positive rays and obtained evidence that neon contained atoms of different masses. Returning to Cambridge in 1919, he developed the mass spectrograph to distinguish the isotopes more clearly. Electromagnetic focusing turned their small mass differences into separable records. He then extended the method to other elements. The Nobel biography credits him with discovering 212 naturally occurring isotopes across his research career; that total should not be read as a count already reached in 1922. Improved instruments also let him measure departures from the whole-number rule with increasing precision. Earlier work on electrical discharges and vacuum apparatus had helped develop the experimental skills behind this programme.

terms.definition: A discovery showing that isotopic masses are close to whole-number multiples of a common unit across many elements.
An instrument that uses electric and magnetic fields to separate charged particles according to mass-to-charge ratio and records the resulting pattern.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Principles of Benavente's dramatic craftsmanship
sections.body: The 1922 presentation praised Benavente for making stage action convincing without relying on exaggerated emotion or spectacle. It treated his attention to character, competing wishes and social surroundings as the basis of his dramatic skill. Psychology, in this reading, clarified what people did rather than becoming a separate subject for analysis. The speech placed his work mainly within Spanish comedy, using that term broadly for plays without tragic endings. It also recognised darker works, including La Malquerida, and smaller romantic or fantastic pieces. Its argument was that Benavente could prompt reflection and challenge prejudice while preserving credible characters and situations. These are the committee speaker’s critical judgments about his craft, rather than claims that fiction provides an objectively complete record of society.

sections.heading: Evolution of Benavente's dramatic style and literary works
sections.body: After leaving law studies, Benavente travelled and wrote journalism; Cartas de mujeres helped establish his reputation as a stylist. His dramatic career began with The Fantastic Theatre in 1892, followed by successes including Gente conocida, a satire of Madrid society. The Nobel biography describes a movement from social portraiture towards tighter dramatic construction. Its examples of rural psychological drama are Señora ama and La Malquerida. It calls Los intereses creados his most frequently staged play and interprets it as an allegory about the necessity of evil. Such descriptions reflect a critical reading of his work. His publications extended beyond the stage, including poetry in 1893. The ten-volume collected plays dated 1941–1955 belong to the much later publication history, after his 1922 award.

terms.definition: In the presentation’s account of Spanish theatrical terminology, a broad category of plays without tragic endings, extending beyond overtly humorous works.
Plays that expose or make comic use of a social group’s conventions, pretensions and behaviour; a form associated with Benavente’s social observation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Methods for analyzing muscle heat and chemical metabolism
sections.body: Hill and Meyerhof approached muscle activity with different measurements. Hill used thermoelectric methods to follow the timing of heat production. Meyerhof compared changes in muscle carbohydrates and lactic acid with oxygen consumption during recovery. His measurements showed that the oxygen used accounted for only part of the disappearing lactic acid. He interpreted the remainder as being reconverted into carbohydrate, coupling chemical analysis with the heat measurements. The award presentation set out this historical account of muscle recovery. Meyerhof also studied finely chopped muscle kept in liquid, where the reactions proceeded faster than in intact preparations. This made it easier to vary conditions such as acidity and phosphate concentration and investigate how the processes were connected.

sections.heading: Techniques for measuring thermal changes in muscle and nerves
sections.body: During his research, Hill utilized the Blix apparatus and learned myothermic observation techniques from Bürker. He integrated a galvanometer into his investigations after being introduced to the device by Paschen. These methods allowed him to study how heat production relates to muscle fiber length. Later, he developed highly sensitive techniques capable of measuring temperature fluctuations as small as 0.003°C occurring within hundredths of a second. His work eventually extended these thermal measurements to observe heat produced during the passage of nerve impulses.

sections.heading: Meyerhof's investigations into cellular oxidation and glycolysis
sections.body: Meyerhof moved from psychiatry and philosophy towards cell physiology under Otto Warburg’s influence. He combined gas analysis with measurements of heat to study metabolism in bacteria, blood cells and sea-urchin eggs. Work with yeast extracts led him to examine factors involved in respiration and fermentation. His frog-muscle experiments related oxygen use to the disappearance of lactic acid during recovery. Later, in 1925, he extracted a functioning glycolytic enzyme system from muscle. Together with colleagues, he used such preparations to investigate individual reactions outside intact cells. This work helped test and extend Gustav Embden’s proposed reaction sequence in the 1930s. Those later investigations expanded the chemical understanding of muscle beyond the measurements recognised in 1922.

terms.definition: Measuring heat-related changes through the electrical response produced by a temperature difference.
A specialized technique used to study and measure heat production and thermal changes associated with muscle function and activity.
A sequence of enzyme-catalysed reactions that breaks down sugars; Meyerhof investigated it using muscle extracts.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Diplomatic negotiations and prisoner repatriation logistics
sections.body: As a League of Nations representative, Nansen negotiated with Soviet, German and other governments over prisoners’ release, food and transport. He chartered ships that Germany was due to hand over to Britain under the peace settlement, using them on Baltic repatriation routes. Prisoners in Eastern Siberia required transport through Vladivostok; other return journeys used the Black Sea. The different routes created distinct logistical and financial problems. His refugee work also involved negotiating with potential host countries and appointing representatives to assist. By the time of the 1922 presentation, a further mission was under way to help people displaced by the Greco-Turkish War, including those arriving in Greece and Balkan countries from Asia Minor and Eastern Thrace.

sections.heading: Diplomatic negotiations and humanitarian relief efforts
sections.body: In 1917–1918 Nansen negotiated in Washington for relaxation of the Allied blockade so that essential food could reach Norway. His later work included prisoner repatriation, relief during the Russian famine of 1921–1922, and assistance to people without recognised nationality. Nansen passports provided identity documents that were eventually accepted by fifty-two governments. His refugee work continued after the award and included involvement in the Greek–Turkish population exchange. In 1925 he prepared an Armenian settlement plan centred on Erivan, but the League did not implement it. The Nobel biography credits the later Nansen International Office for Refugees with settling some 10,000 people in Erivan and 40,000 in Syria and Lebanon. Those later outcomes should not be credited to successful implementation of his original plan.

terms.definition: A senior official assigned responsibility for a defined international task, such as Nansen’s coordination of refugee assistance for the League of Nations.
An identity and travel document for stateless refugees, eventually recognised by fifty-two governments; its acceptance developed over time.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Spectral analysis and the principle of correspondence
sections.body: Spectral measurements produced precise regularities before physicists could explain them. Balmer found a pattern in hydrogen’s lines, while Rydberg extended the search for numerical relationships. Bohr’s atomic theory attempted to connect such patterns with allowed states of electrons. It addressed a central difficulty of classical orbital pictures: an accelerating charge should radiate energy and spiral towards the nucleus. The presentation discussed Sommerfeld’s extension of the early model to elliptical orbits as a way to account for closely spaced spectral lines. It then emphasised Bohr’s correspondence principle, relating quantum predictions to classical behaviour and helping constrain possible transitions. The detailed trajectories described in 1922 belong to that early atomic model. Their historical role should be distinguished from the later quantum-mechanical account of electrons.

sections.heading: Early theoretical investigations and academic developments
sections.body: Bohr’s early investigations included measuring surface tension with oscillating liquid jets, work that earned a Danish academy prize. His doctoral studies examined metals using electron theory and brought him into contact with the implications of Planck’s quantum ideas. After visiting Cambridge’s Cavendish Laboratory, he worked with Rutherford in Manchester, where his theoretical study of alpha-ray absorption preceded investigations of atomic structure. He later headed Copenhagen’s Institute for Theoretical Physics. After the 1922 award, his programme expanded: nuclear research became prominent during the 1930s, including a liquid-drop picture discussed in 1936. He also developed complementarity as part of his interpretation of quantum phenomena. These later contributions grew from a continuing theoretical career and should be distinguished from the atomic-structure work recognised in 1922.

terms.definition: The principle that quantum predictions should agree with classical physics in the appropriate limit, providing guidance for connecting the two descriptions.
The idea that descriptions tied to mutually exclusive experimental arrangements can both be needed for a full account of a quantum system.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Refining elemental analysis through micro-analytical techniques
sections.body: Pregl transformed quantitative analysis by converting established methods used for large quantities into micro-analytical procedures. By introducing new apparatus and techniques, he reduced the required material to as little as 3–5 milligrams or even less. This advancement allows a single amount of substance, previously needed for one carbon-hydrogen determination, to support up to fifty different analyses. These improvements facilitate the study of various elements within organic compounds and aid investigations into chemical constitution. Such precision is vital when analyzing substances like enzymes, vitamins, or hormones that are difficult to obtain. His revised methods for carbon-hydrogen determination provide an essential tool for researchers in fields such as biochemistry, where original material is often extremely limited.

sections.heading: Development of quantitative organic micro-analysis techniques
sections.body: Pregl’s investigation of bile acids and protein-related substances was restricted by how little material he could obtain. This practical difficulty drove his search for analytical methods using smaller samples. At Innsbruck between 1910 and 1913, he concentrated on quantitative organic microanalysis and then continued the work at Graz. By 1912, his procedures could determine carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur and halogens in samples of 5–13 milligrams; later refinements reduced the requirement to 3–5 milligrams. The work combined adapted apparatus, sensitive weighing and careful procedures. Pregl also wanted the techniques to function outside his own laboratory. He delayed publishing individual experimental reports until satisfied that other laboratories could reproduce the methods, then brought them together in a monograph in 1917. Chemists subsequently came to Graz to learn the procedures under his guidance.

terms.definition: A method of quantitative analysis using very small quantities of substances to determine the elemental contents of organic compounds.
Determining the quantities of chemical elements present in a sample, rather than directly determining the complete arrangement of its atoms.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of the Celtic Revival and Irish Drama
sections.body: The 1923 presentation placed Yeats at the centre of a wider revival of Irish literature. Writers drew on Irish traditions while working in English, connecting national material with an international literary language. Yeats’s organising helped build both an audience and a stage for new Irish drama. The Countess Cathleen, published in 1892, became part of that theatrical programme. His verse plays also included Deirdre, The Green Helmet and The King’s Threshold. He later experimented with a different theatrical vocabulary: masks, stylised gestures, music and compressed dialogue could replace some of the expectations of ordinary stage realism. The speaker praised the lyrical effects of these experiments while acknowledging that their possibilities were still developing. This account connected Yeats’s roles as poet, playwright and organiser within the literary movement.

sections.heading: Evolution of dramatic style and theatrical contributions
sections.body: Yeats’s early career included substantial work for the Irish theatre movement alongside Lady Gregory. His plays drew on Irish legends as well as his interests in mysticism and spiritualism. After 1910, his theatrical experiments increasingly used masks, dance and music, with Japanese Noh plays providing an important influence. Some were intended for small audiences. His poetry developed alongside this work. The Wild Swans at Coole appeared in 1919 and Michael Robartes and the Dancer in 1921, before the Nobel award. The Tower followed in 1928 and The Winding Stair and Other Poems in 1933. The Nobel biography interprets the later poetry through recurring concerns such as the relationship between art and life and cyclical views of history. These later collections continued a poetic career already established when he received the prize.

terms.definition: A cultural and literary revival drawing on Irish traditions, in which Yeats and many other writers helped develop modern Irish literature.
A theatrical organization founded by Yeats and Lady Gregory that eventually transitioned into the well-known Abbey Theatre.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of pancreatic extract through duct ligation
sections.body: Banting suspected that digestive enzymes destroyed the pancreatic substance needed to control blood sugar. He proposed tying off the pancreatic duct so that enzyme-producing tissue would deteriorate while the islets remained. In May 1921, he and Charles Best began dog experiments in Macleod's Toronto laboratory. The team studied changes in blood sugar, metabolism and liver glycogen, as well as the danger of excessive falls in blood sugar. Making an extract suitable for patients required further purification. James Collip's improvements led to successful treatment of Leonard Thompson in January 1922 after an earlier, less effective injection. This progression connected an experimental hypothesis with animal studies, biochemical preparation and clinical testing.

sections.heading: The anatomical idea behind pancreatic extraction
sections.body: Banting's proposal drew on earlier work linking diabetes with the pancreas and its islets of Langerhans. Researchers had proposed an internal secretion that controlled sugar metabolism, but attempts to give patients pancreas material or extracts had been unreliable. Banting read Moses Baron's account of what happened when a pancreatic duct was tied off: much of the tissue associated with digestive secretion deteriorated while the islets remained. He hoped this would provide material from which the proposed hormone could be extracted without being destroyed by digestive enzymes. Charles Best assisted the experiments in Macleod's laboratory. The biography describes the reasoning behind this initial approach, rather than a complete account of the later preparation used clinically.

sections.heading: Macleod's research on carbohydrate metabolism
sections.body: Macleod had investigated carbohydrate metabolism and diabetes since 1905, publishing studies of blood-sugar regulation and experimentally produced glycosuria. He believed the pancreas was involved but had not established its exact role. His Toronto laboratory provided the setting for Banting and Best's experiments; he contributed physiological knowledge and supervision as the research developed. Producing a clinically useful preparation also required Collip's purification work. The biography places the insulin result within Macleod's longer investigation of metabolism, rather than presenting his laboratory as an incidental venue. It also records that the manufacturing process was patented and that patent proceeds were directed toward medical research.

terms.definition: Tying off a duct; Banting used this approach hoping to reduce digestive-enzyme-producing tissue while preserving the pancreatic islets.
Clusters of cells within the pancreas associated with insulin secretion, which Banting’s proposed experiment aimed to preserve.
The presence of glucose in urine, a sign investigated in Macleod’s experimental work on sugar metabolism.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
University of Toronto: discovery of insulin and Leonard Thompson’s treatment

sections.heading: Measuring the elementary unit of electric charge
sections.body: Electrolysis had shown that the amounts of substances deposited by an electric current were related to their atomic weights and ionic charges. Estimating the elementary charge from this evidence nevertheless required uncertain knowledge of how many atoms were present. Millikan instead followed individual charged oil droplets. He timed their movement past cross-hairs in a telescope and applied a voltage between metal plates so that the electrical force could oppose their fall. Exposing a droplet to ions changed its charge. Repeated measurements showed changes in multiples of a common unit. The award presentation described the resulting precision as one part in a thousand. Following a single small object through controlled changes made the charge measurement much more direct than the earlier bulk estimates.

sections.heading: Research on light polarization and Planck's constant
sections.body: Before his major achievements in electricity, Millikan conducted research regarding how light emitted from incandescent surfaces becomes polarized. This work involved utilizing molten silver and gold at the U.S. Mint to facilitate his investigations. Following this, he performed experiments between 1912 and 1915 that achieved the first direct photoelectric determination of Planck’s constant. His scientific output also included studying Brownian movements in gases, which helped resolve disputes regarding atomic and kinetic theories of matter. Additionally, during the period from 1920 to 1923, he investigated hot-spark spectroscopy. This research explored the spectral region located between X-radiation and ultraviolet light, successfully extending the known ultraviolet spectrum downwards far beyond its previous limits.

terms.definition: The magnitude of the charge carried by one electron, which Millikan measured by observing changes in the charges of oil droplets.
A method of studying elements by exploring the spectrum between ultraviolet and X-radiation to extend known spectral limits.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Influences and stylistic elements of Chlopi
sections.body: Per Hallström’s prize essay described The Peasants as both a response to Zola and a work shaped by his example. Reymont objected to the rural society depicted in La Terre and wanted to draw on his own experience of the people among whom he had grown up. Yet Hallström also identified debts to Zola’s detailed settings, collective scenes and realism. He praised the novel’s arrangement around the four seasons, whose contrasts give a large and varied story a coherent rhythm. For Hallström, Jagna was both a character and a poetic symbol, embodying qualities he found attractive as well as destructive. He observed that Reymont maintained tragic tension even where he offered no clear moral judgment. These are the prize committee chairman’s interpretations of the novel’s artistic effects.

sections.heading: Early literary development and professional transitions
sections.body: Before achieving international recognition, Reymont engaged in various roles, including working in technical railway services and producing amateur theatre. His early education involved learning Latin from a curate using a breviary as a textbook. During periods of isolation near railway stations, he wrote extensively, though he frequently destroyed his own dramatic and novelistic drafts. After sending six short stories to a Warsaw critic, he secured publication through a recommended publisher. In his autobiographical account, publication was followed by dismissal from the railway company, whose management wanted workers rather than writers. Following this transition, he moved to Warsaw with his manuscripts to pursue a literary career, later producing works such as Bunt in the early 1920s.

terms.definition: A stylistic approach characterized by uncompromising, searching descriptions of the environment and a faithful representation of reality.
A literary style that emphasizes detailed environmental descriptions within a narrative to portray the connection between people and surroundings.

sections.heading: Technical development of the string galvanometer
sections.body: Einthoven's work involved analyzing how the string galvanometer curve depended on string tension, mass, and damping from air resistance or electromagnetic means. Following a 1906 analysis, he published a detailed instrument description in 1909. Before this, he used a correction method developed in 1894 to derive electrocardiograms from capillary electrometer curves, labeling specific details as P, Q, R, S, and T. He later demonstrated that the string galvanometer's recorded action current matched results from the capillary electrometer method. His research showed that while individuals possess unique traces, most follow a general type. Furthermore, his 1906 publication described ECG patterns observed in patients with conditions including mitral insufficiency and heart block.

sections.heading: Development of the string galvanometer and mathematical refinements
sections.body: Einthoven used a capillary electrometer to investigate the heart’s electrical activity. Its sluggish response distorted the recorded trace, so he studied the instrument’s behaviour and developed mathematical corrections for its photographic records. Applying these methods to an electrocardiogram associated with A. D. Waller helped establish what a more faithful trace should look like. Einthoven then refined the string galvanometer over several years so that it could record rapid, weak signals more directly, reducing the need for laborious corrections. Sensitivity alone was insufficient: the instrument also needed to follow changes quickly. His work extended to separate investigations of heart sounds with P. Battaerd and retinal electrical currents with W. A. Jolly. The combination of instrument design and physiological interpretation made electrical recordings useful for studying cardiac function.

terms.definition: A historical term for electrical changes accompanying biological activity, here the heart’s changing electrical signals during a beat.
An instrument in which a thin conducting string moves in a magnetic field in response to an electric current, permitting sensitive recording.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Advancements in X-ray spectroscopy and elemental analysis
sections.body: The prize presentation described a substantial expansion in the measured X-ray spectra of elements. For 27 elements, all four principal K-series lines had been measured; investigations also extended to fainter lines. The L-series studies covered about 50 elements, while the newly explored M-series was examined in 16. Measurements of the N-series reached very heavy elements, including uranium and thorium. These results mattered because precise wavelengths gave atomic theories a large body of evidence to explain. Siegbahn also worked, sometimes with his pupils, on practical instruments. One apparatus used two X-ray exposures for qualitative analysis, identifying the elements present through their characteristic radiation. The presentation reported a range from sodium to uranium. Such an analytical method connects a spectrum with chemical composition, while the precision measurements also test models of atomic structure.

sections.heading: Advancements in X-ray spectroscopy and instrumentation
sections.body: Siegbahn enhanced radiation intensity by constructing new X-ray tubes and improved air pumps. His development of numerous spectrographs, alongside crystal or linear gratings, increased measurement accuracy, allowing for the discovery of new series within characteristic X-radiations. These precision techniques provided an empirical foundation for interpreting quantum-theoretical phenomena regarding electron shell energy and radiation conditions. His spectrographs were held at a constant temperature. A precision goniometer, read through two microscopes on opposite sides, allowed very small angular differences to be measured. Furthermore, he authored the scientific book Spektroskopie der Röntgenstrahlen in 1923, which detailed these spectroscopic findings. These instrumental improvements facilitated more precise observations of atomic radiation patterns and energy levels.

terms.definition: A field of research involving the investigation of X-radiation in different elements through the measurement of spectral lines.
An instrument for measuring angles; in X-ray spectroscopy, precise angles help determine radiation wavelengths.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of the ultramicroscope and nucleus method
sections.body: Working with the Zeiss optician Henry Siedentopf, Zsigmondy developed an instrument that viewed a strongly illuminated solution at right angles to the incident light. Scattered light revealed particles too small for ordinary microscopic observation. He used it to establish that gold colloids contained distinct particles. For still finer particles, his nucleus method added a reducing solution so that metallic gold deposited onto existing particles until they became detectable. Investigations of silver solutions likewise supported a particulate explanation instead of an assumed new form of silver. By counting particles in a measured volume and comparing that count with the amount of material present, he could estimate their size, assuming spherical shapes. These measurements made the heterogeneity of colloids experimentally accessible.

sections.heading: Development of slit-ultramicroscopy and gold hydrosol preparation
sections.body: Zsigmondy studied organic chemistry under W. von Miller in Munich before working with the physicist August Kundt in Berlin. His interest in lustre colours for glass and china drew him towards colloid chemistry. He worked at the Schott glass works in Jena, then left in 1900 to continue his research independently. His subsequent work included reproducible preparations of gold hydrosols and, with Siedentopf, development of the slit-ultramicroscope. These strands complemented each other: reproducible samples made observations comparable, while improved observation helped reveal their particles. He later directed the Institute of Inorganic Chemistry at Göttingen. His publications included Lehrbuch der Kolloidchemie and, with P. A. Thiessen, Über das kolloide Gold, extending the account of his methods and findings.
