terms.definition: In historical colloid research, a term for substances such as dissolved salt that diffused readily and could pass through membranes such as parchment.
An instrument that uses an intense, narrowly directed beam to make very small particles detectable through the light they scatter.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of Shaw's dramatic style and classical approach
sections.body: The presentation described Shaw as an advocate of Ibsen who challenged conventional English and French theatre. It located his originality less in stage structure than in the directness and variety of his arguments. Plays Unpleasant, published in 1898 alongside Plays Pleasant, confronted audiences with subjects such as exploitation instead of offering uncomplicated entertainment. The speaker interpreted Shaw’s humour as a way to keep audiences engaged with difficult ideas, even when critics dismissed it as buffoonery. Shaw also used substantial prefaces to develop arguments beyond the performance itself. In this account, his claim to classicism meant a preference for reasoned debate over romantic sentiment. That was a particular interpretation of Shaw’s dramatic practice, rather than a complete definition of classical theatre.

sections.heading: Evolution of Shaw's dramatic methods and political writing
sections.body: Shaw’s advocacy of Ibsen, including The Quintessence of Ibsenism, accompanied his move from novels to plays. As a Fabian Society member he also wrote political pamphlets. The Nobel biography describes his theatre as a forum for ideas, where verbal wit and competing arguments could take precedence over action. It points to the Life Force discussions in Man and Superman and interprets Major Barbara through the relationship between individual fulfilment and political activity. Back to Methuselah is presented as an example in which discussion threatens to overwhelm drama. Saint Joan, by contrast, connects a medieval story with later perspectives. These are critical interpretations of how the plays work. Other comedies challenged the medical profession and prevailing attitudes towards relations between women and men.

terms.definition: In the presentation’s account of Shaw, an approach favouring rational argument and dialectical debate over romantic sentiment.
A dramatic form where witty argumentation and intellectual debate often take precedence over traditional dramatic action or plot.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Economic and diplomatic mechanisms for European stability
sections.body: An expert committee chaired by Dawes investigated Germany’s capacity to pay reparations and produced its report in April 1924. It proposed a different payment structure intended to make the obligations workable. In October of the following year, negotiations at Locarno addressed a separate but related security problem. Germany, Belgium, France, Britain and Italy reached agreement concerning the Rhineland. Germany also concluded arbitration agreements with Belgium, France, Poland and Czechoslovakia. The financial and diplomatic measures were different contributions to reducing postwar tension; the joint award did not make them a single project carried out at one time.

sections.heading: Diplomatic negotiations and the Locarno Agreements
sections.body: During his tenure as foreign secretary, Chamberlain rejected the Geneva Protocol because it granted the League of Nations Council authority to enforce decisions during crises. Instead, he proposed supplementing the Covenant with special arrangements for specific needs. This approach facilitated the 1925 meeting in Switzerland involving seven powers. The resulting Locarno Agreements included the Rhine Guarantee Pact and various arbitration treaties between Germany and former enemies. These documents also featured a collective note regarding Germany's entry into the League of Nations.

sections.heading: Financial reforms and the Dawes Report
sections.body: As Director of the Budget, Dawes reformed United States governmental procedures by requiring departments to prepare true budgets projecting future expenditures. He also integrated supply procurement and distribution systems for the American Expeditionary Force and created an inter-Allied purchasing board. In 1924, he submitted a report regarding German reparations that analyzed Germany's resources and budget. This document proposed currency stabilization measures and established a sliding scale payment schedule to address international financial instability.

terms.definition: The 1924 expert committee’s plan for reorganising German reparation payments and supporting financial stabilisation.
The package of treaties and related agreements initialled in 1925 to provide security guarantees and arbitration among several European countries.
A plan for expected income and expenditure. Dawes required government departments to project their spending and operate within their budgets.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Refining electron-gas collision methods
sections.body: Franck and Hertz refined an approach pioneered by Lenard: sending electrons through a gas and observing how collisions change their motion. Their experiments made electron impact a tool for investigating atoms and other constituents of matter. The central significance was the evidence that atoms exchanged energy in distinct amounts. Comparisons between these losses and atomic radiation connected electrical measurements with spectroscopy. The 1926 presentation for the 1925 award celebrated this as confirmation of Bohr’s hypotheses. More precisely, the experiments supported discrete atomic energy states and the relationship between energy changes and radiation. They did not establish every feature of Bohr’s model. Other researchers also developed the experimental field, using collisions to probe different gases and particles.

sections.heading: Franck's investigations into electron kinetics and molecular dissociation
sections.body: Franck’s early work in Berlin examined ion mobility and electrical conduction through gases. With Gustav Hertz, he then studied how electrons lose energy in collisions with atoms. Other investigations, often conducted with students and collaborators, explored excited atoms and photochemical reactions. At Göttingen he studied the fluorescence of gases and vapours. In 1925, he proposed an explanation of iodine molecules breaking apart under illumination: the electronic change occurred so rapidly that the nuclei scarcely moved during it. Edward Condon subsequently developed this idea into a theory predicting which vibrational transitions would be favoured. This became the Franck–Condon principle, a distinct development from the electron-collision experiments recognised by the joint prize.

sections.heading: Hertz's research on ionization potentials and spectral lines
sections.body: Hertz’s doctoral research examined how carbon dioxide absorbs infrared radiation as pressure and partial pressure change. In 1913 he began electron-impact experiments with James Franck, investigating energy transfer in gases before his wartime mobilisation. Their research related the energy lost by colliding electrons to the distinct energy states associated with atomic spectral lines. It supplied quantitative experimental support for the emerging quantum account of atoms. Hertz later worked on a different problem: separating isotopes of neon. At his Berlin institute, he developed a diffusion cascade for that purpose. This extended his experimental career beyond the collision measurements recognised by the Nobel award.

terms.definition: A collision in which some of an incoming electron’s kinetic energy is transferred to internal excitation of an atom or molecule.
The approximation that nuclei barely change position during a rapid electronic transition, used to understand the strengths of molecular spectral transitions.
A sequence of diffusion stages used to increase the separation of isotopes; Hertz applied the method to neon.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental verification of molecular existence and particle distribution
sections.body: Svedberg tested predictions about the movement and distribution of tiny particles in liquids. Observing colloidal particles with an ultramicroscope provided evidence for the unseen molecular motion producing their irregular movement. With collaborators, he also counted how the number of particles in a very small region fluctuated over time. For radioactive solutions, related measurements used flashes produced when emitted particles struck a zinc-sulphide screen. These experiments tested statistical predictions about small systems. Another part of his work greatly accelerated settling by spinning solutions. The 1926 presentation described an ultracentrifuge operating at 40,000 revolutions per minute, with an arrangement that allowed the changing distribution of material to be observed and photographed. It connected measurements of dispersed particles with studies of dissolved molecules, extending the experimental tools available for investigating extremely small constituents of matter.

sections.heading: Investigating colloids and macromolecular compounds
sections.body: Svedberg’s 1908 doctoral thesis described a method for producing colloidal particles and presented experimental support for the Brownian-motion theories of Einstein and Smoluchowski. With many collaborators, he studied diffusion, light absorption and sedimentation. These observations connected the behaviour of dispersed particles with the statistical ideas used to describe gases. His ultracentrifuge then made sedimentation useful for studying large dissolved molecules. The Nobel biography surveys the instrument’s broader development and applications, including proteins, carbohydrates and synthetic polymers, and reports forces reaching approximately a million times gravity. Measurements could be related to molecular size and shape. In studies of particular purified proteins, Svedberg found a uniform molecular size; the technique could also reveal contaminants.

terms.definition: Light flashes produced when radioactive particles strike a screen that has been coated with zinc sulphide.
Substances consisting of small particles distributed through another substance, which Svedberg studied regarding their physical properties and molecular existence.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary inspirations from Sardinian landscapes and customs
sections.body: The presentation for Deledda’s prize connected her writing with the landscapes and oral traditions around Nuoro. Folk songs, hymns and legends belonged to the world from which she drew material. In La via del male, funeral scenes include closed doors and shutters, extinguished fires and hired mourners improvising laments. Such details gave a specific social setting to the novel’s human conflicts. The Academy’s speaker emphasised how closely characters and landscape were joined in her fiction, using imagery of people rooted in Sardinian soil. His comparisons with Homer and his praise of the work’s clarity are literary judgements. The explanation of the award moved from this regional specificity to broader questions of desire, suffering and moral struggle: local customs supplied the setting, while the characters’ difficulties could be recognised by readers elsewhere.

sections.heading: Development of Deledda's literary career
sections.body: In her autobiographical account, Deledda recalled that a teacher encouraged her to publish the stories she wrote during private Italian lessons. She said she sent a story to a fashion magazine at thirteen and saw it accepted. Her novel Fior di Sardegna appeared in 1892. She identified Elias Portolú, published in 1903, as her first major success: a translation appeared through the Revue des deux mondes, and translations into other European languages followed. Her subsequent books included Canne al vento and La Madre, alongside numerous short-story collections. She continued writing after the Nobel award. Land of the Wind, published in 1931, combined invented narrative with autobiographical material. The later biographical note interprets such works through her continuing concern with suffering, human resilience and faith.

terms.definition: Vivid, concrete representation that makes people and places seem clearly shaped; the award citation applied this phrase to Deledda’s writing.
A literary method used in later works to combine imaginary elements with the author's own life experiences.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental methods for inducing gastric growths
sections.body: In his research, Fibiger utilized cockroaches that had ingested worm eggs, allowing larvae to develop within the insect muscles. By feeding these cockroaches to healthy rats, he observed the production of growths in the stomachs of many animals. This method was presented as a way to move beyond unauthenticated hypotheses toward demonstrable theories regarding cancer etiology. The process involved the larvae transforming into adult forms within the rats' stomachs. While this work was celebrated for providing an experimental method to study how external stimuli might provoke changes in normal cells, later investigations overturned his claimed cancer results, identifying the lesions as nonmalignant and noting that vitamin A deficiency influenced the findings.

sections.heading: Fibiger's academic career and institutional roles
sections.body: Following his medical qualification in 1890, Fibiger held several positions within the University of Copenhagen, including assistant at the Department of Bacteriology and prosector at the Institute of Pathological Anatomy. His professional trajectory involved directing the Central Laboratory of the Army and serving as a professor of pathological anatomy. Alongside his research and teaching, he contributed to scientific literature as a founder-member and joint-editor of Acta Pathologica et Microbiologica Scandinavica. Fibiger also engaged in international scientific governance, as a member of the International Commission for Intellectual Cooperation. His extensive involvement in medical organizations included leadership roles within the Danish Medical Society and the Danish Medical Association’s Cancer Commission, alongside memberships in various foreign academies and societies dedicated to biological and pathological research.

terms.definition: The study of the causes or origins of a disease, which researchers aim to understand through precise and demonstrable theories.
The study of structural changes in tissues and organs associated with disease, the discipline Fibiger taught and practised in Copenhagen.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Hitchcock and Bell (1952): Studies on the Nematode Parasite, Gongylonema neoplasticum, and Avitaminosis A in the Forestomach of Rats

sections.heading: Diplomatic developments and the Locarno agreements
sections.body: The 1926 presentation connected Locarno with earlier efforts to settle reparations and end the Ruhr occupation through the Dawes Plan. It also recalled the League’s 1924 Geneva Protocol proposal for arbitration and security. Germany’s note of February 1925 offered a possible security agreement and held out the prospect of wider arrangements. Negotiations at Locarno in October produced a regional settlement: a Rhineland guarantee involving Germany, France, Belgium, Britain and Italy, together with arbitration agreements between Germany and France, Belgium, Poland and Czechoslovakia. The committee treated this as evidence of renewed willingness to negotiate. The result was a set of specific agreements, rather than the worldwide convention envisaged as a possible further goal.

sections.heading: Diplomatic methods and security pact developments
sections.body: Briand’s diplomacy helped turn a German offer of mutual guarantees into the Locarno agreements. He worked with Stresemann and Austen Chamberlain to find terms governments could accept and used informal personal contact alongside formal negotiation. The agreements combined western-frontier guarantees with arbitration arrangements. After the Nobel award, he sought to extend the renunciation of war through an agreement with the United States. Frank Kellogg proposed broadening the approach from a bilateral treaty to a multilateral pact. Fifteen countries signed the resulting Paris Pact in August 1928. Briand later outlined a European union in a memorandum circulated in May 1930. These were subsequent diplomatic initiatives, building on the approach to cooperation associated with Locarno.

sections.heading: Stresemann's diplomatic shift toward international stability
sections.body: After the First World War, Stresemann pursued agreements that could improve Germany’s position through negotiation. As foreign minister, he supported the Dawes Plan’s restructuring of reparations arrangements and proposed a security pact in February 1925. At Locarno, Germany accepted guarantees concerning its western boundaries, while separate arbitration agreements addressed relations with several neighbours. Stresemann then worked to secure acceptance of the settlement at home. His diplomacy also included the Treaty of Berlin with the Soviet Union in April 1926. Germany entered the League of Nations that September after an earlier unsuccessful attempt. These measures connected reconciliation with Western powers, relations with the Soviet Union and participation in an international institution.

terms.definition: A 1924 League proposal linking peaceful dispute settlement with security and disarmament; it was a proposal, not a universally operating system.
A method of international relations characterized by persuasiveness and addressing the core of problems through informal amiability.
A mechanism used to restructure German reparations according to the nation's actual ability to make payments.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental methods using gamboge emulsions
sections.body: To investigate molecular existence, Perrin developed a system of small particles with uniform weight and size. He utilized gamboge, a substance derived from vegetable sap that can be manipulated like soap, to create this emulsion. By rubbing the material between his hands under water, he initially produced spherical particles of varying dimensions. Through months of meticulous work, he successfully isolated specific decigrams of particles from one kilogram of the raw material to achieve the necessary uniformity. Using these emulsions, Perrin performed measurements on Brownian movement and particle rotation to calculate Avogadro’s number. His results for the number of molecules in two grams of hydrogen aligned with the kinetic theory of gases, providing indirect evidence for molecules through the observation of molecular impacts.

sections.heading: Calculating Avogadro's number through colloidal particle studies
sections.body: Beyond his work on cathode rays and X-rays, Perrin investigated the nature of colloids to validate Einstein’s theoretical research. He demonstrated that these particles follow gas laws, which allowed for the calculation of Avogadro’s number. This value matched results from different experimental methods, such as his observations regarding sedimentation equilibrium in suspensions featuring uniform microscopic gamboge particles. His broader scientific investigations also included studying fluorescence, the disintegration of radium, and how X-rays affect gas conductivity. Through these various studies on physical phenomena, he provided evidence for the discontinuity of matter. His published works, including the 1913 book Les Atomes, helped communicate these findings regarding molecular reality to a wide audience.

terms.definition: A method of explaining natural phenomena by reducing them to the laws governing the movements of individual molecules.
A steady distribution of suspended particles in which settling under gravity is balanced by their random thermal movement.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Chemical connections between bile acids and cardiac poisons
sections.body: The presentation connected Wieland's bile-acid studies with related investigations by Adolf Windaus. Wieland obtained and characterized a saturated parent acid from bile. Windaus then produced the same substance, cholanic acid, from cholesterol, providing chemical evidence of a relationship between cholesterol and bile acids. Wieland also studied bufotoxin from toad secretions. Windaus's purification and investigation of digitalis compounds helped connect plant-derived cardiac poisons with these other substances. The significance lay in finding structural relationships among materials previously studied in separate fields. Wieland's bile-acid work also contributed to understanding bile's role in the absorption of food. The combined account celebrated complementary contributions by different researchers, rather than assigning all of these results to Wieland.

sections.heading: Chemical investigations into nitrogen oxides and organic radicals
sections.body: Wieland's wider career included extensive work on nitrogen-containing organic compounds. He investigated reactions of nitrogen oxides and studied both persistent and short-lived nitrogen radicals, helping establish methods for examining these reactive intermediates. His later work ranged across natural substances, including alkaloids, mushroom poisons and butterfly pigments. The biography also makes clear that bile-acid research continued after the award: publications beginning in 1912 culminated in clarification of the steroid carbon framework in 1932. Those later results should be distinguished from the knowledge recognized in 1927. Another longstanding interest was biological oxidation, particularly processes involving removal of hydrogen. Together these subjects show the connections between his organic-chemistry experiments and investigations of substances produced by living organisms.

terms.definition: A reference structure used to relate a family of chemical substances; cholanic acid served this role in the bile-acid investigations.
The study of organic chemical species with unpaired electrons, including the nitrogen-centered radicals investigated by Wieland.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Philosophical foundations of duration and intuition
sections.body: In his doctoral thesis, Essai sur les données immédiates de la conscience, Bergson defines time as a reality inseparable from the human self. He introduces duration, or living time, describing it as a dynamic, increasing stream characterized by constant qualitative variations that elude reflection. This concept contrasts with the measurable time tracked by clocks or solar revolutions. Within his 1907 work, L’Évolution créatrice, Bergson argues that the most fruitful philosophical systems originate in intuition. He utilizes this method to challenge the rationalistic biology of the late nineteenth century, arguing that life's fluid nature escapes a purely rationalist account. In an argument against determinism, he suggests that predicting another person's life requires following their experiences and voluntary acts to achieve a state of identity with them.

sections.heading: Philosophical methods and explorations of consciousness
sections.body: Bergson used introspection to explore what he regarded as a deeper self, associated with freedom and creative change. Time and Free Will (1889) introduced this approach, which he developed further in An Introduction to Metaphysics (1903). Matter and Memory (1896) examined consciousness and the relationship between mind and body, giving memory an important role in freedom of choice. His interests also extended to art: Laughter (1900) presented a theory of comedy within a wider discussion of aesthetics. Essays appeared in Mind-Energy in 1919. His career continued after the Nobel award: The Two Sources of Morality and Religion (1932) considered the moral implications of his philosophy, and Thought and Motion (1934) collected further essays. Those later books extend the record of his thinking but were not available when the 1927 prize was decided.

terms.definition: A concept representing living time as a dynamic, continuous stream of qualitative changes that cannot be fixed or measured by clocks.
Examination of one’s own experience from within; Bergson used it to investigate consciousness and lived time.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Historical reports of malaria treatment
sections.body: In 1917 Wagner-Jauregg inoculated nine patients with general paralysis with blood carrying malaria. He chose a form whose fever could be treated with quinine, hoping the induced illness would improve the neurological condition. The 1927 presentation described subsequent use in thousands of patients and reported that about 30 percent had recovered sufficiently to work; some series claimed higher proportions. It also cited follow-up of 400 patients, with roughly 30 percent described as remaining well for two to ten years. These were historical treatment reports, not evidence that malaria was harmless or that fever cured mental illness generally. The intervention deliberately caused another infection in patients with a severe complication of syphilis. Modern treatment uses antibiotics rather than malaria inoculation.

sections.heading: Medical investigations into febrile treatments for psychoses
sections.body: Wagner-Jauregg investigated the effects of fever-producing diseases on psychiatric symptoms from 1887. He later tried tuberculin, introduced by Robert Koch in 1890, but this and related approaches did not produce satisfactory results. The later malaria experiments therefore followed earlier unsuccessful attempts; their reported benefit concerned general paralysis specifically. His research at Graz also examined goitre and associated developmental disorders. The Nobel biography credits his advice with helping prompt government provision of iodine-containing salt in affected areas. His career spanned neurological and psychiatric clinics in Graz and Vienna, including the institution at Steinhof. He also worked on the legal assessment of mental illness and helped formulate Austrian certification law. These activities show a broader medical career than the single treatment recognised by the prize.

terms.definition: A historical name for a severe form of neurosyphilis that damages the brain and can cause profound mental and physical deterioration.
Enlargement of the thyroid gland. Iodine deficiency is one possible cause, explaining the relevance of adding iodine to salt.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
CDC: Neurosyphilis, Ocular Syphilis, and Otosyphilis treatment guidance

sections.heading: Reorienting public opinion through education and organized advocacy
sections.body: The Nobel Committee’s presentation emphasized changing public opinion in France and Germany. It argued that diplomacy needed support from people willing to regard cooperation as an alternative to war. Buisson, an educational reformer, advocated public education as a means of opposing militarism and had attended the League of Peace and Liberty’s founding congress in 1867. He and fellow campaigners arranged exchanges between French and German peace supporters, and he personally joined a visit to Germany. Quidde worked to maintain cooperation among German peace organizations despite disagreements and wartime pressure. The speech credited his mediation with holding the movement together and increasing its support. The award thus recognized sustained public advocacy as well as work within organized peace movements.

sections.heading: Educational reforms and pacifist advocacy
sections.body: Buisson utilized his background in philosophy and literature to promote secularism and peace. While teaching in Switzerland, he participated in the Geneva congress that established the Ligue internationale de la paix et de la liberté. He authored works such as L’Abolition de la guerre par l’instruction to advocate for peace through instruction. In France, he collaborated on laws establishing compulsory, secular primary education and served as director of primary education. Additionally, he helped found the League of the Rights of Man to support justice following the Dreyfus Affair.

sections.heading: Ludwig Quidde’s historical research and political activism
sections.body: Quidde utilized his background in historical research, supported by Professor Weizsäcker, to edit medieval German Reichstag documents. His career shifted toward politics following the 1894 publication of Caligula: A Study of Imperial Insanity. He held various offices, including the Bavarian Assembly and the Weimar National Assembly, while leading organizations like the German Peace Society. His later advocacy included budgetary restrictions on armaments. After the Nobel award, he fled to Geneva in 1933, where he founded the Comité de secours aux pacifistes exilés to support political refugees from Nazi Germany.

terms.definition: An outlook that gives military power and methods a dominant role in political and social life.
Schooling organized independently of religious doctrine or denominational control, a central aim of Buisson’s reforms.
Agreed restrictions on military weapons or expenditure, proposed as one way to reduce the resources available for war.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of X-ray scattering and particle track visualization
sections.body: Compton studied the radiation scattered when X-rays of a well-defined wavelength struck matter. Part of the scattered radiation had a longer wavelength, with the change depending on scattering angle. The explanation linked the light quantum with a recoiling electron: the photon transferred energy and momentum, emerging with lower energy and therefore longer wavelength. Wilson’s separate contribution provided a way to see particle paths. Expansion of moist gas allowed droplets to form around ions left along charged-particle tracks. Photographs of these droplets recorded the paths of particles such as alpha particles and electrons. Together the methods connected quantitative measurements of radiation with visible evidence of particle interactions.

sections.heading: X-ray scattering and the coincidence method
sections.body: During his studies of X-ray scattering, Compton identified that incident radiation increases in wavelength when scattered by free electrons. This phenomenon implies that scattered quanta possess less energy than the original beam. To validate this, Compton and A.W. Simon utilized the coincidence method to demonstrate that recoil electrons and scattered photons appear simultaneously. Additionally, working with C.F. Hagenow, he identified total reflection and complete polarization of X-rays. These investigations into X-ray intensity and reflection helped researchers study the arrangement of atoms and electrons.

sections.heading: Development of the cloud chamber for particle observation
sections.body: Inspired by observing colored rings in mist, Wilson investigated how moisture condenses on nuclei within a dust-free air volume. His early experiments used X-rays to demonstrate that increased condensation resulted from ionization. By 1911, he successfully photographed individual electron, alpha-, and beta-particle tracks, with electron tracks appearing as cloud threads. After the 1927 prize, cloud chambers also helped demonstrate pair creation, annihilation and nuclear transformations. The instrument also facilitated the identification of Compton recoil electrons, confirming the reality of the Compton effect.

terms.definition: The change in a photon’s wavelength when it scatters from an electron and transfers energy and momentum to it.
A technique used to establish that individual scattered photons and recoil electrons appear at the same instant.
Small particles or ions in a gas that cause water vapor to form droplets during the condensation process.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Chemical relationships between sterols and various biological substances
sections.body: Windaus converted cholesterol into cholanic acid, a substance already obtained from bile acids, providing experimental evidence of a structural relationship. He also isolated several digitalis compounds and their components in pure form. Their chemistry linked these plant substances with cholesterol and bile acids, and with compounds studied in animal cardiac poisons. His work on ergosterol, found in yeast and ergot, connected this structural chemistry with nutrition. Ultraviolet irradiation transformed material containing ergosterol so that it acquired vitamin D activity and could counter rickets. The important point was a conversion: unchanged ergosterol was a precursor, not simply vitamin D under another name. These investigations used chemical transformations to identify relationships among substances whose biological roles otherwise seemed very different.

sections.heading: Chemical transformations of sterols and imidazole derivatives
sections.body: Windaus’s research went beyond sterols. With Knoop, he investigated reactions of ammonia with sugar while exploring possible routes to amino acids. The resulting imidazole compounds prompted further study of related chemical structures in proteins. This work helped clarify the structure of the amino acid histidine and led to research on histamine, a biologically active substance important in physiology and pharmacology. The Nobel biography also describes a separate programme on vitamin B1, using material supplied by I.G. Farben. Its emphasis was identifying the molecule’s chemical rings, rather than demonstrating that it shared the imidazole structure first suspected. The account covers a wider research career; the 1928 prize specifically recognised sterols and their connection with vitamins. Throughout, chemical experiments supplied evidence for proposed structures.

terms.definition: A precursor that can be converted into a vitamin; ergosterol is a precursor of vitamin D produced through ultraviolet irradiation.
A research approach where investigations begin with experimental observation rather than starting from theoretical deduction.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary transition from contemporary realism to medieval history
sections.body: Per Hallström’s presentation contrasted the women in Undset’s early contemporary fiction with the characters in her medieval novels. He read the earlier works as portrayals of people pursuing independence while facing isolation and difficult choices. In the historical novels, he praised the integration of individual lives with family, honour and religious obligations. Undset’s knowledge of the past, developed from childhood interests and historical study, supported this reconstruction. Hallström nevertheless recognised a difficulty: the emotional and psychological detail sometimes sounded modern, while medieval documents did not directly supply it. He defended the novelist’s freedom to imagine inner lives beyond the surviving record. His argument therefore concerned both the strength of Undset’s historical art and the boundary between documented history and imaginative interpretation.

sections.heading: Early professional life and literary beginnings
sections.body: Undset attended a commercial school in Christiania and then worked in an office for ten years, from seventeen to twenty-seven. Her first books, Fru Marte Oulie and Den lykkelige alder, appeared in 1907 and 1908 while she was still employed there. A scholarship later enabled travel in Germany and Italy. Her Catholic conversion in 1924 became important to her subsequent writing. The later biographical note describes some of that work as apologetic, meaning concerned with defending religious belief. Its examples include contemporary novels published after the prize: Gymnadenia in 1929 and Den trofaste hustru in 1936. Reflective and autobiographical volumes, including Etapper and Elleve aar, also appeared after 1928. These later works show how her career continued beyond the medieval novels honoured by the award.

terms.definition: The liberty of a poet to use intuitive human understanding to represent emotional truths, even when historical records are silent.
Writing that explains or defends a religious belief; in Undset’s later work, the term refers to her Catholic commitments.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental verification of typhus transmission via body lice
sections.body: Nicolle noticed that typhus transmission around hospital admissions was associated with patients and their clothing before bathing and changing. This suggested a carrier that could be removed even while the patient remained ill. Animal experiments allowed the idea to be tested. In 1909 he infected chimpanzees and then other monkeys using infected blood. His team subsequently showed that lice which had fed on infected animals could pass infection to healthy ones, establishing the body louse’s role as vector. Further work with guinea pigs revealed infection without obvious illness: some infected animals showed neither fever nor other apparent symptoms. Nicolle called this inapparent infection. It widened the investigation from visibly sick hosts to infections that could escape ordinary clinical observation.

sections.heading: Scientific contributions at the Pasteur Institute in Tunis
sections.body: Nicolle’s work at the Pasteur Institute in Tunis extended beyond epidemic typhus. The institute combined bacteriological investigation with production of vaccines and sera for the infectious-disease problems of its period. He studied infections including tick fever, scarlet fever, measles and influenza. He also cultivated Leishmania donovani and Leishmania tropica using artificial media, allowing these parasites to be investigated under laboratory conditions. Another line of work examined whether serum from people recovering from an infection could offer protection against typhus or measles. These investigations belonged to the developing experimental study of immunity. The Nobel biography also distinguishes louse-borne epidemic typhus from murine typhus transmitted by rat fleas. Identifying these different transmission routes helped separate illnesses that had previously been difficult to distinguish and directed prevention towards their respective carriers.

terms.definition: A form of infection where animals carry the germ without presenting any apparent symptoms or fever.
The liquid component obtained from the blood of someone recovering from an infection, studied for its potentially protective properties.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Application of electron streams in amplification and X-ray regulation
sections.body: The 1929 presentation for Richardson’s 1928 award illustrated thermionic emission through telephone amplifiers and X-ray equipment. In an amplifier, a weak electrical signal representing speech controls an electron current supplied by a heated filament. The larger varying current can preserve the pattern of the original signal. The speech described a long demonstration telephone route between Sweden and North America using many amplifiers, with words still clearly audible. A second example involved producing X-rays by directing fast electrons onto a solid target. A heated filament supplied a controllable electron source. These technologies were the work of many people. Richardson’s contribution was to investigate the emission process itself and establish a quantitative account of it. The presentation recalled years of testing alternative explanations, including the possibility that chemical reactions involving impurities were responsible for the observed effect.

sections.heading: Mathematical formulation of electron emission law
sections.body: Richardson began investigating electrical emission from heated bodies at Cambridge’s Cavendish Laboratory after graduating in 1900. In November 1901, he presented an early mathematical expression relating the saturation current to temperature. Its physical proposal was that negatively charged particles escaped from the hot metal itself. He continued investigating this account at Cambridge and, from 1906 to 1913, at Princeton, alongside work on photoelectric phenomena and the gyromagnetic effect. His books The Electron Theory of Matter and The Emission of Electricity from Hot Bodies appeared in 1914 and 1916. His interests later extended to soft X-rays and molecular hydrogen; the book Molecular Hydrogen and its Spectrum was published in 1934, after the Nobel award. This career connected the original temperature-dependent emission problem with a wider programme in electron and molecular physics.

terms.definition: A heated component that emits a stream of electrons used to facilitate signal amplification and regulate Röntgen ray intensity.
The current reached when the available emitted electrons are collected, so increasing the collecting field does not draw an additional supply from the source.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of sugar decomposition and phosphorization
sections.body: Harden and his colleagues separated yeast juice with a gelatin ultrafilter. Neither the material retained by the filter nor the liquid that passed through could sustain fermentation alone; mixing them restored activity. This showed that the fermenting system depended on cooperating components. The smaller, filter-passing component became known as cozymase. Harden also demonstrated the importance of phosphate: adding it affected fermentation and produced compounds containing both sugar and phosphate. Von Euler-Chelpin and his students further investigated these compounds and the role of cozymase. The 1929 presentation offered a developing interpretation of the reaction sequence. Its lasting experimental point was that cell-free fermentation required an interacting chemical system, which could be separated, recombined and analysed.

sections.heading: Research into fermentation and enzyme chemistry
sections.body: Von Euler-Chelpin investigated the early stages of fermentation, particularly phosphate-containing intermediates and cozymase. Karl Myrbäck played a major part in the cozymase research, which helped clarify its composition and structure. Other collaborations examined enzymes including saccharase and catalase. Von Euler-Chelpin also began vitamin studies in the 1920s, working with colleagues including Paul Karrer and Margareta Rydbom. His broader research programme continued beyond the prize: the volumes of Chemie der Enzyme appeared between 1925 and 1934. The Nobel biography describes this as an important synthesis of enzymology. Research at his Stockholm institute also applied enzyme chemistry to blood serum and heredity, extending the methods beyond the original fermentation problem.

sections.heading: Harden's research on glucose breakdown and metabolism
sections.body: While serving as chemist for the British Institute of Preventive Medicine, Harden investigated the chemical action of bacteria and alcoholic fermentation. He studied how glucose breaks down and explored the chemistry within yeast cells. His long-term research into sugar fermentation by yeast juice contributed to understanding intermediary metabolism across all living forms. Beyond fermentation, he published papers regarding the occurrence of antineuritic and antiscorbutic vitamins in various food and drink products, applying his chemical expertise to these biological phenomena.

terms.definition: A sugar molecule carrying one or more phosphate groups, an important type of intermediate investigated in fermentation chemistry.
The study of enzymes, including their properties, actions and roles in sequences of chemical reactions.
The series of chemical processes and breakdown products occurring within living forms, studied through investigations into glucose and fermentation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The development of the German realistic novel
sections.body: The 1929 presentation positioned Buddenbrooks within a European tradition of realistic fiction associated with writers such as Dickens, Balzac and Tolstoy. Its assertion that Mann filled a gap in German literature was the speaker’s critical judgement. Published in 1901, the novel follows a merchant family through generational change. The speech read that change as a movement from practical self-confidence towards sensitivity, reflection and uncertainty. It praised the combination of social observation with an interest in experiences that ordinary realism might struggle to express. Schopenhauer and Nietzsche belonged to Mann’s intellectual background, while music supplied an important means of revealing his characters’ inner lives. In this interpretation, the family narrative connected public circumstances with private tensions between commercial existence, aesthetic experience and philosophical questioning. The award’s emphasis on the novel reflected this perceived combination of breadth and depth.

sections.heading: Literary development and diverse prose works
sections.body: In his autobiography, Mann described a largely self-directed education after an unhappy experience of school in Lübeck. Following a period as an insurance clerk, he attended university lectures in history, economics, art history, and literature to prepare for journalism. His early bibliography includes the short story collection Der kleine Herr Friedemann and the volume Tristan, which contains the novella Tonio Kroger. He also composed the Renaissance dialogues known as Fiorenza. During wartime, his intellectual self-inquiry resulted in the 1918 publication of Reflections of an Unpolitical Man. After the award, he published Joseph and his Brothers (1933–1943), drawing on Old Testament narratives, and Doctor Faustus (1947), which connects an artist’s destructive fate with Germany’s catastrophe.

terms.definition: Fiction that closely represents recognisable people, settings and social conditions, often linking individual experience with a wider society.
A novel of formation or education, tracing a central character’s intellectual, moral or personal development.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental investigations into polyneuritis and growth requirements
sections.body: Eijkman investigated a nerve disease in chickens resembling human beriberi. The protection associated with rice bran initially led him to propose that it neutralized a poison. His successor, Grijns, clarified the alternative: food must supply substances needed by the body. Hopkins approached nutrition through controlled feeding. Young rats stopped growing on purified starch, lard, casein and necessary salts. Adding only two or three millilitres of milk daily restored growth, although it contributed little energy. Even incompletely purified casein could supply enough of the missing substances to support some growth. These experiments showed why removing apparently minor food components could make an otherwise adequate diet fail.

sections.heading: Eijkman's investigations into beriberi and bacterial growth
sections.body: At Batavia’s Medical Laboratory, Eijkman connected protection against beriberi-like illness with material in the outer layers of rice. His later work at Utrecht extended into bacteriology. He developed a fermentation test using coli bacteria as an indicator of faecal contamination in water. He also investigated how bacteria died under different external conditions, questioning a simple logarithmic description of those experiments. In separate studies he examined how bacterial growth on solid media slowed and eventually stopped. Applying Beyerinck’s auxanographic method, he studied enzymes that broke down casein or affected red blood cells, and demonstrated fat breakdown by lipases. These investigations formed part of his broader work on laboratory methods and public hygiene.

sections.heading: Biochemical research and analytical developments at Cambridge
sections.body: At Cambridge, Hopkins developed the chemical aspects of physiology within the Balfour Laboratory before moving to the Sir William Dunn Institute of Biochemistry. His analytical contributions included a new colour reaction for lactic acid and methods for isolating tryptophan and identifying its structure. He also isolated glutathione, demonstrating it is a tripeptide composed of glutamic acid, glycine, and cysteine. He also studied xanthine oxidase, an enzyme involved in converting xanthine and hypoxanthine to uric acid. This returned him to a subject of earlier research: in 1891 he had published a method for measuring uric acid in urine.

terms.definition: The historical name for the protective dietary factor associated with beriberi, later identified as vitamin B1.
An enzyme that breaks down fats through hydrolysis, a chemical reaction involving water.
The study of the chemical substances and reactions involved in living organisms.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Expansion of the international war outlawry movement
sections.body: The movement to proclaim war illegal and label it a crime gained significant momentum in the United States following the First World War. While the concept of the outlawry of war was promoted by Salmon O. Levinson, the U.S. Secretary of State transformed a bilateral proposal into a global initiative. Following a 1927 draft treaty from France regarding perpetual friendship and the renunciation of war as a national policy instrument, Kellogg proposed a broader arrangement. He sought to concert with the French government to conclude a treaty involving the world's principal powers. This expanded framework aimed to invite signatures from all nations, focusing on the peaceful settlement of international disputes through collective condemnation of war.

sections.heading: From a bilateral proposal to the Pact of Paris
sections.body: Kellogg supported legal arbitration and arranged bilateral treaties with nineteen foreign countries. The Pact of Paris grew from a different proposal: Briand's 1927 open letter offered a Franco-American agreement renouncing war between the two nations. Kellogg proposed making the commitment multilateral, opening participation to other states. The pact eventually attracted sixty-four signatories and was officially proclaimed in 1929. This diplomacy formed part of a varied record as secretary of state. Disputes with Mexico over oil and land were addressed through legal rather than military means, while policy toward Nicaragua included armed intervention. The treaty therefore represented a particular effort to establish a general renunciation of war, rather than proof that all of Kellogg's diplomacy avoided force.

terms.definition: A movement and expression focused on making war illegal and designating it as a criminal act.
An agreement involving more than two states, as distinct from the original proposal for a treaty between France and the United States.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental validation of matter wave theory
sections.body: Professor C.W. Oseen explained that Louis de Broglie initially proposed his theory without supporting experimental facts. De Broglie predicted that electron streams passing through small holes in opaque screens would exhibit phenomena similar to light rays. While the original investigation differed from this specific setup, researchers utilized the way electron beams reflect off crystalline surfaces or penetrate thin sheets to provide evidence. These various methods produced results that substantiated the idea that matter possesses a wave nature. This discovery bridged the perceived gap between the world of light waves and the world of atoms and electrons, revealing a single universe where properties are explained by both wave and corpuscular theories.

sections.heading: The thesis Recherches sur la Théorie des Quanta
sections.body: In 1924, Louis de Broglie earned his doctorate at the Faculty of Sciences at Paris University by presenting a thesis titled Recherches sur la Théorie des Quanta. This work presented findings developed over approximately two years regarding quanta problems. His theoretical ideas later provided the foundation for wave mechanics, a theory that transformed atomic-scale physical knowledge. While his initial concepts caused astonishment due to their novelty, they were subsequently confirmed in 1927 through the discovery of electron diffraction by crystals by Davisson and Germer. Alongside his continuing research, de Broglie took up teaching and subsequently taught theoretical physics at the Institut Henri Poincaré in Paris. His academic career included managing various courses and guiding numerous doctoral students through research involving extensions of wave mechanics.

terms.definition: A concept asserting that a light ray is composed of small particles, or corpuscles, projected into space.
A formulation of quantum physics that describes particles through waves and their behavior, providing a framework for atomic-scale phenomena.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Chemical structure and synthesis of haemin
sections.body: Determining the internal chemical constitution of haemin presented a massive challenge due to its complex arrangement of over seventy atoms. Research involved analyzing how the molecule converts into iron-free porphyrins, which can further break down into pyrrole derivatives consisting of four carbon atoms and one nitrogen atom in a closed ring. Through this detailed examination of pyrroles and porphyrins, Fischer established the complete constitution of haemin and its decomposition products. He also investigated the shared chemical framework linking chlorophyll with blood pigments. His work connected the bile pigment bilirubin with blood pigments and demonstrated haemin in yeast. The prize presentation illustrated the wider reach of porphyrin chemistry with examples from bird feathers and eggshells.

sections.heading: Chemical investigations into pyrrole and pigment synthesis
sections.body: Fischer focused his scientific research on investigating the constitutive properties of pigments found in bile, leaves, and blood. His investigations specifically addressed the chemistry of pyrrole to facilitate the synthesis of natural pyrrole pigments. His investigations also connected the chemistry of bilirubin, a bile pigment, with that of blood pigments. His academic career included roles at the University of Innsbruck as a professor of medical chemistry and later at the Technische Hochschule in Munich as a professor of organic chemistry. Much of his research findings were documented through numerous papers published in scientific journals such as Hoppe-Seylers Zeitschrift für physiologische Chemie and Liebigs Annalen der Chemie. His laboratory achievements included the synthesis of haemin, which contributed to his 1930 Nobel Prize recognition.

terms.definition: Large ring-shaped molecules built from linked pyrrole units; related structures can bind metals, as iron does in the haem group.
A molecule with a five-membered ring containing four carbon atoms and one nitrogen atom, a building block in the pigments Fischer investigated.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary themes and notable works in Lewis's fiction
sections.body: Lewis utilized detailed observation to explore social dynamics and professional life. In Main Street, he depicts Gopher Prairie, a Minnesota town characterized by seasonal extremes and tensions between rural and urban needs. His novel Arrowsmith portrays the scientific journey of a researcher who faces delays in announcing discoveries due to continuous testing, eventually being preceded by a scientist at the Pasteur Institute. Through Elmer Gantry, Lewis employs somber satire to examine hypocrisy within religious structures. Additionally, his work Dodsworth follows an American character exploring his English ancestry. Erik Axel Karlfeldt’s prize presentation read these depictions of professions, social hierarchy and identity as examples of American literature examining its own society.

sections.heading: Development of a literary career through publishing and editing
sections.body: Before achieving international recognition, Lewis engaged in various roles within the publishing industry. In 1914 he was working as an editor for the George H. Doran Publishing Company, while simultaneously writing novels during his evenings. His professional background included several unromantic positions at a magazine, a newspaper syndicate, and two different publishing houses. These roles involved tasks such as reviewing books, writing catalogues, and reading manuscripts. He recalled that five novels published between 1914 and 1919 attracted little attention before Main Street challenged idealized images of American village life. This period of professional service in the city of letters preceded his 1930 Nobel Prize, following a sequence of notable publications including Babbitt, Arrowsmith, Mantrap, Elmer Gantry, The Man Who Knew Coolidge, and Dodsworth.

terms.definition: A characteristic of new American literature involving the examination of one's own nation through observant and critical writing.
A metaphor for the professional landscape of publishing, encompassing roles like editing, manuscript reading, and book advertising.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Classification and properties of human blood groups
sections.body: Landsteiner’s blood-mixing experiments revealed consistent differences between people. Serum from one person could cause another person’s red cells to clump. In 1901 he published a classification into three groups; von Decastello and Sturli subsequently identified a fourth. The resulting ABO system distinguishes cells carrying the A antigen, the B antigen, both or neither. Group O means absence of A and B, rather than absence of every blood-cell antigen. The relationship between these cell features and antibodies in serum explained why some mixtures reacted and others did not. It made an important source of transfusion incompatibility predictable. ABO grouping is one part of compatibility assessment, since other red-cell antigens can also matter. The 1930 presentation additionally described uses in studying inheritance and comparing blood samples, including stains, extending the discovery beyond transfusion medicine.

sections.heading: Immunological discoveries and blood group classification
sections.body: Landsteiner brought chemical methods to the study of immunity. In addition to blood grouping, he investigated antibodies, syphilis-related serological reactions and substances he called haptens. His research examined how chemical differences affected the specificity of immune reactions. Work in The Hague between 1919 and 1922 included protein conjugates and comparisons of haemoglobins from different animal species. After moving to the Rockefeller Institute in New York, he continued studying blood groups with collaborators including Philip Levine and Alexander Wiener. This wider programme extended the range of recognised blood-cell differences beyond the original ABO classification. Throughout his later career he investigated the chemistry of antigens and antibodies as well as their reactions. The contribution linked laboratory chemistry with the observation that apparently similar blood samples could behave very differently when mixed.

terms.definition: The clumping of red blood cells when antibodies react with matching antigens on their surfaces.
The study of blood serum and its reactions, particularly interactions involving antibodies and antigens.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Spiritual contributions to international peace efforts
sections.body: Presenting the award, Johan Ludwig Mowinckel argued that treaties needed support from people’s convictions and behaviour. He quoted Söderblom’s warning that the Kellogg Pact would be valuable only if actions matched its declarations. The speech developed this into an argument for churches using their influence to challenge acceptance of war. It also quoted Robert de Traz’s hope that churches would refuse to bless weapons in another conflict. That was an aspiration for their future conduct, not evidence that religious institutions had already secured peace. Mowinckel treated Söderblom’s contribution as adding moral and religious work to political, economic and legal efforts. His case for the award rested on changing attitudes as well as negotiating formal agreements.

sections.heading: Ecumenical efforts and religious scholarship
sections.body: Söderblom’s studies in Greek, Hebrew, Arabic and Latin supported his research in theology and religious history. As editor of the Student Missionary Association review from 1888, he published work at the beginning of a bibliography that eventually reached some 700 items. He later held university chairs at Uppsala and Leipzig. With colleagues and students at Uppsala, he encouraged comparative religion and study of Luther. His international church work culminated in the 1925 Stockholm conference, bringing together Anglican, Protestant and Orthodox participants; the Roman Catholic Church was not represented. His book Stockholm 1925 described the meeting. The conference sought common action for peace while addressing tensions between inward religious life and social responsibility. It pursued cooperation across divisions rather than achieving complete Christian unity.

terms.definition: The international agreement renouncing war as an instrument of national policy, whose practical effectiveness the presentation linked to public conduct and conviction.
A twentieth-century effort to promote unity among different Christian denominations through shared social action and religious cooperation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Discovery of the Raman effect through light scattering
sections.body: Raman’s investigation of scattered light revealed weak spectral lines absent from the incoming illumination. When he changed the frequency of that illumination, the new lines shifted with it, retaining characteristic frequency differences from the incident line. This pattern mattered because it linked the changes to the scattering substance rather than simply to the colour of the source. He found the effect in many substances. The quantum interpretation explained it through energy exchanged between light and matter: a scattered photon could emerge with a different energy, and therefore a different frequency. This added a process in which scattering changes photon energy to the familiar case where it does not. Measuring the shifts offered a way to investigate molecules through their interaction with light.

sections.heading: Scientific investigations in optics and acoustics
sections.body: Raman began research in optics and acoustics while studying at Presidency College in Madras. After joining the Indian Finance Department, he continued experiments at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science in Calcutta. His early publications examined sustained vibrations and musical instruments, including a 1918 study of the violin family. In 1922 he published work on molecular diffraction of light, beginning a series of investigations with collaborators that led to the 1928 scattering discovery. His interests continued after the Nobel award. Studies of light diffraction by ultrasonic and hypersonic sound waves appeared between 1934 and 1942. Later research also considered crystal dynamics and the optical properties of materials such as diamond, opal and pearls. These belong to the extended career, not the original prize-year record.

terms.definition: A phenomenon where scattered light contains new wavelengths different from the primary light source, discovered through studying molecular scattering.

terms.term: Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science
terms.definition: A scientific institution in Calcutta where Raman performed experimental research while serving in the Indian Finance Department.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Industrial advancements in high-pressure chemical methods
sections.body: Bosch’s work turned laboratory ammonia synthesis into industrial production. Making nitrogen and hydrogen react under demanding conditions required equipment that could withstand both high pressure and high temperature. The 1931 presentation stressed this engineering step between scientific demonstration and economical manufacture. Ammonia could then provide nitrogen in forms useful for fertilisers and other products. Bergius addressed a separate problem: adding hydrogen under pressure to coal and heavy carbon-rich materials to obtain liquid fuels. The presentation discussed applications to hard coal, lignite and petroleum processing, while also mentioning possible uses with wood-derived material. The shared award recognised the development of high-pressure chemical methods across these separate applications.

sections.heading: Development of high-pressure coal hydrogenation
sections.body: Bergius’s work with Nernst and Haber encouraged his interest in reactions under pressure. At Hanover in 1909 he developed practical laboratory methods for pressures up to 300 atmospheres. When university facilities became insufficient, he established a private laboratory in 1910 and expanded it with workshops and collaborators. Experiments in 1912–1913 investigated hydrogen’s action on coal and heavy oils. Turning these results into a practical process required much larger equipment and funding. A development plant was established at Rheinau near Mannheim. Bergius subsequently sought collaboration from German firms, Shell and British industrial groups. The scale and cost of this work made commercial organisation part of the technical challenge.

sections.heading: Industrial scaling of high-pressure ammonia synthesis
sections.body: After BASF acquired Haber’s ammonia process, Bosch led its development for industrial operation. The task involved more than enlarging a laboratory vessel. Equipment had to tolerate high pressure and temperature, while the feed gases needed economical production and purification. Bosch and his collaborators also replaced the original costly osmium and uranium catalysts with an iron-based catalyst containing suitable additives. They worked through progressively larger manufacturing units. The Oppau works began production in 1913, establishing a practical route to synthetic ammonia on an industrial scale. Further processing made the ammonia useful in agriculture and other industries. The achievement combined materials, apparatus, catalyst development and gas preparation within a production system.

terms.definition: A chemical process utilizing intense pressure and temperature to transform substances, such as nitrogen gas or carbon-bearing materials, into useful products.
A chemical process in which hydrogen is added to a substance; Bergius applied it to coal and heavy oils.
A chemical method involving extreme pressure and heat to transform substances, used here to produce ammonia and nitrogen fertilizers.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Linguistic character and lyrical development in Karlfeldt's poetry
sections.body: The 1931 presentation described Karlfeldt’s poetry as unusually dependent on the rhythm and weight of Swedish words. Its claim that translation could convey only part of his individuality was a critical assessment of his language. The speaker traced a career beginning with nature poetry in 1895 and developing through a relatively small, carefully selected body of verse. Fridolin served as a poetic alter ego, giving form to feelings, longing and humour without straightforward personal confession. Local landscapes and customs supplied concrete material, including harvest festivities associated with Pungmakarebo. The speech read this regional world as capable of expressing wider human experience. By the time of Hösthorn in 1927, it saw increasingly complex tensions within the poetry. This account emphasised both continuity with his home region and the artistic transformation of that inheritance.

sections.heading: Academic and Institutional Career of Erik Axel Karlfeldt
sections.body: Following his graduation from Västerås in 1885 and studies at Uppsala University, Karlfeldt held various instructional roles. He taught at a private grammar school in Djursholm and an adult education school in Molkom during the mid-1890s. His professional trajectory included five years at the Royal Library in Stockholm and a 1903 appointment as librarian for the Agricultural Academy. Within the Swedish Academy, he achieved significant administrative influence, becoming a member of the Nobel Institute and Nobel Committee before serving as permanent secretary starting in 1912. His literary output expanded through collections such as Vildmarks-och kärleksvisor, Fridolins visor, and Hösthorn. Additionally, his scholarly contributions included writing a life of the poet Lucidor and producing a necrologue for Carl Fredrik Dahlgren.

terms.definition: Poetry that gives concentrated expression to feelings, perceptions or a speaking voice, often with particular attention to rhythm and language.
A prestigious institution where Karlfeldt served as a member, Nobel Committee participant, and permanent secretary.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of intracellular combustion and metallic catalysis
sections.body: Warburg investigated cellular respiration through measurements made in living cells. The respiratory catalyst was present in very small quantities and difficult to isolate without destroying its activity, so he used indirect tests of its chemical behaviour. Compounds that interacted with iron affected the process, suggesting an iron-containing catalyst. Carbon monoxide inhibited respiration, but light could reverse the inhibition. Comparing the effects of different light wavelengths with the behaviour of carbon-monoxide compounds of related pigments gave a more specific chemical clue. Mathematical analysis of these responses supported the identification of an iron-containing respiratory pigment related to blood pigments. The work showed how a substance’s properties could be investigated inside a functioning biological system through controlled interference with its activity. This connection between quantitative measurement and chemical identification was central to the achievement recognised in 1931.

sections.heading: Chemical investigations into cellular oxidation and metabolism
sections.body: Warburg brought physical and chemical measurements to problems of living cells. His research ranged from carbon-dioxide assimilation in plants to tumour metabolism and the chemical components of respiration. This approach sought measurable reactions behind processes that could otherwise appear too complex for chemical analysis. After the respiratory-enzyme work recognised in 1931, he continued investigating how enzymes transfer hydrogen and participate in oxidation and reduction. Studies of flavins and nicotinamide identified important active components in these systems. They broadened the understanding of cellular chemistry without reducing all metabolism to one enzyme or one reaction. His institute in Berlin-Dahlem provided a setting for this sustained experimental programme. The different lines of work shared an interest in connecting biological activity with particular substances and quantitative changes.

terms.definition: A fundamental vital process where substances in or supplied to cells are broken down using oxygen to release energy.
Linked chemical processes involving the transfer of electrons; enzymes help organise such reactions within cells.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: American contributions to international peace efforts
sections.body: The 1931 presentation connected two different strands of American peace work. Addams encouraged women to act across national divisions, including at the 1915 congress in The Hague, where delegates came from countries on opposing sides of the war. Butler pursued institutional and financial support for international cooperation. He became president of the American branch of International Conciliation in 1907 and broadened its activities. He also helped persuade Andrew Carnegie to establish the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in 1910. The speaker praised the continuity and resources this gave the movement. Addams’s organising and Butler’s institution-building were distinct contributions, brought together by the committee’s hope of renewing public commitment to peace.

sections.heading: Jane Addams's social work and peace activism
sections.body: A visit to London’s Toynbee Hall helped Addams develop her plans for a settlement in Chicago. In 1889, she and Ellen Gates Starr leased the building that became Hull-House. It offered educational and social activities, including a kindergarten, art gallery, labour museum and public kitchen. Addams connected this local work with international activism. She published Newer Ideals of Peace and later led the Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom. Her opposition to American entry into the First World War brought public criticism. She nevertheless supported Herbert Hoover’s efforts to provide food relief to women and children in enemy countries. Peace and Bread in Time of War, published in 1922, reflected on this period.

sections.heading: Educational administration and international arbitration efforts
sections.body: Butler applied philosophical pedagogical theories by establishing an institute that became Teachers College. During his presidency of Columbia University from 1902 to 1945, he expanded graduate studies and professional schools like journalism and dentistry while significantly increasing student enrollment and faculty. His peace-related work included chairing the Lake Mohonk Conferences on International Arbitration from 1907 to 1912. Additionally, he led the American branch of International Conciliation and managed the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, where he founded a European branch in Paris and directed international education and communication.

terms.definition: Efforts to reduce conflicts between nations through communication, mutual understanding and peaceful agreement.
A community center established to provide educational, philanthropic, and social services to residents living in underprivileged urban districts.
A concept frequently spoken about by Butler regarding his advocacy for achieving world peace through global cooperation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of monomolecular gas adsorption
sections.body: Langmuir’s model proposed that surface atoms possess partially unsaturated residual valences directed outward. These forces bind gas particles at fixed points and distances, creating a monomolecular film. Experimental evidence supports this through hydrogen uptake on glass, where calculated atom counts match observed quantities. Additionally, using a sensitive micro-balance to measure air retained by gold during pressure transitions revealed a layer only one molecule thick. Further investigations involving electron bombardments and interference determinations showed that hydrogen atoms form regular patterns on nickel crystals, with spacing twice that of the nickel atoms. This research extends beyond gas-solid boundaries to include thin films between gases and liquids, as well as adsorption on liquid surfaces, utilizing oil film spreading to determine lateral pressure.

sections.heading: Research on vacuum phenomena and adsorbed films
sections.body: Langmuir investigated atomic and molecular mechanisms by studying vacuum phenomena, specifically examining electric discharges within high vacuums and low-pressure gases. His research into filaments in gases resulted in the discovery of atomic hydrogen and the invention of gas-filled incandescent lamps. He observed stable, monatomic adsorbed films on platinum and tungsten filaments, which helped him formulate a general theory regarding adsorbed films after conducting experiments with oil films on water. Additionally, he explored the catalytic properties of these films and investigated space charge effects. His interest in reaction mechanisms also led to studies concerning valence and structure, contributing to the development of the Lewis theory of shared electrons.

terms.definition: The accumulation of atoms or molecules at a surface; Langmuir investigated conditions under which a layer only one particle thick could form.
Stable layers of atoms or molecules that form on surfaces, such as monatomic layers observed on tungsten and platinum filaments.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Evolution of Galsworthy's Literary Focus and Trilogy Structures
sections.body: Galsworthy’s writing progressed from early short stories published as John Sinjohn to significant long-form narratives. The Island Pharisees targeted the egoism within England's ruling classes, while The Man of Property initiated his famous Forsyte Saga. This saga expanded fifteen years later with In Chancery and To Let, incorporating two short story interludes. He subsequently developed A Modern Comedy, a trilogy comprising The White Monkey, The Silver Spoon, and Swan Song, which utilized a similar structural format. His literary approach transitioned from radical social criticism toward a more objective, liberal appreciation of humanity. Through these works, he documented the oscillations of a family across three generations, illustrating how hereditary dispositions and social laws influence individual portraits within his expansive historical accounts.

sections.heading: Evolution of Galsworthy's dramatic and novelistic themes
