sections.body: Galsworthy utilized drama to address specific social grievances, such as the legal double standard between classes in The Silver Box and the conflict between capital and labour in Strife. His play Justice prompted prison reform in England. While his early novel The Man of Property offered harsh criticism of the upper middle classes, his later writing showed a shifting perspective. This change is visible through his evolving attitude toward Soames Forsyte within The Forsyte Saga. Beyond this series, he explored the impact of war in The Mob, depicting a statesman's voice lost to war-hungry masses, and examined family enmity in The Skin Game. His literary output also included various short stories and the collection On Forsyte Change.

terms.definition: A trilogy consisting of three novels and two short story interludes, following a structure similar to the Forsyte Saga.
A vast, continuous work of fiction, such as The Forsyte Saga, composed of multiple interconnected novels and interludes.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of Reflex Action and Nerve Impulse Transmission
sections.body: Sherrington investigated how sensory inputs, connecting neurons and motor outputs cooperate in reflexes. Adrian approached nervous activity through electrical recording. Radio amplifiers made weak signals large enough to study, but recordings from a whole nerve mixed activity from many fibres: their electrical contributions could reinforce or cancel one another in the record. Isolating a single fibre made the pattern clearer. In experiments involving stretched muscle, stronger stimulation increased the frequency of impulses rather than simply increasing each impulse’s size. Additional fibres could also become active. These observations connected the all-or-none behaviour of individual nerve impulses with the nervous system’s ability to represent differing stimulus intensities.

sections.heading: Electrical methods for measuring nerve impulses
sections.body: Adrian used electronic amplification, a capillary electrometer and a cathode-ray tube to detect very small electrical signals. Thermionic valves amplified recorded impulses by about 5,000 times. A preparation linking a single sensory ending in frog muscle to its nerve fibre made it possible to examine individual impulses. His wider recordings studied responses to muscle tension, pressure, touch, hair movement and needle pricks. By 1928 he described a pattern of adaptation: a sustained stimulus initially produced frequent impulses, followed by a declining rate as stimulation continued. The size of the individual impulses remained approximately constant. The changing frequency therefore provided information that a measurement of impulse size alone would miss.

sections.heading: Sherrington's research on spinal reflexes and muscle innervation
sections.body: Sherrington investigated spinal reflexes and the nerves supplying muscles. This required distinguishing sensory fibres carrying information from the muscle toward the central nervous system from motor fibres carrying commands outward. At Liverpool, he studied pairs of muscles that produce opposing movements. Reflex inhibition helped explain coordination: activity in one muscle could accompany reduced activation of its antagonist. He also examined connections between the brain and spinal cord through the pyramidal tract. His 1906 book The Integrative Action of the Nervous System, based on his Silliman Lectures at Yale, brought together this work on how individual nervous elements cooperate in organized behaviour.

terms.definition: Nerve cells that receive and transmit signals through their cell bodies and processes, including axons and dendrites.
Vacuum-tube electronic components that can amplify small electrical signals, making nerve activity easier to record.
Reduction of neural activity within a reflex pathway, helping coordinate responses such as relaxing a muscle that opposes a movement.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
The Physiological Society: Sherrington’s work on sensory innervation, 75th anniversary volume, printed p. 51

sections.heading: Foundations of Heisenberg's quantum mechanics
sections.body: Heisenberg developed his version of quantum mechanics by focusing on physical quantities that allow for direct observation. His method involves finding laws that link these observable quantities together, a process that includes establishing a rule regarding the relationship between an electron's velocity and its position coordinate. By incorporating Planck’s constant into these calculations, he created a framework applicable to electrons, atoms, and molecules. This approach enabled the systemization of atomic spectra and led to the prediction that hydrogen molecules exist in two distinct forms. His theoretical work has been applied by himself and other researchers to study the properties of atomic and molecular spectra, yielding results that align with experimental research findings.

sections.heading: Foundations of Quantum Mechanics and Matrix Theory
sections.body: Heisenberg’s 1925 approach began with observable quantities associated with atomic radiation rather than assumed paths of orbiting electrons. Mechanical quantities such as position and velocity came to be represented by matrices, allowing a new form of calculation. The method helped explain atomic and molecular behaviour and predicted two forms of molecular hydrogen, a result highlighted in the Nobel award. Heisenberg subsequently formulated the uncertainty relation: position and momentum cannot both be specified with arbitrarily small uncertainty. This is a limitation built into quantum mechanics, rather than simply a defect in laboratory instruments. Moving from imagined electron orbits to mathematical relations between observable quantities was central to the change in how physicists described atoms.

terms.definition: A framework for describing matter and radiation at atomic scales, including the discrete energies and probabilistic behaviour of quantum systems.
Rectangular arrays of numbers that can represent physical quantities and their mathematical relationships in quantum mechanics.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary traditions and realistic depictions in Bunin's prose
sections.body: The prize presentation placed Bunin within nineteenth-century Russian literary traditions. It praised his depictions of nature, memories of old estates and restrained prose. The Village (1910) attracted fierce discussion because its bleak rural world challenged idealized accounts of the peasantry associated with Slavophile thinking. In later works such as Mitya’s Love, psychological observation and sensory impressions became central to the depiction of intense young emotions. The Well of Days drew on autobiographical material while broadening its portrait of Russian life. The Academy’s speaker contrasted Bunin’s independence with contemporary literary movements, including symbolism and futurism. That comparison expressed a critical judgment about his work’s place in literary history, rather than a rule that realistic writing must reject artistic experimentation.

sections.heading: Literary genres and academic recognition
sections.body: Bunin’s autobiographical account describes a career in poetry, prose and translation from English. He grouped his published writing into volumes of original poems, two volumes of translations and ten of prose. His short fiction included The Gentleman from San Francisco, while The Village contributed to his wider reputation. Recognition included the Russian Academy’s Pushkin Prize and election as an honorary member in 1909. Bunin emphasized his independence from organized literary schools, saying that he did not identify as a decadent, symbolist, romantic or naturalist. He also described a life spent largely in the countryside and travelling. These statements explain how he presented his own career and artistic position alongside the Academy’s assessment of his prose.

terms.definition: A literary approach emphasizing plausible characters, everyday conditions and specific social or psychological detail.
A literary prize awarded by the Russian Academy of Sciences; Bunin received it before his Nobel award.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Integration of microscopic and statistical methods in heredity
sections.body: Morgan’s research group connected statistical breeding results with the behaviour of chromosomes seen under the microscope. Genes did not always assort independently: some traits tended to be inherited together. The group interpreted these associations as linkage between genes on the same chromosome. Crossing-over could break such associations through exchange between corresponding chromosomes. Comparing inheritance patterns then made it possible to infer the relative order of genes along a chromosome. The resulting genetic maps were deductions from breeding data, rather than direct pictures of individual genes. The 1933 presentation emphasised that later microscopic observations supported the chromosome interpretation. It also described the correspondence between linkage groups and chromosomes: a group of linked genes could be associated with a particular chromosome type. Together, these findings extended Mendelian analysis into a physical account of how hereditary factors were organised and transmitted.

sections.heading: Genetic discoveries through Drosophila analysis
sections.body: At Columbia, Morgan and his colleagues used large breeding populations of fruit flies to investigate inheritance. White eyes provided a striking example of a trait whose transmission was associated with sex. Other mutations supplied further markers, allowing many combinations of traits to be followed across generations. The work connected patterns previously called coupling and repulsion with a single underlying phenomenon, linkage. Large numbers of offspring were important because the frequency of different combinations could reveal relationships that isolated examples could not. The group’s interpretation developed into a linear arrangement of genes on chromosomes. The Mechanism of Mendelian Heredity, published in 1915, was a joint book by Morgan, Alfred Sturtevant, Hermann Muller and Calvin Bridges. It brought together experimental results and their chromosome-based explanation, helping make the research programme accessible beyond the laboratory.

terms.definition: An inferred order and relative spacing of genes on a chromosome, constructed from how often their inherited associations are broken by recombination.
The tendency of genes on the same chromosome to be inherited together, although recombination can separate their associations.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
The Mechanism of Mendelian Heredity — University of Pennsylvania library catalogue

sections.heading: Educational role in shaping international public opinion
sections.body: Acting as an educator of public opinion, Angell utilized journalism and lectures to promote peace reforms. His early work, Patriotism under Three Flags, addressed South African War issues, while Europe’s Optical Illusion gained significant fame through the influence of Lord Esher. In his expanded text, The Great Illusion, he argued that war provides no economic advantage and is an ineffective method for resolving disputes. He specifically criticized imposing war indemnities, noting that such payments are unpayable unless accepted as imports. To spread these concepts, the Garton Foundation funded research and publications regarding his ideas. Angell also contributed to the development of the League of Nations plan through contact with President Wilson and later studied social psychology problems.

sections.heading: Intellectual influences and early political writings
sections.body: Angell's political perspectives were shaped by observing various nationalistic sentiments, including French chauvinism during the Dreyfus affair and British jingoism in the Boer War. These experiences led to his 1903 publication, Patriotism under Three Flags: A Plea for Rationalism in Politics. His later works utilized diverse methods to communicate complex ideas; for instance, in The Money Game, he created a specific card game designed to make currency issues visual. He also addressed the necessity of educating common citizens within The Unseen Assassins. Beyond his books, Angell contributed to international discourse through roles in organizations like the World Committee against War and Fascism and by editing Foreign Affairs between 1928 and 1931.

terms.definition: A payment demanded from a defeated state. Angell questioned how a victor could benefit while also restricting the defeated country’s exports.
A theory suggesting that military power provides no commercial advantage and that nations cannot enrich themselves by subjugating others.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Foundations and developments in modern atomic physics
sections.body: Schrödinger’s wave equation made it possible to calculate allowed atomic energies rather than simply postulate electron orbits. In bound systems, suitable solutions occurred at particular energy values, with Planck’s constant setting the quantum scale. The theory was applied to optical phenomena and to atoms in electric or magnetic fields. Dirac developed a relativistic quantum theory of the electron. Its interpretation led to the prediction of a particle with the electron’s mass and an electric charge equal in magnitude but opposite in sign: the positron. The award recognised two distinct mathematical advances in atomic theory.

sections.heading: Mathematical developments in quantum mechanics and relativity
sections.body: Dirac independently developed a noncommutative algebra for calculating atomic properties after Heisenberg introduced his quantum mechanics. His relativistic electron theory followed in 1928, combining quantum mechanics with special relativity. Subsequent interpretation led to the prediction of a positively charged counterpart to the electron, with the same mass and equal but opposite charge. Anderson discovered the positron experimentally in 1932; Blackett and Occhialini supplied further evidence through particle-pair phenomena in 1933. These experimental achievements were distinct from Dirac’s mathematical prediction. His publications included papers in the Proceedings of the Royal Society and the book The Principles of Quantum Mechanics.

sections.heading: Schrödinger's development of the wave equation
sections.body: During his time at the University of Zurich, Schrödinger focused on various theoretical physics subjects, including thermodynamics and atomic spectra. Driven by dissatisfaction with Bohr’s orbit theory, he sought to determine atomic spectra through an eigenvalue problem. This approach led to his 1926 discovery of the wave equation. His earlier studies involved mastering eigenvalue problems in continuous media while at the University of Vienna. Although he later attempted to establish a theory using only waves, this pursuit caused controversy with other physicists regarding the standard dual wave-particle description.

terms.definition: A photon: a quantum of light whose energy equals Planck’s constant multiplied by its frequency.
An algebra in which reversing the order of multiplication can change the result, unlike multiplication of ordinary numbers.
A mathematical problem seeking particular values, such as energies, for which an equation has nonzero solutions satisfying specified conditions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Isotope separation through liquid hydrogen distillation
sections.body: Urey calculated that a heavier form of hydrogen should be less volatile than ordinary hydrogen, suggesting a way to concentrate it by distilling the liquid. He lacked the necessary low-temperature apparatus, so he asked Ferdinand Brickwedde at the Bureau of Standards to prepare the sample. Urey and George Murphy worked on predicting the heavier isotope’s spectrum. Spectroscopic examination of the concentrated sample established its presence, and the result was published in January 1932. The 1934 presentation then considered the consequences of replacing ordinary hydrogen with deuterium. Heavy water has a greater density and a higher freezing point than ordinary water, and reactions involving the two forms can proceed at different rates. Gilbert Lewis and colleagues produced pure heavy water in 1933. The discovery therefore opened a way to compare chemically related substances whose hydrogen atoms differed greatly in mass.

sections.heading: Methods for concentrating heavy hydrogen isotopes
sections.body: During his research into atomic structure and diatomic gases, Urey developed a specific technique to concentrate potential heavy hydrogen isotopes. This process involved the fractional distillation of liquid hydrogen, which facilitated the discovery of deuterium. Following this achievement, Urey collaborated with E.W. Washburn to evolve an electrolytic method designed for separating hydrogen isotopes. His investigations extended to analyzing the vapor pressure of both hydrogen and deuterium, alongside studying equilibrium constants of exchange reactions. These chemical studies contributed to his broader work on molecular structures and atomic properties. After the award, he moved to Chicago in 1945 and later investigated planetary origins and the chemical history of Earth.

terms.definition: Variations of elements that possess different atomic weights but share similar chemical properties.
Separation based on differences in volatility; Urey applied the method to concentrate the heavier component of liquid hydrogen.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary output and thematic focus
sections.body: Pirandello worked across short fiction, novels and drama. His Novelle per un anno assembled stories with varied settings and tones, while Si gira examined a world shaped by mechanisation and cinema. The 1934 presentation treated these prose works as a background to his theatrical experiments. It emphasised his ability to turn psychological uncertainty into action on stage. In its reading of Henry IV, identity becomes a struggle against the passage of time. The speaker also explored the title Maschere nude, or Naked Masks, used for Pirandello’s collected plays. A social identity could act as a covering through which an elusive person was seen, while dramatic analysis exposed contradictions beneath it. The account traced these ideas to images and situations drawn from life, showing how theatrical characters could sustain competing perceptions without resolving into a single stable self.

sections.heading: Literary themes and prolific written works
sections.body: Pirandello produced a vast quantity of literature, including the fifteen-volume collection Novelle per un anno and several notable novels such as Il fu Mattia Pascal and Uno, nessuno e centomila. His dramatic works, published under the title Maschere nude, frequently explore the tension between illusion and reality. In plays like Enrico IV, characters experience a confusion of imagination and reality, while Vestire gli ignudi depicts a protagonist losing various identities. His essay L’Umorismo outlines fundamental attitudes found throughout his dramas. These writings often examine how individuals navigate contradictory perceptions held by others or struggle with the dissolution of a unified self through changing social facets.

terms.definition: Naked Masks, the title of Pirandello’s collected plays; the presentation connected it with the unstable identities through which people appear to themselves and others.
An early essay by Pirandello containing fundamental attitudes expressed throughout his various dramatic works.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental foundations of liver therapy for anaemia
sections.body: Whipple investigated blood regeneration in dogs after controlled blood loss. Different foods affected recovery differently even when their calorie contribution was comparable. These experiments encouraged Minot and Murphy to test a liver-rich diet in people with pernicious anaemia in 1926. The improvement in blood formation pointed towards a useful substance in liver, although these experiments did not identify it chemically. Their work connected dietary investigation with a clinical problem that had previously been extremely difficult to treat. The 1934 presentation also recognised the treatment’s practical burden: patients had to consume large quantities of liver. Subsequent work on extracts and the active factor grew from the need to understand the response and make treatment more manageable.

sections.heading: Development of liver therapy for pernicious anaemia
sections.body: Following Whipple's research on experimental anaemia in dogs, Minot and Murphy described a method using liver to treat pernicious anaemia in 1926. Minot later collaborated with Edwin J. Cohn to demonstrate that specific fractions of liver substance were effective. His investigations also included studying blood coagulation, platelets, and reticulocytes. He utilized reticulocyte reactions to evaluate therapeutic procedures and explored the impact of dietary deficiencies on conditions like alcoholic polyneuritis. These studies contributed to understanding gastro-intestinal functions and iron therapy for various blood disorders.

sections.heading: Medical methods for treating various types of anaemia
sections.body: Murphy’s clinical research addressed pernicious anaemia and other blood disorders, alongside investigations of diabetes. With Minot, he developed liver treatment for patients, drawing on the experimental background supplied by Whipple’s animal studies. He later used injected liver extracts and investigated their effects in several blood conditions. The Nobel biography records an American Medical Association bronze medal in 1934 for an exhibit of his anaemia-treatment methods. His book Anemia in Practice: Pernicious Anemia appeared in 1939, after the Nobel award. This programme followed the progression from a demanding dietary regimen towards preparations that could be administered more conveniently. It belongs to the historical development of treatment before the active vitamin factor was isolated.

terms.definition: The tissue within bones where new blood cells are formed; restoring normal blood formation was central to the liver-therapy results.
A change in the number of immature red blood cells, used to assess renewed blood-cell production during treatment.
A preparation made from liver, investigated historically as a means of delivering the substance responsible for the blood-forming response.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Diplomatic roles and the League of Nations Disarmament Conference
sections.body: Beyond his leadership in disarmament negotiations, Henderson held significant positions within international and domestic structures. In 1924, he served as a delegate to the League of Nations Assembly and participated in the Committee of Security and Disarmament. During this time, he was elected to the Committee of Twelve, where he helped draft protocols regarding security and sanctions. He maintained a specific policy stance that disarmament must be achieved prior to implementing decisions on sanctions. While serving as British foreign secretary starting in 1929, his capacity for international action grew. Even after the fall of the MacDonald government in 1931, which ended his tenure as foreign secretary, he continued presiding over the Disarmament Conference despite not being a member of the British delegation.

sections.heading: Diplomatic efforts regarding reparations and international protocols
sections.body: During his political career, Henderson addressed significant global issues through various diplomatic frameworks. As home secretary in 1924, he focused on implementing the Dawes Plan for German reparations and drafting the Geneva Protocol to settle international disputes via arbitration. While serving as foreign secretary starting in 1929, he managed several complex international developments. These included maneuvering the creditor nations and Germany toward accepting the Young Plan for reparations and coordinating with Briand to facilitate the evacuation of French troops from the Rhineland before the Versailles Treaty deadline. Additionally, his tenure involved restoring British diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union, and supporting the movement for Egyptian independence.

terms.definition: An intergovernmental organisation formed after the First World War to promote international cooperation and help settle disputes peacefully.
The 1924 League of Nations proposal linking arbitration, security and disarmament, which Henderson helped draft.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Synthesis of new radioactive elements via alpha particle bombardment
sections.body: The Joliot-Curies bombarded aluminium with alpha particles from polonium. The award presentation described polonium as a practical source because a usable quantity supplied intense radiation for the experiment. Only a tiny fraction of the incoming particles produced the required nuclear collision, so the researchers had to detect a small amount of newly formed material. Their product was a radioactive isotope of phosphorus: its nuclei had the same positive charge as ordinary phosphorus but a different mass. Artificial production made such short-lived substances available for investigation, even when researchers could not obtain useful quantities from natural sources.

sections.heading: Irène Joliot-Curie’s work before and after the discovery
sections.body: Irène Curie had studied radiation well before the joint discovery. During the First World War she worked as a nurse radiographer, and her 1925 doctoral thesis examined alpha rays from polonium. The 1934 work with Frédéric Joliot was summarized in their paper on artificially producing radioactive elements and chemically demonstrating transmutation. Her research continued after the 1935 award. The biography identifies her 1938 investigations of neutron action on heavy elements as an important step toward the discovery of uranium fission. These are distinct stages of her scientific career: earlier work with radiation, the joint artificial-radioactivity result, and subsequent studies of heavy nuclei.

sections.heading: Creation of isotopes through particle bombardment
sections.body: Beyond the aluminium experiments, alpha-particle bombardment of boron and magnesium produced other unstable nuclei. The biography lists nitrogen-13, phosphorus-30, silicon-27 and aluminium-28 among the isotopes obtained in this research. These products belonged to familiar chemical elements, but their unstable nuclei decayed after they had been made. Depending on the isotope, the decay involved the emission of positive or negative electrons. Producing several radioactive isotopes showed that the effect could be investigated across different starting materials. It expanded the study of radioactivity from naturally available sources to products created through controlled nuclear reactions.

terms.definition: An unstable form of an element with the same nuclear charge as its other isotopes but a different mass, which changes through radioactive decay.
The conversion of one chemical element into another through a change in its atomic nucleus.
Radioactivity produced by creating unstable atomic nuclei in an experiment, for example by bombarding a target with alpha particles.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of developmental mechanics and tissue transplantation
sections.body: Spemann’s laboratory used fine glass tools and hair loops to manipulate newt and frog embryos. Transplanting tissue tested whether its future role was already fixed. At suitable early stages, tissue normally destined to become skin on the embryo’s underside could instead develop as nervous tissue when placed in a different environment. In the crucial organizer experiments performed by Hilde Mangold in Spemann’s laboratory, a graft from the blastopore lip induced neighbouring host tissue to contribute to a second body axis. Differently coloured donor and host embryos helped distinguish the tissues’ contributions. The result was more than growth of the graft itself: it redirected surrounding cells. Further transplantation studies explored how early tissue regions influenced spinal cord, brain and other organ development.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of embryonic induction and organizer function
sections.body: Spemann utilized micro-surgical techniques on amphibian eggs to investigate how specific embryonic regions direct development. The organizer work, including Hilde Mangold’s crucial grafts, showed that transplanted tissue could induce additional embryonic structures. Further experiments showed that different regions could favour different structures, with anterior tissue tending toward head formation and posterior tissue toward tails. Spemann further observed that grafting tail organizers into a head region might result in heads due to environmental influences from the existing head organizer. Additionally, his experiments involving the transplantation of optic cups into abdominal layers showed they could induce eye lens production. These findings established the theory of embryonic induction, suggesting secondary organizers operate following initial primary induction, providing a foundation for modern experimental morphogenesis.

terms.definition: An experimental approach to embryology that tests causal relationships by manipulating developing cells and tissues.
An embryonic region that possesses the ability to induce neighboring cells to form organized, secondary body structures.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
University of Freiburg: the Spemann–Mangold discovery and Hilde Mangold’s transplantation experiments

sections.heading: Journalistic contributions to peace movements
sections.body: After serving as an ordinary soldier, the recipient transitioned from administrative roles to active journalism. He previously served as secretary for the German Peace Society, an organization led by Nobel laureate Mr. Quidde. Moving away from office work, he utilized newspapers and periodicals to promote his pacifist ideas through elegant and witty essays. His writing style often employed a sharp, rapier-like approach to cover various aspects of modern politics while focusing on peace. Beyond his written work, he was recognized as a gifted orator. His candidacy for this distinction gained significant momentum when six former Nobel Peace Prize recipients provided their support, demonstrating the international impact of his efforts to advocate for freedom of thought and expression.

sections.heading: Journalistic opposition to secret German rearmament
sections.body: As editor of Die Weltbühne, Ossietzky published material challenging unauthorized German military activity. A 1927 article by Berthold Jacob criticized the Reichswehr's tolerance of paramilitary organizations; Ossietzky, as the responsible editor, was convicted of libel. In 1929 he published Walter Kreiser's report as part of his campaign against secret rearmament in violation of the Treaty of Versailles. Charged with betraying military secrets, he was convicted in 1931 and sentenced to eighteen months in Spandau Prison. He was released after seven months in the Christmas amnesty of 1932. Earlier, as secretary of the German Peace Society, he had founded its monthly information bulletin and contributed under the name Thomas Murner to another periodical. These roles show how publication itself became a means of peace advocacy and a source of personal danger.

terms.definition: In this presentation, a commitment to free thought, intellectual debate, freedom of expression and respect for the achievements of other nations.
A publication where Ossietzky served as editor-in-chief, maintaining an editorial policy focused on exposing secret German rearmament.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental verification of the neutron's properties
sections.body: Chadwick tested whether the penetrating radiation emitted from bombarded beryllium was electromagnetic radiation or a stream of neutral particles. The Joliot-Curies had observed that this radiation expelled protons from hydrogen-containing materials such as paraffin. Treating it as gamma radiation required implausibly large energies. Chadwick instead calculated the energy transferred when neutral particles struck atomic nuclei and found agreement with the measurements. Charged particles could be traced in a cloud chamber; the neutron had to be inferred from its interactions. He also examined nuclear transformations, including the reaction of a helium nucleus with beryllium that produces carbon and a neutron. Comparing the masses involved helped establish that the neutron’s mass was close to that of the proton.

sections.heading: Nuclear transmutation and neutron properties
sections.body: Following his work in the Physical Laboratory in Manchester under Professor Rutherford, Chadwick moved to Cambridge's Cavendish Laboratory. There, he collaborated with Rutherford on transmuting light elements through alpha particle bombardment and investigated atomic nuclei structures. His 1932 discovery identified neutrons as particles lacking electrical charge. Unlike charged helium nuclei, these neutral particles do not face repulsion from the electric forces within heavy atoms. This characteristic makes them useful for inducing nuclear reactions and prepared the way for the later discovery of neutron-induced uranium fission. For this research, he received the 1932 Hughes Medal from the Royal Society before earning his Nobel Prize in Physics in 1935.

terms.definition: An electrically neutral particle found in atomic nuclei, with a mass close to that of a proton.
Directing helium nuclei, each containing two protons and two neutrons, at a material to investigate or change its atomic nuclei.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Methods for determining molecular structure and dipole moments
sections.body: Debye developed a theory to verify molecular models by analyzing how X-ray beams of specific wavelengths penetrate gases. By recording diffracted radiation through photography, scientists can check if an atom arrangement matches the observed intensity distribution to ascertain dimensions. He also established methods to calculate dipole moments, which involve measuring variations in density and insulating power relative to temperature. This theory applies strictly to diluted gases but also worked well for dilute solutions in non-polar solvents. These techniques allow researchers to treat groups of atoms or radicals as concentrated moments, similar to how forces act on a body. Such investigations into charge symmetry and electric field effects have helped elucidate the structures of thousands of organic and inorganic substances.

sections.heading: Academic career and institutional leadership
sections.body: Following his studies in electrical technology at the Aachen Institute of Technology, Debye held several significant academic positions across Europe. He served as a lecturer at Munich University and later became a professor of theoretical physics at Zurich University. His career included directing the Theoretical Department of the Physical Institute at the University of Göttingen and leading the entire institute. During his time in Germany, he managed the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics in Berlin-Dahlem. After the 1936 Nobel award, his career moved to the United States in 1940 when he joined Cornell University as a professor of chemistry and head of the chemistry department. He also contributed to scientific publishing by serving as the editor of Physikalische Zeitschrift for twenty-five years.

terms.definition: A measure of the separation of positive and negative charge, including its magnitude and direction; molecular shape affects the resulting moment.
A scientific journal for which Debye served as editor from 1915 until 1940.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Evolution of tragic dramatic techniques
sections.body: The presentation traced O’Neill’s development from short plays grounded in maritime experience towards larger tragic forms. It discussed Desire Under the Elms through its New England setting and Puritan inheritance. In Strange Interlude, characters speak thoughts and memories that other characters do not hear, giving the audience access to conflicts beneath ordinary dialogue. The speaker then interpreted Mourning Becomes Electra as a modern counterpart to Greek tragedy. In that reading, ideas about heredity and the unconscious helped supply the pressure once associated with fate. These were dramatic uses of contemporary hypotheses, not proof that those hypotheses explained human behaviour. The speech’s central argument was that O’Neill adapted inherited tragic effects through modern settings, psychology and carefully connected events.

sections.heading: Development of dramatic technique and psychological analysis
sections.body: O’Neill’s early experience included prospecting in Honduras, seafaring and short-lived jobs. He wrote Bound East for Cardiff in 1914 and then attended George Baker’s dramatic-technique course at Harvard. The Provincetown Players helped bring his early plays to audiences. His Nobel autobiography described this pre-award development, while a later biographical note added achievements that followed 1936. Those included The Iceman Cometh and the posthumous 1956 production of Long Day’s Journey into Night in Stockholm. The note also discussed A Touch of the Poet and More Stately Mansions as parts of an unfinished cycle. Hughie, mentioned alongside them, was a separate one-act play. Keeping these works and dates distinct makes clear how his later reputation extended beyond the career the Nobel committee had judged.

terms.definition: In the speech’s reading of O’Neill, an explanation of tragic fate through inherited traits and psychological causes rather than supernatural intervention.
Exploration of characters’ motives, memories and conflicts as a means of shaping dramatic action and relationships.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Chemical mechanisms of autonomic nervous system signaling
sections.body: The heart offered a clear example of opposing autonomic effects: sympathetic stimulation could accelerate its activity, while parasympathetic stimulation could slow it. Loewi’s experiments investigated whether chemicals carried these effects from nerves to the organ. The substance released during parasympathetic stimulation was difficult to study because blood and tissue rapidly broke it down. Loewi and Navratil found that physostigmine could inhibit this destruction, making detection easier. Further experiments identified the substance with acetylcholine. The work linked a physiological response to a particular messenger and showed why the messenger’s removal mattered as well as its release. It provided a method for investigating chemical transmission rather than merely comparing the effects of stimulating different nerves.

sections.heading: Pharmacological investigations into chemical transmission
sections.body: Dale conducted detailed research regarding the pharmacology of ergot alkaloids and investigated simpler incidental bases like histamine and tyramine. His studies on histamine contributed to understanding anaphylaxis and shock conditions. Additionally, he identified acetylcholine within specific ergot extracts. Through his work at the Wellcome Physiological Research Laboratories and the National Institute for Medical Research, he explored how these substances function. These investigations into chemical messengers provided a foundation for extending the discoveries made by Loewi regarding nerve impulse transmission.

sections.heading: Loewi's investigations into metabolism and nerve transmission
sections.body: Before his nerve-transmission experiments, Loewi investigated metabolism and kidney function. His 1902 work showed that animals could rebuild proteins from amino-acid breakdown products. He also studied carbohydrate metabolism and the effects of drugs on physiological processes. In London in 1902, he worked in Starling’s laboratory and met Henry Dale, beginning a friendship that preceded their shared Nobel award. Research in Vienna with Alfred Fröhlich examined the autonomic nervous system. They observed that cocaine enhanced certain responses to epinephrine and sympathetic stimulation. Loewi’s chemical-transmission experiments followed in 1921; work with colleagues over subsequent years identified the parasympathetic messenger as acetylcholine. This discovery emerged from a longer career linking pharmacology with organ function.

terms.definition: The part of the nervous system that regulates internal organs, including the heart, through sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways.
The study of the effects of chemical substances, such as alkaloids and histamine, on biological systems and physiological processes.
The parasympathetic substance that was later identified by Loewi as being acetylcholine during his research into nerve transmission.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The Argentine Antiwar Pact and international law
sections.body: Saavedra Lamas brought legal scholarship into diplomacy, criticising intervention in other countries’ affairs, particularly policies associated with the United States. As foreign minister, he developed the Antiwar Pact to broaden cooperation against war, including among countries outside the League of Nations. Six Latin American states signed it in Rio de Janeiro in October 1933, and the Montevideo conference endorsed it later that year. His parallel mediation efforts helped secure the 1935 cessation of hostilities between Bolivia and Paraguay. The presentation described provision for referring disputes over implementation to the Permanent Court of International Justice. Such a provision was a commitment about resolving future disagreements, not evidence that the court itself had negotiated or decided the peace settlement.

sections.heading: Scholarly contributions to labor legislation and international law
sections.body: Saavedra Lamas combined diplomacy with academic work in labour legislation and international law. He edited treatises on social and labour law, including the three-volume Código nacional del trabajo of 1933, and drafted legislation concerning workers in Argentina. His teaching career began at La Plata and extended to Buenos Aires, where he taught subjects including political economy and constitutional law. It spanned more than forty years overall, rather than belonging entirely to the period before his Nobel award. He supported the establishment of the International Labour Organization in 1919 and presided over its 1928 conference in Geneva. As minister of justice and education, he also promoted vocational and technical training. These activities connected legal scholarship with the institutions and practical needs of public administration.

terms.definition: The principle that states should not impose themselves on another country’s affairs; a central concern of Saavedra Lamas’s international legal writing.
Laws governing employment and the treatment of workers, including protections, rights and obligations in the workplace.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental investigations of cosmic radiation intensity and particle paths
sections.body: Hess’s balloon flights in 1911–1912 tested how ionisation changed with height. It initially decreased, then rose above about 1,000 metres. The 1936 presentation reported roughly twice the surface intensity at 5,000 metres. Later investigators used unmanned balloons carrying recording instruments and found still greater intensities higher in the atmosphere. Measurements at different latitudes also examined the influence of Earth’s magnetic field. Anderson approached the radiation through particle tracks in a cloud chamber. Improved equipment and further measurements allowed him to establish a positively charged counterpart of the electron in 1932. Track interpretation also required considering particles produced when incoming radiation interacted with the chamber or its walls.

sections.heading: Anderson's research into X-rays and cosmic-ray particles
sections.body: During his doctoral studies at the California Institute of Technology, Anderson investigated how X-rays eject photoelectrons from different gases. Working with Professor Millikan starting in 1930, he transitioned into cosmic-ray investigations. In 1933, alongside Dr. Neddermeyer, he obtained direct evidence that gamma rays from a radioactive source produce positrons when passing through matter. His subsequent research explored the energy loss of high-speed electrons moving through material and the energy distribution of cosmic-ray particles, with findings frequently published in The Physical Review and Science.

sections.heading: Experimental methods and publications of Victor Hess
sections.body: During his early career, Hess studied radioactivity under Professor von Schweidler at the Physical Institute in Vienna. His research between 1911 and 1913 was documented in the Proceedings of the Viennese Academy of Sciences. He authored several significant works, including studies on radium heat production and the electrical conductivity of the atmosphere. To further investigate cosmic rays, he established a specialized observation station at Hafelekar mountain near Innsbruck to monitor radiation intensity fluctuations.

terms.definition: Radiation produced when incoming radiation interacts with matter, rather than simply the original radiation passing through unchanged.
Electrons that are ejected from various gases following exposure to X-rays, as studied during Anderson's doctoral thesis research.
A station for measuring radiation from space and its effects; Hess established one at Hafelekar near Innsbruck.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Chemical structures of carbohydrates and vitamins
sections.body: Haworth and Karrer investigated the structures of different biologically important compounds. Carbohydrates include simple sugars and larger substances built from sugar units; their atoms are principally carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Establishing their composition was only a starting point: the atoms’ connections and spatial arrangement also needed explanation. Haworth’s work extended from carbohydrates to the structure of vitamin C. Karrer studied carotenoids, the pigments responsible for colours in plants such as carrots and peppers. This led to investigations of vitamin A obtained from fish-liver oil and clarification of its structure. His work on flavins also contributed to identifying vitamin B2. The shared award brought together these structural investigations across distinct classes of compounds.

sections.heading: Structural analysis of sugars and polysaccharides
sections.body: Haworth used chemically modified sugars to investigate their structures. Methylated derivatives helped reveal how atoms were connected and how sugar units were linked in larger molecules. By 1928, his work had clarified structures including maltose, lactose and raffinose, as well as ring arrangements in common sugars. He also studied sugar-derived lactones and related their structures to optical rotation, the effect of a substance on polarised light. For polysaccharides, determining chain length was another important problem. His methods helped establish basic structural features of starch, cellulose, glycogen, inulin and xylan. These investigations connected small sugar molecules with the much larger carbohydrate structures found in biological materials.

sections.heading: Chemical structure elucidation of carotenoids and vitamins
sections.body: Karrer’s early research involved complex metal compounds, but his most important investigations turned towards plant pigments. Work on carotenoids established a structural formula for beta-carotene in 1930 and connected some of these pigments with vitamin A formation in animals. This helped clarify the structure of vitamin A itself. He also investigated ascorbic acid and extended his research into flavins. The identification of lactoflavin contributed to separating distinct substances within what had initially been treated as a vitamin B complex. Across these studies, chemical structure linked substances obtained from plants, foods and tissues with their biological roles. The results depended on distinguishing related compounds rather than treating every coloured substance or every vitamin activity as chemically identical.

terms.definition: A class of compounds including sugars and substances built from sugar units, principally containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Modified compounds bearing methyl groups; Haworth used derivatives of sugars as tools for working out their structures.
A family of pigments; some, including beta-carotene, can be converted into vitamin A in animals.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Narrative structure and character analysis in Les Thibault
sections.body: The 1937 presentation read Les Thibault through a contrast between generations and between the two brothers Antoine and Jacques. It saw the father as an embodiment of an older bourgeois world. Antoine’s outlook expressed confidence in intellectual analysis alongside doubt about an individual’s power to change larger events. Jacques’s moral struggle took a different direction as Europe approached war in 1914. The speaker praised the detail with which Martin du Gard reconstructed the political atmosphere and the pressure of collective events on private lives. These were interpretations of the volumes available when the prize was awarded; the cycle’s final publication still lay ahead. Its broad cast and extended narrative made it possible to connect family experience with religious, social and political conflicts. The method gave historical catastrophe both a public setting and an intensely personal dimension.

sections.heading: Scholarly training and literary development
sections.body: Martin du Gard’s training at the École des Chartes as an archivist and palaeographer informed his attention to documents and historical detail. Jean Barois, published in 1913 and written largely as dialogue, examined a life divided between Catholic belief and a freethinking humanist outlook. His work also included the peasant farce Le Testament du Père Leleu. After service during the First World War, he concentrated on Les Thibault. Publication began in 1922 and continued until 1940, so the complete cycle extended beyond the 1937 Nobel award. The Summer 1914 volumes formed a major part of its treatment of the approach to war and Jacques Thibault’s response. Shorter works included the drama Un Taciturne and the village sketches collected in Vieille France, showing forms outside the large family chronicle.

terms.definition: An extended sequence of novels following connected characters and events across a broad span of life.
The study of historical handwriting and written documents, part of Martin du Gard’s scholarly training.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of biological oxidation and catalyst systems
sections.body: Szent-Györgyi and his colleagues developed methods for measuring organic acids during biological oxidation. They found that small quantities of certain acids could sustain oxidation without being depleted overall. The substances therefore appeared to take part in a regenerating system rather than simply serving as fuel. The 1937 presentation discussed oxaloacetic, malic, fumaric and succinic acids and their cooperation with specific proteins. It placed this work within an emerging picture of hydrogen transfer between nutrients and systems associated with oxygen. That account was a historical model of respiration, expressed in the terminology then available. Its central experimental contribution was to connect measurable intermediates with the reactions through which cells release energy, and to show that these substances could act repeatedly within the process.

sections.heading: Research into cellular respiration and organic acids
sections.body: During his early research at Groningen, Szent-Györgyi investigated the chemistry of cell respiration, describing how oxygen and hydrogen activation are interdependent. He made initial observations regarding polyphenol oxidase systems in plants and co-dehydrases. His studies on biological oxidation led to identifying the catalytic function of C4-dicarboxylic acids and investigating flavin compounds. Additionally, he demonstrated that a reducing substance exists within animal and plant tissues. By isolating ascorbic acid from adrenals, he later identified paprika as a significant source of this nutrient. These investigations into organic acids and oxidative processes provided essential insights into how specific chemical components facilitate the metabolic transformations necessary for life.

terms.definition: Interacting substances that help reactions proceed and are regenerated through the process, rather than being consumed as the fuel.
Organic acids containing four carbon atoms and two carboxyl groups; this group included several intermediates studied by Szent-Györgyi in biological oxidation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Promoting Disarmament and International Cooperation
sections.body: Cecil advocated a League of independent states and sought practical ways for them to act together against aggression. His campaigning combined support for disarmament with pressure for an effective international response to breaches of peace. The large public survey he helped organise returned about eleven and a half million questionnaires. The 1937 presentation reported roughly eleven million supporters of the League, ten million supporting economic sanctions and 6.78 million supporting military sanctions. The differing totals show that support for the institution did not imply identical views about every means of enforcement. Through the International Peace Campaign, Cecil also sought cooperation between existing organisations. Its programme called for disarmament and League machinery able to address international conditions that could lead to war. These were proposals for strengthening collective action, not evidence that the system had already prevented all aggression.

sections.heading: Development of international peace mechanisms
sections.body: Cecil’s commitment to global stability involved creating structured diplomatic tools. In 1916, he circulated a memorandum containing proposals for avoiding war, which he later described as an initial document behind official British advocacy of the League of Nations. During his tenure as minister of blockade from 1916 to 1918, he developed procedures intended to apply economic and commercial pressure against enemies. His efforts to promote the League included a five-week tour of the United States in 1923 to explain its functions to American audiences. Additionally, he co-founded the International Peace Campaign alongside a French jurist. Through various publications, such as his collection of lectures titled The Way of Peace, he continued to communicate his dedication to maintaining an international system for peace.

terms.definition: An arrangement in which states cooperate to respond to threats to peace or aggression against members.
A written statement setting out information, arguments or policy proposals for consideration.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Robert Cecil, Viscount Cecil of Chelwood — biography

sections.heading: Experimental verification of de Broglie's wave theory
sections.body: Beginning in 1922, Davisson and Kunsman investigated electron scattering using electron beams on crystal surfaces. While initial results were difficult to interpret due to apparatus challenges, Davisson and Germer later used a cubic nickel crystal to provide evidence for matter waves. Thomson independently confirmed this theory using high-velocity electrons passing through thin celluloid, gold, platinum, or aluminium films. By adjusting electron velocities, researchers can determine wavelengths and calculate distances between atomic planes, establishing a new method for investigating crystal structures similar to X-ray techniques.

sections.heading: Davisson's research and professional development
sections.body: Following his studies under Professor R.A. Millikan at the University of Chicago, Davisson held various academic positions at Purdue University and Princeton University. His doctoral thesis focused on thermal emission from alkaline earth salts. While working at Bell Telephone Laboratories, he conducted investigations between 1919 and 1929 alongside collaborators C.H. Kunsman and L.H. Germer. These efforts led to the discovery of electron diffraction. During the same period he also investigated thermionics and thermal radiation. From 1930 to 1937 he studied electron optics and its engineering applications.

sections.heading: Experimental methods for observing electron wave behavior
sections.body: During his tenure at the University of Aberdeen, George Paget Thomson conducted research regarding electrons passing through extremely thin metal films. These experiments demonstrated that electrons exhibit wave-like properties despite their particle nature. This established the possibility of electron diffraction, a process later utilized to investigate solid surfaces. While Thomson achieved these results through film transmission, C.J. Davisson reached similar conclusions using a different experimental approach at Bell Telephone Laboratories. Such findings confirmed that matter possesses dual characteristics during interaction with specific materials.

terms.definition: The wave behavior associated with particles such as electrons, whose diffraction patterns can test predictions about their wavelength.
The study of how electron beams can be guided and focused, in analogy with the manipulation of light in ordinary optics.
The wave-like interference of electrons that produces characteristic patterns when a beam interacts with the ordered atoms of a crystal.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Investigations into conjugated double bonds and polyene structures
sections.body: Kuhn investigated how chains of conjugated double bonds affected organic compounds. His group synthesized more than 300 substances to compare chemical structure with optical, electrical and magnetic properties. This work connected with studies of natural carotenoid pigments. Alongside independent research by Karrer and Rosenheim, Kuhn helped distinguish α-carotene from β-carotene; in 1933 he identified γ-carotene. Chromatography helped his group separate closely related pigments. Vitamin research presented similarly demanding purification problems. Kuhn and collaborators obtained about one gram of pure riboflavin from 5,300 litres of skimmed milk, and chemical breakdown and synthesis helped establish its structure. The prize account also covers investigations of vitamin B6 reported in 1938–39, undertaken with collaborators including Wendt, Andersag and Westphal.

sections.heading: Chemical investigations of polyenes and carotenoid structures
sections.body: During his research, Kuhn examined theoretical problems in organic chemistry, specifically focusing on the stereochemistry of aliphatic and aromatic compounds. He investigated the acidity of hydrocarbons alongside the syntheses of cumulenes and polyenes. His sustained study of compounds containing double bonds proved significant for understanding the chemical nature of carotenoids. Through this work, he identified eight new types of these substances and analyzed their constitution. His research also extended to studying flavins and the antidermatitis vitamin B6. These investigations into the constitution and color of various organic structures formed a central part of his scientific contributions described in the Nobel biography.

terms.definition: Alternating double and single bonds in a molecular chain or ring, an arrangement that affects properties such as light absorption.
Organic compounds containing more than one carbon–carbon double bond; extended conjugated polyenes are important in the chemistry of many pigments.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Thematic elements in Buck's literary works
sections.body: Buck utilized her experiences living among Chinese peasants to act as an interpreter for the West. In The Good Earth, she depicts Wang Lung, a character whose virtues stem from a deep connection to the soil. The narrative tracks his transformation from a simple farmer into a powerful lord, a shift that brings greed and domestic discord. Through characters like O’Lan, Buck highlights the difficult status of Chinese women. The Mother centres on an unnamed woman. Separately, The Exile portrays Buck’s own mother, Carie, whose resilience the prize presentation also praised. These stories examine how individuals navigate hardships, including famine, revolutions, and the tension between ancient traditions and modernizing forces within China.

sections.heading: Literary works and biographical developments
sections.body: Following her education at Randolph-Macon Woman’s College and earning an M.A. from Cornell University in 1926, Buck expanded her literary output beyond the Wang family trilogy. Her bibliography includes collections such as The First Wife and Other Stories and the translation of the Chinese novel Shui Hu Chuan, titled All Men are Brothers. She also composed biographical works regarding her parents, published as The Exile and Fighting Angel. After the 1938 award, her writing continued to explore encounters between East and West, extending to India and Korea. Her later activities also included political journalism and welfare work, including establishing Welcome House, Inc., an adoption agency for Asian-American children.

terms.definition: An extended narrative centred on rural life and the changing fortunes of farming people and their families.
A series of three related novels, specifically The Good Earth, Sons, and A House Divided, chronicling the Wang family.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of sinus-driven respiratory and blood pressure regulation
sections.body: Heymans and his collaborators changed the composition of blood supplied to the carotid sinus region, varying oxygen, carbon dioxide and acidity. The experiments showed that chemical changes there could stimulate breathing through nerve signals to the medulla. Cutting those nerves prevented the increased breathing seen with low oxygen in the experiment. Carbon dioxide, however, could act both through this reflex pathway and directly on the respiratory centre; the results did not make every breathing response dependent on the sinus nerves. Other experiments linked pressure changes in the region with blood pressure, heart rhythm and respiration. The carotid body, or glomus, was identified as containing receptors sensitive to blood chemistry. Together, these findings distinguished chemical sensing from pressure sensing while connecting both to automatic regulation.

sections.heading: Discovery of reflexogenic chemoreceptors in cardiovascular areas
sections.body: At the J. F. Heymans Institute, Heymans and his collaborators investigated how chemical sensing in the carotid and aortic regions affected breathing. Their work established reflex pathways linking changes in blood composition to respiratory control. The Nobel biography also describes a wider programme in circulation and pharmacology. It included studies of blood flow to the brain, nervous and kidney-related causes of high blood pressure, circulation during muscular exercise, and the survival or recovery of nervous centres after circulation stopped. These subjects belonged to a broad research career rather than being interchangeable descriptions of the prize-winning discovery. The particular achievement recognised in 1938 concerned the role of the carotid and aortic mechanisms in regulating respiration through sensory signals.

terms.definition: An automatic response carried through nerves from the carotid sinus region, where pressure and nearby chemical sensing can influence circulation and breathing.
Sensory receptors that detect chemical changes. Those studied by Heymans respond to blood chemistry and help trigger adjustments in breathing.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Organizational transition and the Nansen Office legacy
sections.body: The Nansen Office was created in 1930 after Fridtjof Nansen’s death. A separate High Commission for refugees coming from Germany was established in 1933. By the time of the 1938 award, these bodies operated from Geneva and London respectively. Both were due to close at the end of that year, but the need for refugee assistance was increasing rather than disappearing. The prize presentation explained that their functions would continue through a combined High Commission based in London. The reorganization was therefore intended to coordinate continuing work, even as the earlier institutions ended. The speech praised the Nansen Office for bringing practical administration together with humanitarian ambition, drawing a connection with Nansen’s own approach to refugee assistance.

sections.heading: Financial mechanisms and humanitarian operations of the Nansen Office
sections.body: The Nansen International Office for Refugees operated as an autonomous body under the League of Nations authority. To fund welfare and relief, the agency relied on private contributions, proceeds from refugee-aid stamps sold in Norway and France, and fees from Nansen Certificates. Beyond providing material assistance, the office managed large-scale resettlement projects, such as constructing villages for 40,000 Armenians in Syria and Lebanon and resettling 10,000 individuals in Erivan. The organization also facilitated the movement of Saar refugees to Paraguay after 1935. Despite these efforts, the agency faced significant challenges, including diminishing League administrative funding, the economic depression, and a growing number of refugees from Germany, Italy, and Spain. These difficulties persisted until the office's dissolution on December 31, 1938.

terms.definition: The process of merging two separate institutions into one single, coordinated High Commission to continue humanitarian activities.
A document used by eligible refugees in place of a national passport; fees associated with it also helped fund refugee assistance.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Nansen International Office for Refugees: mandate, Nansen certificates, relief and institutional limits

sections.heading: Neutron bombardment and isotope production
sections.body: Neutrons offered a new way to investigate nuclei because their lack of electric charge avoided the electrostatic repulsion faced by positively charged projectiles. Fermi and his colleagues found that neutron bombardment could make many materials radioactive. A nucleus might capture a neutron and become an unstable isotope, while other reactions could eject particles. Passing neutrons through water or paraffin often increased the observed activity. Collisions with hydrogen nuclei slowed the neutrons, and the probability of a reaction depended on their speed and the target substance. The presentation compared particularly strong responses at certain speeds with resonance. Researchers then used chemical separation and measurements of radioactive decay to distinguish the products. This was a programme of nuclear transformation and isotope production, rather than a claim that every irradiated nucleus split.

sections.heading: Nuclear transformations through neutron bombardment
sections.body: After Irène Curie and Frédéric Joliot demonstrated artificial radioactivity in 1934, Fermi investigated neutron-induced reactions across many elements. His team’s work revealed the importance of slow neutrons and led to studies of their absorption and diffusion. Papers in Ricerca Scientifica, the Proceedings of the Royal Society and other journals documented these investigations. They supplied methods and questions for later nuclear research, but the 1938 prize should not be read as recognising an already established explanation of nuclear fission. Following the identification of fission, Fermi investigated secondary neutron emission and the possibility of a chain reaction. This continued in the United States after he joined Columbia University in 1939. The later programme built on the neutron expertise recognised by the award.

terms.definition: A pronounced increase in a nuclear reaction’s probability at particular neutron energies, with the relevant energies depending on the target nucleus.
Statistical laws governing particles that are subject to Pauli’s exclusion principle, also known as fermions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Chemical structural analysis of sex hormones and terpenes
sections.body: In 1929, Butenandt, working in parallel with Edward Doisy, isolated crystalline folliculine from pregnant women's urine, later identified as oestrone. By utilizing spectral analysis and the cholesterol formula, he determined that oestrone and oestriol contain a phenanthrene core. He also achieved the synthesis of progesterone from cholesterol in 1939. Ruzicka and his collaborators applied experimental skill to determine the structures of polyterpenes and developed preparative methods for androsterone and testosterone. His work established technical synthesis pathways for these hormones, linking various organic substances like bile acids and sterols through shared chemical relationships.

sections.heading: Advancements in hormone isolation and chemical synthesis
sections.body: Butenandt isolated crystalline oestrone in 1929, independently of parallel work by Edward Doisy, and crystalline androsterone in 1931. His investigations also helped obtain pure progesterone in 1934. These isolated substances gave chemists material for investigating how related hormones differed in structure and biological activity. He studied their interrelationships and examined possible carcinogenic properties of some compounds. In 1935, Butenandt and Ruzicka independently achieved chemical preparation of testosterone, following its isolation from testicular material by Laqueur and colleagues. The important progression was from a biological effect observed in extracts towards identified compounds whose structures and transformations could be studied. This helped establish steroid-hormone chemistry as an experimental field.

sections.heading: Structural Elucidation of Terpenes and Alicyclic Ketones
sections.body: Research into higher terpenes involved the total syntheses of farnesol and nerolidol, alongside establishing the structure of jasmone. Investigations also corrected Tiemann’s irone formula and identified the structures of musk perfumes, specifically muscone and civetone. Through these efforts, Ruzicka and his team prepared a series of alicyclic ketones containing between 9 and over 30 carbon atoms. These ring-membered compounds were previously thought to be impossible to exist. His wider research programme benefited from industrial connections and later support from the Rockefeller Foundation.

terms.definition: A diverse group of higher terpenoids found in the vegetable kingdom that Ruzicka studied to understand complex organic structures.
An ovarian structure that produces progesterone and supplied material for early investigations of that hormone.
The study of non-aromatic carbon-ring compounds; Ruzicka showed that large rings occurred in natural musk substances.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary style and thematic focus of the laureate
sections.body: The Academy’s address praised Sillanpää’s economy of language and his attention to ordinary rural life. It made an explicit admission: the committee members had read him in translation and did not know Finnish. Their judgement concerned the qualities they could perceive through those translations. The speaker compared his handling of landscape with watercolour and music, metaphors for artistic effect rather than descriptions of another medium he used. His peasants’ connection with the land supplied a central subject, while small events could acquire significance through close observation. The address also turned from literature towards Finland’s situation in late 1939, praising the courage and endurance of its people. Keeping that public tribute separate from its reading of the fiction helps explain how the speech combined literary appreciation with the immediate historical moment.

sections.heading: Scientific training and early literary development
sections.body: Sillanpää pursued biology as his primary subject, engaging in intensive laboratory work that involved microscopic examination and detailed anatomical drawing. This period of study lasted five years before financial constraints forced him to return to his family's impoverished croft. His transition into professional writing began when he submitted a short story to a major city newspaper using a pseudonym. The piece achieved immediate front-page success, earning both a significant fee and recognition from the Helsinki literary community. This early achievement led to an offer from a prominent publisher, who offered a financial advance to support his future book production. His subsequent bibliography includes notable works such as The Maid Silja and the 1945 novel The Loveliness and Wretchedness of Human Life.

terms.definition: Descriptive language and comparisons that shape how a reader perceives a scene, character or experience.
The study of living organisms and their processes; Sillanpää’s training included laboratory observation and microscopy.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Research at IGEFA on streptococcal infections
sections.body: At the Elberfeld laboratories of I.G. Farben, Domagk directed animal experiments seeking compounds active against streptococcal infection. Chemists Josef Klarer and Fritz Mietzsch supplied preparations for testing, including compounds associated with dye chemistry. In experiments begun in December 1932, mice received a bacterial strain obtained from a patient with blood poisoning. Untreated controls died, while Prontosil-treated animals survived. Publication in 1935 prompted investigations in other countries. These helped establish that the sulphonamide part of Prontosil was central to its activity and encouraged the preparation of related drugs. The Nobel account also describes subsequent compounds, including work directed at pneumonia treatment. The advance came from combining chemical synthesis, controlled infection experiments and further investigation of the active component, rather than assuming a dye’s laboratory properties would predict its effect inside an animal.

sections.heading: Research on Prontosil rubrum at I.G. Farbenindustrie
sections.body: Domagk’s industrial laboratory programme tested chemicals against infection in animals. Prontosil rubrum, a red dye preparation, protected animals in experiments with bacteria including haemolytic streptococci. Its structure included a sulphanilamide component; sulphanilamide itself had been synthesised by Paul Gelmo in 1908. The important discovery concerned antibacterial action, not the first creation of that chemical substance. Domagk continued working with Klarer and Mietzsch on sulphonamides and also investigated quaternary ammonium compounds. His later career extended to tuberculosis chemotherapy, including thiosemicarbazones and isonicotinic acid hydrazide. Those later investigations followed the Prontosil work recognised by the 1939 prize. The programme illustrates how one successful treatment experiment could lead to further chemical variations and tests against other infections.

terms.definition: Treatment of disease using chemical agents; here the historical term refers to medicines investigated against infections.
A substance that acts against bacteria; effectiveness depends on the organism and the conditions in which it is used.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Advancements in particle acceleration and isotope production
sections.body: Lawrence and his collaborators developed cyclotrons into increasingly powerful sources of particles. A magnetic field kept ions turning while an alternating electric field accelerated them repeatedly, so their paths widened as they gained energy. The Nobel account reported alpha-particle energies of up to 38 million electronvolts in November 1939, substantially above those of natural alpha sources. Deuterons, the nuclei of heavy hydrogen, were also useful projectiles for inducing nuclear reactions. The resulting radioactive isotopes supplied material for further physical, biological and medical studies. This practical production capability was central to the award. The research was collective: the account stresses the many collaborators involved in enlarging and improving the machines. Lawrence and students also constructed a linear resonance accelerator, exploring a different arrangement of successive acceleration stages.

sections.heading: Early research and cyclotron advancements
sections.body: Before developing cyclotrons, Lawrence investigated ionisation and measured the ionisation potentials of metal vapours. He also devised a method for measuring extremely short intervals in spark discharges and worked on precise measurement of the electron’s charge-to-mass ratio.
