These projects reflect an interest in experimental methods as well as particular physical questions. His nuclear research later expanded through larger accelerators and a growing laboratory team. Subsequent machines supported studies of mesons and, later, antiparticles, extending the programme beyond the work recognised in 1939. The Nobel biography records fifty-six papers bearing his name between 1924 and 1940, with much of his research appearing in The Physical Review and the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. His role joined invention, collaborative experiment and the development of a laboratory capable of pursuing new particle and nuclear problems.

terms.definition: A method using a constant homogeneous magnetic field and an oscillating electrical field to achieve stepwise particle acceleration.
A facility at the University of California, Berkeley, directed by Lawrence starting in 1936 for nuclear physics research.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Applications of radioactive isotopes in chemical and biological research
sections.body: Hevesy’s unsuccessful attempt to separate radioactive lead from ordinary lead suggested a new experimental use. Their closely similar chemical behaviour meant the radioactive atoms could accompany the ordinary ones through a process, while their radiation revealed where they went. He used this approach to measure the small quantities of lead dissolved from compounds such as lead sulphide and lead chromate. Later radioactive tracers made biological investigations possible. Phosphorus-labelled preparations allowed his group to follow redistribution from blood into tissues and organs, including the skeleton. Experiments also examined the movement and excretion of sodium and potassium. Phosphorus tracing helped show that phospholipids were synthesised within chicken embryos. Across these studies, the marker provided a measurable signal for an element participating in an otherwise difficult-to-follow chemical or biological process.

sections.heading: Development of neutron bombardment activation analysis
sections.body: On returning to Copenhagen, Hevesy investigated artificially produced radioactive isotopes and developed activation analysis. In this approach, neutron bombardment makes suitable atoms radioactive, allowing the resulting signal to help identify or measure the material present. It added another analytical method to his earlier work with fluorescent X-rays. From 1934, his programme of physiological investigations expanded through the use of labelled atoms, supported by several research foundations. This built on earlier applications of isotope tracers to living systems. His later work in Sweden continued the biological direction, including studies of iron transport in healthy and cancerous organisms and the effect of X-rays on nucleic-acid formation in normal tissues and tumours. These projects extended the tracer approach from tracking an element’s location to investigating changing processes within cells and tissues.

terms.definition: Different species of an element that possess the same nuclear charge but differ in their atomic weight.
A method of investigating an element through the process of neutron bombardment to create detectable radioactive signals.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of Vitamin K and Blood Coagulation
sections.body: Research following Dam's discovery linked vitamin K deficiency with impaired blood coagulation. The presentation explained the sequence through prothrombin, thrombin and the formation of a fibrin network that stabilizes a clot. Vitamin K is needed for normal activity of important clotting proteins; deficiency can therefore lead to abnormal bleeding. These findings helped explain problems affecting some newborns and people with certain liver or intestinal disorders. Researchers identified dietary sources and also found production by intestinal bacteria. Doisy and his collaborators purified forms designated K1 and K2 and investigated their chemical structures. Connecting nutritional observations with chemical isolation made it possible to study the vitamin more precisely.

sections.heading: Research into sterol metabolism and vitamin properties
sections.body: While investigating the metabolism of sterols in chicks, Dam identified vitamin K. His research expanded to examine its physical and chemical properties, alongside its occurrence in plants and animals. Working with P. Karrer, he focused on the purification and isolation of this substance. This investigation also revealed that certain fats, when consumed without vitamin E, cause increased capillary permeability and adipose tissue coloration in experimental animals. Dam later explored nutritional studies regarding gall-stone formation and held leadership roles within the Danish Fat Research Institute.

sections.heading: Chemical distinction of vitamin K analogues
sections.body: During his research, Edward Doisy worked with collaborators including Thayer, MacCorquodale, McKee, and Binkley to examine vitamin K analogues. Their studies established a clear distinction between two specific forms: vitamin K1, which they isolated from alfalfa, and vitamin K2, which was obtained from fish meal. While vitamin K2 possesses an action similar to K1, the researchers identified that it possesses a slightly different chemical constitution. This work followed Doisy's 1939 success in isolating the substance after its presence was noted in alfalfa.

terms.definition: A group of fat-soluble nutrients required for the normal activity of important proteins involved in blood clotting.
A specialized field of study that Dam practiced in Graz, Austria, to investigate chemical processes at a minute scale.
Different chemical forms of vitamin K, such as K1 from alfalfa and K2 from fish meal, possessing slightly different constitutions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The Frankfurt experiment and space-quantization discovery
sections.body: In Frankfurt in 1922, Stern and Gerlach sent a narrow beam of silver atoms from a heated furnace through a vacuum. A non-uniform magnetic field deflected the atoms according to their magnetic properties. Classical expectations suggested a continuous spread of deflections, but the observed beam separated into distinct parts. The result supported quantization: the component of an atom's magnetic moment along the field could take particular values rather than any value in a continuous range. It did not mean that an atom could occupy only certain locations in ordinary space. The beam method subsequently allowed magnetic properties to be measured with greater precision. Stern's later work on the proton found a magnetic moment substantially larger than the simple theoretical expectation.

sections.heading: Experimental applications of molecular beam methods
sections.body: Following his early research in statistical thermodynamics and quantum theory, Stern transitioned toward experimental physics. He utilized the molecular beam method to investigate various atomic and nuclear properties. One significant application involved the experimental verification of Maxwell’s law regarding velocity distribution in gases. Additionally, he conducted experiments involving the production of interference by hydrogen and helium rays, which provided a demonstration of the wave nature found in atoms and molecules. His collaborative work with Gerlach focused on how magnetic fields act upon the magnetic moment of atoms to cause deflection. These techniques allowed for the measurement of magnetic moments in sub-atomic particles, such as the proton, expanding the utility of beam-based investigations into the fundamental characteristics of matter.

terms.definition: The restriction of the component of an atomic magnetic moment along a chosen field direction to discrete values.
Directing a narrow stream of atoms or molecules through an apparatus and measuring effects such as deflection or interference to investigate their properties.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Otto Stern — Nobel Prize facts: the 1922 Stern–Gerlach experiment

sections.heading: The emergence of nuclear chemistry through neutron bombardment
sections.body: Neutrons gave researchers a way to investigate nuclei without the electric repulsion encountered by positively charged projectiles. Between 1936 and 1938, Hahn and Lise Meitner studied products of neutron bombardment of uranium and thorium. They initially interpreted results in terms of relatively small nuclear changes and possible elements beyond uranium. The decisive surprise came when Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found that a supposed radium product behaved chemically as barium, a much lighter element. Meitner and Otto Frisch explained how splitting a heavy nucleus could produce lighter fragments and release substantial energy. Frisch then investigated the energetic fragments experimentally. Evidence that fission also released neutrons suggested the possibility of a chain reaction, in which one splitting event could help cause further ones. The result linked chemical identification with a new account of nuclear behaviour.

sections.heading: Early radioactive discoveries and chemical research methods
sections.body: Before his work on fission, Hahn conducted significant research into radioactive substances. While working in London under William Ramsay, he identified radiothorium during the preparation of pure radium salts. At McGill University, he investigated alpha-rays alongside Ernest Rutherford and discovered radioactinium. His chemical expertise included developing the strontium method for dating geological periods and utilizing the emanation method to test substance compositions. Hahn also explored nuclear isomerism through the discovery of uranium Z. Alongside Lise Meitner, he utilized radioactive recoil to identify new transformation products and investigated beta-ray absorbability. These various radioactive methods allowed him to study the precipitation of minute quantities of substances and the formation of crystals throughout his long career in Berlin.

terms.definition: The study of radioactive substances and transformations involving atomic nuclei, including reactions that change one element into another.
Motion of a nucleus caused by the emission of a particle during radioactive decay, which can help separate or identify decay products.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary themes in Jensen's expansive works
sections.body: Jensen’s diverse literary output includes American novels such as Madame D’Ora and Hjulet, which celebrate modern technology, skyscrapers, and motor cars. His six-volume series, Den lange rejse, imagines a journey from the ice age to Christopher Columbus. The prize presentation described a claimed world-historical role for Scandinavian peoples as one of its central themes. Within this monumental work, he introduces the legendary figure Nornagestr, a character representing the Nordic spirit. Jensen’s writing style frequently balances historical facts with myths, navigating between the realities of the present and the shadows of the past.

sections.heading: Themes and structures in Jensen's prose and myths
sections.body: In Den lange rejse, Jensen imagines human development from early communal life to civilization through six stories. This epic traces developments like mastering fire and inventing locomotion via wagons or sails, eventually reaching the era of Columbus. His Myter series explores diverse realms, ranging from fantasy to factual theories presented with graphic clarity. Additionally, Vor oprindelse examines how humanity began influencing evolutionary forces by perfecting crafts and weapons. Hallström praised the direct, vivid style with which Jensen presented these imaginative accounts of human development.

sections.heading: Integration of natural sciences into literary themes
sections.body: In his autobiographical account, Jensen connected his literary direction with the natural sciences he studied during three years of medical training. Botany, zoology, physics and chemistry furnished subjects and ways of thinking that entered his prose and poetry. He described his poems as a move toward simplicity and admired the energy he found in English and American writing. His fiction, including Den lange rejse, used ideas about evolution to imagine human origins and cultural development. Jensen presented this as a response to what he considered distortions of Darwinism. That is his explanation of his literary project, rather than a claim that the novels established a scientific correction to evolutionary theory.

terms.definition: A connected series of narratives that develops a large story across generations or historical periods.
Short prose works that range across fantasy, observed experience and speculative ideas, united by their author’s vivid style.
Here, the use of ideas about evolution to consider human origins, cultural change and moral questions in literature.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Different nerve fibres have different electrical properties
sections.body: Erlanger and Gasser distinguished three main fibre groups, with further subdivisions of group A. The presentation reported conduction speeds of 5–100 metres per second for A fibres, 3–14 for B fibres and below 2 for C fibres. Speed was associated with other properties, including impulse duration, excitation threshold and the recovery period after an impulse. These properties did not all change in exactly the same way. The work also examined sensitivity to pressure and oxygen deprivation, helping show that a nerve contains fibres with distinct electrical characteristics.

sections.heading: An instrument sensitive enough to record nerve signals
sections.body: In 1922, Erlanger and Gasser adapted the cathode-ray oscillograph to record nerve action potentials. This technical work made their later comparison of nerve fibres possible. It formed part of Erlanger's broader interest in designing instruments for physiological research. He had also developed a recording device for blood-pressure studies and a clamp that could temporarily interrupt conduction through a particular pathway in the heart. Those were separate investigations of circulation and cardiac function, while the Nobel-recognised collaboration concerned the electrical properties of nerves.

sections.heading: Why a nerve recording contains several components
sections.body: Gasser's early nerve research included measurements of action currents in the phrenic nerve. Improved oscillograph recordings revealed complex signals, which the researchers linked to groups of fibres conducting impulses at different speeds. A recording from a nerve therefore combined contributions from fibres with different properties. This helped explain why the response was more complicated than a single uniform signal. The biography connects the work with later progress in studying reflexes and pain, and notes Gasser's contribution to the 1937 book Electrical Signs of Nervous Activity.

terms.definition: Slower changes in electrical potential following an impulse, associated with changes in how readily a nerve fibre can be excited again.
An instrument that displays changing electrical signals; Erlanger and Gasser adapted it to make the small, rapid signals from nerves observable.
The speed at which an impulse travels along a nerve fibre; differences between fibres contribute to the complexity of recordings from a whole nerve.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Access to prisoners and the limits of conventions
sections.body: The presentation credited the ICRC with useful prisoner-of-war camp inspections and assistance with exchanges initiated by the warring states. It also described serious limits to this work. Access was uneven, and the speech linked restrictions in particular countries with the lack of universal participation in the 1929 prisoner-of-war convention. German authorities treated concentration camps as an internal political matter and rejected inspection requests. The presentation distinguished the practical value of some visits and exchanges from the limited effect of protests about violations. Its account shows how humanitarian work depended on permission and cooperation that were often withheld.

sections.heading: Limited relief and failure to protect persecuted people
sections.body: The ICRC's retrospective describes both relief efforts and their severe limitations. It sent more than 122,000 parcels to concentration camps up to May 1945, but the operation did not reach people subjected to the harshest conditions or protect prisoners from torture and massacre. In Budapest, Friedrich Born obtained authorisation for certificates linked to Latin American immigration papers. These offered some protection but did not enable their holders to leave Hungary. Late-war interventions inside some camps had local successes. Such actions did not prevent the mass deportations or provide effective protection to many victims of the Holocaust.

sections.heading: Practical relief and intellectual aid
sections.body: In his 11 December 1945 Nobel lecture, Edouard Chapuisat described how the ICRC organised collective, individual and intellectual relief. Food and clothing shipments addressed physical needs, while an Intellectual Relief Service worked with other organisations to provide books and educational opportunities. He reported distribution of more than 1.3 million books between 1940 and 1945, helping establish camp libraries and support secondary or university study. The lecture also described the use of funds from Jewish assistance organisations to obtain provisions and clothing for persecuted people in Romania and Hungary. These figures and descriptions form the organisation's own postwar account of its relief activities.

terms.definition: An international agreement governing the treatment of captured combatants; participation and access restrictions shaped the ICRC's ability to act during the war.
Direct dealings with particular authorities, the approach the ICRC continued after deciding against a public appeal about wartime violations in 1942.
Support for prisoners' mental and educational needs, including access to books, camp libraries and opportunities to continue formal study.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
ICRC retrospective: the Holocaust and the organization’s acknowledged failure to protect persecuted civilians
Edouard Chapuisat: ICRC activities during the war, 1939–1945 — Nobel lecture, 11 December 1945

sections.heading: Reading a resonance from a dip in the beam
sections.body: Rabi placed a wire loop connected to a variable-frequency circuit inside the magnetic field traversed by the beam. Tuning this circuit changed the frequency of its oscillating field. At a matching frequency, the field could drive transitions between allowed magnetic states of the particles. The resulting change in magnetic deflection meant that some particles no longer reached the detector. A dip in the detector count therefore marked the resonance. Measuring the frequency of that dip precisely, together with the known applied field, provided a precise way to determine magnetic properties. The presentation compared the frequency adjustment to tuning a radio receiver.

sections.heading: From magnetic crystals to nuclear measurements
sections.body: Rabi's doctoral research concerned the magnetism of crystals. After working with several European physicists, including Otto Stern, he joined Columbia University in 1929 and turned to nuclear magnetism. He refined Stern's molecular-beam approach by combining it with resonance. Instead of relying solely on how a beam was deflected, the apparatus used electromagnetic oscillations at a frequency matched to the response of particles in a magnetic field. This made it possible to investigate particular quantum states and determine nuclear angular momentum and magnetic moments. The biography presents this development as the central experimental advance of his nuclear research.

terms.definition: A change between allowed quantum states; in this experiment, a matching radio frequency could change a particle's magnetic state.
The regular precession of a magnetic moment around an applied magnetic field; its frequency provides the reference for the resonance condition.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Controlling the processes that spoil stored fodder
sections.body: Virtanen studied the acidity needed to preserve green fodder in storage. Acidification reduced plant-cell respiration, which consumes soluble carbohydrates, and suppressed fermentations and protein breakdown that could spoil the feed. The presentation described better retention of vitamins and other nutrients under the method. It also emphasised a practical advantage in Finland: autumn grass could be stored even when weather made drying it into hay difficult. The aim was to preserve a useful feed through the winter and support dairy production. The method concerned ensiling green material, not simply treating already dried hay.

sections.heading: Agriculture as a problem in biochemistry
sections.body: Virtanen's laboratory investigated bacterial fermentation, plant nutrition and the chemistry of agricultural products. Early studies examined the role of cozymase and phosphorylation in sugar breakdown, helping identify shared steps in different fermentation pathways. Other work concerned nitrogen fixation in legume root nodules and the chemical composition of plants. His biography describes a research programme extending beyond the prize-winning preservation method and continuing after the award. The common thread was the use of biochemical experiments to understand processes that affected crops, animal nutrition and dairy production.

terms.definition: Virtanen's method of preserving green fodder by controlled acidification, reducing biological processes that consume nutrients or spoil the stored feed.
A structure on the roots of legumes that houses bacteria involved in fixing atmospheric nitrogen, one subject of Virtanen's agricultural research.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Grief, childhood and the wider landscape
sections.body: The presentation traced different emphases across Mistral's collections. Desolación brought intense expressions of grief, while Ternura gathered songs and rounds for children. Tala, published in Buenos Aires in 1938 to aid child victims of the Spanish Civil War, placed greater emphasis on landscape and elemental images such as bread, salt and water. The speech interpreted these changes as a widening of personal feeling into a larger poetic world. Her work with children and education formed another connection between the poems and public life, rather than a complete explanation of every poem through one personal tragedy.

sections.heading: Poetry alongside education and international service
sections.body: Mistral's Sonetos de la muerte brought wider recognition in 1914, before the publication of Desolación in 1922. Ternura and Tala developed recurring concerns with childhood and maternal feeling. Her biography also records a substantial public career: work in education in Chile and Mexico, cultural activity associated with the League of Nations, and Chilean consular appointments in European cities. She taught Spanish literature at institutions in the Americas as well. These activities show that the poet's international presence involved teaching and cultural service alongside the circulation of her books.

terms.definition: Poetry giving concentrated expression to feelings, perceptions or a speaking voice, the form central to Mistral's award.
A fourteen-line poetic form; Mistral's Sonetos de la muerte used the form in poems associated with love and loss.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: From a clear patch on a plate to an active preparation
sections.body: Fleming’s earlier investigation of antibacterial substances made the mold’s effect worth following up. He grew it in broth, removed the mold and tested the remaining liquid. Even highly diluted filtrate inhibited susceptible bacteria, showing that an active substance had entered the broth. Different bacterial species responded differently. The later Oxford program investigated this activity systematically and worked through the difficulties of preparing penicillin for treatment. The sequence distinguishes observing an effect, testing its range and producing a medically useful preparation, each requiring additional experimental work.

sections.heading: Biochemistry turned an old observation into a research program
sections.body: Chain emigrated from Nazi Germany to England in 1933, worked on phospholipids at Cambridge and moved to Oxford in 1935. His research there included lysozyme, metabolism and methods for analyzing small biological samples. In 1939 he and Florey began a systematic investigation of antibacterial substances produced by microorganisms. Reexamining Fleming’s penicillin became the most consequential part of that program. The biography places its therapeutic development within a broader biochemical approach: isolate active material, investigate its properties and test whether laboratory activity could translate into treatment.

sections.heading: Testing antibacterial activity in biological fluids
sections.body: Fleming sought substances that could inhibit bacteria without comparable damage to animal tissues. His work on lysozyme and on measuring antibacterial activity in blood and other fluids supplied methods he later used for penicillin. The accidental mold contamination in 1928 was therefore followed by deliberate experiments, including dilution tests of the culture liquid. Those tests helped establish the strength of its effect against staphylococci. The discovery depended on recognizing an unexpected observation and then investigating it with laboratory methods developed through earlier research.

terms.definition: Liquid remaining after microorganisms are removed from a culture, which can contain substances they released during growth.
Chemical analysis of very small biological samples, useful when active substances are scarce or difficult to isolate.
A test measuring how a substance affects bacterial growth or survival under specified conditions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Trade disputes as a problem for peace
sections.body: Hull believed that retaliatory tariffs and discrimination in trade could damage international trust and contribute to wider conflict. In 1917 he proposed an international trade-agreement congress intended to address these practices through mutual agreement. The presentation traced this connection between economic policy and diplomacy across his career. It also described the resistance such proposals met when governments were driven by domestic pressures. The argument was Hull's theory about reducing causes of conflict, rather than evidence that lowering tariffs alone would prevent war.

sections.heading: Reciprocal agreements and regional diplomacy
sections.body: The Trade Agreements Act of 1934 gave Hull a means to negotiate reciprocal reductions in trade barriers with other countries. His diplomatic work also included the Montevideo conference and subsequent inter-American meetings, where he sought improved relations between the United States and Latin American states. The biography links this approach with the Good Neighbor policy. Alongside regional and commercial diplomacy, he worked on plans for a postwar international organisation. These activities supplied different parts of the case for his peace award: practical agreements, relations between states and institutional planning.

terms.definition: Economic self-sufficiency with limited reliance on international trade, a tendency Hull opposed in his efforts to encourage commercial cooperation.
An agreement in which countries exchange trade concessions, such as reductions in tariffs, rather than acting only unilaterally.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A rule that organizes atomic structure
sections.body: Pauli’s 1925 exclusion principle emerged from analyzing the atomic evidence available at the time. An electron’s state required four quantum numbers, and two electrons in an atom could not share the same complete set. This does not mean that two electrons can never have the same energy: states with the same energy may differ in other quantum properties. The additional two-valued property was subsequently connected with electron spin. By restricting which states electrons could occupy, the principle explained patterns in the arrangement of electrons and helped account for chemical behavior, magnetism and electrical conduction. Its scope also extends to identical protons or identical neutrons.

sections.heading: Beyond the exclusion principle
sections.body: Pauli also helped develop quantum field theory and established a connection between particle spin and the statistical rules governing collections of particles. He proposed the neutrino to account for energy carried away in beta decay; this was a theoretical inference, not an experimental detection. The historical biography calls the neutrino massless, reflecting an older understanding. Experiments recognized by the 2015 physics prize subsequently showed that neutrinos change type and are not all massless. This distinction separates Pauli’s enduring proposal of an unseen neutral particle from a property that later evidence revised.

terms.definition: Numbers labeling allowed quantum states or their properties; the complete set distinguishes the electron states relevant to Pauli’s atomic rule.
An electrically neutral elementary particle involved in processes such as beta decay; neutrino oscillation experiments show that neutrinos have mass.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Neutrino oscillations and mass — official 2015 physics announcement

sections.heading: Advancements in enzyme purification and viral crystallization
sections.body: Building on earlier discoveries, John Northrop at the Rockefeller Institute developed methods to obtain crystallized digestive enzymes like pepsin, trypsin, and chymotrypsin. Working with collaborators such as Kunitz, he performed extensive studies regarding the purity and homogeneity of these protein substances. Wendell Stanley utilized similar purification techniques to isolate active crystals from tobacco mosaic virus using large quantities of infected leaves. Subsequent investigation established that the active virus preparations contained nucleic acid as well as protein.

sections.heading: Northrop's enzyme crystallization and protein research
sections.body: During his tenure at the Rockefeller Institute, Northrop conducted kinetic studies on essential enzymes alongside Jacques Loeb. In 1929, he utilized specific techniques to isolate pepsin in a pure crystalline state. These methods subsequently enabled the crystallization of trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase, and pepsinogen. His investigations into viral proteins led to the isolation of a nucleoprotein possessing bacteriophage activity. Furthermore, his published work, Crystalline Enzymes, documented findings regarding the physical chemistry of proteins and the chemical nature of enzymes.

sections.heading: Stanley's research on tobacco mosaic virus and influenza
sections.body: Stanley's work at the Rockefeller Institute produced purified material that retained tobacco mosaic virus activity while also behaving like a chemical preparation. This combination made the material important for investigating the boundary between chemistry and infection. The virus preparation contained protein associated with nucleic acid. His wider research later included preparing and studying influenza viruses and developing a vaccine using centrifugation techniques. He also worked on other chemical topics, including sterols, the stereochemistry of diphenyl compounds, and compounds investigated against leprosy. The biography therefore places the tobacco mosaic work within a broader career spanning chemistry and virology.

terms.definition: Separating the material of interest from other components so that its activity and chemical properties can be investigated more reliably.
The study of how quickly reactions proceed; Northrop investigated the rates of reactions involving enzymes.
Material consisting of protein associated with nucleic acid, as in the tobacco mosaic virus preparations described here.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Influences and psychological developments in Hesse's literary evolution
sections.body: Hesse’s writing evolved through significant personal transitions and intellectual encounters. After fleeing a seminary education, he experienced a profound inner crisis in 1914 that moved his work away from idyllic regionalism toward more daring themes. Seeking relief from doubt and illness, he utilized psychoanalysis, which left permanent marks on his increasingly bold narratives. His maternal lineage connected him to Indian wisdom through his grandfather, Gundert, an Indologist. His interest in Indian thought and Buddhism appears in works such as Siddhartha. Furthermore, his 1943 novel, The Glass Bead Game, depicts a mysterious intellectual order using meditation as therapy. This complex structure mirrors the concept of a game's role in civilization, reflecting his ability to maintain German cultural traditions during periods of political collapse.

sections.heading: Hesse's Literary Development and Philosophical Influences
sections.body: Following a period as a mechanic apprentice and bookseller, Hesse transitioned to full-time writing after the success of Peter Camenzind. His literary output includes various forms, such as the stories Knulp and the poetry collected in 1942. While influenced by Western philosophers like Plato, Spinoza, Schopenhauer, and Nietzsche, he found significant impact in Indian and Chinese philosophy. His later works include Siddhartha, Narziss und Goldmund, and The Journey to the East. His eleven years of work on the two-volume novel The Glass Bead Game extended through much of the Nazi period. Despite facing German nationalism and abusive letters, he maintained international connections through figures like Romain Rolland. His political essays, published in 1946 under War and Peace, reflect his engagement with global conflicts.

terms.definition: An approach to exploring unconscious feelings and conflicts; the presentation linked Hesse’s experience of it with changes in his writing.
The religious upbringing described in Hesse’s autobiography, which he personally experienced as restricting his individuality and ambitions as a writer.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Measuring mutations before trying to induce them
sections.body: Muller's work depended first on finding reliable ways to measure mutation frequency. After leaving Morgan's research group, he spent several years developing procedures that made changes in hereditary factors experimentally detectable and countable. He could then compare the effects of different agents. X-ray irradiation produced many more mutations, turning events that were otherwise relatively rare into material for systematic laboratory study. The presentation identified this experimental control as central to the achievement. It opened possibilities for investigating hereditary changes and their consequences in different organisms, with implications for research on evolution, plant improvement and medicine.

sections.heading: Different causes and forms of hereditary change
sections.body: Muller studied spontaneous mutations as well as those induced experimentally. His biography describes early arguments that many mutations were harmful and recessive, together with proposals about their physical origins. Later research examined how mutation frequency varied with radiation dose, dose rate, other agents and the stage of the cell. The work distinguished small gene changes from larger alterations in chromosome structure, including breaks and rearrangements. He also investigated relationships between spontaneous mutation and ageing. This was a programme of experiments and hypotheses about hereditary change, not a finding that every mutation had the same cause or effect.

terms.definition: How often hereditary changes are detected in a studied population; measuring this enabled Muller to compare the effects of different treatments.
A hereditary change arising without deliberate mutagenic treatment; Muller investigated its frequency and sought to understand its physical origins and consequences.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Social Reform and International Cooperation Methods
sections.body: Balch applied a practical approach to peace by promoting regular collaboration between nations in specific fields. Her efforts included urging the United States to renounce priority for Austrian credits during 1921. She supported the Briand-Kellogg Pact through lectures in England and advocated for League of Nations involvement to counter American isolationism. Additionally, she studied treaty drafts at a 1919 Zurich conference. Mott focused on combating racial prejudice by systematically studying global conditions and presiding over the 1938 International Missionary Council World Congress in India.

sections.heading: Research as a basis for peace advocacy
sections.body: Balch brought economics and sociology into her work for peace. Her research included studies of public assistance in France and Slavic immigrants in America. At the 1915 International Congress of Women, she helped prepare proposals for the warring nations and participated in a delegation to Scandinavia and Russia seeking offers of mediation. She also helped establish the organisation that became the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom. In 1926 she joined its investigation of conditions in Haiti under American military occupation. She edited and wrote much of Occupied Haiti, the committee's report, which supported restoration of Haitian independence.

sections.heading: Building international student networks
sections.body: Following an 1886 interdenominational conference, Mott helped develop the Student Volunteer Movement for Foreign Missions. With Karl Fries, he organised the World's Student Christian Federation in 1895 and travelled to establish national student movements in several parts of the world. His leadership included presiding over the 1910 World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh. During the First World War, he served as general secretary of the YMCA's National War Work Council. Through the YMCA he maintained international contacts where circumstances permitted and helped organise assistance for prisoners of war. These activities connected missionary and student organisations with practical wartime relief.

terms.definition: A political approach involving active engagement with international organizations to promote cooperation and prevent isolationism between different nations.
Direct study of conditions to inform a proposal, illustrated by the committee's examination of Haiti before publishing its report on occupation.

terms.term: Student Volunteer Movement for Foreign Missions
terms.definition: A Christian missionary movement that emerged in 1888 from pledges made by students, including Mott, at a conference two years earlier.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Containing extreme pressures
sections.body: Bridgman's apparatus combined a pressure-producing chamber with a separate experimental chamber connected through a fluid. A piston compressed the fluid, which transmitted the pressure to the sample. His sealing arrangement tightened more effectively as pressure increased, while external support helped vessels resist the forces inside them. Work at the highest pressures required very small samples and close study of the strength of the apparatus. The presentation described experiments at pressures hundreds of thousands of times greater than atmospheric pressure. X-ray examination of thin flakes recovered from one experiment indicated that their original crystalline structure had been lost. Developing the equipment therefore went hand in hand with discovering how materials change under pressure.

sections.heading: Measurements and the meaning of physical concepts
sections.body: Bridgman's high-pressure programme, begun in 1905, examined properties including compressibility, electrical and thermal conductivity, tensile strength and viscosity. His biography reports measurements on more than a hundred compounds, using improved seals and externally supported vessels. He also worked on growing single crystals and on electrical effects in metals. His books included The Physics of High Pressure and The Logic of Modern Physics. The latter belongs to his interest in how physical concepts are interpreted. The biography describes him as an advocate of an operational viewpoint that connects such concepts with what can be observed.

terms.definition: Noncrystalline: lacking an ordered crystal structure. The presentation describes high pressure producing this change in the small material samples examined.
An approach connecting the meaning of physical concepts with how they can be observed, advocated by Bridgman in his philosophical writing.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A theory connecting plant chemistry and synthesis
sections.body: The presentation described Robinson's proposals for how plants could construct alkaloids from amino-acid precursors. His tropinone synthesis illustrated the approach: three relatively simple starting molecules could combine into a much more elaborate structure, avoiding a long sequence of separate steps. This suggested possible routes for biological synthesis and helped chemists reason about relationships between alkaloids. It did not establish that every plant followed the proposed route. Robinson's broader research also covered plant pigments, hormones, antimalarial compounds and reaction mechanisms. The Academy nevertheless identified his work on alkaloids as the particular basis of the award.

sections.heading: Working out how atoms are arranged
sections.body: Robinson investigated both the construction of organic compounds and the arrangement of atoms within them. His studies of plant pigments expanded into alkaloid chemistry, where he contributed to structural work on morphine, papaverine and narcotine. Establishing a structure was a practical research problem: chemists needed to explain how a compound's atoms were connected and how its reactions fitted that arrangement. His wider programme also addressed mechanisms of organic reactions and the development of antimalarial drugs. The biography describes these connected interests across a long career, extending beyond a single successful synthesis or a single class of plant compounds.

terms.definition: Plant pigments responsible for many red, purple and blue colours; Robinson studied their chemical structures as part of his wider organic chemistry research.
The arrangement and connections of atoms within a molecule; identifying this was central to Robinson's investigations of complex natural compounds.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Contradiction as a literary method
sections.body: The Nobel presentation interpreted Gide's work through recurring conflicts: belief and doubt, discipline and freedom, self-denial and attachment to life. It described these tensions as a continuing dialogue rather than a settled doctrine. The Counterfeiters stood out for its experimental narrative technique and examination of young French characters. The speech also praised the intention behind Gide's autobiographical writing: to reveal uncomfortable experiences rather than offer a flattering self-portrait. That is the presenter's assessment of his literary ambition, not independent proof of every autobiographical claim. The award's language of literary integrity concerns the writing and does not absolve the conduct it describes.

sections.heading: Different narrative forms and political reports
sections.body: Gide distinguished between several kinds of narrative. He described works such as Lafcadio's Adventures as soties, while placing Strait is the Gate and The Pastoral Symphony among the more restrained récits. He regarded the structurally experimental The Counterfeiters as his novel. His writing also extended beyond fiction to literary criticism, translation and accounts of political experience. Reports from the Congo addressed economic exploitation, while his account of Russia expressed disillusionment. The biography describes these activities as part of a career that moved from relatively specialised literary circles to wider and often contentious public influence.

terms.definition: Writing that examines and reveals the author's own experiences or failings; candour is an intention of the form, not a guarantee of factual completeness.
A narrative or account; Gide used the label for comparatively restrained works such as Strait is the Gate, distinguishing them from his other fictional forms.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Hormones could change the response to insulin
sections.body: Houssay's contribution addressed regulation of sugar metabolism at the level of the whole animal. In experiments removing the pituitary gland or its anterior lobe, animals became unusually sensitive to insulin and had reduced glycogen stores in the liver. The observations showed that pituitary activity could oppose insulin's effects and that blood-sugar regulation involved interactions between hormones. This was distinct from the Coris' biochemical investigation of glycogen reactions, which received the other half of the prize.

sections.heading: Reproducing glycogen chemistry outside the organism
sections.body: In 1936, the Coris isolated glucose-1-phosphate and connected its formation with phosphorylase activity. Studying this intermediate helped them reproduce enzymatic formation of polysaccharides in the laboratory. Purifying and crystallising enzymes then allowed particular reactions to be examined more closely. The important distinction is between demonstrating what an enzyme system can do under controlled conditions and explaining every route used in a living cell. Their work supplied identifiable intermediates and experimental reactions on which a fuller understanding of carbohydrate metabolism could build.

sections.heading: Moving from whole animals to individual biochemical steps
sections.body: The Coris' joint programme began with questions about how sugar was used in animals and how insulin and epinephrine affected it. Their investigations progressively moved through isolated tissues and extracts to purified enzymes. They also studied glucose breakdown in tumours. This change of experimental scale helped connect bodily effects with particular chemical processes. Gerty Cori continued the collaboration as a research associate after the move to St. Louis and became professor of biochemistry in 1947. The biography describes their research as a sustained partnership across these different approaches.

terms.definition: The front part of the pituitary gland, whose hormonal activity was central to Houssay's experiments on sugar metabolism.
Glucose-1-phosphate, the sugar phosphate isolated by the Coris and associated with phosphorylase-catalysed reactions involving glycogen.
A sequence of reactions breaking down glucose and releasing usable energy, investigated by the Coris in tissues including tumours.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Relief across the divisions of war
sections.body: The presentation described Quaker relief as assistance offered across national and political divisions. After the First World War, the American committee organised food for undernourished children in Germany at Herbert Hoover's request. Relief teams also worked in Poland, Serbia and France, and later assisted people on both sides of the Spanish Civil War. The committee connected these activities with a longer tradition of peace work and social service. Its emphasis was on practical help for people in need, including those associated with former enemies, rather than on military or political victory.

sections.heading: From emergency assistance to reconstruction
sections.body: The AFSC's early work in France included repairing homes, assisting refugee children and helping establish a maternity hospital with British Friends. After the armistice, its activities spread to other countries affected by war, hunger and disease. Teams eventually handed projects over, leaving small centres to support continuing work. New crises in the 1930s brought assistance to refugees from Nazi Germany and children affected by the Spanish Civil War. The history describes repeated movement between immediate relief and longer-term recovery, rather than one continuous programme with the same tasks everywhere.

sections.heading: International centres as places for dialogue
sections.body: The Friends Service Council brought together earlier British Quaker organisations. One predecessor had developed international centres in cooperation with the American Friends Service Committee. Described informally as Quaker embassies, they provided meeting places where people of different nationalities could exchange information and views. The historical account connects this constructive peace work with relief for refugees and victims of war. Some activities belonged to predecessor organisations before the council itself existed. The centres were part of a religious and humanitarian network, not embassies representing a government.

terms.definition: The religious movement also known as the Quakers, represented in the award by two organisations carrying out relief and peace work.
Emergency assistance followed by work to restore homes, services and livelihoods, two connected parts of the AFSC's humanitarian programmes.
Meeting places intended to support dialogue, understanding and practical peace work across national divisions, sometimes informally called Quaker embassies.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
American Friends Service Committee: foundation, First World War relief and work through the Second World War
Friends Service Council: roots of British Quaker overseas service, relief and peacemaking (1972 historical account)

sections.heading: Using interference to detect an atmospheric layer
sections.body: Appleton and Barnett varied radio frequency and observed interference between a signal travelling near the ground and another returning from the upper atmosphere. The changing interference provided evidence of the longer path and a way to estimate the height of the reflecting region, around 100 kilometres in the early experiment. Subsequent work distinguished higher regions with different behaviour. The presentation explained that the upper layer could retain ionisation through much of the night because recombination was slower in the rarefied air. This persistence belonged to the higher Appleton layer, not simply to the lower region first measured.

sections.heading: Developing methods for sounding the ionosphere
sections.body: The early experiments used a BBC transmitter at Bournemouth to investigate radio signals returning from above the Earth. Later research identified a higher and more strongly ionised region, known as the Appleton layer, important for long-distance short-wave communication. Appleton also developed methods using brief bursts of radio energy and recording their returning echoes with a cathode-ray instrument. These approaches made the atmosphere an object of repeated measurement rather than only a proposed explanation of distant reception. His research extended to northern latitudes and the relationship between solar activity and ionospheric behaviour.

terms.definition: A technique using changes in signal interference as radio frequency is varied to infer the difference between two propagation paths.
Investigating the atmosphere by sending radio signals and measuring their returned echoes or propagation characteristics to infer properties such as layer height.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Separating components without losing their identity
sections.body: Proteins posed a difficult analytical problem: separating a mixture could change the very substances being studied. Tiselius refined electrophoresis, observing how dissolved components moved under an electric field. His experiments separated the globulin portion of blood serum into three fractions, each containing related molecules, rather than treating it as one uniform substance. He also improved analysis by adsorption, extending the usefulness of chromatographic methods beyond visibly colored materials. The presentation speech emphasizes that these advances supported quantitative measurement as well as recognition of different components. They gave researchers more reliable ways to characterize complex biological mixtures.

sections.heading: From physical chemistry to biochemical analysis
sections.body: Tiselius’s early work combined studies of protein movement with research on diffusion and adsorption in zeolites. Contacts with American scientists during a Princeton fellowship encouraged him to apply physical methods to biochemical problems. His improved electrophoretic method, published in 1937, became particularly valuable for investigating blood-serum proteins. The biography also describes the broader research program at the Uppsala institute, including chromatography, partition methods and gel filtration. That account extends beyond the 1948 award: the institute acquired its new building in 1950–1952. These later developments should not all be read as techniques already completed when the prize was given.

terms.definition: Movement of charged particles or molecules through a medium under an electric field, used to analyze or separate mixture components.
An electrophoretic approach that follows the movement of boundaries between regions of solution as dissolved components migrate.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Allusion, fragmented form and a changing poetic voice
sections.body: The presentation speech describes The Waste Land as a difficult but influential experiment combining symbolic language, fragments and references to earlier writing. It connects these techniques with Eliot’s view that a complex civilization requires poetry capable of indirect and layered expression. The speech then contrasts the poem’s fragmentation with the sustained meditation and recurring phrases of Four Quartets. This is the Academy’s interpretation of a developing body of work: changing forms gave different expression to questions about disorder, meaning and spiritual experience. Eliot’s critical account of tradition also treated new writing as changing how earlier literature is read.

sections.heading: Poetry within a wider literary career
sections.body: Eliot’s influence extended through editing, criticism and drama. He edited The Criterion throughout its 1922–1939 run and became an editor and later a director at Faber & Faber. His philosophical training accompanied a critical interest in the relationship between inherited literature and new writing. The biography also discusses the religious concerns of plays such as Murder in the Cathedral and The Family Reunion. It treats his advocacy of tradition alongside his poetic experimentation, suggesting that these activities belong to the same intellectual career rather than separate, unrelated identities.

terms.definition: An indirect reference to another text, event or cultural tradition, asking the reader to bring those associations into the work.
A regularly issued publication carrying writing and criticism, such as The Criterion, through which an editor can shape literary discussion.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of DDT as a contact insecticide
sections.body: Müller sought an insecticide for plant protection and tested hundreds of organic compounds on flies in a Peet-Grady chamber. Earlier chemical work suggested testing substances containing CCl3 groups, eventually leading him to DDT's strong contact action against flies, Colorado beetles and other insects. He developed preparations including dusts, emulsions and solutions, and found that treated surfaces could remain active for months. Contact action made it possible to target blood-feeding insects without requiring them to eat a poison. Persistence was initially valued because applications continued working. Later evidence changed the assessment of that same property: DDT remains in the environment, accumulates in organisms and can harm wildlife. The original insecticidal finding remained valid, while claims of harmlessness and the acceptability of widespread use required reassessment.

sections.heading: Development of synthetic contact insecticides and DDT
sections.body: Beginning his research into new synthetic contact insecticides in 1935, Müller conducted four years of intensive investigation. This work led to the synthesis of dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane, known as DDT, for which a Swiss patent was issued in 1940. While an Austrian student had originally created the compound in 1873, it lacked significant attention until Müller's efforts. His field trials demonstrated effectiveness against various pests, including mosquitoes, lice, and the Colorado beetle. By 1942, products such as Gesarol and Neocide were marketed. These formulations became vital to British and American medical entomologists during World War II when pyrethrum supplies were low. Müller's earlier professional experience included studying chemical oxidation and developing synthetic tanning agents like Irgatan FL at J. R. Geigy A.G.

terms.definition: A substance that kills insects through direct physical contact rather than requiring the organism to ingest an oral poison.
A professional who applies chemical knowledge within a scientific-industrial laboratory setting to develop substances like pesticides or dyes.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
US EPA: DDT history, persistence, accumulation and environmental effects

sections.heading: Development of the automatic Wilson apparatus
sections.body: To increase efficiency in cosmic ray research, Blackett and Occhialini created an automatic version of the Wilson chamber. This device utilized two Geiger counters positioned above and below the expansion chamber, linked to a quick electrical relay. The mechanism triggered the chamber's expansion only when simultaneous discharges occurred in both counters, indicating a particle had likely passed through the chamber. Using this improved apparatus, they observed electron–positron pairs appearing in cosmic radiation, where tracks were deflected in opposite directions by a superposed magnetic field. They also identified 'gerbes,' which are large numbers of tracks appearing as showers on a single photographic plate. Furthermore, working with Chadwick, they demonstrated that hard gamma rays from radioactive substances could produce these same electron–positron pairs.

sections.heading: Photographs of transmutation and particle creation
sections.body: Blackett's cloud-chamber work began before the automatic apparatus. In 1924 he obtained photographs showing the conversion of nitrogen into an oxygen isotope. The later collaboration with Occhialini made cosmic-ray events easier to capture. In 1933 they observed showers containing approximately equal numbers of positive and negative electrons. Guided by Dirac's theory, they interpreted these observations as evidence that gamma radiation could create an electron and a positron, with additional energy appearing as their motion. The reverse process is annihilation, in which an electron and a positron produce gamma radiation. These ideas connected the visible tracks in photographs with transformations involving radiation and matter. Blackett continued cosmic-ray investigations at Birkbeck and later at Manchester.

terms.definition: A technique using an expansion chamber filled with water vapour to form visible cloud-drops around ions produced by passing particles.
Radiation produced when an electron and a positron meet and are converted into photons; the biography contrasts this with pair production.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Cooling below liquid helium temperatures
sections.body: Giauque's measurements helped researchers calculate chemical equilibria by combining information about reaction heat, temperature and entropy. Reaching lower temperatures also opened a new experimental range. In the method described at the award ceremony, crystals such as gadolinium sulphate were magnetised while heat was carried away through a liquid-helium bath. After the crystals were isolated from their surroundings, removing the field caused further cooling. The presentation reported temperatures within a few thousandths of a degree of absolute zero and described opportunities to investigate magnetic behaviour and superconductivity.

sections.heading: Comparing measurements with molecular spectra
sections.body: Giauque's doctoral work compared the entropies of crystalline and glassy glycerine. He later carried out extensive low-temperature measurements, particularly on condensed gases, and compared thermodynamic properties with results derived from molecular energy levels and quantum statistics. With H. L. Johnston, he investigated oxygen using both heat-capacity measurements and its band spectrum. The comparison led to identifying atmospheric oxygen isotopes 17 and 18 and exposed a mismatch between the atomic-weight scales used by chemists and physicists. His studies of magnetic fields and the entropy of paramagnetic substances also led to adiabatic demagnetisation, first demonstrated with D. P. MacDougall. These related experiments provided different ways to test the third law.

terms.definition: A thermodynamic quantity related to microscopic disorder; its changes, together with temperature and reaction heat, help determine chemical equilibria.
A cooling method using changes in a magnetic field, demonstrated by Giauque and MacDougall to reach temperatures below one kelvin.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A changing South and changing narrative forms
sections.body: The award presentation interpreted Faulkner's fiction through the history of the American South: slavery, the Civil War, the decline of older social structures and the growth of an industrial economy. It connected this setting with the pressures experienced by his characters, including poverty, resentment, fear and ambition. The speech also emphasised his willingness to change narrative methods between books. His language ranged across older literary idioms and regional speech, and his prose could move from long, densely constructed sentences to short sequences. In the Academy's account, this technical variety allowed him to explore difficult psychological experiences within a closely observed regional world.

sections.heading: The growth of a fictional county
sections.body: Faulkner's stories contribute to a shared fictional history through the inhabitants of Yoknapatawpha County. The biography contrasts the declining Sartoris and Compson families with the rising Snopes family. The Sound and the Fury presents the Compsons through several characters' minds, linking changes in viewpoint with an altered experience of time. Light in August and Absalom, Absalom! examine racial prejudice, while The Hamlet, published in 1940, begins the Snopes sequence. That sequence continued after the Nobel award with The Town in 1957 and The Mansion in 1959. The biography also discusses The Reivers, published in 1962, as a later continuation of his writing.

terms.definition: Changing established ways of telling a story, including sentence patterns, narrative structure and forms of speech, to create different effects.
Presenting a character's unspoken thoughts; Faulkner uses this access to different minds to shape the reader's experience of events and time.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Two different approaches to brain function
sections.body: Hess used fine wires implanted in cats under anaesthesia to investigate small brain regions. Observing the effects of stimulation, and of local damage, helped him map coordination of bodily functions. Moniz's separate work involved severing connections in the white matter of the frontal brain. He proposed that this might relieve severe psychiatric symptoms. The presentation praised that therapeutic rationale, reflecting the judgement made at the time. It should be read as a historical account of why the operation was rewarded, rather than evidence that the procedure was harmless or that its claimed benefits justified its consequences.

sections.heading: Coordinating internal organs and bodily movement
sections.body: Hess's investigations connected regulation of internal organs with coordinated bodily responses. Stimulation studies also produced effects on movement, posture and muscle tone, leading him to examine links with the body's balance apparatus. These findings expanded the picture of what the diencephalon helped organise. The biography includes later work as well: an atlas published in 1956 and a study of the biological aspects of psychology in 1962 drew together experimental observations and their interpretation. Those publications followed the Nobel award and should not be mistaken for work already published in 1949.

sections.heading: Angiography was a separate part of Moniz's work
sections.body: Moniz's career included cerebral angiography as well as the leucotomy recognised by his Nobel award. His publications on angiography addressed diagnosis of brain tumours and applications in anatomy, physiology and clinical practice. The biography lists substantial work on this method during the 1930s alongside separate publications on psychiatric surgery. Keeping the two programmes distinct matters: a diagnostic technique for investigating the brain is different from an operation intended to change psychiatric symptoms. His bibliography also ranged beyond these subjects into neurological medicine, biography and cultural history.

terms.definition: A psychiatric operation that cut connections in the frontal brain; Moniz's share of the award recognised this intervention, whose serious harms are discussed in the reassessment.
A region of the forebrain that includes structures involved in coordinating internal bodily functions; Hess investigated these roles through precisely located experimental interventions.
Imaging of the brain's blood vessels, developed by Moniz as a diagnostic technique; it is distinct from prefrontal leucotomy.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Hunger in a world with surplus food
sections.body: The presentation described a contradiction that shaped Boyd Orr's approach: food could be plentiful in some places while people elsewhere went hungry because they lacked the money to buy it. Nutrition policy therefore involved access and purchasing power as well as agricultural production. After the Second World War, the FAO sought cooperation over food supplies that remained scarce. The International Emergency Food Council helped coordinate their distribution between countries, operating until the summer of 1949. Boyd Orr argued that governments should accept responsibility for adequate nutrition and cooperate internationally to achieve it. These were policy objectives, not a claim that the council had eliminated hunger.

sections.heading: From nutrition surveys to an unsuccessful world food plan
sections.body: Boyd Orr's research interests expanded from animal nutrition to human diets, including studies of milk consumption and surveys of nutritional conditions. His 1936 report Food, Health and Income helped shape British wartime food policy. As FAO director-general, he encountered limits in the organisation's authority and funding. He sought a more comprehensive international food system, but his proposed World Food Board failed in 1947 after Britain and the United States withheld support. The biography makes clear that his programme combined scientific investigation with political advocacy, and that international agreement on food distribution was much harder to secure than recognition of nutritional need.

terms.definition: A body that coordinated the distribution of scarce food after the Second World War, described in the award presentation as a form of international rationing.
Boyd Orr's proposed institution for a comprehensive international food programme; it failed to gain the necessary political support in 1947.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Using the range of a force to predict a particle
sections.body: Yukawa adapted ideas from electromagnetic field theory to describe a force acting only over nuclear distances. His calculation connected the short range of that force to the mass of an exchanged particle, giving an estimate around 200 electron masses. He also argued that sufficiently energetic collisions could produce such particles outside nuclei, making cosmic rays a promising place to search. The presentation distinguished the later discovery of a strongly interacting particle from an earlier, lighter particle that did not interact with nuclei strongly enough. Matching an approximate mass alone was insufficient: the observed particle also had to possess the predicted nuclear interaction.

sections.heading: Turning a proposal into a research programme
sections.body: Yukawa published On the Interaction of Elementary Particles. I. in 1935 while working at Osaka University. The paper developed his proposed field theory of nuclear forces and its prediction of a new particle. He continued developing the theory as cosmic-ray experiments revealed new particles and raised questions about their properties. His career also included teaching and explaining the emerging subject: he wrote Japanese introductions to quantum mechanics and elementary-particle theory and began editing the English-language journal Progress of Theoretical Physics in 1946. The biography traces a sustained programme of theoretical work beyond the initial prediction.

terms.definition: A way of describing an interaction through particles exchanged between its participants; Yukawa used this approach to explain forces between protons and neutrons.
A framework in which physical fields describe interactions; Yukawa proposed a new field associated with the short-range force within nuclei.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A ring assembled from two reacting components
sections.body: In the classical reaction, a conjugated diene supplies four carbons and a compatible unsaturated partner supplies two. Bond rearrangement joins them into a six-membered ring. With an alkene partner, the product retains one double bond. The presentation emphasised how readily many suitable combinations react, although the required conditions depend on the reactants. The method proved useful both for making compounds and for investigating the structures of natural products. It also found industrial applications involving resins, materials and synthetic fuels.

sections.heading: Studying selectivity and related reaction types
sections.body: Alder continued investigating the principles of diene synthesis after the original collaboration with Diels. His research included stereochemical questions about which products form when unsaturated compounds react. He also examined double bonds in strained carbon rings and the relationship between addition and substitution processes. The biography places the named reaction within this wider study of organic reactivity. It describes research continuing under difficult conditions in Cologne during the 1940s, with attention to patterns connecting apparently different kinds of chemical transformation.

sections.heading: Using chemical transformations to investigate structures
sections.body: Diels also developed a method using selenium to remove hydrogen from hydroaromatic compounds. Applied to cholesterol and related substances, it produced an aromatic framework that helped chemists investigate steroid structures. This was a separate contribution from the ring-forming reaction developed with Alder. Both lines of work illustrate the value of controlled chemical transformations: reactions can reveal aspects of an existing molecule as well as construct a new one. His biography records these research tools alongside his long involvement in teaching organic chemistry.

terms.definition: The unsaturated reaction partner that combines with a diene in a Diels–Alder reaction, contributing two atoms to the new ring.
A reaction in which components combine, often across an unsaturated bond; diene synthesis was an important example in Alder's investigations.
Removal of hydrogen from a compound; Diels used selenium-mediated dehydrogenation to help investigate the carbon frameworks of steroids.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Reasoned criticism addressed to a wider public
sections.body: The Nobel presentation praised Russell's clarity and wit in writing about difficult questions for non-specialist readers. Books such as Human Knowledge and Sceptical Essays accompanied his historical and technical work. The speech placed him in a tradition of empiricism associated with Locke and Hume, while stressing that his political views could not be reduced to one simple position. He examined socialism, warned about bureaucracy and defended individual freedom against collective pressures. The literary award concerned this wide-ranging practice of argument and public criticism as well as the qualities of the prose.

sections.heading: Technical philosophy under difficult public circumstances
sections.body: Russell's 1903 book The Principles of Mathematics was his own work, distinct from the later Principia Mathematica written with Alfred North Whitehead. His biography connects these investigations with the logic of Peano and Frege. It also describes how public events affected his writing: opposition to conscription led to loss of his Cambridge lectureship, and he wrote Introduction to Mathematical Philosophy during imprisonment in 1918. Analysis of Mind grew from a privately supported lecture series. His technical and public careers therefore developed together, rather than as a simple progression from mathematics to unrelated literary work.

terms.definition: An approach to knowledge emphasising experience and observation; the presentation connected Russell with this philosophical tradition.
The study of logical structures and methods used in mathematical reasoning, a central subject of Russell's early work and collaboration with Whitehead.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Separating hormones with different biological effects
sections.body: The adrenal cortex produced a mixture of substances that required chemical separation and characterization. Similar molecular structures did not imply identical activity. Reichstein developed a semisynthetic route to one useful cortical hormone, while cortisone, initially called Compound E, was isolated in several laboratories. Hench and Kendall had already investigated possible treatment with cortical preparations before cortisone became available. Their clinical report with Slocumb and Polley in 1949 described marked improvement in rheumatoid arthritis. The achievement linked difficult chemical work with observation of a specific physiological effect.

sections.heading: Clinical observations suggested an experimental treatment
sections.body: Hench noticed that rheumatoid arthritis symptoms sometimes improved during pregnancy or episodes of jaundice. These observations suggested that a changing bodily substance might influence the illness. Collaboration with Kendall connected that clinical question to isolated adrenal steroids. Compound E was difficult and expensive to obtain, delaying testing, but trials in 1948–1949 demonstrated its anti-inflammatory activity. Hench also investigated ACTH, a pituitary hormone that stimulates adrenal activity. The reasoning proceeded from an observed association to a testable treatment hypothesis; pregnancy or jaundice was not itself being proposed as a therapy.

sections.heading: Independent chemical programs met a clinical question
sections.body: Kendall’s group in Minnesota and Reichstein’s group in Zurich independently investigated adrenal-cortex hormones. Isolation, identification and production were gradual achievements, followed by larger-scale preparation that made physiological and clinical studies possible. Hench’s observations supplied a reason to test one of those hormones in rheumatoid arthritis. Cortisone reduced inflammation and symptoms, but that benefit did not remove the underlying disease. The biography thus distinguishes discovery of a useful therapeutic effect from a permanent cure and shows why access to sufficient purified material was essential for testing the idea.

terms.definition: Preparing a compound by chemically modifying a substance obtained from a natural source, rather than building it entirely from simpler materials.
Adrenocorticotropic hormone, produced by the pituitary gland, which stimulates hormone secretion from the adrenal cortex.
The outer region of the adrenal gland, which produces steroid hormones involved in several bodily functions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Keeping negotiations possible despite mistrust
sections.body: Bunche proposed using a ceasefire as the opening for negotiations on an armistice, with a final political settlement left for later. The presentation emphasised the difficulty of sustaining communication between parties marked by mutual suspicion.
