sections.heading: Diplomatic efforts within the United Nations framework
sections.body: Pearson’s work at the United Nations preceded the Suez Crisis. At the 1945 San Francisco Conference he advised Canada’s delegation and criticized the great powers’ veto. He also chaired the Political Committee during the UN’s 1947 consideration of Palestine. These activities were separate from his proposal during the Suez fighting in 1956. Believing a call for a ceasefire insufficient, Pearson sought an international force to help secure it. On 4 November 1956 he submitted a resolution asking the Secretary-General to prepare a plan within forty-eight hours. The force was intended to supervise the cessation of hostilities in the conflict area. The presentation speech contrasted this initiative with Pearson’s unsuccessful advocacy of a UN mission during the Hungarian uprising, illustrating both the possibilities and limits of international action.

sections.heading: Diplomatic foundations and international treaty development
sections.body: Before his work in Suez, Pearson gained diplomatic experience through various international commissions and conferences. He participated in the Hague Conference on Codification of International Law and several London Naval Conferences during the 1930s. His involvement extended to the Geneva World Disarmament Conference and sessions of the League of Nations. In Washington, he assisted in establishing the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration and the Food and Agriculture Organization. Pearson also drafted the speech used by Louis St. Laurent to propose the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. He also played a prominent role in UN discussions about the future of Palestine in 1947.

terms.definition: An international force operating under UN authority; Pearson’s Suez proposal sought troops to secure and supervise a cessation of hostilities.
The United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, established during the Second World War to organize international relief and recovery efforts.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Investigation of Right-Left Symmetry in Particle Reactions
sections.body: Lee and Yang initiated a revision of right-left symmetry by examining strange observations regarding K mesons. They identified that existing weak-interaction experiments had not adequately tested the symmetry assumption because they were arranged to yield identical results regardless of its validity. To address this, they proposed new experimental tests for various particle transformations. Following their lead, Chien-Shiung Wu used a magnetic field to orient cobalt nuclei at low temperatures. This setup revealed that electrons were emitted unequally in opposite directions relative to the nuclei’s orientation, demonstrating parity violation in this weak-interaction process.

sections.heading: Lee's academic development and early research
sections.body: Following graduate studies at the University of Chicago under Enrico Fermi, Lee held various positions including a research associate role at Yerkes Astronomical Observatory. His early scientific contributions involved complex problems in fields such as statistical mechanics and astrophysics. At Columbia University, he developed the renormalizable field theory model, frequently referred to as the Lee Model. By 1956, his rapid academic progression led him to become the youngest full professor in the history of the Columbia University faculty.

sections.heading: Foundational research in nuclear reactions and symmetry
sections.body: During his doctoral studies under Professor E. Teller, Yang investigated the angular distribution in nuclear reactions alongside coincidence measurements. His academic development involved studying group theory and molecular spectra for his undergraduate thesis, as well as order-disorder transformations for his master's work. These investigations established his primary research interests in symmetry principles and statistical mechanics. Following his education in China, he moved to the University of Chicago, where he studied under Professor E. Fermi before joining the Institute for Advanced Study.

terms.definition: The condition that a physical process follows the same laws under spatial reflection; Lee and Yang questioned whether weak interactions obeyed it.
A framework describing fields and their interactions throughout space and time; Lee developed a simplified model within this approach.
Ideas about transformations, such as rotations or spatial reflections, under which physical laws may remain unchanged.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Methods for Determining Insulin Chain Sequences
sections.body: Sanger used dinitrofluorobenzene to label free amino groups, including those at the ends of protein chains. The attached label survived acid hydrolysis, allowing the terminal amino acids to be identified among the breakdown products. Insulin’s two chains could then be studied separately. Partial digestion with acids or enzymes produced overlapping fragments, which Sanger and colleagues separated using chromatography and electrophoresis. Matching these overlaps allowed the original amino-acid order to be reconstructed. Insulin contains 51 residues: 21 in the A chain and 30 in the B chain. The presentation speech’s figures of 20 and 31 are erroneous. Locating the disulfide links joining the chains completed another part of the structural problem. The achievement established that a protein had a definite, experimentally recoverable sequence rather than an indefinite or merely repetitive arrangement.

sections.heading: From amino-acid metabolism to later sequencing methods
sections.body: Sanger’s doctoral work with A. Neuberger concerned lysine metabolism and was completed in 1943, before the insulin programme. Protein-structure research then occupied much of his work and led to the achievement recognised in 1958. After insulin, he developed methods for studying enzyme active centres. His biography’s later addendum describes a further change around 1960 toward RNA and DNA. Methods for identifying short RNA sequences preceded the development of rapid DNA sequencing in the 1970s. The dideoxy method was used to sequence bacteriophage φX174 DNA in 1977, followed by human mitochondrial DNA and bacteriophage lambda. These later accomplishments belong to the continuation of his career, rather than the evidence available for the 1958 prize.

terms.definition: A technique using a dye reagent to mark terminal amino acids, allowing researchers to identify chain ends after molecular fragmentation.
A DNA-sequencing method using chain-terminating nucleotides to produce fragments whose lengths reveal the sequence of bases.

sections.heading: The Refusal of the 1958 Nobel Prize
sections.body: The Academy’s announcement records two sharply different telegrams. On 25 October 1958, Pasternak responded to the award with gratitude and pride. On 29 October he said he must reject it because of the meaning attached to the honour in his society. Although his message described the rejection as voluntary, that wording must be read in the context of the Soviet pressure placed on him. It should not be treated as proof of an unconstrained personal choice or as the Academy withdrawing its judgment of his writing. The Academy stated that refusal did not alter the validity of the award. The practical consequence was that the presentation to him could not take place. The exchange distinguishes being selected as a laureate from being able to accept the prize.

sections.heading: Evolution of literary styles and translation work
sections.body: Pasternak's early career involved six years studying musical composition, inspired by Scriabin before he transitioned to philosophy in Germany. His poetic development included the sober style found in Themes and Variations and the psychological depictions within The Childhood of Luvers. He also explored historical subjects in verse, including the poem Lieutenant Schmidt. Beyond original poetry, he engaged in extensive translation of major dramas by Shakespeare, Goethe, Schiller, Kleist, and Ben Jonson. The biography describes Doctor Zhivago as combining lyrical description with an expansive dramatic narrative. These diverse literary efforts, ranging from short stories like Aerial Ways to autobiographical sketches, defined his multifaceted contribution to the Russian literary landscape.

terms.definition: A laureate’s rejection of the offered distinction; in Pasternak’s case, it did not annul the award and occurred under political pressure.
Narration that places individual actions and conflicts within a broad historical canvas; critics used the term for one aspect of Doctor Zhivago.

sections.heading: Development of Neurospora biochemistry research
sections.body: Beadle's scientific path included studying Mendelian asynopsis in Zea mays at Cornell University. During his time at the California Institute of Technology, he investigated crossing-over in Drosophila melanogaster alongside collaborators like Th. Dobzhansky and A.H. Sturtevant. Following a period at the Institut de Biologie physico-chimique in Paris with Boris Ephrussi, he focused on eye pigment development in fruit flies. These investigations eventually transitioned into studying the biochemistry of the fungus Neurospora, research which led to his 1958 Nobel Prize alongside Edward Lawrie Tatum.

sections.heading: Lederberg's academic career and microbiological research
sections.body: After studying medicine at Columbia, Lederberg went to Yale as a research fellow and graduate student with Edward Tatum. His research investigated genetic structure and function in microorganisms. He joined the University of Wisconsin in 1947 and organized its Department of Medical Genetics in 1957. After the Nobel award, he organized Stanford's Department of Genetics in 1959 and later directed the Kennedy Laboratories for Molecular Medicine. From 1978 to 1990 he was president of Rockefeller University. The biography's later addendum describes his continuing work on the relationship between gene function and mutagenesis in bacteria.

sections.heading: Biochemical research and nutrient requirements in Neurospora crassa
sections.body: During his collaboration at Stanford University, Tatum managed the chemical components of joint studies regarding Drosophila melanogaster eye-colour genetics. Upon transitioning their research focus to the fungus Neurospora crassa, Tatum identified that biotin was essential for cultivating this organism on simple inorganic media. This finding enabled cultivation of the fungus for the genetic investigations that led to the 1958 Nobel Prize. His earlier doctoral thesis focused on bacterial metabolism and nutrition under the direction of Edwin Broun Fred and William Harold Peterson.

terms.definition: A genus of fungi used in biochemical genetics; Beadle and Tatum turned to it after their earlier experiments on fruit-fly eye pigmentation.
The production of genetic mutations, a process Lederberg studied in relation to gene function in bacteria.
A nutrient Tatum found necessary to cultivate Neurospora crassa successfully on the otherwise simple medium used for their genetic experiments.

sections.heading: Expansion of Aid to Displaced Persons
sections.body: Pire's Aid to Displaced Persons developed from Belgian relief work into an international organisation in 1957. Its sponsorship scheme linked refugees with people outside the camps through letters and parcels. At the 1958 ceremony, the committee reported 15,000 sponsors in twenty countries; these figures describe the award period. Personal contact could offer encouragement, but it did not itself provide a way out of a camp. Pire therefore established four Belgian homes for elderly refugees and developed European Villages where displaced people could begin rebuilding their lives. The organisation's statutes called for material and moral assistance regardless of nationality or religion. Its Europe of the Heart appeal sought solidarity around people without a secure home, connecting practical help with relationships across national boundaries.

sections.heading: Development of humanitarian aid organizations and village construction
sections.body: Pire's refugee work grew from earlier Belgian relief organisations. His family-aid service and open-air camps, founded in 1938, fed children during and after the war. His later refugee programme combined sponsorship, homes for elderly people and purpose-built villages. The villages were placed near cities to allow residents to establish roots and economic independence while avoiding isolation, an aim rather than an automatic result of the design. The Fridtjof Nansen Village in Belgium opened in 1958. The eventual seven-village programme also included Wuppertal in 1959 and Euskirchen in 1962, after the Nobel award. Pire's international activities continued through the Europe of the Heart fundraising movement and, in 1960, the University of Peace at Huy. The latter brought people together for education and dialogue across national divisions.

terms.definition: Pire's name for a movement of solidarity with refugees, linking sponsorship, housing and other assistance across national and religious divisions.
Pire's small housing communities intended to help displaced families leave refugee camps and establish more independent lives near existing cities.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Applications of the Cerenkov effect in nuclear physics
sections.body: Cherenkov's observation of blue light from irradiated water led to a useful method of detecting fast charged particles. Such particles can emit Cherenkov light when they exceed the speed of light in the material they cross. Detectors use that emission to reveal particles and help measure their speeds. The biography describes applications in nuclear physics and cosmic-ray research, including an instrument aboard Sputnik III. Cherenkov also contributed to electron-accelerator construction and to studies of photon-induced nuclear and meson-producing reactions at the Lebedev Institute. These activities show how an initially puzzling optical observation became part of the experimental toolkit for investigating energetic particles.

sections.heading: Ilja Frank's research in nuclear and neutron physics
sections.body: Frank's early investigations concerned photoluminescence and photochemistry. After joining the Lebedev Institute in 1934, he began nuclear-physics work in Skobeltzyn's laboratory, including experiments on pair production by gamma rays and their measurement. Later research extended to neutron physics and reactions involving light nuclei and mesons. Alongside this experimental programme, he worked on the theory of Cherenkov radiation and related problems. He led the institute's Atomic Nucleus Laboratory from 1941 and, from 1957, also directed the neutron laboratory at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. His career combined theoretical interpretation with experimental questions about the behaviour of radiation and nuclei.

sections.heading: Tamm's theoretical physics contributions
sections.body: Tamm's early research, influenced by Leonid Mandelstam, examined the optical properties of crystals and the quantum theory of light scattering in solids. He later studied relativity, quantum mechanics and interactions between nuclear particles. With Frank he developed the theoretical explanation of Cherenkov radiation, relating the emission to a charged particle moving faster than light travels in the surrounding material. His wider research included cosmic-ray showers, the neutron's magnetic moment and ideas for controlling thermonuclear reactions. From 1934 he led the Lebedev Institute's theoretical division. These activities place the prize-winning explanation within a broad programme of mathematical work on radiation, matter and nuclear physics.

terms.definition: An instrument that detects light emitted by charged particles travelling faster than light propagates in a particular material, helping identify their passage and speed.
Radiation emitted when a charged particle travels through a material faster than light propagates in that material, without exceeding light's speed in vacuum.
The study of how light propagates through and interacts with crystals, including how their internal structure affects optical behaviour.

sections.heading: Development and application of the polarograph
sections.body: Inspired by suggestions from Bohumil Kucera regarding mercury capillarity, Heyrovsky transitioned from weighing mercury drops to measuring electrical current between a capillary and a collection point. To prevent substances from sticking to surfaces and disturbing experiments, he utilized falling mercury droplets to provide a continuously clean surface for chemical reactions. Alongside his collaborator Shikata, he constructed the polarograph, an apparatus that records how currents vary with applied tension to produce characteristic step curves. This method allows researchers to identify specific substances and determine their concentrations from the voltage positions and current heights of the steps. While initially used in his own laboratory, the technique eventually enabled industrial applications, such as accurately detecting metal impurities, and remains useful for analyzing various chemical elements and organic groups.

sections.heading: Development of the polarographic method and research institutions
sections.body: Following his studies in London under Professors Ramsay, Lewis, and Donnan, Heyrovsky focused his scientific career on expanding the branch of electrochemistry known as polarography. After inventing this method in 1922, he established a specialized school of Czech polarographers at Charles University in Prague. His leadership in this field led to his appointment as Director of the Polarographic Institute in 1950. This institution eventually became part of the Czechoslovak Academy of Sciences in 1952. Beyond his research, Heyrovsky held various international roles, including serving as Vice-President of the International Union of Physics from 1951 to 1957 and acting as the inaugural President of the Polarographic Society in London.

terms.definition: An analytical method that records current as applied voltage changes, using a renewed mercury-drop electrode to identify and measure substances in solution.
A scientific organization established in 1950 and later incorporated into the Czechoslovak Academy of Sciences for specialized research.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Classical influences and wartime transitions in Sicilian poetry
sections.body: The presentation speech connects Quasimodo’s poetry with Sicily’s classical inheritance: ancient temples, theatres and myths form part of the imaginative landscape it describes. It presents his classical studies and translations as sources of discipline in language, rather than models for simple imitation. His collections include Ed è subito sera, Giorno dopo giorno, La vita non è sogno, Il falso e vero verde and La terra impareggiabile. Across his developing work, the speech identifies a growing engagement with the suffering of contemporary Italy, sharpened by war and fascism. Biblical language appears alongside classical mythology. Quasimodo understood poetry as a creative activity with a public human purpose, capable of challenging isolation and helping people recognise one another’s experience.

sections.heading: Evolution of poetic form and linguistic purpose
sections.body: Quasimodo described a transition from lyric to epic poetry to address global torment through rational and emotional means. In the lecture he credited his 1940 Lirici Greci translations with renewing readers’ engagement with classical poetry. Separately, he recalled his own lyrics appearing in love letters and on prison walls. He rejected linguistic revolution or dialect-heavy styles, favoring a concrete language reminiscent of Dante’s simple style. Quasimodo argued that poets possess the exclusive right to develop written language, resisting political attempts to render poetry immobile through conformist criticism. He viewed the poet as an embodiment of contemporary experiences, navigating a path between religious expression and civic duty while avoiding the limitations of purely abstract or missionary-driven verse.

terms.definition: A heritage of ancient Greek literature and mythology that serves as a foundational background for modern poetic expression.
In Quasimodo’s lecture, poetry that moves beyond private feeling to address shared historical experience and human suffering.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Salvatore Quasimodo: The Poet and the Politician — Nobel lecture, 11 December 1959

sections.heading: Experimental laboratory synthesis of nucleic acids
sections.body: The prize recognized experiments showing that enzymes could assemble nucleic-acid chains outside cells. Kornberg’s DNA polymerase used an existing DNA strand to direct the sequence of a complementary strand. The presentation speech described both laureates’ results as template copying, but that historical account requires qualification. Ochoa’s polynucleotide phosphorylase can synthesize RNA chains without copying a template. Its important laboratory use did not establish that it normally carried out DNA-directed RNA synthesis in cells; later work clarified roles in RNA breakdown and processing. The distinction separates a demonstrated chemical reaction from an initially mistaken interpretation of its physiological function.

sections.heading: Enzymatic pathways in nucleotide and DNA synthesis
sections.body: Kornberg investigated the enzymatic synthesis of coenzymes and inorganic pyrophosphate before focusing on nucleic acid biosynthesis. He identified PRPP as an intermediate during his study of pyrimidine and purine nucleotide synthesis pathways. This research led to his discovery of DNA polymerase, the enzyme that assembles building blocks into DNA. These enzymes are essential for DNA replication, repair, and rearrangements. The updated biography links the wider study of DNA-processing enzymes with the later development of recombinant-DNA technology and biotechnology.

sections.heading: Enzymatic processes in biological oxidation and synthesis
sections.body: Ochoa investigated various enzymatic mechanisms involving energy transfer and metabolic steps. His research explored the reductive carboxylation of pyruvic and ketoglutaric acids, alongside the photochemical reduction of pyridine nucleotides during photosynthesis. He studied the biological functions of vitamin B1 and the role of condensing enzyme within the Krebs citric acid cycle. Additionally, his work addressed the biosynthesis of nucleic acids and the metabolic pathways of fatty acids and carbohydrates, contributing to knowledge of oxidative phosphorylation. The biography also includes genetic-code research from his later career.

terms.definition: An existing nucleic-acid strand whose sequence guides the order of building blocks in a complementary strand.
A ubiquitous class of enzymes that assembles nucleotide building blocks into DNA, essential for genetic replication, repair, and rearrangements.
The enzyme that joins an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to oxaloacetate, forming citrate in the citric acid cycle.

sections.heading: Diplomatic contributions and League of Nations involvement
sections.body: Following his service in the Quaker Ambulance Unit, Noel-Baker supported Fridtjof Nansen during relief efforts in Greece and Russia. While working for the Foreign Office, he assisted Sir Robert Cecil during the 1919 Paris peace negotiations, helping draft the League of Nations Covenant and the International Labour Organization’s founding documents. His League of Nations career included serving as head of the Mandate Section and acting as an adviser to Arthur Henderson. He continued working on international disarmament efforts in the early 1930s. In his 1926 book, The League of Nations at Work, he detailed the organization's structure. Later, he influenced the United Nations Preparatory Commission, promoting the International Refugee Organization and proposals for a European economic commission.

sections.heading: Academic foundations and scholarly contributions to disarmament research
sections.body: Noel-Baker established a rigorous academic background through honors in economics and history at King’s College, Cambridge, alongside studies as a Whewell scholar in international law. His scholarly output focused on analyzing global security frameworks and arms control. He authored several significant works, including The Geneva Protocol for the Pacific Settlement of International Disputes and Disarmament. His 1958 publication, The Arms Race: A Programme for World Disarmament, synthesized extensive research with his direct experiences from the 1919 Paris Peace Conference. This analytical study later received the Albert Schweitzer Book Prize. Beyond legal scholarship, he applied his expertise to administrative roles, such as defining the responsibilities and privileges of United Nations staff members during the organization's formative period.

terms.definition: An association of states established to prevent war and promote international cooperation regarding health, welfare, and economic areas.
A Cambridge scholarship distinction in international law, held by Noel-Baker during the academic training that preceded his diplomatic and disarmament work.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Testing Dirac's theory of particles and antiparticles
sections.body: Finding the proton’s antiparticle tested whether the particle–antiparticle relationship extended beyond the electron and positron. Producing proton–antiproton pairs required much more energy than producing electron–positron pairs. Cosmic rays could supply high energies, but an accelerator offered more controlled conditions. Berkeley’s Bevatron reached energies of about six billion electronvolts, sufficient for this search. The presentation speech emphasized that the machine alone did not make the discovery: Chamberlain, Segrè and their colleagues needed methods capable of detecting and identifying rare antiprotons. Subsequent experiments with antineutrons extended experimental knowledge of antimatter to a particle with no electric charge.

sections.heading: Research into proton scattering and antiproton interactions
sections.body: Following work on neutron diffraction, Chamberlain studied proton–proton scattering with Segrè and Clyde Wiegand. Experiments on polarization included triple scattering with Thomas Ypsilantis and Robert Tripp. Chamberlain, Segrè, Wiegand and Ypsilantis discovered the antiproton in 1955. Over the following years, the group studied antiproton interactions with hydrogen, deuterium and other targets, and used antiprotons to produce antineutrons. Chamberlain’s updated biography also describes work after the Nobel award: from 1960, he, Carson Jeffries and Gilbert Shapiro developed polarized proton targets. These enabled studies of how high-energy scattering depends on spin, including tests involving pi mesons, protons and electrons.

sections.heading: Segrè's research in atomic and nuclear physics
sections.body: Before his work with Chamberlain, Segrè focused on atomic spectroscopy, specifically studying the Zeeman effect and forbidden lines. His early nuclear investigations included neutron research alongside Enrico Fermi between 1934 and 1935. Through various collaborations, he helped identify the elements technetium and astatine, as well as the isotope plutonium-239 and its fission properties. His scientific career also involved investigating spontaneous fission, isomerism, and nucleon interactions. His research later extended to high-energy physics; in 1955 at Berkeley he discovered the antiproton with Chamberlain, Wiegand and Ypsilantis.

terms.definition: The creation of a particle and its antiparticle in an energetic process, as in proton–antiproton production.
A target in which proton spins have a preferred orientation, allowing experiments to test how particle interactions depend on spin.
The study of light emitted or absorbed by atoms to investigate their structure and behaviour, including spectral lines and magnetic-field effects.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms and applications of carbon-14 dating
sections.body: Cosmic-ray reactions produce carbon-14 in the atmosphere. It enters carbon dioxide and circulates through living systems. Once a sample stops exchanging carbon with its surroundings, radioactive decay reduces its carbon-14 content. Libby’s methods made these very low activities measurable and compared them with an estimate of the original activity to infer age. Experiments with materials of known age tested the approach. The 1960 presentation speech described uses in archaeology, geology and studies of ocean circulation. Its explanation assumed an approximately steady production and distribution of atmospheric radiocarbon; the statement that all living material has exactly the atmospheric ratio should not be taken as universal. The speech’s quoted working range of roughly 500–30,000 years also reflected the methods then available, rather than the full reach of later radiocarbon dating.

sections.heading: Libby's professional roles and scientific specializations
sections.body: A specialist in radiochemistry, Libby focused on isotope tracer work, hot atom chemistry, and tracer techniques. During the 1940s, his research at Columbia University involved the Manhattan District Project while he was on leave from Berkeley. Following World War II, he joined the University of Chicago's Institute for Nuclear Studies, where he gained recognition for studying natural tritium for applications in geophysics and hydrology. His scientific influence extended to government service through appointments to the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission's General Advisory Committee and the Plowshare Advisory Committee. Beyond laboratory research, Libby authored the 1952 book Radiocarbon Dating and served on editorial boards for prestigious publications like Science and the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

terms.definition: The time required for half the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay, leaving half of the original amount.
A field of chemistry involving the study of radioactive isotopes, including tracer techniques and hot atom chemistry.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Poetic style and structural characteristics
sections.body: The 1960 presentation speech highlighted a dense poetic form combining prose and verse. It described biblical rhythms blending with the French Alexandrine to produce a solemn flow. The early cycle Pour fêter une enfance evokes childhood memories of Guadeloupe through vivid images of its plants and animals. Anabase presents a mysterious military expedition through Asian deserts. The committee traced related formal qualities through Exil and Vents, and read Chronique as containing veiled references to the contemporary world. In its interpretation, the difficult symbols and expansive imagery served a broadly human purpose: portraying creativity, displacement and the struggle with natural forces. The speech connected this ambition to the classical French rhetorical tradition. These are the committee’s readings of his poetry, rather than a claim that every poem has a single decipherable message.

sections.heading: Poetry and science as shared modes of investigation
sections.body: In his 1960 Nobel banquet speech, Saint-John Perse addressed the perceived dissociation between poetic activity and a materialistic society. He argued that both scientists and poets engage in disinterested thought to explore common mysteries. While physics utilizes doctrines like the general theory of relativity and quantum uncertainty, the poet uses imagination to approach reality. This connection is further illustrated by scientific innovators who use intuition to support reason or describe modern cosmology through equations. Perse suggested that poetry serves as a way of life that preserves spiritual needs when mythologies vanish. He viewed the poetic mind as an essential force capable of breaking through inertia and reflecting the human condition amidst the challenges of the atomic age.

terms.definition: A traditional French verse line of twelve syllables, whose rhythm the committee heard within Perse’s flowing poetic prose.
Inquiry pursued without immediate personal gain or practical utility; Perse used the idea to connect the intellectual aims of scientists and poets.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Saint-John Perse: poetry, scientific inquiry and imagination — Nobel banquet speech, 10 December 1960

sections.heading: Mechanisms of immunological tolerance development
sections.body: Burnet proposed that recognition of the body's own tissues develops through exposure during early life. This suggested a test: could foreign cells introduced during immune development also become tolerated? Medawar, Billingham and Brent introduced donor cells into developing mice and later tested skin grafts. Many recipients accepted grafts from the donor strain while retaining the ability to reject unrelated tissue. The result established specificity: tolerance to one donor did not mean loss of every immune response. The experiment challenged the idea that rejection between genetically different individuals was unavoidable. The ceremony's account of fetal immunity reflects the historical framework of the discovery; it should not be read as a claim that fetuses possess no immune functions.

sections.heading: Burnet's research on influenza and viral cultivation
sections.body: Burnet's influenza research formed a separate strand from the immune-tolerance work recognised by the prize. He isolated an Australian influenza A strain in 1935 and investigated variation in the virus's properties, including virulence and serological reactions. His work with W. I. B. Beveridge used the chorioallantoic membrane of chicken embryos to grow viruses. Counting the lesions produced on these membranes offered a way to estimate the relative concentration of infectious material. In 1947, Burnet and Stone identified a receptor-destroying enzyme in Vibrio cholerae, contributing to further biochemical investigations of influenza. These experiments joined virus cultivation with measurement, enabling researchers to compare samples and investigate their biological behaviour.

sections.heading: From graft rejection to experimentally acquired tolerance
sections.body: During the Second World War, Medawar investigated why skin from one person usually fails to survive as a permanent graft on another. This work established principles of transplantation immunity. At Birmingham from 1947, he and Rupert Billingham examined skin grafting and pigmentation in cattle, including whether graft responses could distinguish identical from non-identical twins. Ray Owen's findings helped suggest that acceptance of another individual's tissue might be acquired during development and reproduced experimentally. After moving to London in 1951, Medawar continued the tolerance research with Billingham and Leslie Brent. The progression from graft rejection to early-life tolerance experiments linked surgical observations, developmental biology and immunology.

terms.definition: A specific lack of an immune response to particular material; in these experiments, early exposure enabled later acceptance of donor-strain grafts.
Growing viruses on an extraembryonic membrane of a developing chicken embryo; visible lesions can provide an experimental measure of infectious material.
A tissue graft between genetically different individuals of the same species, now usually called an allograft.

sections.heading: Political development and leadership within the African National Congress
sections.body: Lutuli joined the African National Congress in 1944, entered its Natal committee in 1945 and became national president in 1952. His leadership coincided with a move from petitions toward boycotts, strikes and defiance campaigns against discriminatory laws. The presentation speech emphasised his commitment to nonviolent action and his effort to navigate differing views within the movement. Government restrictions increasingly limited his travel, public speaking and political activity. He nevertheless expressed his position through articles in the newspaper Post and a political review sent to the South African Institute of Race Relations. The speech’s implication that his presidency ended when the ANC was banned in 1960 is misleading: a ban on the organisation did not terminate his leadership. The prize honoured his contribution to the struggle against racial oppression.

sections.heading: Lutuli's leadership and political transition
sections.body: Lutuli joined the ANC in 1944, served on its Natal committee from 1945 and became provincial president in 1951. In 1952 he helped organise campaigns defying discriminatory laws. The government then demanded that he choose between his position as chief and his ANC membership. He refused to surrender either voluntarily and was removed from the chieftainship. A month later, he was elected ANC president-general. The conflict showed how a locally rooted leader’s responsibilities had broadened into opposition to racial restrictions across South Africa. His activism addressed limits on political representation and the pass laws controlling movement, as well as the wider system of apartheid.

terms.definition: A policy of using peaceful means, such as boycotts and strikes, to oppose political discrimination without resorting to violence.
The system of racial segregation and white-minority domination intensified by South Africa’s National Party government after its 1948 election victory.

sections.heading: Mechanism and development of the bubble chamber
sections.body: Glaser achieved the first radiation-sensitive bubble chamber in 1952 by utilizing a liquid heated near its boiling point. By rapidly reducing pressure, perhaps via a mobile piston, the liquid enters an unstable superheated state. When an energetic charged particle traverses this medium, it produces ions that act as centers for bubble development. These small bubbles form along the particle's path, creating a track that can be captured with a light flash before general boiling occurs. Some later large chambers used liquid hydrogen at very low temperatures, with powerful magnets to curve charged-particle paths. Such advanced chambers also incorporate automatic read-off apparatuses connected to mathematical computers to process information from the tracks.

sections.heading: Experimental research into elementary particles
sections.body: Before developing the bubble chamber, Glaser investigated several detection methods, including parallel-plate spark counters and diffusion cloud chambers. His later experimental work at facilities like the Bevatron at Lawrence Radiation Laboratory and the Cosmotron at Brookhaven National Laboratory provided data regarding the spins, decay modes, and lifetimes of particles including neutral kaons and hyperons. He also studied pion-proton scattering and branching ratios in positive K meson decay. These investigations into strange particles were conducted alongside various colleagues and students while he held positions at the University of Michigan and the University of California, Berkeley. His research efforts received support from the United States Atomic Energy Commission and the National Science Foundation.

terms.definition: A liquid above its boiling temperature at the prevailing pressure that temporarily remains liquid until bubble formation is initiated.
A detector maintaining a supersaturated vapour in which ionisation along a charged particle’s path triggers visible droplets.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of carbon dioxide fixation and regeneration
sections.body: Calvin and his collaborators used carbon-14 to follow carbon dioxide into the products of photosynthesis. They identified a ribulose-derived acceptor that combines with carbon dioxide, leading to phosphoglyceric acid. Further reactions reduce this product towards the carbohydrate level using a reducing agent and an energy-rich phosphate supplied through light-dependent processes. A crucial problem was regeneration: carbon fixation uses the acceptor, so continued assimilation requires it to be rebuilt. The ceremony described a regeneration pathway involving numerous intermediates and enzymes. This distinction matters because the cycle does not simply run once from carbon dioxide to a finished sugar. It continually regenerates the molecule needed to capture more carbon, while light-driven processes replenish the chemical resources consumed by the cycle.

sections.heading: Development of Isotopic Carbon Techniques
sections.body: Carbon-14 became readily available to Calvin's programme after the Second World War, enabling techniques for tracing carbon through photosynthesis. His research interests had developed across several areas of chemistry. A 1935 doctoral thesis examined the electron affinity of halogens; work with Michael Polanyi in Manchester then stimulated an interest in coordination catalysis and metalloporphyrins. At Berkeley, interactions with Gilbert Lewis and G. E. K. Branch helped shape his approach to molecular structure and behaviour. These chemical interests converged in the investigation of photosynthetic carbon assimilation. The biography describes a laboratory drawing researchers from physics, chemistry and biology, reflecting the combination of tracing techniques, molecular analysis and biological experiments needed for the problem.

terms.definition: The incorporation of inorganic carbon, such as carbon dioxide, into organic molecules through biochemical reactions.
A radioactive isotope of carbon used as a tracer, allowing labelled carbon atoms to be followed through chemical reactions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of the Bosnian trilogy and psychological studies
sections.body: During the German occupation, Andrić composed three novels known as the Bosnian trilogy. These works share a historical setting symbolized by the cross and crescent. The Bridge on the Drina, published in 1945, depicts a bridge serving as a site for armies and caravans to connect East and West within the Ottoman Empire. His 1945 work, Bosnian Story, explores the Napoleonic Wars through the rivalry of Austrian and French consuls amidst religious tensions. Additionally, his 1945 novel, The Woman from Sarajevo, provides a psychological study regarding the pathological nature of avarice. Later, his 1954 story, Devil’s Yard, utilizes an Istanbul prison setting to combine modern psychological insight with the fatalism found in the Arabian Nights.

sections.heading: Evolution of literary forms and thematic focus
sections.body: Andrić transitioned from poetry, contributing to Hrvatska mlada lirika, to lyrical prose such as the diary-style Nemiri. His early novella, Put Alije Djerzeleza, demonstrated a method of using Bosnian life to address universal human issues. During the Second World War, he produced significant chronicles including Na Drini cuprija and Travnicka hronika. Gospodjica examines the psychology of wealth, while other works return to earlier historical settings. For instance, Devil’s Yard depicts a Bosnian Franciscan imprisoned under Ottoman rule. His later output included collections such as Lica and essays like Zapisi o Goji, maintaining a focus on regional history and diverse populations shaped by clashing Eastern and Western influences.

terms.definition: A group of three novels sharing a common historical setting symbolized by the crescent and the cross.
A narrative following events across time; Andrić used this form to connect fictional lives with the history of Bosnia and its communities.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of sound transmission and cochlear vibration
sections.body: Sound vibrations travel through the ossicle chain to the stirrup footplate, which moves against the oval window. This motion engages the cochlear fluid, initiating waves along the basilar membrane. Using a thin needle as both a mechanical stimulus and an electrode, Békésy demonstrated that local pressure creates shearing forces on hair cells. He observed that these vibrations form a wave complex moving from the stiff base toward the flexible apex. The peak amplitude of this wave shifts based on sound frequency, appearing near the base for high frequencies and the apex for low frequencies. Additionally, his research identified the endocochlear potential and slow potential shifts in receptor cells, helping connect mechanical vibration with electrical changes in the receptors that lead to nerve signals.

sections.heading: Development of a mechanical inner ear model
sections.body: While working at Harvard University's Psycho-Acoustic Laboratory, Békésy focused on creating a mechanical model of the inner ear. This experimental setup utilized the skin of an arm to represent the necessary nerve supply. The construction demonstrated such significant similarities to actual hearing phenomena that it became a practical tool for investigating long-standing specific problems. Previously, his research at the Hungarian Post Office laboratory involved studying long-distance telephone transmission and the ear's role in transmission systems. He also created a patient-operated audiometer during his time in Sweden. This device proved versatile enough to measure changes in pigeon eye sensitivity during dark adaptation, demonstrating utility beyond traditional audiology applications.

terms.definition: The role of the cochlea in separating sound characteristics based on the specific location of membrane vibrations.
An experimental apparatus using physical components, such as arm skin, to represent biological nerve supply and simulate hearing phenomena.

sections.heading: Principles of the United Nations Secretariat
sections.body: As Secretary-General, Hammarskjöld established that the Secretariat must obtain objective information regarding member nations while ensuring the leader personally forms opinions based strictly on UN Charter rules. He operated as an international civil servant, prioritizing the organization's ideals over individual political interests. This approach enabled him to manage critical conflicts, such as the 1958 crisis involving Lebanon, Jordan, and Arab States. His methods also facilitated the suspension of hostilities between France, Great Britain, Israel, and Egypt through the establishment of a UN force to supervise borders. When instructions were unclear or members failed to agree, he used personal initiative to address disputes. The crisis following Congo’s independence in 1960 presented a further challenge to applying the United Nations’ principles.

sections.heading: Implementation of preventive diplomacy and peacekeeping operations
sections.body: To enhance international effectiveness, Hammarskjöld utilized preventive diplomacy to manage global conflicts. He drafted specific regulations for a 4,000-person Secretariat to ensure staff remained independent from narrow national interests. During the 1956 Suez Canal crisis, he engaged in personal diplomacy and worked with the United Nations to nullify force used by Great Britain, France, and Israel. This period saw him commission the United Nations Emergency Force, to supervise the ceasefire and withdrawal of invading forces. His operational leadership extended to the Congo following its 1960 independence, where he managed a peacekeeping force amidst army mutiny, Belgian troop intervention, and the secession of Katanga. Earlier, in 1954–1955, he negotiated the release of Americans whom Chinese forces had captured during the Korean War.

terms.definition: An official serving an international organization rather than one national government; Hammarskjöld understood this as responsibility to the United Nations and its Charter.
Diplomatic action intended to prevent disputes from escalating or spreading into wider conflict.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
United Nations: Dag Hammarskjöld biography and the 1955 prisoner negotiations

sections.heading: Experimental methods for investigating nuclear structure and radiation
sections.body: To study nuclei, Hofstadter utilized a linear accelerator at Stanford University to bombard targets with electrons with energies of nearly one billion electronvolts. Using magnetic spectrometers, he measured how these high-energy electrons deviated to map electric charge distributions. Meanwhile, Mössbauer investigated resonance absorption by observing gamma radiation in solids. He demonstrated that atoms bound in crystals can emit radiation without the frequency changes caused by recoil. This discovery allows for studying nuclear energy level shifts and verifying relativity through the Doppler effect using extremely small velocities.

sections.heading: Development of electron-scattering and scintillation detection methods
sections.body: At Princeton, Hofstadter found that thallium-activated sodium iodide crystals could detect radiation and measure the energy of gamma rays and energetic particles. After moving to Stanford in 1950, he developed equipment for electron-scattering experiments while continuing detector research. His Stanford work included fast inorganic scintillators and Cerenkov counters, distinct types of detector. High-energy electron scattering then became his main focus. Measurements revealed the size and surface thickness of nuclei and, later, the distributions of charge and magnetic moment within protons and neutrons. The biography places many principal nucleon results in 1954–1957, followed by more precise form-factor measurements.

sections.heading: Experimental discovery of recoilless nuclear resonance absorption
sections.body: Mössbauer investigated gamma-ray absorption during his doctoral research at the Institute for Physics within the Max Planck Institute for Medical Research in Heidelberg. Work there led to the observation of recoilless nuclear resonance absorption, with direct experimental evidence established in 1958. He also developed a theoretical interpretation of the phenomenon. After a period at the Technical University in Munich, he moved to the California Institute of Technology in 1960 and continued his investigations of gamma absorption. The research joined questions about nuclear transitions with the behaviour of atoms bound in solids.

terms.definition: Absorption that occurs when a photon’s energy matches the energy difference between suitable nuclear states, allowing the nucleus to make that transition.
A detector that converts deposited radiation energy into brief flashes of light, which can be counted and used to measure particle or photon energies.
Gamma-ray absorption by nuclei bound in a solid without appreciable recoil-energy loss, allowing nuclear resonance to be observed with exceptional precision.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Heavy atom incorporation for protein structure determination
sections.body: To overcome structural determination difficulties, researchers utilized heavy atoms to alter diffraction patterns. In 1953, Perutz incorporated mercury into specific positions within the haemoglobin molecule to facilitate more direct analysis. Similarly, Kendrew used mercury or gold atoms within myoglobin to proceed with his investigations. Determining the myoglobin structure required measuring intensities from approximately 250,000 X-ray reflections across 110 crystals. This massive computational task was made practicable through the use of a large electronic computer, allowing for the mapping of these complex globular proteins.

sections.heading: Protein structure research at Cavendish Laboratory
sections.body: Following wartime research on radar and reaction kinetics, Kendrew joined the Cavendish Laboratory to collaborate with Perutz under Lawrence Bragg. This work occurred within the Medical Research Council Unit, an organization that later became the Laboratory of Molecular Biology. Focusing on X-ray analysis of myoglobin, Kendrew produced a three-dimensional model at 6Å resolution in 1957 and achieved an almost complete structure by 1960. His research contributions also included founding and serving as Editor-in-Chief for the Journal of Molecular Biology.

sections.heading: Development of haemoglobin structural research
sections.body: Perutz initiated his investigation into haemoglobin following a 1937 conversation with F. Haurowitz. Working with G.S. Adair, who produced horse haemoglobin crystals, Perutz learned X-ray photography and interpretation from Bernal and Fankuchen. While conducting X-ray work at the Cavendish Laboratory, he utilized biochemical facilities at the Molteno Institute provided by D. Keilin. An early study examined crystals of both haemoglobin and chymotrypsin. Difficulties with the twinned chymotrypsin crystals encouraged Perutz to concentrate on haemoglobin. His efforts helped bridge the gap between physics and biology through integrated laboratory work.

terms.definition: Determining how a molecule’s atoms are arranged in space, including their relative positions and distances from one another.
The level of detail visible in a molecular model; Kendrew’s early myoglobin model was refined to reveal increasingly precise atomic structure.
Investigating protein structure through crystals and their X-ray diffraction patterns, combining protein preparation with physical measurement and interpretation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Conscience and the costs of progress
sections.body: The presentation speech defended the continuing force of Steinbeck’s later writing, especially The Winter of Our Discontent, published in 1961. Its central character, a New England grocery clerk from a declining family, faces pressure to pursue material success at the expense of personal integrity. The committee praised Steinbeck’s ability to explore public questions through ordinary situations and an individual conscience. It also discussed Travels with Charley, published in 1962, as a journey through American society. Steinbeck’s account combines local observations with unease about changes presented as progress, including the destruction of wooded land for urban development. These examples helped the committee explain the connection between realistic detail, imagination and social criticism. Its appraisal concerned the moral questions raised by the writing, rather than a claim that every book offered a single sociological argument.

sections.heading: Evolution of Steinbeck's literary themes and styles
sections.body: After attempting a freelance writing career in New York, Steinbeck returned to California following unsuccessful efforts to establish himself. His early publication, Tortilla Flat, utilized humorous narratives regarding Monterey paisanos. He subsequently transitioned toward more serious fiction characterized by aggressive social criticism. This shift is evident in In Dubious Battle, which examines strikes among migratory fruit pickers on plantations. His later bibliography includes the travelogue Travels with Charley, recounting impressions from a three-month truck tour across forty American states. While his novels frequently function as social novels addressing rural labor's economic difficulties, the Nobel biography also identifies an attachment to the land that can sit uneasily beside a matter-of-fact sociological interpretation.

terms.definition: The ability to observe and interpret the experiences of people and the complexities of society through realistic and imaginative writing.
Fiction that explores social conditions and their effects on people’s lives, including the economic problems of rural labour in Steinbeck’s writing.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Molecular structure and the genetic code
sections.body: DNA combines sugar–phosphate chains with four kinds of bases. X-ray diffraction at King’s College, including work by Wilkins and by Franklin with Gosling, supplied essential structural evidence. Watson and Crick proposed two intertwined chains with specific complementary base pairs. This arrangement connected molecular structure to biological information: the order of bases can vary, while pairing allows each strand to guide formation of its complement. The presentation speech also discussed the emerging relationship between nucleic-acid sequences and protein synthesis. Its tentative wording about RNA reflects knowledge at the time. Determining the double helix and subsequently deciphering the genetic code were related but distinct achievements.

sections.heading: Francis Crick's scientific development and research contributions
sections.body: After working for the British Admiralty during the war, Crick transitioned from physics to biology. Supported by a Medical Research Council studentship, he conducted research at Cambridge's Strangeways Research Laboratory and later joined M. F. Perutz's unit. With W. Cochran and V. Vand, he developed a general theory regarding X-ray diffraction by a helix. Following his 1953 proposal for the DNA double-helical structure with J. Watson, Crick also suggested theories for small virus structures and investigated polyglycine II, collagen, and polyadenylic acid structures.

sections.heading: Development of the double-helical DNA model
sections.body: Seeing Wilkins’s DNA diffraction pattern at a Naples meeting in 1951 helped turn Watson toward molecular structure. At Cambridge, he and Crick combined model building with evidence from King’s College. Their failed 1951 attempt preceded the complementary double-helix model of March 1953. That evidence included Franklin and Gosling’s work, whose contribution is essential to the wider discovery story. Watson also investigated tobacco mosaic virus, obtaining evidence for its helical construction in June 1952 using improved X-ray equipment. His subsequent work at Caltech with Alexander Rich examined RNA structure. These were connected interests in biological molecules, but the virus experiment and the DNA model were separate results.

terms.definition: The correspondence between nucleotide triplets and amino acids or stop signals during protein synthesis; it is more specific than simply the information stored in DNA.
The scattering of X-rays into patterns that reveal spatial organisation within a sample, allowing structural models to be tested.
A sequence of linked nucleotide units forming a strand of a nucleic acid such as DNA or RNA.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Campaigning against radioactive fallout and nuclear testing
sections.body: During the middle of the 1950s, Pauling focused his efforts on protesting nuclear explosions due to the increasing atmospheric radioactive fallout. He performed personal investigations and calculations to estimate how such fallout might impact human health and hereditary factors in future generations. To prevent the detonation of a fifty-megaton bomb, Pauling sent telegrams to Premier Khrushchev and President Kennedy, requesting that both nations avoid atmospheric testing. While visiting the Academy of Science in Moscow in 1961, he delivered lectures regarding disarmament and submitted a draft agreement for a test ban to the Soviet leader. In October 1962, he estimated that US and Soviet tests during the previous year or so had released twice the fallout of the preceding sixteen years of testing.

sections.heading: Scientific advocacy for nuclear test bans
sections.body: Pauling utilized scientific analysis to advocate against the expansion of nuclear arsenals. He calculated estimates regarding the probable frequency of congenital deformity in future generations caused by radioactive fission products and carbon 14 released during testing. As a member of Einstein’s Emergency Committee of Atomic Scientists, he protested hydrogen bomb production and promoted multilateral disarmament. In 1958, he presented a petition to the UN signed by 9,235 scientists protesting further nuclear testing. He also published No More War!, which proposed creating a World Peace Research Organization within the UN structure. Following the Soviet Union's 1961 announcement of resumed nuclear testing, Pauling worked to convince American, British, and Russian leaders of the necessity of a test ban treaty.

terms.definition: Radioactive particles from a nuclear explosion that spread through the atmosphere and settle back onto the Earth.
A group active from 1946 to 1950 that included Albert Einstein and addressed issues regarding nuclear warfare.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Quantum investigations of helium and electron behavior
sections.body: Landau’s theory of superfluid helium treated the liquid’s collective motion rather than starting with separate atomic motions. Excited states could be described through quasiparticles with particular energies and momenta. He combined calculations with experimental information to establish their properties. Neutron-scattering experiments in Stockholm in 1957 directly tested this description of excitations. His work also explained second sound, a form of wave propagation distinct from ordinary sound. A separate theory, developed in 1956–1958, addressed the lighter isotope helium-3 at very low temperatures. That theory predicted another kind of wave, zero sound. The 1962 presentation speech described the experimental search for zero sound as ongoing; it did not report its detection in the 1957 neutron experiments. These distinctions matter because the two helium isotopes obey different quantum statistics and require different theories.

sections.heading: Development of quantum liquid theories and phase transition formulations
sections.body: Landau’s scientific work ranged from fluid mechanics to quantum field theory, but condensed matter formed a major part of it. In 1936 he developed a general thermodynamic approach to continuous, or second-order, phase transitions. Following experimental discoveries of superfluidity, he investigated quantum liquids at very low temperatures. His papers of 1941–1947 treated Bose-type liquids, including ordinary helium-4. Between 1956 and 1958 he developed the theory of Fermi-type liquids, including helium-3. The distinction reflects the different quantum statistics governing their constituent particles. These theories supplied ways to understand collective behaviour that ordinary classical descriptions could not adequately capture. Landau also collaborated with E. M. Lifshitz on the Course of Theoretical Physics, for which they received the Lenin Science Prize in 1962.

terms.definition: A liquid state exhibiting flow without ordinary viscous resistance, including the ability to pass readily through very fine channels.
The study of matter in solid and liquid forms, including how interactions among many particles produce collective properties.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of Ziegler catalysts and stereoregular polymer formation
sections.body: Ziegler studied reactions in which small molecules joined growing chains associated with organometallic compounds. Combining aluminium compounds with other metal compounds produced catalyst systems useful for controlled polymerisation. Natta extended this chemistry to the spatial order of the resulting chains. Certain catalysts repeatedly arranged newly added units in the same relative configuration, producing stereoregular polymers. This is not simply a claim that every reaction occurs at an aluminium atom or that all side groups point in one fixed direction in space. Isotactic chains can adopt helical conformations with side groups facing outward. Their regular structure changes how chains pack together and therefore changes material properties.

sections.heading: Stereospecific polymerization and industrial polymer development
sections.body: Supported by Montecatini, research into organometallic catalysts enabled the discovery of polymers with sterically ordered structures, including isotactic, syndiotactic, and di-isotactic types. These studies produced isotactic polypropylene, which was manufactured at a Ferrara plant in 1957 for use as Moplen, Meraklon, Merakrin, or Moplefan. Additionally, investigations into butadiene polymerization created cis-1,4 polymers with high steric purity. Using X-ray investigations, the exact arrangement of chains within the lattice of these new crystalline polymers was determined, alongside the synthesis of alternating copolymers.

sections.heading: Organometallic Catalyst Development and Olefin Polymerization
sections.body: During his tenure at the Max-Planck-Institut fur Kohlenforschung, Karl Ziegler conducted extensive research regarding reactions involving organ aluminium compounds. He discovered organometallic mixed catalysts specifically used for the polymerization of olefins. This chemical process enabled the synthesis of high-density polyethylene. His scientific contributions also included investigations into multi-membered ring systems and the chemistry of radicals with trivalent carbon. These advancements in organometallic chemistry provided the essential mechanisms for creating specific polymer structures through controlled catalytic reactions.

terms.definition: Describing a polymer whose successive stereochemical units have the same relative configuration, creating regularity along the chain.
A process involving organometallic catalysts to create polymers possessing a specific, sterically ordered molecular structure.
A compound containing a carbon–carbon double bond; olefins such as ethylene can be joined by polymerisation into long molecular chains.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Poetic techniques and mythological integration
sections.body: Seferis utilizes a subtle, rhythmical, and metaphorical language to interpret ancient Greek heritage. His poetic method involves using imagination to explore names from the Iliad, such as in The King of Asine. He often employs a central narrative figure, resembling an Odysseus with characteristics of Smyrna seamen, to dramatize historical Greek disasters and valor through a mask of anonymity. Technically influenced by T. S. Eliot, his work incorporates echoes of ancient Greek chorus music. Seferis also presents the Argonauts' story as a parable blending myth and history. His verse captures the Mediterranean landscape, portraying Greece as a maritime kingdom of islands and sea, while connecting contemporary wartime events in the Mediterranean to classical mythological figures.

sections.heading: Evolution of poetic themes and stylistic development
sections.body: Seferis's writing developed from the Symbolist-influenced rhymed lyrics of Strophe (Turning Point, 1931) towards a sustained encounter between classical myth and modern experience. Mythistorema (1935) consists of twenty-four short poems that recast Odyssean themes in contemporary language. The Logbook collections, published between 1940 and 1955, continue this exploration of wandering, alienation and the presence of the past. The King of Asine begins from a fleeting Iliad reference and imaginatively examines what remains of a largely forgotten figure. Seferis also wrote prose criticism, collected in Dokimes (1962). His stylistic development continued after the Nobel award: Three Secret Poems, published in 1966, includes short lyrics approaching surrealism. That later collection is part of his subsequent career, not a publication assessed for the 1963 prize.

terms.definition: A speaking voice or figure through which a poem expresses experience; it need not be identical to the poet.
The language and forms of expression of a contemporary period; Seferis used them to recast ancient myths rather than simply retell them in archaic language.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Measuring ionic permeability using electronic methods
sections.body: Using electronics and microelectrodes, researchers recorded electrical processes by amplifying signals a million times for display on cathode ray tubes. In voltage-clamp experiments on the squid giant nerve fibre, Hodgkin and Huxley held membrane voltage at chosen levels and measured the current needed to maintain it. This allowed calculation of membrane resistance and conductance. Findings revealed that the rising impulse phase involves sodium ions flowing inward, while the falling phase occurs as potassium ions migrate outward. These transient, selective permeability changes were described by a quantitative model capable of predicting fundamental attributes of excitability.

sections.heading: Electrophysiological research on synaptic transmission
sections.body: During his Oxford period, Eccles investigated synaptic transmission within the central nervous system and sympathetic ganglia using amplifiers and cathode ray oscilloscopes. His later research involved studying excitatory and inhibitory synapses through microelectrode insertion into nerve cells. Collaborating with Coombs and Fatt at the Australian National University, he explored the biophysical properties of synaptic transmission. This work built upon ionic membrane activity hypotheses developed by Hodgkin, Huxley, Katz, and Keynes. Additionally, his investigations contributed to the development of the ionic sieve hypothesis regarding inhibitory synaptic action.

sections.heading: Experimental methods for studying ionic mechanisms
sections.body: To investigate ionic processes in living cells, Hodgkin utilized techniques learned at Woods Hole to dissect squid axons. Working with A. F. Huxley, he conducted experiments on giant nerve fibres, often utilizing the Marine Biological Association Laboratory in Plymouth. This research into cellular mechanisms was supported by grants from the Rockefeller Foundation and the Nuffield Foundation. Additionally, his work involved applying principles of cable-theory and using amplifiers to measure electrical changes within these biological structures.

terms.definition: Changes in a nerve cell’s input that make it more or less likely to fire an impulse, respectively.
The study of electrical activity and properties in biological cells and tissues, using tools such as electrodes and amplifiers.
A mathematical description of how electrical currents and voltages spread along an elongated structure such as a nerve fibre.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Founding and organizational structure of the Red Cross
sections.body: Dunant's experience of the wounded after the 1859 Battle of Solferino inspired his appeal for organised relief. A Geneva committee of five, including Dunant, helped convene the 1863 conference at which sixteen countries discussed the project. The red cross on a white background provided a recognisable protective emblem. By the 1963 centenary, the movement included national societies, the International Committee and the League. The ceremony described their international conference as a meeting with representatives of governments party to the Geneva Conventions. Its decisions carried moral authority for national societies, rather than making the movement a single government-controlled organisation. This structure brought voluntary relief societies and international humanitarian commitments into a shared forum.

sections.heading: Functions of the Red Cross movement
sections.body: MacAulay's 1963 lecture distinguished the League's federation of national societies from the International Committee's work as a humanitarian intermediary in conflict. The League, founded in 1919, helped societies develop their capacity to assist people during disasters and other emergencies. Its development programme supplied financial and material help, technical specialists and training seminars. Support was intended to fit local conditions and strengthen cooperation between established societies and newer ones. The lecture also emphasised the contribution of volunteers and youth programmes. This account describes the League's work at the time of the award, including efforts to turn international solidarity into practical local services.

sections.heading: Operational methods of the ICRC
sections.body: In his 1963 lecture, Boissier described the ICRC's governing committee as an independent Swiss body whose members were invited by existing members. Its humanitarian mission was international. He explained how delegates visited detention facilities, examined diet, medical care and living conditions, and spoke with prisoners without witnesses. Reports and requests for improvements were addressed to the responsible authorities. The lecture reported approximately eleven thousand camp visits during the Second World War. It also traced the committee's involvement in developing humanitarian law, from the 1864 Geneva Convention to later protections for prisoners of war. This combined confidential practical work with efforts to strengthen the legal obligations of states.

terms.definition: A meeting of the movement's components and governments party to the Geneva Conventions to discuss humanitarian commitments and cooperation.
An international federation of national societies acting as a corporate body to promote humanitarian service and development through organized aid.
A recruitment method used by the International Committee of the Red Cross where existing members invite new individuals to join.

John A. MacAulay: The Red Cross in a Changing World — League of Red Cross Societies Nobel lecture, 11 December 1963

sections.heading: Nuclear force properties and symmetry principles
sections.body: Wigner's 1933 work used experimental evidence to establish the very short range and great strength of nuclear forces. He also showed how symmetry could reveal nuclear properties without a complete account of those forces. A symmetry identifies a change under which the relevant laws retain the same form. His investigations included the similar nuclear behaviour of protons and neutrons, and questions about left-right and time-reversal symmetry. These methods became tools for interpreting elementary-particle experiments as well as nuclei. The presentation speech also connects his work with the later revision of assumptions about left-right symmetry by Yang and Lee: such symmetries must be examined, rather than assumed to hold universally.

sections.heading: Academic career of J. Hans D. Jensen
sections.body: After studying physics, mathematics, physical chemistry, and philosophy at the Universities of Hamburg and Freiburg im Breisgau, Jensen earned his Ph.D. in 1932. He served as a scientific assistant at the University of Hamburg's Institute for Theoretical Physics before becoming a docent in 1937 and a Professor of Theoretical Physics at the Technische Hochschule in Hannover in 1941. His academic trajectory included a professorship at the University of Heidelberg starting in 1949 and various visiting positions at institutions such as the Institute of Advanced Study, Princeton.

sections.heading: Development of nuclear shell model and magic numbers
sections.body: While working at the S. A. M. Laboratory, Goeppert Mayer investigated separating uranium isotopes through photochemical reactions. After moving to Chicago, she transitioned into nuclear physics through discussions with scientists like Enrico Fermi. In 1948, she began researching magic numbers, eventually finding an explanation for these values a year later. Her findings were reinforced when Haxel, Jensen, and Suess provided the same explanation simultaneously. This work contributed to the shell model, which explains how specific proton or neutron counts produce unusual stability within the nucleus.

terms.definition: Properties of physical laws that remain unchanged under specified transformations, allowing physicists to constrain how a system can behave.
A scientific publication that J. Hans D. Jensen co-edited alongside O. Haxel beginning in 1955.
Particular numbers of protons or neutrons associated with especially stable nuclei, rather than the total number of both kinds of particle combined.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Evolution of structural determination methods
sections.body: Early structural analysis relied on classical chemical methods, which involved breaking large molecules into known components to understand how they joined. These techniques used nineteenth-century knowledge regarding carbon bond geometry but struggled with complex organic compounds. While X-ray diffraction, discovered by Max von Laue, allowed scientists like the Braggs to locate atoms within crystals, early applications dealt mainly with simple inorganic structures. By the 1940s, advancements enabled the solution of organic structures that classical chemical methods had not resolved. Hodgkin utilized new X-ray crystallographic methods and intensive work starting in 1942 to resolve penicillin's structure. Her efforts, supported by electronic computers and interdisciplinary cooperation between physicists and chemists, eventually led to the landmark determination of the highly complex vitamin B12 structure.

sections.heading: Early research and academic development in crystallography
sections.body: Following a special course in crystallography, Hodgkin began research on thallium dialkyl halides under H.M. Powell. Her academic path included a summer visit to Professor Victor Goldschmidt’s laboratory in Heidelberg and two years at Cambridge working with J.D. Bernal. While her early interests involved analyzing glass tesserae from Jerash, she transitioned toward sterols after Bernal shifted his focus to them in 1932. At Oxford, she worked within the subdepartment of Chemical Crystallography and sought funding for X-ray apparatus with Sir Robert Robinson. Her research group, which included students and visitors, investigated natural products such as insulin, penicillin, and vitamin B12. She also participated in meetings in 1946 that led to the foundation of the International Union of Crystallography.

terms.definition: Chemical techniques using bond geometry knowledge to break large molecules into known components for structural analysis.
A method used for the analysis of natural products through the study of X-ray diffraction patterns.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
