The effort also trained scientists across disciplines, linking laboratory knowledge with field production. The presentation speech described resistance to adoption in West Pakistan, including administrative obstacles and unfounded rumours that the wheat caused human sterility. It reported expansion beyond Mexico, India and Pakistan to other countries. This account concerns a programme involving collaborators, farming practices and local implementation, rather than a single seed that automatically produced high yields everywhere.

sections.heading: Scientific management of the Cooperative Wheat Research and Production Program
sections.body: In 1944, Borlaug directed the Cooperative Wheat Research and Production Program in Mexico, a joint venture between the Mexican government and the Rockefeller Foundation. This initiative integrated diverse scientific disciplines, including genetics, plant pathology, entomology, agronomy, soil science, and cereal technology. Through this work, he identified high-yielding, disease-resistant, short-strawed wheat varieties. He later directed the International Wheat Improvement Program at the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT), an autonomous international research training institute. The 1970 biography reported training young scientists from approximately sixteen countries in research and production methods. Additionally, his experimental work included investigations of triticale, a man-made grain species created by crossing wheat and rye to potentially improve productivity and nutritional quality.

terms.definition: Large increases in crop production associated with improved varieties and supporting agricultural practices; Borlaug’s wheat programme was a major part of this development.
An autonomous international research training institute established by the Rockefeller and Ford Foundations in cooperation with the Mexican government.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of Plasma Motion and Magnetic Alignment
sections.body: Alfvén showed that magnetic fields and electrically conducting plasma must be studied together. Motion of charged particles produces currents; the interaction between currents and magnetic fields can change the plasma's motion. This coupling supports disturbances called Alfvén waves. The 1970 presentation discussed their use in theories of solar-system formation, rather than establishing one definitive account of how planetary orbits arose. Néel's work addressed a different magnetic problem in solids. He modelled materials with interpenetrating arrangements of opposing magnetic moments. In antiferromagnets those moments can cancel, while in ferrimagnetic materials such as magnetite their unequal contributions leave a net magnetisation. The award thus joined advances in plasma dynamics and the internal magnetic organisation of materials.

sections.heading: Academic career and published monographs of Hannes Alfvén
sections.body: After earning his doctorate in 1934, Hannes Alfvén served as a physics lecturer at Uppsala University. His professional trajectory included roles as a research physicist at the Nobel Institute for Physics in Stockholm and various professorships at the Royal Institute of Technology, covering electricity, electronics, and plasma physics. He authored several significant monographs, including Cosmical Electrodynamics in 1948 and Origin of the Solar System in 1956. Additionally, he co-authored Cosmical Electrodynamics, Fundamental Principles in 1963 alongside C.-G. Fälthammar.

sections.heading: Louis Néel's magnetic research and institutional leadership
sections.body: Néel began his magnetism research in Pierre Weiss's Strasbourg laboratory between 1928 and 1939. After being called up for wartime service in 1939, he devised protection for French ships against German magnetic mines. This military work followed his earlier laboratory research. After the 1940 armistice, he established an electrostatics and metal-physics laboratory at Grenoble, which became a CNRS laboratory in 1946. His theoretical interests extended beyond antiferromagnetism and ferrimagnetism to nickel's specific heat, magnetic viscosity and hysteresis. He also built research institutions, founding Grenoble's nuclear research centre in 1956 and contributing to the decision to install a Franco-German high-flux reactor. These activities show the connection between theoretical magnetism, practical applications and laboratory infrastructure.

terms.definition: An electrically-conducting gas consisting of electrons and ions, recognized as a fourth state of matter alongside solid, liquid, and gaseous.
Specialized books or detailed written works on a single subject, such as those published by Alfvén regarding electrodynamics and solar origins.
The dependence of a material's magnetisation on its previous exposure to magnetic fields, rather than only the field currently applied.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Spectroscopic investigation of molecular energy and radical structures
sections.body: By measuring how molecules absorb light-energy in the ultraviolet and infrared regions, researchers can derive properties like size and shape. Because light-energy is packaged as quanta, these measurements provide accurate data regarding molecular energy contents. Herzberg applied quantum mechanical descriptions to interpret these experimental investigations, specifically focusing on the properties of over thirty free radicals, including methyl and methylene. His research showed that the geometry of a radical can depend strongly on its energy state. These precision determinations required developing specialized spectroscopic techniques to capture short-lived species, some lasting only millionths of a second, facilitating the study of complex chemical systems.

sections.heading: Spectroscopic applications in astrochemistry and molecular structures
sections.body: Beyond studying reactive fragments like free methyl and methylene, Herzberg utilized spectroscopic studies to identify specific molecules within comets, planetary atmospheres, and interstellar space. His research involved determining the structural compositions of various diatomic and polyatomic molecules. During his career, he held significant leadership roles, including serving as Director of the Division of Pure Physics at the National Research Council. He also contributed to the international scientific community through positions such as Vice President of the International Union of Pure and Applied Physics. Before returning to Canada in 1948, he was professor of spectroscopy at the University of Chicago’s Yerkes Observatory. His work connected laboratory measurements of molecules with their identification far beyond Earth.

terms.definition: A field of research involving measuring light-energy absorption to determine the size, shape, and energy contents of molecules.
Molecules containing two atoms and molecules containing more than two atoms, respectively; Herzberg investigated the structures of both groups.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Quantitative methods for analyzing economic growth and change
sections.body: Kuznets utilized extensive statistical material to provide quantitative precision to economic magnitudes related to social change. He developed specific methods for calculating national income size and fluctuations while avoiding abstract models that lack empirical testing opportunities. In the historical data he examined, Kuznets identified long growth cycles lasting approximately twenty years, which are significantly influenced by population growth rate variations. Additionally, he observed that the amount of real capital required for specific production volumes showed a falling trend, with physical capital growing less than proportionally to production. He also noted that household savings propensities had remained remarkably stable across decades in most industrial nations, though short-run savings vary during cyclical fluctuations. His work, including Economic Growth of Nations, incorporates institutional factors like technology and industrial structure.

sections.heading: Quantitative analysis of global economic growth
sections.body: While conducting research at the National Bureau of Economic Research, Kuznets investigated capital formation and national income within the United States. His scholarly activities expanded to include comparative quantitative analysis of economic growth across different nations through his leadership of the Social Science Research Council Committee on Economic Growth. During the mid-twentieth century, he directed research for the War Production Board's Planning Committee and oversaw the Falk Project for Economic Research in Israel. Furthermore, his investigations extended to the economy of China while serving as chairman of a specialized committee. These diverse roles allowed him to apply empirical methods to various international economic structures, moving beyond domestic studies to examine how different countries experience developmental processes and shifts in wealth.

terms.definition: Quantifiable economic elements that Kuznets sought to provide with precision to better understand processes of social change.
A method used by Kuznets to study the economic growth patterns of various nations through numerical data.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Evolution of poetic direction and social purpose
sections.body: The presentation speech reads Neruda’s development as a movement from isolation in his early love poems toward harmony between humanity and the Earth. While Residence on Earth depicted a sense of being alone among shifting matter, his later work transitioned into poetry focused on political and social preparedness. In Canto General, partly written during exile caused by his political opinions, he utilized visions of the future to address themes of redress. His later collections, such as Estravagario, reflect a path shaped by diverse global experiences and the observation of terror in various parts of the world. Additionally, works like La Barcarola explore new relationships with the origins of life and womanhood, demonstrating a shift from dissonance toward community with existence.

sections.heading: Evolution of poetic styles and political engagement
sections.body: Neruda's early literary career included contributing to the daily La Mañana and the journal Selva Austral under a pen name inspired by Jan Neruda. His collection Crepusculario appeared in 1923, followed by his famous love poems. During his diplomatic service, he produced the surrealistic work Residencia en la tierra. The Spanish Civil War and the death of García Lorca influenced his transition toward social themes, leading to the creation of España en el Corazón. Later, while serving as consul in Mexico, he expanded Canto General de Chile into a broader epic of the continent’s landscapes, peoples and history. His later works, such as Odas elementales, utilized an alphabetic structure to describe objects and events, while Las Uvas y el Viento documented his experiences during exile.

terms.definition: The speech’s description of Neruda’s movement toward connection with humanity and the natural world, drawing on his own language of harmony.
A collection of poems that uses an alphabetic form to present various objects, events, and relations.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanism of epinephrine and glucose liberation
sections.body: Sutherland investigated how epinephrine, also called adrenaline, mobilizes stored energy. The hormone acts as a signal from the adrenal glands to other tissues. His experiments identified cyclic AMP as an intermediate carrying that signal into the cell’s metabolic machinery. The hormone could act at the cell surface without itself carrying the message through the cell interior. Evidence from Sutherland and other researchers showed that several hormones use this kind of signalling. Their different effects depend in part on which receptors a cell possesses and how it responds internally. The discovery therefore revealed a shared signalling principle while leaving room for different tissues and hormones to produce different outcomes.

sections.heading: Mechanism of epinephrine-induced glycogen degradation
sections.body: Sutherland’s work on epinephrine and liver glycogen connected a surface signal with a chain of intracellular reactions. Hormone binding activates a membrane-associated enzyme, adenylyl cyclase, which produces cyclic AMP inside the cell. This second messenger initiates reactions that activate glycogen phosphorylase, helping mobilize stored carbohydrate. Cyclic AMP does not itself directly turn glycogen into glucose. The discovery explained how a signal arriving outside a cell could regulate its metabolism without the hormone entering it. This is a mechanism used by many hormones, not a rule that every hormone remains outside cells. It also clarified why identifying intermediate steps was essential to understanding an observed physiological response.

sections.heading: Academic career and professional appointments
sections.body: Following his medical training at Washington University, Sutherland held several pharmacology and biochemistry positions within the same institution's School of Medicine. His academic progression included roles as an instructor and assistant professor before he moved to Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio. There, he served as a professor of pharmacology and directed the department. Later, he transitioned to Vanderbilt University School of Medicine in Nashville, Tennessee, where he held a professorship in physiology starting in 1963.

terms.definition: An intermediate chemical substance, such as cyclic AMP, that transmits signals from a hormone to the interior of a cell.
Cyclic adenosine monophosphate, a nucleotide that acts inside cells as a second messenger in several hormone-signalling pathways.
The study of drugs and other active substances, including how they act on living systems and produce biological effects.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Diplomatic initiatives for European détente
sections.body: As Foreign Secretary and later Chancellor, Brandt implemented specific strategies to transition from confrontation to co-operation between Eastern and Western Europe. His government's 1969 declaration outlined four essential clauses to achieve this goal. These included efforts to expand the European Economic Community and strengthen political unity within it. Furthermore, his administration pursued a non-violence agreement with the Soviet Union and sought to normalize relations through talks with Poland. Brandt also moved to sign a non-proliferation treaty during his first year in office. By utilizing West European economic and political co-operation, these actions aimed to reduce Germany's isolation and foster international trust, providing a foundation for meaningful dialogue between opposing sides of the continent.

sections.heading: Early political activities and humanitarian work
sections.body: Before his chancellorship, Brandt engaged in international cooperation to oppose Nazism. During the Spanish conflict in 1937, he functioned as a political observer and acted for humanitarian relief organizations. His resistance included involvement with German anti-Nazi forces and operating within the Berlin underground. Captured in Norway in 1940 and released without being identified as a German opponent of Nazism, he fled to Sweden. After the war, he worked in Germany as a correspondent for Scandinavian newspapers. His political ascent continued through roles such as press officer for the Norwegian Mission in Berlin and various positions within the Social Democratic Party. He eventually served as Mayor of Berlin from 1957 to 1966 before his later diplomatic achievements.

terms.definition: A policy of reducing tensions and moving from confrontation toward co-operation between Eastern and Western European nations.
Organizations providing assistance to people affected by war or other hardship; Brandt represented such groups while working in Spain in 1937.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Preserving wave phase through holographic interference
sections.body: Gabor addressed the loss of three-dimensional geometry in photography by finding a way to retain the phase of a wave-field on a photographic plate. He achieved this by superimposing a reference wave with the wave-field from an object, creating an interference pattern where waves either reinforce or extinguish each other based on their phase. While Gabor initially intended to use electron rays for two-step microscopy, technical limitations prevented testing that specific method. Instead, he used light to prove his principle through three papers published between 1948 and 1951. The recorded phase information also supports precise optical measurements. Multiple exposures of a changing object, such as a vibrating membrane, can produce interference lines that reveal changes in shape between exposures.

sections.heading: Development of wavefront reconstruction and electron holography
sections.body: Gabor’s 1948 experiments in wavefront reconstruction grew from an ambition to improve electron microscopy enough to resolve atomic lattices and individual atoms. Work with the AEI Research Laboratory at Aldermaston from 1950 to 1953 produced results but fell short of that objective. In his autobiography, Gabor explained that the supporting techniques had not yet matured. Optical holography developed more successfully after the laser became available, while electron holography needed further technical advances. He joined Imperial College in 1949 and pursued many related problems with research students, including a holographic microscope, an electron-velocity spectroscope and instruments for communication and display. His account shows how an unsuccessful route toward one instrument produced a principle with much wider uses.

terms.definition: A record of interference between an object wave and a reference wave, encoding information that allows the object’s wavefront to be reconstructed.
Recording information about a wave and later using it to recreate the wavefront; Gabor first pursued the idea for electron microscopy.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Molecular mechanisms of ribonuclease catalytic activity
sections.body: Research on ribonuclease revealed how specific amino acids drive enzymatic functions. Moore and Stein identified that the active site contains amino acids with much higher reactivity than those in free form. By using chemical modification to label two specific histidine residues, they determined their positions within the peptide chain. This method provided a detailed view of the active site before its three-dimensional structure was known. These studies connected particular residues and their unusual chemical reactivity with the enzyme’s catalytic function.

sections.heading: Ribonuclease structural investigations and amino acid sequence determination
sections.body: Anfinsen’s ribonuclease experiments showed that the amino-acid sequence contains information needed for the enzyme’s active conformation under suitable conditions. His thermodynamic interpretation concerned the most favourable free-energy state in a given environment, rather than an environment-independent rule that every protein automatically folds. Moore and Stein addressed a complementary problem: knowing a sequence alone does not reveal which residues meet in the active site. Folding can bring together groups widely separated along the chain. They used unusually reactive groups as targets for chemical modification, then located those groups in the sequence. This connected linear chemical structure with the localized region responsible for catalysis.

sections.heading: Experimental verification of the thermodynamic hypothesis
sections.body: Anfinsen investigated reversible denaturation to test if amino acid chemistry determines tertiary structure. By cleaving disulfide bonds and disrupting protein structures, he demonstrated that several proteins could spontaneously recover their native forms when suitable conditions were restored. This process led to the acceptance of the thermodynamic hypothesis. Additionally, his research identified a microsomal enzyme that catalyzes sulfhydryl-disulfide interchange. This specific enzyme accelerates the in vitro refolding of denatured proteins containing disulfide bonds, approaching rates sufficient to account for folding during protein biosynthesis.

terms.definition: A process involving substances called catalysts that accelerate chemical reactions without being consumed during the reaction itself.
A limited part of an enzyme molecule where the reacting substance interacts with the enzyme to accelerate chemical reactions.
The proposal that a protein’s amino-acid sequence determines its energetically favoured native conformation under appropriate environmental conditions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Advancements in general equilibrium and decision-making theory
sections.body: Hicks built a model of interconnected markets from assumptions about consumers and producers. Differential analysis allowed him to examine how changes in harvests, tastes or business expectations spread through prices, production and employment. Arrow and Gérard Debreu later used more general mathematical tools. Their 1954 model established conditions for the existence of a competitive equilibrium; existence does not imply that the equilibrium is unique or that an economy will automatically reach it. Arrow also studied decisions under uncertainty and the conditions imposed on methods for combining individual rankings into collective choices. His social-choice results exposed tensions among apparently reasonable requirements, rather than ruling out every form of democratic decision-making.

sections.heading: Innovations in equilibrium and welfare theory
sections.body: Hicks utilized differential analysis to build a model featuring aggregated markets for money, credit, commodities, and production factors. His work introduced multiperiod analysis and a capital theory centered on profit maximization assumptions. Arrow later applied the mathematical theory of convex sets to reformulate equilibrium systems, focusing on solubility and stability properties. Alongside Gérard Debreu, he produced a 1954 paper that initiated significant research. Additionally, Arrow explored uncertainty within equilibrium frameworks and, with Leonid Hurwicz, analysed decentralised decisions when a central authority fixes the price system.

sections.heading: Arrow's research on social choice and information
sections.body: Arrow’s work on Pareto efficiency and social choice began during his association with the Cowles Commission and RAND. He subsequently explored information as something economically valuable to produce and use. Two papers in 1962 addressed distinct questions: how efficiently markets encourage innovation, and how learning by doing affects economic growth. In 1963 and later work, he analysed medical care and insurance through differences in the information available to participants. His 2005 autobiographical addendum also recalled later work on demand for information, information as a productive input, and racial discrimination. This broad programme extended beyond the particular equilibrium and welfare contributions cited in the 1972 award.

terms.definition: The difference between the maximum price a person would pay for a commodity and the actual market price paid.
The study of sets that contain the whole line segment between any two of their points; convexity supports important equilibrium-existence arguments.
A difference in relevant knowledge among participants in a transaction, which can affect how markets for services such as medical care and insurance operate.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Arrow and Debreu: Existence of an Equilibrium for a Competitive Economy (1954)

sections.heading: Themes of homelessness and human aesthetics in Böll's literature
sections.body: Böll’s literary program utilizes a range of styles, from satire to parody, to explore the aesthetics of the humane. His writing addresses fundamental human needs, including religion, food, and neighborhood. Through works like Und sagte kein einziges Wort, Haus ohne Hüter, and Das Brot der frühen Jahre, he depicts a displaced era marked by famine and dictatorship. While proficient in meticulous detail, Böll often employs irony or suggests figures with minimal lines, seeking a habitable language within his era's social displacement.

sections.heading: Renewing literature after destruction
sections.body: The announcement distinguished Böll’s contribution from novelty of form alone. He generally worked within realistic narrative, but could shift between dense, ironic detail and a few lines sufficient to establish a character. The committee interpreted his achievement against the destruction experienced by his generation: hunger, dictatorship, war and their aftermath. It read the titles of his three breakthrough works from 1953–1955 as expressions of this inheritance. Group Portrait with a Lady, published in 1971, represented his broadest undertaking available at the award. Renewal here meant rebuilding a humane literary culture after catastrophe, rather than claiming that post-war West Germany itself remained under the Nazi dictatorship.

sections.heading: Postwar literary development and professional background
sections.body: Before establishing himself as a freelance writer in Cologne, Böll began a bookselling apprenticeship at Matth. Lempertz in Bonn in 1937, leaving it the following spring. His academic path included studying Germanistics and Classical Philology, though he initially resumed studies formally to secure food rationing cards. Following his wartime experiences, he published short stories between 1946 and 1949. Through participation in Gruppe 47 starting in 1951, Böll connected with various postwar writers, helping to reduce the isolation of authors living within a fragmented, destroyed Germany.

terms.definition: A literary concept involving a passionately engaged aesthetic that explores the essential requirements for leading a human life.
Narrative that represents recognisable people, settings and social experience; Böll used its conventions flexibly, including through irony and selective detail.
A group of German postwar writers that helped liberate authors from isolation during the period of a fragmented Germany.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Methods for analyzing antibody molecular structure
sections.body: Porter and Edelman independently broke antibody molecules into smaller components to investigate their construction. Porter used the protein-cutting enzyme papain under controlled conditions. It produced three fragments: two retained specific antigen binding, while the third had other functions. Edelman broke disulfide cross-links and separated the molecule into individual protein chains. Comparing these approaches helped establish the four-chain organisation of the basic antibody unit: two matching light chains and two matching heavy chains. The methods answered different questions. Cutting across parts of the molecule revealed functional regions; separating linked chains exposed its structural building blocks. Combining the results connected antibody architecture with selective binding.

sections.heading: How antibody structure divides recognition from other functions
sections.body: The familiar Y-shaped antibody unit contains two light chains alongside two longer heavy chains. At each branch tip, a light-chain region and a heavy-chain region cooperate to form an antigen-binding site. The stem consists of the remaining heavy-chain regions and supports other immune functions. The 1972 announcement explained that heavy-chain differences distinguish antibody classes and influence activities such as complement activation or passage across the placenta. These properties are not identical in every class. Structural analysis therefore explained more than the molecule's outline: it showed how a shared architecture can combine specific recognition with different biological effects. Porter's fragment experiments and Edelman's chain-separation work provided complementary routes to that model.

sections.heading: From protein chemistry to later studies of cell interactions
sections.body: Alongside antibody chemistry, Edelman used fluorescent probes and spectroscopy to investigate proteins and developed methods for separating molecules and cells. His award-era biography also mentions research on plant mitogens and cell surfaces. A later, 2005 addendum describes the subsequent expansion into cell growth, development and interactions between cells. This programme led to work on cell adhesion molecules, which help organise tissues and nervous systems. The addendum also discusses experiments on synthetic promoters and internal ribosomal entry sites. These later projects illustrate the breadth of his career, but they were not the discoveries for which the 1972 antibody prize was awarded.

terms.definition: A molecular target specifically recognised by an antibody or other immune receptor; an antigen need not be foreign to the body.
One of the longer protein chains in an antibody; its regions contribute both to antigen binding and to the molecule's class-specific functions.
Proteins involved in attaching cells to other cells or their surroundings, helping organise tissues during development and other processes.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
US National Cancer Institute: antigen, including antigens on the body’s own tissues

sections.heading: Mechanisms of the BCS theory and superconductivity
sections.body: BCS theory describes a collective quantum state of electrons in conventional superconductors. An interaction involving vibrations of the crystal lattice allows electrons to form pairs. The pairs participate coherently in a state extending across the material; this is not simply a picture of electrons travelling in orderly lines instead of moving randomly. The theory connected microscopic interactions with the disappearance of electrical resistance below a critical temperature. The 1972 speech also discussed emerging uses, including magnets for particle accelerators, and hopes for electrical-power applications. Those engineering possibilities were distinct from the central achievement: explaining superconducting behaviour through a microscopic many-electron theory.

sections.heading: An energy gap and new experimental tests
sections.body: The paired state in BCS theory has an important energetic consequence: creating certain excitations, including breaking a pair, requires a minimum energy. This gap helps connect the microscopic theory with observable properties. The 1972 announcement credited both the original work and subsequent extensions by other researchers with explaining superconductors in increasing detail. It also highlighted new research on quantum tunnelling, magnetic-flux quantisation and Josephson effects. These should not all be attributed as predictions made by the three laureates in their initial 1957 paper. Rather, their theory supplied a foundation from which a wider community developed and tested further consequences.

sections.heading: Bardeen's academic path and research focus
sections.body: Before his work on superconductivity, Bardeen studied electrical engineering at the University of Wisconsin and mathematical physics at Princeton. His early career involved interpreting magnetic and gravitational surveys at Gulf Research Laboratories. During his time at Harvard, he investigated metal cohesion and electrical conduction. Following service as a civilian physicist at the Naval Ordnance Laboratory, he joined Bell Telephone Laboratories. His research interests expanded to include semiconductor surface properties, atom diffusion in solids, and the development of methods for geophysical prospecting.

terms.definition: A state with zero electrical resistance below a critical temperature, accompanied by characteristic magnetic behaviour.
Correlated pairs of electrons; in conventional BCS superconductors, an effective attraction involving lattice vibrations supports their formation.
The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from a material into the surrounding vacuum.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental expansion of sandwich compound structures
sections.body: After ferrocene's structure was established, Fischer and Wilkinson tested how widely the sandwich arrangement could be extended. They prepared related compounds using different metals and organic groups. Fischer produced a chromium atom held between two benzene rings, showing that the bonding pattern was not restricted to ferrocene's iron and cyclopentadienyl rings. Further compounds retained a ring on one side while other groups occupied the remaining positions around the metal: the so-called open sandwiches. Wilkinson also prepared a compound containing a direct rhenium–hydrogen bond. These syntheses expanded the range of structures available for studying organometallic bonding and stability.

sections.heading: Expansion of organometallic sandwich compound chemistry
sections.body: Following their 1952 identification of ferrocene's structure, researchers expanded this field by synthesizing various metal-based variations. Fischer produced a surprising chromium and benzene sandwich compound, while others developed open sandwiches using carbon monoxide or methyl groups to replace one plate molecule. Wilkinson prepared a notable rhenium-hydrogen sandwich compound. These developments facilitated international scientific discussions regarding the unexpected stability of such molecules, which significantly influenced modern understanding of how these compounds function as catalysts in reactions involving hydrogen.

sections.heading: Fischer's research into metal complexes and reaction mechanisms
sections.body: Fischer's doctoral work with Walter Hieber investigated carbon monoxide reactions of nickel(II) salts in the presence of dithionites and sulfoxylates. After completing the doctorate in 1952, he specialised in transition-metal and organometallic chemistry. His teaching qualification examined complexes of cyclopentadienes and indenes. Later investigations broadened to metal complexes with aromatic rings and olefins, and to metal-carbonyl carbene and carbyne complexes. His biography describes these subjects as the basis of international lectures and collaborations. This progression places the sandwich-compound work within a wider investigation of how metals bind organic groups.

terms.definition: A molecular structure consisting of a metal atom positioned between two flat molecules, acting like a filling.
A substance that increases a reaction's rate through a different reaction pathway and is regenerated overall rather than consumed in proportion to the products.
The chemistry of compounds with bonding between a metal and carbon in an organic group, including many ring-bound metal complexes.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Applications of the input-output method
sections.body: The input-output method serves as a mathematical and statistical model for empirical analysis. It functions as a complement to market processes, aiding in economic planning and forecasting. This tool allows researchers to calculate how shifts in oil prices or wages spread through an economy via infinite series of effects. The method was used to estimate how United States disarmament after World War II and rearmament during the Korean War would affect sectoral production and employment. Additionally, it helps study environmental residuals from high-technology production processes.

sections.heading: Development and application of input-output analysis
sections.body: Leontief outlined his technique during the 1930s, later publishing a comprehensive version in his 1941 book, The Structure of American Economy, 1919-1929. This method utilizes technical coefficients to define required intermediary product quantities per unit produced. Analysts use it to determine necessary production increases to satisfy final demands for consumption, investment, and exports. Beyond studying price transmissions or military mobilization, the 1973 announcement described extensions incorporating production residuals like smoke and water pollution. This allows researchers to study how industrial processes impact the environment through these various sectors.

sections.heading: Development of input-output theory and economic modeling
sections.body: Seeking an empirical general equilibrium theory, Leontief utilized a research grant in 1932 to compile the first American economy input-output tables for 1919 and 1929. His methodology developed alongside computing: he began using a large-scale mechanical calculating machine in 1935 and later used Harvard’s Mark I. Following his 1941 publication, Structure of the American Economy, 1919-1929, he expanded the theory's applications. Later research focused on analyzing economic growth alongside environmental disruption, while also investigating scientific methodology and broader social and economic policy issues.

terms.definition: A mathematically and statistically formulated model designed to capture complicated interdependences within a production process through empirical analyses.
Quantities of intermediary products required per unit produced for each commodity within a production sector.
Studying a restricted part of an economic system separately; Leontief instead sought to model the interdependence of the production system as a whole.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Characterization of individuals in Australian literature
sections.body: White utilizes a psychological approach to portray characters as unique individuals rather than mere settlers. In works like Voss, he uses the wilderness to dramatize Nietzschean willpower and self-sacrifice. His narratives frequently feature outsiders, such as mystics, zealots, or maladjusted people, to explore human qualities. In Riders in the Chariot, these alienated figures experience persecution yet achieve a mystical victory. This method focuses on internal lives, often exploring themes of guilt, atonement, and the tension between passion and puritanism.

sections.heading: Narrative techniques in White's major novels
sections.body: White utilized diverse literary methods across several key works. In The Aunt’s Story, he portrays an unmarried Australian woman's life spanning Europe and America. His novel Voss features a character study of an explorer within the Australian interior, while Riders in the Chariot uses symbolism in a sacrificial drama. The Solid Mandala presents a double portrait of two brothers defined by rational and intuitive traits. Additionally, The Vivisector functions as an imaginary biography, scrutinizing an artist's motives and their struggle to express the utmost.

sections.heading: Development of an epic narrative style
sections.body: White's literary progression involved early poetry and plays before publishing his first novel, Happy Valley, in London. During World War II, he served as an air force intelligence officer, traveling through locations including Greenland, the Azores, and Cairo. Following his demobilization, he settled on a farm at Castle Hill. While writing there, he developed A Life Sentence on Earth into The Tree of Man. This work challenged the naturalistic tradition, despite local criticism regarding his background in the grazier class.

terms.definition: A literary method used by White to portray characters from the inside, focusing on individualized problems that transcend local or national contexts.
Storytelling that combines broad narrative scope with close attention to the inner lives of individual characters.
Fiction emphasizing close observation of everyday life and social conditions, a tradition White challenged through psychological and symbolic writing.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Studying inherited patterns and experience
sections.body: Ethologists combined observation with experiments to explain behaviour in terms of evolution and development. They investigated stereotyped actions, including elements of courtship and nesting, that could appear without prior practice. Early accounts called these fixed action patterns and described the features that elicited them as key stimuli. Experiments with artificial models allowed researchers to vary those features and compare animals’ responses. Exaggerated features sometimes elicited stronger responses than natural examples. The research also showed the importance of experience during sensitive periods. Taken together, these approaches examined both inherited organization and learning; they did not reduce all animal behaviour to an inflexible sequence of automatic actions.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of behavioral elicitation and communication
sections.body: Karl von Frisch used experiments to investigate communication among bees. Round dances and waggle dances helped distinguish information about nearby and more distant food sources. Konrad Lorenz examined patterns appearing in inexperienced young birds, while also studying imprinting and the importance of early experience. Nikolaas Tinbergen tested behavioural hypotheses with controlled changes to artificial models. By varying the form, colour and contrast of a model gull’s bill, he investigated features that elicited a chick’s food-begging response. Exaggerated features could be more effective than the natural object. These different methods made behaviour experimentally testable, linking an animal’s responses to both its inherited capacities and its surroundings.

sections.heading: Karl von Frisch's investigations into bee sensory systems
sections.body: Von Frisch studied zoology in Munich and Vienna before receiving his doctorate in Vienna in 1910. That year he became Richard Hertwig’s assistant in Munich. His research examined how bees sense colour, shape, smell and taste, as well as how they communicate. Studies listed in his biography investigated polarized skylight as an orientation cue in bee dances and the sun’s role as a compass. His 1965 book brought together work on dance language and orientation. These investigations connected the signals bees produce with the sensory information available to the animals receiving and using them.

terms.definition: Stereotyped sequences of behaviour, traditionally described as inherited patterns elicited by particular stimuli; the concept concerns some behaviour, not everything an animal does.
A science focused on the comparative study of behavior patterns, examining how they are organized, elicited, and shaped by evolution.
The preferred directions in which light waves oscillate; patterns of polarized skylight can provide bees with orientation information.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The 1973 Vietnam ceasefire negotiations
sections.body: Following nearly four years of discussions initiated in Paris in 1969, negotiators reached agreement on January 23, 1973, before the formal signing on January 27. This arrangement between the United States and the Vietnamese Democratic Republic followed significant military actions, including American air attacks on North Vietnamese targets and supply lines through Laos and Cambodia. While the systematic withdrawal of American forces began in 1969, reducing troop levels from half a million to 27,000 by December 1972, combat persisted through major offensives in South Vietnam. The Nobel Committee recognized this specific achievement as an important step toward full peace, despite acknowledging that the agreement was a ceasefire rather than a complete peace settlement and that population sufferings remained ongoing.

sections.heading: Henry Kissinger's academic and professional diplomatic background
sections.body: Before serving as United States Secretary of State, Henry Kissinger held several influential academic and advisory roles. He was a faculty member at Harvard University within the Department of Government and the Center for International Affairs, where he also served as Associate Director. His research expertise included directing the Special Studies Project for the Rockefeller Brothers Fund and leading the Harvard Defense Studies Program. Additionally, his work involved studying nuclear weapons and foreign policy for the Council on Foreign Relations. Kissinger's scholarly contributions include his doctoral dissertation, A World Restored: Metternich, Castlereagh and the Problems of Peace 1812-22. His professional experience also encompassed service in the U.S. Army Counter Intelligence Corps and various consulting roles for the Department of State and the Rand Corporation.

terms.definition: An agreement to stop fighting under specified terms; reaching or signing one does not by itself establish compliance or lasting peace.
A field of study involving the analysis of international affairs, foreign policy, and the historical development of global diplomacy.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms and developments in solid state tunnelling
sections.body: Esaki’s semiconductor junction experiments led to the tunnel diode. Giaever used evaporated metal films separated by a thin oxide layer to study superconductors’ energy gaps, revealing fine structures associated with lattice vibrations. Josephson then predicted a further current carried by coupled electrons, or Cooper pairs. His theory showed that a supercurrent could cross an insulating barrier without an applied voltage. With a constant voltage, the current would instead oscillate at high frequency. These predictions made it possible to control superconducting currents with electric and magnetic fields and investigate quantum behaviour on a macroscopic scale. The presentation speech described sensitive measurements of temperature and electromagnetic fields among the applications of quantum interferometry.

sections.heading: Experimental and theoretical discoveries in tunneling phenomena
sections.body: In 1958, Leo Esaki used simple experiments to demonstrate a new semiconductor tunneling type, enabling tunnel diode technology. Ivar Giaever later utilized thin oxide layers between metals at General Electric to show the tunnel effect, providing evidence for the energy gap in superconductors and creating an accurate spectroscopic method. Inspired by these experiments, Brian Josephson predicted the Josephson effects in 1962. These theoretical predictions included a supercurrent flowing through barriers without applied voltage and high-frequency currents generated by a constant voltage difference.

sections.heading: Development of semiconductor quantum structures
sections.body: At Sony, Leo Esaki researched heavily doped germanium and silicon, work that led to the Esaki tunnel diode. In 1960 he joined IBM’s Thomas J. Watson Research Center, where he continued semiconductor research. Beginning in 1969, he and his colleagues investigated deliberately designed semiconductor quantum structures, including artificial superlattices. These structures extended his exploration of quantum behaviour beyond the original diode. His biography records later recognition for work on superlattices and quantum wells as part of this continuing career. The 1973 Nobel Prize specifically recognized his pioneering work on electron tunnelling in solids.

terms.definition: Sensitive measurement using quantum phenomena in superconducting currents, with applications including the electromagnetic fields around the heart and brain.
Theoretical phenomena involving a supercurrent flowing through tunnel barriers without voltage and high-frequency currents produced by constant voltage differences.
Artificial semiconductor structures, such as the superlattices investigated by Esaki and colleagues, created to explore quantum behaviour in materials.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Statistical Theory of Chain Molecule Interactions
sections.body: Flory developed statistical ways to describe the many shapes a flexible polymer chain can adopt. Its average size depends on interactions among chain segments and with the surrounding solvent. In suitable polymer–solvent systems, cooling makes the solvent less favourable and the coil contracts before the polymer becomes insoluble. Theta conditions identify a balance at which the chain has its unperturbed dimensions, providing a useful reference for comparing different molecules. This is a change in coil shape and size, not a shortening of the molecule’s chemical chain. Flory also investigated chain formation, crystallization, rubber elasticity and the rotational behaviour of chain links.

sections.heading: Connecting polymer formation with measurable properties
sections.body: Flory connected theories of long molecules with measurements that could test them. The award announcement described the use of viscosity, light scattering, ultracentrifugation and diffusion to characterize polymers in solution. His work also addressed how the molecules are made: small units join through addition or condensation reactions, and the reaction conditions influence the distribution of chain lengths. Chain transfer was another important mechanism. A growing chain can stop growing while transferring the capacity for further growth to another molecule. This helped explain why a polymer sample contains chains of different lengths. Together, the chemical and physical approaches linked the preparation of a material with its measurable molecular properties.

sections.heading: Excluded volume effect and smoothed density model
sections.body: During his Baker Lectureship, Flory investigated how the exclusion of one chain segment from the space occupied by another affects configuration. He utilized a simple smoothed density model to demonstrate that this perturbation increases without limit as chain length grows. This approach allowed for the reinterpretation of hydrodynamic theories developed by Kirkwood and Debye. By accounting for intramolecular interactions in dilute solutions, he showed agreement with experimental data regarding sedimentation velocities, diffusion coefficients, and viscosities, contributing to hydrodynamic characterization and recognition of theta conditions, where the net excluded-volume effect is neutralized.

terms.definition: A temperature, specific to a polymer–solvent system, at which competing interactions balance so the chain has its unperturbed dimensions.
A reaction in which growth stops on one polymer chain while the active centre for growth is transferred to another molecule.
A phenomenon where a chain segment is prevented from occupying space already taken by another part of the same molecule.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Interdisciplinary approaches to economic and social systems
sections.body: Beyond pure economic theory, these researchers investigated how institutional, legal, and demographic factors influence societal structures. Myrdal utilized equilibrium models and dynamic analysis of cumulative processes to examine the social and economic position of Black Americans in An American Dilemma. He identified how various strategic factors, such as health and discriminatory attitudes, create vicious circles of deterioration. Meanwhile, Hayek examined the difficulties of socialist calculation and evaluated proposals for decentralized market socialism. His research assessed system viability based on how efficiently organizations utilize information spread among individuals and enterprises.

sections.heading: Friedrich von Hayek's academic career and published works
sections.body: After studying at the University of Vienna, Hayek conducted postgraduate work at New York University. He directed the Austrian Institute for Trade Cycle Research before holding professorships at the London School of Economics and the University of Chicago. His extensive bibliography includes Monetary Theory and the Trade Cycle, which originated as Geldtheorie und Konjunkturtheorie in 1929. Other significant publications include The Road to Serfdom, Prices and Production, and The Pure Theory of Capital, many of which were translated into multiple languages.

sections.heading: Gunnar Myrdal's research on economic and social development
sections.body: After studying in Germany and Britain, Myrdal explored the evolution of economic theory in his book The Political Element in the Development of Economic Theory. Commissioned by the Carnegie Corporation of New York, he directed a study of the social and economic conditions faced by Black Americans, which became An American Dilemma: The Negro Problem and Modern Democracy. Later, while working for the Twentieth Century Fund, he investigated economic trends and policies within South Asian nations. This research produced Asian Drama: An Inquiry into the Poverty of Nations and The Challenge of World Poverty.

terms.definition: Cumulative processes of deterioration arising from the interdependence between various economic and social factors within a population.
A 1929 publication by Hayek, later released in English as Monetary Theory and the Trade Cycle.
A field of study involving the relationship between politics and economics, which Myrdal taught as a docent and professor.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Social transformation and literary breakthroughs
sections.body: The rise of working-class writers represents a significant cultural shift. Eyvind Johnson, whose formal schooling ended at thirteen, collaborated with Willy Brandt to publish the Scandinavianism mouthpiece, A Handshake, during the occupation years. Harry Martinson, once a child of the parish, drew elemental realism from his experiences as a sea stoker and road wanderer. These authors brought new creative energy to literature, mirroring a broader societal transformation where a new class gained access to the heights of cultural achievement.

sections.heading: Eyvind Johnson's early literary and professional development
sections.body: Before his literary success, Johnson held various roles including sawmill worker, locomotive cleaner, and projectionist. In 1920, he co-founded the magazine Vår Nutid and joined the writer society De gröna. While living in Paris, he supported himself through jobs as a cement worker and hotel dishwasher. His early bibliography includes the short story collection De fyra främlingarna, completed in 1924. These diverse experiences in Sweden, Germany, and France preceded his later established works of narrative art.

sections.heading: Martinson's literary development and thematic explorations
sections.body: Martinson drew inspiration from six years working on various ships and in foreign countries during the 1920s. His early prose captured memories of coal-heated vessels, while subsequent autobiographical books explored a child's perception of life. He developed nature studies in prose by combining observation with words through a method he called thinking out in the meadow. His novel Vägen till Klockrike examines the tension between wandering and settled impulses within people, whereas his epic Aniara utilizes an imagined space flight to reflect contemporary human fears.

terms.definition: Working-class poets and authors who entered the literary landscape, enriching it with their unique experiences and creative energy.
A literary magazine founded by Johnson and other young writers during the metalworkers' strike of 1920.
A method used by Martinson in his prose nature studies that combines linguistic expression with direct observation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Technological advancements in cell biology research
sections.body: The availability of the electron microscope in 1938 offered immense promise for observing tiny cellular structures. While initial attempts to prepare cells for this technology faced difficulties, Claude and his colleagues achieved a breakthrough in the mid-forties by successfully preparing cells for microscopy. Additionally, Claude pioneered a method involving grinding cells into fragments and using a centrifuge to sort components on a large scale. These methodological developments allowed researchers to analyze individual cell parts separately to understand their specific chemical compositions and functional roles.

sections.heading: Techniques for studying cellular structure and composition
sections.body: Claude helped combine high-resolution images with biochemical analysis. Electron microscopy revealed small structures, while cell fractionation allowed researchers to investigate their chemical activities. Cells or tissues were gently broken apart, then centrifuged in successive steps. Components sedimented at different rates; nuclei could be collected in an early fraction, with other components recovered in later steps. Each sedimented fraction could then be analysed. This was a separation by sedimentation behaviour, not simply the formation of neat layers ordered by weight. Examining fractions such as mitochondria or microsomes helped researchers connect the structures seen in micrographs with biological functions. The strength of the approach was the combination of evidence from imaging and chemistry.

sections.heading: Albert Claude's academic and professional trajectory
sections.body: After earning a medical degree from the Université de Liège in 1928, Albert Claude traveled to Berlin for research. He worked at the Institute für Krebsforschung and later within the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute, Dahlem, specifically in Albert Fischer's tissue culture laboratory. In the summer of 1929, he joined the Rockefeller Institute. His career included roles as a professor at the University of Brussels and the Université Catholique de Louvain, where he also directed a laboratory focused on cellular biology and cancer research.

terms.definition: The study of cells, including their internal structures, chemical activities, functions and interactions.
Separating cell components by repeated centrifugation steps that collect particles with different sedimentation rates, which depend on properties including size and density.
Maintaining living cells or tissue outside the organism under controlled laboratory conditions, allowing their behaviour to be studied.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Diplomatic achievements in regional security and human rights
sections.body: The presentation speech praised Satō’s use of negotiation in securing the return of the Ogasawara Islands and Okinawa to Japanese sovereignty. It highlighted public non-nuclear commitments and Japan’s 1970 signature of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. These were the committee’s grounds for encouragement, rather than proof that all security disputes had been resolved. MacBride’s contribution concerned a different kind of international protection. As Irish foreign minister during the drafting of the European Convention on Human Rights, he supported treaty-based limits on state power. The convention was signed in 1950. His wider ambition for universal protection went beyond this regional instrument, including the idea of an international human-rights court.

sections.heading: Seán MacBride's international legal and human rights leadership
sections.body: Beyond his early Irish political involvement, MacBride held several significant global positions. He served as the Secretary-General of the International Commission of Jurists from 1963 to 1971 and chaired the Amnesty International Executive between 1961 and 1975. His administrative work included acting as Vice-President of the Organization for European Economic Cooperation and leading the Special Committee of International Non-Governmental Organizations on Human Rights in Geneva. Additionally, he was appointed by the United Nations General Assembly as the Commissioner for Namibia.

sections.heading: Eisaku Satō's professional background and political career
sections.body: After studying German jurisprudence at Tokyo Imperial University, Eisaku Satō entered the civil service following successful examinations. His early career involved roles within the Ministry of Railways, including serving as Director of the Osaka Railways Bureau and Vice-Minister for Transportation. He transitioned into politics through an appointment as Chief Cabinet Secretary in 1948. Following his election to the House of Representatives in 1949, he held various government and party positions. His collected speeches, titled In Quest of Peace and Freedom, supported his Nobel candidacy.

terms.definition: Treaty rules and institutions that place limits on state treatment of individuals; the European Convention established a regional, not worldwide, framework.
Organisations operating across national boundaries independently of governments; MacBride worked with several concerned with legal standards, peace and human rights.
The study of German law and legal principles, which formed Satō’s university specialisation before he entered Japan’s civil service.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Techniques for observing cosmic radio sources
sections.body: A single radio telescope large enough for the desired angular resolution could be impractical. Ryle and colleagues instead developed aperture synthesis, combining observations from separated antennas. Moving antennas and using Earth’s rotation sampled different spacings and orientations, allowing detailed radio maps to be reconstructed. A separate Cambridge programme used a fast receiver to study rapid fluctuations in radio-source intensity. During that survey in 1967, Jocelyn Bell identified unusually regular pulses that led to the discovery of pulsars, in work supervised by Hewish. Pulsars were understood as rotating neutron stars. The award joined Ryle’s imaging methods with Hewish’s role in a discovery whose essential observational contribution came from Bell.

sections.heading: Radio astronomy research and antenna development
sections.body: At the Cavendish Laboratory, researchers utilized radio interferometers to study radiation propagation through inhomogeneous media. Hewish developed theories regarding diffraction from phase-modulating screens to measure ionospheric plasma clouds and estimate wind speeds. He also applied interplanetary scintillation techniques to achieve high angular resolution in radio astronomy. To conduct large-scale sky surveys of radio galaxies, a giant phased-array antenna was constructed by 1967. This instrument featured high sensitivity at long wavelengths and multi-beam capabilities, which enabled the survey in which Jocelyn Bell identified the first pulsar signals.

sections.heading: Development of radio astronomy at Cambridge
sections.body: Following a suggestion from J.A. Ratcliffe, Ryle joined a research group at the Cavendish Laboratory to investigate solar radio emissions. This work utilized techniques derived from radar equipment used during the war. Supported by Lawrence Bragg, the team developed aperture synthesis methods, which shared similarities with X-ray crystallography techniques. During the period between 1948 and 1952, Ryle's research group expanded as Antony Hewish and four other members began their investigations. This academic progression eventually led to Ryle's appointment to a Chair of Radio Astronomy in 1959.

terms.definition: Combining measurements from separated antennas to reconstruct an image with resolution corresponding to a much larger observing aperture.
Rapid fluctuations in the apparent intensity of compact radio sources caused by plasma in the solar wind, useful for studying source sizes and the intervening medium.
Combining signals received at separated radio antennas to measure spatial information that a single small antenna cannot resolve.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of enzymatic synthesis and molecular geometry
sections.body: Research into biological synthesis revealed how enzymes navigate complex pathways. Cornforth investigated the fourteen-step production of squalene from mevalonic acid, determining which specific hydrogen atoms are eliminated at each stage. He achieved this by utilizing ordinary, heavy, and radioactive hydrogen isotopes as tracers. Concurrently, Prelog explored how the flexible shapes of medium rings, containing eight to eleven carbon atoms, influence chemical reactions. His work with carbon isotopes and small molecules helped map enzyme active sites, demonstrating how geometric fit dictates the success of oxidation or reduction processes.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of molecular stereochemistry and isotopic marking
sections.body: Cornforth utilized three hydrogen isotopes—mass 1, deuterium, and tritium—to identify which specific atoms enzymes replace during biological reactions. By leveraging the differing reaction speeds of these isotopes, he tracked transformations such as steroid synthesis from mevalonic acid via squalene. Prelog investigated how the geometric forms of molecules influence chemical courses, specifically studying medium-sized rings containing 8 to 12 carbon atoms. His work explored how mobile ring structures allow remote parts to contact each other, alongside research into chiral molecules and reactions involving alkaloids or antibiotics.

sections.heading: Isotopic substitution and steroid synthesis research
sections.body: At the National Institute for Medical Research, Cornforth and George Popják combined chemistry and biochemistry to investigate cholesterol synthesis. They devised a carbon-by-carbon degradation of the nineteen-carbon portion containing the steroid ring framework and used radioactive tracers to identify how acetate units contributed to it. As intermediate stages became known, they could design experiments that resolved more detailed questions. At the Milstead Laboratory of Chemical Enzymology, which they co-directed from 1962, Cornforth developed studies of enzyme reactions using asymmetry introduced through isotopic substitution. Work with Hermann Eggerer helped address the configuration of isotopically asymmetric methyl groups. The approach made otherwise similar atomic positions experimentally distinguishable.

terms.definition: Describing a structure that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, like a left hand and a right hand.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons and therefore different masses; distinguishable isotopes can serve as tracers in reactions.
Replacing an atom with another isotope of the same element; selected substitutions can create distinguishable positions or introduce molecular asymmetry.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mathematical techniques for optimal resource use
sections.body: Kantorovich invented linear programming to maximize factory production by finding the maximum value of a linear function under linear inequality constraints. This method produces shadow prices, which serve as useful accounting prices for decentralized profitability calculations in planned economies. Independently, Koopmans developed related methods for routing empty ships while working in wartime Washington. He developed activity analysis to link technical efficiency with price systems and explored optimal methods for dividing national income between present consumption and future investment during the 1960s.

sections.heading: Methods for optimizing resource use and economic planning
sections.body: Kantorovich utilized linear programming to show improvements for Soviet economic planning, specifically examining how individual enterprise efficiency relates to the broader economy in his book, The Best Use of Economic Resources. He demonstrated that decentralizing decisions in a planned economy requires a rational price system featuring a uniform accounting interest rate for investment. Meanwhile, Koopmans developed activity analysis through works like Analysis of Production as an Efficient Combination of Activities. This method interprets input-output relationships to link production efficiency with calculation prices and explores optimum growth rates.

sections.heading: Development of linear programming and production planning methods
sections.body: While consulting for the Laboratory of the Plywood Trust in 1938, Kantorovich addressed maximizing equipment productivity by distributing raw materials. He identified that various economic challenges, such as rational material cutting and transport flow distribution, shared a mathematical form involving maximizing linear functions on convex polytopes. This led to his method of resolving multipliers. In 1939, he published The Mathematical Method of Production Planning and Organization, which introduced algorithms for linear programming. His later work, The Best Use of Economic Resources, expanded these optimal approaches to include pricing and decentralization.

terms.definition: A technique used to find a linear function's maximum value subject to constraints made of linear inequalities.
Analysis of how resources ought to be allocated under specified goals or standards, as distinct from describing existing economic choices.
A bounded region defined by linear inequalities; in these optimization problems it represents the combinations of choices allowed by the constraints.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Poetic resistance and linguistic precision
sections.body: During the fascist dictatorship, Montale utilized hermeticism to maintain free expression despite atmospheric suppression. His stylistic evolution moved toward an anti-eloquence, stripping away embellishment to achieve a laconic, precise artistry. This method is evident in works like La bufera e altro and his later diary, Diario, which employs irony and epigrams. His poetry reflects a fundamental pessimism regarding historical lessons and human decline, yet functions as a subtle voice of conscience through concentrated structures that avoid traditional rhetorical flourishes.

sections.heading: Evolution of Montale's poetic volumes
sections.body: Montale published his major poetry collections at long intervals. After his 1925 debut, Ossi di seppia, later volumes included Le Occasioni, La Bufera e altro, Satura and Diario del ’71 e del ’72. Each collection strengthened his literary standing while developing his restrained approach. The award announcement connects the rocky Ligurian coastline with the hardness and resistance of his poetic language. His rejection of rhetorical fanfare expressed an outlook on modern life, not simply a preference for a particular style. Refusing political conformity also had practical consequences: excluded from his library post, he supported himself in part through translation.

sections.heading: Evolution of Montale's poetic style and literary output
sections.body: Montale's creative trajectory moved from early critical contributions in Primo Tempo to significant collections like Le occasioni, which established a metaphysical, classical-modern imprint. His work often utilized linguistic ambiguity, notably in the bestseller Satura, to disrupt traditional patterns through provocative humor and existential themes. Beyond poetry, he produced imaginative prose in La farfalla di Dinard and explored autobiographical elements in later volumes. His verse frequently sought hidden presences, such as spectres or amulets, while reflecting on the tragic consequences of historical conflicts.

terms.definition: Dense, indirect poetry using compressed images and associations; the presentation speech links this style with writers’ resistance to fascist demands for conformity.
Writing that rejects grand flourishes and easy emotional effects in favour of concentrated expression, a defining emphasis of Montale’s poetry.
Language that permits more than one interpretation, which Montale used to unsettle familiar poetic forms and expectations.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of viral genetic integration and information reversal
sections.body: Dulbecco’s work showed that DNA from certain tumour viruses can join cellular DNA, creating heritable changes in the infected cells. Temin proposed that RNA tumour viruses also pass through a DNA stage, an idea initially met with scepticism. In 1970, Temin and Baltimore independently identified the enzymatic activity that makes DNA using RNA as a template. Reverse transcriptase supplied a mechanism for this RNA-to-DNA step. It changed understanding of information transfer between nucleic acids; it did not reverse the transfer from nucleic acids into protein. Viral sequences incorporated into chromosomes can also be inherited across generations, rather than persisting for millions of years within one individual organism.

sections.heading: Later research on cancer-causing proteins
sections.body: Baltimore’s 2005 autobiographical addendum describes research after the Nobel award, when his laboratory combined immunology with virology. Studies using the Abelson mouse leukaemia virus connected its ability to transform cells with an oncoprotein that acts as a tyrosine-specific protein kinase. Tyrosine-specific kinase activity was also identified in related work by Tony Hunter. Understanding these cancer-associated enzymes helped create the scientific basis for targeted drugs, including Gleevec. This later development was distinct from the reverse-transcriptase work recognized in 1975. The biography illustrates how studying viral mechanisms could reveal processes relevant to cancer more broadly.

sections.heading: Development of animal virus assay techniques
sections.body: Renato Dulbecco established a method to assay animal viruses using cell cultures and a plaque technique, adapted from phage studies. This innovation enabled quantitative research in animal virology and was applied to studying poliovirus biological properties. His laboratory investigations into the polyoma virus explored how lytic infection and transformation interact with host cells. Additionally, his work with Howard Temin and Harry Rubin focused on the Rous Sarcoma Virus, which helped initiate his specific interest in the field of tumor viruses.

terms.definition: The synthesis of DNA from an RNA template, catalysed by the enzyme reverse transcriptase.
An enzyme that transfers phosphate groups to tyrosine residues in proteins, changing how those proteins function.
A method of measuring infectious virus by counting localized areas of damage, called plaques, in a layer of cultured cells.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Human rights advocacy and the Committee for Human Rights
sections.body: To bring his proposals to a broader audience, Sakharov established the Committee for Human Rights in 1970 alongside colleagues. This organization sought to implement constructive reforms through legal frameworks, following the principles found in the 1948 United Nations Declaration of Human Rights. His activism focused on resisting power abuses and promoting government based on the rule of law. The speech connects his advocacy with Section VII of the 1975 Helsinki Agreement, in which participating states committed to respect freedoms including conscience and religion. By emphasizing that individual rights are necessary for lasting international cooperation, Sakharov used his public letters to authorities and his 1968 manifesto to advocate for disarmament and global peace.

sections.heading: Evolution of socio-political views and human rights activism
sections.body: Following his nuclear physics thesis defense in 1947, Sakharov joined a research group led by I.E. Tamm to develop nuclear weapons. During the period between 1953 and 1962, he participated in nuclear experiments while becoming increasingly aware of inherent moral problems. In 1968, he published the article Progress, Peaceful Coexistence and Intellectual Freedom to express these growing concerns. His activism expanded through the Committee for Human Rights, which he operated alongside individuals such as Valery Chalidze and Tverdokhlebov. From 1970 onwards, his focus shifted toward defending victims of political trials. After the Nobel award, he was exiled to Gorky in 1980 following his criticism of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. Despite KGB persecution, he continued advocating human rights and used hunger strikes to seek medical treatment for Yelena Bonner.

terms.definition: An organization founded by Sakharov in 1970 to promote legal reforms and human rights based on United Nations principles.
Freedom to develop, express and debate ideas without political suppression, a central concern of Sakharov’s 1968 essay and subsequent human rights advocacy.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of nuclear deformation and collective excitations
sections.body: Rainwater proposed that outer, or valence, nucleons could change the shape of the nuclear core. The effect was mutual: the core’s distribution also determined the field in which those particles moved. Several nucleons in similar orbits could produce a lasting deformation. Rainwater’s model explained this through the pressure associated with their motion; the nucleus has no literal solid wall. Bohr independently considered the interaction and in 1951 developed a theory coupling nuclear surface oscillations to individual nucleon motion. His analysis predicted both shape vibrations and collective rotation. This rotation was not simply the motion of a rigid body: the presentation speech described a wave travelling around the nuclear surface.

sections.heading: Testing the model against nuclear energy levels
sections.body: A successful nuclear model had to account for measured properties, not only offer a plausible picture. The liquid-drop and shell models each captured part of nuclear behaviour, but neither initially explained the strongly non-spherical charge distributions found in some nuclei. Bohr’s theory included vibrations and rotation about an axis perpendicular to the nucleus’s symmetry axis.
