In three papers published in 1952–1953, Bohr and Mottelson compared the theory with experimental results. The arrangement of particular nuclear energy levels matched a rotational spectrum, giving strong support to the collective model. This agreement encouraged further experiments and refinements. Later work with David Pines connected features of nuclear matter with behaviour resembling superconductivity.

sections.heading: Development of nuclear structure theory
sections.body: Discussions with I.I. Rabi during a 1948 visit to Columbia drew Aage Bohr into research on deuterium’s hyperfine structure. This led to a longer association with Columbia from January 1949 to August 1950. Following this, he established a long-term scientific cooperation with Ben Mottelson. Together, they worked to document nuclear structure understanding through a multi-volume monograph. The first volume, focusing on single-particle motion, was published in 1969, while the second volume, covering nuclear deformations, followed in 1975. Their research efforts were supported by the scientific environment at the Niels Bohr Institute and Nordita.

terms.definition: Protons or neutrons in outer nuclear states whose motion can influence the shape of the remaining nuclear core.
Nuclear phenomena including the rotation of the entire nucleus or periodic changes in its shape around a mean value.
A detailed study of one subject; Bohr and Mottelson organized theirs into volumes on single-particle motion and nuclear deformation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Advancements in Borane Structural Analysis
sections.body: Since 1954, Lipscomb addressed the challenges of studying unstable, chemically aggressive boranes. Because these compounds often require investigation at very low temperatures, he utilized X-ray methods and advanced theoretical computations to determine molecular geometry. His work explored various forms, including electrically neutral molecules and charged ions. By calculating possible combinations within conceivable bond types, he helped establish a systematic understanding of how boron atoms bind. These research efforts enabled scientists to predict molecular stability and reactions, significantly advancing the field of preparative borane chemistry.

sections.heading: Why familiar bond pictures were insufficient
sections.body: The boranes posed a problem for a simple comparison with hydrocarbons. A conventional covalent bond joins two atoms through a shared electron pair, but boron has fewer available bonding electrons than carbon. Drawing every connection that way could not satisfactorily account for the structures. Lipscomb used topological reasoning to identify combinations of bond types consistent with the molecules. Experimental geometries from X-ray diffraction and quantum-mechanical calculations then constrained those possibilities. His work included neutral boranes, charged clusters and related compounds, turning apparently exceptional structures into a field with systematic relationships. The resulting descriptions helped chemists reason about stability and reactions under different conditions.

sections.heading: Academic transitions and early research publications
sections.body: After studying physics at the California Institute of Technology, Lipscomb transitioned to chemistry in 1942 under Linus Pauling. Following his doctoral studies, he held faculty positions at the University of Minnesota and Harvard University. His foundational investigations into boron hydrides were documented in his 1963 book, Boron Hydrides. Beyond borane research, his work since 1960 explored how enzyme three-dimensional structures relate to catalytic reactions and regulation through allosteric transformations.

terms.definition: A type of bond where two electrons cooperate to bind three atoms together, addressing electron deficiency in boron compounds.
Ways of analysing how atoms can be connected, used here to identify feasible combinations of bonding types in borane structures.
Structural changes in an enzyme that couple events at one site to changes in activity at another site.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Impact of monetary theory and policy lags
sections.body: Friedman's research revitalized the importance of money in explaining inflation and business cycles, challenging post-Keynesian tendencies to neglect monetary policy. He introduced specific terms for difficulties in timing stabilization efforts, namely observation-, decision-, and effect-lags. His analysis demonstrated how varying delays in money supply changes can create destabilizing effects, leading to recommendations for simplified monetary goals focused on stable long-term growth of the money supply. Additionally, his historical work argued that Federal Reserve policy helped deepen the Great Depression. Beyond monetary theory, he proposed an international currency system based on free exchange rates and reshaped consumption theory by using permanent income rather than current annual income to explain consumption expenditure.

sections.heading: Development of income and consumption theories
sections.body: Friedman's economic ideas emerged from diverse research experiences and academic influences. While working at the National Resources Committee in 1935, he contributed to a large consumer budget study, which became a primary component of his later Theory of the Consumption Function. His work on professional incomes, conducted alongside Simon Kuznets at the National Bureau of Economic Research, led to the publication of Incomes from Independent Professional Practice. This research introduced the distinction between permanent and transitory income. By combining these earlier consumption studies with his analysis of professional income, he developed the permanent income hypothesis. His academic training was further shaped by mentors like Arthur Burns, who emphasized scientific standards, and Homer Jones, who introduced him to rigorous economic theory.

terms.definition: A Chicago School concept emphasizing the significant role of money in explaining inflation and economic activity.
Concepts introduced in research regarding professional incomes to distinguish between lasting and temporary changes in an individual's earnings.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Anti-heroes, disappointment and human values
sections.body: The presentation speech read Bellow’s fiction as a search for human values amid difficult realities. His protagonists are exposed and questioned rather than conventionally glorified. Dangling Man and The Victim established a restrained attention to inner life, a line the committee also found in Seize the Day. Their formal discipline differs from the more expansive structure of his later narrative style. Across these forms, the speech identified characters who endure repeated disappointment yet continue seeking a worthwhile life. It treated their persistence as a kind of heroism and emphasised Bellow’s ability to turn their struggles into comedy. This was an interpretation of his compassionate scrutiny of people, not a description of every protagonist as simply defeated.

sections.heading: Evolution of American narrative art and style
sections.body: Bellow transitioned away from the rigid, choppy prose of the hard-boiled style toward a more expansive method. His early writing utilized restrained perceptions reminiscent of Flaubert and Henry James to examine protagonists' inner selves. Later, he developed a unique mixture of picaresque elements and cultural analysis. This mature phase incorporated exuberant ideas, irony, and comedy into works like The Adventures of Augie March and Henderson the Rain King. These narratives feature loose-jointed structures that allow for detailed descriptions of diverse societies, ranging from Manhattan to Africa.

sections.heading: Literary achievements and diverse writing contributions
sections.body: Bellow expanded his literary repertoire through various formats beyond novels. His dramatic works include the play The Last Analysis and the short play collection Under the Weather, which reached Broadway in 1966. He also produced non-fiction, such as the personal account To Jerusalem and Back, documenting a 1975 trip to Israel. Additionally, his prose appeared in numerous periodicals including The New Yorker and Esquire. His career included roles as a war correspondent for Newsday during the 1967 Arab-Israeli conflict and teaching positions at Princeton University.

terms.definition: A central character who lacks conventional heroic qualities; the committee saw Bellow’s flawed, disappointed protagonists as nevertheless committed to human values.
A novel style characterized by entertaining adventure and a loose structure used to explore different societies and colorful characters.
A category of writing, such as Bellow's personal account of his travels to Israel, based on factual records.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Long incubation periods challenged ideas about infection
sections.body: Gajdusek investigated kuru, a fatal neurological disease among the Fore people of New Guinea. Progressive brain damage occurred without the fever and inflammatory signs commonly associated with infection. Experiments nevertheless showed that material from affected people could transmit a similar disease to chimpanzees. Symptoms took roughly one and a half to three years to appear in those experiments. The delay demonstrated why an infectious cause could be difficult to recognise. The 1976 presentation also emphasised the agent's unusual resistance to treatments that inactivate many viruses. These were observations distinguishing kuru from conventional viral infections, not a general claim that its agent was indestructible or bypassed every bodily defence.

sections.heading: An unexpected blood marker revealed hepatitis B infection
sections.body: Blumberg's investigations of variation in blood proteins uncovered a marker called Australia antigen. Initially it was considered a possible inherited serum protein. Work during 1966–1968 connected it instead with the infection then often called serum hepatitis, now hepatitis B. The marker proved to be associated with the virus's surface. Detecting it made it possible to identify some people carrying the infection even when they were not visibly ill, a major advance for screening donated blood. This connection between a blood marker and an infectious agent grew from research that had begun with human biological variation, rather than a direct search for the cause of hepatitis.

sections.heading: Research on blood polymorphisms and hepatitis B
sections.body: Blumberg's studies of inherited protein variation involved specimens from different populations, including the Fulani and their domestic animals. Continuing this comparative approach eventually led to Australia antigen and hepatitis B. His group developed an HBV radioimmunoassay to improve screening; more sensitive and convenient tests from other laboratories strengthened the programme. Identifying infected donor blood greatly reduced transfusion-associated hepatitis B, although it did not eliminate hepatitis from other causes. Vaccine development used surface-antigen particles obtained from carriers' blood. That describes the early vaccine approach discussed in his retrospective account, rather than every later hepatitis B vaccine. The research linked population studies, laboratory assays and prevention.

terms.definition: The interval between exposure to an infectious agent and the appearance of symptoms; it can be unusually long in diseases such as kuru.
A protein associated with the outer surface of hepatitis B virus, originally called Australia antigen, whose detection can indicate infection.
A laboratory measurement using antibody binding and a radioactive label to detect or quantify a particular substance.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Grassroots mobilization against violence in Northern Ireland
sections.body: After three children died in a Belfast incident involving a car and a shooting, Betty Williams began a door-to-door appeal against violence. Media attention helped the appeal spread, and she joined the children’s aunt, Mairead Corrigan, in building a peace movement. The presentation speech stressed participation by ordinary people across divided communities. It described the campaign as a way to challenge fear, break barriers between neighbours and make the desire for peace publicly visible. The committee argued that this rejection of violence could weaken support for armed conflict. That was a strategic hope attached to the movement, rather than evidence that marches had already ended Northern Ireland’s conflict.

sections.heading: Community work beyond the first marches
sections.body: Corrigan’s later biographical account describes the Community of Peace People’s continuing work after its initial mobilisations. Summer camps in other European countries allowed Catholic and Protestant young people from Northern Ireland to meet outside their usual divisions. Outreach also supported prisoners and their families. Corrigan advocated nonviolent solutions through writing and public speaking. Separately, she helped found the Committee on the Administration of Justice, a non-sectarian organisation concerned with human rights and emergency legislation. These details trace the movement and her activities over subsequent years; they should not all be read as projects already completed when the reserved 1976 prize was awarded in 1977.

sections.heading: Later advocacy for children affected by violence
sections.body: Long after the Nobel award, Williams extended her advocacy toward children threatened by war and other violence. She founded the Global Children’s Studies Center in 1992 and World Centers of Compassion for Children International in 1997. Her biographical account describes gathering children’s testimony to argue for stronger legal protection. It also presents a project for a City of Compassion in Basilicata, southern Italy, within a wider proposal for safe communities for vulnerable children. These are later activities and ambitions described in that account, not evidence that a place was automatically protected from attack or that every planned project was completed.

terms.definition: A grassroots initiative formed to promote reconciliation and reject violence through community participation and the removal of street barriers.
Activities such as summer camps for youth designed to help opposing groups from Northern Ireland know one another.
A proposed community intended to provide vulnerable children with safety and care, part of Williams’s later advocacy programme.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Two experiments and one unexpected resonance
sections.body: The two teams used different experimental routes but found the same striking signal in 1974. Richter’s group studied electron–positron collisions at Stanford, while Ting’s apparatus at Brookhaven identified electron–positron pairs produced after proton collisions. Both saw a heavy particle with an unusually narrow energy profile. Brookhaven named it J and Stanford named it psi, producing the combined name J/psi. Its narrow resonance was part of the surprise that demanded a new explanation. The result became decisive evidence for charm. Although the historical speech discussed the wider field of elementary particles, J/psi itself is understood as a bound charm quark–antiquark state, not an indivisible constituent.

sections.heading: Different collision methods
sections.body: To create heavy particles, scientists must concentrate large amounts of kinetic energy using massive accelerators. Richter utilized a storage ring at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, where electron and positron streams collided head-on at precisely adjustable beam energies to produce the psi particle. Conversely, Ting’s team used a proton machine at Brookhaven National Laboratory, directing high-speed protons into a stationary beryllium target. This method identified parent particles by measuring resulting electron and positron daughter pairs, despite the difficulty of isolating rare signals from millions of other particles.

sections.heading: Collider development before and after the prize
sections.body: Richter’s 2005 autobiography spans several different stages of accelerator development. In 1963 he established a SLAC group designing a high-energy electron–positron machine. While seeking funding, his group also built spectrometer equipment for pion and kaon photoproduction experiments. Later work, beyond the 1976 award, explored converting SLAC’s long linear accelerator into a collider. Electrons and positrons would be accelerated together, then separated and redirected by magnets into head-on collisions. This later facility contributed to beam-dynamics research and planning for still higher-energy machines. It should not be confused with the storage-ring experiment that discovered J/psi.

terms.definition: A pronounced peak in a reaction rate at a particular energy, indicating formation of a particle state with characteristic mass and lifetime.
A circular accelerator system that holds particle beams for repeated circulation; Stanford’s ring brought electrons and positrons into head-on collisions.
An accelerator arrangement that brings beams accelerated along straight paths into collision, rather than repeatedly accelerating them around a storage ring.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Non-linear thermodynamics and open systems
sections.body: Prigogine and collaborators including Glansdorff, Lefever and Nicolis investigated nonlinear processes in systems maintained far from equilibrium. Exchanges with the environment can sustain organised patterns in space or time. The problem was to determine when such states arise and whether they remain stable under small disturbances. This extended analysis beyond the near-equilibrium regime where linear approximations are useful. The 1977 presentation suggested that the stability methods could illuminate varied problems, from chemical and biological organisation to traffic and population models. Their relevance depends on the particular system and model; they do not establish that every open system becomes ordered.

sections.heading: Extension of thermodynamics to non-equilibrium systems
sections.body: Prigogine studied how organised patterns can persist when a system is continually driven away from equilibrium. An illustrative case is convection in a liquid heated from below. Beyond an instability threshold, organised circulation can replace simple heat conduction, sometimes forming regular cellular patterns. Continued heat flow maintains that organisation; removing the driving conditions allows it to disappear. The example connects local order with ongoing dissipation. It does not contradict thermodynamics: the system exchanges energy with its surroundings while producing entropy. The framework helped researchers study stability and pattern formation in chemical reactions and other nonlinear systems.

sections.heading: Development of stability criteria and evolution theorems
sections.body: Prigogine's early work developed a minimum-entropy-production theorem for stationary states within a restricted near-equilibrium regime. It built on De Donder's use of chemical affinity to connect reaction rates and entropy production. Later, with Glansdorff, he sought criteria useful beyond that linear regime. Their analysis examined stability and identified critical conditions where an existing state could become unstable and new branches of behaviour emerge. Fluctuations could then help initiate organised patterns sustained by exchanges with the surroundings. Their 1971 book presented this work on thermodynamic structure and stability. The distinction between the two regimes is essential: minimum entropy production is not a universal rule for all far-from-equilibrium systems.

terms.definition: A system exchanging matter and energy with its surroundings; such exchanges can help maintain a state away from equilibrium.
Ordered patterns that exist only through symbiosis with their surroundings, requiring a continuous exchange of energy or matter.
A thermodynamic quantity describing the driving tendency of a chemical reaction and its relation to entropy production.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of international trade and economic policy
sections.body: In the Heckscher-Ohlin model, differences in countries' supplies of land, labour and capital help explain trade patterns. Countries tend to export goods that use their abundant factors intensively, such as land-intensive wool from Australia. Under the model's assumptions, trade can also bring factor prices, such as wages and land rents, closer together. This is the factor price equalization result, rather than a claim that all production costs become identical. Meade investigated how economic policy changes international trade, including the effects of tariffs, customs unions and free trade areas. His work also examined interest rates, exchange rates and policies for maintaining balance in both the domestic economy and international payments.

sections.heading: Foundations of international trade and capital movement theory
sections.body: Bertil Ohlin's Interregional and International Trade explores how trade patterns and the division of labor are determined. His research links international commerce to industrial location, resource allocation, and income distribution while comparing intra-national and global trade. James Meade, in The Theory of International Economic Policy, investigates stabilization methods for economies dependent on foreign trade. He analyzes the requirements for internal and external balance, focusing on how total demand levels and price-cost relations influence successful economic policy within these open systems.

sections.heading: James Meade's research on international economic policy
sections.body: During his tenure at the London School of Economics, James Meade developed significant works regarding global commerce. His project resulted in two primary books: The Balance of Payments and Trade and Welfare. In these texts, he utilized mathematical appendices to examine international relations between national economies built upon a Keynesian model. Additionally, he applied economic welfare theory to international transactions. While his initial research goals were expansive, these specific studies regarding trade and payments contributed to his recognition for excellence in the field.

terms.definition: A theoretical framework where trade arises from differences in the supplies of various production factors among different nations.
Economies connected to others through trade and international transactions; Meade particularly examined countries strongly dependent on foreign trade.
A model linking aggregate demand with output and employment, which Meade used to examine relations between national economies.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Evolution of Spanish poetic styles and creative consciousness
sections.body: Aleixandre's career shifted from railway administration to poetry following a serious bout of renal tuberculosis in 1925. As a member of the Pleiades group, he participated in a movement that utilized baroque-inspired ornamentation alongside rustic folksong variations. While influenced by French surrealism, he rejected automatic writing in favor of creative consciousness. His later significant collections include Poemas de la consumación and Diálogos del conocimiento. His poetic trajectory moves from a cosmic perspective toward realistic close-ups, often exploring themes where destruction and love are interconnected.

sections.heading: Evolution of Spanish Surrealist Expression
sections.body: Aleixandre's poetic development moved from complex structures toward a simplicity of expression and warm openness. While his work shared characteristics with French surrealism, such as abrupt allusion techniques, it maintained independence by incorporating baroque imagery and motifs from everyday life. His prolific output includes significant works like Nacimiento último and En un vasto dominio. Despite facing severe renal tuberculosis that restricted his physical movement, he achieved a peak in his career through later collections like Diálogos del conocimiento, demonstrating a continuous capacity for renewal.

sections.heading: Evolution of Spanish Poetic Works
sections.body: Aleixandre devoted himself entirely to literature from 1925; his first poetry collection, Ambit, appeared in 1928. His creative progression includes the 1933 National Literary Prize-winning work, Destruction or Love. Despite facing four years of silence under new authorities after the Civil War, he continued publishing significant texts. In 1944, he released The Shadow of Paradise while maintaining independence from the prevailing political situation. His extensive bibliography eventually led to his recognition by the Swedish Academy for the totality of his literary contributions.

terms.definition: A concept representing creative consciousness used by Aleixandre to move away from the practice of automatic writing.
A literary movement sharing imagery with French surrealism but utilizing baroque ornamentation and everyday motifs to maintain distinct Iberian independence.
A distinction received by Aleixandre in 1933 specifically for his poetic work titled Destruction or Love.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Measuring protein hormones and brain chemical links
sections.body: Yalow and Berson found antibodies against insulin in people who had received insulin treatment. This observation helped them develop a way to measure minute hormone concentrations. In a laboratory sample, unlabelled insulin competes with radioactively labelled insulin for antibody binding; the measured binding indicates how much insulin the sample contains. The assay itself does not require injecting radioactive insulin into a patient. A separate challenge faced Guillemin and Schally: identifying the hormones through which the hypothalamus controls the pituitary. Their teams processed enormous quantities of sheep and pig hypothalamic tissue to obtain tiny purified samples. In 1969, they identified the structure of thyrotropin-releasing hormone.

sections.heading: Discovery and analysis of peptide hormones
sections.body: Guillemin’s and Schally’s teams isolated hypothalamic compounds that cause pituitary tissue to release hormones. Thyrotropin-releasing factor, also called TRF, stimulates release of TSH, which then acts on the thyroid. In 1969 its structure was established as a small peptide built from three amino acids; Guillemin’s group synthesized it that year. Radioimmunoassay addressed the complementary problem of measuring hormones at very low concentrations. Yalow and Berson’s original insulin assay used competition between labelled and unlabelled insulin for antibodies. Adaptations required the appropriate labelled substance and antibody for each target hormone. The award announcement cited measurements of ACTH below one picogram per millilitre as an example of the method’s sensitivity.

sections.heading: Research into hypothalamic releasing factors
sections.body: Guillemin became interested in how the hypothalamus controls pituitary secretion while studying the body’s response to stress. Contacts with Claude Fortier and Geoffrey Harris helped direct him toward chemical mediators. Schally later joined him at Baylor, where they initially hoped to identify corticotropin-releasing factor quickly. This early collaboration preceded the independent, competing programmes that produced the prizewinning results. Guillemin’s biography points readers to accounts of thyrotropin-releasing factor and luteinizing-hormone-releasing factor as key developments. He returned to Houston in 1963 after a period in France and moved to the Salk Institute in 1970 to establish neuroendocrinology laboratories.

terms.definition: A laboratory method that measures a substance by its competition with a radioactively labelled version for binding to a specific antibody.
Substances built up by chains of amino acids that function as signals within the body's endocrine system.
The study of interactions between nervous and hormonal signalling, including the hypothalamus’s control of pituitary function.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Amnesty International's organizational methods and principles
sections.body: The 1977 presentation speech described impartiality and independence as essential to Amnesty’s credibility. It reported that national sections supplied almost all its funding and that donations could not be allowed to restrict its work. Small adoption groups worked for prisoners from differing political backgrounds, using information about their circumstances and the relevant justice systems. They coordinated with the London office to trace prisoners, seek outside investigation and press for release. The speech also described Amnesty’s proposal for a United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. These were the organization’s methods and proposals at the time of the award.

sections.heading: Expansion of Amnesty International's global human rights activities
sections.body: Following its 1963 establishment of an international secretariat, the organization expanded into a world-embracing movement. By February 1977, the group comprised 1874 voluntary groups across 33 countries. Its core tasks under the 1974 statutes included campaigning against torture, ill-treatment, and capital punishment. To address global issues, the movement collected signatures for an appeal directed to the United Nations General Assembly. Its prisoner campaigns focused on releasing individuals detained for their faith, skin colour, or ethnic origin, provided they have not used or incited violence.

sections.heading: Human rights as a foundation for global peace
sections.body: The 1977 Nobel lecture described Amnesty as a movement of 168,000 members in 107 countries. This work connects human rights to peace by viewing injustice as a source of conflict. Through the Amnesty International Report 1977, the group surveyed human rights situations in 117 nations, documenting violations occurring within various political or ideological blocs. The organization emphasizes that protecting fundamental freedoms requires strengthening legal machinery, such as the Human Rights Committee, and mobilizing public opinion to defend individuals against repression by governments or political organizations.

terms.definition: Small organizational units that monitor prisoners from different political backgrounds using detailed information regarding their situation and justice systems.
Individuals arrested due to their convictions, ethnic origin, skin colour, or faith, who have not utilized or encouraged violence.
A collection of international instruments, including the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, designed to protect fundamental human freedoms.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Amnesty International: organizational history and activities as described for the 1977 award
Mümtaz Soysal: Amnesty International’s methods and human-rights principles — Nobel lecture, 11 December 1977

sections.heading: Electronic Structure Theory in Magnetic and Disordered Systems
sections.body: The laureates investigated how electron behaviour determines electrical and magnetic properties. Van Vleck developed crystal-field and ligand-field theories, which describe metal atoms in their surroundings and have applications in chemistry, geology and laser technology. Anderson showed that geometrical disorder can confine electronic states to particular regions of a material. This localization need not restore a regular atomic arrangement. Mott studied transitions between conducting and insulating behaviour, including the role of mutual repulsion between electrons. Together, these approaches showed why neither perfect crystal order nor a picture of independent electrons is sufficient to describe every solid. The award speech emphasized their fundamental contributions, while also recognizing the practical possibilities of controlling disorder.

sections.heading: Theoretical investigations of electronic structures
sections.body: Van Vleck developed crystal field and ligand field theories to describe how electric fields from host crystals influence foreign atoms. His work on the Jahn-Teller effect explained lattice distortions caused by electronic incompatibility with environmental symmetry. Anderson expanded upon electron correlation concepts to explain how impurities can produce local magnetic moments in metals such as silver or copper. Additionally, Mott utilized refined theories involving electron-electron interactions to explain why nickel oxide acts as an insulator despite predictions from band theory.

sections.heading: Continuing localization research after the prize
sections.body: In his later autobiography, Anderson described how he, Elihu Abrahams, T. V. Ramakrishnan and Don Licciardello extended localization theory after the Nobel award. Their scaling approach produced quantitative predictions that experiments could test as magnetic field, interactions and dimensionality changed. This was a continuation of the prizewinning research, rather than work completed before the 1977 award. Anderson also recalled a separate collaboration with S. F. Edwards on a replica theory of spin glasses in 1975. His account places these developments in a longer career supported by colleagues at Bell Laboratories and appointments at Cambridge and, from 1975, Princeton.

terms.definition: A transition between conducting and insulating behaviour in which interactions between electrons play a crucial role.
The study of solid materials and how their atomic arrangement and electrons determine properties such as electrical conductivity and magnetism.
Quantitative predictions for how localization behaviour changes with conditions such as magnetic field, interactions and the dimensionality of a system.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of Bioenergetics and Protonmotive Force
sections.body: Bioenergetics investigates how living cells obtain and use energy. In respiration and photosynthesis, electron-transfer reactions are associated with biological membranes, including those of mitochondria and chloroplasts and the membranes of bacteria. Earlier explanations sought a chemical intermediate that would couple electron transfer directly to ATP formation. Mitchell instead emphasized the orientation of membrane proteins and the directed movement of protons across a membrane. The resulting electrochemical gradient stores energy that can be used elsewhere. He called this form of biological power transmission proticity, drawing an analogy with electricity. The award speech described applications beyond ATP synthesis, including nutrient uptake, ion transport and bacterial movement.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of biological energy transfer
sections.body: The chemiosmotic theory describes how electron-transfer chains drive protons across membranes in mitochondria, chloroplasts, and bacterial cells. This movement creates a protonmotive force consisting of an electric potential difference and a pH variation. In processes like oxidative phosphorylation and photophosphorylation, the return flow of protons down the gradient drives ATP synthesis. Beyond ATP synthesis, this mechanism supports nutrient uptake, ion transport, and bacterial motion. Mitchell also used the term proticity to describe this biological power transmission through an analogy with electricity.

sections.heading: Establishment of the Glynn Research Institute
sections.body: Mitchell established the Chemical Biology Unit at Edinburgh University in 1955 and remained there until illness led to his resignation in 1963. He then spent 1963–1965 restoring Glynn House in Cornwall and adapting it for laboratories. His former colleague Jennifer Moyle supported the project, and together they founded the charitable company Glynn Research Ltd. An endowment donated by Mitchell and his brother Christopher financed the work. In 1965 Mitchell and Moyle began their programme on chemiosmotic reactions at Glynn with technician Roy Mitchell and administrative assistance. The institute provided a small, independently supported setting for fundamental research into the energy-converting processes described by chemiosmotic theory.

terms.definition: The study of chemical processes responsible for supplying energy to living cells through various biological activities.
The electrochemical drive on protons across a membrane, combining a difference in proton concentration with a difference in electrical potential.
A charitable company founded by Peter Mitchell and Jennifer Moyle to finance fundamental biological research at Glynn House laboratories.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Decision-making processes in economic organizations
sections.body: In his 1947 book Administrative Behavior, Simon describes the company as an adaptive system comprising physical, personal, and social components linked by intercommunications and cooperation. He rejects classical assumptions of omniscient entrepreneurs, instead utilizing the psychology of learning to model decision-makers with limited memory and calculating capacity. Because these individuals lack knowledge regarding total consequences, they seek satisfactory alternatives rather than a single best choice. This approach applies to planning, budgeting, and control techniques within business and public administration. Simon observes that firms must strive for internal equilibrium among various organizational components while managing partly contradictory goals. His research focuses on how multiple cooperating decision-makers attempt to find acceptable solutions to acute problems by considering the actions of others.

sections.heading: Foundations of decision-making research and computer simulation
sections.body: Simon's early research career involved investigating municipal administration through operations research as a research assistant. He directed a municipal-administration research group at Berkeley from 1939 to 1942. Later work with Charles Holt derived decision rules and a certainty-equivalence theorem for handling uncertainty. His descriptive studies of organizational decision-making also included collaborations with Harold Guetzkow, James March, and Richard Cyert. Seeking better theories for human problem-solving, Simon and Allen Newell later developed computer models to investigate cognition. Additionally, Simon worked with Yuji Ijiri on stochastic models regarding the skewed size distributions of business firms. His broader scientific goals included strengthening social science tools and fostering cooperation between natural and social scientists to address complex public policy questions.

terms.definition: A system that adjusts to changing conditions; Simon described firms as interacting physical, personal and social components held together by communication and cooperation.
Using programmed models to reproduce selected aspects of a process; Simon and Allen Newell applied this approach to human problem-solving.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Themes of tradition and renewal in Singer's narrative art
sections.body: Singer’s literary development involved navigating the conflict between pious mysticism and modern secular currents. His writing explores the clash between traditional other-worldliness and the rise of free thought, doubt, or nihilism. In epic family chronicles such as The Family Moskat, The Manor, and The Estate, he depicts how new age demands split Jewish families socially and humanly. His 1935 work, Satan in Goray, examines themes of false Messiahs, mass hysteria, and the collapse of illusions. Through short stories and novellas, Singer integrates supernatural elements like demons and spectres from Jewish popular belief into his prose. He utilizes Yiddish as a storehouse for centuries of folklore, anecdotes, and superstitions to bring historical shadows back to life.

sections.heading: Passion, comedy and the supernatural
sections.body: The Nobel biographical essay highlights Singer’s ability to give human passions imaginative, sometimes supernatural forms. The Magician of Lublin follows an unconventional protagonist through restless desires toward an ascetic transformation. Its comic adventures coexist with darker consequences, making moral change part of the story rather than a simple lesson imposed from outside. In the shorter fiction, demons, ghosts and other figures from Jewish folklore embody obsession and destructive emotion while also appearing as presences within the fictional world. The essay points to collections including Gimpel the Fool, The Spinoza of Market Street and A Crown of Feathers. It also discusses In My Father’s Court, where memories of childhood Warsaw combine humour with an awareness of a world subsequently destroyed. These examples show the range between recollection, comic invention and the fantastic.

terms.definition: A narrative following a family through changing generations and circumstances; Singer used the form to explore conflicts between inherited traditions and modern life.
An episodic narrative following a roguish or unconventional protagonist through adventures and changing social encounters, a form the essay relates to The Magician of Lublin.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of DNA cleavage and genetic mapping
sections.body: Arber investigated host-controlled restriction and modification, a phenomenon previously observed by Bertani and Weigle. He proposed that bacteria could recognise foreign DNA and cut it while chemically modifying their own DNA to protect it. Smith then purified a restriction enzyme and determined the sequence features associated with its cuts. Nathans used such enzymes to fragment and map the DNA of simian virus 40, providing an important early demonstration of restriction mapping, not the first genetic map of any kind. Reproducible cuts allowed scientists to compare defined DNA segments and investigate genome organisation. The same tools also helped make recombinant-DNA experiments possible, including transferring selected genes between organisms.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of bacterial restriction and modification
sections.body: Arber and Daisy Dussoix found that bacterial restriction and modification acted directly on DNA without producing mutations. The effects were not confined to invading bacteriophages: experiments on conjugation showed that bacterial DNA transferred between cells was also affected. Later work examined the chemical modification responsible for protection. Stuart Linn developed laboratory studies of the Eco B restriction and modification activities, drawing on contacts with researchers studying Eco K. Experiments established that modification in these systems involved nucleotide methylation. Urs Kühnlein and John Smith subsequently tested and extended the findings in cells and in laboratory preparations. This distinguished protective chemical marking from the separate restriction process that cuts susceptible DNA.

sections.heading: Mapping Simian Virus 40 DNA via restriction enzymes
sections.body: After learning of a restriction endonuclease discovered in Hemophilus influenzae, researchers surveyed various enzymes for their ability to cleave Simian Virus 40 DNA. Working with Stuart Adler, Daniel Nathans utilized these enzymes to produce DNA fragments. Collaborators Kathleen Danna and George Sack then used these fragments to construct a cleavage map of the viral genome. This mapping allowed scientists to localize genes and template functions, create deletion or point mutants at specific restriction sites, and analyze genomes from naturally occurring viral variants.

terms.definition: Chemical alteration of DNA by the host cell that can protect it from the host's own restriction enzymes, without changing its nucleotide sequence.
Adding methyl chemical groups to particular DNA bases; in the restriction–modification systems studied, this marks DNA and can protect it from cleavage.
A map of where particular restriction enzymes cut a DNA molecule, which can then help researchers locate genes and other features.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The framework agreements of Camp David
sections.body: The committee grounded the 1978 award in two frameworks signed at Camp David on 17 September. One addressed peace in the Middle East more broadly; the other set out a basis for an Egypt–Israel agreement. They were foundations for further negotiation, not the final bilateral treaty. The presentation speech connected this breakthrough with earlier diplomacy after the 1973 Yom Kippur War and with President Jimmy Carter’s mediation. Sadat’s visit to Jerusalem in November 1977, including his address to the Knesset, had opened the way to direct talks with Begin. The committee hoped negotiations would replace repeated war with diplomatic, economic and cultural connections. The historical sequence matters: the frameworks preceded the award, while the Egypt–Israel treaty followed in March 1979.

sections.heading: Political development of Menachem Begin
sections.body: Before becoming Prime Minister, Menachem Begin held various leadership roles within Zionist movements. At age sixteen, he joined the Betar nationalist youth movement, eventually heading its Polish organization department in 1932 and later managing the movement in Poland by 1939. During his time in Palestine, he commanded the Irgun, also known as Etzel, directing operations against British rule while evading capture in Tel Aviv. Following Israel's establishment, he founded the Herut Movement and participated in the first Knesset elections. His political career included serving as a Minister without Portfolio within the 1967 Government of National Unity. After his party won the May 1977 elections, he presented his government to the Knesset and assumed the role of Prime Minister.

terms.definition: An agreement establishing principles and a route for further negotiations, while leaving a final settlement or detailed implementation to later steps.
A nationalist youth movement associated with the Zionist Revisionist Movement that Begin joined at age sixteen.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Helium liquefaction and superfluidity
sections.body: Kapitsa’s equipment made substantial quantities of liquid helium available for low-temperature research. That practical achievement mattered because reliable access to the liquid enabled sustained experiments close to absolute zero. After moving from Cambridge to Moscow, he continued investigating its unusual properties. Below the lambda transition, near 2.2 kelvin, helium-4 enters a superfluid phase that can flow with extraordinarily little resistance in appropriate experiments. Its behaviour involves a frictionless superfluid component alongside a normal component that can still exhibit viscosity. The 1978 prize recognised both experimental inventions and discoveries about matter under these conditions. Kapitsa’s work formed a separate half of the award from the cosmic-background discovery.

sections.heading: Distinguishing cosmic radiation from receiver noise
sections.body: Penzias and Wilson adapted a sensitive Bell Laboratories receiver originally built for satellite communications. At a wavelength near seven centimetres they expected little astronomical background, yet measured an unexplained excess. They investigated instrumental and atmospheric noise before concluding that the signal came from space. It was remarkably uniform across the sky within the precision of their measurements, rather than absolutely identical in every direction. Identifying it as radiation from a hot early universe required the connection with cosmological theory; subsequent spectral measurements strengthened that interpretation. The discovery was a faint microwave background with profound significance, not simply an intense radio source.

sections.heading: Kapitsa's advancements in magnetic fields and helium liquefaction
sections.body: During his career, Kapitsa developed techniques for generating intense magnetic fields reaching 320 kilogauss. He proposed a method with N.N. Semenov to determine atomic magnetic moments using inhomogeneous fields, which later supported Stern-Gerlach experiments. In 1934, he created an original apparatus for helium liquefaction utilizing the adiabatic principle. His research continued with a low-pressure cycle for air liquefaction using high-efficiency expansion turbines. These developments in cryogenics and strong magnetic fields facilitated his investigation into the properties of liquid helium and its superfluidity.

terms.definition: The transition temperature, near 2.2 kelvin under ordinary low-pressure conditions, at which liquid helium-4 enters its superfluid phase.
Radiation observed across the sky at microwave wavelengths, interpreted as a cooled remnant of the universe’s hot early state.
A change occurring without heat exchange with the surroundings; gas expansion can lower temperature when the gas performs work.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
David M. Lee: Nobel lecture on superfluid helium and its normal component

sections.heading: Advancements in organic synthesis through boron and phosphorus reagents
sections.body: Brown developed boron compounds into versatile reagents for organic synthesis. Borohydrides, including sodium borohydride, provided useful ways to carry out reductions, while organoborane chemistry supplied methods for additions, rearrangements and carbon–carbon bond formation. Wittig's phosphorus-containing reagents addressed another central task: building a carbon–carbon double bond. A phosphorus ylide reacts with a carbonyl compound, replacing the carbonyl oxygen with a carbon-containing group. These complementary tools expanded the transformations available when planning a synthesis. The Wittig reaction became particularly important in industrial vitamin A production, illustrating how a new laboratory reaction could support manufacture of a biologically important compound.

sections.heading: Advancements in Boron and Phosphorus Reagents
sections.body: Brown developed hydroboration, using boron hydrides to add boron and hydrogen across carbon–carbon multiple bonds. The resulting organoboranes could be transformed in many useful ways. His work on sodium borohydride and modified borohydrides also supplied selective reducing agents. Wittig developed a separate carbonyl-to-alkene transformation using phosphorus ylides. Its product contains a carbon–carbon double bond in place of the starting carbon–oxygen double bond. The Wittig reaction's use in vitamin A manufacture showed its practical value, while both programmes became standard parts of synthetic chemistry. Reagent design gave chemists greater choice over which part of a molecule would react and what structure would result.

sections.heading: Brown's research in organic and inorganic chemistry
sections.body: A gift from Sarah Baylen, Alfred Stock's book on boron and silicon hydrides, helped direct Brown towards graduate work with H. I. Schlesinger. This interest preceded his doctorate, awarded in 1938. His later research extended beyond borane reagents to the effects of molecular crowding, quantitative measures of steric strain and debates over non-classical ions. He also investigated aromatic reactivity and developed substitution constants used to correlate electrophilic reactions. At Purdue, his programme initially crossed physical, inorganic and organic chemistry, before he concentrated mainly on organic chemistry. The biography shows reagent development alongside broader efforts to understand why molecular structure changes reactivity.

terms.definition: The planned construction of organic molecules through a sequence of chemical reactions that form or modify particular bonds.
Organic compounds containing bonds between boron and carbon; hydroboration provides an important route to them.
Changes in molecular behaviour caused by the space occupied by atoms or groups, including crowding that can alter stability or hinder reactions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Models of economic development and trade dynamics
sections.body: Lewis utilized a dual economy model featuring a subsistence agricultural sector alongside a modern, market-oriented industrial sector. Under its labour-surplus assumption, migration can supply the capitalist sector with workers without immediately raising wages, while reinvested profits finance expansion. Additionally, Lewis analyzed trade terms between rich and poor nations by examining the exchange of raw materials for industrial goods. Schultz systematized how investments in education influence agricultural productivity and broader economic growth, specifically studying productivity imbalances within the United States and Third World nations.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of agricultural productivity and trade dynamics
sections.body: Schultz utilized a disequilibrium approach to analyze the gap between traditional production methods and more effective available techniques. His research, including Transforming Traditional Agriculture, emphasized how vocational skills, schooling, and research application drive efficiency. Meanwhile, Lewis examined how agricultural productivity levels influence long-term terms of trade between rich and poor nations. He modeled trade involving food, raw materials, and industrial products, specifically looking at the relationship between productivity in developing and developed countries to determine trade outcomes.

sections.heading: Lewis's development of the dual economy model
sections.body: While walking in Bangkok in 1952, Lewis formulated a solution to discrepancies regarding relative prices and historical wage stagnation. He rejected the neoclassical assumption of fixed labor quantities, proposing a model in which a large available supply of workers can keep wages low. This mechanism facilitates high profits and cheap production. His research involved analyzing colonial reports on mining and agriculture, alongside studying industrial economics and world economic history. These investigations informed his 1955 book and the dual-economy model, in which one sector supplies labour for another.

terms.definition: An economic framework describing a developing nation composed of a traditional subsistence agricultural sector and a modern, market-oriented industrial sector.
A method used by Schultz to analyze development potential by examining the gap between traditional methods and more effective production techniques.
A model assumption that workers remain available at prevailing wages during expansion; it does not mean the population or labour supply is literally infinite.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Integration of Surrealism and Greek Myth
sections.body: The poet's work represents a significant intersection between modernism and inherited myth. Rejecting the automatic writing characteristic of the surrealist school, he utilized deliberate creation and strict form rather than unchecked chance associations. His poetry avoids remoulding ancient tales into Western patterns, instead repeating the process by which myths are produced. This method moves from current reality toward potentiality, using the Aegean Sea as a foundation to explore a humanity that seeks a golden age which remains unrealized.

sections.heading: Symbolic elements and surrealist influences in Greek poetry
sections.body: The adopted name Elytis alludes to Greece, hope and freedom, and to Helen as a figure of beauty; the announcement reads it as a condensed manifesto. His verse utilizes sensory details like sea urchins, salt, and sunlight to elevate the perceptible world into a symbolic reality. Influenced by Paul Éluard and French surrealism, he used these impulses to connect with the classical Greek tradition without stagnation. Through works like the poetic cycle To Axion Esti, he integrated strains from the Bible, Hesiod, and Byzantine hymns into a polyphonic structure that mirrors modern western avant-gardism.

sections.heading: Development of poetic reform and inner architecture
sections.body: Beginning with his 1935 debut in Nea Grammata, the poet introduced a new style that contributed to a lasting poetical reform. His technical approach utilized an "inner architecture," a method clearly perceptible in works such as Axion Esti. Beyond verse, he engaged in translating theatre and creating collage pictures. His theoretical perspectives were documented in his essay series, My Cards To Sight. Through these efforts, he sought to build modern Hellenic mythology by complementing natural elements with ethical powers and achieving transparency in expression.

terms.definition: An artistic movement exploring unexpected associations and imaginative freedom; Elytis drew inspiration from it while retaining deliberate form instead of automatic writing.
An arrangement of multiple voices or expressive strands within one work; Axion Esti brings together mythical, biblical and hymnic elements.
The deliberate internal organization of a poem’s parts into a larger whole, a structural quality the biography highlights in Axion Esti.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Advancements in computerized tomography technology
sections.body: While calculating radiation dosages at Groote Schuur Hospital, Allan Cormack identified imprecisions in conventional X-ray techniques regarding tissue-density distribution. He developed mathematical solutions to reconstruct cross-sections of irregular objects using a desktop calculator, publishing findings in 1963 and 1964. Independently, Godfrey Hounsfield constructed the EMI scanner, the first clinically usable computerized tomograph, designed for head examinations. This device overcame previous limitations where overlapping structures and lack of density values obscured anatomy. Consequently, clinicians could distinguish brain gray matter, white matter, and liquid-filled cavities clearly.

sections.heading: Development of computer-assisted tomography
sections.body: Cormack’s 1963 and 1964 papers presented an independent method for reconstructing X-ray attenuation within a cross-section from measurements along many paths. Related mathematical problems had been studied earlier in other contexts. He validated his theory via model experiments using gamma radiation to demonstrate agreement between theory and experiment. Working independently, Hounsfield constructed the first practical medical system, describing its complete architecture in a 1968 patent application. This technology allows clinicians to analyze scaled images of organs at tumor levels, facilitating precise radiation field selection and monitoring tumor shrinkage during treatment.

sections.heading: Development of CT-scanning mathematical methods
sections.body: Cormack returned from Cambridge to a lectureship in Cape Town in 1950. His main research interests were nuclear and particle physics, but in 1956 he became interested in the problem later known as CAT scanning. A subsequent sabbatical at Harvard involved nucleon–nucleon scattering experiments and led to an offer from Tufts University. He pursued the imaging problem intermittently and published results in 1963 and 1964. With little response to those papers, he continued his other research and teaching. Developments he learned about in 1970–1972 drew him back to CT with renewed attention. The biography shows the long interval between an early mathematical result and wider recognition of its practical importance.

terms.definition: A method using X-ray tubes, radiation detectors, and powerful computers to produce clear cross-sectional views through the human body.
The reduction in an X-ray beam’s intensity as it passes through material; CT reconstructs how this varies within a cross-section.
Experiments on how protons and neutrons scatter when they interact, a focus of Cormack’s nuclear-physics work.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of the Missionaries of Charity
sections.body: In 1948, Mother Teresa received permission to leave the Loreto community’s established setting and work among people living in Calcutta’s slums. She adopted a simple sari and undertook nursing training before starting this work. Former pupils and other women joined her, forming the community that became the Missionaries of Charity. Alongside the usual religious vows, members committed themselves to free service to the poorest. Papal recognition followed in 1965. The 1979 speech described an expanding range of work: mobile clinics, leprosy centres, children’s homes, food kitchens and vocational training, with activities extending beyond India into other countries.

sections.heading: Expansion of religious order activities
sections.body: After departing a teaching position at a Roman Catholic girls' school in Calcutta, Mother Teresa led a religious order that expanded its operations beyond the city's slums. This organization grew to include various Indian cities and international locations. Her methodology involved enlisting assistants from different religious denominations to provide aid. The work focused on assisting refugees and children while emphasizing the inherent dignity of every person. These efforts aimed to address global poverty and distress, which the Norwegian Nobel Committee identifies as threats to peace.

sections.heading: Expansion of the Missionaries of Charity
sections.body: Mother Teresa received permission to establish the Missionaries of Charity in 1950. A branch of Brothers followed in 1963, and Contemplative Brothers in 1979. The biography also describes later developments beyond the Nobel year, including the Priest branch established in 1984. As the religious family expanded geographically, its work included disaster relief, assistance to refugees and homes for people otherwise lacking care. Later activities in North America, Europe and Australia included support for homeless people, people with alcohol dependence and people with AIDS. These later details describe the organization’s continuing development, rather than the specific scope of its work at the time of the award.

terms.definition: The religious community Mother Teresa founded, whose members added a commitment to free service to the poorest alongside their other religious vows.
The inherent value accorded to every person, regardless of poverty or social standing, which the committee emphasized in its explanation of the award.
The central governing authority of the Roman Catholic Church, which granted permission for the establishment of Mother Teresa’s congregation in 1950.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Vatican biography of Mother Teresa: permission in 1948 and foundation in 1950

sections.heading: Predictions of the weak neutral current
sections.body: The unified theory predicted a new type of weak interaction. Previously, scientists believed weak processes only occurred via charged currents, where particles like electrons change identity and charge. This framework instead implies that neutrinos or electrons can participate in neutral current interactions without changing their identity. Experiments in the 1970s provided strong evidence for these predicted neutral-current processes. Such advancements provide a pattern for describing the strong nuclear force and integrating further elementary particle interactions within a single scientific description.

sections.heading: Unified theory of electromagnetic and weak interactions
sections.body: During the 1960s, these physicists developed a common formalism to unify the weak and electromagnetic interactions. This framework utilized a generalization of the gauge principle established by Yang and Mills. The theory predicts a neutral current where reacting particles do not change charges, unlike neutron beta-decay. Experimental evidence for this interaction emerged from neutrino bombardment at CERN in 1973. Additionally, high energy electron scattering on deuterium nuclei at SLAC demonstrated a direct interplay between the electromagnetic and weak components of this unified interaction.

sections.heading: Development of the electroweak SU(2) x U(1) structure
sections.body: During his 1958–1960 fellowship, spent mainly in Copenhagen, Glashow identified the SU(2) × U(1) structure for electroweak theory. His earlier Harvard thesis under Julian Schwinger had already explored vector mesons in particle decays. After returning to Harvard, he worked with John Iliopoulos and Luciano Maiani on arguments for charmed hadrons. His autobiography also describes subsequent collaborations with Álvaro de Rújula and Howard Georgi. It recalls an early-1974 prediction that charm would be found in neutrino physics or electron–positron annihilation. The discovery of the J/ψ particle helped bring these strands of particle-physics research together. This broader research history accompanied the electroweak contributions recognized by the Nobel Prize.

terms.definition: A weak interaction process in which a particle undergoes a change of identity and electric charge.
A weak-interaction process in which the participating particles retain their electric charges, unlike the conversion of a neutron into a proton.
The combined mathematical symmetry structure used in electroweak theory, joining the two symmetry groups denoted SU(2) and U(1).

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Methodological advancements in genetic material analysis
sections.body: Berg and colleagues constructed a recombinant DNA molecule by joining material from different biological sources. The presentation speech’s human–bacterial example described the general idea, not that first experiment. He applied this technique to analyze viral chromosomes in detail. Independently, Gilbert and Sanger created distinct methods for determining exact nucleotide sequences. Gilbert investigated bacterial DNA segments that control genetic message transcription. Sanger successfully mapped the entire nucleotide sequence for a small virus containing more than 5,000 nucleotide building blocks. These chemical tools enable researchers to study how DNA governs cellular machinery and enzyme production.

sections.heading: Development of recombinant DNA technology
sections.body: During his time at Stanford University, Paul Berg sought methods to introduce new genes into mammalian cells using SV40. He and his colleagues created a general process for joining two DNAs in vitro. The constructed molecule joined SV40 DNA with a segment carrying three E. coli genes for galactose metabolism. This was an in-vitro construction, distinct from the broader goal of transferring genes into living mammalian cells. This achievement established recombinant DNA technology, offering a significant tool for analyzing how mammalian genes function and their structures.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of protein synthesis and genetic control
sections.body: Gilbert’s move from physics into biology began with experiments on messenger RNA and protein synthesis. He showed that one messenger molecule could serve several ribosomes and studied how a growing protein chain remains attached to transfer RNA. With Benno Müller-Hill, he later isolated the lactose repressor, making a genetically predicted control mechanism accessible to biochemical study. Further experiments examined the repressor’s interaction with DNA. In the mid-1970s, Gilbert and Allan Maxam developed rapid chemical DNA sequencing. His biography links these investigations of gene expression and control with the sequencing method recognized by the prize, while also describing related recombinant-DNA techniques such as blunt-end ligation.

terms.definition: A DNA molecule assembled by joining genetic material from different sources; the sources need not always belong to different species.
Performed outside a living organism in a laboratory system, as when isolated DNA molecules are joined together.
A protein that binds DNA to reduce transcription of genes involved in lactose use, helping regulate when those genes are expressed.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of interdependent simultaneous equation systems
sections.body: Klein’s models drew on statistical advances associated with Trygve Haavelmo, treating interdependent equations as a simultaneous system. This flexible approach allowed for larger, more detailed structures as statistical material increased. Through the Survey Research Center at Michigan, he helped develop statistics regarding consumer attitudes and consumption. His paradigm established a procedure for generating forecasts and policy consultations. Additionally, his Project LINK integrates macromodels from various nations, including developing and centrally planned economies described in the 1980 speech, to study international economic relationships and trade movements.

sections.heading: Development of international econometric forecasting projects
sections.body: Klein collaborated with Arthur Goldberger to create famous models and led the Brookings-SSRC Project to forecast American economic development. He also developed the Wharton Econometric Forecasting Model, which analyzes variables like taxation, public expenditure, and oil prices. As an initiator of the LINK project, Klein coordinated econometric models across various nations, including OECD and socialist countries. This international coordination aimed to study how business fluctuations and political measures diffuse between different economies, specifically examining how oil price increases influence inflation, employment, and trade balances.

sections.heading: What large modelling projects could teach
sections.body: At Pennsylvania, Klein developed the Wharton models and participated as a principal investigator in a major Social Science Research Council project on a short-run US model. His autobiography records an important limitation: no working model survived that project’s decade of research. Nevertheless, the methods and results shaped later work. His international interests included modelling centrally planned economies, introducing econometric techniques in China and bringing additional countries into Project LINK. He also advised Wharton Econometric Forecasting Associates as a professional consultant, rather than describing himself as its manager. This account shows both the practical ambitions of forecasting and the learning that can come from a project without a lasting operational model.

terms.definition: A coherent system of quantitative relations representing a country's development using yearly or quarterly data regarding variables like production and wages.
A large research initiative initiated by Klein to coordinate econometric models across multiple countries for analyzing international economic movements.
An economy in which central authorities make major decisions about production and resource allocation, among the systems Klein sought to model.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary style and structural complexity
sections.body: The author's writing utilizes a polyphonic structure characterized by many voices and dramatic shifts in mood. His work moves between the elegiac and the furious, ranging from abstract concepts to extremely concrete imagery. This intellectual approach incorporates pastiches, ironies, and breaches of style. While his prose and poetry contain deep philosophical references, they also maintain an inherent linguistic sensuousness. He uses surprising imagery derived from memory, imagination, and the empirical world to seek a defense against destructive global forces.

sections.heading: Exile and conflicting loyalties
sections.body: The 1980 announcement interprets exile as both a circumstance of Miłosz’s life and a recurring condition in his writing. He broke with the Polish government in 1951, settled in France, and moved to Berkeley in 1960. Yet his connections to Polish intellectual life remained. The committee connected his work with tensions between loyalty and independence, destruction and creativity, and belief and doubt. Childhood memories of nature coexist with the violent histories of Lithuania and Poland. Its discussion of his essays and political analysis stressed how these writings illuminate the poetry. Exile, in this reading, was not only separation from a country but also a way to express the divided experience of being human.

sections.heading: Literary beginnings and academic career in Berkeley
sections.body: After debuting in 1930, Miłosz co-founded the Zagary literary group. His early professional years included working for Polish Radio and contributing to underground presses in Warsaw. After breaking with the Polish government in 1951, he lived and wrote in France before moving to Berkeley in 1960. He served as a Professor of Slavic Languages and Literatures starting in 1961. His career also involved receiving the Prix Littéraire Européen in 1953 and various recognitions for poetry translations and research lectureship.

terms.definition: A many-voiced literary arrangement that utilizes various roles, styles, and dramatic shifts between different moods and levels of abstraction.
Separation from a homeland; in the committee’s reading of Miłosz, also a metaphor for spiritual estrangement and conflicting loyalties.
A literary group co-founded by Czesław Miłosz during his early years as a writer.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Genetic regulation of the major histocompatibility complex
sections.body: The major histocompatibility complex brought together discoveries made through different experimental routes. Snell used inbred mouse strains to investigate why transplanted tumours were accepted in some genetic combinations and rejected in others. His work identified the importance of the H-2 region. Dausset studied antibodies reacting with human white blood cells, helping establish the related human HLA system. Benacerraf found inherited differences in guinea pigs' responses to particular antigens, linking immune-response genes with the same general chromosomal complex. The work connected transplant compatibility with cooperation between immune cells. It did not show that a single gene determines every immune response or that tissue compatibility alone guarantees a successful transplant.

sections.heading: Genetic regulation of cell-surface protein-carbohydrate complexes
sections.body: Snell used mouse strains whose members were highly similar genetically to test transfer of tumours and normal tissues such as skin. His experiments connected rejection with inherited cell-surface antigens and identified the importance of histocompatibility genes. Dausset investigated antibodies against white blood cells in transfusion recipients and women who had been pregnant, helping identify the human HLA system. Benacerraf's guinea-pig experiments revealed that inherited factors also influence responses to specific antigens. Some of these immune-response factors mapped to the same chromosomal region. Together the findings linked cell-surface differences with transplantation and broader immune regulation. They did not imply that every gene in the region performs the same function.

sections.heading: Genetic regulation of immune response mechanisms
sections.body: Benacerraf found that genetically varied animals exposed to certain restricted groups of antigens separated into responders and nonresponders. In the systems studied, responsiveness followed dominant autosomal inheritance. Work on these immune-response genes connected them with the major histocompatibility complex. At the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases from 1968, inbred guinea-pig strains supported further experiments by his colleagues on how the genes functioned. After moving to Harvard in 1970, he continued research on specific immunity, suppression and recognition by cytotoxic T lymphocytes. These were successive stages in a collaborative programme, not all experiments performed at the same institution.

terms.definition: A chromosomal region containing genes important for immune recognition and tissue compatibility; related systems include mouse H-2 and human HLA.
Histocompatibility antigens are inherited cell-surface molecules whose differences between donor and recipient can provoke immune responses against transplanted tissue.
Genes affecting responsiveness to particular antigens; the MHC-linked examples studied by Benacerraf helped explain inherited differences in immune recognition.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Nonviolent strategies for social and political liberty
sections.body: As Secretary-General of Paz y Justicia, Esquivel utilized nonviolence as a strategic tool to pursue economic and social reforms. He supported landless peasants' demands for land and workers' rights to organization. To combat human rights violations in Latin America, his organization drafted evidence for a United Nations commission and sought international support through European visits. His approach rejected terror as a weapon, instead drawing inspiration from Mohandas Gandhi to advocate for liberation while warning against territorial conflicts between nations like Argentina and Chile.

sections.heading: Management of Servicio Paz y Justicia
sections.body: In 1974 Pérez Esquivel took on the daily leadership of Servicio Paz y Justicia, leaving teaching to concentrate on human rights. The 1980 announcement described a Buenos Aires headquarters and a continental network linking national and local groups. Shared commitments allowed these groups to coordinate action while relying on nonviolent methods. The committee placed the work against a background of political violence and severe military repression in Argentina. It interpreted the defence of basic rights as part of the pursuit of peace.
