This account describes the network and political circumstances around the award, rather than its present organisational structure.

sections.heading: Documentation, legal aid and persecution
sections.body: Pérez Esquivel’s work connected international attention with practical support. A 1976 campaign gathered documentation of human-rights violations in Latin America and sought action through the United Nations. The movement also provided legal assistance to rural workers seeking land and unions defending workers’ rights. Its understanding of human rights included social and economic conditions, not only protection against imprisonment or torture. Pérez Esquivel was himself imprisoned in 1977 and released in May 1978 under restrictions. The biography situates the movement within a Christian outlook and contacts with critical clergy, while emphasising its insistence on nonviolent action despite repression.

terms.definition: Active resistance to injustice without using physical violence, including organising, protest and efforts to obtain political or legal change.
Service Peace and Justice, a Latin American movement linking human-rights work with nonviolent action and cooperation among local groups.
Rights concerning conditions of living and working, including the material security and worker protections emphasised in Pérez Esquivel’s programme.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Neutral K-meson decay experiment at Brookhaven
sections.body: The 1964 Brookhaven experiment tested a decay expected to be forbidden if CP symmetry held exactly. Cronin, Fitch and collaborators studied long-lived neutral kaons and found a small fraction decaying into two pions: about two events per thousand decays. The qualification matters. This was not a statement about every kaon species, nor a violation of the laws of physics as such. It showed that a particular symmetry assumption about weak decays was not exact. Earlier work by Gell-Mann and Pais had clarified the unusual neutral-kaon system, providing a setting where such a test was possible. The unexpected result made a small decay probability a major problem for fundamental theory.

sections.heading: Testing combined particle and spatial transformations
sections.body: Brookhaven’s AGS accelerator produced particles from which a neutral beam was selected. A specially designed detector measured kaon decays in flight. The crucial symmetry question combined two operations: reflecting spatial coordinates and replacing particles with antiparticles. Earlier parity violation had shown that reflection alone was insufficient; this experiment showed that the combined CP operation also failed to preserve all weak-decay behaviour. Neutral-kaon states involve quantum mixing between particle and antiparticle states, rather than a literal object made by putting two classical halves together. The result concerned CP directly; inferring time-reversal violation additionally uses CPT symmetry.

sections.heading: Experimental developments in particle physics research
sections.body: Cronin first investigated parity violation in hyperon decays at Brookhaven. A 1958 failure of the Cosmotron magnet moved those experiments to Berkeley, where working with experienced instrument builders influenced his approach. He joined Princeton later that year with encouragement from Fitch. There he helped develop spark chambers as practical research instruments and continued hyperon studies with students. Collaboration with Fitch on neutral kaons led to the 1964 CP-violation discovery. After a year at Saclay, he returned to Princeton in 1965 and investigated further CP-violating decay modes through 1971. The sequence shows how apparatus development and successive decay experiments prepared the ground for the central result.

terms.definition: An electrically neutral meson; its particle and antiparticle states can mix, giving combinations with distinct decay behaviour.
Brookhaven’s Alternating Gradient Synchrotron, which accelerated protons used to produce the secondary particles for the kaon experiment.
A particle detector in which an electric discharge makes a charged particle’s ionised path visible as a series of sparks.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Predicting chemical reaction pathways and molecular transformations
sections.body: Fukui showed how selected molecular orbitals could provide useful predictions of reactivity without calculating every detail of a reaction. His frontier-orbital approach helped explain why different positions in an aromatic molecule such as naphthalene react differently. Hoffmann and Woodward emphasised another feature: the symmetry of orbitals as bonds reorganise. Their analysis supplied rules for understanding which concerted reaction pathways are favoured under particular conditions. The 1981 ceremony connected these theoretical advances with the challenges of complex synthesis, including vitamin B12. The achievement was a practical simplification of quantum chemistry: energy and symmetry patterns could guide experimental choices and explain otherwise puzzling outcomes.

sections.heading: Frontier electron density and aromatic hydrocarbon reactivity
sections.body: In 1952, Kenichi Fukui identified a correlation between frontier electron density and the chemical reactivity of aromatic hydrocarbons. Influenced by Mulliken’s work on charge-transfer forces in donor-acceptor complexes, Fukui provided a theoretical foundation for these findings. His approach focused on the importance of electron delocalization between the frontier orbitals of reactant species. To make the role of these orbitals more distinct, he utilized diagrams to visualize the geometrical shapes of reacting molecules. This research expanded into various directions regarding chemical reactivity theory.

sections.heading: Development of the extended Huckel method and orbital analysis
sections.body: Hoffmann used computational and qualitative methods to study the electronic structure of stable molecules and reactive intermediates. His extended Hückel method provided approximate descriptions of both sigma and pi electrons, helping estimate molecular shapes and energy changes during structural rearrangements. With Woodward, he applied arguments about symmetry and bonding to concerted reactions, in which bond changes occur in a coordinated step. He also examined intermediates such as carbonium ions and diradicals using semiempirical calculations. These approaches combined approximate numerical models with interpretable orbital pictures, giving chemists ways to reason about structures and reaction pathways.

terms.definition: The highest occupied and lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals, whose interactions often have particular importance in determining chemical reactivity.
The spreading of electronic states over several atoms or interacting molecular regions, rather than confinement to a single atom or localised bond.
An approximate molecular-orbital calculation scheme that includes sigma and pi electronic structure and can help estimate molecular geometry and relative energies.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Transmission mechanisms between financial and real markets
sections.body: Tobin utilized a mathematical risk theory to analyze how households and firms allocate portfolios among cash, bonds, shares, and physical assets based on yield and risk. By aggregating these individual decisions, his framework explains the total supply and demand for assets, which determines equilibrium interest rates and prices. This analysis identifies transmission mechanisms through which government budget deficits or exchange rate shifts reach real markets. A central component involves the ratio of an asset's market value to its reproduction cost. When this ratio is below unity, firms may find it more profitable to acquire existing companies rather than investing in new equipment. Furthermore, his work addresses how wage and price stickiness causes restrictive policies to impact production volume and employment levels.

sections.heading: Research foundations and institutional influences
sections.body: During his career, Tobin sought to provide more rigorous foundations for Keynesian economics while refining the logic of monetary theory. His academic development included a doctoral dissertation focused on the statistics and theory of the consumption function. While serving as a Junior Fellow at the Society of Fellows, he engaged in writing about statistical demand analysis, rationing theory, and macroeconomics. He also collaborated on the sociological-economic book, The American Business Creed. Later, his research benefited from the Cowles Foundation at Yale, an institution that inaugurated modern activity analysis and econometrics. Through this center, he explored how monetary theory and macroeconomics could be integrated into existing lines of economic inquiry, supported by a collegial environment of researchers.

terms.definition: A ratio expressing the market value of a physical asset compared to the cost of producing that same asset again.
A research center at Yale that pioneered modern econometrics and activity analysis through various scientific inquiries.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary themes and analytical works
sections.body: Canetti's fiction includes the novel Die Blendung, which features fantastic elements reminiscent of Gogol and Dostoevsky. This work serves as a metaphor for the threat posed by the mass man. His historical analysis in Masse und Macht examines how mass movements originate and react, specifically targeting the religion of power. Additionally, his aphoristic notes utilize satire to observe human behavior, while his three absurd plays function as acoustic masks. His memoirs further document the political and cultural life of early twentieth-century Vienna through vivid descriptions.

sections.heading: Themes of death and mass movement dynamics
sections.body: Canetti's literary investigations explore the connection between power and mortality, suggesting that the threat of death underlies every command. His research into mass movements, detailed in Masse und Macht, examines the origins and reaction patterns of groups. In his novel Die Blendung, he utilizes a Viennese apartment house to present a metaphor for the danger posed by the mass man. Additionally, his plays, such as Hochzeit and Die Befristeten, employ what he calls acoustic masks to portray extreme situations and human vulgarity.

sections.heading: Development of literary and analytical works
sections.body: Canetti's intellectual path was shaped by lectures from Karl Kraus. He first outlined a book on crowd psychology in 1925, then concentrated on Masse und Macht from 1939 through the following two decades before its publication in Hamburg in 1960. His dramatic output included the play Hochzeit and Die Befristeten, the latter premiering in Oxford. He also produced various memoirs and sketches, such as Aufzeichnungen 1942-48. Other notable publications include Die Stimmen von Marrakesch and several collections of essays and autobiographical writings produced throughout his career.

terms.definition: A concept used by critics to describe a fundamental threat within individuals, explored through the metaphor of Canetti's novel.
The condition of being subject to death; Canetti treats its threat, and the desire to survive, as central to the exercise of power.
The study of how people behave in crowds and how collective movements form and act, a central concern of Canetti’s research.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of visual processing and cortical plasticity
sections.body: Hubel and Wiesel built on Stephen Kuffler’s studies of retinal signals by recording activity from nerve cells in the visual cortex. They found cells that responded selectively to features such as contrast, oriented lines and movement. The organization of cells into columns showed that cortical processing had a systematic structure. Their recordings helped explain how the brain analyses information arriving from the eyes, rather than simply receiving a complete picture. A related research programme examined visual development. Experience during early life could strongly affect the organization and responses of cortical cells, demonstrating the importance of sensory input during sensitive periods. These findings concerned specific visual mechanisms, not a complete explanation of every higher brain function.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of visual processing and hemispheric specialization
sections.body: Sperry investigated learning in animals after connections between the cerebral hemispheres were cut. Under his experimental conditions, information learned by one hemisphere was not available to the other. Studies of patients who had undergone similar surgery for severe epilepsy revealed differences in what each separated hemisphere could do. In a distinct programme, Hubel and Wiesel recorded impulses in the visual cortex and identified cells organized into columns and larger groupings. These cells responded to features of the retinal image. Animal experiments also showed that depriving one eye of patterned vision during early development could cause lasting changes in cortical function. This finding depended on developmental timing, not simply closing an eye at any age.

sections.heading: Development of visual cortex recording techniques
sections.body: At the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research, Hubel compared the spontaneous firing of single cortical cells in sleeping and waking cats. He chose the visual cortex partly because relatively little muscle covered it, making electrode access easier. Recording from freely moving cats required a suitable method and a tungsten microelectrode strong enough to penetrate the dura. Developing these tools took more than a year. In 1958, Hubel moved to Stephen Kuffler’s laboratory at the Wilmer Institute, Johns Hopkins Hospital, where he began collaborating with Torsten Wiesel. The technical experience with single-cell recordings helped support their subsequent investigations of visual processing.

terms.definition: The capacity of cortical organization and responses to change with experience, especially pronounced during sensitive periods of early visual development.
A neurosurgical technique used on patients with severe epilepsy that involves severing the nerve fibers connecting the two cerebral hemispheres.
A fine tungsten electrode used to record nerve-cell activity; Hubel developed one strong enough to penetrate the brain’s protective dura.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Evolution of international refugee protection and institutional mandates
sections.body: The 1981 award speech placed UNHCR within a longer effort to make refugee protection an enduring international responsibility. After earlier relief by the International Refugee Organisation and others, the new High Commissioner’s office initially had an uncertain future. In 1953 the General Assembly extended its life to 1959. The speech emphasized the 1951 Refugee Convention as a foundation for protection, while acknowledging that not every government had accepted it. A separate African convention adopted in 1969 reaffirmed its importance in addressing refugee problems on that continent. UNHCR’s practical work depended on diplomacy with governments and cooperation with other organizations. The speaker also warned that the economic difficulties of the early 1980s would complicate resettlement in industrial countries. These were the historical circumstances surrounding the award, rather than a description of current refugee policy.

sections.heading: Global refugee trends and humanitarian assistance
sections.body: In its 1981 announcement, the Nobel Committee estimated that there were fourteen to eighteen million refugees worldwide. It cited approximately two million refugees from Afghanistan and a similar number from Ethiopia, alongside the exodus from Vietnam by land and sea. These were contemporary estimates, not present-day totals. The committee praised UNHCR’s assistance despite political obstacles, while stressing that other international organizations, governments and voluntary groups also contributed. It particularly recognized organizations and authorities in Asian and African developing countries that accommodated large refugee populations. The announcement argued for opportunities to rebuild lives when return was unsafe and, over the longer term, for preventing the conditions that forced people to flee. It linked protection of human rights with more peaceful relations between states.

terms.definition: An international treaty establishing refugee status and protections, central to the framework discussed in the award speech.
Relief and practical support for people in distress, including refugees who have been forced to leave their homes.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
African Union: 1969 Convention Governing the Specific Aspects of Refugee Problems in Africa

sections.heading: Foundations of electron spectroscopy and non-linear optics
sections.body: Kai Siegbahn utilized instruments designed for analyzing beta decays to study electrons expelled during the photoelectric process. This technique allowed researchers to determine atomic electron binding energy with increased accuracy, facilitating tests of new atomic models. His work also enabled chemical analysis through ESCA. Separately, Nicolaas Bloembergen and collaborators developed a theory for responses to intense laser light that go beyond a simple linear description. This work helped establish non-linear optics, which includes mixing multiple laser beams to generate different wavelengths for applications like studying combustion.

sections.heading: Development of nonlinear optics and maser research
sections.body: Bloembergen's research group investigated nuclear quadrupole interactions in alloys and imperfect ionic crystals, alongside studying the Knight shift anisotropy in noncubic metals. His work included exploring scalar and tensor indirect nuclear spin-spin coupling in insulators and metals. In 1956, his team proposed a three-level solid state maser. Later, he established a nonlinear optics program that produced a 1965 monograph. A 1991 autobiographical update describes continued research after the award on how picosecond and femtosecond laser pulses interact with condensed matter.

sections.heading: Development of the optical maser
sections.body: At Bell Telephone Laboratories from 1951 to 1961, Schawlow worked mainly on superconductivity, with some studies of nuclear quadrupole resonance. He also collaborated with Charles Townes on Microwave Spectroscopy, published in 1955. In 1957–1958 they examined how maser principles could be extended to optical wavelengths. Schawlow then investigated optical properties and spectra of solids relevant to laser materials. After moving to Stanford in 1961, he pursued experimental physics with students, visitors and colleagues, including Theodor Hänsch. His biography also credits the technicians who built and maintained the apparatus. This account distinguishes the earlier optical-maser proposal from the later programme of laser-based research.

terms.definition: The study of light–matter interactions in which the material’s response is not simply proportional to the applied optical field, enabling effects such as frequency mixing.
A microwave amplifier or oscillator using three energy levels to establish the population difference needed for stimulated emission.
An early name for a laser: a device that applies stimulated-emission principles to optical radiation rather than microwaves.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mathematical manipulation of low contrast electron microscopy images
sections.body: Klug developed a technique to extract structural information from electron microscopy pictures that appear to lack sufficient contrast. By applying mathematical manipulation to these images, he could study the structure of molecular aggregates within biological systems. His virus research illuminated self-assembly: interactions among components can organize them into complex structures. This does not mean every cellular assembly forms unaided. Additionally, his investigations into chromatin provided clues regarding the structural control involved in reading DNA genetic messages. These methods allow for the study of large assemblies that are rarely obtainable in crystal forms suitable for traditional X-ray diffraction. Such work offers long-term perspectives for understanding how genetic material regulates cell growth and division.

sections.heading: Mathematical methods for structural analysis
sections.body: During his early research, Klug developed a technique using molecular structure factors to solve crystal structures while analyzing small organic compounds. His academic training provided foundational knowledge in Fourier theory and optics through lectures on phenomena like conical refraction. While studying the cooling of steel, he utilized numerical methods to solve partial differential equations regarding heat flow during phase transitions. He later applied these computational approaches to analyze kinetic curves for chemical reactions involving hemoglobin and oxygen. At Birkbeck, he joined Rosalind Franklin’s work on tobacco mosaic virus and interpreted unusual curved layer lines in her X-ray photographs in terms of helical parameters. Working with collaborators like Kenneth Holmes and John Finch, he mapped the general structural outline of this virus.

terms.definition: Assemblies containing multiple molecules; examples in Klug’s work include viruses and chromatin made from nucleic acids and proteins.
Computational techniques for obtaining solutions to mathematical problems, including the heat-flow and reaction-rate calculations that informed Klug’s early work.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Research on information costs and regulatory drivers
sections.body: Stigler demonstrated that searching for prices and product qualities involves costs, meaning buyers rarely achieve full information. Information costs can help explain persistent differences in prices and quality, as well as price rigidity. He also investigated how the costs of monitoring members and enforcing sanctions constrain cartels. Furthermore, his empirical work on adjustment lags showed that the delays in moving capital and labour between industries had sometimes been given exaggerated empirical importance. Finally, he explored how specific groups influence legislation to favor their own interests rather than the general public.

sections.heading: Research on market processes and regulatory causes
sections.body: Stigler utilized strong empirical orientation to investigate how economic legislation affects markets. He explored the role of information in market processes and examined the survivor principle, which identifies surviving firm categories before seeking their specific properties. His research investigated how regulation can protect producer interests rather than the general public. Additionally, he studied the effects of rent controls and minimum-wage legislation in the USA. Through these studies, he treated legislation as an outcome influenced by economic interests, rather than only as a rule imposed from outside the economy.

sections.heading: Evolution of economic research and price theory investigations
sections.body: Stigler's academic development involved graduate training at the University of Chicago under Frank H. Knight, who supervised his thesis on production and distribution theories. His early research included an approximate solution to a minimum-cost diet problem and testing kinked oligopoly demand curve theory during the 1940s. He later proposed a survivor method for determining efficient enterprise sizes. Through the National Bureau of Economic Research, he utilized total factor productivity measures to study service industries and investigated price dispersion, which led to his 1961 publication, The Economics of Information.

terms.definition: A research area established by analyzing how costs related to searching for and disseminating market data affect economic performance.
A field of research established by Stigler focusing on the causes and consequences of public regulatory legislation.
An approach that compares which categories of firms survive or expand, then investigates the properties associated with their efficiency.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
George Stigler: The Cost of Subsistence (1945)

sections.heading: Literary influences and narrative techniques
sections.body: García Márquez utilizes a diverse range of inspirations, blending European surrealism, Spanish baroque, and oral folk traditions. His storytelling often features the imaginary town of Macondo, where miraculous events converge with realistic descriptions resembling reportage. Across his fiction, characters encounter political conflict and the destructive pressures of history. This narrative approach frequently centers on death, using recurring figures to explore themes of fate, political oppression, and the complex human condition.

sections.heading: Narrative range and the pressure of history
sections.body: The 1982 announcement placed One Hundred Years of Solitude within a wider achievement. It compared The Autumn of the Patriarch with that earlier novel and praised the disciplined shorter forms of No One Writes to the Colonel, In Evil Hour and Chronicle of a Death Foretold. The committee saw versatility across novels and stories. It also described a tension between mortality and narrative energy: death frequently organises a plot, while comedy and grotesque invention keep the fictional world alive. Recurring characters appear under different pressures and from different angles. In this interpretation, the invented world reflects social conflict without becoming a simple chronicle of historical events.

sections.heading: Journalistic background and international residence
sections.body: García Márquez’s upbringing with his maternal grandparents in Aracataca supplied a background distinct from his later international career. He began law studies but turned to journalism. Newspaper work took him abroad; he later lived in Paris, New York, Barcelona and Mexico. The Nobel biography describes this life abroad as partly enforced exile. It also qualifies its own account: his later autobiography names Geneva, rather than Rome, as his first newspaper destination. Journalism did not simply end when fiction began. He continued reporting and writing articles alongside novels, stories and screenplays, maintaining several forms of writing throughout his career.

terms.definition: An imaginary town within García Márquez's fiction where extraordinary, miraculous elements and tangible, realistic descriptions exist together.
A literary mode combining exaggerated, disturbing and comic elements; the announcement describes García Márquez’s humour as capable of both cruelty and reconciliation.
Living away from one’s homeland under political or other pressures; the biography characterises García Márquez’s residence abroad as partly compulsory.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of the Prostaglandin Regulatory System
sections.body: Bergström, Samuelsson and Vane investigated a family of short-lived chemical signals with diverse effects. Bergström identified unsaturated fatty acids as precursors of prostaglandins. Samuelsson traced related pathways and characterised compounds including leukotrienes; some of these signals attract white blood cells and promote their attachment near inflamed tissue. Vane showed that aspirin inhibits prostaglandin formation, connecting a familiar medicine with a defined biochemical pathway. His group also discovered prostacyclin, which helps oppose platelet aggregation and maintain blood flow. The ceremony used Vane's description of these substances as defence hormones to emphasise their roles in protection and regulation. Their effects depend on the particular substance and tissue, rather than forming one uniform response.

sections.heading: Sune Bergström's academic and professional trajectory
sections.body: Bergström's international research experience preceded his 1944 medical and biochemistry qualifications at Karolinska Institutet. He held a London fellowship in 1938, worked at Columbia in 1940–1941 and at the Squibb Institute in 1941–1942. He later became professor of physiological chemistry at Lund in 1947, returning to Karolinska as professor of chemistry in 1958. His scientific career was accompanied by administrative responsibilities: he served as medical-faculty dean, then rector, and became chairman of the Nobel Foundation's board in 1975. These dates distinguish the training and institutional setting of his research from the biochemical discoveries recognised by the prize.

sections.heading: Biochemical pathways of arachidonic acid transformation
sections.body: Samuelsson initially studied cholesterol metabolism and the mechanisms of chemical reactions. After investigating prostaglandin structures with Bergström during 1959–1962, he concentrated on substances formed from arachidonic acid. His group studied endoperoxides, thromboxanes and leukotrienes, connecting chemical identification with biochemical pathways and biological activity. These compounds participate in regulatory processes, so identifying them helped explain how a common starting material can lead to signals with different effects. The research had implications for understanding thrombosis, inflammation and allergy. The biography describes a progression of research interests; it does not mean that the prostaglandin pathways were simply cholesterol reactions applied to a different substance.

terms.definition: Vane's descriptive label for locally acting chemical signals involved in protective and regulatory processes, including inflammation and blood-vessel function.
The study of chemical substances and reactions involved in the functioning of living organisms, closely related to biochemistry.
An unsaturated fatty acid that serves as a starting material for several signalling compounds, including prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: United Nations disarmament negotiations and public opinion
sections.body: The laureates gained international recognition through their work within United Nations disarmament negotiations. Beyond diplomatic efforts, they focused on informing global opinion regarding armaments problems. This process involved arousing public acceptance of collective responsibility for global events. Myrdal also contributed to the development of the modern Swedish welfare state and served as the first female department head at the United Nations. Their methods emphasized using constructive proposals rather than simple slogans to promote peace and address the nuclear arms race.

sections.heading: Methods of promoting global disarmament
sections.body: The announcement treated formal negotiations and public mobilisation as complementary ways to oppose nuclear armament. Myrdal worked in Geneva and other international forums while using her writing to make technical and political issues accessible to a wider public. García Robles likewise combined diplomacy with efforts to increase awareness of nuclear danger. Separately from his participation in United Nations special disarmament sessions, he had been a driving force behind the 1967 agreement establishing a nuclear-weapon-free zone in Latin America. The committee valued both sustained negotiation and pressure from informed opinion. Neither approach was presented as sufficient by itself to end the arms race.

sections.heading: Diplomatic efforts in disarmament and social welfare
sections.body: Myrdal’s international work grew from earlier involvement in social welfare. She and Gunnar Myrdal jointly wrote The Population Problem in Crisis, while she also worked on housing and education. In 1943 she joined a party committee drafting a post-war programme and a government commission on reconstruction aid. Later, as Sweden’s disarmament representative in Geneva, she helped non-aligned countries press the superpowers for concrete measures. Her book The Game of Disarmament expressed frustration with American and Soviet reluctance. She also helped establish the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, reflecting her belief that effective disarmament advocacy required technical knowledge as well as commitment.

terms.definition: Diplomatic processes within the United Nations aimed at reducing military armaments and addressing the destructive potential of nuclear weapons.
A region covered by treaty commitments prohibiting nuclear weapons; such a zone concerns nuclear armament rather than eliminating every military activity.
Countries outside the opposing superpower military blocs; in these negotiations they sought to press both sides toward practical disarmament.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Renormalization group theory and scale fluctuations
sections.body: Near a continuous phase transition’s critical point, fluctuations occur over many length scales, from microscopic distances toward the size of the sample. A calculation focused on only one scale misses their interaction. Wilson developed renormalisation-group methods that handle successive changes of scale, replacing an unmanageable simultaneous calculation with a sequence of related descriptions. His 1971 papers supplied a systematic approach to critical behaviour and practical ways to calculate important quantities. The result was not a claim that every phase transition has identical fluctuations or that every associated calculation is exact. It provided a tractable framework connecting small-scale interactions with collective behaviour near criticality.

sections.heading: Why different materials can behave alike
sections.body: Wilson’s approach explained universality: physically different systems can share the same patterns of behaviour near critical points. Many microscopic details become less important at large scales, while features such as dimensionality and the structure of the order parameter remain decisive. Within appropriate classes of systems, this makes common critical behaviour possible despite different chemical constituents. The 1982 announcement linked the theory with successful calculations and experiments, and described possible applications to other problems involving many scales. Turbulence was presented as a challenge for future work, not a solved problem. Particle-physics applications likewise represented extensions rather than a universal solution of every strong-interaction question.

sections.heading: Contributions to particle theory and scientific computing
sections.body: Wilson made several contributions to elementary particle theory, including a short distance expansion for operator products and the formulation of lattice gauge theory in 1974. He discovered that the strong coupling limit of lattice theory exhibits quark confinement. Beyond theoretical physics, he helped initiate a computing support project at Cornell using a Floating Point Systems Array Processor and helped write its initial Fortran compiler. His later research involved applying Monte Carlo Renormalization Group methods to the three dimensional Ising model and exploring large scale scientific computing organizational challenges.

terms.definition: A method that tracks how a system’s effective description changes as short-distance details are combined into progressively larger-scale descriptions.
The sharing of critical behaviour by different physical systems whose relevant large-scale features place them in the same class.
An approach combining statistical computer sampling with changes of scale to investigate collective behaviour, applied by Wilson to the three-dimensional Ising model.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Tracing electron transfer through a shared ligand
sections.body: Taube examined a reaction between a cobalt(III) complex bearing ammonia and chloride ligands and a chromium(II) ion surrounded by water molecules. The products revealed both electron transfer and transfer of chloride from cobalt to chromium. This provided a way to investigate the route taken by the reaction. In the proposed intermediate, a water molecule leaves chromium's coordination sphere and chloride connects the two metal centres. An electron moves from chromium(II) to cobalt(III), giving chromium(III) and cobalt(II). When the bridge separates, chloride remains attached to chromium. Tracking the ligand therefore supplied evidence for an inner-sphere mechanism involving a shared bridge. The example concerns this particular pathway; other electron-transfer reactions can occur without such a shared ligand.

sections.heading: Academic training and professional research trajectory
sections.body: Taube earned a B.S. at Saskatchewan in 1935 and an M.S. there in 1937 under J. W. T. Spinks. He completed his doctorate at Berkeley with W. C. Bray in 1940. Teaching and research posts at Berkeley and Cornell preceded his move to Chicago, where he served as chemistry-department chairman. At Stanford from 1962, he again held departmental leadership roles. His research interests extended from atom- and electron-transfer mechanisms to mixed-valence compounds, ruthenium and osmium chemistry, and the effects of charge transfer on ligand reactivity. These topics shared an interest in how electronic structure and bonding influence the behaviour of metal complexes.

terms.definition: A chloride ion that connects two metal ions within a larger complex to facilitate electron transfer during a reaction.
The presence of an element in more than one formal oxidation state within the same compound, often prompting questions about how electrons are localised or shared.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of the Arrow-Debreu model
sections.body: The Arrow-Debreu model outlines specific conditions that guarantee a general equilibrium exists within a competitive economy. Under specified assumptions, it also establishes conditions for efficient resource use according to consumer preferences. While originally formulated for economies lacking uncertainty or a public sector, these advancements allowed the theory to expand into analyzing taxes, environmental issues, and collective goods. Furthermore, this mathematical approach supports cost-benefit analysis and the creation of computable general equilibrium models used to study entire economic systems. By introducing new analytical techniques and tools, this work provides an essential frame of reference for economists. Prices convey information about production costs and consumer demand, making individual plans mutually consistent in the model. The existence proof does not show that actual markets automatically reach such an equilibrium.

sections.heading: Mathematical developments at the Cowles Commission
sections.body: During the early 1950s, the Cowles Commission served as a central hub for mathematical economics research. Within this supportive environment, Debreu made rapid progress on utility theory, Pareto optima, and the existence of general economic equilibrium. His research was influenced by practical challenges, such as managing uncertain water levels in hydroelectric reservoirs at Électricité de France. This work led to his study of economic uncertainty, which he included in his 1959 monograph, Theory of Value. Later, while at the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences, he focused on a complex proof regarding a general theorem on economic equilibrium existence. His subsequent research interests expanded to include differentiable utility functions and the characterization of an economy's excess demand function.

terms.definition: A framework for studying simultaneous balance between supply and demand across interdependent markets under specified assumptions.
A research institution that functioned as a focal point for mathematical economics through weekly meetings and seminars.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Narrative structures and themes of human depravity
sections.body: Golding utilizes schematic dramatic skeletons to explore the capacity for human wickedness. Rites of Passage uses a nineteenth-century shipboard setting to examine social aggression and the scapegoat mechanism, while The Inheritors approaches human violence through a vision of prehistory. Through novels like The Spire, he depicts characters driven by complex motives, including humility and arrogance. These stories often feature a mythic Fall, where aggressive intelligence and individualism drive violence. His writing combines adventurous plots with deep ambiguity to investigate how innate human traits can transform good into something destructive.

sections.heading: Mythic patterns and narrative complexity in Golding's novels
sections.body: Golding utilizes mythic patterns to explore fundamental human conflicts and deep ambiguity. His works, such as Rites of Passage and The Inheritors, blend exciting adventure with profound layers that engage both scholars and general readers. While his writing features colorful tales and biting irony, it also examines the capacity for wickedness within humanity. Through a dualistic lens, he explores themes like the myth of a Fall, presenting a world where humans possess both the ability to murder and a belief in God.

sections.heading: Golding's naval service and academic transitions
sections.body: After studying at Brasenose College, Oxford, Golding shifted his focus from science to English literature and Anglo-Saxon studies. His wartime experiences in the Royal Navy included encounters involving aircraft, submarines, and the sinking of the Bismarck. Serving as a Lieutenant in command of a rocket ship, he was present during the D-Day invasion and at Walcheren. Naval service interrupted his teaching career; after the war he returned to the classroom and to writing. His later achievements included the Booker Prize for Rites of Passage.

terms.definition: A literary pattern in Golding's work representing the loss of an original state of innocence through human wickedness.
A structural method in Golding's writing used to explore basic human experiences, conflicts, and the concept of a Fall.
The Old English language and literature of early medieval England, a field that interested Golding during his university studies.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Genetic mechanisms identified through maize kernel variegation
sections.body: McClintock connected patterns of maize-kernel colour with visible chromosome changes and controlled breeding experiments. On chromosome 9, she traced mobile elements whose insertion could disrupt pigment-gene activity and whose movement was associated in some cases with chromosome breaks. Between 1948 and 1951 she investigated several families of these controlling elements, showing effects beyond pigmentation. The work challenged the view of chromosomes as fixed arrangements of genes. She also suggested that comparable mobile elements might exist in other organisms. Later research established their wider occurrence. This contribution concerns transposable elements; other forms of genome rearrangement, including antibody-gene assembly, should not be treated as the same mechanism.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of mobile genetic elements in maize
sections.body: McClintock compared the timing and patterns of kernel pigmentation with changes in chromosomes. Insertion of a controlling element could inactivate a gene; departure of the element could restore its activity. A change arising during development could therefore produce a differently coloured sector within a kernel. Some elements depended on another element in the system for their ability to move, revealing an interaction that could be studied through crosses. Movement could occur within or between chromosomes and, in some cases, was associated with breaks or other structural changes. These were experimentally observed relationships between genetic elements and gene activity, rather than a simple universal rule that every transposition breaks a chromosome.

sections.heading: Early training and cytogenetics research at Cornell University
sections.body: While taking C. B. Hutchison’s genetics course in 1921, McClintock also studied cytology with Lester W. Sharp. These interests shaped her subsequent graduate work. This training focused on chromosome structures and behaviors during mitosis and meiosis. After earning her Ph.D. in 1927, she worked at Cornell to associate specific genes with each of the ten maize chromosomes. Collaborating with Dr. Charles R. Burnham, she helped complete this mapping task. Her research interests centered on cytogenetics, exploring how chromosomes function as bearers of heritable factors.

terms.definition: Mobile genetic material that alters the function of neighboring genes by changing positions on a chromosome.
Movement of a genetic element to a different genomic position, either within a chromosome or between chromosomes.
A scientific field focusing on the study of chromosome structure and their behaviors during mitosis and meiosis.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Strategy of peace and negotiation for workers' rights
sections.body: The presentation speech emphasised negotiation as a strategy for gaining workers’ rights. Wałęsa sought independent organisations and a voice in discussions about social and economic conditions. Negotiation required willingness to compromise in a difficult political setting. The committee described the Polish church’s support as a source of moral strength rooted in concern for human dignity. Although immediate demands concerned labour rights, the speech acknowledged their unavoidable political significance. Intellectuals within Solidarity and the church increasingly expressed the connection to broader human rights. The award recognised specific organising efforts and the committee’s conviction that respect for rights was essential to lasting peace.

sections.heading: Promoting workers' rights through nonviolent negotiation
sections.body: The Norwegian Nobel Committee recognized the efforts to secure the right for workers to establish their own organizations. Through Solidarity, Wałęsa attempted to create a dialogue with authorities using cooperation instead of violence. This approach aimed to address national problems while contributing to the relaxation of international tension. Such activities support the universal freedom to organize, which is defined as a human right by the United Nations. The Committee viewed these peaceful methods as essential for resolving conflicts during an era requiring detente.

sections.heading: Development of independent trade unionism in Poland
sections.body: Dismissed from the shipyard in 1976 because of his organising activities, Wałęsa joined activists building independent unions in 1978. During the August 1980 Gdańsk strike, he led negotiations producing the agreement of 31 August, which recognised workers’ rights to strike and organise an independent union. He travelled internationally in 1980–1981 and became Solidarity’s elected chairman in September 1981. Martial law in December brought the suspension of Solidarity and his internment. After release in November 1982, he maintained contact with underground Solidarity leaders despite surveillance. The 1983 prize came while restrictions remained, before the movement achieved the political changes of later years.

terms.definition: Collective action to secure basic freedoms and human dignity; the Nobel Committee interpreted Solidarity’s labour campaign within this broader framework.
A universal human right, as defined by the United Nations, involving the ability of workers to establish their own organizations.
A 1980 accord that granted Polish workers the legal right to strike and establish their own independent trade unions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Physical processes during stellar evolution
sections.body: Gravity contracts interstellar gas, raising its temperature until nuclear reactions can begin. Hydrogen fusion supplies energy during a long stable phase; later reactions depend on a star’s mass and history. Successive fusion stages in massive stars build heavier nuclei toward the iron group, while neutron capture contributes to producing still heavier elements. Stellar endings also differ: some stars leave white dwarfs, while more massive ones may undergo collapse associated with a supernova and leave neutron stars or black holes. Chandrasekhar investigated the structure and stability of stars, especially compact remnants. Fowler studied the relevant nuclear reactions through experiments and theory. The award united complementary explanations of stellar change and element formation.

sections.heading: Chandrasekhar's research periods and published monographs
sections.body: Chandrasekhar organized his scientific career into distinct periods of study. His early work from 1929 to 1939 focused on stellar structure and white dwarf theory, producing papers on highly collapsed configurations and maximum mass. Later investigations included stellar dynamics, radiative transfer, and the mathematical theory of black holes. These research phases resulted in several monographs, such as An Introduction to the Study of Stellar Structure and Radiative Transfer. His academic development also involved studying at the Institut för Teoretisk Fysik in Copenhagen under the advice of P.A.M. Dirac.

sections.heading: Laboratory investigations into stellar nucleosynthesis
sections.body: Bethe’s 1939 carbon–nitrogen-cycle work gave astrophysical significance to proton reactions already being measured at Kellogg. After wartime defence research, Fowler and the Lauritsens focused the laboratory on reactions in stars. Separate experiments established gaps in stable nuclei at mass numbers five and eight, important obstacles for understanding how heavier elements form. Fowler then worked with Fred Hoyle and with Margaret and Geoffrey Burbidge. Their 1957 paper, Synthesis of the Elements in Stars, assembled a broad account of nuclear processes producing elements from carbon to uranium. Fowler stressed the continuing experimental task: measuring reaction probabilities in the laboratory and converting them into rates appropriate to stellar conditions.

terms.definition: The series of physical processes stars undergo from birth out of interstellar matter until their eventual extinction.
A detailed written work or book produced from a specific period of scientific study or research.
A scientific field focusing on nuclear reactions occurring within stars and the resulting production of various chemical elements.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Advancements in solid matrix peptide synthesis
sections.body: Merrifield attached the first amino acid to an insoluble polymer formed into small beads. The growing peptide remained on this support while further residues were added; only the completed chain was released. Soluble reagents and by-products could therefore be washed away between steps without repeatedly isolating the desired intermediate. This arrangement simplified handling and made automation practical. Washing did not, however, guarantee a perfect sequence or remove every incorrect chain still attached to the support. A notable achievement was the synthesis of active ribonuclease, containing 124 amino-acid residues. Other researchers extended the strategy of synthesis on a solid matrix to oligonucleotides used in nucleic-acid research.

sections.heading: Why small losses matter in long syntheses
sections.body: The announcement illustrates the cumulative cost of imperfect reactions and product isolation. If each of 100 steps retains 90% of the desired material, the final yield is only about 0.003%. At 99.5% per step, the corresponding calculation gives about 61%. These figures are an illustration, not a guaranteed yield for every peptide. Solid-phase synthesis made high step yields achievable while simplifying separation. The chemistry still required protecting groups so that the intended amino and carboxyl groups reacted in a controlled sequence. A selected protecting group could then be removed before adding the next amino acid. Efficient handling and controlled chemistry worked together.

sections.heading: Development of solid-phase peptide synthesis
sections.body: Following graduate research at UCLA regarding pyrimidine quantitation, Merrifield joined the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research. Working under Dr. D.W. Woolley, he investigated dinucleotide growth factors and previously discovered peptide growth factors. These investigations into growth factors created a requirement for peptide synthesis. In 1959, this necessity prompted his concept for solid-phase peptide synthesis. His laboratory work focused on the application of this technique, which transitioned from initial ideas into a developed method for assembling chemical chains.

terms.definition: A method for performing multistep chemical reactions by attaching a starting material to an insoluble, solid support.
A temporary chemical modification that prevents a functional group from reacting until it is deliberately exposed for the appropriate synthesis step.
A compound containing two linked nucleotides; Merrifield studied a dinucleotide growth factor before developing solid-phase peptide synthesis.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of integrated national accounting systems
sections.body: While assisting John Maynard Keynes at the British Treasury during the Second World War, Stone applied double-entry accounting to manage vast statistical data. His method aimed for full integration across sub-sectors, ensuring every expenditure item recurred as a corresponding income item in another account. This framework encompassed household finances, enterprise revenues, public sector spending, and balances of payments with other nations. Following the war, Stone directed an international expert group under the United Nations to create standardized accounting forms for global use. He continued directing work on international accounting standards and revisions. By employing large systems of equations, he demonstrated economic interdependence, establishing a common foundation for comparing national structures and cyclic positions across industrialized and developing countries.

sections.heading: Development of standardized international accounting frameworks
sections.body: Stone recalled that early wartime accounts used residual estimation: some figures were obtained as the amount needed to balance other entries. Their balance therefore did not independently prove accuracy. More encouraging was agreement between residuals derived from largely independent sets of information. He remained responsible for official estimates under Keynes until leaving government service after the war. International work followed, including a memorandum in the United Nations’ 1947 report on national income and social accounts. A Cambridge unit he directed for the Organisation for European Economic Cooperation produced systems published in 1950 and 1952. He also applied the linear expenditure system of Lawrence Klein and Herman Rubin to British data, relating commodity spending to prices and income. These activities connected measurement standards with empirical economic analysis.

terms.definition: A method where every expenditure recorded in one account must appear as a corresponding income item in another.
Estimating an unknown entry as the difference between a total and known components; the resulting balance alone does not validate the measurements.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Evolution of Seifert's poetic style and political engagement
sections.body: Initially influenced by socialistic revolution, Seifert utilized an unembellished style featuring folk song elements and everyday scenes. He rejected formalist, elevated styles in favor of clarity and musicality. While his early work sought a future without oppression, he later dissociated from communist dogmatism. During Nazi occupation, he defended Czechoslovakian freedom and eventually eulogized the 1945 Prague rebellion. Despite pressures to produce social realism propaganda, he refused such slogans, instead focusing on human empathy and resisting political dictates that reduce individuals to mere cogs.

sections.heading: Prague, memory and resistance in the poems
sections.body: The announcement links Seifert’s work with particular places and historical pressures. His early City in Tears draws on a working-class childhood. Collections such as Turn off the Lights, Robed with Light and Bridge of Stone later expressed resistance and sustained national confidence under threat and occupation. Helmet with Clay responded to the Prague rebellion and liberation in 1945. After the communist takeover, The Song of Viktorka drew accusations of political betrayal. The committee also emphasised another form of independence: poems celebrating love, remembered spring and Prague itself. These experiences mattered because they preserved imaginative life outside the demands of official slogans.

sections.heading: Seifert's early political involvement and editorial career
sections.body: During his early years, Seifert worked for communist publications such as Rovnost, Srsatec, and Reflektor. He also contributed to the publishing house and bookstore while serving on various avant-garde editorial staffs. In 1929, he joined six other writers in signing a manifesto against Bolshevik tendencies within the Czechoslovakian Communist Party's leadership, resulting in his expulsion. Later, he held editorial roles at Národní práce, Práce, and Kytice. After being forced to leave journalism in 1949, he turned to focus entirely on literature, eventually leading the Czechoslovakian Writers’ Union.

terms.definition: A metaphor drawn from midwifery; the committee used it to describe poetry as bringing forth forms of life beyond restrictive dogmas.
Poetry expressing opposition to oppression or occupation and sustaining collective confidence, a function the announcement identifies in several Seifert collections.
Artists and writers experimenting with forms that challenge established conventions; Seifert participated through poetry, translations and editorial work in the 1920s.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of Immune Selection and Hybridoma Production
sections.body: Jerne's 1955 theory proposed that antigens select among antibody specificities already present in the body. This shifted attention from an antigen acting as a template towards selection from an existing repertoire. In 1974 he proposed an immune network in which antibodies could themselves be recognised by other antibodies, potentially contributing to regulation. These were influential theoretical proposals, not a complete established mechanism of immunity. Köhler and Milstein addressed a practical problem: obtaining a reproducible supply of one antibody. They fused antibody-producing cells with tumour cells capable of continued growth, then selected and cloned useful hybrids. A hybridoma could combine a chosen antibody specificity with sustained multiplication. This made monoclonal antibodies available for identifying and purifying scarce molecules and for diagnostic research.

sections.heading: Niels Jerne's medical training and early research
sections.body: Jerne began with two years of physics at Leiden before changing to medicine at Copenhagen. His early experimental research examined antibody binding, culminating in a 1951 thesis on antibody avidity. The subject concerned how strongly antibodies bind their targets, providing a concrete experimental setting before his better-known theoretical work. His later proposals addressed different levels of immune organisation: selection among existing specificities, development of immune cells and possible networks of interactions between antibodies. The brief autobiography records the transition from physics to medicine and antibody research; the network ideas remained theoretical proposals rather than a complete description of immune regulation.

terms.definition: Hybrid cells created by fusing antibody-producing cells with tumor cells to produce large, continuous quantities of identical monoclonal antibodies.
The overall strength of binding between an antibody and its target, reflecting the combined effects of the binding interactions involved.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Objectives for a democratic South African society
sections.body: As leader of the South African Council of Churches, Tutu pursued a democratic society free from racial segregation. His specific platform included securing equal civil rights for every citizen and ending the Pass Laws. He advocated for a unified educational system and demanded an end to the forced deportation of black individuals into homelands. Through these goals, his leadership within the church organization sought to utilize reason and spirit to oppose the apartheid system's racial discrimination.

sections.heading: The nonviolent struggle for racial equality
sections.body: As General Secretary of the South African Council of Churches, Tutu acted as a unifying figure within the movement to resolve apartheid. This campaign utilized peaceful methods to unite black and white South Africans, aiming to lead the nation out of crisis and conflict. The Nobel Committee recognized this effort as part of a broader global struggle for human rights and racial equality. Such nonviolent approaches are considered vital for peace across the African continent and throughout the world, highlighting the importance of dignity and democracy.

sections.heading: From teaching to national church leadership
sections.body: Tutu trained as a teacher before turning to theology and being ordained in 1960. Further study in England from 1962 to 1966 led to a master’s degree, followed by theological teaching in South Africa. In 1975 he became the first black Dean of St Mary’s Cathedral in Johannesburg. He served as Bishop of Lesotho from 1976 to 1978, then became the first black General Secretary of the South African Council of Churches. That position gave him a platform linking religious leadership with opposition to apartheid. The biography describes the council as a contact body for churches whose firm stance against racial domination also produced disagreements within South African Christianity.

terms.definition: A political system of racial discrimination and segregation that the Nobel Committee regarded as a threat to global peace.
A peaceful campaign for liberation and racial equality involving united groups working to resolve national conflict and crisis.
An interchurch organisation through which South African churches cooperate; under Tutu’s leadership it became a prominent voice against apartheid.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The CERN antiproton project and particle detection
sections.body: At CERN, researchers utilized the SPS accelerator as a storage ring to circulate protons and antiprotons in opposite directions. These beams crossed the French-Swiss border 100,000 times per second, facilitating high-energy collisions. To achieve this, van der Meer developed stochastic cooling to build an intense antiproton beam within a special storage ring. Two separate teams operated large detectors at different collision points; Rubbia led the team responsible for the larger detector. These experiments allowed scientists to observe the rare creation of heavy W and Z particles through energy conversion into mass.

sections.heading: Development of the CERN superaccelerator project
sections.body: The project brought a proposed test of the weak interaction together with a practical accelerator solution. Heavy W and Z particles had been predicted as its carriers, but producing them required sufficiently energetic collisions and intense beams. In 1976 Rubbia proposed converting an existing large accelerator to store protons and antiprotons circulating in opposite directions. The antiprotons had to be produced and accumulated; van der Meer’s cooling method helped make a useful beam possible. First collisions in the converted SPS occurred in 1981. Specially designed detectors then supplied the evidence for W and Z discoveries announced in 1983. The sequence separates the proposed experiment, operational machine and eventual discovery.

sections.heading: Stochastic cooling and antiproton accumulation techniques
sections.body: To enable proton–antiproton collisions, researchers proposed using the SPS or Fermilab ring as a collider. This required accumulating necessary antiprotons through cooling processes. Simon van der Meer worked on stochastic cooling, a method initially developed to increase ISR luminosity. Following successful experiments in the ICE ring involving stochastic stacking, van der Meer served with R. Billinge as joint project leader for constructing the accumulator. His work also led to the proposal of the stochastic extraction method, which was later utilized in the Low-Energy Antiproton Ring.

terms.definition: A feedback technique that measures beam fluctuations and applies corrective electromagnetic kicks, reducing the spread of particle motion.
CERN’s Super Proton Synchrotron, converted for this project to store counter-circulating proton and antiproton beams.
Accumulating successive groups of antiprotons in a storage ring by cooling and combining them into an increasingly intense stored beam.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Direct method for solving the phase problem
sections.body: X-ray diffraction measures intensities but does not directly record the phases needed to reconstruct electron density. Hauptman and Karle developed statistical relationships that constrain those missing phases using information in the diffraction data. Their papers of 1950–1956 drew on physical properties such as nonnegative electron density and the availability of many measured reflections. This reduced reliance on guessing a complete molecular structure before analysing the data. The approach still used physical constraints and probabilistic reasoning; its name did not mean that every structure followed automatically without assumptions or validation. Increasing computing power helped turn the mathematics into practical tools for chemical structure determination.

sections.heading: Direct methods for determining crystal structures
sections.body: Hauptman and Karle related measured X-ray intensities to restrictions on the missing diffraction phases. Electron density cannot be negative, which limits the combinations of phases compatible with a physical crystal. Their equations express probabilistic relationships, so many measurements and an overdetermined set of constraints improve reliability. Solving these relationships requires substantial computation. The resulting phases can be combined with measured amplitudes to reconstruct an electron-density map, from which atomic positions are inferred. This connects mathematical relationships among diffraction measurements with a three-dimensional molecular structure. The method became a practical tool for many organic and inorganic compounds.

sections.heading: Probabilistic methods in X-ray crystallography
sections.body: In their 1953 monograph, Solution of the Phase Problem I. The Centrosymmetric Crystal, researchers introduced probabilistic methods to address phase determination. They utilized joint probability distributions of several structure factors as a primary tool. This work also established structure invariants and seminvariants, which are special linear combinations of phases. These concepts helped create recipes for origin specification within all centrosymmetric space groups. Later developments extended these mathematical foundations to non-centrosymmetric space groups, using these invariants to link observed diffraction intensities with necessary structure factor phases.

terms.definition: Crystallographic techniques that infer phase relationships from measured diffraction intensities using physical constraints and statistical relationships.
The distribution of electrons through space; crystallographic maps of this distribution help locate atoms within a crystal.
Combinations of diffraction phases that remain unchanged when the coordinate origin is shifted, allowing phase information to be related to observed intensities.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The Life-Cycle Hypothesis and Saving Determinants
sections.body: In 1954, Franco Modigliani and Richard Brumberg introduced the life-cycle hypothesis to resolve the Keynes-Kuznets paradox. This theory posits that individuals accumulate savings during active years to fund retirement consumption. Unlike previous models, this mathematical formulation suggests saving depends on wealth, age, and expected future income rather than just current income. Furthermore, Modigliani demonstrated that aggregate household saving is influenced by population growth, age structure, and interest rates acting as a capitalization factor, while also noting how the multiplier effect relates to marginal tax rates.

sections.heading: When financing does not change a firm’s value
sections.body: Modigliani and Merton Miller’s 1958 theorem asks whether changing a company’s debts changes its value. Under perfect financial markets, with no taxes or bankruptcy costs, its total market value is independent of how its assets are financed. That value combines the market values of debt and equity and depends on the expected returns from the assets, discounted appropriately for risk. Within this model, investment decisions can therefore be separated from financing decisions. The assumptions matter: the theorem is not a claim that debt, taxes or bankruptcy risk never affect real companies. It provided a precise starting point for the theory of corporate finance.

sections.heading: Foundations of economic and econometric research
sections.body: Modigliani studied econometrics and mathematical theory under Jacob Marschak and participated in a New York seminar with researchers including Abraham Wald and Tjalling Koopmans. At the Institute of World Affairs, he worked with Hans Neisser on research later published as National Income and International Trade. During that period he also made the early saving contribution known as the Duesenberry-Modigliani hypothesis. In 1948 he moved to Chicago and joined the Cowles Commission as a research consultant. His subsequent work at Cowles and the University of Illinois developed amid advances in choice under uncertainty and statistical inference from non-experimental observations.

terms.definition: A theory of household saving where individuals accumulate wealth during active years to support consumption throughout their retirement.
A result showing that, under specified ideal market conditions, a firm’s total value is independent of its financing structure.
The use of mathematical and statistical methods to investigate economic relationships using data, a foundation of Modigliani’s training with Marschak.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Linguistic development and narrative structure
sections.body: Simon's prose evolved through works like Le Vent and L’Herbe, moving toward a method resembling linguistic montages or collages. Influenced by Faulkner, his technique avoids realistic continuity in time and space, instead joining fragments via emotional correspondences or content-based associations. In novels such as Histoire and Les Géorgiques, language functions as an independently living organism that buds and grows. This approach utilizes parallel actions and stories within stories to break traditional narrative frameworks, often drawing parallels between modern warfare experiences and the Napoleonic era.

sections.heading: War memories woven through fragmented scenes
sections.body: La Route des Flandres, published in 1960, made Simon internationally known. Its account of the French collapse in 1940 draws on his experience as a cavalryman and prisoner of war, but it does not present those events as a straightforward military history. Memories, family stories and parallel actions unfold around Georges’s night with Corinne. Scenes connect through associations rather than a single chronological sequence. Simon’s experiences of the Spanish Civil War recur in Le Palace and Les Géorgiques. Across these books, apparently ordered plans dissolve into cruelty, confusion and individual struggles to survive. Fragmented narration makes that disorder part of the reader’s experience.

sections.heading: Artistic training and literary development
sections.body: Simon's literary approach was informed by his studies in painting at the André Lhote Academy. His extensive travels through countries including Spain, Germany, Italy, and the Soviet Union provided further influence for his writing. During the Second World War, he participated in the battle of the Meuse and later joined the resistance after escaping captivity. These experiences shaped works such as Histoire, which earned him the Médicis prize in 1967, following his earlier success with La Route des Flandres.

terms.definition: A French literary movement featuring prose works that reject conventional realistic stories and coherent, lucid chronological progression in favor of fragmentation.
The joining of fragments from different moments through associations and contrasts, rather than arranging every scene in chronological order.
An institution where Claude Simon undertook courses in painting to develop his artistic perspective.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of cellular cholesterol regulation and LDL receptor function
sections.body: Through systematic investigations using connective tissue cell cultures, the researchers demonstrated how LDL particles bind to surface receptors and move into the cell interior. Once inside, the receptor is released back to the cell surface to repeat the process while the particle disintegrates. This influx of cholesterol suppresses HMG CoA reductase activity to reduce endogenous synthesis and activates enzymes for storage. They also observed that cells from patients with familial hypercholesterolemia had reduced or absent functional LDL receptors, disrupting uptake and feedback regulation.

sections.heading: Mechanism of receptor-mediated endocytosis in cholesterol uptake
sections.body: LDL binds receptors concentrated in coated pits on the cell surface. The membrane folds inward and pinches off, carrying the bound particles into the cell in vesicles. This receptor-mediated endocytosis delivers LDL for intracellular processing and release of its cholesterol; the endosome should not be equated with the whole breakdown process. Brown and Goldstein compared cultured fibroblasts from healthy people and patients with familial hypercholesterolemia. Added LDL-containing serum inhibited cholesterol production in normal cells. In severely affected cells lacking functional receptors, LDL could not produce the same feedback response. The comparison linked a specific defect in uptake to a failure of cellular regulation.

sections.heading: Enzyme purification and cholesterol biosynthesis regulation
sections.body: While working at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical School, Brown achieved the partial purification and solubilization of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase. This specific enzyme catalyzes the rate-controlling step in cholesterol biosynthesis. Building on his earlier work at the National Institutes of Health, where he studied nucleotide-controlled regulatory enzymes, Brown and Goldstein hypothesized that defects in regulating this enzyme cause familial hypercholesterolemia. Their collaborative research investigated how these genetic abnormalities lead to excess cholesterol accumulation within blood and various tissues.

terms.definition: The intracellular process where cells manage cholesterol by balancing internal synthesis with amounts obtained from circulating blood lipoproteins.
A spherical, cholesterol-containing particle composed of proteins and fats that circulates in the blood and is taken up by cells.
An enzyme that catalyzes the rate-controlling step during the biological process of cholesterol biosynthesis.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A professional network across Cold War divisions
sections.body: IPPNW gave physicians from opposing political systems a shared forum for explaining the consequences of nuclear war. The 1985 presentation described support from international institutions as well as national medical communities. At an earlier congress in Amsterdam, the organisation received messages of support from the UN Secretary-General, Pope John Paul II and political leaders. UNESCO awarded it a peace-education prize in 1984. The World Health Organization distributed its reports on the medical effects of nuclear explosions and established an official relationship with it in March 1985. These connections helped carry the physicians' arguments beyond their own membership. The committee regarded cross-border cooperation and public education as contributions to the campaign for disarmament.

sections.heading: How public awareness could affect negotiations
sections.body: The award announcement set out the committee's reasoning for recognising a medical campaigning organisation. It judged that information about nuclear war's consequences could increase public pressure against the spread of atomic weapons. Greater attention to health and humanitarian costs might, in turn, change the priorities brought into arms-limitation talks.
