The committee gave particular weight to the organisation's origin in cooperation between Soviet and American physicians and its support in more than forty countries. Bernard Lown and Yevgeny Chazov were invited to receive the prize on the organisation's behalf. The announcement described an influence the committee hoped this public work would have on diplomacy, rather than an arms agreement already achieved.

terms.definition: Joint work across national boundaries, exemplified by IPPNW's collaboration between physicians from countries on opposing sides of the Cold War.
Diplomatic talks aimed at restricting weapons; the committee hoped greater awareness of medical and humanitarian consequences could influence their priorities.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A precise effect in a thin electron layer
sections.body: At the high-field laboratory in Grenoble in 1980, von Klitzing cooled semiconductor samples to a few degrees above absolute zero and applied a strong magnetic field. In the transistors he used, electrons were confined to an interface and moved effectively in two dimensions. The Hall conductance changed in steps, with plateaux determined by fundamental constants rather than varying continuously. The presentation reported agreement at about one part in ten million. That reproducibility made the effect a candidate for an international resistance standard. It also showed that an electrical measurement on a laboratory-sized device could reveal a sharply defined quantum effect.

sections.heading: From semiconductor measurements to strong magnetic fields
sections.body: Von Klitzing's earlier research already concerned how materials behave electrically. His diploma work at Braunschweig examined lifetime measurements in indium antimonide. At Würzburg, his doctoral research investigated tellurium's galvanomagnetic properties in strong magnetic fields. Research visits took him to Oxford's Clarendon Laboratory in 1975–1976 and Grenoble's High Magnetic Field Laboratory in 1979–1980. His biographical record identifies the 1980 Physical Review Letters paper as the central publication associated with the Nobel discovery. This sequence places the result within a programme of semiconductor and high-field research, rather than presenting it as an observation without an experimental background.

terms.definition: Electrons confined to a thin interface so that their motion is effectively limited to two dimensions, as in the semiconductor samples studied.
Electrical properties examined in the presence of a magnetic field, the subject of von Klitzing's doctoral work on tellurium.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Measuring what emerges from a molecular collision
sections.body: Chemical reactions can involve extremely brief molecular encounters. Crossed-beam experiments isolated these events at low pressure, allowing streams of atoms or molecules to meet under controlled conditions. Researchers could vary the energy of the incoming particles and measure what emerged: the products' identities, speeds, directions and internal rotational or vibrational energy. These observations supplied a much richer description than the overall reaction equation. They also gave theorists experimental evidence with which to test explanations of the molecular rearrangements between the starting materials and the final products.

sections.heading: Extending crossed-beam experiments beyond alkali reactions
sections.body: Herschbach's early apparatus revealed preferred product recoil angles and translational energies in reactions involving alkali atoms. After the research group moved to Harvard, Yuan Lee joined in 1967 and led construction of a more versatile instrument. It combined improved differential pumping, supersonic beam sources and mass-sensitive detection using ion counting. These changes expanded the range of reactions accessible to crossed-beam experiments. Herschbach's account also describes distinct reaction patterns, including abrupt bond exchange and the formation of longer-lived intermediate complexes, which could be related to the target molecule's electronic structure.

sections.heading: Mapping the products of reactive encounters
sections.body: After his doctorate, Lee worked with Ron Gentry on collisions between ions and molecules. Their apparatus measured how reaction products were distributed in energy and direction, producing a detailed map for a reaction between ionised nitrogen and hydrogen. At Harvard, Lee then worked with Doug McDonald and Pierre LeBreton to construct a more widely applicable crossed-beam instrument. Completed in 1967 with help from the machine shop, it enabled experiments on neutral reactions outside the alkali systems studied earlier, including chlorine atoms reacting with bromine molecules.

terms.definition: One trillionth of a second, a unit used in the presentation to convey the very short timescales of molecular reactions.
Pumping separate parts of an apparatus to maintain suitable low pressures, an important feature of the improved crossed-beam instrument.
A collision in which particles react to form new products; measuring the products' energies and directions reveals details of the encounter.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Studying the incentives inside political institutions
sections.body: Public choice extended economic analysis to voters, administrators, politicians and organised interests. The presentation distinguished explaining how institutions behave from prescribing how they ought to behave. Models of individual incentives could help explain, for example, why well-organised producer groups sometimes gain influence over more dispersed consumers. They also showed why an intervention intended to correct a market problem might produce a different policy problem. Buchanan's work asked economists to examine the incentives and constraints of public institutions alongside those of private markets, rather than assume that public decisions automatically served a single common interest.

sections.heading: Choosing the rules before choosing particular policies
sections.body: Buchanan treated political cooperation as a possible means of obtaining mutual benefits, while stressing that outcomes depend on the rules governing decisions. The press release used trade policy as an example: changing the basic rules of trade could matter more than lobbying over an individual tariff. Inspired by Wicksell, Buchanan also examined unanimity as a basis for agreement about public expenditure and taxation. This was a framework for analysing consent and institutional design. It did not establish that actual political decisions always reflected voluntary agreement or that a particular existing constitution achieved mutual advantage.

sections.heading: A programme of work on debt, taxation and rules
sections.body: Buchanan's bibliography shows the range of questions behind his institutional approach. Books on public debt and fiscal theory preceded The Calculus of Consent, written with Gordon Tullock in 1962. Later collaborations included Democracy in Deficit with R. Wagner and The Power to Tax and The Reason of Rules with G. Brennan. His separately authored Liberty, Market and State also appeared before the award. Together these publications place the prize within a long programme examining public finance, collective decisions and the constraints imposed by political rules.

terms.definition: The application of economic reasoning about incentives and choices to political decision-making and public institutions.
The underlying rules that govern collective decisions, including who may decide, how agreement is reached and what limits apply.
The study of government revenue, expenditure and borrowing, subjects that recur throughout Buchanan's published work.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Myth, satire and moral conflict
sections.body: The presentation described Soyinka's use of inherited myths as a source of dramatic thought rather than decorative folklore. His work combines Yoruba traditions with a wide reading of other literatures, an approach he called selective eclecticism. Plays such as Death and the King's Horseman use ritual, poetry and satire to explore moral responsibilities and conflicts that exceed a simple opposition between cultures. The speech also connected the increasingly difficult ambiguities in his work with wartime and prison experiences. These were interpretations of the drama's complexity, rather than a single formula explaining every play.

sections.heading: Ritual relationships and the experience of confinement
sections.body: The award announcement discussed links between Soyinka's plays and both Yoruba ritual and European theatrical traditions. A Dance of the Forests brings spirits and deities into the drama, while Death and the King's Horseman explores relationships among the living, the dead and those yet to be born. His writing also draws on direct political experience. A Shuttle in the Crypt and The Man Died respond to his imprisonment during Nigeria's civil war, addressing survival, human contact, anger and forgiveness. Mythic structures and personal testimony therefore form distinct resources within the work.

sections.heading: Writing for performance and reworking earlier plays
sections.body: Soyinka worked with theatre companies as well as writing dramatic texts, founding The 1960 Masks and Orisun Theatre Company. His theatre draws on combinations of speech, music, dance and action, alongside influences such as J. M. Synge. He also reworked existing dramatic material: The Bacchae of Euripides adapts the Greek play, while Opera Wonyosi draws on works by John Gay and Bertolt Brecht. These examples show an active engagement with theatrical form and performance, extending beyond the use of any one set of myths or literary sources.

terms.definition: Soyinka's description of choosing deliberately among varied literary traditions and influences when making his own work.
Drama shaped by ceremonial actions and beliefs; the announcement connected this element in Soyinka's work with Yoruba cultural traditions.
The reworking of an existing text for a new artistic context or performance, as in Soyinka's version of Euripides' Bacchae.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: How a growth signal reaches the cell interior
sections.body: Cohen’s work on epidermal growth factor connected an external signal with a biochemical response inside a cell. A target cell needed a suitable surface receptor. One part of that receptor bound EGF outside the membrane, while another part inside the cell had enzyme activity that increased after binding. This provided a molecular explanation of signaling, beyond observing that a substance stimulated growth. The presentation speech also links this kind of enzyme activity with proteins encoded by certain cancer-causing viruses. The connection helped explain why growth regulation and abnormal proliferation could be studied through related biochemical mechanisms.

sections.heading: Biochemical training behind the growth-factor research
sections.body: Cohen’s doctoral work examined a change in earthworm nitrogen metabolism during starvation, when the main waste product shifted from ammonia to urea. He later learned to use radioactive tracers while studying carbon dioxide incorporation in frog eggs and embryos. These experiences connected chemical measurements with biological questions. In 1953 he joined Levi-Montalcini’s effort to isolate the nerve-growth activity she had found in mouse tumors, while also learning experimental embryology. His later work at Vanderbilt developed the investigation of epidermal growth factor. The biography highlights the combination of different experimental skills behind these discoveries.

sections.heading: Research continued under persecution and war
sections.body: Italy’s antisemitic laws of 1938 excluded Levi-Montalcini from an academic career. After returning to Turin, she set up a small laboratory in her bedroom and investigated chick-embryo development, prompted by Hamburger’s experiments on removing developing limbs. Giuseppe Levi, her former teacher, joined the work. Bombing later forced her to rebuild the laboratory in a country cottage, and further persecution drove the family into hiding in Florence. After the war, work with Hamburger in St. Louis continued the developmental investigations. The home experiments were an important stage in a longer research trajectory, rather than the completed growth-factor discovery itself.

terms.definition: A membrane protein that binds epidermal growth factor and activates intracellular enzyme activity, initiating signals that influence cell behavior.
A radioactively labeled substance used to follow the movement or chemical transformation of material in a biological experiment.
An experimental procedure removing a developing limb structure to study how its absence affects other tissues, including the nerves that would supply it.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Rita Levi-Montalcini — Women who changed science

sections.heading: The danger of looking away
sections.body: The presentation described Wiesel's writing as an attempt to confront the ideas and behaviour that made the Holocaust possible, alongside preserving testimony about its victims. It interpreted his opposition to indifference as a call for responsibility: people should recognise suffering and act against persecution rather than assume it is someone else's concern. The speech connected this message with his advocacy beyond the Jewish experience. Its language about moral complicity expresses that ethical argument, not a legal finding that every indifferent observer bears the same criminal responsibility as a perpetrator.

sections.heading: Testimony as a form of public responsibility
sections.body: The committee presented Wiesel's personal testimony as central to his contribution to peace. His writing returned to experiences of humiliation and persecution, asking readers to consider their wider implications for human dignity. The announcement also recognised practical advocacy and described a commitment extending beyond the suffering of his own community. These were the committee's reasons for honouring an author with the Peace Prize: the work was understood as a public intervention against violence, racism and repression, as well as an act of remembrance.

sections.heading: Writing, teaching and institutional remembrance
sections.body: The French-language memoir La Nuit appeared in 1958, bringing Wiesel's camp experiences into a work known in English as Night. His public activity also included journalism, teaching and lectures about persecution. From 1980 to 1986 he chaired the United States Holocaust Memorial Council, and at Boston University he taught courses on memory and literature. The Nobel biography later received a 1999 update mentioning advocacy for victims in Bosnia and Kosovo. Those later activities belong to the continuing career, not to the evidence available when the 1986 prize was awarded.

terms.definition: A lack of concern or response to others' suffering; Wiesel challenged it as an obstacle to protecting human dignity.
An account grounded in a person's witnessed or lived experience; Wiesel used it to communicate the consequences of persecution and the need for responsibility.
A written account of selected personal experiences, such as Wiesel's recollection of imprisonment and survival in Night.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Two ways to obtain information beyond optical resolution
sections.body: In electron microscopy, a magnetic field produced by a coil can act as a lens for an electron beam, with the resulting image recorded on a screen or photographic medium. Scanning tunnelling microscopy uses a different measurement: current across a very small gap between a conducting surface and a sharp tip. Because that current changes strongly with separation, a feedback system can control the tip's height as it scans. The recorded signal reveals fine surface structure. Its interpretation also concerns the electronic properties involved in tunnelling, rather than simply a mechanical tracing of physical bumps.

sections.heading: The experimental team behind the tunnelling microscope
sections.body: Binnig's account describes his move from studying physics to enjoying its experimental practice. He joined IBM's Zürich laboratory in 1978 and worked with Heinrich Rohrer, Christoph Gerber and Edmund Weibel. The biography emphasises the exchange of ideas and the research environment in which the scanning tunnelling microscope developed. This adds a collaborative dimension to an award naming Binnig and Rohrer: designing and building the instrument involved colleagues as well as the two laureates. Binnig presented the experience as a renewal of his curiosity about physics.

sections.heading: Rohrer's earlier work on magnetic materials
sections.body: Before the tunnelling-microscope collaboration, Rohrer spent years investigating condensed-matter physics at IBM. His research included changes in electrical resistance in magnetic fields and studies of magnetic phases in an antiferromagnetic material. Work with colleagues led him towards critical phenomena, where a system changes behaviour near a transition. The biography distinguishes this earlier programme from the new direction he later pursued with Binnig. It places the microscope project within a career already concerned with sensitive measurements and the behaviour of materials under controlled conditions.

terms.definition: A quantum process allowing electrons to cross a barrier that would prevent classical passage, producing current across the microscope's small tip–surface gap.
An instrument that scans a sharp tip across a conducting surface and uses tunnelling current to obtain information at very small scales.
A map showing which magnetic states occur under different conditions, such as temperature and applied magnetic field.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Selectivity depends on the match between host and guest
sections.body: Pedersen’s crown ethers contain rings of carbon and oxygen atoms that can bind metal ions. A particular ring may fit potassium well while accommodating a larger ion less effectively; this preference depends on the host’s size and chemistry, not on a universal inability to bind large ions. Cram and Lehn extended molecular design to more elaborate cavities and binding arrangements. The presentation describes hosts recognizing positive ions, negative ions and neutral molecules, including discrimination between mirror-image forms. These results made selective recognition a property chemists could deliberately investigate and design.

sections.heading: A laboratory program connected with teaching and collaboration
sections.body: Cram’s biography describes research as a collective enterprise involving more than two hundred coworkers over his career. Alongside experimental chemistry, he taught large undergraduate classes and wrote textbooks with collaborators, including Organic Chemistry with George Hammond. His monograph Fundamentals of Carbanion Chemistry addressed a more specialized research subject. These activities show how laboratory methods and chemical reasoning circulated through training and books as well as papers. His later autobiographical addition also credits the Nobel recognition with strengthening interest in molecular recognition and extending his own research career.

sections.heading: From ion-binding cavities to organized molecular assemblies
sections.body: Lehn dates the beginning of his work on cation cryptates to 1967. Designing molecules that enclosed and recognized positive ions grew into the broader field he called supramolecular chemistry. His research also explored artificial photosynthesis and chemical storage of solar energy. A later addition to the biography, dated 2006, describes expanded work on self-organization: molecular components assembled through selected interactions into more complex architectures. Keeping that later account separate from the 1987 award makes the longer trajectory visible without placing every subsequent structure among the original prize-winning results.

terms.definition: The study of a host molecule selectively associating with a guest ion or molecule through complementary shape and chemical interactions.
The planned construction of carbon-containing molecules through chemical reactions, central to making hosts with chosen shapes and binding properties.
Chemistry of organized associations among molecules and ions, focusing on their interactions and collective structures rather than covalent molecules alone.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of capital intensity and long-run growth
sections.body: Solow's model utilizes a savings propensity to determine how national income is saved. Within this framework, a high savings ratio decreases capital costs relative to wages, increasing capital intensity by raising real capital per worker. Conversely, a low savings ratio makes capital more expensive, reducing capital intensity. While these shifts influence short-run growth rates, the model demonstrates that capital per worker and production per worker eventually reach a constant state under fixed technology. In this model, continued growth in output per worker requires technological progress; research and development can generate new production methods. Additionally, Solow investigated embodied technical progress, where innovation is integrated into capital goods, contributing to the vintage approach in growth theory and providing empirical foundations for studying major growth factors.

sections.heading: Solow's academic development and empirical research contributions
sections.body: Following his studies in sociology and anthropology, Solow pursued economics under Wassily Leontief, whose mentorship introduced him to empirical methods. While serving as a research assistant, he generated the initial capital-coefficients for the input-output model. His mathematical training expanded through intensive statistical study at Columbia University, where he engaged with scholars like Abraham Wald and T.W. Anderson while developing a Ph.D. thesis using interacting Markoff processes to model wage income distributions. Beyond theoretical work, Solow helped found the Manpower Demonstration Research Corporation, a non-profit group dedicated to the experimental testing of policy interventions for disadvantaged populations. His 2005 biographical update also describes later collaboration with Martin Baily on McKinsey Global Institute studies of international differences in industrial performance.

terms.definition: The amount of real capital available per worker, which fluctuates based on the relationship between savings ratios and capital costs.
A non-profit research group that performs rigorous experimental testing of policy interventions intended to improve employment and earning power.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Language as a way of seeing
sections.body: Brodsky treated Russian and English as different ways of approaching the world. His poetry drew on the Russian tradition of Mandelstam, Akhmatova and Pasternak, while English-language influences included Donne, Frost and Auden. The award presentation also explored his belief that words can redirect thought, rather than simply record an already formed consciousness. In this account, writing becomes an active struggle with language. Brodsky extended that view to political history, arguing that a shared language sustains an empire's cultural existence.

sections.heading: Time, exile and the poet's public voice
sections.body: The Academy connected Brodsky's experience across languages and countries with the historical range of his poetry. His poem 1972 imagines a gradual loss of bodily features and elements of speech after leaving the Soviet Union. History of the Twentieth Century, written in English, uses parody and a mocking tone to approach its subject. His essays in Less Than One examine another problem: how a poet can speak within society. The announcement contrasts the suppression of voices under totalitarianism with the danger of being overwhelmed by information in an open society. These are different pressures on the poet's ability to be heard.

sections.heading: Translation and an expanding readership
sections.body: Brodsky translated English metaphysical poets and Czesław Miłosz into Russian, while other translators carried his own poetry into additional languages. George L. Kline translated the Selected Poems issued in London in 1973 and New York in 1974, with a foreword by W. H. Auden. A Part of Speech appeared in 1980. The essay collection Less Than One followed in 1986, extending his published work into discussions of art and politics. The biography also records later books: To Urania in 1988 and Watermark, essays about Venice, in 1992. Those publications continued his career after the 1987 award.

terms.definition: Brodsky's view that words can alter the direction of thought, making language an active participant in the process of writing.
An imitative, often mocking mode of writing; the Academy identifies it as part of Brodsky's approach in History of the Twentieth Century.
Rendering poetry in another language; Brodsky translated other poets into Russian, while translators made his own work available to wider audiences.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Combining gene segments to generate variety
sections.body: The presentation explained antibody diversity through the assembly of inherited DNA segments. For an antibody's light chain, variable and joining segments are brought together, while a constant region supplies another part of the instruction. Different combinations multiply the possibilities. Variation at the joins adds further diversity, and combining light chains with heavy chains increases the number of possible antibodies again. This explains how a limited collection of inherited segments can support an enormous repertoire across many B cells. The process does not mean that every rearrangement produces a useful antibody.

sections.heading: The antibody-producing cell has rearranged DNA
sections.body: Tonegawa's 1976 experiments showed that DNA regions separated in embryonic cells were brought together in antibody-producing cells. Subsequent work explained how rearrangement could move, combine or remove stretches of DNA during B-cell development. The press release illustrates the heavy chain with three groups of segments, V, D and J, that join to form its variable-region instruction. The finding changed the question from how many complete antibody genes were inherited to how inherited segments could be assembled. It provided a physical genetic mechanism for generating many different recognition sites.

sections.heading: Applying molecular tools to an immunological puzzle
sections.body: Tonegawa brought molecular-biology methods to the debate over antibody diversity, including restriction enzymes and recombinant-DNA techniques. His account credits collaborators and describes rapid progress during his Basel years. The work established that diversity involves rearrangement of inherited gene segments as well as somatic mutation. After moving to MIT, his laboratory also investigated how rearranged antibody genes are activated and studied the genes encoding T-cell antigen receptors. These projects extended the investigation from antibody diversity to regulation and another major branch of immune recognition.

terms.definition: A portion of inherited DNA that can contribute to a functional antibody gene when combined with other segments during B-cell development.
A molecular structure recognised by an antibody; different antibody binding sites can recognise different antigens.
Rearrangement of inherited DNA segments in developing immune cells, producing combinations that differ from the original inherited organisation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of the Central American peace plan
sections.body: The peace process built upon the 1983 Contadora group's preliminary twenty-one-point agenda, which involved Mexico, Venezuela, Colombia, and Panama. Although that initial proposal failed to produce a treaty, it gained support from Canada and Western Europe. Following his 1986 election, Oscar Arias worked to complete these intentions. He collaborated with the presidents of Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador, and Honduras to create a new plan. This finalized agreement, signed in August 1987, emphasized that outside powers must cease actions contributing to ongoing civil wars.

sections.heading: The committee's assessment of a new agreement
sections.body: The Nobel Committee announced its decision in October 1987, only months after the agreement signed in Guatemala on 7 August. Its statement recognised Arias as the plan's principal architect while also emphasising cooperation among all five signatory states and the earlier Contadora initiative. The award concerned the agreement's potential to help restore stability after civil conflict. The committee connected that prospect with democratic freedoms, equality and continued cooperation between countries. This explains the timing and nature of the recognition: the accord was treated as an opening for peace whose wider aims still depended on subsequent developments.

sections.heading: From an unresolved meeting to a signed plan
sections.body: Arias met the presidents of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua in May 1986 to discuss the Contadora proposals. That meeting did not produce full agreement. Early in 1987 he convened another meeting and submitted his own plan, which differed in some respects from the earlier approach. The five presidents approved it in Guatemala on 7 August. His negotiating position combined opposition to the activities of US-supported Contras on Costa Rican territory with criticism of Nicaragua's political system. He nevertheless sought to include Nicaragua in the peace process, making dialogue with neighbouring governments a central part of his approach.

terms.definition: A diplomatic collective including Mexico, Venezuela, Colombia, and Panama that presented a preliminary peace agenda for Central American nations.
Freedom and equality for citizens, identified by the Nobel Committee as conditions it considered necessary for a lasting peace in the region.
Discussions among neighbouring governments seeking a shared agreement, exemplified by the successive meetings that preceded approval of Arias's peace plan.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A higher transition temperature and magnetic effects
sections.body: Earlier superconducting alloys had reached transition temperatures of about 23 kelvin. Bednorz and Müller searched outside that familiar group and found a sharp drop towards zero resistance in a lanthanum–barium–copper oxide ceramic. The transition occurred at a temperature roughly fifty percent higher on the absolute scale. The presentation also explained the magnetic behaviour associated with superconductivity: a material entering the superconducting state can expel magnetic flux. Under suitable conditions this allows a nearby magnet to levitate. Both electrical resistance and magnetic response therefore mattered when examining the unusual properties of these new materials.

sections.heading: Testing a new family of oxide materials
sections.body: Beginning in 1983, Bednorz and Müller investigated copper-containing oxides, pursuing an idea that interactions between electrons and the crystal might favour superconductivity. Adding barium to lanthanum–copper oxide produced a ceramic with a transition temperature about twelve degrees above the previous record. After purifying the material, they also demonstrated the magnetic behaviour associated with superconductivity. Other laboratories quickly investigated related compounds. By early 1987, transition temperatures above 90 kelvin had been reached. Those later materials could use liquid nitrogen as a coolant, making the temperature improvement practically significant as well as scientifically surprising.

sections.heading: Learning to grow and characterise crystals
sections.body: Bednorz developed experimental skills in crystal growth, materials characterisation and solid-state chemistry while working with Hans Jörg Scheel. His diploma research involved growing and studying strontium titanate crystals. At ETH Zürich, he continued with perovskite-type solid solutions, examining their structure and electrical properties under the supervision of Heini Gränicher and Alex Müller. After joining IBM in 1982, he began an intensive search with Müller for a superconducting oxide in 1983. His account describes several years of experimental work before the 1986 result, connecting the discovery with experience in preparing and measuring suitable material samples.

terms.definition: The temperature boundary below which a material enters its superconducting state, used to compare the performance of different superconductors.
The exclusion of magnetic flux associated with entering a superconducting state, providing a magnetic signature alongside the disappearance of electrical resistance.
Preparing crystalline samples for measurement; Bednorz used this experimental skill to investigate how a material's structure related to its electrical properties.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Why one membrane structure mattered more widely
sections.body: The reaction-centre structure provided a physical arrangement against which theories of biological electron transfer could be tested. It showed how components positioned within a membrane protein supported very rapid transfer over substantial molecular distances. The presentation also pointed beyond photosynthesis: nutrient transport, hormone responses and nerve signalling involve membrane proteins too. Solving this structure offered principles and experimental methods that could help investigate other members of this difficult class. Prospects such as artificial photosynthesis were presented as possible future applications, not outcomes already achieved by the prize-winning structural study.

sections.heading: From a promising crystal to a refined structure
sections.body: Deisenhofer joined the reaction-centre project after Michel reported successful crystallisation in 1982. His account describes a collaborative effort involving Huber, Kunio Miki and Otto Epp, supported by crystallographic software and computer modelling. By the end of 1983 the prospects looked promising, but completing the structure took almost two more years. Refining the model at 2.3 ångström resolution required a further two years. The sequence illustrates why obtaining a crystal and determining a reliable molecular structure are different stages, each involving substantial experimental and computational work.

sections.heading: Proteins as flexible structures
sections.body: Huber's laboratory investigated many proteins in addition to the photosynthetic reaction centre. Work on digestive enzymes and their inhibitors helped show that flexibility and disorder could be meaningful molecular properties. The trypsinogen system was examined using low-temperature crystallography and other experimental and computational methods. His account also credits colleagues involved in developing tools for structure determination, refinement, data processing and computer graphics. This wider programme provided experience and methods for tackling difficult structures, while challenging the idea that a protein's function could always be understood from one rigid arrangement.

terms.definition: A protein associated with a biological membrane; some span the membrane and participate in processes such as transport, signalling or electron transfer.
Adjustment of a structural model to improve its agreement with measured diffraction data, carried out after an initial model has been obtained.
Changes in a protein's conformation or flexibility; Huber's research examined how such properties mattered alongside its overall structure.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Equilibrium, adjustment and decisions under risk
sections.body: Allais investigated both the conditions for economic equilibrium and the processes by which an economy might approach it. The presentation discussed his auction-like model of price adjustment and his analysis of when that process would be stable. His work also extended to growth, overlapping generations and the demand for money. A different line of research examined choices under uncertainty. The Allais paradox drew attention to observed patterns that conflict with expected-utility theory in particular decisions, motivating a reconsideration of the theory's assumptions about consistent choice.

sections.heading: Linking mathematical models to resource allocation
sections.body: Building on Walras and Pareto, Allais used models of household and firm decisions to formulate conditions for market equilibrium and efficient resource use. The press release highlights his major works of 1943 and 1947. It also describes analysis of the conditions under which price adjustments could restore equilibrium after a disturbance. These ideas influenced French economists working on large public enterprises, including electricity and railways, where pricing and resource allocation were practical problems. The analysis depended on specified conditions; it was not a finding that every market automatically returned to an efficient outcome.

sections.heading: Efficiency and the organisation of an economy
sections.body: Allais developed his early economic work while also holding administrative responsibilities in mining. In his autobiography, he connected theoretical results about equilibrium and efficiency to a broader argument for decentralised markets. He believed such organisation could matter in economies with different ownership systems, including collectivist ones. The account also asks how a market economy should be implemented and what ethical questions arise. These passages describe his interpretation of the implications of his theory, rather than settling every institutional or ethical choice involved in organising an actual economy.

terms.definition: A pattern of choices under risk that conflicts with an assumption of expected-utility theory, highlighting a gap between that model and observed behaviour.
Whether a system returns towards equilibrium after a disturbance; Allais studied conditions under which price adjustment could have this property.
An arrangement in which economic decisions are distributed among participants; Allais argued that this was important for efficient use of scarce resources.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A range extending beyond social realism
sections.body: The presentation contrasted the broad picture of contemporary life in the Cairo Trilogy with the allegorical and spiritual concerns of Children of Gebelawi. The latter's 114 chapters echo the number of chapters in the Quran. This variety was central to the committee's interpretation of Mahfouz's achievement: psychological realism, experiment and reflection on time all contributed to his narrative art. The speech also described connections with classical Arabic literature and European writing. Its praise concerned a varied body of work, rather than a single unchanging method of representing Cairo.

sections.heading: From ancient settings to modern urban life
sections.body: Mahfouz's early novels used settings in ancient Egypt while also inviting comparisons with contemporary society. Later Cairo novels placed modern urban lives at their centre. In Midaq Alley, the shared setting brings together a varied group of characters, allowing their different ambitions and pressures to interact. The announcement also discussed works where reality and illusion become harder to separate, including the novel known in English as Adrift on the Nile. It read these formal changes alongside Mahfouz's continuing interest in the social and intellectual life of his country.

sections.heading: Political meaning through indirect forms
sections.body: After a pause following the 1952 revolution, Mahfouz resumed fiction with Children of Gebelawi in 1959. His biography describes a new phase in which allegory and symbolism carried political meanings. The Thief and the Dogs and Miramar belong to this wider development, followed by further experimental work. Alongside writing, he held civil-service posts, including responsibilities connected with censorship and cinema, until retiring in 1972. The account records a substantial continuing output after retirement, showing that the familiar Cairo novels were one phase of a longer career.

terms.definition: A narrative approach that gives convincing attention to characters' motives, feelings and conflicts within their social circumstances.
Fiction concerned with questions about reality, existence and meaning, often extending beyond a straightforward account of observable events.
The use of characters, objects or events to suggest meanings beyond their immediate place in a story, including indirect political meanings.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Adrift on the Nile — publisher’s edition record

sections.heading: Designing drugs around biological targets
sections.body: Black sought compounds that would block particular receptors. Blocking cardiac beta receptors could reduce the heart’s demand for oxygen; blocking a different histamine receptor could reduce stomach-acid secretion. Elion and Hitchings pursued another route, using differences in biochemical processes to guide compounds against infections or abnormal cell growth. Their work included drugs affecting nucleic-acid metabolism and the development of acyclovir, whose activation favors virus-infected cells. The common principle was to organize drug research around a biological mechanism. Selectivity was a research achievement to establish experimentally, not a promise that a medicine would have no unwanted effects.

sections.heading: Reducing the heart’s demand for oxygen
sections.body: Black’s work with surgeons treating narrowed coronary arteries suggested a different strategy from increasing oxygen supply: reduce the heart’s demand. He used the distinction between adrenaline receptor types to guide a search for a selective blocker, taking the program to ICI. His biography emphasizes the collaboration required to turn that idea into a medicine. Bert Crowther led chemical development, while Bill Duncan developed measurements of drug levels and metabolites that supported toxicity studies and clinical investigation. Propranolol emerged from a sustained program combining physiological reasoning, chemistry and careful measurement.

sections.heading: Connecting the making of compounds with testing their effects
sections.body: Elion entered Hitchings’ laboratory after chemistry training and work that included analytical quality control. The new position offered increasing responsibility and the opportunity to cross disciplinary boundaries. She began as an organic chemist but became closely involved in microbiology and in measuring what her compounds did to biological systems. This connection between synthesis and biological testing was central to her research development. Her biography also describes later leadership in cancer research and international work on malaria chemotherapy, showing the range of disease problems to which her drug-research experience was applied.

terms.definition: Drug research guided by knowledge of biological processes or targets, with candidate compounds then tested for useful and harmful effects.
A substance that blocks a receptor’s response to an activating signal, such as adrenaline at a beta receptor.
A measurable effect of a substance on cells, organisms or a biological process, used to investigate potential drug actions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A force supporting negotiation rather than replacing it
sections.body: The Suez crisis of 1956 led to the first armed UN peacekeeping force, expanding a practice that had already included observer missions. The presentation highlighted principles associated with Dag Hammarskjöld: cooperation from the parties, UN command and an emphasis on persuasion and negotiation. Troops and unarmed observers could monitor ceasefires and help prevent renewed fighting while political discussions continued. The General Assembly established the Suez force through the Uniting for Peace process when the Security Council was blocked. The operation illustrates the relationship between an international mandate and practical conditions on the ground.

sections.heading: Making space between an armistice and a peace agreement
sections.body: The committee's announcement focused on situations where hostilities had stopped but a lasting political settlement had not yet been reached. In such circumstances, the presence of peacekeepers could reduce tensions and help negotiations begin or continue. The prize recognised personnel serving in difficult and hazardous conditions on behalf of the wider international community. The committee also expressed confidence in the UN's growing role at that moment. This was an assessment of contributions made by 1988, rather than a promise that every mission would secure agreement or prevent future violence.

terms.definition: A General Assembly procedure for considering recommendations for collective measures when Security Council action is blocked by disagreement among permanent members.
An agreement to stop fighting, which may precede a broader peace settlement; peacekeeping can support this uncertain interval.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
UN University — General Assembly practice on peace operations
UN General Assembly resolution 377 (V): Uniting for Peace

sections.heading: A large beam, heavy shielding and very few events
sections.body: The Brookhaven experiment produced energetic neutrinos from fast-moving mesons decaying in flight. Even with about one hundred trillion neutrinos, only a few dozen useful interactions were recorded. The team built a detector weighing about ten tonnes and placed roughly thirteen metres of steel shielding in front of it, using material from scrapped battleships. They also had to distinguish genuine events from cosmic-ray muons entering from outside. This combination of beam production, shielding and background rejection made neutrino interactions experimentally useful and helped establish a method later applied to many particle-physics questions.

sections.heading: Learning to make particle tracks observable
sections.body: Lederman's doctoral assignment at Columbia was to build a Wilson cloud chamber for work associated with the Nevis accelerator laboratory. He joined the project in 1948, working with Eugene Booth and learning from researchers brought into the programme by I. I. Rabi. This was an earlier stage of his experimental career, not the detector used in the later neutrino-beam discovery. The biography describes an environment in which building instruments and training researchers developed together, giving context to his subsequent work on difficult particle-detection problems.

sections.heading: Research after the neutrino-beam experiment
sections.body: Schwartz moved from Columbia to Stanford in 1966, after the neutrino work recognised by the prize. There he pursued different questions, including charge asymmetry in the decay of long-lived neutral kaons. Another project produced and detected fast-moving hydrogen-like bound systems made from a pion and a muon. These later studies should not be attributed automatically to the same collaborators as the Columbia neutrino experiment. His biography distinguishes successive research programmes and also describes a later move into work connected with computing and industry.

terms.definition: A pairing of a charged lepton with its associated neutrino, as with the muon and muon neutrino established by this research.
A detector in which charged particles leave visible condensation tracks in supersaturated vapour, making their paths observable.
An exotic bound system made from a pion and a muon, analogous in some respects to the two-particle structure of hydrogen.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: RNA challenged the assumed monopoly of protein catalysts
sections.body: The experiments showed that catalytic activity need not reside in a protein. Altman’s RNase P studies established that an RNA component could perform cleavage under suitable laboratory conditions. Cech’s work demonstrated an RNA molecule carrying out its own splicing reaction. These were different experimental routes to the same broader conclusion: RNA could participate directly in chemistry as well as carry information. The presentation connected this dual capability with hypotheses about early life. It made an RNA-centered origin more plausible, without demonstrating that the actual historical origin of life had been reconstructed.

sections.heading: Separating components revealed where activity resided
sections.body: RNase P from E. coli contained both protein and RNA. Separating those components stopped its activity, while recombining them restored it. This established that RNA was necessary, but did not yet prove it was the catalyst. Later experiments showed that the RNA component could perform cleavage on its own under appropriate conditions. The distinction between those two results is crucial: a molecule can be required as a supporting component without itself carrying out the chemical transformation. The successive experiments moved from identifying an essential component to establishing its catalytic role.

sections.heading: A change of discipline led to RNA processing
sections.body: Altman moved from physics into biophysics and molecular biology, studying DNA-related problems before joining the MRC laboratory in Cambridge. There he began work that led toward RNase P, helped by John Smith and other colleagues. Isolating a precursor to transfer RNA supplied an experimental starting point and helped him secure a Yale position in 1971. The decisive catalytic-RNA results emerged from the longer program that followed. His biography therefore describes the Cambridge period as the beginning of the investigation, rather than the location where the entire later discovery was already complete.

terms.definition: An RNA molecule with catalytic activity, such as the RNA component of RNase P studied by Altman.
Rebuilding an active system from separated components to test which parts are required and how they contribute.
An initial RNA molecule that undergoes processing before reaching its mature functional form.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Methodological foundations of modern econometrics
sections.body: Before the 1940s, limitations in data and testing methods often restricted economic research to qualitative conclusions. Haavelmo addressed challenges where theories do not fully match available data due to unaccounted determinants. He also tackled the difficulties of drawing conclusions from observational economic data, where researchers do not control all the influences as in an experiment. In his dissertation, The Probability Approach in Econometrics, he demonstrated that formulating economic theories in probabilistic terms allows mathematical statistics to derive conclusions from random empirical observations. To prevent bias occurring from isolated estimates within large models, Haavelmo proposed simultaneous estimation of the entire model structure. This research program attracted economists to the Cowles Commission in Chicago, facilitating rapid methodological development during the 1940s and establishing foundations for quantitative studies used in decision-making.

sections.heading: Haavelmo's contributions to economic theory and investment research
sections.body: Beyond his work in econometrics, Haavelmo explored diverse areas of economic theory during his tenure at the University of Oslo. In his 1954 book, A Study in the Theory of Economic Evolution, he investigated potential reasons for why certain countries experience economic underdevelopment relative to others. His 1960 publication, A Study in the Theory of Investment, introduced significant theories regarding real capital demand and the sluggishness found in real capital adjustment. Additionally, his research included an early monograph on environmental economics. As a professor and advisor at the Institute of Economics, he mentored numerous students and research recruits, many of whom began their academic writing careers by producing expositions based on his lectures.

terms.definition: Problems arising because economic variables are determined together, making estimates of a single relationship potentially misleading unless those interactions are accounted for.
The use of statistical methods to estimate economic relationships and test model predictions against observed data.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Narrative experiments under censorship
sections.body: The presentation speech traced Cela's challenges to the expectations of postwar Spanish publishing. His 1942 debut, The Family of Pascual Duarte, centres on a murderer recounting his life before execution; the speech describes its secret printing in a Burgos garage. The Hive builds a picture of early Franco-era Madrid through more than 300 characters. Spanish readers were initially denied access despite its circulation in other languages. San Camilo 1936 turns to the week before the Civil War, using an intense, visionary narrative. The speech describes another formal experiment in Oficio de Tinieblas 5, whose arrangement draws on the structure of the Mass.

sections.heading: Crowds, montage and a literary forum
sections.body: Cela often builds a collective picture rather than concentrating on fully developed individual characters. The Academy describes The Hive as a montage that captures a crowd's movement and activity. San Camilo 1936, published in 1969, combines images of violence and sexual obsession with a narrative set just before the Civil War. The announcement reads events within this small social world as a reflection of national upheaval. Cela also worked as an editor: Papeles de Son Armadans, which he published from 1956 to 1979, gave younger writers opposed to the dictatorship a place to appear. This editorial work formed another part of his role in Spanish literary life.

sections.heading: Writing across genres
sections.body: Cela's bibliography extends beyond the novels most closely associated with his reputation. It includes poetry such as Pisando la dudosa luz del día and travel writing such as Viaje a la Alcarria. Collections including Mesa revuelta gather shorter articles, while María Sabina belongs to his dramatic writing. Diccionario secreto represents a different undertaking: work concerned with words and their meanings. The range of these forms helps make the award's emphasis on a varied body of prose more concrete. His work as founder and director of Papeles de Son Armadans also placed him within the production and circulation of other writers' work.

terms.definition: Restrictions on what may be published or read; the presentation places Cela's novels in conflict with the authorities' control of expression.
Building a narrative from juxtaposed scenes and voices; in The Hive, the effect directs attention toward a crowd rather than one individual.
Writing concerned with recording words and their meanings, represented in Cela's bibliography by the two volumes of Diccionario secreto.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A cancer-associated viral gene had a normal cellular relative
sections.body: The Rous sarcoma virus contained a gene needed for tumour induction but not for viral replication. Bishop, Varmus and their collaborators developed a molecular probe to look for related genetic material. Finding it in normal cells across different species showed that the viral tumour gene had a cellular origin. The wider research then connected cancer-associated alterations with genes involved in normal growth-control systems, from signals at the cell surface to responses in the nucleus. The distinction matters: a normal growth-regulating gene is not inherently a cancer-causing version of that gene.

sections.heading: Designing a probe that could answer the origin question
sections.body: The researchers compared a version of Rous virus containing the tumour-inducing gene with a version lacking it. This difference helped them construct a nucleic-acid probe selective for the relevant genetic material. They could then search normal cellular DNA for corresponding sequences. Their 1976 publication concluded that the viral gene had originated in the host cell and had been acquired by the virus. The experiment supplied a way to connect a cancer-causing viral sequence with its normal cellular counterpart, directing attention towards changes in the cell's own growth-regulating machinery.

sections.heading: Following the altered src gene
sections.body: Bishop's account distinguishes the question of where src came from from the question of what its protein product did. Experiments performed mainly by Dominique Stehelin and Deborah Spector helped establish the gene's cellular origin. A normal cellular sequence had been acquired by the retrovirus through recombination and altered into a cancer-causing version. Bishop and Varmus later contributed to understanding the protein's biochemical function as well. The account credits a collaborative sequence of investigations, rather than presenting the origin, acquisition and action of the gene as one experiment.

terms.definition: A normal cellular gene that can contribute to cancer when altered or inappropriately activated; the viral tumour gene studied here originated from such cellular material.
A piece of genetic material used to detect a corresponding sequence; here it helped identify the cellular counterpart of a viral tumour gene.
In this context, the process by which a cellular gene is incorporated into a retroviral genome through recombination.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Peace proposals and negotiated autonomy
sections.body: The 1989 presentation examined the Dalai Lama's proposals for Tibet as attempts to create room for negotiation. His 1987 plan called for a zone of peace and included environmental protection. The committee linked concern about Himalayan forests with the effects of erosion and flooding beyond Tibet. In his 1988 address to the European Parliament, he proposed internal autonomy while accepting Chinese responsibility for foreign affairs and defence. He was also prepared to accept a Chinese military presence pending a regional peace arrangement. The speech presented these positions as evidence of willingness to compromise, while acknowledging that negotiations had not begun. They were proposals about Tibet's future, not an agreed settlement.

sections.heading: Institutions in exile and proposals for Tibet
sections.body: The Dalai Lama's education included examinations in Buddhist philosophy and monastic learning leading to the Geshe Lharampa degree. After going into exile in India in 1959, he worked to sustain Tibetan educational, cultural and religious institutions. His residence in Dharamsala began in 1960. In 1963 he promulgated a draft constitution proposing democratic government for Tibet. His Five-Point Peace Plan, presented to the Congressional Human Rights Caucus in 1987, addressed peace, population transfers, rights, the environment and negotiations. It included proposals concerning nuclear weapons and waste. In Strasbourg the following year he elaborated a proposal for democratic self-government in association with China, emphasising that Tibetans should decide the outcome of negotiations.

terms.definition: Authority over internal affairs while some powers remain elsewhere; the proposal left foreign policy and defence with China while seeking Tibetan self-government.
A doctorate in Buddhist philosophy awarded through monastic examinations, including preliminary assessments at major universities and a final examination in Lhasa.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Precise timing as an experimental tool
sections.body: The presentation connected precision spectroscopy with applications extending well beyond individual atoms. Hydrogen masers provided stable frequency references for comparing radio signals received on different continents, helping measurements of continental drift through very-long-baseline interferometry. A hydrogen maser carried by a rocket to a height of 10,000 kilometres was also compared with one on the ground to test a prediction of general relativity about time at different gravitational potentials. Trapping individual electrons and ions opened another route to precision, allowing prolonged observation and stringent tests of quantum electrodynamics. These examples show how improved measurement methods could test theories and support other fields.

sections.heading: Controlling and monitoring atomic clouds
sections.body: Dehmelt's 1955 work on phosphorus resonance developed techniques using a buffer gas. In 1956 he applied that experience to producing and monitoring a cloud of optically polarised sodium atoms. His account also describes spin-resonance experiments with electrons held in a neutralising ion cloud that diffused slowly through the gas. These were steps in learning to control particles and observe their behaviour for longer periods. The optical monitoring method found additional uses: Earl Bell and Arnold Bloom at Varian Associates used it in developing rubidium-vapour magnetometers and frequency standards, with Dehmelt acting as a consultant.

sections.heading: Focusing particles and developing new instruments
sections.body: Paul's research included mass spectrometry and isotope separation with W. Walcher, followed by experiments involving energetic electrons. He also developed methods for focusing molecular beams using quadrupole and sextupole lenses, work begun with H. Friedburg and continued with colleagues and students. His autobiography explicitly credits research students with conceiving and investigating the quadrupole mass spectrometer and ion trap. These instruments belonged to a wider programme of building equipment that made different experiments possible. The account therefore places the prize-winning trapping work within collaborative efforts in molecular beams, mass analysis and particle control.

terms.definition: An instrument using hydrogen atoms as a stable frequency reference, enabling precise comparisons of timing in experiments and other measurements.
A surrounding gas used to control particle motion and diffusion in experiments, including Dehmelt's work with atomic and ion clouds.
Controlling particle paths within a beam; Paul and colleagues developed specialised lenses that enabled new types of molecular-beam experiments.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Planning routes and inventing the reactions they required
sections.body: Corey's contribution combined strategic planning with experimental chemistry. The presentation credited his programme with around a hundred natural-product syntheses and roughly fifty new or substantially improved reactions by the time of the award. Some routes depended on organometallic reagents; others used catalysts that strongly favoured one mirror-image form of a product. These methods supplied practical tools for carrying out plans that would otherwise remain on paper. The award therefore recognised connected achievements in theory, reaction development and the laboratory construction of complicated molecules.

sections.heading: A plan that could be expressed as a sequence of choices
sections.body: Retrosynthetic reasoning made synthesis planning sufficiently explicit to explore with computer programs. A target structure could be analysed through successive simplifications until the proposed starting compounds were known or available. Chemists then had to judge whether the corresponding forward reactions were practical. The press release connected this approach with syntheses of complex natural products, including the plant hormone gibberellic acid and biologically active eicosanoids. Computer-assisted planning supported the comparison of possible routes; the chemical transformations still had to be achieved experimentally.

sections.heading: Connecting electronic structure with three-dimensional reactions
sections.body: Corey's early research applied molecular-orbital ideas to the three-dimensional arrangements involved in chemical reactions. He investigated transition states and the relation between electronic effects and stereochemistry. As his group expanded, he began more demanding projects on the structures and synthesis of natural products, later extending into metal complexes, selective synthesis and enzyme chemistry. His biography presents this breadth as deliberate: theoretical reasoning, molecular shape and biological chemistry were treated as connected parts of the same discipline. That background helps explain the combination of strategic analysis and practical reaction development in his later work.

terms.definition: Synthesis designed to favour one mirror-image form of a chiral product, a capability developed in several of Corey's catalytic methods.
Reasoning backwards from a target structure to simpler possible precursors; the imagined disconnections guide a subsequent forward synthesis rather than physically breaking up the target.
A description of electrons in orbitals extending over a molecule, used by Corey to analyse bonding and the geometry of chemical reactions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Different levels of financial decision-making
sections.body: The presentation connected three distinct problems. Markowitz formalised portfolio choice as a trade-off between expected return and variance, with efficient portfolios found through quadratic optimisation. Sharpe's model linked expected return to exposure to market-wide risk, expressed through beta. Miller's corporate-finance work, initially with Modigliani, examined why financing and dividend choices would not alter firm value under specified idealised conditions. These results provided benchmarks for investigating how taxes and other departures from the models' assumptions matter. They did not remove uncertainty or guarantee the performance of an investment.

sections.heading: Why the relationships between investments matter
sections.body: Markowitz's account describes the step from valuing an individual security to choosing a portfolio. Expected return alone could not explain why investors diversify, so he considered variance as a measure of risk. Portfolio variance depends on how returns move together as well as on each security's separate variability. This led to the analysis of efficient combinations of risk and expected return. His later computational work drew on optimisation methods learned from George Dantzig at RAND, helping make the calculation of such combinations more practical.

sections.heading: From company financing to financial-market institutions
sections.body: Miller's collaboration with Modigliani began at Carnegie, producing their first joint corporate-finance paper in 1958 and further work into the mid-1960s. At Chicago, he continued investigating company financing before expanding his interests towards the institutions through which securities are traded. His biography describes research on economic and regulatory problems facing financial services and exchanges. It also records his involvement with the Chicago trading exchanges, including an academic examination of the 1987 crash. These later activities show the widening application of his interests beyond the original financing theorems.

terms.definition: A model linking an asset's expected return to its exposure to market risk under stated assumptions; beta measures that exposure.
A measure of how two returns vary together, used in calculating the risk of a portfolio rather than treating its investments independently.
The study of companies' financing decisions, including borrowing, equity and distributions to shareholders.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Time and intimacy in the poetic imagination
sections.body: The presentation read Paz's poetry through encounters between thought and sensory experience. In Sun Stone, different times and identities seem to converge in an intense present. It connected this imagery with surrealism, but also emphasised intimacy and love as ways the poems imagine overcoming separation. A Tree Within offered another example of that recurring concern. These are claims about the poems' imaginative movement: the experience of time is transformed through language, memory and relationship. The speech treated this joining of intellectual reflection with bodily experience as central to Paz's voice.

sections.heading: Language and the meeting of cultural traditions
sections.body: The award announcement connected Paz's writing with pre-Columbian traditions, Spanish history, Western modernism and experiences in India. It examined how his poetry changes the associations and meanings of words, making language itself part of the subject. Sun Stone's 584-line cycle links poetic form with the cycle of Venus, while The Labyrinth of Solitude investigates Mexican identity through essays. His study of Sor Juana examines a writer within the religious and cultural conditions of her time. The range joins poetry with sustained historical and cultural inquiry.

sections.heading: Journals, travel and a public intellectual life
sections.body: Paz helped found Taller after returning from the anti-fascist writers' congress in Spain. Later diplomatic postings brought him into contact with surrealists in France and with cultural and intellectual life in India. In 1968 he resigned from the diplomatic service in protest at the government's violent suppression of student demonstrations in Mexico. He subsequently founded Plural and Vuelta, journals concerned with literature, art and politics. The biography places his books alongside these editorial and public activities, showing several ways in which he participated in debate across national boundaries.

terms.definition: A recurring poetic idea in which different times or identities appear to meet in an intensified present, discussed in the presentation's reading of Paz.
An artistic movement drawing on dreamlike associations and unexpected connections, an important influence on Paz's handling of language and perception.
A periodical publishing writing and criticism; Paz used journals such as Taller, Plural and Vuelta as forums for artistic and intellectual exchange.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Sunstone — publisher’s account of the poem’s structure

sections.heading: Overcoming different immune barriers to transplantation
sections.body: Murray’s successful kidney transplant between identical twins avoided the usual genetic incompatibility. Extending transplantation to other donors required approaches such as irradiation and, later, immunosuppressive drugs including azathioprine. Thomas faced an additional problem in marrow transplantation: donor immune cells could attack the recipient. His work combined donor matching, preparation of the patient and treatments such as methotrexate to reduce this reaction. Marrow cells introduced into the bloodstream could then establish blood formation. These advances addressed distinct barriers and developed over time; they were not a single procedure that made every transplant successful.

sections.heading: Burn care raised a fundamental question about rejection
sections.body: At Valley Forge General Hospital during the war, Murray treated severely burned patients who lacked enough uninjured skin for grafts from their own bodies. Skin from other people could provide temporary coverage but was eventually rejected. The contrast made him ask how the body distinguished its own tissue from a donor’s. His colleague James Barrett Brown had documented lasting skin-graft survival between identical twins and considered how genetic relationship affected acceptance. These observations connected an immediate surgical problem with the immunological questions that later shaped organ transplantation.

sections.heading: Showing that donor marrow cells could restore blood formation
sections.body: Early animal studies found that marrow infusion could protect against otherwise lethal irradiation. Researchers initially considered whether a soluble stimulating factor explained the effect. Experiments showing donor-cell chromosomes in recipients, together with acceptance of skin from the marrow donor, supported a different explanation: living donor cells survived and rebuilt the blood-forming system. Thomas’s clinical program drew on this evidence, studies of immune compatibility and irradiation, and a specialized care team. It eventually demonstrated successful treatment for some patients with leukemia, aplastic anemia and inherited disorders, while confronting substantial risks and technical difficulties.

terms.definition: An immune reaction in which transplanted donor immune cells attack tissues of the recipient; it can cause serious or fatal disease.
Skin transplanted between genetically different individuals of the same species, as distinct from an autograft taken from the patient’s own body.
The degree of compatibility between donor and recipient tissue characteristics relevant to immune recognition and transplant outcomes.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: An award made during an unfinished transformation
sections.body: The presentation described the Soviet Union's reforms as a difficult process still under way. Greater democracy, economic change and increased autonomy for the republics were presented as aims and expectations, not as fully achieved conditions. The committee connected Gorbachev's openness and willingness to compromise with new opportunities for arms agreements and East–West cooperation. It also acknowledged severe economic, social and political problems. The award was intended partly as encouragement during that uncertainty, making the speech a record of hopes in 1990 rather than a settled judgement on everything that followed.

sections.heading: Recognising a change in international relations
sections.body: The 1990 announcement emphasised negotiation replacing confrontation, movement towards arms control and greater freedom in parts of Europe. It credited Gorbachev with important contributions while explicitly acknowledging that the changes had several causes. The committee also hoped that improved relations would allow more effective international cooperation through the United Nations and across ideological divisions. These statements explain the award's focus on a developing peace process. They should be understood in their historical setting, rather than as a claim that all regional conflicts or disagreements between states had been resolved.

sections.heading: A reformer emerging from the party hierarchy
sections.body: Gorbachev's career began within the Soviet Communist Party and its youth organisation. He held regional responsibilities in Stavropol, later joined the Central Committee and became a full Politburo member in 1980. His election as party general secretary followed in March 1985. The biography then records events after the Nobel award, including the failed coup in August 1991 and his resignation as Soviet president that December. It also notes his subsequent role in a social, economic and political research foundation. These later entries are distinct from the leadership record considered in 1990.

terms.definition: The policy of greater openness associated with Gorbachev's reforms, which the committee connected with increased international confidence.
Negotiated measures limiting or regulating weapons, distinguished from broader political changes and from the complete elimination of armaments.
The Communist Party's senior political leadership body in the Soviet system, which Gorbachev joined before becoming general secretary.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Evidence for constituents inside the proton
sections.body: High-energy electron scattering at SLAC produced results inconsistent with treating the proton simply as a smooth, extended object. The electrons behaved as though they were encountering compact constituents. Interpretation by theorists, including Bjorken and Feynman, connected this evidence with the quark picture. The presentation also noted indications of electrically neutral constituents, which became part of the broader description involving gluons. The measurements were scattering patterns requiring theoretical interpretation, rather than photographs of individual quarks or a direct visual record of the forces holding them together.

sections.heading: Measuring energy and direction after a collision
sections.body: The SLAC–MIT programme used magnetic spectrometers to measure electrons after they struck targets containing protons or neutrons. Recording both the outgoing energies and scattering angles allowed researchers to compare different conditions and infer how momentum was distributed within the target. The results supported a description of nucleons in terms of quarks. This was more informative than merely observing that collisions occurred: the pattern of outcomes across energies and angles constrained possible models of the internal structure. Subsequent understanding placed quarks and gluons within that picture.

sections.heading: Correcting the spectra before interpreting them
sections.body: Friedman developed experience with electron scattering while working in Hofstadter's group at Stanford.
