Earlier studies of deuterons required calculations to account for radiative effects in the measured spectra. Henry Kendall independently developed a related technique, and they later combined their work in a correction program for the SLAC experiments. These corrections mattered because the measured electron energies include effects beyond the simplest collision picture. The biography describes the ensuing MIT–SLAC programme from 1967 into the mid-1970s as a collaborative investigation across a newly accessible energy range.

terms.definition: Scattering at large energy and momentum transfer that probes a particle's internal structure while leaving the target changed or broken into other particles.
An instrument using magnetic deflection to analyse charged particles, used in these experiments to measure scattered electrons.
Calculations accounting for radiation-related effects that alter measured scattering spectra, needed when comparing experimental results with an underlying interaction model.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Extracting more information from weak magnetic signals
sections.body: Pulse experiments excite a range of nuclear responses, and Fourier analysis separates the recorded time signal into its frequency components. This greatly improved the usefulness of weak NMR signals, including those from less abundant isotopes such as carbon-13 and nitrogen-15. Multidimensional experiments then spread information across additional frequency axes. Carefully chosen pulse sequences can reveal connections through bonds, proximity in space or chemical exchange. The gain is both sensitivity and interpretability: a congested spectrum can be separated into relationships that help identify a molecule’s structure.

sections.heading: Instrument building and theory developed together
sections.body: Ernst’s early work with Hans Primas combined calculations of experimental performance with construction of improved NMR instruments. Primas worked on field modulation, frequency locking and magnet design, while Ernst developed sensitive radio-frequency preamplifiers and probe assemblies. Improving the ratio of useful signal to background noise was a recurring concern. Ernst also investigated excitation by random signals as a way to study nuclear responses. These efforts show the practical foundation beneath the later methods: stable fields, sensitive electronics and an understanding of how the instrument transforms molecular behavior into a measurable signal.

terms.definition: A mathematical operation converting a signal described over time into its frequency components, central to interpreting pulse NMR measurements.
The strength of the information-bearing measurement compared with unwanted fluctuations that make it difficult to detect or interpret.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The role of transaction costs in institutional structure
sections.body: In his essay The Nature of the Firm, Coase addressed why economic activity occurs within administrative structures rather than through simple market contracts. He proposed that firms emerge when the resources required to manage activities internally are lower than those needed for market purchases and sales. This theory relies on the concept of transaction costs, which include the time and work necessary to enter agreements and manage institutions. Coase further demonstrated that economic transactions involve rights to dispose of resources rather than just physical goods. In a thought experiment with clearly assigned rights and zero transaction costs, parties could trade those rights to achieve the highest output regardless of their initial assignment. Real transaction costs are not zero, so legal and institutional arrangements matter.

sections.heading: Development of transaction costs and law and economics
sections.body: Coase developed the concept of transaction costs and explained firm existence by the summer of 1932. His 1937 article, The Nature of the Firm, served as a basis for his Nobel Prize. During his time at the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences, he studied the Federal Communications Commission to examine United States broadcasting regulation and radio frequency spectrum allocation. He proposed that a pricing system awarding use to the highest bidder would be preferable. Later, as editor of the Journal of Law and Economics from 1964 to 1982, he promoted research into how markets operate and how governments regulate economic activities. This editorial work helped establish the new academic subject known as law and economics.

terms.definition: The time, work, and other resources used to enter into contracts and manage firms or similar economic institutions.
The application of economic reasoning to legal rights, rules and institutions, including their effects on markets and people’s decisions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Political history through individual lives
sections.body: The presentation speech explains Gordimer's achievement through the relationship between character and historical setting. In its reading, her fiction makes racial segregation visible through particular people's lives rather than through a programme of political argument. Novels such as A Guest of Honour, Burger's Daughter and July's People place choices and relationships under the pressure of public events. The speech also emphasises her short stories, including the collections Six Feet of the Country, A Soldier's Embrace and Something Out There. It identifies precision of language and close characterisation across both forms, connecting the political setting with the distinct experiences of individuals.

sections.heading: A reversal of dependence in July's People
sections.body: In July's People, a white family escapes armed rebellion with help from July, their servant, and takes shelter in his village. Their growing dependence on him reverses the familiar relationship between employer and employee. The Academy draws attention to the title's two meanings: July's people can be the family he serves or his own community. The novel also examines how the upheaval changes language and family relationships; the children adapt more readily than the adults. These fictional events explore the fragility of established privilege. Gordimer's later My Son's Story uses two narrative perspectives to examine love and political responsibility within an oppressive society.

sections.heading: Fiction, nonfiction and a continuing career
sections.body: Gordimer worked across novels, short stories and nonfiction. Her biography lists A Sport of Nature alongside novels such as The Conservationist and Burger's Daughter. Jump belongs to her short-story writing, while The Essential Gesture, On the Mines and The Black Interpreters are identified as nonfiction. The page also includes material added after the Nobel award. A 2005 update records later fiction including The Pickup and Get a Life, as well as the story collection Loot. These later books show the continuation of her career; they were not works available to the Academy when it made the 1991 decision.

terms.definition: The depiction of individual people in fiction; the presentation argues that Gordimer makes historical pressures perceptible through their particular lives.
Presenting a story through two viewpoints, allowing Gordimer to reveal different aspects of characters and relationships in My Son's Story.
Writing presented outside the invented narratives of novels and stories; Gordimer's biography groups The Essential Gesture and The Black Interpreters here.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Recording the current through one channel
sections.body: Neher and Sakmann used a fluid-filled glass pipette with a tip only a few micrometres wide. Close contact between glass and cell membrane isolated a small patch electrically, allowing extremely small currents through its channels to be measured. An open channel conducts ions; when it closes, that contribution to the current stops. The resulting steps reveal individual channel openings and closings, with currents around a trillionth of an ampere. Combining such recordings with changes to channel molecules allowed researchers to investigate which parts influenced ion selection or responses to chemical signals.

sections.heading: Electrical signals and vesicle secretion
sections.body: Different ion concentrations inside and outside a cell contribute to a voltage across its membrane. Opening ion channels changes the electrical current and can rapidly change that voltage, as happens during nerve signalling. Channel proteins discriminate among ions through their molecular structure. Neher also extended electrical recording to secretion: when a vesicle fuses with the cell membrane, it adds membrane area and changes the cell's electrical properties. Sensitive measurements could detect individual fusion events. Introducing substances through a pipette then helped researchers examine steps controlling secretion from within the cell.

sections.heading: Development of single channel recording techniques
sections.body: While working at the Max-Planck-Institut für Psychiatrie, Neher investigated voltage-clamping snail neurones. To address space-clamp issues, Dieter Lux suggested utilizing suction pipettes for measuring local current density. Neher later joined a physical chemistry laboratory in Göttingen to gain experience with single channel recording in artificial membranes. Collaborating with Bert Sakmann, who brought expertise regarding the neuromuscular junction, they published their initial single channel records in 1976. Supported by Young Investigator Laboratories, they refined these recording configurations alongside several postdoctoral fellows.

terms.definition: A protein pore in a cell membrane that allows particular ions to pass when it is open.
The electrical voltage difference between the inside and outside of a cell, influenced by ion distributions and the membrane's permeability.
Fine glass tubes using suction to contact a small membrane region, enabling local electrical measurements.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Political proposals and the formation of the NLD
sections.body: Returning to Burma in 1988 to care for her mother, Aung San Suu Kyi entered a period of mass protest and military repression. Her open letter proposed independent advisers to prepare multiparty elections and called for political prisoners' release and restraint from violence. She then addressed a large gathering at Rangoon's Shwedagon Pagoda. The military established the State Law and Order Restoration Council in September and imposed martial law. Soon afterwards, she and other opposition figures formed the National League for Democracy. The 1991 presentation highlighted her subsequent campaigning across ethnic divisions despite bans on public meetings.

sections.heading: The committee's reasoning in 1991
sections.body: The announcement credited Aung San Suu Kyi with leading nonviolent opposition to military rule and promoting reconciliation among divided regions and ethnic groups. Her involvement in the 1988 democracy movement was described as a renewed struggle for freedom, rather than a new campaign to end colonial rule. The committee cited the opposition's decisive victory in the May 1990 election and the regime's refusal to accept the result. Its award supported peaceful demands for democracy and human rights while she remained under house arrest. These were the circumstances and judgments underlying the 1991 prize.

sections.heading: Civil disobedience and international pressure
sections.body: As NLD general secretary, Suu Kyi adopted nonviolence and civil disobedience. During late 1988 she toured the country speaking to large crowds despite restrictions on gatherings of more than four people. The Nobel chronology also records later efforts to exert pressure from outside Burma: she discouraged foreign tourism and business investment while military rule continued. In 1992, after receiving the Nobel award, she announced that its money would establish a health and education trust for Burmese people. These details describe different stages of her activism, not a single initiative undertaken before the prize.

terms.definition: A group asked to advise on public decisions; Suu Kyi proposed independent members to help prepare multiparty elections.
Pursuing political change through protest, persuasion and other methods that do not use physical violence.
Deliberately breaching a law or official restriction as a form of nonviolent political protest, illustrated here by meetings held despite military bans.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mathematical models for liquid crystals and polymers
sections.body: De Gennes identified connections between seemingly unrelated physics fields by generalizing descriptions of order. He applied mathematical models from magnetic and superconducting materials to understand nematic phases, where molecules align similarly to atoms in a ferromagnet. In polymer physics, he demonstrated that the size of a molecule in solution increases by a specific power of its monomer count, mirroring behavior near a magnet's critical temperature. These findings enabled the formulation of scaling laws, allowing researchers to deduce unknown properties through simple relations between different material characteristics.

sections.heading: Mathematical descriptions of complex order phenomena
sections.body: De Gennes used mathematical frameworks to connect ordering in magnetic systems, liquid crystals and polymers. He found deeper similarities between polymer configurations and magnetic behaviour near phase transitions than had previously been recognised. His work also addressed superconductivity, the stability of microemulsions and the motion of polymer chains. Collaborators developed these descriptions for concentrated solutions, where chains become entangled, and for polymer melts. His 1979 book Scaling Concepts in Polymer Physics presented this approach. It helped show how a complicated material could have useful general relationships despite the many details of its molecular structure.

sections.heading: Research developments in polymers and interfacial dynamics
sections.body: As a participant in the STRASACOL joint action involving Strasbourg, Saclay, and Collège de France, de Gennes investigated polymer physics. His scientific focus expanded from studying superconductors in Orsay to exploring liquid crystals starting in 1968. Later research interests included interfacial problems, specifically the dynamics of wetting. He also examined the physical chemistry of adhesion and cellular adhesion. During his tenure as director of the Ecole de Physique et Chimie, he oversaw a center dedicated to training research engineers in physics, chemistry, and biology.

terms.definition: Relations describing how one physical quantity changes with another, often through a power law, allowing behaviour across different sizes or conditions to be compared.
A change between distinct states of matter or collective organisation, brought about by changing conditions such as temperature.
A joint scientific action involving the institutions of Strasbourg, Saclay, and the Collège de France focused on polymer physics.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mathematical modeling of electron transfer energy barriers
sections.body: Willard Libby suggested applying the Franck–Condon principle to electron transfer: the electron moves too quickly for surrounding nuclei to follow it during the transition. Marcus examined the unexpectedly slow exchange between iron ions with different charges in water. Water molecules around the ions must first rearrange into a configuration compatible with transfer, requiring energy. His 1956 model calculated this barrier using quantities including ionic charges and radii. Later extensions produced a quadratic relationship and a cross-relation that could be tested for transfers between different reactants. The framework connected experiments in biological, inorganic, organic and photochemical systems. Its surprising prediction concerned strongly favourable reactions: beyond a particular driving force, making transfer still more favourable could increase the barrier and slow it. In 1965 Marcus proposed chemiluminescent reactions as possible examples; subsequent experiments established the inverted behaviour more widely.

sections.heading: Development of RRKM theory and reaction rate studies
sections.body: During his early career, Marcus conducted experimental research on gas phase and solution reaction rates, including the kinetics of nitration at McGill. In 1951, he published a specific case of what B. Seymour Rabinovitch later named RRKM theory. This work integrated statistical concepts from 1920s RRK theory with mid-1930s transition state theory. Following this, Marcus wrote a generalization for other reactions in 1952. His theoretical approach was heavily influenced by his experimental background at the National Research Council and Brooklyn Polytechnic. While studying electrostatics in 1954 and 1955, he prepared to address electron transfer problems. Later, while at the University of Illinois, he explored reaction dynamics through natural collision coordinates and action-angle variables.

terms.definition: The regime in which increasing an electron-transfer reaction’s driving force raises its activation barrier and reduces its rate.
A theoretical framework blending statistical ideas from RRK theory with transition state theory to describe unimolecular reaction rates.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The household as a production unit
sections.body: Becker treated a household as producing services for its members using time alongside purchased goods. This changes the meaning of a cost: childcare performed at home uses time that could instead earn wages. In his model, rising market wages therefore increase the opportunity cost of time-intensive household production. Families may shift some activities to businesses, schools or childcare providers and increase paid work. The framework also connects the cost of parents’ time with choices about family size and investment in children’s education. These are modelled responses to incentives, not predictions that every household makes the same choices. The contribution was to include unpaid household activity within an explicit analysis of production and resource allocation.

sections.heading: Studying education and training as investments
sections.body: Becker helped formalise human-capital theory, which examined how acquiring skills and knowledge relates to earnings. His 1964 book Human Capital developed work first presented in earlier articles. The framework connected education and workplace training with returns, wage differences and earnings patterns over a working life. The award announcement explicitly noted that the concept predated Becker; his contribution was to develop its microeconomic foundations and applications. Other economists extended the approach to migration, health and economic growth. Growing availability of individual records, including observations following people over time, made its predictions easier to investigate empirically. This links a theoretical account of investment decisions with evidence about unequal earnings.

sections.heading: Expanding economic theory into social and family structures
sections.body: Becker’s dissertation research examined how prejudice affected minority earnings, employment and occupations. At Columbia, he introduced a doctoral research workshop based on an existing Chicago model; Jacob Mincer later became its co-director. His research subsequently encompassed marriage, divorce, parents’ investment in children and concern for other family members. Articles from the 1970s developed into A Treatise on the Family in 1981, followed by an expanded edition in 1991. He also investigated how changes in family composition could affect inequality and growth. Research by Becker, colleagues and students was discussed in the Chicago workshop he ran with Sherwin Rosen. The account shows both the breadth of his questions and the collaborative setting in which they developed.

terms.definition: Creation of services for household members by combining their time with purchased goods and other inputs.
Skills, knowledge and capabilities developed through investments such as education and training that can affect productive capacity and earnings.
Concern for other people’s welfare, including family members, which can be incorporated into a model of individual choices.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary synthesis of European and Caribbean traditions
sections.body: The Nobel presentation describes Walcott’s poetry as bringing European literary traditions into conversation with Caribbean language and experience. Omeros gives the fisherman Achille, the taxi driver Hector and the housemaid Helen names that recall Greek epic while placing their lives in a contemporary island world. The speech treats these echoes as part of a wider pattern throughout Walcott’s writing. The sea joins distant histories to present experience: in The Sea Is History, biblical memories of captivity resonate with slavery’s Caribbean legacy. Historical scale and immediate sensory detail coexist. The committee’s account therefore emphasises a reshaping of inherited literature through a particular place, rather than a simple transplantation of a classical story.

sections.heading: Development of Caribbean drama and poetic collections
sections.body: Walcott's literary progression included his debut with 25 Poems at age eighteen, followed by the significant collection In a Green Night in 1962. To foster an indigenous drama, he established the Trinidad Theatre Workshop in 1959, which served as a venue for producing many of his early plays. His academic background involved studying at St. Mary’s College in Saint Lucia and the University of the West Indies in Jamaica. While working as an art and theatre critic in Trinidad after 1953, he integrated various cultural elements into his writing. His creative approach reflected a society shaped by African, Asiatic, and European influences, rooted in his experiences on the volcanic island of Saint Lucia.

terms.definition: An extended poetic narrative connecting individual lives and actions with a wider community, history or cultural world.
An organization founded by Walcott in 1959 to produce early plays and develop an indigenous Caribbean drama.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of cellular regulation through protein phosphorylation
sections.body: During the 1950s, researchers demonstrated how muscles release energy-rich sugars from storage by phosphorylating a protein. This process involves coupling small phosphate groups to proteins to alter their properties. Such regulation can occur in successive steps, creating a cascade that amplifies effects similarly to hydraulic braking. While Krebs and collaborators studied preceding proteins in these chains, Fischer focused on different areas, including purifying a specific type of phosphate-removing protein. These reversible modifications allow cells to respond to various signals, such as stress hormones or voluntary actions.

sections.heading: Enzymatic regulation of glycogen phosphorylase
sections.body: Studies of muscle glycogen phosphorylase in the mid-1950s revealed a reversible way to change enzyme activity. A protein kinase transfers a phosphate group from ATP to phosphorylase, converting it to a more active form under the conditions studied. A phosphatase removes the group and reverses that modification. These opposing enzymes regulate the breakdown of glycogen, the stored carbohydrate that can supply fuel for muscle activity. The discovery showed how a cell could rapidly change the behaviour of a protein it already possessed by adding or removing a small chemical group.

sections.heading: A question about AMP led to a different discovery
sections.body: Fischer began collaborating with Krebs after moving to Seattle. Krebs brought experience with muscle phosphorylase from the Coris' laboratory; Fischer had previously purified potato phosphorylase in Geneva. AMP was thought to serve as a cofactor for the muscle enzyme, yet the potato enzyme did not require it. This contrast prompted their investigation. They did not initially resolve AMP's role, which Fischer's biography connects to later allosteric explanations. Instead, their experiments revealed a different regulatory mechanism: phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of muscle phosphorylase. Fischer recalled the close collaboration, with experiments planned together and either researcher able to continue the other's work.

terms.definition: A series of successive chemical reactions where phosphate groups are coupled to proteins, creating an amplified end effect within cells.
An enzyme that catalyzes the attachment of a phosphate group to a protein, altering its biological properties and activity.
An explanation of regulation in which binding at one location on a protein changes its behaviour at another location.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Founding of the Revolutionary Christians and UN involvement
sections.body: The Nobel speech described Menchú’s participation in founding the Revolutionary Christians and her understanding of revolutionary change as transformation. It presented her preference for political advocacy over taking up arms as important to future reconciliation. Exile in Mexico also allowed her to bring Indigenous rights into international forums, including the United Nations. The committee connected these activities with a difficult ethical question: how to resist brutal oppression without abandoning the possibility of later coexistence. Its account emphasised keeping communication and recognition of other people’s humanity possible, even during conflict. This was the committee’s explanation of the peaceful approach it sought to honour.

sections.heading: Advocacy for Indigenous Rights and Ethno-cultural Reconciliation
sections.body: The 1992 announcement situated Menchú’s advocacy against a history of inequality and repression affecting Guatemala’s Indigenous peoples. It stressed the particularly severe violence of the 1970s and 1980s and the persecution experienced by her family. The committee’s focus was on social justice combined with respect across ethnic and cultural divisions. It understood peace as a long-term objective of her political work, rather than simply an absence of open fighting. The recognition also gave international visibility to Indigenous rights beyond Guatemala. These were the grounds on which the committee presented her as a symbol of reconciliation, not a claim that the country’s conflict had already been settled.

sections.heading: Advocacy through organized resistance and international storytelling
sections.body: Menchú’s Nobel biography describes activism with the CUC, a Guatemalan peasant organisation, including work around farm labour and resistance to military repression. After fleeing to Mexico in 1981, she helped organise opposition abroad and participated in establishing the RUOG coalition in 1982. Her account, recorded by Elisabeth Burgos Debray and published as I, Rigoberta Menchú, became an influential form of international testimony. She also narrated the documentary When the Mountains Tremble about Maya experiences. These activities combined organising with communication to audiences outside Guatemala. Describing the book as testimony identifies the form through which her account circulated, rather than treating every autobiographical claim as independently established by the award.

terms.definition: Pursuit of political or social change through argument, organisation and other methods that avoid the use of physical violence.
A process of fostering peace and social justice by promoting respect between different ethnic groups and their respective cultural identities.
A Guatemalan peasant organisation in which Menchú participated in labour activism and the struggle for Indigenous rights.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Requirements for advanced particle detectors
sections.body: Particle experiments need detectors that respond quickly, identify where a particle passed and send their signals directly to computers. Large arrangements of detectors must cover extensive surfaces and reconstruct trajectories extending over metres. They must also work inside strong magnetic fields. Charpak's multiwire proportional chamber met these practical demands and became the basis of several forms of tracking detector. The 1992 presentation described its widespread use in particle physics and growing applications in medicine. The advance combined sensitive position measurements with a form of electronic recording suited to processing many collisions.

sections.heading: Advancements in particle detection speed and resolution
sections.body: Charpak used modern electronics to connect his detector directly to a computer, replacing photographic recording followed by laborious picture analysis. The Nobel announcement reported a thousandfold increase in data collection speed over earlier track-recording methods, often with better position measurements. Several chambers placed at different distances could reconstruct a particle's trajectory. Such rapid recording helped researchers identify extremely rare interactions among enormous numbers of collisions. Multiwire proportional chambers were used in the 1974 discovery associated with the charm quark and in the 1983 discovery of the intermediate bosons at CERN. These are examples of how an instrument can enable discoveries beyond its inventor's own experiments.

sections.heading: From particle tracking to biological imaging
sections.body: Charpak's research extended across several detector technologies. His biography lists nonphotographic scintillation chambers developed during 1961–1967, followed by the introduction of multiwire proportional chambers in 1968. In 1974, spherical drift chambers were introduced at Orsay for studying proteins by X-ray diffraction. Later work included multistage avalanche chambers and photon counters for imaging ionising radiation. He also participated in Fermilab experiments during 1985–1991. The biography records instruments for biological research using beta-ray imaging in Geneva, showing how techniques for registering particles could also support the study of biological material.

terms.definition: A gas-filled detector containing parallel wires that collect and amplify signals produced when charged particles ionise the gas.
A device featuring a central wire and high voltage that generates an electric signal through gas ionization and electron avalanches.
Radiation capable of removing electrons from atoms, producing charged particles that a detector can register.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Chemical manipulation of DNA outside living cells
sections.body: PCR made it possible to amplify a selected DNA segment in a test tube through repeated copying cycles. Under ideal doubling conditions, twenty cycles can produce over a million copies from one starting target. This greatly expanded the uses of small DNA samples. The 1993 presentation highlighted research, infection testing and forensic analysis among its applications. Smith's site-directed mutagenesis addressed a different problem: making a chosen change at a specified position in a gene. Producing the resulting altered protein lets researchers test questions about folding, catalytic activity and interactions with other molecules. The two methods therefore support both obtaining genetic material and investigating the consequences of changing it.

sections.heading: Development of PCR and synthetic chemical linkers
sections.body: Mullis recalls conceiving PCR while working at Cetus, where he made oligonucleotides. The idea came during a drive to a cabin in northern California. His autobiography connects the discovery with the expanding biotechnology industry and his practical work in synthetic DNA chemistry. A separate project appears in a 2005 addendum: Altermune aimed to redirect immune responses using synthetic chemical linkers. Mullis described work involving chemists, immunologists and infectious-disease researchers, reporting experiments in rodents while expressing hope for eventual human use. This later research was distinct from the PCR invention recognised by the Nobel Prize.

sections.heading: Chemical synthesis of nucleoside phosphates and protecting groups
sections.body: In Vancouver, Michael Smith worked under Gobind Khorana to develop efficient procedures for synthesising nucleoside-5′ triphosphates. This research involved investigating carbodiimide reactions with acids, including phosphoric acid esters. He also established a method for preparing nucleoside-3′,5′ cyclic phosphates. During this period, he developed methoxyl-trityl protecting groups for nucleoside-5′-hydroxyl groups. In his Nobel autobiography, Smith noted that this family of protecting groups remained in use in automated synthesis of DNA and RNA fragments. These earlier projects developed the chemical tools and experience that preceded his work on changing gene sequences.

terms.definition: A general method for producing mutations at specific, predetermined positions within a gene rather than through random processes.
Short chains of nucleotides, the building blocks of DNA or RNA; synthetic DNA oligonucleotides can serve as primers in PCR.
Temporary chemical groups that protect a nucleoside's 5′ hydroxyl from unwanted reaction during a sequence of synthetic steps.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Methodologies for analyzing economic and institutional change
sections.body: Researchers utilized counterfactual analyses and social cost-benefit analysis to evaluate historical developments. Fogel demonstrated that railways were not an essential prerequisite for growth, prompting more restrained views on the impact of major innovations. He also examined how demographic factors and nutritional standards relate to mortality rates. North investigated how organizational changes increased transoceanic shipping productivity and studied how the English Industrial Revolution benefited from weak guilds and small state regulation. His work highlights how institutional stability or lack thereof influences economic dynamism.

sections.heading: Methods and models in new economic history
sections.body: Researchers in this field utilize cliometrics to explain economic growth or decline by integrating economic theory with quantitative methods and hypothesis testing. This approach involves constructing or reconstructing databases to reassess earlier results and eliminate irrelevant theories. North developed an explanatory model for American growth before 1860, using an export base model to show how cotton plantations stimulated interregional trade. Additionally, his research on ocean shipping productivity demonstrated that organizational changes were more significant than technical changes, while his work on Western Europe highlighted how property rights influence economic incentives.

sections.heading: Quantitative methods in economic history research
sections.body: Fogel sought to investigate how specific technologies, including steel mills and railroads, influenced nineteenth-century economic growth. To address these questions, he mastered advanced statistical and analytical techniques to move beyond traditional historical approaches. This methodology allowed for the identification of necessary evidence categories and the development of suitable measurement techniques. By applying mathematical models, researchers could assess result robustness and examine the factory system's role in institutional change through measurable analytical issues.

terms.definition: The written and unwritten rules and usages that influence human activity, affecting the costs of production and consumption.
A branch of economic history that combines economic theory, quantitative methods, and hypothesis testing to explain economic growth and decline.
Numerical observations and measurements used to investigate a historical claim; statistical methods help researchers analyse this evidence.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literature, race and the search for identity
sections.body: The Academy's presentation connected Morrison's fiction with the argument of her essays in Playing in the Dark. She examined how Black presence shapes American literature even when it remains unacknowledged, and how literary ideas of whiteness depend on a racial other. In Song of Solomon, Milkman Dead's search for himself leads through family history and the songs of children's games. The speech highlighted a family name assigned through an official's misunderstanding and accepted as a way to erase the past. Recovering ancestry therefore becomes part of the novel's exploration of identity. These examples show how Morrison joins close attention to language with questions about whose histories become visible.

sections.heading: Improvisation, folklore and narrative form
sections.body: In Jazz, the opening gives the outline of a story that the narrator subsequently changes, elaborates and intensifies. The Academy compared this movement to musical performance: readers encounter events through a developing voice rather than a single fixed account. In Beloved, realistic detail and folklore work together. The announcement emphasised Sethe's terrible response to the future she imagined for her child, and the consequences for her own life. These examples illustrate why the committee admired variation between Morrison's novels, as well as their coherence. Her formal choices shape how readers approach characters and difficult histories.

sections.heading: Teaching, editing and literary recognition
sections.body: Morrison studied humanities at Howard and Cornell before an academic career that included Texas Southern, Howard and Yale. She took a chair at Princeton in 1989. Alongside teaching, she edited books for Random House, wrote criticism and lectured publicly on African-American literature. Her 1970 debut began a career in fiction that attracted both reviewers and a wider readership. By the Nobel award, her honours included election to the American Academy of Arts and Letters in 1981 and a Pulitzer Prize in 1988. The Nobel biography particularly praised her dialogue and the poetic energy of her portrayals of Black American life.

terms.definition: A group represented as different from a dominant identity; Morrison examined how such representations help construct literary whiteness.
Storytelling that develops through variation and elaboration, compared by the Academy to jazz performance in its discussion of Morrison's novel.
Literature by African-American writers, including the novels, essays and criticism that Morrison wrote and studied.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Interrupted genes and the processing of RNA
sections.body: The 1977 adenovirus studies showed that sequences retained in a mature RNA message could correspond to separated regions of DNA. This required RNA processing: intervening sequences are removed and retained segments joined. The finding also suggested ways gene segments could be rearranged in DNA over evolutionary time, generating new combinations. That evolutionary rearrangement is distinct from the splicing of an RNA copy during ordinary gene expression. The ceremony also linked splicing to disease. Some inherited defects causing thalassemia disrupt RNA processing, producing faulty messages and inadequate functional protein. This is one mechanism of thalassemia, not a description of every form.

sections.heading: Making the interrupted structure visible
sections.body: Roberts's group found that late adenovirus-2 messages shared a short beginning whose DNA source was distant from the main part of the message. Richard Gelinas had helped investigate the RNA ends. To test the proposed split arrangement, the team paired intact RNA with selected DNA fragments and examined the hybrids by electron microscopy. Louise Chow and Tom Broker supplied crucial expertise in visualising the structures. The experiment made the relationship between separated DNA regions and a continuous RNA message visible. It grew out of the laboratory's earlier DNA mapping and extensive work discovering and characterising restriction enzymes.

sections.heading: Mapping viral genes before the split-gene discovery
sections.body: At Cold Spring Harbor, Sharp studied adenovirus gene expression with collaborators including Ulf Pettersson and S. Jane Flint. Restriction enzymes cut the roughly 35,000-base-pair viral genome into fragments that could be mapped and analysed. Comparing RNA from infected and experimentally transformed cells helped identify which DNA regions were expressed. Work during this period linked the E1 region with oncogenic transformation in experimental systems. The laboratory also investigated how differences in restriction patterns could support genetic mapping. These tools made the viral genome manageable enough to relate particular regions to their messages and functions.

terms.definition: A gene whose RNA transcript contains retained exons separated by introns that are removed during splicing.
A DNA virus used as an experimental model for gene organisation and RNA production, including the split-gene studies.
Enzymes that cut DNA at particular recognition sequences, producing fragments useful for mapping and studying genes.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Negotiating institutions for a democratic transition
sections.body: The 1993 presentation pointed to concrete changes since Mandela's 1990 release: negotiations over a provisional constitution, a broadly representative Transitional Executive Council and agreement on democratic elections for 27 April 1994. The committee regarded reconciliation and compromise as essential to replacing institutionalised racial oppression. It also stressed that the process remained unfinished. Some groups had stayed outside the talks or withdrawn, and violence and fear continued. The award therefore recognised a negotiated route toward democracy while supporting a transition whose electoral test still lay ahead.

sections.heading: De Klerk's change of political direction
sections.body: De Klerk's earlier ministerial career included support for segregated universities; he had not been known as a reformer while leading the National Party in Transvaal. After becoming party leader in February 1989, he called for negotiations and a nonracist South Africa. He became State President that September. On 2 February 1990 he announced the lifting of bans on opposition organisations and Mandela's release. These steps opened negotiations toward equal voting rights and constitutional protections. His role in that transition followed participation in the apartheid government, a contrast acknowledged by the Nobel biography itself.

sections.heading: Mandela's trials, imprisonment and ANC leadership
sections.body: Mandela was acquitted in 1961 after the treason trial that had begun in 1956. That case was distinct from the later proceedings that brought his life sentence. After the ANC's banning in 1960, he advocated armed resistance, helping establish Umkhonto we Sizwe. He was arrested in 1962, received a five-year sentence, and subsequently stood trial with other leaders accused of planning violent overthrow. In June 1964 he was sentenced to life imprisonment. His imprisonment included Robben Island and Pollsmoor. Released in February 1990, he became ANC president at its 1991 conference inside South Africa.

terms.definition: Rebuilding relations after conflict or oppression through acknowledgement, dialogue and negotiated accommodation; the committee stressed the compromises required in South Africa.
The South African party that governed under apartheid and was led by de Klerk during negotiations to dismantle that system.
The armed organisation associated with the ANC, formed after its banning as Mandela and others turned to violent resistance against apartheid.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A pulsar clock reveals an orbiting companion
sections.body: PSR 1913+16 emitted radio pulses about 59 milliseconds apart. Hulse and Taylor found that this interval varied periodically: motion toward Earth shortened the observed spacing, while motion away lengthened it. The Doppler pattern revealed an unseen companion and allowed the orbit to be studied. This particular pulsar rotates roughly seventeen times per second; the speech's discussion of much faster rotation concerned pulsars generally. Continued timing then showed a different, gradual change: the orbital period itself was shrinking. That long-term energy loss matched the prediction for gravitational-wave emission, providing indirect evidence through the behaviour of the binary system.

sections.heading: Early scientific development and computational training
sections.body: During his time at Cooper Union, Hulse utilized an IBM 1620 to teach himself FORTRAN programming. He applied this skill to perform orbit simulations, a task that preceded his physics degree in 1970. His interest in radio astronomy began with home projects, such as constructing an amateur radio telescope using television parts and military surplus power supplies. After completing his Ph.D. at the University of Massachusetts in Amherst in 1975, he held a post-doctoral appointment at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory.

sections.heading: Radio electronics and the analysis of astronomical signals
sections.body: Taylor learned radio electronics through childhood projects using surplus equipment and discarded television parts. Later, a senior honours project at Haverford allowed him to build a working radio telescope. He described it as training in problem solving rather than an original research discovery. At Harvard, his doctoral work in radio astronomy developed those skills further under Alan Maxwell. Ron Bracewell's book The Fourier Transform and its Applications supplied insights needed to analyse his thesis data, and helped prepare him for signal-processing methods subsequently important in pulsar studies.

terms.definition: A change in an observed signal's frequency caused by relative motion between its source and the observer.
A programming language developed for numerical and scientific computation; Hulse learned it through orbital simulations.
An instrument that collects radio waves from astronomical sources so their signals can be measured and studied.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Examining carbonium ions and their reactions
sections.body: Olah combined exceptionally strong acids with solvents that did not immediately react with the resulting carbocations. At low temperatures, ions could persist in sufficient concentrations for spectroscopic investigation. This distinguished three-coordinate carbenium ions from carbonium ions with five-coordinate carbon, challenging the assumption that carbon could connect to no more than four surrounding atoms. Superacids could even protonate saturated hydrocarbons, allowing the resulting ions and their further reactions to be examined. The 1994 presentation described practical consequences: rearranging straight-chain alkanes into branched products with higher octane ratings, and using methane to build larger hydrocarbons. It also discussed superacid-catalysed breakdown of heavy oils and conversion of coal under comparatively mild conditions. These were applications of understanding reactive intermediates, rather than simply observations of unusual ions.

sections.heading: Activating already electron-deficient reagents
sections.body: Olah extended his superacid research by asking whether an already electron-deficient reagent could be made much more reactive. Acyl cations, halonium ions and other electrophiles could interact further with strong Brønsted or Lewis acids. He called the resulting enhancement superelectrophilic activation. His account distinguished the highly reactive species responsible for a reaction from more stable intermediates that chemists might actually isolate or observe. It also cautioned that activation need not produce a distinct ion carrying two positive charges: association or solvation by the acidic medium could provide the necessary assistance. This qualification matters when interpreting a proposed reaction mechanism. In separate later work, Olah promoted methanol as an energy carrier and chemical feedstock, including production from carbon dioxide and hydrogen. He acknowledged that producing the required hydrogen would itself demand substantial energy.

terms.definition: A class of carbocations that includes ions with five-coordinate carbon, extending beyond the three-coordinate arrangement of carbenium ions.
Enhancement of an electrophile’s reactivity through further interaction with a strong acid; a separately observable doubly charged intermediate is not always formed.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Analyzing Strategic Interactions and Information Asymmetry
sections.body: Strategic interaction arises when one participant’s outcome depends on others’ actions, as with competing firms. A Nash equilibrium rules out a profitable unilateral change while everyone else keeps their strategy unchanged. It need not give a good collective outcome: individually rational choices can leave participants worse off than other possible arrangements. Harsanyi’s three articles from the 1960s extended analysis to situations with incomplete information. Selten’s refinements addressed a further difficulty: a game may have several Nash equilibria, including ones supported by threats or promises that would not be credible when a decision actually arose. These refinements helped analysts distinguish among equilibrium predictions.

sections.heading: Harsanyi's mathematical contributions to game theory
sections.body: After studying mathematics and statistics at Stanford under Ken Arrow, Harsanyi applied these tools to expand strategic analysis. He demonstrated the mathematical equivalence between Zeuthen’s and Nash’s bargaining models in 1956. Later, he extended the Shapley value to games lacking transferable utility. His significant work included a three-part series published between 1967 and 1968, which transformed games of incomplete information into those with complete yet imperfect information. Additionally, he showed that most mixed-strategy Nash equilibria can be reinterpreted as pure-strategy strict equilibria using randomly fluctuating payoff functions.

sections.heading: Nash's academic transition and early research developments
sections.body: At Carnegie, Nash changed from chemical engineering to chemistry and then mathematics. His difficulty with laboratory tasks belonged to the second transition, alongside encouragement from mathematics faculty. An international-economics elective prompted the idea behind The Bargaining Problem. At Princeton, that interest led him toward game theory, where von Neumann and Morgenstern’s work was influential. Nash also obtained results about manifolds and real algebraic varieties. He recalled keeping those results as a possible alternative dissertation topic if his game-theory ideas were rejected. The non-cooperative-games work was accepted for his mathematics doctorate; he wrote up Real Algebraic Manifolds later while teaching at MIT.

terms.definition: A method for studying situations where participating parties are unable to enter into binding agreements regarding their strategic choices.
A situation in which a player lacks knowledge of some feature of the game, such as another player’s preferences or payoffs.
The problem of analysing a negotiated agreement among participants whose interests and possible outcomes differ.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Narrative structures and recurring themes in Oe's literature
sections.body: The Nobel presentation follows recurring situations across Ōe’s fiction: conflicts between brothers, the return of earlier rebellions, the birth of a child with a disability and the threat of nuclear catastrophe. In The Silent Cry, ancestral history enters the lives of characters in the present. The speech connects these recurrences with responsibility, human dignity and questions shaped partly by Ōe’s reading of Sartre. A Personal Matter and M/T and the Tale of the Wonders of the Forest contribute to a larger network in which books answer and reshape one another. First-person narration can create an autobiographical impression while remaining a constructed fiction. The committee presents this use of recurring narrative patterns as a way to approach realities that resist straightforward description.

sections.heading: Literary influences and thematic developments in Oe's writing
sections.body: Ōe’s early fiction, including the Akutagawa Prize-winning The Catch, explored rural life disrupted by war. His later work drew on French literature and philosophy while investigating histories and cultures outside a Tokyo-centred perspective, including Okinawa. His biography links those interests with his reading of Mikhail Bakhtin and the joining of village myths to modern experience in The Silent Cry. Cultural anthropology supplied further ideas, including matriarchal and trickster patterns used in Contemporary Games. Another strand connected family experience with public responsibility: Hiroshima Notes recorded encounters with atomic-bomb survivors and their thoughts. These strands sometimes meet, bringing the imagined forest village, contemporary politics and the difficulties of living with others into the same literary world.

terms.definition: An image, situation or theme that returns across a work or several works, acquiring new meanings through repetition and variation.
The study of human cultures and social practices; Ōe drew on its ideas when constructing myths and relationships in his fiction.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The three-step process of transmembrane signal transduction
sections.body: Rodbell's model separated a signalling system into three functional parts. A discriminator, or receptor, recognises the incoming chemical message. A transducer connects that recognition to an amplifier that produces an internal response. Rodbell showed the importance of guanine nucleotides to this coupling step. Gilman and colleagues then used genetic and biochemical approaches to isolate G proteins and investigate how they operate as timed switches. Different combinations of receptors, G proteins and downstream components allow cells to respond differently to signals. The same broad principle helps explain signalling in sensory systems, including vision and smell.

sections.heading: Pharmacological research and academic influences
sections.body: Alfred Gilman's scientific path was shaped by his father’s work in physiological chemistry at Yale Medical School. His father co-authored the influential textbook The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics with Louis S. Goodman. During his training, Gilman explored thyroid gland research and later utilized the Pharmacology Research Associate Training Program from the National Institute of General Medical Sciences. His laboratory environment benefited from advancements like ligand binding assays for receptors and the development of S49 cells by Gordon Tomkins and associates.

sections.heading: From isolated fat cells to membrane signalling
sections.body: Rodbell used a collagenase preparation to digest the matrix around fat cells, freeing intact cells that could be separated by flotation. Their response to insulin showed that they remained metabolically active. He also found that phospholipases could mimic insulin's effects on glucose use and protein synthesis, providing indirect evidence for action at the cell surface. He subsequently prepared fat-cell ghosts by removing much of the fat while preserving structural and metabolic features. Work with Torben Clausen on hormone effects in these preparations showed that a hormone could influence different transport processes through separate routes.

terms.definition: A component that converts or relays a signal; in Rodbell's model, the G-protein switch couples receptor recognition to an internal amplifier.
A major pharmacology textbook created through a collaboration between Louis S. Goodman and Alfred Gilman's father.
Preparations made by removing fat from fat cells while retaining components used to investigate membrane-related and metabolic processes.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The significance of the Oslo Accords
sections.body: The Nobel speech emphasised the mutual recognition associated with the 1993 Oslo process as a change in relations between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization. Its significance was an opening for negotiation between former adversaries. Arafat, Peres and Rabin were credited with following the talks closely and taking difficult decisions about concessions. The committee described trust as a political risk: each side needed reason to believe the other’s offer of negotiation was serious. It also saw connections between the Israeli–Palestinian process and relations with neighbouring Arab states. These were opportunities identified in 1994, not a completed resolution of the disputes left for further negotiation.

sections.heading: An award intended to encourage continued negotiation
sections.body: The 1994 announcement honoured political decisions that enabled the Oslo agreements and efforts to follow them up. It connected those decisions with Alfred Nobel’s aim of encouraging fraternity between nations. The committee acknowledged the suffering caused by decades of conflict and praised the courage required to pursue cooperation across the divide. Recognition also had a prospective purpose: the announcement explicitly hoped to encourage Israelis and Palestinians working toward lasting peace. The prize therefore expressed both a judgement about steps already taken and support for further work. That distinction helps explain why the award was made during a continuing process, while major questions remained unresolved.

sections.heading: Evolution of the Palestine Liberation Organization
sections.body: Arafat helped build Fatah in the late 1950s as a clandestine movement promoting armed struggle. After the 1967 war, it became the leading group within the Palestine Liberation Organization, whose executive committee he chaired from 1969. He developed a more independent Palestinian nationalist organisation with its own armed forces. Conflict with Jordan’s government led to the PLO’s expulsion; later, an Israeli invasion forced its leadership out of Lebanon. Headquarters moved to Tunis. In 1988, Arafat publicly renounced terrorism as part of a shift toward diplomacy. This history supplies context for the later decision to negotiate with Israel, rather than portraying his political career as an uninterrupted peaceful initiative.

terms.definition: The Israeli–PLO agreements establishing a framework for interim self-government and further negotiations toward a lasting settlement.
Cooperation and peaceful relations among peoples, an aim cited from Alfred Nobel’s will in the committee’s explanation of the award.
The Palestinian nationalist movement co-founded by Arafat that became the leading faction within the Palestine Liberation Organization.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Neutron scattering applications in condensed matter research
sections.body: Reactors made intense neutron beams available for research after the Second World War. Shull used neutron scattering to locate atoms, including hydrogen in ice, and investigate magnetic structures. Brockhouse developed instruments that measured energy gained or lost by neutrons as they interacted with matter. Those energy changes revealed atomic vibrations in crystals, diffusion in liquids and fluctuations in magnetic materials. By 1994, these methods were being used to investigate ceramic superconductors, catalytic surfaces, polymers and interactions between proteins and viral genetic material. The range of applications arose from two complementary questions: how matter is arranged and how its constituents move.

sections.heading: Development of neutron scattering techniques for condensed matter
sections.body: Neutron scattering provides different information through changes in direction and changes in energy. Scattering patterns can reveal the arrangement of atoms; changes in neutron energy reveal movements within the material. Shull's work included locating hydrogen atoms in ice and organic compounds. Brockhouse's triple-axis spectrometer selected an incoming neutron energy, directed the beam at a sample, then analysed the scattered neutrons with another crystal. Measuring the energy transferred to or from the sample made it possible to investigate collective atomic vibrations. This explains why structural measurements and studies of motion require related but distinct observations.

sections.heading: Advancements in neutron spectroscopy and spectrometer development
sections.body: Brockhouse's early experiments with Myer Bloom and D. G. Hurst investigated neutron scattering by cadmium, samarium and gadolinium, testing the Breit–Wigner formula. A modified apparatus later measured inelastic scattering in aluminium, graphite and diamond. Instrument development continued along several paths. Quartz single-crystal filters improved the proportion of slow neutrons in the beam, making useful signals easier to distinguish from background. A beryllium-filter method provided another way to measure energy distributions. Brockhouse also converted an instrument into a rotating-crystal spectrometer for liquids and polycrystalline materials; an improved successor operated at the NRU reactor.

terms.definition: Matter in solid or liquid states, whose properties depend on the arrangements and interactions of its many constituent particles.
An instrument with independently rotatable components for selecting an incident neutron beam, orienting a sample and analysing the energy of scattered neutrons.
The strength of the useful measured signal relative to unwanted counts or other background contributions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Atmospheric chemical processes and ozone depletion
sections.body: Ozone's effects depend on where it occurs. In the stratosphere it shields life from ultraviolet radiation; near the ground it is a harmful component of photochemical smog. The laureates investigated how atmospheric reactions change its abundance. The 1995 presentation linked nitrogen oxides with combustion, distinguishing high-altitude aircraft emissions from pollution released near the ground. It also highlighted CFC emissions from refrigeration, air conditioning and aerosol propellants. Chemicals once valued for their practical usefulness could have consequences far from their point of release. These findings supplied evidence for environmental controls, including the Montreal Protocol's restrictions on ozone-depleting substances.

sections.heading: Crutzen's transition to stratospheric chemistry research
sections.body: At Stockholm's meteorological institute, Crutzen was initially offered a research project on numerical modelling of a tropical cyclone. Around 1965, a different assignment asked him to help model the distribution of forms of oxygen in the upper atmosphere. That work stimulated his interest in ozone photochemistry and led to an intensive study of the literature. He chose stratospheric chemistry instead of the proposed cyclone project. The institute also studied clouds, the carbon cycle and acid rain, but Crutzen recalled selecting ozone out of interest in natural processes, without anticipating the environmental importance the subject would acquire.

sections.heading: Researching CFCs and polar stratospheric cloud chemistry
sections.body: After joining Rowland's group at Irvine, Molina investigated what could eventually remove chemically unreactive CFCs from the atmosphere. This led to their ozone-depletion hypothesis. A later research phase followed the 1985 discovery of seasonal Antarctic ozone loss. At JPL, Molina's group reproduced reactions associated with polar stratospheric clouds, some of which contain ice crystals. They showed that ice could promote chlorine-activation reactions under polar conditions. The group also investigated chlorine peroxide, helping explain the rapid gas-phase reactions that destroy ozone. These laboratory studies connected the earlier CFC hypothesis with the distinct chemistry responsible for severe polar depletion.

terms.definition: An international agreement controlling ozone-depleting substances, including CFCs, to protect the stratospheric ozone layer.
A mathematical representation evaluated through numerical calculations to investigate how a system behaves under specified conditions.
Reactions that convert chlorine from relatively unreactive reservoir forms into forms that can participate in ozone destruction.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Why a policy change can alter a statistical relationship
sections.body: Lucas analysed how inflation expectations affect the relationship between inflation and employment. In his models, a policy that predictably raises inflation cannot maintain an employment gain by repeatedly surprising people. This challenged attempts to treat a historical Phillips curve as a permanent menu of policy choices. His critique also applied to estimated relationships involving consumption, investment, wages, interest rates and taxes. If a new policy changes expectations and decisions, the old relationship may no longer provide a reliable forecast. Lucas proposed theoretical and statistical approaches that explicitly account for those behavioural responses.

sections.heading: Two collaborations behind Lucas's economic models
sections.body: At Carnegie Tech, Lucas studied dynamical systems and optimisation over time while investigating firms' investment decisions. With Leonard Rapping, he developed a neoclassical account of US wages and employment from 1929 to 1958. A separate collaboration with Edward Prescott produced Investment under Uncertainty, which reformulated John Muth's rational-expectations idea. Lucas's biography describes learning general-equilibrium theory, functional analysis and probability through this work. Edmund Phelps also encouraged Lucas to place the labour-supply model developed with Rapping within a general-equilibrium setting. These exchanges helped connect individual decisions with the behaviour of the wider economy.

sections.heading: Treating policy as a rule people can anticipate
sections.body: Lucas extended rational expectations from single-market analysis to general-equilibrium models. He treated policy as systematic behaviour with both predictable and unpredictable components. A central bank's recurring response to inflation and unemployment could therefore enter people's expectations. He also developed methods for solving the resulting models, making their implications operational. In one model discussed by the prize committee, a shift towards persistently higher inflation did not raise average employment once expectations adjusted. That was a conditional model result. The broader research programme sought to estimate behavioural parameters that would remain useful when comparing different policy rules.

terms.definition: The warning that historical statistical relationships may change when policy changes people's expectations and behaviour.
A modelling assumption that expectations use available information consistently with the model, while still allowing uncertainty and prediction errors.
A systematic pattern linking policy actions to economic conditions, which people may learn about and incorporate into their expectations.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Bogland, memory and the individual
sections.body: The Academy's presentation treated Heaney's bogland as a landscape of identity and historical memory, alongside the potato's association with the Great Hunger. His poem about Tollund Man, whose Iron Age body survived in a Danish peat bog, brings ancient sacrifice into contact with silenced human voices. The speech also stressed his attention to individual victims of the Troubles rather than political slogans. The Redress of Poetry collected his Oxford lectures; his essays and poems drew on Celtic, Catholic and pre-Christian inheritances. Describing poetry as soil to be turned over, or creativity as a natural process, expressed a critical metaphor for his writing.

sections.heading: Poetic form and ethical responsibility
sections.body: Heaney's essays in The Government of the Tongue and The Place of Writing considered what poets owe to their art and their society. The experience of writers such as Osip Mandelstam informed his concern for preserving beauty under tyranny. His translation of Sophocles' Philoctetes, The Cure at Troy, was staged by Field Day Theatre in 1990. The Academy connected it with his continuing exploration of difficult ethical questions. In the Squarings sequence of Seeing Things, twelve-line poems place varied images within a restrained form. Lightenings viii draws on a miracle story associated with Clonmacnoise, bringing legendary material into contact with everyday experience.

sections.heading: Languages and changes in poetic style
sections.body: Heaney studied Latin and Irish at school and Anglo-Saxon at Queen's University Belfast. His early poems often used strongly stressed, densely packed lines. Later collections drew more visibly on Mediterranean literary traditions: Dante influenced Station Island, while Seeing Things included echoes of Virgil and a translation from Book VI of the Aeneid. His engagement with Irish produced Sweeney Astray, a translation of the Middle Irish story Suibhne Gealt. His 1970–71 visiting lectureship at Berkeley also encouraged a change in working life. After returning, he left Queen's and moved to County Wicklow to concentrate on poetry and freelance writing.

terms.definition: Peat-bog landscape used in Heaney's poetry to connect Irish identity with traces of the past.
Reserve or reluctance to speak openly, which Heaney valued but also saw as a possible obstacle to writing and confronting injustice.
A grouping of Northern Irish writers associated with Heaney, including Michael Longley, Derek Mahon and a younger generation, despite differences in style.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Patterning segments and assigning their identities
sections.body: Nüsslein-Volhard and Wieschaus screened fruit-fly mutations for defects in the larval body plan. Their fifteen key genes fell into groups acting at different scales: broad regions along the body, alternating segments and finer structures within individual segments. The screen revealed a hierarchy of patterning processes. Lewis studied a distinct question: how segments acquire their identities. He found that the order of certain developmental genes along DNA corresponds to the order of the body regions they affect. The two lines of research therefore connected formation of a segmented pattern with the specification of what each region should become.

sections.heading: Academic career and professional recognitions of Edward B. Lewis
sections.body: After earning his Ph.D. from the California Institute of Technology in 1942, Edward B. Lewis served as a meteorologist and oceanographer for the United States Army Air Force. He later joined the Caltech faculty, eventually becoming the Thomas Hunt Morgan Professor of Biology. His international academic engagements included roles as a Rockefeller Foundation Fellow at Cambridge University and a Guest Professor at the University of Copenhagen. Throughout his career, he received numerous honors, including the National Medal of Science and the Albert Lasker Basic Medical Research Award.

sections.heading: Making embryo screens practical
sections.body: Collecting eggs and inspecting their patterns had been slow and difficult. With Jeanette Holden and David Ish Horowicz, Nüsslein-Volhard developed an egg-collection block system and ways to compare material from many fly lines. With Jitse van der Meer, she devised fixation and clearing methods that made the larval cuticle's structure easier to score. These improvements supported systematic searches for developmental mutants. Her earlier plan also proposed injection experiments to look for activities missing from mutant embryos. Restoration of development could point to a missing activity, which would still need further work to identify its molecular source.

terms.definition: The fruit-fly species used in these experiments, with a short life cycle and genetic tools suited to studying development.
A research position held by Lewis at Cambridge University in England between 1947 and 1948.
An experiment testing whether an intervention restores a mutant's normal feature, providing evidence about an activity lost or impaired in the mutant.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Scientific expertise and responsibility
sections.body: Rotblat combined concern about nuclear weapons with research on radiation biology and medical applications. He signed the Russell–Einstein Manifesto in 1955 and became a leading organiser of Pugwash. The 1995 presentation described its conferences as a way for scientists to communicate across political divisions and offer expertise to decision-makers. It judged that Pugwash probably contributed to negotiations leading to the 1963 test-ban treaty, the 1968 non-proliferation treaty and arms agreements in 1972. That was a supporting, often private role rather than sole authorship of those agreements. The committee also stressed scientists' responsibility to examine possible consequences before new discoveries were put to use.

sections.heading: Scientific responsibility and disarmament efforts
sections.body: The Pugwash Conferences operate on the principle that scientists bear responsibility for their inventions. This organization facilitates collaboration between researchers and decision-makers to develop constructive proposals aimed at reducing nuclear threats. By bringing participants together across political divides, the group works toward the destruction of all nuclear arms. Their activities include addressing the catastrophic consequences of using new weapons and seeking alternatives to war for resolving international disputes. At the July 1995 conference in Hiroshima, participants judged that opportunities existed to move closer to these goals.

sections.heading: Scientific Contributions and Nuclear Education Initiatives
sections.body: Beyond his peace advocacy, Rotblat led significant technical developments in nuclear physics. He chaired the UK Nuclear Physics Committee's Photographic Emulsion Panel, which produced sensitive emulsions used to discover pi-mesons. Additionally, he supervised building cyclotrons for Liverpool and Harwell through the committee's Cyclotron Panel. To educate the public on both military and peaceful uses of nuclear energy, he organized the Atom Train Exhibition, a large-scale tour across Britain, Europe, and the Middle East. He also co-founded the Atomic Scientists Association.

terms.definition: Scientists' social and moral obligation to consider the consequences of their work and help address harms arising from scientific discoveries.
An organization where scientists and decision-makers collaborate across political divides to propose reducing nuclear threats and achieving disarmament.
A large-scale educational effort touring Britain, Europe, and the Middle East regarding nuclear energy applications.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Discoveries in two particle families
sections.body: The Standard Model organises quarks and leptons into three generations. Familiar ordinary matter mainly uses the lightest members, while accelerators can produce heavier relatives. Reines and Cowan detected electron antineutrinos using a nuclear reactor, making an exceptionally weakly interacting particle experimentally accessible. Perl's team later found evidence for the tau, a charged lepton thousands of times heavier than the electron. The tau was the first discovered member of the third generation. The two halves of the award therefore recognised distinct steps in building the particle picture: detecting an elusive member of the lightest family and revealing a heavier repeated family.

sections.heading: Experimental training and doctoral research methods
sections.body: During his doctoral studies at Columbia University under advisor I.I. Rabi, Perl utilized the atomic beam resonance method. This specific technique allowed him to measure the quadrupole moment of the sodium nucleus by employing an excited atomic state. Although he lacked extensive physics coursework upon entering the program in 1950, his research focused on these precise measurements. His experimental preparation also involved drawing apparatus designs, a task he performed despite lacking natural craftsmanship or proficiency in college drafting classes.

sections.heading: Neutrino detection methods and experimental developments
sections.body: To observe the electron antineutrino, Reines and Cowan transitioned from considering nuclear bomb tests to utilizing the Hanford reactor in Washington. They later moved operations to the Savannah River facility in South Carolina, which provided ideal conditions for their 1956 observation. Reines also conducted research in a South African gold mine to identify atmospheric neutrinos produced by cosmic rays. His experimental programs further investigated nucleon decay and studied fundamental symmetry principles, such as the conservation of lepton number and baryon number.
