terms.definition: A generation of quarks and leptons following a repeated pattern in the Standard Model, with corresponding particles differing greatly in mass.
An atomic state with more energy than the lowest-energy state; Perl's sodium-nucleus measurement required such a state.
Neutrinos produced through cosmic-ray interactions in Earth's atmosphere, which Reines's underground programme investigated.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental discovery and verification of fullerene structures
sections.body: The original experiment vaporised a small amount of carbon with a short laser pulse. As the vapour cooled, clusters with different numbers of atoms formed, with a particularly strong signal from sixty-atom clusters. Their abundance suggested unusual stability, but the tiny quantities did not permit rigorous structural determination. In 1990, work by Donald Huffman, Wolfgang Krätschmer and their collaborators made much larger samples available through an inexpensive, reproducible preparation method. Researchers could then apply complementary structural measurements to test the proposed cage. The family extended beyond C60: the presentation also described other closed carbon clusters and cages containing a metal atom inside.

sections.heading: Researching microwave spectra and stable free radicals
sections.body: Curl’s postdoctoral work at Harvard with E. Bright Wilson introduced him to microwave measurements of barriers to internal molecular rotation. After moving to Rice in 1958, he inherited George Bird’s instrument and graduate students. With Jim Kinsey he studied the microwave spectrum of chlorine dioxide, including its fine and hyperfine structure; this helped launch further investigations of stable free radicals. His biography emphasised the collaborative nature of his research. In the fullerene work, he credited graduate students James Heath and Sean O’Brien as equal participants in the scientific discussions who also performed most of the experiments, alongside contributions from other colleagues.

sections.heading: Testing the cage with separated samples
sections.body: Kroto hoped that a C60 sample would give a single carbon-13 NMR signal, because all sixty carbon atoms in the proposed cage occupy equivalent environments. The 1990 bulk-production breakthrough made such tests practical. At Sussex, Jonathan Hare extracted fullerenes from soot; Roger Taylor, with Jim Hanson’s help, developed chromatography to separate C60 from C70. Tony Avent detected the expected single signal for C60 and five signals for C70. Kroto’s account credits these measurements and separation methods as decisive additional evidence. It also records a correction: one preliminary C70 assignment had been confused with a nearby benzene signal before the final paper was published.

terms.definition: Carbon molecules whose connected atoms form a closed cage, including the sixty-atom buckminsterfullerene molecule.
A pattern of molecular responses to microwave radiation that provides evidence about molecular structure and motion.
A method for separating components of a mixture, used here to obtain distinct C60 and C70 samples for structural measurements.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms for managing information imbalances in markets
sections.body: In a sealed-bid auction, bidding strategy can conceal how much participants are willing to pay. Vickrey analysed a rule under which the highest bidder wins but pays the next-highest bid. Under the model’s assumptions, reporting one’s own value is in the bidder’s interest. His auction research influenced the design of mechanisms for government securities, air-traffic rights and radio spectrum. Vickrey also formulated an income-tax problem in which the government cannot observe individuals’ productivity and must account for their responses to taxation. Mirrlees later developed a tractable analysis of that problem. Related work investigated contracts that align an agent’s incentives with a principal’s objectives despite unequal information.

sections.heading: Designing mechanisms for information asymmetry
sections.body: Economic research addresses situations where decision-makers possess different information. William Vickrey studied auction properties to generate economic efficiency and analyzed the New York subway fare system for efficient public service pricing. He also formulated a mid-1940s model regarding income taxation, balancing efficiency with individual work incentives. James Mirrlees later provided a thorough solution to optimal income tax problems. Additionally, Mirrlees and Peter Diamond analyzed consumption tax structures, demonstrating that maintaining full production efficiency is worthwhile under general conditions despite social inefficiencies caused by tax wedges.

sections.heading: Development of optimal income tax theory
sections.body: Mirrlees began work on nonlinear incentive relationships during a sabbatical at MIT between his Cambridge and Oxford appointments. An initial version of his income-tax paper circulated before its mathematical justification was complete. His biography describes the additional work needed to finish that argument. Collaboration with Peter Diamond on optimal taxation was central to this development and influenced his sole-authored papers too. With Ian Little, he also worked on a manual of cost–benefit analysis. These projects connected mathematical questions about incentives with decisions about taxation and public investment. The income-tax research became part of a broader analysis of relationships between a principal designing an arrangement and an agent responding to it.

terms.definition: A condition where one party in an economic transaction possesses more knowledge than the other, potentially allowing for strategic exploitation.
An incentive problem in which one party’s actions affect outcomes but cannot be fully observed or controlled by another party.
Analysis of how a tax schedule can balance distributional objectives with the effects of taxation on people’s choices and work incentives.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Reconsidering language after ideological certainty
sections.body: The Nobel presentation places Szymborska among Polish poets whose careful attention to language challenged the damage done by ideological slogans. It describes precision in words as a responsibility, not merely a decorative accomplishment. Reading her poems, the speaker finds a movement away from collapsed certainties toward everyday experiences, tenderness, fear and humour. Allegro ma non troppo becomes an example of carefully shaped thought that admits uncertainty about how to describe life. The speech’s idea of beginning again through negation is a critical interpretation: questioning a ready-made answer makes room for a fresh comparison. It does not identify a literal process by which poetry purifies an entire society.

sections.heading: Evolution of Szymborska's Poetic Style and Themes
sections.body: The announcement distinguishes Szymborska’s later poetry from the ideologically conforming collections of 1952 and 1954 that she subsequently disowned. It highlights The Joy of Writing and On Death, without Exaggeration as examples of poetry confronting mortality through the power of representation. Restraint makes her irony sharper: apparently modest or naive questions unsettle assumptions about civilisation and human superiority. The English selection View with a Grain of Sand, translated by Stanisław Barańczak and Clare Cavanagh, appeared in 1995 and gathered one hundred poems. Its range allowed readers to follow changes from Calling Out to Yeti to The End and the Beginning. The committee emphasised technical precision alongside inventiveness and empathy.

sections.heading: Literary career and published collections
sections.body: Szymborska studied Polish literature and sociology at the Jagiellonian University from 1945 to 1948. Her first published poem appeared in a daily newspaper in March 1945. From 1953 to 1981 she worked as a poetry editor and columnist for the Kraków weekly Zycie Literackie. Her reading essays, Lektury nadobowiazkowe, later appeared in book form. The 1996 biography listed sixteen poetry volumes, including selected collections as well as books such as Sól and Koniec i poczatek. She also translated French poetry. These activities place the individual poems alongside sustained editorial work, literary commentary and translation, rather than treating the bibliography as sixteen entirely new collections.

terms.definition: Denial or refusal of an existing claim; in this reading of the poetry, a way to reopen questions rather than accept inherited answers.
A discrepancy between what words appear to say and what they imply, which can expose assumptions without stating an argument directly.
A series of essays written by the author that appeared in a Kraków literary weekly and was later published as books.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Why matching cell markers matter
sections.body: At the John Curtin School of Medical Research, Doherty and Zinkernagel compared immune responses in different mouse strains. Killer T cells could attack infected targets from another strain only when the relevant transplantation-antigen variant matched. This connected two areas previously considered separately: recognition of infected cells and the compatibility of transplanted tissues. Subsequent research established how these molecules bind and display fragments that T cells can recognise. Differences in the molecules help explain differences between individuals' immune responses. The experiment's significance was the combination of viral material and an appropriate self marker, rather than viral infection alone, in recognition by these T cells.

sections.heading: Early research influences and academic development
sections.body: Doherty's veterinary training exposed him to ecology, parasitology, population genetics and infectious disease. Books by F. M. Burnet and R. M. Stanley helped develop his interest in viruses; his final-year thesis concerned ultraviolet-induced eye cancer in Hereford cattle. At the Moredun Research Institute, he studied louping-ill virus while enrolling part-time at the University of Edinburgh medical school. In sheep experiments with H. W. Reid, the collaborators divided the work: Reid handled virology and serology, while Doherty examined disease-related tissue changes using light microscopy and ultrastructural methods. This background brought veterinary infection research and the study of tissue injury into his later immunology.

sections.heading: A shared laboratory and complementary experiments
sections.body: Zinkernagel and Doherty shared laboratory space at the John Curtin School of Medical Research in Canberra. They began collaborating on immune responses to lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus. Doherty collected cerebrospinal fluid and investigated inflammation and tissue injury in the brain; Zinkernagel performed assays measuring the killing of target cells. He had learned such techniques in Lausanne, although an earlier attempt to apply chromium labelling to bacteria had proved inconclusive. His later work on how the thymus influences T-cell recognition took place at Scripps in California. The biography distinguishes this subsequent research from the Canberra experiments that established MHC restriction.

terms.definition: Cell-surface molecules, including major histocompatibility complex proteins, whose variants affect transplant compatibility and the presentation of molecular fragments to T cells.
The processes through which a disease develops and produces its effects in an organism.
A test that labels target cells with radioactive chromium and measures the radioactivity released as the cells are killed.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mediation across political divisions
sections.body: Ramos-Horta's diplomacy included efforts to reconcile East Timorese political groups. The award presentation described him as a moderate Fretilin leader who favoured social democracy. Returning during the internal conflict in 1975, he sought reconciliation; after Indonesia's invasion, he collected and communicated evidence of repression while working to unite nationalist groups. Belo's local interventions likewise sought to reduce confrontation and protect lives. The committee placed both men's work within a broader principle: lasting peace depends on respect for human rights. Its presentation explicitly connected that approach with the 1960 award to Albert Lutuli.

sections.heading: An award intended to encourage a settlement
sections.body: The October 1996 announcement presented the prize as encouragement for further diplomacy. It recognised Belo's dialogue with Indonesian authorities and Ramos-Horta's reconciliation talks and regional peace plan while East Timor's future remained unresolved. The committee described severe human losses from starvation, disease, war and terror under occupation. Its stated objective was a diplomatic settlement respecting the population's right to self-determination. The award therefore combined recognition of sustained advocacy with an attempt to draw attention to a conflict still requiring a peaceful solution.

sections.heading: Diplomatic advocacy and international representation
sections.body: José Ramos-Horta represented the East Timorese independence movement at the United Nations for more than a decade beginning in 1975. His advocacy reached the Security Council, the UN Commission on Human Rights and the European Parliament. His award-era biography also records studies at the Hague Academy of International Law and the International Institute of Human Rights. Alongside public diplomacy, he wrote books including Funu: The Unfinished Saga of East Timor. In 1996, he served as a representative of the National Council of Maubere Resistance, an umbrella body bringing together nationalist political forces and resistance groups.

terms.definition: The committee's principle that protecting fundamental human rights is central to building lasting peace.
A people's right to determine its political future, which the committee identified as a basis for settling the East Timor conflict.
The National Council of Maubere Resistance, the non-partisan East Timorese resistance umbrella organisation described in his 1996 biography.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental detection of helium-3 superfluid phases
sections.body: The Cornell researchers were investigating magnetic behaviour in solid helium-3 when pressure measurements showed two small irregularities at temperatures a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. Their initial interpretation assigned the changes to the solid. Further magnetic-resonance measurements showed that the liquid was responsible. Identifying the phase transitions required attention to small departures from the expected measurements and a willingness to revise the first explanation. The resulting research revealed a richer phase structure than that of superfluid helium-4. It also provided sharply defined transitions useful in low-temperature measurement. The discovery demonstrated collective quantum behaviour in a liquid whose individual atoms are fermions.

sections.heading: Research developments in low temperature physics at Cornell
sections.body: Lee established a low-temperature laboratory at Cornell, including responsibility for a helium liquefier. The growing group pursued several distinct lines of research. Erlend Graf, John Reppy and Lee identified a tricritical point in mixtures of liquid helium-3 and helium-4. William Halperin, Richardson and colleagues discovered antiferromagnetic ordering in solid helium-3. Lee also collaborated with Jack Freed on nuclear spin waves in spin-polarised atomic hydrogen gas. These were separate collaborations within a wider programme, rather than all being results of the three-person Nobel discovery team. The biography places the superfluid discovery within a sustained experimental environment supporting different techniques, students and questions.

sections.heading: Investigating magnetic ordering in solid helium-3
sections.body: At Bell Laboratories, Osheroff investigated magnetic ordering in solid helium-3 after the superfluid discovery. By late 1979, his group had observed antiferromagnetic resonance in samples grown from the superfluid directly into the magnetically ordered solid. A University of Florida group independently detected the resonances. Osheroff’s team used nuclear demagnetisation of copper for cooling, allowing single crystals to be formed and magnetic-domain orientations studied. With Mike Cross and Daniel Fisher, he determined the magnetic sublattice symmetry and proposed a detailed structure subsequently confirmed by polarised neutron scattering. The resonance-frequency shifts made the solid a useful model for investigating magnetic behaviour.

terms.definition: A collective quantum state of a liquid that exhibits flow without ordinary viscosity.
The study of matter at very low temperatures, where effects such as superfluidity and unusual magnetic ordering become accessible.
Cooling by reducing a magnetic field after nuclear spins have been aligned, while limiting heat entering the system.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The binding change mechanism of ATP synthase
sections.body: Boyer's binding change mechanism explains ATP synthesis through changes in the shapes of three catalytic sites. As a central shaft rotates, the sites pass through states suited to binding ADP and phosphate, forming ATP and releasing it. The rotating shaft is asymmetric, allowing the sites to occupy different states at the same moment. Walker and colleagues' 1994 X-ray structure of the catalytic F1 portion revealed an asymmetric central protein surrounded by units with different conformations. That structural evidence strongly supported the proposed mechanism. It showed how coordinated changes in a molecular machine could connect ion-driven rotation with ATP production.

sections.heading: Development of the binding change mechanism
sections.body: During his research, Paul Boyer identified that energy input primarily promotes the release of tightly bound ATP rather than forming the molecule itself. His team further revealed that three catalytic sites participate sequentially and cooperatively through rotational catalysis. This work involved investigating isotope exchanges during enzyme catalysis and exploring complex magnesium and ADP inhibition. Through studies involving chloroplasts, E. coli, and thermophilic bacteria, researchers unveiled essential facets of cooperative catalysis and the properties of six nucleotide binding sites.

sections.heading: Research on the sodium-potassium pump
sections.body: Skou's investigation into local anaesthetics led to his 1957 identification of the sodium-potassium pump, an enzyme responsible for active cation transport across cell membranes. His research group explored various aspects of Na+,K+-ATPase, including phosphorylation, ligand binding, and kinetics. Collaborators investigated the effects of cardiac glycosides, vanadate, and lipids on the system. Further studies involved enzyme solubilization, molecular weight determination, and electron microscopy. This work eventually expanded into studying how pump activity connects to vasoconstriction and the reconstitution of the enzyme into liposomes.

terms.definition: A mechanism in which catalytic sites change conformation in sequence to bind substrates, form ATP and release it as the central shaft rotates.
Catalysis in which interacting sites influence one another's activity; ATP synthase's three catalytic sites work through a coordinated sequence.
A membrane enzyme that performs active transport of sodium and potassium ions across a cell membrane.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Pricing derivatives without a risk premium
sections.body: A central difficulty in option valuation was choosing an appropriate risk premium. Within the model's assumptions, constructing a matching hedge allowed the option's value to be derived without separately specifying that premium. The method linked valuation to the underlying asset and the absence of arbitrage. It also supported analysis beyond traded stock options. A company able to switch between energy sources possesses a form of flexibility whose value can be studied as an option. Related methods were applied to corporate liabilities, insurance and guarantees. These are model-based valuations whose usefulness depends on how well the assumptions describe the particular problem.

sections.heading: Merton's research on continuous-time models and financial applications
sections.body: Merton's graduate work developed dynamic approaches to consumption, portfolio choice and asset pricing. Three thesis chapters were published before submission; another, on continuous-time consumption and portfolio rules, was presented in 1970 and published in 1971. He later shifted emphasis towards applications. Work during 1978–1987 examined how social security and different pension arrangements distribute risk. He also used option-pricing ideas to analyse deposit insurance, market-timing information, corporate investment and implicit employment contracts. In his autobiography, Merton stressed the importance of choosing useful abstractions from complex reality, as well as the mathematical methods used to analyse them.

sections.heading: Research on taxation and asset pricing
sections.body: At MIT's Sloan School, Scholes interacted with Robert Merton and Fischer Black on asset and derivative pricing. He worked with Black on option-pricing methods and with Black and Michael Jensen on tests of the capital asset pricing model. During his later Chicago years, taxation became a major research theme. With Merton Miller, he studied dividend taxation and executive compensation; with Robert Hamada, capital structure and taxes; and with George Constantinides, tax effects on asset liquidation. These were distinct stages and collaborations in a broader programme on financial decisions, incentives and valuation.

terms.definition: A financial contract whose payoff depends on an underlying asset or financial variable, as an option depends on the asset it covers.
A mathematical model in which variables and decisions can be analysed throughout time rather than only at separate preset dates.
Valuing financial claims whose payments depend on future events or the future value of an underlying asset.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Satirical influences and theatrical development
sections.body: Fo's dramatic method integrates diverse historical and literary influences to expose unrighteousness. He draws from the oral traditions of commedia dell’arte, Roman playwrights like Plautus, and Brecht’s didactic theatre. In Mistero Buffo, he utilizes old material, such as scenes depicting a landlord violating a worker's wife. His plays undergo a long-term development through an interplay with spectators, utilizing improvisation and witty rhythms. In Accidental Death of an Anarchist, a Hamlet-like figure named il Matto uses madness to reveal official falsehoods during cross-examinations.

sections.heading: Satirical techniques and historical influences in dramatic works
sections.body: Fo utilized diverse literary impulses, including Brecht, Mayakovski, and commedia dell’arte, to construct his multifaceted oeuvre. His 1970 play, Accidental Death of an Anarchist, addressed the 1969 right-wing extremist bombings and the suspicious death of a suspect in Milan. Through characters like the Maniac, he exposed official lies. Additionally, his later works with Franca Rame addressed women's issues. He also developed grammelot, a jesting language using onomatopoeia and dialect, which presents unique challenges for translators attempting to preserve his topical references.

sections.heading: Collaborative Theatre and Social Activism
sections.body: Dario Fo collaborated extensively with Franca Rame, who managed the Fo-Rame Company and contributed to writing many plays. Their work often addressed contemporary struggles, such as the La Comune collective staging performances between 1971 and 1985 to support striking factory workers. Through productions like Tutta casa, letto e chiesa, they utilized grotesque and comic elements to illustrate women's situations. Fo also developed Mistero buffo with an open-ended structure, allowing the performance to evolve by incorporating various contemporary issues that interested him and his audience over many years.

terms.definition: A comic performer who uses wit and mockery; Fo drew particularly on medieval jesters who challenged abuses despite lacking legal protection.
A jesting language created from onomatopoeia and dialect used within Fo's texts to provide engagement and amusement.
The theatre collective whose performances supported striking workers; Fo's biography records hundreds of such benefit performances between 1971 and 1985.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: How an infectious protein shape can spread
sections.body: The puzzle was that the protein associated with infectivity had a normal counterpart in healthy brains. The crucial difference was its three-dimensional shape, rather than a separate protein present only in diseased tissue. Prusiner proposed that an abnormal form could induce normal host protein to adopt the same harmful conformation. That process propagates a protein state without requiring the infectious agent to carry its own DNA or RNA genome. The host still makes the normal protein from its own gene. This distinction helps explain how prion disease can be acquired through infection, arise sporadically or be associated with inherited mutations.

sections.heading: Testing the role of the host protein
sections.body: Early purification experiments required long waits for disease in mice. Hamster models shortened that incubation period and made testing faster. Genetic experiments then connected disease to the host's prion protein. Mice carrying disease-associated versions of the gene developed a scrapie-like illness. Mice lacking the gene resisted experimental infection, while restoring it restored susceptibility. These results supported the requirement for normal host protein in propagation. The announcement also described abnormal protein aggregation, but acknowledged that the detailed link between aggregates and nerve-cell destruction was still poorly understood. Evidence for the protein mechanism was therefore stronger than knowledge of every step causing tissue damage.

sections.heading: A molecular toolkit for studying prions
sections.body: After the prion protein was isolated, Leroy Hood determined part of its amino-acid sequence, enabling further molecular work. Prusiner collaborated with Charles Weissmann on cloning the PrP gene, and with George Carlson and David Kingsbury on its relationship to scrapie incubation time in mice. Antibodies helped identify normal PrP and allowed Stephen DeArmond to study disease development in transgenic animals. Ruth Gabizon dispersed prions into liposomes and used PrP antibodies in purification. Karen Hsiao identified a familial-disease mutation and reproduced disease in transgenic mice. These named contributions show how biochemical, genetic and tissue studies built the evidence together.

terms.definition: An infectious protein-based agent whose conformation can propagate by inducing a change in the folding of host protein.
A mouse in which a particular gene has been inactivated, allowing researchers to test which processes require that gene.
A protein that recognises a particular molecular target; antibodies against PrP helped detect and purify it in these experiments.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Building support for the Ottawa treaty
sections.body: The Nobel presentation described a strategy of seeking a clear prohibition rather than weakening the proposed treaty to attract hesitant governments. Canada's invitation in October 1996 helped mobilise political support; by December 1997, 121 countries had signed in Ottawa. The campaign had developed from a 1991 agreement between the Vietnam Veterans of America Foundation and Medico International into a coalition of more than a thousand organisations. Its broad support placed pressure on larger states that remained outside the agreement. The committee interpreted the campaign as evidence that popular mobilisation could renew international negotiations. It also stressed that destroying mines and helping victims remained enormous unfinished tasks.

sections.heading: Why the committee honoured a campaign network
sections.body: The October 1997 announcement awarded equal shares to the ICBL and Williams, recognising both a dispersed coalition and the work of its coordinator. The committee linked mines' indiscriminate effects to obstacles to social and economic development in affected countries. It saw more than a thousand organisations as a way to connect public commitment with decisions by small and medium-sized governments. At that point, the Ottawa signing ceremony was still ahead. The suggestion that this cooperation could guide future disarmament was a hope for wider adoption, rather than a claim that the landmine problem had been solved.

sections.heading: Research and humanitarian expertise
sections.body: Williams coordinated and spoke for a coalition launched by six nongovernmental organisations in 1992. Her expertise also developed through research and earlier humanitarian work. With Shawn Roberts, she coauthored After the Guns Fall Silent, a 1995 study drawing on two years of field research in four mine-affected countries. She advised the United Nations study on children and armed conflict led by Graça Machel, wrote for the International Review of the Red Cross, and addressed the European Parliament and the Organization of African Unity. Before the landmine campaign, she had directed relief projects for Medical Aid for El Salvador and led fact-finding delegations through the Nicaragua-Honduras Education Project.

terms.definition: The cooperation between campaigning organisations and supportive governments that led to the 1997 treaty banning antipersonnel mines.
Organisations working together toward a shared objective; the ICBL connected many independent groups with public mobilisation and diplomatic action.
Effects on people's social and economic lives, the subject of Williams and Roberts's study of landmine contamination.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Using light to slow and confine atoms
sections.body: A photon transfers momentum when an atom absorbs it. By choosing laser frequencies so that atoms preferentially absorb light travelling against their motion, researchers create a braking force. Opposing beams along three directions form optical molasses, slowing motion without by themselves providing the same confinement as a trap. A magneto-optical trap combines laser light with a magnetic field to keep the cooled atoms near a central region. The 1997 presentation also described subrecoil methods reaching temperatures below a millionth of a kelvin. Cooling and trapping together make dilute atoms accessible for observation without simply letting them form an ordinary liquid or solid.

sections.heading: From atom traps to individual molecules
sections.body: Chu's groups demonstrated cooling and trapping methods, including work on the magneto-optical trap. At Stanford he developed a theory of cooling atoms with multiple internal levels, independently of work by Cohen-Tannoudji and Jean Dalibard. His group also demonstrated atomic-fountain techniques and atom interferometry using light pulses. In biological experiments, Chu applied optical tweezers by attaching tiny polystyrene beads to DNA. The beads served as handles that light could trap, allowing individual molecules to be manipulated. This extended an approach developed through optical trapping, including Arthur Ashkin's work on small particles, into experiments on molecular behaviour.

sections.heading: Energy landscapes and cooling below recoil
sections.body: Cohen-Tannoudji's group treated an atom and its interacting light together as a dressed atom, helping explain behaviour in intense laser fields. This approach suggested a cooling mechanism in which light creates spatially varying energy levels. Changes between those levels make atoms repeatedly expend motion energy climbing potential hills. The group called this Sisyphus cooling. A related low-intensity mechanism helped explain the unexpectedly low temperatures measured by Phillips, with Chu's group reaching similar conclusions. Cohen-Tannoudji also worked with Alain Aspect and Ennio Arimondo on velocity-selective coherent population trapping, using quantum interference to cool below the recoil-energy scale associated with a single photon.

terms.definition: A change in the frequency perceived by an observer moving relative to a wave source; an atom's motion changes the light frequency it experiences.
A technique using focused light to hold and move small objects; attached beads can serve as handles for manipulating a DNA molecule.
An atom described together with the light field interacting with it, allowing their combined energy levels to be analysed.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Two routes to practical quantum calculations
sections.body: Pople developed a model chemistry in GAUSSIAN: defined approximations and computational procedures for estimating molecular properties. The aim was to make quantum calculations usable and systematically assess their accuracy. Kohn’s work with Hohenberg offered a different starting point. Ground-state electron density determines the external potential up to an additive constant, and energy can be expressed as a functional of that density. Density depends on three spatial coordinates, whereas a many-electron wavefunction depends on every electron’s coordinates. Practical density-functional calculations still require approximations, but the reformulation greatly expands the systems that can be studied.

sections.heading: From scattering methods to ground-state density
sections.body: At Harvard, Kohn studied with Julian Schwinger, who proposed a three-body scattering problem. Kohn found an alternative formulation that became his variational principle for scattering, useful in nuclear, atomic and molecular work. With N. Rostoker he later developed a band-structure method using geometric information and scattering properties of a cell in a periodic potential. In the work leading to density-functional theory, he investigated whether ground-state density determines the external potential. His biography credits collaboration with Pierre Hohenberg in developing the result. These projects show how techniques and questions from scattering and solid-state physics informed his later contribution to computational chemistry.

sections.heading: Early research into molecular structures and liquid theory
sections.body: Beginning his career in 1948 under Sir John Lennard-Jones, Pople investigated the water molecule to examine lone electron pairs. This work aimed toward developing a theory for hydrogen bonding and studying liquid water structure. Seeking practical computational possibilities with limited early resources, he worked on simplifying theories, including developments related to PPP theory. This specific model applied to systems containing only one significant electron per atom. His research interests also transitioned from the statistical mechanics of liquids toward nuclear magnetic resonance techniques by 1955.

terms.definition: A framework using electron density as its basic quantity for determining electronic properties, with practical methods approximating the required energy functional.
The spatial distribution of electrons in a system's lowest-energy state, central to Kohn's density-based description.
A simplified electronic-structure model treating one selected, chemically relevant electron per atom rather than every electron explicitly.

sections.heading: Interpersonal comparisons and social choice theory
sections.body: Traditional social choice theory assumed individuals rank alternatives based on personal utility without allowing for comparing one person's evaluation to another. This limitation prevented meaningful conclusions regarding inequality. Sen expanded this field by demonstrating how specific assumptions about the possibility of making interpersonal comparisons influence the identification of consistent social preferences. He showed that applying utilitarian principles, which seek the highest average welfare, requires the ability to compare differences in personal utility between individuals across different social states. By deriving indicators for poverty and income inequality from a small number of reasonable axioms, he provided tools to evaluate various social conditions. His research also identifies specific vulnerable groups, such as nomadic cattleherds, by analyzing imbalances between needs and resources during events like the 1970s Sahel drought.

sections.heading: Development of social choice theory and economic applications
sections.body: Sukhamoy Chakravarty drew Sen’s attention to Kenneth Arrow’s 1951 study of social choice. Arrow’s impossibility theorem showed that, under its specified conditions, no non-dictatorial aggregation rule could deliver a consistent social ranking. This was a problem about combining particular requirements, rather than a claim that every collective decision procedure must fail. Sen’s 1970 book, Collective Choice and Social Welfare, presented a broad treatment of the field. Work with colleagues and students, including Prasanta Pattanaik, explored constructive possibilities alongside impossibility results. Sen’s biography describes applications to poverty, unemployment, income distribution, gender inequality and the assessment of liberty and rights. These linked formal questions about social evaluation to the practical interpretation of economic statistics, including national-income measures that account for distribution.

terms.definition: A collective ranking or evaluation of alternatives derived from information about individuals’ preferences or welfare; it need not represent unanimous agreement.
A field of study examining how individual preferences and values are aggregated into collective decisions and economic policy-making.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary methods and narrative structures
sections.body: The Nobel presentation describes a pattern in Saramago’s fiction: suspend one decisive rule of ordinary reality, then follow the consequences with close observation and sustained logic. In The Stone Raft, the Iberian Peninsula breaks away and floats into the Atlantic, creating opportunities for social and political satire. In Baltasar and Blimunda, the heroine gathers the wills of dying people to power a fantastical flight, while the narrative also depicts the suffering involved in building the convent at Mafra. The speech connects this mixture of invention and historical detail with a narrator who handles traditional storytelling techniques with ironic distance. Its account presents the novels as different ways of approaching an elusive reality.

sections.heading: Literary themes and narrative techniques in Saramago's prose
sections.body: The award announcement traces Saramago’s experimentation across several novels. Manual of Painting and Calligraphy examines the emergence of an artist while combining love, travel, ethical questions and reflections on society. The Year of the Death of Ricardo Reis places one of Fernando Pessoa’s invented literary identities in 1936 Lisbon, where the dead Pessoa visits him. In The Stone Raft, a drifting Iberian Peninsula provides an impossible setting for recognisable political behaviour. The History of the Siege of Lisbon begins with a proofreader deliberately inserting the word “not”, reversing a historical statement and opening another narrative. These devices make storytelling itself part of the inquiry: an invented departure from reality changes what can be explored.

sections.heading: Development of a unique narrative style
sections.body: Saramago’s 1947 debut appeared as The Land of Sin, although he had called the manuscript The Widow. He later worked in publishing at Estúdios Cor and as a translator and journalist. After losing his newspaper post in 1975, he committed himself to literature. Weeks spent observing and taking notes in Lavre in 1976 informed his 1980 novel Raised from the Ground. In his biography, he identifies that book as the starting point of his characteristic narrative manner. This development followed a long working life around books and newspapers, rather than an uninterrupted sequence of early successful novels. His account connects a particular encounter with rural life to a lasting change in how he told stories.

terms.definition: A narrative voice able to describe events and characters beyond the limited knowledge of any one participant.
A story whose events invite interpretation beyond the immediate plot, often illuminating moral, social or philosophical questions.
Saramago’s 1980 novel, in which he located the emergence of the narrative style associated with his later fiction.

sections.heading: The sandwich experiment and nitric oxide identification
sections.body: Furchgott combined two pieces of aorta: one retained its endothelial lining but could not contract or relax; the other could respond mechanically but lacked that lining. Stimulation caused the second piece to relax when the pieces were together. This showed that a transferable substance from the endothelium could act on neighbouring tissue. The experiment established the existence of a signal before its chemical identity was known. At a 1986 meeting, Furchgott and Ignarro independently argued that the factor was nitric oxide. Ignarro's additional evidence included matching spectral changes when reduced haemoglobin reacted with either the endothelial factor or nitric oxide.

sections.heading: Earlier clues from isolated blood vessels
sections.body: Furchgott's studies of aortic strips raised questions that led to later discoveries. In work published in 1954, blocking many receptors still left a strong contraction response to an agonist such as epinephrine. This encouraged his interest in spare receptors. His laboratory also investigated relaxation caused by light. With Eugene Greenblatt and Stuart Ehrreich, he measured an action spectrum peaking near 310 nanometres. Adding sodium nitrite made the strips more sensitive to light and shifted the peak to about 355 nanometres. These experiments illustrate how carefully controlled tissue preparations could reveal unexpected relationships between a stimulus and a blood vessel's response.

sections.heading: Nitric oxide mechanism and guanylate cyclase activation
sections.body: Ignarro's group reported in 1979 that nitric oxide rapidly relaxed strips of bovine coronary artery that had first been contracted with phenylephrine. They introduced diluted nitric oxide gas into the organ bath containing the tissue. Haemoglobin and methylene blue prevented the relaxation in these experiments, helping connect the effect to nitric oxide and guanylate cyclase. Studies also linked nitric oxide's inhibition of platelet aggregation to cyclic GMP. Following earlier work by Phil Needleman, Ignarro's laboratory investigated the role of thiols and found them necessary for guanylate-cyclase activation by nitroglycerin in the experimental systems studied.

terms.definition: An arrangement of two vessel preparations that tests whether a substance released by one can alter the response of the other.
Receptors beyond those needed to produce a maximal response, so a strong effect can occur without activating the entire receptor population.
Cyclic guanosine monophosphate, an intracellular signalling molecule produced by guanylate cyclase that mediates several effects of nitric oxide.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Institutional frameworks for conflict resolution
sections.body: The Good Friday Agreement provided institutions through which unionists and nationalists could pursue disagreements peacefully while retaining different constitutional aspirations. The May 1998 referendum and June Assembly election were steps toward putting that framework into practice. The Nobel speech emphasised Hume’s insistence on inclusive talks, including an opportunity for people associated with violent political campaigns to enter a peaceful process. Such engagement attracted criticism, especially during renewed violence. The committee saw leadership and institutional guarantees as complementary: dialogue opened possibilities, while agreed arrangements could help sustain them. The new Assembly brought former adversaries into a shared political setting without requiring them to abandon every substantive difference.

sections.heading: Foundations of the Good Friday Agreement
sections.body: At the time of the award, the committee described a conflict that had killed more than 3,500 people over three decades. It highlighted different contributions by the two laureates. Hume had consistently advocated a peaceful settlement, while Trimble persuaded support for negotiated solutions at a crucial stage within a traditionally dominant unionist party. Their significance lay partly in addressing constituencies with opposed aspirations. The announcement also credited other Northern Irish leaders and the British, Irish and United States governments. It expressed hope that the foundations established in 1998 would lead to durable peace and encourage negotiated approaches elsewhere. This was recognition of a collective political opening whose implementation was still developing.

sections.heading: John Hume's political leadership and community development
sections.body: Before leading the SDLP, Hume organized the University for Derry campaign and helped establish the Derry Credit Union and Derry Housing Association. His early career included serving as a Stormont MP for Foyle and participating in the 1974 Power-Sharing Executive as Minister of Commerce following the Sunningdale Agreement negotiations. As a Member of the European Parliament, he contributed to regional policy and authored a report on Irish regional problems. He also initiated talks with Gerry Adams to pursue an end to violence through All Party Talks.

terms.definition: Structures within a political agreement designed to provide a framework for resolving conflicts through peaceful means rather than violence.
A series of efforts and political contributions involving multiple leaders and governments to find a peaceful solution to conflict.
A government in which parties representing different communities share executive responsibility, as in Northern Ireland’s 1974 arrangement.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Measuring collective behaviour in a thin electron layer
sections.body: Precision semiconductor structures confined electrons to effectively two-dimensional motion, providing the setting for the experiments. Under very strong magnetic fields and at temperatures near absolute zero, Störmer and Tsui observed an unexpected plateau in the Hall response. Its value suggested behaviour involving a third of the usual electronic charge; the experiment did not isolate a piece cut from an electron. Laughlin explained the fractional effect through interactions among many electrons forming a correlated quantum fluid. Excitations of that state could behave as fractionally charged objects. The result linked advanced materials fabrication, sensitive electrical measurements and a theory of collective behaviour.

sections.heading: From the integer effect to a fractional state
sections.body: Laughlin’s earlier explanation of precise integer Hall quantisation used a thought experiment with a ring-shaped sample and related current to changes in energy. That work preceded his account of the fractional effect. For the latter, he studied a proposed correlated ground state using methods borrowed from plasma physics, including Monte Carlo calculations. Comparing energies showed his trial state was more favourable than the crystalline alternatives then considered. A further adiabatic thought experiment constructed excitations carrying one-third of the electron’s charge. Their estimated energies could be compared with activation energies measured in experiments. The calculation tested a particular many-electron state, rather than extending a single-electron picture unchanged.

sections.heading: Experimental discovery of the fractional quantum Hall effect
sections.body: Störmer dates the discovery measurement to October 1981, when he and Tsui took an exceptionally clean, low-density sample to MIT’s high-field laboratory to look for an electron crystal. Art Gossard and William Wiegmann had fabricated it. The result instead revealed the fractional quantum Hall effect. Crucial materials work began earlier: Störmer and Ray Dingle discussed separating dopant impurities from the region occupied by mobile electrons. Gossard and Wiegmann implemented the selective doping in grown semiconductor layers. Loren Pfeiffer and Ken West subsequently led major improvements in sample quality. These contributions made electronic behaviour visible that disorder and scattering could otherwise obscure.

terms.definition: A state of matter whose collective behaviour depends essentially on quantum effects; here, a correlated state of many electrons.
A collective disturbance that behaves as a charge carrier with a fraction of the electron’s charge.
Doping that separates the impurities supplying carriers from the region where those carriers move, reducing impurity scattering.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of femtochemistry and laser-based observation
sections.body: Zewail's experiments used laser pulses lasting only tens of femtoseconds to investigate molecular change. An initial pulse starts a reaction in a population of molecules; later pulses detect how that population changes. Coordinating the start makes it possible to reconstruct events that would otherwise be blurred together. Early experiments followed the stretching and breaking of bonds in relatively simple reactions, followed by studies of more complex systems. The field also reached biology: the Nobel presentation described research on the rapid change in retinal's shape following light absorption, an early step in vision. Such measurements made molecular motion accessible through time-resolved signals.

sections.heading: Using delayed pulses to reconstruct a reaction
sections.body: In pump–probe experiments, a strong pulse excites molecules and a delayed probe detects the starting material or a changed form. Varying the delay builds a record of the reaction's progress. Mirrors can lengthen the probe's path and therefore alter its arrival time. Spectral signals are compared with calculations of molecular structures and energies to interpret the changes. Zewail's early work followed the dissociation of ICN into iodine and CN on a timescale of about 200 femtoseconds. Experiments on sodium iodide also revealed how molecular motion and changes in electronic character are coupled during dissociation.

sections.heading: Research into molecular physics and laser technology
sections.body: Zewail's early research ranged across molecular spectroscopy: the Stark effect, the Zeeman effect, optical detection of magnetic resonance and double-resonance techniques. During his postdoctoral work with Charles Harris, he helped build a picosecond laser. He recalled that the demanding project taught him the principles and physics of lasers. This combination of spectroscopy and hands-on instrument development preceded his later ultrafast experiments at Caltech. In a 2006 addendum to his biography, he described continuing research on dynamical chemistry and biology, including elementary processes in complex systems, as director of Caltech's Physical Biology Center for Ultrafast Science and Technology.

terms.definition: The study of chemical reactions on femtosecond timescales, using ultrashort pulses to resolve changes as bonds break and form.
A method in which one light pulse initiates a change and a later pulse measures the system after a controlled delay.
A laser producing pulses on the scale of picoseconds; one picosecond is one trillionth of a second.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The Mundell-Fleming model and exchange rate policy
sections.body: The Mundell–Fleming framework showed how policy effects depend on both capital mobility and the exchange-rate regime. In its high-capital-mobility case, monetary policy has strong short-run effects under floating rates, while exchange-rate changes offset fiscal expansion. Under fixed rates, the comparison reverses because maintaining the peg constrains independent monetary action. These are results within a model, not universal descriptions of every economy. Mundell also went beyond short-run comparisons to analyse adjustment over time, including mechanisms behind persistent balance-of-payments imbalances. His research considered how different policy instruments could be assigned to objectives such as domestic stability and external balance.

sections.heading: Stabilization policy under different exchange rate regimes
sections.body: With very mobile capital and a credible fixed exchange rate, domestic interest rates are tied closely to foreign rates. A central bank defending the peg must intervene in currency markets, causing the money supply to adjust and limiting independent monetary policy. In the model, fiscal expansion can raise activity without the usual rise in interest rates or exchange-rate appreciation. Under floating rates, fiscal expansion instead attracts capital and appreciates the currency, reducing net exports and offsetting the stimulus in the limiting case. Monetary expansion can work through the opposite exchange-rate channel. The assumptions explain why the same policy can have different effects across exchange-rate arrangements.

sections.heading: Economic theories regarding monetary and fiscal policy
sections.body: Mundell pioneered several foundational economic frameworks, including the theory of the monetary and fiscal policy mix and the monetary approach to the balance of payments. His research also explored the relationship between inflation, interest, and growth. Beyond his work on currency areas, he co-founded supply-side economics and authored significant texts such as The International Monetary System: Conflict and Reform. His expertise extended to advising international organizations like the World Bank and the IMF, alongside various governments in Europe and Latin America.

terms.definition: The ability of funds to move across borders in response to investment opportunities, returns and financial conditions.
The use of monetary and fiscal measures to manage economic activity and influence national income within open economies.
The combination of monetary and fiscal instruments used to pursue economic objectives such as domestic stability and external balance.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary methods and narrative techniques in Grass's work
sections.body: Grass's fiction challenges grand accounts of history through parody and irreverence. The award presentation compares The Tin Drum to a carnival, with events viewed from the unusually low vantage point of its narrator. It also highlights the many voices in his prose, likening them to conversations in a noisy inn. Animals and food recur across his books. In The Flounder, the presentation reads the stories of female cooks as an alternative account of civilisation, connecting everyday nourishment with historical memory. These were features of the Academy's interpretation of his literary achievement.

sections.heading: Literary techniques and thematic explorations in Grass's prose
sections.body: Grass utilizes diverse narrative methods to examine historical truth. In The Tin Drum, he employs a protagonist with infernal intelligence to break realist boundaries through dadaism. His work Dog Years presents a modernist structure lacking a determinable centre, serving as an arena for various voices. In The Flounder, he adopts a grand style to depict civilization as a struggle between destructive masculine dreams and female achievement. Additionally, his writing in Ein weites Feld explores the tension between artistic imagination and political power within German history.

sections.heading: Literary development and political engagement
sections.body: Following his studies in Düsseldorf and Berlin, Grass worked as a sculptor and graphic artist. He joined the literary group Gruppe 47 in 1955; his first poetry appeared in 1956 and his first play was produced in 1957. The Tin Drum then established his international reputation and became part of the Danzig Trilogy with Cat and Mouse and Dog Years. His political activity included campaigning for Willy Brandt and the Social Democrats. The award biography also connects The Flounder and The Rat with his involvement in peace and environmental movements.

terms.definition: The presentation speaker's term for the connection between cooking and historical reflection in The Flounder.
Grass's self-description as a belated Enlightenment thinker, expressing a commitment to reason in an era he saw as tired of it.
Three works of fiction connected with Danzig: The Tin Drum, Cat and Mouse and Dog Years.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental verification of protein translocation mechanisms
sections.body: To validate his signal hypothesis, Blobel created an ingenious test tube system that allowed for the individual study of each step in the protein transport process. This experimental setup utilized components sourced from mouse, rabbit, and dog cells to observe how proteins move across membranes. His research demonstrated that proteins intended for various organelles or membrane integration possess specific topogenic signals. These guiding principles are highly conserved across evolution, functioning within plant, animal, and yeast cells. Beyond basic biology, these discoveries allowed the pharmaceutical industry to use cultured cells as efficient mini-factories for producing protein-based drugs like insulin, growth hormone, and coagulation factors. His work established a framework for understanding hereditary diseases caused by proteins becoming mislocalized.

sections.heading: Development of molecular analysis of cellular functions
sections.body: Following his medical studies at the University of Tübingen, Blobel moved to Madison via Montreal to pursue graduate research. Under the mentorship of Van R. Potter, he eventually joined George Palade’s Laboratory of Cell Biology at Rockefeller University. This period marked a transition toward the molecular analysis of cellular functions, moving beyond the initial identification of structures like the endoplasmic reticulum. While researchers like Keith Porter, Ernest Fullam, and Albert Claude had previously used the electron microscope to reveal cytoplasmic networks, Blobel helped initiate this third phase of research. His work contributed to relating specific cellular structures to their biological functions through molecular investigation, building upon the foundational discoveries made at the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research.

terms.definition: The proposal that proteins destined for the secretory pathway carry a signal directing them to, and through, the endoplasmic-reticulum membrane.
A phase of cellular research focused on investigating specific cellular functions through the study of molecular components.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Independence and the dilemmas of humanitarian action
sections.body: The 1999 presentation described MSF's founders as seeking a flexible organisation able to reach people quickly and speak publicly about abuses. They claimed freedom to make medical decisions on humanitarian grounds, without treating prior political approval as the determining criterion. Such public criticism was controversial: the speech acknowledged fears that it could obstruct access to people needing help. It also described reliance on private donations for half the organisation's income as an independence safeguard at that time. The committee praised MSF for exposing a wider dilemma of aid: good intentions do not guarantee beneficial consequences, particularly when armed groups intrude into humanitarian work. Its account therefore concerned both emergency medicine and the difficult judgments involved in delivering it.

sections.heading: Humanitarian assistance as a contribution to peace
sections.body: The 1999 announcement explained the award through a principle of assistance according to need, regardless of borders or political sympathies. It credited MSF's independence with helping the organisation act on that commitment. The committee also identified roles beyond treatment: drawing attention to emergencies, opposing abuses through public testimony and, in some violent settings, opening possibilities for contact between adversaries. These were the committee's reasons for connecting medical humanitarian work with the Peace Prize. It did not claim that aid alone resolves conflict. Its emphasis on the dignity of individual patients linked practical care to a wider hope for reconciliation.

terms.definition: Judging action by its likely practical consequences as well as its motivating convictions; the presentation applied this tension to humanitarian aid.
In this announcement, the commitment to give disaster victims prompt professional assistance without selecting recipients by political allegiance or national boundaries.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Making finite predictions from difficult calculations
sections.body: The researchers needed consistent calculations in theories linking electromagnetism with the weak interaction. Their methods used auxiliary ghost fields during intermediate steps; these were mathematical components, not newly predicted particles observable in detectors. They also calculated in a number of dimensions displaced slightly from four. This allowed divergent terms to be isolated and treated systematically before obtaining physical predictions. The approach did not propose that spacetime literally had a fractional dimension. Its success made precise theoretical comparisons with accelerator experiments possible, including measurements at CERN's Large Electron–Positron collider.

sections.heading: Why massive force carriers were a challenge
sections.body: In his biography, 't Hooft recalls Veltman's concern that apparently simple mass terms made weak-interaction calculations fail to yield finite answers. Experimental evidence nevertheless pointed toward a Yang–Mills framework. The algebra was complicated enough that Veltman developed computer tools to handle it. Researchers also doubted whether scalar fields and symmetry breaking could fit into a consistent theory. 't Hooft and Veltman refined methods that made the relevant models calculable, allowing experiments to distinguish competing versions. The biography later discusses strong interactions and asymptotic freedom as another research direction, rather than making that entire subject part of the electroweak breakthrough.

sections.heading: Veltman's early research and doctoral work
sections.body: After completing graduate studies in 1956, Veltman pursued a PhD under Van Hove. His thesis, titled Intermediate particles in S-matrix theory and calculation of higher order effects in the production of intermediate vector bosons, addressed unstable particles and Coulomb corrections for vector boson production by neutrinos. While working at CERN, he performed extensive calculations regarding vector boson production to assist experimentalists with data analysis. Additionally, Veltman served as an editor for Physics Letters, where he managed a high volume of daily submissions.

terms.definition: A calculation technique that temporarily varies the number of dimensions to expose divergent terms, enabling them to be handled before physical results are obtained.
Expressing a theory's predictions in terms of physical parameters so that problematic infinities can be handled consistently and measurable results calculated.
A framework relating particles' initial and final states in an interaction, used to calculate scattering and transition probabilities.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Doping and transport along polymer chains
sections.body: Polyacetylene has a conjugated backbone with alternating single and double bonds. Removing electrons by oxidation, for example with iodine, changes its charge state and allows much greater electrical conduction. This is p-doping. Charge transport depends both on motion along a chain and on transfer between different chains, so their packing and order matter. The Nobel background compared highly conductive doped polyacetylene with metals, while identifying the undoped material as a semiconductor. Conductivity varies with preparation and doping; the comparison does not mean that every treated polymer film automatically performs like copper.

sections.heading: An unexpected film and a deliberate chemical test
sections.body: An accidental excess of catalyst during acetylene polymerisation produced a silvery film instead of the expected material. The researchers recognised an opportunity to investigate its electrical behaviour. Treating polyacetylene with iodine vapour oxidised the polymer and increased conductivity by many orders of magnitude. Oxidation removes electrons from the conjugated system, producing positively charged carriers often described as holes. Their motion contributes to current along the chains. The important sequence combined an unexpected observation with deliberate chemical modification and measurement. It opened a field investigating how the molecular structure and charge state of polymers determine their electrical properties.

sections.heading: From conducting chains to possible devices
sections.body: In these conjugated polymers, doping changes the number of electrons in the molecular system: oxidation removes them and reduction adds them. The resulting charge carriers can move through the material. The 2000 announcement described applications already in use or under industrial development, including antistatic coatings for photographic film, electromagnetic shielding and windows that change their transmission of sunlight. It also highlighted work on semiconducting polymers for light-emitting devices, solar cells and small displays. These examples represented different stages of development at the award year. They illustrate the broader move from treating polymers mainly as insulators to designing their electronic behaviour.

terms.definition: A connected pattern of alternating single and multiple bonds whose electrons can be distributed across more than one bond.
A useful unexpected discovery arising from chance together with the ability to recognise and investigate its significance.
Changing a material's charge-carrier population; in these polymers, oxidation or reduction creates carriers that can increase electrical conductivity.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Correcting a wage study for who works
sections.body: A wage survey observes earnings for people who work, but cannot directly record what non-workers would earn if they took jobs. If entry into employment is related to earning potential, the observed workers may not represent the whole population. Heckman’s two-stage procedure models the probability of working, then uses a correction derived from that model when estimating the wage relationship. Education and age can remain explanatory variables, alongside the selection correction. The method’s validity depends on its modelling assumptions; its purpose is to account explicitly for how observations entered the sample. The official explanation connects this methodological work to Heckman’s earlier empirical research on married women’s labour supply.

sections.heading: Applications of microeconometric methods in social science
sections.body: Heckman’s methods were used to evaluate labour-market and educational programmes, study discrimination, and investigate how unemployment duration relates to the chance of finding work. McFadden’s discrete-choice models supported transport planning: researchers could estimate how travellers might respond to petrol prices, easier subway access or demographic change. His applications included the San Francisco Bay Area’s BART network, telephone-service investment and housing for older people. The 2000 presentation also described using his model to estimate environmental damage from the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill. These examples show the range of questions that individual-level economic information can address, while the statistical problems and appropriate models differ across applications.

sections.heading: Two different obstacles in individual data
sections.body: The award announcement distinguishes missing observations from the form that observed choices take. For Heckman, characteristics the researcher cannot observe may influence who works or enters education; ignoring that selection can distort estimated relationships. Related issues arise when evaluating social programmes or connecting unemployment duration with job-finding chances. For McFadden, the outcome may be a category, such as a residence or occupation, selected from a finite set. His contribution connected statistical models of these choices to economic theory. Both researchers developed methods in close contact with applied problems. Larger datasets and faster computers made more studies possible, but did not remove the need to model how the data were generated.

terms.definition: A process in which people’s own choices determine who enters the observed sample.
Records about individual people, households or firms, rather than only totals or averages for a whole population.
Selection among distinct alternatives, rather than a continuously varying quantity.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary structures and psychological foundations in Gao's works
sections.body: The Nobel presentation reads Gao’s fiction through a tension between solitude and companionship: relationships relieve loneliness while exposing the individual to struggles over power. In its account of Soul Mountain, the narrative “I” projects a “you”, which in turn creates a “she”; shifting pronouns open different perspectives on human relationships. Stories, shamanistic practices and Daoist ideas encountered in southern China provide alternatives to demands for ideological conformity. The speech also describes One Man’s Bible as a companion novel confronting different positions during the Cultural Revolution: rebel leader, victim and silent observer. These are critical interpretations of the novels’ forms and concerns. Framing chapters and shifts in perspective allow memory and imagination to be examined alongside the experiences they represent.

sections.heading: Literary development and experimental dramatic techniques
sections.body: Gao earned a degree in French in 1962. His 1981 discussion of modern fiction provoked debate over literary modernism, while his experimental plays drew partly on Brecht, Artaud and Beckett. Signal Alarm was staged in Beijing in 1982; Bus Stop followed in 1983 and was condemned during a campaign against intellectual pollution. Wild Man attracted both controversy in China and attention abroad, and The Other Shore was banned in 1986. His biography describes journeys through the Chinese countryside alongside this period of writing and pressure. He left China in 1987 and settled in Paris the following year. The chronology shows the interaction of formal experimentation, theatrical production and political constraints without reducing his work to a single political purpose.

terms.definition: Use of pronouns such as “I”, “you” and “she” to divide or shift narrative perspectives, here interpreted as different projections of a central self.
A broad movement of artistic experimentation that questions inherited conventions of form, representation and perspective.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of signal transduction and synaptic change
sections.body: Carlsson's experiments used reserpine to deplete brain dopamine in animals. Giving L-DOPA restored dopamine and movement, helping establish the basis for its use in Parkinson's disease. Greengard investigated events inside the receiving nerve cell: receptor activation can generate second messengers, activate protein kinases and change proteins by adding phosphate groups. These changes regulate functions including ion-channel activity. Kandel studied how learning alters synapses in Aplysia. Repeated harmless stimulation reduced transmitter release, while stimuli producing long-lasting memory engaged signalling pathways that led to new protein production and changes in synaptic form and function.

sections.heading: Early pharmacological research at the University of Lund
sections.body: At Lund, Carlsson and Georg Theander investigated how long the stimulant pentylenetetrazol acted. It initially failed to counter the anaesthetic effect of nitrous oxide. After a small dose of barbital was added, the stimulant could counter the combined depressant effect. They measured its action through the additional nitrous oxide pressure needed to suppress an animal's righting reflex. Their 1946 paper showed a longer duration of stimulant action than observations in animals without depressant treatment had suggested. In another project, Carlsson and Folke Serin found a daily rhythm in the lethal effects of nikethamide. These were historical pharmacology experiments in animals.

sections.heading: Integrating biophysical and biochemical techniques in neuroscience
sections.body: Hodgkin's lecture on the ionic basis of nerve impulses prompted Greengard to combine biophysics with biochemistry. At Johns Hopkins, his doctoral supervisors brought those disciplines together: Frank Brink was a biophysicist and Sidney Colowick a biochemist. After graduating in 1953, Greengard worked in Europe with Henry McIlwain, E. C. Slater and Wilhelm Feldberg. He recalled that pharmacology departments then offered an unusual combination of electrophysiological and biochemical facilities. That setting allowed him to investigate the relationship between electrical activity and chemical processes in nerve cells, developing the approach behind his later studies of intracellular signalling.

terms.definition: The conversion of a signal received by a cell into changes in its internal activity or behaviour.
A drug that stimulates the central nervous system; drugs in this group were historically studied for counteracting depressant effects.
The study and measurement of electrical activity in cells and tissues, including nerve impulses.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Principles of Human Rights and Regional Diplomacy
sections.body: The Nobel speech praised Kim’s defence of human rights as universal, rejecting arguments that they belonged only to Western culture. It cited his support for Aung San Suu Kyi’s democratic struggle in Burma and South Korea’s contribution of troops to international efforts in East Timor. Toward North Korea, his sunshine policy favoured gradually expanding cooperation and common interests. Its name recalled Aesop’s contest between wind and sun: warmth persuades a traveller to remove a cloak that forceful wind only makes him grip tighter. The committee also acknowledged unfinished reform in South Korea in 2000, including concerns about security legislation, political imprisonment and labour rights. Its support for Kim accompanied recognition of those continuing problems.

sections.heading: Political opposition and the transition to presidency
sections.body: Kim opposed Park Chung Hee’s efforts to prolong authoritarian rule and endured kidnapping, imprisonment and house arrest. A death sentence imposed after his 1980 arrest was later reduced. His prison term was suspended in 1982, allowing him to travel to the United States. He returned in 1985 and was placed under house arrest again; his civil and political rights were fully restored in 1987. After unsuccessful presidential campaigns, he won the December 1997 election. His inauguration brought an opposition party to power through an electoral transition. The presidency began amid a severe financial crisis. Alongside economic reform, he pursued engagement with North Korea and signed a joint declaration with Kim Jong-il on 15 June 2000.

terms.definition: Kim Dae-jung’s policy of engagement with North Korea through dialogue, exchanges and cooperation intended to build conditions for reconciliation.
The constitutional system imposed under Park Chung Hee that concentrated presidential power and enabled prolonged authoritarian rule.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Developments in semiconductor heterostructures and integrated circuits
sections.body: The advancement of microelectronics relied on overcoming limitations in component assembly and transistor speed. Jack Kilby addressed the error-prone task of soldering discrete transistors by designing a circuit using a single semiconductor material processed in various ways, demonstrating its functionality on September 12, 1958. To improve amplification and frequency, Herbert Kroemer proposed a heterostructure consisting of two semiconductors with compatible atomic structures but different electronic properties in 1957. In 1963, Kroemer and Zhores Alferov independently suggested using a double heterojunction to confine electrons, holes, and photons within a thin layer.
