Working in Leningrad, Alferov and his team produced a continuous-operation laser in May 1970 that functioned without intensive cooling. These innovations enabled technologies ranging from mobile phone base stations to optical broadband links.

sections.heading: Development of semiconductor heterostructure technologies
sections.body: Alferov’s earlier work on semiconductor devices examined where charge carriers recombined. Under the working current densities he studied, recombination in heavily doped outer regions could dominate over the middle region. This helped motivate his interest in a layered laser structure that controlled carriers and light more effectively. His group’s gallium-arsenide and aluminium-containing heterostructures demonstrated several distinct effects, including efficient one-sided injection, superinjection, tunnelling and carrier and optical confinement. These findings supported lasers, light-emitting diodes, solar cells and other devices. In the double-heterostructure laser, a thin active layer sits between other semiconductor layers, concentrating the relevant carriers and light where emission occurs. The account connects device engineering with investigations of how carriers behave at material boundaries.

terms.definition: A structure joining semiconductor materials with different electronic properties, used to control charge carriers and light in electronic and optical devices.
A thin active semiconductor layer between two surrounding semiconductor layers with different properties, enabling carrier and optical confinement.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Developments in catalytic asymmetric synthesis
sections.body: A chiral catalyst supplies an asymmetric environment that favours one product enantiomer. Knowles's team at Monsanto combined rhodium with the diphosphine ligand DiPAMP for industrial L-DOPA production. Noyori and colleagues developed BINAP, whose metal complexes supported a broader range of selective reactions. Rhodium–BINAP chemistry was used in amino-acid synthesis and as part of industrial menthol production. Replacing rhodium with ruthenium expanded the range of hydrogenation substrates. One application produced the desired form of 1,2-propanediol for making levofloxacin. These examples show why both the metal and its surrounding ligands matter: together they determine which reactions are practical and which molecular form is favoured.

sections.heading: Applications of chiral catalysis in industrial chemistry
sections.body: The development of selective catalysts has significant practical utility in large-scale production. Ryoji Noyori created more general and selective hydrogenation catalysts, which are used industrially to manufacture various antibiotics. K. Barry Sharpless introduced methods for epoxidation and dihydroxylation reactions, providing new ways to construct complex molecules. These advancements support the creation of medicines for high blood pressure and ulcers. Such catalytic tools also accelerate academic progress in fields including materials science, biology, and medicine by enabling more efficient molecular construction.

sections.heading: William Knowles's early chemical research and industrial work
sections.body: While studying organic chemistry at Harvard under Louis Fieser, William Knowles learned about the tetrahedral carbon atom and optical isomerism. During his career at Monsanto, he worked on producing benzyl benzoate for mite repellant and participated in a DDT project. He also contributed to the custom manufacture of the antibiotic chloramphenicol. Later, using kinetic studies and mathematical methods, he improved industrial processes to double production within existing equipment. His professional background also included working on steroid synthesis alongside Professor Woodward.

terms.definition: Having a structure that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, as a left hand cannot be superimposed on a right hand.
An oxidation reaction guided to favour one mirror-image product or configuration, as in the selective reactions developed by Sharpless.
Research involving the measurement of reaction rates used by Knowles to improve chemical production efficiency without additional capital.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Why good products can disappear from a market
sections.body: Akerlof's used-car example begins with a seller who knows more about a car's quality than the buyer. If buyers cannot distinguish good cars from poor ones, the price they offer reflects that uncertainty. Owners of better cars may then find selling unattractive, leaving a worse selection on the market. Under some conditions, this feedback can shrink trade severely or eliminate it. Akerlof also examined institutions that address information problems. Dealer guarantees, brands, chain stores and contractual arrangements can help provide reassurance or incentives. The lesson concerns both the failure information gaps can produce and the ways markets develop responses.

sections.heading: Signals and contract choices reveal different information
sections.body: Spence studied when an informed participant can send a credible signal. An observable action must be sufficiently more costly for the type trying to imitate the signal; expense alone does not establish credibility. Education offered a model example in employment. Stiglitz examined the complementary problem of what the less-informed side can do. An insurer can offer contracts with different premiums and deductibles, encouraging customers to select terms suited to their risk. In the model, a low premium paired with a high deductible helps distinguish lower-risk customers because the combination is less attractive to higher-risk customers.

sections.heading: Information gaps beyond used cars
sections.body: The informed side changes from one market to another. Borrowers may know more about repayment prospects than lenders; managers may know more about profitability than shareholders; prospective policyholders may know more about accident risk than insurers. The laureates' work supplied tools for investigating these differences. Akerlof discussed issues including insurance access and labour-market discrimination. Signalling research considered education and corporate dividend decisions, while Stiglitz analysed phenomena such as unemployment and credit rationing. The common contribution was to make the distribution of information part of the economic model, rather than assume that all participants know the same relevant facts.

terms.definition: A process in which hidden information changes who participates in a transaction, potentially leaving a worse mix of products or risks.
Offering a set of choices designed so that participants' selections reveal information about characteristics they privately know.
A market condition where actors on one side possess significantly better information than those on the opposing side.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: How archival research changed Naipaul's writing
sections.body: While researching The Loss of El Dorado, Naipaul found archival traces of the Indigenous people whose name had passed to the town where he spent his early years. The award presentation describes this as an enlargement of his understanding that fiction alone had not supplied. He subsequently applied a related method to travel notes, recovering individual lives from documents and testimony. Fiction, autobiography, reportage and historical research came together in his prose. The emphasis was on detailed voices and circumstances, shaped into literature without relying on grand myths to explain them.

sections.heading: Naipaul's integration of diverse literary forms
sections.body: Naipaul developed a unique style by merging autobiography, documentary elements, and fictional narratives. In works like The Enigma of Arrival, he utilized observations to depict the decline of colonial ruling cultures. His process involved studying archives for projects such as The Loss of El Dorado, where he prioritized authentic details and voices over simple fictionalization. This method allowed him to document the histories of the vanquished across India, Africa, and the Islamic world, often blurring the boundaries between non-fiction and fiction through precise, vigilant prose.

sections.heading: A biographer's reading of agency and identity
sections.body: The biographical essay hosted with Naipaul's award was written by David Pryce-Jones. It interprets his travels in India and Africa as an investigation of identity during decolonisation, and reads his books as arguments for individual responsibility and intellectual independence. Pryce-Jones also notes that critics regarded this position as insufficiently attentive to the constraints of culture and history. His account therefore documents a debate about Naipaul's outlook. The accompanying bibliography records books spanning these concerns, including India: A Wounded Civilization and Beyond Belief. The essay's judgments are critical interpretations, rather than neutral descriptions of whole societies.

terms.definition: Writing that builds an account of the past from documents and other evidence; Naipaul combined it with several literary forms.
The Academy's metaphor for Naipaul as a writer whose travels and research ranged across societies shaped by empire.
A person's capacity to make choices and act within historical and social circumstances, a central concern in this interpretation of Naipaul.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A conserved control system across different organisms
sections.body: Hartwell identified CDC genes in baker's yeast, including CDC28, which controls the Start step of the cycle. Nurse found the related cdc2 regulator in a distantly related yeast. In 1987 he isolated the corresponding human gene by introducing human genetic material into yeast and showing that it could supply the required function. This demonstrated conservation of the control mechanism across a large evolutionary distance. Hunt's sea-urchin experiments identified cyclin, whose amount rose before division and then fell abruptly. Together these findings connected genetic control, a kinase regulator and periodic protein destruction as parts of the cell-cycle system.

sections.heading: Kinases, cyclins and controlled progression
sections.body: Before dividing, a cell must copy and distribute its chromosomes in the proper sequence. CDK proteins help drive these transitions by phosphorylating other proteins. The cdc2 gene studied by Nurse encodes such a kinase; the human counterpart became known as CDK1. Cyclins regulate CDK activity, and Hunt's discovery that they are periodically destroyed revealed an important way to change that activity during the cycle. Hartwell's checkpoint concept explained how progression can be halted when DNA is damaged or an earlier step is incomplete. The mechanisms help coordinate division; defects can contribute to the chromosome abnormalities seen in cancer cells.

sections.heading: Genetic research methods using yeast and temperature-sensitive mutants
sections.body: To investigate cellular DNA synthesis, Leland Hartwell utilized Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a model eukaryotic organism for genetic studies. He employed the isolation of temperature-sensitive mutants to analyze macromolecule synthesis and cell division at restrictive temperatures. This methodology drew from his previous experience with conditional mutants in phage morphogenesis. While working in Seattle, he also utilized time-lapse photomicroscopy to observe the cell cycle. His research direction was influenced by suggestions to find a single-celled eukaryote with accessible genetics for studying growth control.

terms.definition: Control mechanisms that delay progression when required events have not been completed or when damage needs attention.
Adding a phosphate group to a molecule; CDKs use this chemical modification to alter the behaviour of other proteins.
Genetic variants that function normally at one temperature but develop a defect at another, allowing the affected biological process to be investigated.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The UN's institutions and development ambitions
sections.body: The Nobel presentation contrasted the UN with the failed League of Nations. A stronger Security Council combined an ambition of universal membership with special powers for major states, including authority to use force to maintain peace. The speech noted that the planned standing forces had still not materialised in 2001. It placed the UN's humanitarian and social achievements alongside these institutional limits. Annan's report on the organisation's role in the new century also informed the Millennium Declaration. The declaration linked poverty, education, HIV/AIDS and environmental protection with the prevention of armed conflict, showing how broadly the UN understood the conditions for peace.

sections.heading: Human rights and the limits of state power
sections.body: The committee praised Annan's efforts to renew the UN while recognising that its capacity depended on what member states permitted. His concern for more effective use of limited resources accompanied a wider argument about accountability: sovereignty should not enable governments to hide human rights violations. The announcement placed this position beside the UN's established security responsibilities and its responses to HIV/AIDS and international terrorism. Awarding the institution itself, alongside its Secretary-General, also expressed the committee's commitment to cooperation through the UN despite its recorded setbacks. This was a judgment about the importance of collective institutions, not a claim that they had solved the problems they addressed.

sections.heading: UN Reform and Global Health Initiatives
sections.body: As Secretary-General, Annan implemented a comprehensive reform programme to revitalize the organization. He promoted the rule of law and human dignity while strengthening traditional work in international security. To address global crises, he proposed a Global AIDS and Health Fund through his 2001 Call to Action. Additionally, he introduced the Global Compact to encourage businesses to respect environmental, employment, and human rights standards. His 2000 report outlined essential actions for ending poverty, improving education, and protecting populations from violence.

terms.definition: An agenda adopted by national leaders in 2000, informed by Annan's report and setting shared ambitions for development, human welfare and peace.
A state's authority to govern itself; Annan argued that this authority should not shield human rights violations from scrutiny.
An initiative designed to encourage businesses to uphold specific standards regarding the environment, employment laws, and human rights.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental methods for achieving Bose-Einstein condensation
sections.body: To reach temperatures around 100 nanokelvin, researchers used advanced cooling and trapping techniques for neutral atoms. Laser cooling followed by evaporative cooling reduced typical atomic speeds to a few millimetres per second. The experiments kept the atoms in dilute gases; rubidium-87 and sodium-23 have integer atomic spin and weak repulsive interactions. Experiments with sodium demonstrated that portions of a condensate could be released in pulses, producing an atom-laser effect. Overlapping condensates also showed interference patterns, revealing coherent behaviour of matter waves.

sections.heading: Experimental methods for achieving atomic condensation
sections.body: To reach temperatures below one millionth of a kelvin, researchers combined laser-based cooling and trapping with evaporative cooling, which removes energetic atoms so the remaining gas becomes colder. Wieman helped establish this approach, and Cornell solved a remaining obstacle after extensive work by the Colorado team. Their rubidium results were reported in 1995. Working independently, Ketterle produced larger sodium condensates later that year. Experiments with their interference demonstrated coherent matter waves, and controlled release of atoms from the condensate produced an early atom-laser beam.

sections.heading: Condensates as coherent matter waves
sections.body: Cornell and Wieman produced a condensate of about 2,000 rubidium atoms at 20 nanokelvin in 1995. Ketterle independently produced larger condensates using sodium, allowing additional experiments on their properties. When two condensates expanded into one another, their overlapping matter waves formed a pattern of alternating density. This showed coherent wave behaviour, rather than atoms simply behaving as independent classical particles. Ketterle also released successive portions of a condensate that fell under gravity. These pulses provided an early atom-laser demonstration: coherent matter emerging from a trapped condensate, analogous in a limited sense to coherent light from an optical laser.

terms.definition: Particles with integer spin that can occupy the same quantum state; many can accumulate in the lowest-energy state at sufficiently low temperature.
Cooling a trapped gas by allowing its more energetic atoms to escape, lowering the energy and temperature of the atoms that remain.
Alternating regions of stronger and weaker signal produced when waves overlap; here, the visible pattern appeared in the density of expanding atoms.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Turning large molecules into measurable ions
sections.body: Mass spectrometry requires ions in the gas phase, a challenge for large proteins that can fragment during preparation. Fenn's electrospray forms charged droplets from a solution. As solvent evaporates and droplets divide, protein ions become available for analysis. Multiple charges reduce the mass-to-charge ratio enough for conventional instruments to handle large molecules. Tanaka demonstrated that suitable laser-desorption conditions could also release large molecules without destroying them. These techniques analyse prepared samples; they do not simply weigh proteins inside an intact living cell. Wüthrich's NMR work addressed a complementary question by obtaining structural information from proteins in solution.

sections.heading: Mass measurements and structural constraints
sections.body: Mass spectrometers distinguish ions by mass-to-charge ratio. Flight-time methods are one way to do this, but mass spectrometry is not limited to that instrument design, and charge matters as well as mass. Fenn and Tanaka made large biomolecules accessible as ions through different preparation methods. Wüthrich instead tackled overlapping NMR signals from proteins. Assigning signals to particular nuclei and obtaining information about distances between them supplied constraints for calculating three-dimensional structures. The result was a model consistent with molecular measurements in solution, rather than an ordinary photograph of the protein.

sections.heading: Learning precision measurement through electrolyte research
sections.body: At Yale, Fenn worked with Gosta “Gus” Akerlof on electrolyte solutions. He measured voltages between platinum–hydrogen and silver–silver chloride electrodes in hydrochloric-acid solutions with different concentrations and methanol–water mixtures. He prepared three pairs of cells, allowed them to equilibrate overnight and checked that duplicate readings agreed. A controlled water bath then allowed measurements at successive temperatures, usually ten degrees apart. He recalled obtaining about 3,000 acceptable readings. This demanding routine developed experience in controlling conditions and checking reproducibility, decades before his work on electrospray ionisation.

terms.definition: Releasing large molecules from a sample with laser energy under conditions that preserve sufficiently intact ions for mass analysis.
Measurement of the resonant responses of certain atomic nuclei in a magnetic field, used to investigate their molecular surroundings and relationships.
The voltage a source such as an electrochemical cell provides when no current is drawn; Fenn measured it between pairs of electrodes.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Testing Economic Models Through Laboratory Experiments
sections.body: Smith and his colleagues compared auction rules in controlled markets. In the experiments described by the committee, English ascending-bid auctions and sealed-bid second-price auctions produced similar seller revenues. Dutch descending-price auctions and first-price sealed-bid auctions behaved differently, despite a theoretical prediction of equivalence. These are findings for the studied conditions, rather than a universal ranking of auction formats. Smith also used computer-assisted experiments to evaluate airport-slot allocation and energy-market arrangements in Australia and New Zealand. Such trials offered a way to investigate complicated rules before implementation. Monetary rewards were designed both to motivate participants and to improve the relevance of laboratory behaviour to larger real markets.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of psychological and experimental economic research
sections.body: Kahneman and Amos Tversky investigated shortcuts in judgement, including excessive confidence in small samples. People could give a small sample’s average as much weight as a large sample’s, overlooking greater sampling uncertainty. Prospect theory also described choices relative to a reference point, rather than only absolute wealth. Smith investigated another question: how people interact under market rules. His experimental buyers and sellers were not told the overall supply and demand conditions, yet trading prices could approach the theoretical equilibrium. Further experiments showed that the rules of exchange affected price adjustment. The findings concerned specific patterns in decisions and institutions, rather than a blanket verdict on rationality.

sections.heading: When remembered discomfort shapes later choices
sections.body: Kahneman distinguished experienced utility—how an outcome feels while it happens—from utility inferred from subsequent choices. In one experiment described in his biography, participants immersed a hand in painfully cold water for sixty seconds. A second episode repeated those sixty seconds and added thirty more during which the water became slightly warmer but remained painful. Most participants chose to repeat the longer episode. Its improved ending left a less unpleasant memory despite the extra discomfort. Kahneman and his collaborators used such findings to investigate how peak intensity and the ending of an experience shape recollection, while duration can receive little weight. This separates a specific memory effect from a general preference for longer experiences.

terms.definition: A sealed-bid auction in which the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest submitted bid.
An ironic name for the mistaken belief that small samples represent a population about as reliably as large samples.
The pleasure or discomfort of an outcome as it is actually experienced, distinguished from what later choices or recollections imply.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Interconnectedness of Kertész's literary works
sections.body: The Nobel presentation invites readers to follow connections across Kertész’s books rather than treat each as isolated. It links Fiasco, with its account of a writer’s difficulties under a totalitarian system, to The English Flag and the reflective fragments of Galley Diary. It also connects Kaddish for a Child Not Born with Fateless through themes and allusions. The speech uses organic and musical metaphors to describe this unity: separate texts contribute to a larger body of work. Its central interpretation is that Kertész repeatedly examines an individual’s resistance to losing personal will within a collective identity. References to other writers become part of that continuing literary conversation.

sections.heading: Existential analysis of individual survival and conformity
sections.body: The announcement interprets Fateless through its unsettling narrative distance. The young Köves responds to camp life through immediate practical experiences, often without the explanations or moral language a reader expects. This exposes the reader to both brutality and the disturbing capacity to adapt. The committee connects that problem with Kaddish for a Child Not Born, reading its treatment of childhood, love and continued existence as an inquiry into conformity. These are interpretations of literary voices and situations, not claims that persecution was acceptable or that survivors endorsed it. Galley Diary extends the inquiry through fragments engaging writers and thinkers including Kafka and Camus, maintaining the individual perspective against collective explanations.

sections.heading: Literary influences and the trilogy of György Köves
sections.body: Kertész supported himself partly by translating German-language writers, including Nietzsche, Freud and Wittgenstein, whose work influenced his prose. His biography distinguishes Fateless from straightforward autobiography: it uses an autobiographical novel’s form while transforming experience into fiction. The book’s difficult publication and reception became material for Fiasco. The biography presents that novel, Fateless and Kaddish for a Child Not Born as a commonly recognised trilogy, connected by the problem of living and writing after Auschwitz. Galley Diary takes another form, gathering fictionalised diary material spanning 1961–1991. A later volume continued the inner monologue through notes from 1991–1995. These changing forms let him revisit experience without making every work a literal life record.

terms.definition: The body of work produced by an artist or writer, considered together rather than as isolated pieces.
The relationship between a narrator’s way of understanding events and the perspective or judgement a reader brings to them.
Fiction shaped by the author’s life experiences while remaining a constructed narrative rather than a direct factual account.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A reproducible pattern of cell death
sections.body: Brenner made the small worm Caenorhabditis elegans an experimental model for linking genes to development. His 1974 work showed that mutations could produce visible changes in organ formation. Sulston exploited the animal's transparency to follow cell divisions and construct a lineage: a record of which cells give rise to which descendants. Particular cells repeatedly died at predictable stages, showing that their elimination formed part of normal development. Horvitz then systematically searched for genes controlling that process. The findings turned an observable pattern of cell loss into a biological mechanism whose genetic components could be tested experimentally.

sections.heading: Different genes control death and cleanup
sections.body: Genetic experiments distinguished several steps in cell elimination. Sulston found that nuc-1 was needed to degrade DNA in cells that had died. Horvitz identified ced-3 and ced-4 as genes required for the death process itself. The gene ced-9 had a protective role, preventing cells from entering that process. This distinction matters: failure to destroy a dead cell's DNA is different from failure to kill the cell. Related genes were subsequently identified in humans, connecting the worm experiments to conserved mechanisms of cell survival and elimination. These studies helped explain how development depends on regulated cell loss as well as cell production.

sections.heading: Sydney Brenner's scientific training and early research
sections.body: Brenner began medical studies at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg at fifteen. Because he would have been too young to practise medicine when the course ended, he was allowed to spend a year on a research-oriented anatomy and physiology degree. Working in small groups introduced him to microscopy, physical chemistry and experiments on cells. He stayed for further research and an MSc in cytogenetics, supporting himself partly as a laboratory technician. His early publications included work on histochemical reactions. This training in observing cells, building equipment and investigating chromosomes preceded his later work in molecular genetics and C. elegans development.

terms.definition: Cell elimination controlled by biological mechanisms, including the reproducible removal of particular cells during normal development.
A gene related to another through common evolutionary ancestry; corresponding genes in different organisms can retain related functions.
The study of chromosomes and their relationship to heredity and variation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Methods of mediation and human rights advocacy
sections.body: The Nobel speech connected Carter’s presidential diplomacy with his later mediation. His administration negotiated the Panama Canal treaties, while his post-presidential work included the 1994 effort in Haiti. He sought to broaden mediation through the International Negotiation Network, which included several Nobel Peace laureates. By the 2002 award, the committee reported that Carter and his centre’s staff had observed about three dozen elections in twenty countries. It credited the development of observation procedures as well as individual missions. Human rights linked these activities across different stages of his career. The speech treated negotiation, election observation and institution-building as complementary ways of pursuing peace, rather than limiting his contribution to formal diplomatic office.

sections.heading: Post-presidency conflict resolution and global health initiatives
sections.body: Through the Carter Center, which reached its twentieth anniversary in 2002, Carter pursued extensive conflict resolution across multiple continents. His work involved serving as an observer for numerous worldwide elections to support democratic processes. Beyond political mediation, he engaged in efforts to combat tropical diseases and foster economic growth within developing nations. These activities utilized principles of international law and cooperation to address global challenges, emphasizing human rights and social development even during periods characterized by the threat of power-based force.

sections.heading: Diplomatic achievements and presidential foreign policy
sections.body: Carter’s administration negotiated major international agreements, including the Panama Canal treaties, the Camp David Accords, the Egypt–Israel peace treaty and SALT II with the Soviet Union. It also established diplomatic relations with the People’s Republic of China. These were distinct diplomatic processes, with different requirements for putting agreements into effect. His biography places them alongside a domestic programme that created the Departments of Energy and Education, changed regulation in several industries, and expanded environmental protection. It specifically identifies the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act. This broader record provides context for a peace award that also recognised two decades of work after the presidency.

terms.definition: A network including several Peace Prize Laureates used by Carter to create a broader foundation for mediation efforts.
An organization used by Jimmy Carter to conduct long-term conflict resolution, election observation, and initiatives to fight tropical diseases.
Negotiated limits or other agreed rules concerning weapons and military capabilities.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Investigating a shortage of solar neutrinos
sections.body: Davis extracted tiny numbers of argon atoms produced by neutrino interactions in chlorine-rich liquid. The total was below expectations, and control experiments tested whether inefficient recovery could explain the deficit. Kamiokande supplied different information: light flashes registered individual event times and directions, connecting the signal with the Sun. Its successor, Super-Kamiokande, later found atmospheric-neutrino behaviour indicating changes between neutrino types. The official explanation linked such oscillations with the solar-neutrino puzzle and with non-zero neutrino mass. Thus, instruments built to investigate stars also exposed questions in particle physics. The result depended on complementary measurements, rather than treating a low count alone as proof of a new particle property.

sections.heading: Going underground and above the atmosphere
sections.body: The experiments required different ways of avoiding interference. Davis and Koshiba placed neutrino detectors deep underground to reduce background signals, while neutrinos could still reach them. Cosmic X-rays, by contrast, are absorbed by the atmosphere, requiring instruments carried above it. Giacconi’s pioneering 1962 rocket experiment sought solar X-rays reflected from the Moon. Instead it revealed a strong cosmic signal and an X-ray source beyond the Solar System. Further telescope and satellite development made these high-energy sources accessible to detailed study. The new view included compact objects releasing enormous amounts of energy, with some sources interpreted as containing black holes.

sections.heading: Large instruments for very rare interactions
sections.body: The announcement illustrates the scale mismatch between a detector and the events it records. Davis’s tank held roughly six hundred tonnes of liquid, yet over decades it yielded evidence for only about two thousand solar-neutrino interactions. In February 1987, the Kamiokande team registered twelve events from a supernova burst even though an estimated ten quadrillion neutrinos passed through the detector. Large amounts of material and sensitive measurements were necessary because interactions were so rare. Those few events nevertheless supplied evidence about a distant stellar explosion. Detecting particles from the Sun and a supernova established a way to investigate astronomical processes alongside observations of light.

terms.definition: Changes in the probability of detecting a neutrino as different types, or flavours, as it travels.
Study of celestial sources through their X-ray emission, using instruments above the atmosphere because air absorbs most cosmic X-rays.
Investigation of astronomical sources and processes by detecting neutrinos that reach Earth.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of water and ion transport
sections.body: Agre tested water transport both in cells and in liposomes, artificial membrane vesicles. Adding the candidate protein increased water permeability, while mercury inhibited transport through it. MacKinnon's 1998 structure of the bacterial KcsA channel explained a different kind of selectivity. Potassium ions shed their surrounding water molecules on entering the narrow filter. Oxygen atoms in the protein then provide an arrangement resembling the ion's interactions with water. The smaller sodium ion is not accommodated in the same favourable way. Thus the filter selects ions through the molecular interactions that replace their water shell, rather than simply admitting every ion small enough to enter.

sections.heading: Unexpected findings and deliberate structural research
sections.body: Agre encountered the protein later identified as a water channel while investigating another problem in red blood cells. Recognising the significance of that unexpected result required further experiments on the protein's function. MacKinnon pursued a different challenge: obtaining an atomic-level structure of an ion channel, a difficult membrane protein. Together, the discoveries connected everyday physiology with particular molecular structures. Water recovery by the kidneys depends on controlled water movement, while movements of ions across nerve-cell membranes contribute to electrical signalling. The award highlighted both the value of pursuing an unexpected observation and the deliberate development of methods for a demanding structural question.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of membrane transport and ion channel signaling
sections.body: The protein Agre isolated in 1988 was subsequently established to function as a water channel. Its identification enabled biochemical, physiological and genetic investigations of related channels in bacteria, plants and mammals. Researchers could examine how such pores admit water while excluding ions and other molecules. MacKinnon's potassium-channel structure addressed the selective movement of charged particles. Ion channels also have gates that respond to cellular signals, controlling when ions can cross the membrane. Coordinated channel opening and closing supports electrical pulses in nerves and is important in muscle function. These mechanisms connect molecular selectivity with controlled transport across the surfaces of cells.

terms.definition: Net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane towards a solution with a higher effective concentration of substances that cannot cross.
An unexpected scientific finding that occurs while a researcher is actively working to solve an entirely different problem.
An electrical pulse propagated along a nerve cell surface through the sequential opening and closing of ion channels.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Analyzing Long-Run Economic Equilibrium and Short-Run Fluctuations
sections.body: Researchers use time series to study macroeconomic variables like consumption or GDP. While many series are nonstationary, Granger discovered that combining multiple nonstationary variables can create a stationary combination. This allows for studying long-run equilibrium relationships, such as between exchange rates and price levels, despite short-term deviations. In 1987, Engle and Granger introduced methods to test for cointegration and estimate error-correction models. These tools help identify how variables adjust toward equilibrium after random disturbances, capturing both simultaneous adjustment forces and temporary fluctuations around an adjustment path.

sections.heading: Forecasting changing volatility
sections.body: Engle investigated a feature that constant-volatility models missed: financial markets alternate between calmer periods and periods of large fluctuations. The ARCH approach models systematic changes in uncertainty over time, using patterns in observed data to forecast volatility. This became useful for comparing the risk of assets, valuing derivatives and assessing portfolios exposed to large losses. The Nobel presentation noted that the work began partly from questions about macroeconomic uncertainty before finding especially broad applications in finance. Its contribution was a way to model the changing size of unpredictable movements, alongside models of an average trend or return.

sections.heading: Statistical modeling of volatility and nonstationary economic data
sections.body: Many macroeconomic series contain persistent trends: a disturbance can alter their future path for a long time. Applying methods designed for stationary data to such series can produce misleading results. Granger's work showed that particular combinations of nonstationary variables can nevertheless be stationary. This lets researchers investigate relationships constrained in the long run even when individual series fluctuate substantially in the short run. Wealth and consumption, or exchange rates and price levels, provide examples of the questions that motivated the approach. Recognising the statistical properties of the data therefore becomes part of choosing a credible model of economic relationships.

terms.definition: A stationary combination of nonstationary variables that allows researchers to identify long-run relationships between economic factors despite short-run deviations.
The degree of variability in a series, such as financial returns, used as one measure of uncertainty and risk.
Describing a time series whose statistical properties change over time, for example through a persistent stochastic trend.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Allegory and resistance in Coetzee's prose
sections.body: The Academy's presentation emphasised Coetzee's use of invented situations to explore power and moral responsibility. In Life and Times of Michael K., it reads the protagonist's withdrawal from war, money and authority as a form of resistance that frustrates opposing political forces. Its discussion of Waiting for the Barbarians connects the wish to possess another person with the desire to explain and control them. Coetzee's restrained language gives these conflicts intensity. The presentation also identifies his defence of literature and imagination as ways to understand lives that power silences or despises.

sections.heading: Literary themes and structural techniques in Coetzee's novels
sections.body: In the Heart of the Country makes the reader depend on a woman's contradictory notes, leaving the sequence of events uncertain. Foe turns attention towards storytelling itself: its narrator wants a place in a major narrative but is offered a smaller role. The Academy also highlighted the variety of Coetzee's forms, including the fictionalised self-examination of Boyhood and Youth. Across these different books, it identified a recurring pattern in which loss of status can expose both vulnerability and unexpected strength. These formal choices make questions about power and moral judgment part of the reader's experience.

sections.heading: Academic background and literary bibliography
sections.body: Coetzee earned honors degrees in English and mathematics from the University of Cape Town before completing a PhD at the University of Texas at Austin. His doctoral research focused on the early fiction of Samuel Beckett. Throughout his career, he held various academic roles, including serving as a professor at the University of Cape Town and teaching at institutions like Harvard and the University of Chicago. His notable bibliography includes works such as In the Heart of the Country, which earned the CNA Prize, and the Booker Prize-winning Disgrace.

terms.definition: A narrative whose characters and events invite broader political, moral or philosophical meanings beyond the literal story.
A novel that draws attention to storytelling and the making of narratives, as Foe does through its narrator's struggle over her story.
A work that uses a fictional speaker and lecture setting to explore ideas through narrative, as in The Lives of Animals.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Adding location to magnetic-resonance signals
sections.body: Nuclear magnetic resonance had been used to investigate chemical compounds through their spectra. Lauterbur introduced magnetic-field gradients so the signals also carried information about where they originated. Analysing those signals allowed a two-dimensional image to be reconstructed. Mansfield developed further uses of gradients and mathematical analysis that made reconstruction more effective, and demonstrated possibilities for rapid imaging. Together these contributions turned resonance measurements into a spatial method for examining internal structures. The medical importance lay in obtaining useful images from physical differences within tissues, rather than requiring an invasive view of the organ itself.

sections.heading: Water tubes and faster image acquisition
sections.body: In 1973, Lauterbur described an image of ordinary-water tubes surrounded by heavy water. Adding field gradients let him locate the signals and reconstruct a cross-section, illustrating how resonance information could become an image. Mansfield developed methods for analysing spatially encoded signals and for collecting them much faster. His echo-planar approach used rapid gradient changes. The 2003 announcement noted that this technique became useful in clinical practice about a decade after its development. The history therefore involved both the initial physical demonstration and subsequent improvements needed to make imaging practical.

sections.heading: From tissue measurements to spatial imaging
sections.body: While temporarily leading a company in New Kensington, Lauterbur observed measurements on tissue specimens from tumour-bearing rats. Normal and tumour samples showed different proton relaxation behaviour, but he considered those measurements alone too complex and insufficiently understood for reliable medical decisions. He began thinking about how to locate NMR signals within an object and form images of their distribution. This episode belonged to his company work, not his earlier Army Chemical Center service. Later publications explored spatially resolved NMR, tumour imaging and ways magnetic agents could change tissue-water signals. His biography connects the imaging idea with a wish to investigate intact objects more usefully.

terms.definition: The response of magnetic atomic nuclei to radio-frequency excitation in a magnetic field, producing signals that can reveal properties of the surrounding material.
A rapid MRI acquisition method using fast changes in magnetic-field gradients to collect spatial information.
Lauterbur's early term for forming images by combining NMR measurements with spatial information introduced through magnetic-field gradients.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Children's rights and equal citizenship
sections.body: The 2003 presentation described Ebadi as the founder and leader of the Association for Support of Children's Rights in Iran. At that time, it reported around 5,000 members, a Tehran centre, school information materials and an emergency telephone service for children. The committee hoped the award would bring wider attention to children's rights. It also highlighted her advocacy for refugees and for citizens whose rights were threatened because of religion, ethnicity or political opinion. Her opposition to unequal treatment of women belonged to this broader insistence on equality before the law. These examples show how legal advocacy could extend into education, practical support and public debate.

sections.heading: Principles of non-violence and democratic governance
sections.body: Ebadi advocates for political authority to be established through democratic elections. Her approach to resolving conflicts and altering societal attitudes relies on the use of dialogue and enlightenment. Within her framework, she maintains that there is no contradiction between Islamic faith and fundamental human rights. She promotes a method of intercultural engagement that utilizes shared values as a starting point for communication between different religions and cultures, while consistently supporting non-violence during eras of global conflict.

sections.heading: From judicial office to human rights cases
sections.body: After a law degree and six months of judicial training, Ebadi began serving as a judge in March 1969. She obtained a doctorate in private law in 1971 and became President of Bench 24 of Tehran's City Court in 1975. Following the 1979 revolution, she and other women judges were removed from judicial posts and assigned clerical work. After early retirement and years without permission to practise, she gained a lawyer's licence in 1992. Her later clients included relatives of people killed in political murders or a university-dormitory attack. She also handled child-abuse and press-related cases.

terms.definition: The ability to communicate opinions and ideas; Ebadi defended this right across differences of religion, ethnicity and political belief.
A method used to resolve conflicts and change attitudes by focusing on the shared values between different cultures and religions.
The process of deciding legal cases, for which Ebadi trained before beginning her work as a judge.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Magnetic vortices and different forms of superfluid order
sections.body: Abrikosov used the Ginzburg–Landau framework to explain how magnetic flux can enter a type-II superconductor through vortices. More vortices appear as the applied field increases; at sufficiently high field, superconductivity disappears as their cores overlap. The theory therefore describes a material remaining superconducting while admitting magnetic flux within a particular range of fields. Leggett addressed a different problem: superfluid helium-3. Its paired atoms have internal and magnetic degrees of freedom, allowing several distinct kinds of order. The resulting phases depend on temperature, pressure and magnetic field. His framework helped connect this structure with the measurements experimentalists observed.

sections.heading: Describing collective order mathematically
sections.body: Ginzburg and Landau introduced an order parameter to describe the superconducting state and how it responds to currents and magnetic fields. Abrikosov showed that solutions with vortices explain how magnetic flux can coexist with superconductivity in type-II materials. Superfluid helium-3 requires a richer description. Its fermionic atoms form pairs whose internal motion and spin permit several arrangements. The order parameter has eighteen real components, rather than the two used in the simplest superconducting description. Leggett connected these possible forms of order with observable properties, giving experiments a framework for distinguishing and investigating the superfluid phases.

sections.heading: Type-II superconductors and vortex structures
sections.body: Working with N.V. Zavaritskii, Abrikosov tested Ginzburg–Landau predictions for the critical magnetic fields of thin films. He then studied bulk type-II superconductors, showing that their magnetic response changes between two limiting fields. Within that range, magnetic flux enters in narrow structures surrounded by circulating currents. These quantum vortices can form a regular Abrikosov vortex lattice. His wider research also included gapless superconductivity, the response of superconductors to high-frequency fields, and the thermodynamics and kinetics of nonsuperfluid helium-3.

terms.definition: In a type-II superconductor, a structure with circulating superconducting current around a core through which magnetic flux penetrates.
A mathematical quantity describing a collectively ordered state; it may require several components to capture the different arrangements a system permits.
A regular structure formed by thin threads of magnetic flux that penetrate a superconductor between two limiting critical fields.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: How a protein receives a degradation signal
sections.body: The pathway uses several steps. ATP-dependent activation prepares ubiquitin through an E1 enzyme; E2 carries it, and E3 helps select a target and attach the label. Repetition can build a ubiquitin chain that the proteasome recognises. The tag is removed for reuse as the target is unfolded and passed into the proteasome, where it is cut into peptides. This makes degradation selective rather than indiscriminate. Ubiquitin attachment can be reversed; destruction of the target protein is the irreversible outcome. The distinction matters because a regulatory tag and the process it triggers are not the same event.

sections.heading: Why controlled destruction requires energy
sections.body: The laureates investigated an ATP-dependent system of protein breakdown in cell extracts. They found a tagging pathway involving three classes of enzymes. Energy activates ubiquitin and supports the controlled processing that selects and disposes of targets. The small tag can be recovered and reused. The ceremony emphasised that destruction is more than removal of defective proteins: eliminating a functioning protein can switch off or change a cellular process. Such regulation contributes to cell-cycle progression, DNA repair and immune defence. This explains why a carefully controlled route to breakdown is as important as making proteins in the first place.

sections.heading: Protein turnover as a means of regulation
sections.body: Selective protein destruction allows a cell to change its activity by removing particular molecules at a particular time. The award announcement linked this control with division, DNA repair, quality control of newly made proteins and parts of immune defence. It also connected disturbances in the pathway with disease, mentioning cystic fibrosis and cervical cancer as examples of its medical relevance. Understanding the mechanism opened opportunities for drug research. These were reasons to investigate the pathway further, rather than evidence that the discovery had already supplied treatments for every disease named.

terms.definition: Attaching a chain of ubiquitin molecules to a protein; particular chain signals can direct that protein toward proteasomal degradation.
A small protein that can be attached to other proteins as a regulatory tag, including signals directing selected targets to degradation.
A large cellular protein complex that unfolds and cuts selected proteins into smaller peptides as part of regulated protein breakdown.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Integrating economic growth and business cycle analysis
sections.body: In their 1982 article, the researchers established microeconomic foundations for analyzing business cycles by integrating them with long-run growth studies. Their model utilized assumptions of profit-maximizing firms and utility-maximizing consumers to examine how productivity growth variations transmit through investments and relative price movements. This approach demonstrated that supply-side fluctuations can generate short-run economic movements around a long-run path. By studying the transmission of technology growth rates, they showed that cyclical changes in consumption, investment, and GDP could originate from the economy's supply side.

sections.heading: Comparing a simulated economy with observations
sections.body: Kydland and Prescott’s 1982 model showed how changes in technological progress could generate fluctuations resembling much of the postwar United States business-cycle pattern. This was evidence that supply-side disturbances could matter greatly, rather than proof that they explain every recession. Their approach also changed how models were constructed and compared with data. Information from studies of individual economic behaviour helped calibrate a model, which was then simulated to produce artificial time series for macroeconomic variables. Household and firm decisions were coordinated through wages, prices and interest rates. The resulting fluctuations could be compared with observed patterns in consumption, investment and output.

sections.heading: Commitment problems even with shared objectives
sections.body: Kydland recalled adapting computer programs from the collaborators’ policy research to calculate equilibria in business-cycle models. Early versions used linear technology and quadratic household utility functions. A separate 1980 paper examined a growth model in which labour and capital taxes financed government purchases. Within that model, low capital taxation served the representative household’s welfare, but an inability to commit could lead to higher taxes. The example addressed a misconception: time inconsistency need not arise because policymakers want something different from the public. Their model deliberately gave the government the same preferences as the otherwise identical households. The difficulty was maintaining a previously desirable plan when later incentives changed.

terms.definition: The efficiency with which productive inputs are turned into output; changes in it can affect investment, prices and economic growth.
An account of aggregate economic behaviour built from models of the decisions and interactions of individual households and firms.
A situation in which a plan chosen as best initially would no longer be chosen when the time comes to implement it.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Linguistic manipulation and genre deconstruction
sections.body: The Nobel presentation describes Jelinek’s writing as an investigation of the assumptions hidden in ordinary language. Advertising, news, pornography, popular fiction and television supply phrases and patterns that she rearranges until their violence or absurdity becomes visible. Her prose resists the relief of smooth, conventional storytelling. The speech connects Women as Lovers, Wonderful, Wonderful Times, The Piano Teacher, Lust and Gier with different forms of domination and submission. It also describes her theatrical writing as material organised around speech rather than conventional character roles. Distorted quotations and macabre images unsettle familiar cultural pictures, including idyllic representations of Austria. This is the committee’s account of how literary form carries her social criticism, rather than a claim that the reproduced prejudices express her own beliefs.

sections.heading: Evolution of Jelinek's linguistic and dramatic techniques
sections.body: Jelinek’s musical training overlapped with her emergence as a writer: her first poetry collection appeared in 1967, before she completed her organist diploma in 1971. Early satirical novels such as wir sind lockvögel baby! challenged popular culture’s promises of a good life. The Academy’s 2004 notes then trace a growing emphasis on drama. In works including Totenauberg and Raststätte, speech carries multiple psychological and historical voices instead of simply distinguishing realistic characters. The notes describe the resulting encounters as clashes between kinds of language. Her princess dramas similarly examine the stereotypes through which women are imagined and constrained. These techniques connect gender and class criticism with the organisation of the text itself.

terms.definition: A familiar expression or representation repeated until it seems self-evident; Jelinek reworks such material to expose its underlying assumptions.
Extended speeches that interweave different voices, registers or perspectives, rather than functioning solely as the speech of one psychologically unified character.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Elfriede Jelinek — Swedish Academy bio-bibliographical notes

sections.heading: Genetic structure of mouse olfactory receptors
sections.body: The mouse studies described in the 2004 presentation revealed an unusually large family of receptor genes, estimated at about a thousand. An individual olfactory sensory cell expresses one receptor type. Cells expressing the same type send their nerve fibres to particular small regions of the olfactory bulb. Other neurons then relay information towards cortical regions involved in smell perception. This organisation preserves information about which receptor populations were activated. Because an odorant can stimulate a combination of receptor types, the pattern across these pathways helps distinguish smells. A receptor's identity therefore matters both for detecting molecules and for organising their representation in the brain.

sections.heading: Organization of the olfactory system and receptor genes
sections.body: Odorant receptors belong to the family of G protein-coupled receptors. When an odorant activates one, signalling through G proteins leads to production of cyclic AMP and the opening of ion channels. The resulting electrical signal travels along the sensory cell's nerve fibre towards the olfactory bulb. Cells with the same receptor type converge on specialised regions called glomeruli. Information from different receptor populations is subsequently combined in other brain regions. This links a molecular event at the nose's surface to a pattern of neural activity: the first stage identifies chemical features, while later stages combine those signals into the perception of a smell.

sections.heading: Using genes to investigate sensory perception
sections.body: Before the olfaction work, Axel's laboratory developed methods for introducing DNA into cultured mammalian cells, with important contributions from Michael Wigler and Sol Silverstein. These techniques made it possible to investigate gene function as well as isolate genes. Axel and Linda Buck later approached smell as a problem in molecular recognition: how could receptors detect such a wide variety of odorous substances? They expected a large gene family, and Buck devised the experimental approach that identified it. Axel's biography recalls the late-night presentation of her results. Subsequent genetic manipulation in mice helped connect receptor identity with the organisation of sensory pathways.

terms.definition: A signalling pathway that preserves information about a particular receptor type through connections and relays to other brain regions.
Micro domains in the olfactory bulb where nerve processes from receptor cells carrying the same receptor type converge.
Genes encoding proteins that detect odorant molecules and initiate signalling in olfactory sensory cells.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Environmental protection as a path to peace
sections.body: The Norwegian Nobel Committee recognized that securing the living environment is essential for global stability. Maathai addressed deforestation and soil erosion, which destroyed livestock grazing areas and forced women to travel further for cooking wood. By founding the Green Belt Movement, she mobilized women to plant millions of trees to combat desertification. Her activism also included protesting a proposed 62-storey skyscraper in Nairobi's Uhuru Park. This holistic approach links ecological preservation with human rights, democracy, and sustainable social, economic, and cultural development.

sections.heading: Strategies for Sustainable Development and Grassroots Mobilization
sections.body: The 2004 announcement presented tree planting as part of a wider effort to improve people’s capacity to shape their lives. It credited the Green Belt Movement with mobilising poor women to plant thirty million trees over nearly three decades. Alongside environmental work, it described education, nutrition, family planning and resistance to corruption. Maathai’s challenges to Kenya’s former authoritarian government linked local organising with democratic rights. The committee emphasised that protecting existing forests was only one aspect of the programme: the movement also sought to strengthen the social conditions for lasting environmental care. These connections explain why a conservation initiative was recognised with a peace prize.

sections.heading: Expansion of the Pan African Green Belt Network
sections.body: Maathai introduced community tree planting while active in the National Council of Women of Kenya, before her later term as its chair. The idea developed into organising women’s groups around environmental conservation and livelihoods. In 1986 the Green Belt Movement established a Pan African network to share its methods. Participants adapted them in countries including Tanzania, Uganda, Malawi, Lesotho, Ethiopia and Zimbabwe. This spread involved training and local adaptation rather than simply extending one central planting operation. Maathai also served as a co-chair of the Jubilee 2000 Africa Campaign, which sought cancellation of debts that poor African countries could not repay. Her organising thus extended from land and forests to wider constraints on development.

terms.definition: Development that improves human living conditions while protecting the environmental basis on which those conditions depend.
Organising people within local communities to participate directly in collective action affecting their lives.
A campaign seeking cancellation of unpayable debts owed by poor African countries, linked to the international Jubilee 2000 initiative.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Testing the theory through particle showers
sections.body: Asymptotic freedom made the short-distance part of energetic collisions calculable. The official explanation uses electron–positron annihilation as an example: the collision can produce a quark and antiquark that move apart. Subsequent strong interactions turn their energy into showers of observable particles, retaining information about the original directions. Predicted probabilities for two-shower events could be compared with measurements. Three-shower events, observed at DESY in the late 1970s, supplied further evidence through their interpretation as gluon emission. These tests connected the mathematical description of quarks and gluons with patterns in detectors, even though the experiments did not observe isolated free quarks.

sections.heading: The mathematical discovery of asymptotic freedom
sections.body: The mathematical challenge was to find a theory whose effective interaction became weaker when probed at shorter distances. Calculations in familiar theories had suggested the opposite behaviour. In 1973, Gross and Wilczek, and independently Politzer, found the required negative sign in the scale dependence of a non-Abelian gauge interaction. That result made a consistent theory of the strong interaction possible. The sign described how the effective coupling changed, rather than a universal numerical value for a physical force. Subsequent accelerator tests compared predictions with measured processes. By the 2004 award, the committee highlighted their precision as evidence that the theoretical approach captured the observed behaviour of quarks.

sections.heading: The mathematical framework of Quantum Chromodynamics
sections.body: Quantum chromodynamics describes the strong interaction through quarks, gluons and colour charge. Asymptotic freedom explains why a high-energy probe can encounter quarks behaving approximately as independent particles inside a proton. At larger scales their interactions are strong, and the freely observable particles are bound combinations rather than isolated quarks. The award announcement used a stretched rubber band as an analogy for binding, but that image is not a literal force law. The achievement was to connect apparently incompatible observations within a mathematical framework: strong binding alongside weak effective interactions at very short distances. QCD became the strong-interaction part of the Standard Model.

terms.definition: The quantum-field framework describing elementary quarks, leptons and their electromagnetic, weak and strong interactions.
Weakening of an interaction’s effective coupling at sufficiently high energy scales or short distances.
The quantum theory of the strong interaction involving quarks, gluons and colour charge.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The intermediate that explains partner exchange
sections.body: Chauvin's mechanism places a metal–carbon double bond at the centre of metathesis. This metal alkylidene reacts with an alkene to form a four-membered ring containing one metal atom and three carbon atoms. Breaking a different pair of bonds opens the ring to produce a new alkene and a new metal alkylidene. Further reaction continues the exchange and regenerates a catalytic species. This cycle explains how groups attached to carbon–carbon double bonds can change partners. It also gave chemists a design principle: a useful catalyst needed a metal alkylidene that was reactive enough to enter the cycle yet stable enough to handle.

sections.heading: Development of efficient metathesis catalysts
sections.body: Understanding the reaction cycle left a practical challenge: designing catalysts with useful activity and selectivity. Schrock investigated different metals and the groups attached to them, presenting highly active molybdenum catalysts in 1990. Grubbs's ruthenium catalyst, reported in 1992, offered greater tolerance of ordinary handling conditions and higher selectivity, although the early comparison favoured Schrock's catalysts for reactivity. These properties presented chemists with different tools for different synthetic problems. By the 2005 award, metathesis had applications across pharmaceutical, polymer and other chemical industries. The advance joined fundamental mechanism research with compounds that could be used reliably in laboratories and production.

sections.heading: Why a shorter synthesis can matter
sections.body: The 2005 announcement emphasised practical consequences of improved metathesis catalysts. A useful reaction can replace a longer sequence of transformations, reducing the number of operations, resources consumed and material lost along the way. Catalysts that tolerate air and work under accessible conditions also simplify handling. The resulting methods expanded possibilities for making pharmaceuticals and advanced plastics. Some routes can use less hazardous solvents or generate less hazardous waste. These are potential advantages of choosing an effective synthetic route; the environmental result depends on the particular process, its materials and its operating conditions.

terms.definition: A chemical reaction where double-bonding atom groups in alkenes exchange places, breaking and forming new carbon-carbon bonds.
The tendency of a catalyst to favour a desired reaction or product over competing transformations.
Designing chemical products and processes to reduce resource use and the generation or use of hazardous substances.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of strategic interaction and cooperation
sections.body: Thomas Schelling applied game theory to global security and arms race issues, exploring how short-run concessions might build long-term confidence. His book, The Strategy of Conflict, introduced ideas regarding credible threats and limitations on alternatives. Robert Aumann utilized mathematical analysis to demonstrate that peaceful cooperation can serve as an equilibrium solution in repeated games, even when parties have conflicting interests. Additionally, Aumann developed the correlated equilibrium concept, which explains how an impartial mediator might advantageously provide different information to negotiating parties.

sections.heading: Why restricting options can strengthen a position
sections.body: Strategic interaction involves players acting based on available information and expectations regarding others' future moves. Thomas Schelling demonstrated that a party can strengthen its position by limiting its own options, such as burning ships. He also showed that uncertain, gradual retaliation can be more credible than immediate responses. Robert Aumann provided a formal analysis of repeated games, illustrating how frequent interaction allows parties with conflicting interests to sustain cooperation. These methods help explain managing common-pool resources and market behaviors like price wars.

sections.heading: Conditions that sustain repeated cooperation
sections.body: Aumann's repeated-game analysis asks which outcomes can persist when participants expect future encounters. Cooperation can become harder when groups are larger, meetings less frequent or relationships more likely to end. Difficulty observing others' actions also matters because behaviour cannot easily influence a later response if it goes unnoticed. The framework has been used to study price wars, trade disputes and the management of shared resources. It also helps explain institutions that organise long-term relationships, from merchant associations to wage bargaining and international agreements. The analysis identifies conditions supporting particular outcomes, rather than guaranteeing that repeated contact will produce cooperation.

terms.definition: An equilibrium in which players use correlated signals to choose actions and, given their information, none benefits by unilaterally departing from the recommended strategy.
A credible restriction on future choices that can change other participants' expectations and behaviour.
A model in which the same underlying game is played repeatedly without a final round.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Theatrical mechanisms of menace and linguistic power
sections.body: Pinter's dramatic technique utilizes language as a tool for aggression, evasion, and torture within his comedies of menace. In plays such as The Birthday Party, The Dumb Waiter, and The Hothouse, dialogue functions as a metaphor for various forms of authoritarian intervention, including the influence of religion, family, and the state. His characters navigate unpredictable dialogues where unsaid threats and shifting secrets redistribute power. By using the rhythms of character voices to drive action rather than a fixed plot, he explores how individuals are undermined by ingrained reflexes. Through works like Mountain Language, his writing also addresses the necessity of promoting justice and unconditional generosity to resist the pain caused by totalitarianism.

sections.heading: Continuities across Pinter's changing forms
sections.body: Pinter's early plays, including The Room and The Birthday Party, establish enclosed spaces and unpredictable exchanges. Critics have divided his career into psychological, lyrical and political phases, citing Landscape and later Mountain Language. The Academy's notes explicitly caution that this scheme is too simple: attention to threat, injustice and the instability of memory runs across his work. They cite No Man's Land and Ashes to Ashes as works that resist tidy periodisation. Pinter also wrote for radio, television and film. His screenplays include The Go-Between and The French Lieutenant's Woman, extending his dramatic writing into another medium.

terms.definition: Drama mixing humour with unease or threat, often allowing aggression and struggles for power to surface through everyday conversation.
A script written for film, combining scenes, action and dialogue; Pinter's work included adaptations of novels for the screen.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Harold Pinter — Swedish Academy bio-bibliographical notes

sections.heading: From stomach biopsies to an infection hypothesis
sections.body: Warren observed spiral bacteria near inflamed stomach lining in biopsy specimens. Marshall's culture attempts succeeded after plates remained incubating over Easter 1982, allowing the organism later named Helicobacter pylori to grow. Clinical studies linked it with gastritis and many gastric or duodenal ulcers. Marshall's self-inoculation produced stomach inflammation, supporting the bacterium's ability to cause gastritis; it did not itself demonstrate the development of an ulcer. Further treatment studies showed that eliminating infection could alter the course of associated ulcer disease. The case for the discovery came from microscopy, culture, clinical comparisons and follow-up evidence together.

sections.heading: Literature searches and early clinical observations
sections.body: At Royal Perth Hospital, Marshall used the new Medline connection to search earlier work on gastric bacteria. Their appearance reminded him of Campylobacter organisms already known from gastrointestinal disease. Biopsy collections included infected specimens with inflammation and uninfected specimens usually lacking it, providing an observational comparison. His biography also describes later experimental treatment at Fremantle, where some severely affected ulcer patients improved after antibiotics and bismuth and avoided planned surgery. These are historical observations in the development of the hypothesis, alongside the larger studies needed to establish the infection's role.

sections.heading: Staining tissue and finding suitable controls
sections.body: Warren developed an interest in staining bacteria in tissue sections. After noticing organisms in a stomach biopsy in 1979, he collected examples and examined their association with chronic gastritis. Finding appropriate negative controls was difficult because biopsies from different stomach regions had been coded together. He eventually found twenty normal antral biopsies without the bacteria. Collaboration with Marshall added clinical histories, endoscopy findings and culture samples to the pathology. Warren later contributed tissue analysis to a study conducted over seven years, reporting that ulcer recurrence was uncommon after successful eradication but usual when infection persisted.

terms.definition: Inflammation of the stomach lining, the condition produced in Marshall's self-inoculation experiment.
A comparison group used to help interpret a study's findings; here, uninfected biopsy specimens were compared with infected ones.
The microscopic study of tissue structure, commonly using prepared and stained sections to make cells and other features visible.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: From Atoms for Peace to international oversight
sections.body: Eisenhower's 1953 Atoms for Peace speech proposed that nuclear powers supply uranium and fissile material to an international agency for peaceful uses. This was a founding vision, not a description of a system controlling the allocation of all nuclear material worldwide. The IAEA was established in 1957 to encourage peaceful nuclear activities while limiting military misuse. The Nobel presentation emphasised the significance of allowing an international body to perform oversight previously reserved to national authorities. It also criticised nuclear-weapon states for demanding restraint from others while continuing their own weapons programmes. ElBaradei's advocacy therefore sat within a wider debate about shared obligations and unequal nuclear power.

sections.heading: Cooperation against nuclear proliferation
sections.body: The committee recognised the IAEA and ElBaradei for efforts to prevent military misuse of nuclear energy and promote safe peaceful applications. Its 2005 announcement placed the award against stalled disarmament and concern that nuclear weapons could spread to additional states or terrorist groups.
