It praised ElBaradei's advocacy of measures to strengthen the international system for limiting that spread. The committee connected this work to Alfred Nobel's concern with reducing armies, arguing that nuclear dangers required cooperation across states. The award acknowledged this work and its importance; it did not certify that nuclear proliferation had been prevented everywhere.

sections.heading: Diplomacy and international law
sections.body: ElBaradei began in the Egyptian Diplomatic Service in 1964, handling political, legal and arms-control matters at Egypt's UN missions in New York and Geneva. He completed a doctorate in international law at New York University in 1974. Before becoming IAEA Director General, he served as its Legal Adviser and later Assistant Director General for External Relations. His work also included international-law education: he joined the UN Institute for Training and Research in 1980 and held an adjunct professorship at NYU from 1981 to 1987. Across his career, he lectured and published on international organisations, arms control and peaceful nuclear uses.

terms.definition: Eisenhower's 1953 proposal to use international cooperation and an atomic-energy agency to direct nuclear materials toward peaceful purposes.
International arrangements intended to limit the spread of nuclear weapons and prevent diversion of peaceful nuclear activities to weapons programmes.
Rules and agreements governing relations among states and other international actors, including arrangements relevant to arms control.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: What photon detection reveals about light
sections.body: Glauber's 1963 theory connected quantum descriptions of light with observations made by photodetectors. It explained why thermal light can show bunching: detections close together are more likely than in an ideal coherent laser beam. Correlating several detectors reveals information that a simple average intensity misses. The framework also accommodates antibunching, where closely spaced detections occur less often than in a purely random signal, a behaviour beyond classical wave descriptions. These distinctions made quantum optics a way to test the character of light itself. The Nobel background also connected quantum fluctuations with limits on measurement precision.

sections.heading: A measuring scale for optical frequencies
sections.body: An atomic clock provides a reference, but measuring an unknown optical frequency also requires a reliable way to compare it with that reference. Hall and Hänsch developed frequency-comb techniques that supply a sequence of precisely spaced frequencies. The comb acts like a ruler against which an unknown frequency can be compared. The ceremony speech linked this practical advance with spectroscopy: more precise measurements of light emitted or absorbed by atoms reveal more about their properties. It also stressed that improved accuracy can expose limitations in existing physical theories, rather than merely adding decimal places to familiar measurements.

sections.heading: Coherence and the uses of greater precision
sections.body: The award joined two different contributions. Glauber's theory explained optical coherence and the statistical differences between thermal light and ideal coherent laser light. Hall and Hänsch advanced precise frequency measurement, including frequency-comb methods. The 2005 announcement reported measurements reaching fifteen-digit accuracy and pointed to questions such as whether physical constants remain stable over time. It also identified better clocks and satellite navigation as potential applications. These possibilities followed from improved frequency references; they did not mean that a single instrument could measure every wavelength with identical accuracy or that all proposed applications were already deployed.

terms.definition: A statistical tendency for photon detections to occur close together, characteristic of thermal light and distinct from an ideal coherent laser beam.
Light containing a series of evenly spaced frequency components that can serve as reference marks for measuring other optical frequencies.
The degree to which light maintains predictable phase relationships across space or time, allowing stable wave correlations and interference.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Preparing the machinery for structural study
sections.body: Kornberg’s group spent about a decade refining a yeast system that could supply suitable transcription proteins in sufficient quantities. To capture a copying complex, researchers could withhold a required RNA building block so that synthesis stopped when it was needed. Crystals of the stalled complex then provided structural evidence about DNA, polymerase and RNA positions. Separate work identified Mediator, a complex connecting regulatory signals to the transcription machinery. The 2006 account distinguished these achievements: including Mediator and the full set of general transcription factors in an active structural description remained a further goal. Its discovery was not an inference from an already complete crystal structure of the whole system.

sections.heading: Molecular modeling of the eukaryotic transcription apparatus
sections.body: By utilizing baker’s yeast as a model system, Kornberg investigated how cells regulate genetic expression. He employed biochemical methods alongside X-ray crystallography to generate detailed molecular models where individual atoms are visible. These studies revealed how the transcription machinery selects specific RNA building blocks and identifies starting points on DNA strands. His research also demonstrates how the apparatus moves along DNA during copying. Furthermore, his work describes how additional molecules bind to and cooperate with the transcription machinery to facilitate cellular regulation.

sections.heading: Why controlling transcription matters
sections.body: Copying a gene into messenger RNA makes its information available for protein production outside the nucleus. Which genes are transcribed, and when, therefore matters to how a cell functions. The announcement connected transcriptional regulation with stem cells developing into specialised cell types, and identified disturbances of transcription in diseases including cancer and inflammation. These were reasons for studying the mechanism, rather than evidence that the structural results had already produced treatments. It also distinguished Roger Kornberg’s work from his father Arthur’s earlier prize: Arthur investigated DNA synthesis, whereas Roger examined the machinery copying DNA information into RNA. The two awards concern different steps in the handling of genetic information.

terms.definition: A protein complex that helps convey regulatory signals to the machinery that transcribes genes.
A method that uses X-ray diffraction from crystals to infer the arrangement of atoms, producing structural models rather than ordinary photographs.
Use of genetic information to produce a functional product; transcription into RNA is a central step.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The expectations-augmented Phillips curve and wage-setting models
sections.body: Phelps modelled wage and price decisions using firms’ and workers’ expectations. In the expectations-augmented Phillips curve, holding unemployment fixed, a one-percentage-point increase in expected inflation raises actual inflation by one percentage point. This is a relationship within the model, rather than an unconditional empirical correlation. As expectations adjust, attempts to hold unemployment persistently below its equilibrium level lead to increasing inflation. Stabilisation policy can still moderate short-run fluctuations. The committee’s explanation also noted an empirical qualification: the influence of expected on actual inflation may be weaker at very low inflation rates. Expectations therefore help explain why a short-run policy trade-off cannot simply be extrapolated indefinitely.

sections.heading: Investment and the interests of future generations
sections.body: Phelps’s work on capital formation examined how current consumption competes with investment benefiting future generations. Those future people cannot vote in present decisions, so a policy can involve conflicts across generations even when it raises later output. His analysis explored conditions under which pension arrangements could improve outcomes across generations. The committee also emphasised investment in education and research. In Phelps’s framework, growth could depend on the educational level already attained, as well as on how quickly that level was increasing. This connected the accumulated capacity to use knowledge with economic development, extending the analysis beyond investment in physical equipment alone.

sections.heading: Inflation expectations and the Phillips Curve
sections.body: Phelps’s 1967 and 1968 analyses distinguished temporary employment effects from sustainable outcomes. If a central bank continually sought employment above its equilibrium level, inflation would exceed expectations; revised expectations would then shift the short-run Phillips curve upward. Conversely, reducing inflation expectations could involve a temporary increase in unemployment. His biography explained the role of adaptive expectations: people revised beliefs as actual inflation repeatedly differed from what they had expected. He considered that assumption plausible during an attempted disinflation, when a sceptical public needed evidence of the bank’s commitment. He also stressed that adaptive expectations were not a realistic description in every circumstance. The modelling assumption was therefore part of the argument, not a universal rule of behaviour.

terms.definition: A model stating that inflation depends on both unemployment levels and the anticipations of firms and employees regarding price increases.
Knowledge and capabilities developed through education and related investment that can contribute to production and growth.
Expectations adjusted in response to discrepancies between previously expected and subsequently observed outcomes.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary techniques and thematic conflicts in Pamuk's novels
sections.body: The Nobel speech reads My Name Is Red through the competing artistic ideals staged among miniature painters in 1590s Istanbul. Within the novel, painting inherited stories from memory is set against the appeal of individual style and Western portraiture. These are positions dramatised in fiction, not a complete description of Muslim art. Pamuk also complicates the apparent choice: the speech asks whether a supposedly unique gesture can ever be free of imitation. The Black Book develops related questions through characters drawn into imagined lives and stories of Istanbul. Snow places a poet among conflicting political and religious commitments in a remote Turkish town. Across these examples, the committee emphasises shifting identities and the difficulty of settling into one authoritative perspective.

sections.heading: Literary development and thematic exploration
sections.body: After abandoning architecture for journalism, the author transitioned from painting to prose. His early works, Cevdet Bey and Sons and Silent House, function as family sagas that depict crowded gatherings and domestic disputes. In Silent House, he utilized grandmotherly monologues to investigate the boundary between dreams and wakefulness. Later, while residing in New York and utilizing the Columbia Library, he composed The Black Book. This work emerged from a period of questioning his own history and exploring Ottoman, Persian, Arab, and Islamic cultures. His memoir, Istanbul, also examines his first twenty-two years, though he reflects that autobiographies can serve to help individuals forget their pasts rather than simply preserving them.

terms.definition: A movement between different viewpoints that changes how characters, events or beliefs can be understood.
A narrative following a family’s relationships, conflicts and changes over time, often extending across generations.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Evidence that silencing acts on messenger RNA
sections.body: Fire and Mello used staining to detect messenger RNA in worm embryos. Antisense RNA reduced the signal weakly, whereas matching double-stranded RNA eliminated it in the experiments described. Other observations narrowed down the mechanism. The double-stranded sequence had to match mature messenger RNA; sequences corresponding only to introns did not trigger the same effect. Silencing was specific to the matching gene, and very small quantities of double-stranded RNA were sufficient. The response could spread between cells and tissues and could reach offspring. Together, these results suggested an active cellular process acting after transcription, rather than a simple blocking reaction requiring one injected molecule for every target.

sections.heading: Testing complementary RNA strands together
sections.body: Earlier attempts to alter gene activity had produced puzzling results. Some silencing experiments failed, while adding a pigment gene to flowers could unexpectedly remove colour. Fire and Mello tested RNA in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. A sense strand corresponds to the messenger-RNA sequence; an antisense strand is complementary to it. Mixing the two allows them to pair into a double strand. Injecting this paired material caused a much stronger silencing response than the individual strands. The result identified double-stranded RNA as the effective trigger and helped explain why experiments intended to increase gene activity could instead suppress it.

sections.heading: How the RNA-interference machinery was resolved
sections.body: The components that explain RNA interference were identified in the years after Fire and Mello's 1998 experiments. Dicer cuts double-stranded RNA into short fragments. These are taken up by the RNA-induced silencing complex, or RISC, which retains one strand as a guide. The guide's sequence enables recognition of matching messenger RNA, which can then be degraded. This provides molecular specificity: the guide directs the machinery towards particular RNA targets. It also explains how a small initial quantity of double-stranded RNA can initiate a potent response. The machinery made RNA interference a useful way to investigate what happens when a gene's expression is reduced.

terms.definition: Sequence-specific regulation of gene expression triggered by RNA, including the breakdown of matching messenger RNA in the experiments of Fire and Mello.
A simple nematode worm used as a model organism to study the mechanisms of genetic information flow and regulation.
A protein–RNA complex, abbreviated RISC, that uses a guide RNA to recognise target RNA and suppress its expression.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Economic development through micro-credit mechanisms
sections.body: The 2006 presentation described Grameen as profitable and self-financing, with small loans averaging a little over one hundred dollars at that time. Most ownership was held by poor clients. Lending was connected with local groups, whose regular meetings covered borrowing, repayment, saving and practical concerns in daily life. Networks of these groups also supported community activity, including health and vaccination programmes. The committee viewed this social organisation as important alongside access to money. It presented Yunus’s approach as lending amounts suited to borrowers and supporting financial understanding. These were features and claims of the model as described at the award, not fixed statistics for the bank’s entire subsequent history.

sections.heading: Micro-credit as an instrument for social development
sections.body: The committee’s case for the award connected poverty, participation and peace. It argued that lasting peace required large excluded populations to gain opportunities for economic and social development. Grameen’s small-loan approach was one means toward that goal, especially for women facing restrictive economic conditions. The announcement highlighted international adoption of the model and treated women’s equal participation as essential to the potential of both economic growth and democracy. It also stated a clear limit: Yunus’s ambition to eliminate poverty could not be achieved through microcredit alone. The award endorsed a contribution to a wider development effort, rather than declaring that borrowing by itself would end poverty.

sections.heading: From economics training to a lending institution
sections.body: Yunus studied at Dhaka University and received a Fulbright scholarship for economics at Vanderbilt, where he completed his doctorate in 1969. He subsequently taught at Middle Tennessee State University. His personal loans to poor Bangladeshi artisans in the mid-1970s grew into the institution established as Grameen Bank in 1983. His biography presents the guiding belief as access to credit being a fundamental human right. Loans were intended to fit borrowers’ circumstances and be accompanied by basic financial understanding. By the award-period account, versions of the model operated in more than one hundred countries. That spread records the approach’s influence; its ambitious aim of ending poverty remained a goal.

terms.definition: Small loans; in Grameen’s model, access was offered to people excluded from conventional lending by lack of collateral.
Social and economic improvement built through the participation and initiative of people and communities whose opportunities have been restricted.
Access to financial services for people who have been excluded from conventional providers, exemplified here by access to small loans.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Advancing cosmology through satellite-based radiation measurements
sections.body: A satellite allowed measurements above atmospheric absorption and across the sky. NASA’s 1974 invitation for proposals led to the COBE project, ultimately involving more than one thousand scientists, engineers and other participants. Mather coordinated the effort and led the spectrum experiment. Its early observations closely matched the thermal curve expected for blackbody radiation; the result presented in January 1990 drew an enthusiastic response. Smoot’s experiment addressed a different question by looking for tiny directional variations. The combination tested both the overall thermal character of the background and departures from uniformity, which offered clues to how matter later concentrated into galaxies and stars.

sections.heading: COBE satellite measurements and cosmic temperature variations
sections.body: Launched by NASA in 1989, the COBE satellite enabled researchers to calculate a temperature of nearly 2.7 degrees above absolute zero. John Mather coordinated a large team to identify the blackbody form of the radiation spectrum. George Smoot led efforts to measure anisotropy, which involves detecting tiny temperature differences of roughly one hundred-thousandth of a degree across different directions. These small variations provide clues regarding how matter began to aggregate, a process necessary for the development of stars and galaxies.

sections.heading: Development of the COBE mission instruments
sections.body: Mather’s early mission proposal, developed with colleagues including Hauser, Weiss and Wilkinson, envisioned four instruments: a spectrum interferometer, two anisotropy experiments and an infrared-background instrument. This was a proposed configuration, not a count of instruments ultimately flown. A later mission-definition team brought together members of that group with Smoot and Gulkis from competing proposals. Developing the mission required sustained collaboration with engineering teams. Mather also credited the analysis group with compensating for systematic effects built into the instruments. Their work produced results exceeding the formal sensitivity and accuracy requirements. The scientific achievement therefore depended on the interpretation and calibration of measurements as well as the original instrument concepts.

terms.definition: Thermal radiation with the ideal blackbody spectrum, whose distribution across wavelengths is fixed by temperature.
Dependence on direction; here, small differences in the microwave background’s temperature across the sky.
A consistent distortion arising from instruments or procedures that can bias a measurement.

sections.heading: Identifying the rate-limiting step in nitrogen splitting
sections.body: Ertl distinguished atomic from molecular nitrogen on iron using several surface-sensitive methods. Adding hydrogen reduced the amount of atomic nitrogen, supporting a reaction pathway in which nitrogen molecules first split and the resulting atoms then react with hydrogen. That initial splitting was the slow step in the iron-catalysed process studied. Later steps occurred too quickly to observe easily in the forward reaction. Ertl therefore investigated ammonia breaking down on iron and used heavy hydrogen to probe hydrogen exchange. Studying the reverse process helped him identify intermediates and examine steps hidden by the slow initial dissociation.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of surface catalysis and catalytic converter reactions
sections.body: Ertl investigated how reacting gases and the structure of a solid surface influence each other. His studies of carbon-monoxide oxidation, a reaction relevant to automotive catalytic converters, revealed feedback between surface structure and chemical activity. This interplay could produce moving patterns on the surface. The findings showed that a catalyst's surface can change dynamically as a reaction proceeds. Ertl's broader method combined observations from different experimental techniques to reconstruct molecular events. His work on ammonia synthesis and carbon-monoxide oxidation demonstrated how detailed studies of carefully controlled surfaces can clarify reactions of industrial importance.

sections.heading: Experimental methodologies in surface chemistry research
sections.body: To achieve reliable results, researchers must utilize advanced high-vacuum equipment to observe individual layers of atoms and molecules on extremely pure metal surfaces. This precise approach requires determining exactly which elements enter the system, as contamination can jeopardize measurements. Beyond studying the Haber-Bosch process, investigations into the oxidation of carbon monoxide on platinum help explain how car catalysts clean exhaust emissions. By combining various experimental techniques, a complete picture of surface reactions is constructed, providing a scientific basis for both academic research and industrial chemical development.

terms.definition: The study of chemical processes at surfaces and interfaces, including reactions between gases and solid catalysts.
A process where a solid surface aids atoms of gas molecules to generate new chemical combinations.
An environment with very low gas pressure, used to limit unwanted molecules reaching a clean experimental surface.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Analyzing economic institutions through mechanism design
sections.body: Mechanism design begins with a goal and asks which rules can achieve it when participants have private information and their own incentives. Different objectives can require different rules: an allocation that maximises gains from trade is not necessarily the same as one that maximises a seller's revenue. Auction design offers one application, while insurance and public-good provision pose others. The revelation principle simplifies the search by allowing analysis of direct mechanisms in which participants have incentives to report their information truthfully. Researchers can then relate those results to more practical institutions. The resulting recommendations depend on the objective, information structure and behavioural assumptions.

sections.heading: Methods for analyzing resource allocation and institutional design
sections.body: Mechanism design theory utilizes a three-step analytical process to evaluate economic activity. Researchers first use game theory to predict expected behavior under specific rules. Next, they assess resulting resource allocations, such as production or environmental stress, against a set goal. Finally, the researcher seeks the optimal mechanism. This involves using the revelation principle to identify direct mechanisms compatible with individual incentives. This systematic approach helps determine if institutional arrangements can achieve social welfare, efficiency, or fair distribution despite constraints from private information.

sections.heading: Foundations of mechanism design theory
sections.body: The development of mechanism design theory addresses challenges when information regarding production technologies or individual preferences is dispersed among various actors. Because participants may use private data to advance personal interests, researchers study how different allocation mechanisms perform. This framework evaluates whether specific institutions, such as government regulation, bargaining between interest groups, or transactions within firms, can reach goals like social welfare or private profit. By accounting for incentives and private information, the theory helps identify efficient trading mechanisms, voting procedures, and effective regulation schemes.

terms.definition: A result allowing achievable outcomes to be studied through direct mechanisms where truthful reporting is an equilibrium, simplifying the search for suitable rules.
Designing a mechanism whose equilibrium outcomes meet a specified objective, including addressing unwanted equilibria.
Institutional arrangements or rules used to distribute resources, such as those found in firms, bargaining, or government regulation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary themes and narrative structures in Lessing's work
sections.body: Lessing’s expansive bibliography resists simple genre classification, moving between honest realism, symbolic fable, and myth. Her writing explores the tension between the desire for love and the will to create, particularly in her experimental novel The Golden Notebook. Through characters like Martha Quest in the Children of Violence series, she tracks a journey from colonial life to the British class hierarchy. Her narratives examine the dangers of absorbing into collectives or pursuing utopias, while also addressing global issues like environmental threats and poverty in the Third World. In works such as The Sweetest Dream, she utilizes characters like Frances to explore caretaking, while The Cleft presents a parable set during the dawn of mankind. Ultimately, her prose investigates social ostracism, solitude, and the complexities of human existence.

sections.heading: Literary themes and autobiographical influences
sections.body: Lessing utilized personal memories to construct various literary works. In her novel The Cleft, she incorporated a childhood scene involving a horse and her father's wooden leg. Her writing also drew from experiences of displacement, such as observing hungry children at stations during the Civil War and traveling through Moscow and the Baltic States. She explored themes of social structures in Southern Rhodesia, where white populations commanded large black populations, and utilized dreams to navigate creative blocks. While she initially intended to write an autobiography based on dreams, this effort resulted in Memoirs of a Survivor. Additionally, her work The Sweetest Dream included characters involving children and young people, reflecting her life experiences of adding children to her family.

terms.definition: A strength demonstrated in Lessing's work that resists totalitarian temptations and avoids the deceptive allure of triumphant ideologies.
Scenes and associations drawn from dreams and reshaped as literary material; Lessing said dreams often helped her overcome writing blocks.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Selecting cells with the intended genetic change
sections.body: Early experiments targeted the hprt gene because successful changes were comparatively easy to detect. In 1987, Smithies repaired a defective version in cultured embryonic stem cells using an introduced DNA fragment. Cells with a functional gene could survive in a specially chosen culture medium. Capecchi’s group introduced a sequence into hprt that conferred resistance to a selection antibiotic. The challenge was to identify the few cells carrying the intended alteration among many others. Later selection strategies combined survival of cells containing introduced material with elimination of cells where it had entered an unintended position. These experiments changed DNA encoding an enzyme, rather than targeting the enzyme molecule itself.

sections.heading: From a DNA change to a test of gene function
sections.body: Capecchi and Smithies used DNA resembling a normal gene but containing a deliberate difference to direct a change to the corresponding genomic position. Evans’s embryonic stem cells provided a way for such changes to reach an animal’s germ line and later generations. Researchers could then examine a gene’s effects in the context of development and the whole body. A knockout removes a gene’s function, but targeted modification can also alter it in other ways. The 2007 presentation linked these mouse experiments to understanding disease and developing medicines. It also emphasised weighing expected benefits against animal numbers and suffering. Testing a gene experimentally does not itself establish a treatment’s benefit in humans.

sections.heading: Demonstrating transmission through the germ line
sections.body: Evans initially investigated embryonal carcinoma cells, but their abnormal chromosomes prevented the required contribution to germ cells. He then established chromosomally normal embryonic stem cells from early mouse embryos. Injecting cells from one mouse strain into an embryo of another produced an animal containing contributions from both. Breeding these mosaic animals revealed stem-cell-derived genes in their offspring. Evans subsequently introduced retroviral DNA into the stem cells and demonstrated its transmission through this route. This established the inheritance step needed to combine his work with Capecchi’s and Smithies’s targeted DNA modifications. The initial injected embryo was a mixture of cell lineages; breeding was essential to establishing inherited changes.

terms.definition: Exchange or recombination between DNA sequences with matching regions, usable to introduce a chosen change at a corresponding genomic location.
Cells from early embryos that can be maintained in culture and contribute to the different cell types of a developing animal.
The cell lineage producing eggs or sperm, through which genetic information can pass to offspring.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A shared process for assessing climate research
sections.body: UNEP and the World Meteorological Organization established the IPCC in 1988 to assess climate change, its causes, its consequences and possible responses. The Nobel presentation described an unusual continuing mobilisation of scientific expertise, with governments also reviewing reports. Its figures of more than 130 participating countries and hundreds of authors described the project in 2007. The speech connected the first assessment in 1990 with the subsequent UN environmental summit, and the 1995 report with the 1997 Kyoto agreement. These examples explain how the committee saw scientific assessment informing international policy, without treating the panel itself as the body negotiating those agreements.

sections.heading: Climate risks and the Peace Prize
sections.body: In its 2007 announcement, the committee credited the IPCC's assessments with strengthening understanding of the connection between human activity and global warming. It described collaboration among thousands of scientists and officials across more than a hundred countries. The announcement connected climate risks with peace through possible effects on living conditions: displacement, pressure on resources and heavier burdens on vulnerable countries. It warned that these pressures could increase the danger of violent conflict, rather than asserting that climate change automatically causes war. This concern supported its call to take the evidence seriously and prepare measures against further change.

sections.heading: Gore's work beyond elected office
sections.body: Gore's award-era biography described several roles following his eight years as US vice president. In 2007 he chaired the Alliance for Climate Protection and Generation Investment Management, whose focus was sustainable investing. He also chaired Current TV, a nonfiction television venture drawing on material created by viewers. His technology roles differed: he was an Apple board member and a senior adviser to Google. The biography also listed a visiting professorship at Middle Tennessee State University. These are historical career details from the time of the award, alongside his books and climate documentary, rather than a list of current appointments.

terms.definition: An organised evaluation of research evidence that helps explain what is known, where uncertainties remain and what responses can be considered.
An approach that takes potentially serious harm into account even while some scientific uncertainty remains.
Reporting or nonfiction media produced by members of the public; viewer-created material was central to Current TV's description.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Why thinner magnetic layers improved data reading
sections.body: Early disk read heads used induction coils. Later designs exploited ordinary anisotropic magnetoresistance, in which resistance depends on magnetic orientation. This was the direct predecessor of GMR read heads, which offered greater sensitivity. Making very thin metallic layers, with techniques developed from the 1970s, enabled the new structures. A simple example places a nonmagnetic metal between two magnetic layers. Electrons of different spin scatter differently in the materials and at their interfaces. Changing the layers' magnetic arrangement can therefore produce a much larger resistance change than earlier readout methods, helping detect weaker signals from smaller stored regions.

sections.heading: Electron spin and resistance in magnetic layers
sections.body: Electrons have an intrinsic quantum property called spin, associated with magnetism; it is not the rotation of a tiny solid ball. Relative to a chosen magnetic direction, electrons can occupy two spin states. In a ferromagnetic metal, these states can experience different amounts of scattering and therefore contribute differently to resistance. Fert and Grünberg independently found that alternating very thin magnetic and nonmagnetic layers could make resistance strongly responsive to an applied magnetic field. The result helped establish spintronics, in which electron spin provides an additional property for electronic devices to use alongside electric charge.

sections.heading: Turning stored magnetisation into an electrical signal
sections.body: A hard disk records information in small regions magnetised in different directions. As a read head passes over them, it detects changes in the magnetic pattern. In a GMR device, these changes alter electrical resistance, which the readout circuitry converts into a signal representing stored bits. The effect changes the response of the sensor; it does not create electrical energy by itself. The Nobel announcement identified 1997 as the launch of the first GMR read head. Its greater sensitivity helped make smaller magnetic regions readable and therefore supported denser information storage.

terms.definition: Making and using structures at nanometre scales; a nanometre is one billionth of a metre, and layered structures can have properties unlike bulk materials.
Electronics that uses electron spin and its associated magnetic properties as well as electric charge.
The component that detects a storage disk's magnetic pattern and supplies an electrical signal from which recorded information can be recovered.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms and developments of fluorescent protein technology
sections.body: Shimomura identified that GFP contains a chromophore, a chemical group that absorbs blue or ultraviolet light to emit green light. This process involves the chromophore becoming excited by absorbing energy before releasing it at a green wavelength. To expand the available palette, Tsien's research group redesigned the larger DsRED protein into a stable, single amino acid chain. This advancement enabled the creation of various colored proteins, such as mCherry and mStrawberry, which allow scientists to track different protein interactions and movements within cells.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of GFP fluorescence and protein engineering
sections.body: In the jellyfish, excitation energy from aequorin can transfer to GFP without first being emitted as a photon; GFP then emits green light. Chalfie tested whether other organisms could make fluorescent GFP without jellyfish-specific enzymes. Using a cloned gene supplied by Douglas Prasher, his team demonstrated fluorescence in bacteria and C. elegans. Tsien investigated how the fluorescent group forms within the protein, including oxygen’s role, and engineered a blue-emitting variant. Changing the protein sequence could therefore change its optical behaviour. Further engineering of GFP and related proteins improved properties such as brightness, resistance to bleaching and the time required to become fluorescent.

sections.heading: Counting structures inside touch-sensing neurons
sections.body: Before the GFP experiments, Chalfie studied touch-sensitive cells in C. elegans at the Laboratory of Molecular Biology. John Sulston had identified their conspicuous bundles of microtubules in electron micrographs. Chalfie counted these structures in successive sections and plotted the numbers along a neuronal extension. Counts rose and fell repeatedly, rather than simply declining with distance from the cell body. That suggested that the microtubules did not all begin at the cell body. Working with Nichol Thomson, who prepared additional section series, he showed that microtubules could start and end within the extension. His biography presents this investigation as an example of a simple measurement opening a new research question.

terms.definition: The light-absorbing chemical group responsible for a molecule’s optical properties; in GFP it also emits green fluorescence.
An altered form of a fluorescent protein whose sequence changes can modify colour, brightness, stability or maturation.
An image produced with an electron microscope, used here to examine structures in successive thin sections of neurons.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of the core-periphery model
sections.body: Krugman’s core-periphery analysis asks when economic activity spreads out and when it concentrates. A firm can reduce production costs by operating at scale, but locating far from customers creates transport costs. Workers and customers also move, changing which locations are attractive. Under some conditions, these interactions reinforce an initial concentration, producing a manufacturing centre and a more agricultural periphery. Other conditions favour a less concentrated pattern. The committee presented this as a possible mechanism behind rapid urbanisation and rural depopulation, rather than an inevitable outcome for every region. The result depends on the balance between transport costs and the advantages of concentration.

sections.heading: How firms and workers can reinforce a location’s appeal
sections.body: Krugman combined consumers’ demand for different varieties of goods with production that becomes cheaper per unit at larger scale. In his economic-geography work, labour could also move between regions. A populated location attracted firms because many customers were nearby, reducing delivery costs while supporting larger production runs. For workers, a larger choice of goods made the location attractive. These responses could reinforce one another, concentrating activity in a few regions. The theory also made clear why the outcome was conditional: transport costs, scale economies and consumer demand jointly determined the balance. It offered an explanation for concentration, rather than a rule that every growing city must keep expanding.

sections.heading: Why similar countries exchange similar goods
sections.body: The award announcement used Sweden’s simultaneous exports and imports of cars to illustrate a pattern that differences in national resources alone did not explain well. In Krugman’s framework, consumers value variety and firms benefit from producing at scale. A wider market lets different producers specialise in particular varieties while selling across borders. Trade can therefore arise between countries with similar technology and resources, and within the same broad industry. Consumers can obtain a broader selection at lower prices as production expands. This complements the older explanation based on differences between countries and helps connect international exchange to firms’ location and production decisions.

terms.definition: A model showing how the interaction between transport costs and economies of scale results in either concentration or decentralization.
Falling average production costs as the quantity produced increases.
Exchange across borders of goods from the same broad industry, such as a country both importing and exporting cars.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Evolution of Le Clézio's literary style and form
sections.body: The Nobel presentation places Le Clézio’s early work alongside the French nouveau roman, while distinguishing his confidence in language’s contact with the physical world. The Interrogation combines diary fragments, newspaper material, wordplay and institutional dialogue, unsettling a single continuous narrative. In Fever, he questions inherited divisions among poems, stories and novels. The speech then connects his Central American encounters with a search for knowledge marginalised by dominant cultures. Later writing brings migration and personal history into this exploration. Its account of Désert emphasises an open form moving among periods, places and kinds of discourse. Travel writing, reflection and testimony can enter the novel without being reduced to one conventional plot. These are critical descriptions of his changing literary practice.

sections.heading: Early writing and literary recognition
sections.body: Le Clézio wrote from about the age of seven or eight, trying poems, sagas, tales and short stories before publication. His first novel, Le Procès-verbal, appeared in September 1963 and received the Prix Renaudot. Its English title is The Interrogation. His educational background included undergraduate studies at the Institut d’Études Littéraires in Nice and a doctorate. Later literary recognition included the Académie française’s Grand Prix de Littérature Paul Morand in 1980, the same year Désert appeared.

terms.definition: A movement in French fiction that challenged conventional plot and psychological characterisation, often foregrounding perception and the organisation of description.
Le Clézio’s debut novel, published in 1963 and known in English as The Interrogation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Académie française — Jean-Marie Le Clézio award record

sections.heading: Finding unfamiliar papillomavirus DNA
sections.body: Zur Hausen's team used labelled fragments of viral DNA as probes to search for related sequences. Probes based on known wart viruses initially worked on other skin warts but failed to reveal the sought-after virus in cervical tumours. Relaxing the matching conditions allowed imperfectly complementary sequences to bind. This low-stringency hybridisation helped reveal a previously unknown papillomavirus in cervical tumour material. HPV16 was described in 1983, followed by HPV18 in other samples. The strategy depended on recognising that a family of related viruses could contain members sufficiently different to escape an overly restrictive search.

sections.heading: From identifying HIV to testing and treatment
sections.body: Barré-Sinoussi and Montagnier found HIV in lymph-node material from patients with early signs of immune deficiency. The virus multiplied in white blood cells and damaged the type of cell depleted in AIDS. Its ability to persist in the host genome and its extensive variation helped explain why the infection was difficult to control. Identifying the virus opened the way to tests for infected people and donated blood products. It also provided a foundation for antiretroviral medicines that suppress the disease. The 2008 presentation described the growing availability of such treatment as an important consequence of the discovery.

sections.heading: Evidence that the new virus attacked immune cells
sections.body: The Pasteur researchers cultured cells from swollen lymph nodes and detected reverse-transcriptase activity. They also observed retroviral particles budding from infected cells. The isolated virus infected and killed lymphocytes from both healthy and affected donors, and antibodies from infected patients reacted with it. Unlike previously characterised human cancer-causing retroviruses, it did not make the cells grow uncontrollably. Instead, it caused cell damage and fusion, helping explain the loss of immune function. By 1984, isolates had been obtained from patients with different routes of infection. Several research groups subsequently contributed to the definitive evidence that HIV causes AIDS.

terms.definition: The pairing of complementary DNA strands, used to detect related sequences; relaxed matching conditions can reveal more distantly related sequences.
Treatment using medicines that inhibit stages of a retrovirus's replication and help suppress the infection.
An enzyme that makes DNA using RNA as a template, enabling a retrovirus to produce a DNA copy of its genome.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mediating Namibia's Independence and International Conflicts
sections.body: Ahtisaari’s work on Namibia extended across different UN roles and many years. The independence process involved South African control, Namibian political forces and Cold War rivalries, including the neighbouring war in Angola. Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990. The Nobel speech also described work of a different scale in Iraq: in April 2008, the Crisis Management Initiative and cooperating institutions brought thirty-six Iraqi politicians together in Helsinki. Ahtisaari acted as a senior adviser. The participants agreed principles concerning peace, rather than a settlement ending the Iraqi conflict. These examples show mediation ranging from an extended international transition to efforts to establish common ground among political participants.

sections.heading: The mediator’s role and the parties’ responsibility
sections.body: The 2008 announcement credited Ahtisaari with several kinds of intervention. He and the Crisis Management Initiative were central to the 2005 Aceh agreement, while his Kosovo assignments in 1999 and 2005–2007 confronted particularly difficult circumstances. The committee also noted contributions in Northern Ireland, Central Asia and the Horn of Africa, and ongoing efforts involving Iraq. It explicitly located primary responsibility for avoiding conflict with the parties themselves. The mediator’s contribution was to help create conditions in which they could reach decisions and pursue peaceful alternatives. The range of assignments therefore mattered alongside the most visible agreements, without implying identical methods or equally complete outcomes in every case.

sections.heading: United Nations peacekeeping and transition operations
sections.body: As the UN Secretary-General’s special representative for Namibia, Ahtisaari led the United Nations Transition Assistance Group during 1989–1990. Its work combined military peacekeeping with civilian responsibilities involving elections, policing, human rights and education. This required more than arranging discussions among political leaders: the transition also depended on institutions and practical supervision. After returning to Finland’s foreign ministry, he chaired the Bosnia-Herzegovina Working Group of the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia in 1992–1993. His later Kosovo work produced a proposal for the territory’s future status. The biography connects these assignments through his experience with international transitions and the different political structures needed to support them.

terms.definition: A third party who helps participants communicate and negotiate toward agreement without replacing their responsibility for the outcome.
The organisation through which Ahtisaari and colleagues conducted mediation and supported efforts to resolve conflicts.
A UN operation that combined traditional peacekeeping forces with civilian components managing electoral, police, human rights, and educational matters.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: How a symmetric theory can have an asymmetric state
sections.body: Nambu drew on ideas from superconductivity to develop spontaneous symmetry breaking in particle physics. The underlying laws can retain a symmetry even when the state adopted by the system does not display it. This differs from a violation built into the interactions themselves. His work supplied a framework important to later theories, including the electroweak description in which W and Z bosons acquire mass while the photon remains massless. The 2008 prize also honoured Kobayashi and Maskawa for a separate problem involving particle–antiparticle and mirror transformations. Keeping these contributions distinct explains why the same award involved different meanings of symmetry breaking.

sections.heading: Extending the quark model to explain CP violation
sections.body: Kobayashi and Maskawa investigated how the theory of weak interactions could accommodate observed differences between certain particle and antiparticle processes. Their analysis required six quark types arranged in three families, extending beyond the three then recognised. This made the proposal a substantial extrapolation. The additional quarks were later found, and experimental tests supported the framework. The Nobel speech placed this work alongside Nambu’s but distinguished the question it answered: how an interaction can violate a symmetry, rather than how a symmetric theory can have a ground state that hides it. Together the contributions expanded the role of symmetry reasoning in particle physics.

sections.heading: Research developments at Nagoya and Kyoto Universities
sections.body: Kobayashi’s graduate collaboration with Maskawa at Nagoya concerned chiral symmetry. After moving to Kyoto in April 1972, he resumed working with Maskawa on CP violation; their paper was written by the end of August. This preceded the 1974 discovery of the J/ψ particle and its identification as charmonium. Kobayashi recalled earlier Japanese investigations of four-quark models prompted by hints in cosmic-ray experiments, which had not predicted charmonium’s long lifetime. The tau lepton’s discovery in 1975 brought further interest in a third particle generation and the six-quark proposal. His biography also records related work with Katsuhiko Sato on cosmological constraints on neutrino properties.

terms.definition: A situation in which the governing laws have a symmetry that the state adopted by the system does not share.
Invariance under the combined operations of exchanging particles with antiparticles and reflecting spatial coordinates.
A bound system consisting of a charm quark and its antiquark.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Combining evidence to solve the phase problem
sections.body: Ribosome crystals posed a difficulty beyond obtaining a diffraction pattern. Heavy atoms could help establish the phase information needed to reconstruct a structure, but the ribosome's size made their arrangement difficult to interpret. Steitz's group combined heavy-atom data with electron-microscopy images produced by Joachim Frank. Those images helped locate and orient the ribosomes within the crystal. The resulting 1998 structure of the large subunit had a resolution of nine ångströms: it revealed overall features but could not locate individual atoms. Better crystals and further measurements later produced the detailed structures needed to investigate the chemistry of protein synthesis.

sections.heading: Atomic level insights into ribosomal function and antibiotic action
sections.body: After the initial large-subunit structure in 1998, the laureates' groups reported high-resolution subunit structures in 2000: Steitz's group studied the large subunit, while Ramakrishnan's and Yonath's groups studied the small one. Structures of functional complexes connected shape to activity. Large-subunit work clarified peptide-bond formation, and small-subunit work explained how the genetic message is read accurately. Structures with bound antibiotics revealed where the drugs attach and how they inhibit bacterial ribosomes. They also helped explain changes in the drug target that can cause resistance, providing a basis for developing new antibiotics.

sections.heading: Structural breakthroughs in the 30S subunit
sections.body: Ramakrishnan's biography describes several distinct team contributions. Brian Wimberly used knowledge of protein–RNA interactions to trace the central domain of the 30S subunit and identify protein S20 in its maps. James Ogle led later experiments on the accuracy of decoding. Moving from a subunit to the whole ribosome required further work on purification and crystallisation. Frank Murphy and Mike Tarry developed preparations pure enough to crystallise, while Maria Selmer and Christine Dunham obtained high-resolution crystals containing messenger RNA and transfer RNA. These efforts helped turn a static subunit structure into a series of structures representing the ribosome's functional states.

terms.definition: The process where the ribosome reads messenger RNA information to produce proteins, converting DNA/RNA language into protein language.
The difficulty of obtaining the wave-phase information needed to reconstruct a structure from X-ray diffraction measurements.
The small subunit of a bacterial ribosome, containing RNA and proteins and participating in decoding messenger RNA.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Why a coal mine and power plant may share an owner
sections.body: Williamson's argument can be illustrated by a mine supplying a nearby coal-burning power station. Each may depend heavily on the other if alternative buyers and suppliers are far away. Investments that are valuable mainly within that relationship create difficult bargaining problems when circumstances change. Bringing both operations inside one organisation can provide a way to resolve disputes. When alternative trading partners are readily available, market exchange may work well instead. The Nobel background described evidence linking greater mutual dependence with longer, more complex contracts and, in some cases, common ownership. The relevant comparison is between the costs of different ways to organise the transaction.

sections.heading: How participation affects shared-resource rules
sections.body: Ostrom's studies showed that some groups of resource users develop effective rules for managing common property. The content of the rules matters, but so does the way they are created and enforced. People may be more willing to respect arrangements they helped design, monitor and maintain. Her findings challenged the assumption that shared access necessarily leads to unmanaged overuse. They also made institutional processes part of the explanation: successful governance requires attention to participation and enforcement, not merely a written rule. This complemented Williamson's analysis of how different organisational arrangements handle conflicts of interest.

sections.heading: Researching police performance and resource governance
sections.body: Ostrom's police research compared service arrangements in American metropolitan areas. In the cases studied, large departments did not outperform smaller forces of 25–50 officers in direct services such as patrol and criminal investigation. This challenged the assumption that multiple local units necessarily meant inefficiency. In the mid-1980s, National Research Council work exposed how research on shared resources was fragmented across disciplines and regions. The interdisciplinary workshop she and Vincent Ostrom had established in the early 1970s offered another approach, bringing scholars together to compare institutional arrangements in settings including police services, irrigation and forests.

terms.definition: Costs of arranging, carrying out and enforcing exchanges, including bargaining and resolving disputes.
The rules, institutions and processes through which economic activity is coordinated and disputes or collective decisions are handled.

terms.term: Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis
terms.definition: A research center founded by the Ostroms to study how diverse institutional arrangements influence behavior and outcomes across various settings.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary methods and themes in Müller's prose
sections.body: Müller uses linguistic opposition and collage to compose poetry. The award presentation highlights her departures from conventional plots, combining clear syntax and sharp details with an ambiguous reality. Niederungen depicts the cruelty and confinement of a German-speaking village, while novels such as Herztier and Der Fuchs war damals schon der Jäger explore terror under Ceaușescu. Atemschaukel grew from a project planned with poet Oskar Pastior; Müller completed it after his death. Everyday objects acquire associations with fear, and unexpected images disrupt familiar ways of seeing. These techniques join the concentration of poetry with detailed prose about surveillance, interrogation and exile.

sections.heading: Literary depictions of political oppression and forced labor
sections.body: Atemschaukel draws on Oskar Pastior's detailed recollections of deportation and forced labour in the Soviet Union. Müller had planned to write it with him, but his death during preparation left her to complete it alone. Cristina und ihre Attrappe uses material from her own secret-police dossier to examine the Securitate's pursuit of her, including after she left Romania. Herztier and The Appointment explore surveillance reaching into private life. Her biography also describes her friendships with writers from Aktionsgruppe Banat and her alarm at her father's service in an SS division. These experiences informed her concern with the effects of political ideology on individuals.

terms.definition: A term for writers who are not defeated by displacement through nostalgia, maintaining a critical gaze despite being rootless.
A group of writers who opposed the official literature of the ruling socialist party and the Ceauşescu dictatorship.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of telomere protection and enzymatic extension
sections.body: After Tetrahymena chromosome-end DNA protected artificial chromosomes in yeast, Szostak used the system to search for yeast’s own protective sequences. He removed one telomere and tested different yeast DNA fragments in its place. Most constructs degraded, but some fragments stabilised them. The yeast sequences also contained short repeats, although the precise sequence was not identical across species. Subsequent work showed that repeated telomeric DNA binds proteins that cap chromosome ends and prevent inappropriate joining. Mutations that disrupted telomere maintenance caused yeast cells to grow poorly and eventually stop dividing. The experiments connected a particular DNA structure and its associated proteins with continued cellular proliferation.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of telomere stability and telomerase function
sections.body: The 2009 presentation connected the basic mechanism with human disease. Some inherited defects in telomerase impair renewal of blood-forming cells and produce bone-marrow disorders. Many cancer cells, by contrast, maintain chromosome ends through elevated telomerase activity, helping sustain repeated division. The committee described clinical trials of telomerase-targeting approaches then under way, presenting treatment development as a research prospect. It did not establish that blocking the enzyme would cure cancer. The speech also explicitly treated telomere shortening as one influence on ageing among several. These applications emerged from work in simple organisms revealing that an enzyme could use an internal RNA template to extend chromosome-end DNA.

sections.heading: Solving the problem of copying chromosome ends
sections.body: Ordinary DNA-copying enzymes depend on an existing template and cannot by themselves fully solve the replication problem at chromosome ends. Telomerase supplies an extension: its RNA contains the information used to make additional telomeric DNA, while its protein component performs the catalytic work. The extension supports completion of chromosome-end replication by other DNA-synthesis machinery. Maintaining functional telomeres also protects the ends from damage. Experiments disrupting telomere maintenance caused premature loss of cell division in yeast and Tetrahymena, while later work showed that telomerase could postpone senescence in human cells. These cellular findings do not amount to a general method for preventing ageing of an organism.

terms.definition: A persistent loss of a cell’s ability to divide; telomere dysfunction can trigger it, but it is not simply a temporary slowing of division.
An enzyme complex that uses an RNA template to add telomeric DNA repeats to chromosome ends.
An RNA sequence used to specify a complementary DNA sequence, as in the addition of repeats by telomerase.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Diplomatic ambitions at the time of the award
sections.body: The 2009 presentation cited unanimous Security Council support for the aspiration of a world without nuclear weapons. It also described the US administration's reconsideration of planned missile defences in Eastern Europe. The committee believed this had improved the atmosphere for US–Russian strategic-arms negotiations, while explicitly expressing hope for an agreement still to come. It similarly judged Obama's climate proposals as a promising basis for further negotiations. These assessments explained an award intended to encourage diplomatic initiatives early in his presidency. The committee acknowledged criticism of the timing and welcomed scrutiny of whether his actions would match his ideals. Its argument concerned momentum and opportunities, not a completed record of disarmament or climate agreements.

sections.heading: Community work and legislative experience
sections.body: Before becoming president, Obama worked with churches in Chicago on problems affecting communities after local steel-plant closures. At Harvard Law School he became the first African-American president of the Harvard Law Review. He later returned to Chicago, helped organise voter registration and taught constitutional law at the University of Chicago. His award-era biography credited his Illinois Senate work with ethics reform and expanded health-care access for children and parents. It described his US Senate work on lobbying rules, weapons security and making federal spending information available online. These were parts of his background before the 2009 award, rather than the diplomatic achievements for which the Nobel Committee selected him.

terms.definition: The committee's description of an award intended to encourage further work on particular causes, alongside recognition of efforts already made.
Making information about public decisions and spending available so people can examine what their government does.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The obstacle of losing light in glass
sections.body: Early optical fibres could lose 99 percent of the light entering them within about 20 metres. Kao's research addressed whether glass could be made sufficiently transparent for long-distance communication, rather than merely showing that light could travel inside a fibre. The development also depended on a suitable source: lasers supplied concentrated light that could be introduced into a narrow guide. More practical sources able to operate continuously at room temperature arrived around 1970. Encoding information in rapid changes of light created the opportunity for high-capacity transmission, but reducing losses in the glass remained essential to making it useful over distance.

sections.heading: Recording images as electrical charge
sections.body: Boyle and Smith's 1969 invention provided a circuit able to store and read the distribution of electrical charge across its surface. When used for imaging, that distribution records the pattern of incoming light. Reading it out converts the image into an electrical form that can be processed or transmitted. The 2009 presentation highlighted scientific and medical uses as well as cameras: astronomical telescopes and instruments for keyhole surgery benefited from sensitive electronic image recording. This was a separate contribution from Kao's fibre research, though digital images became an important part of the information carried through optical networks.

sections.heading: From research proposals to practical instruments
sections.body: The announcement distinguished Kao's 1966 calculations about the potential of very pure glass from subsequent engineering: the first ultrapure fibre followed in 1970. Long-distance optical links depended on turning that insight into manufactured materials. For digital imaging, a parallel challenge was collecting and reading signals from many picture elements quickly. A CCD's pixels convert absorbed light into measurable charge, enabling an image to be recorded electronically. The announcement connected this capability with medical investigation and observation of remote environments, from the ocean to space. These applications show why the two awards concerned both communication infrastructure and tools for acquiring information.

terms.definition: The reduction in a signal's strength as it travels; in an optical fibre, it describes how much transmitted light is lost.
A semiconductor device that stores charge in an array and transfers it for readout; in an image sensor, the charge records incoming light.
The release or mobilisation of electrons when light is absorbed; CCD imaging uses light-generated charge to produce an electrical record.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Preserving material through a long synthesis
sections.body: Complex molecules are assembled through many reactions. If each stage sends too much material into unwanted products, little may remain at the end. Palladium-catalysed coupling offered chemists selective ways to join carbon-containing fragments, improving the practicality of such sequences. The official explanation describes the Suzuki reaction’s use in synthesising palytoxin, a large natural toxin. It also identifies a Negishi coupling as a central step in making discodermolide, which was difficult to obtain in useful amounts from its marine source. Producing enough material enabled further biological investigation. The 2010 account presented discodermolide as an experimental drug candidate, rather than an established cancer treatment.

sections.heading: Palladium-Catalysed Cross Coupling Mechanisms
sections.body: The three reactions use different partners for forming a carbon–carbon bond. In the Heck reaction, one partner can be bromobenzene and the other an olefin containing a carbon–carbon double bond. Negishi reported a coupling with carbon attached to zinc in 1977. Suzuki’s 1979 work used a carbon–boron reagent. Palladium participates in the reaction pathway, allowing suitable fragments to be joined selectively under comparatively mild conditions. The methods supplied complementary choices for organic synthesis rather than one recipe suitable for every molecule. Their industrial applications include pharmaceuticals, agricultural chemicals and organic compounds used in electronics.

sections.heading: Selectivity as a tool for organic synthesis
sections.body: The award announcement places the discovery within a wider challenge: constructing carbon-based molecules with the complexity found in nature. Earlier reactions that strongly activated a carbon-containing component could also produce unwanted reactions elsewhere. Palladium-mediated coupling gave researchers more control over which fragments joined. That precision expanded the range of structures they could make and study, from potential medicines to materials for electronic devices. The contribution was a set of broadly useful synthetic methods, rather than the discovery of one finished drug or device. Their value extends from research laboratories to commercial manufacture, with the choice of reaction depending on the particular construction needed.

terms.definition: Construction of a target molecule through a sequence of reactions, whose individual yields affect how much final product is obtained.
A reaction partner containing a carbon–boron bond, used to supply a carbon-containing fragment in a Suzuki coupling.
The planned construction of carbon-based compounds through chemical reactions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: How a small search cost can change prices
sections.body: Diamond’s 1971 model examined buyers searching for prices while sellers chose prices in response to that search behaviour. Under its assumptions, even a small search cost could produce the price a monopolist would charge in the corresponding market. The result differed sharply from the usual competitive benchmark. It showed why apparently minor obstacles to acquiring information could change market predictions substantially. Later search-and-matching models examined labour markets, where wage formation, recruiting and job-seeking interact. Their implications depend on the specified incentives and market conditions. The central lesson is that the process of finding a transaction can matter to the outcome, not just the gains once buyers and sellers meet.

sections.heading: Economic impacts of search frictions and unemployment insurance
sections.body: A job seeker’s greater search effort can make hiring easier for firms while increasing competition faced by other job seekers. These effects are not fully reflected in the individual’s decision, creating a possible role for policies that improve overall outcomes. The laureates’ labour-market framework examines search, recruitment and wage formation together. Unemployment insurance illustrates why policy evaluation needs several considerations. More generous benefits can prolong search, but can also help workers find better-suited jobs and protect income after job loss. The committee emphasised all of these considerations. A prediction about unemployment duration alone therefore does not determine which insurance arrangement provides the greatest welfare.

sections.heading: Why unemployment and vacancies can coexist
sections.body: An unfilled job and a person seeking work need not meet immediately. Searching consumes time and resources, so an economy can have vacancies and unemployment at once. The framework developed by Diamond, Mortensen and Pissarides makes that process part of the analysis instead of assuming an immediate match. It lets researchers examine how benefit arrangements and hiring or dismissal rules affect wages, recruiting and unemployment. The announcement also points to applications outside employment, including housing and monetary theory. These extensions share an interest in how participants establish contact and complete transactions, while the details of what is being matched differ across markets.

terms.definition: A price consistent with participants’ choices and incentives under a model’s assumptions.
Obstacles in markets that require time and effort for buyers and sellers to establish contact and reach transaction agreements.
An unfilled position for which an employer is seeking a worker.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary techniques and thematic explorations in Vargas Llosa's work
sections.body: The Nobel presentation connects Vargas Llosa’s storytelling with both the expansive nineteenth-century novel and modern experiments associated with Faulkner. The Time of the Hero and The Green House examine divisions within society through complex narratives. The Feast of the Goat turns to Rafael Trujillo’s Dominican dictatorship, exploring domination, servility and the abuse of power. The speech emphasises that these novels admit competing voices and interpretations while portraying Latin America’s varied social and cultural worlds. Their political engagement is carried through imagined lives and conflicts. In the committee’s reading, characters may suffer crushing historical forces while retaining a capacity for moral resistance. That tension links the account of power with the formal range of the fiction.

sections.heading: Literary inspirations and political evolution
sections.body: Vargas Llosa’s time at the Leoncio Prado Military Academy helped inspire The Time of the Hero, while a 1958 Amazon journey supplied material for The Green House and other novels. Conversation in the Cathedral drew on experiences of Peru under Manuel Odría. His biography connects a changing political outlook with increasing criticism of authoritarianism: after early support for the Cuban revolution, he moved toward liberal democracy and markets. In Peru he led Movimiento Libertad in opposition to Alan García’s proposed bank nationalisation and later ran for president. A Fish in the Water, published in 1993, recalled those political years. His later activities included El País columns and, from 2005, performing in his own theatrical work. These later stage appearances were not part of the earlier memoir.

terms.definition: Novels that bring multiple voices and perspectives into relation without reducing them all to one controlling viewpoint.
A political outlook supporting individual freedoms and the coexistence of differing views and political positions within democratic institutions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: From egg maturation to a successful pregnancy
sections.body: Edwards's doctoral research in Edinburgh concerned reproduction in mice. He began investigating human reproduction later, after moving to London, and found that human eggs required a different maturation schedule from the animal eggs previously studied. Access to suitable eggs remained difficult. Collaboration with Patrick Steptoe brought laparoscopic methods for collecting them from ovaries, while Edwards developed fertilisation and culture procedures. Early attempts used hormonal stimulation to obtain several eggs, but establishing pregnancy remained a separate obstacle. The team eventually worked with a naturally maturing egg, timing collection through the patient's cycle. That approach led to Louise Brown's birth in 1978. A private donation had helped the work continue after a Medical Research Council funding application was rejected. Edwards and Steptoe later established Bourn Hall Clinic to develop IVF treatment further.

sections.heading: Scientific developments in human egg maturation and fertilisation
sections.body: During the 1960s, Edwards systematically addressed scientific challenges to make in vitro fertilisation a reality. His research clarified how various hormones influence the maturation process of human eggs outside the body. In 1969, he and his colleagues demonstrated that human eggs could undergo fertilisation in an external environment. This work further showed that an egg fertilised outside the body was capable of generating an early embryo. By combining basic scientific research on reproductive biology with clinical investigations alongside gynaecological experts, Edwards transitioned these laboratory insights into a medical treatment. His efforts eventually led to the birth of Louise Joy Brown in July 1978, proving that external fertilisation could result in pregnancy and live birth.

terms.definition: A medical therapy involving fertilizing eggs in culture dishes and transferring embryos back into a woman to establish pregnancy.
Placement of an embryo into the uterus after fertilisation and early development outside the body, with the aim of establishing pregnancy.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Non-violent advocacy and Charter 08
sections.body: On 2 June 1989, Liu and companions began a hunger strike in Tiananmen Square against the declared state of emergency. Their six-point manifesto, written by Liu, opposed dictatorship and called for democracy. He urged a peaceful response to the confrontation with the authorities. His later advocacy continued through essays and literary organisations, including his 2003–2007 presidency of the independent Chinese PEN centre. He was one of the principal authors of Charter 08, released in December 2008. By the 2010 award, the committee described it as having attracted several thousand signatures in China and abroad.
