The document extended his commitment to non-violent argument and political reform.

sections.heading: Advocacy through Charter 08 and constitutional rights
sections.body: The committee placed Liu's work in the context of rights already stated in China's constitution, including speech, press, assembly and association under Article 35. Charter 08 appeared on the sixtieth anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, connecting the reform appeal to an international reference point. In 2009, a court sentenced Liu to eleven years in prison for inciting subversion of state power, with political rights removed for another two years. The announcement reported his argument that the punishment violated both constitutional guarantees and fundamental human rights. It also stressed that many other Chinese people, inside and outside the country, were involved in the wider campaign.

sections.heading: Writing, imprisonment and public solidarity
sections.body: Liu trained in literature at Jilin University and Beijing Normal University, where he also taught. He left a visiting position at Columbia in April 1989 to return to the democracy movement in Beijing. His subsequent writing and appeals led to repeated detention. A 1996 labour-camp sentence followed anti-corruption proposals and calls to reassess the June Fourth crackdown. He was detained again in December 2008 and convicted the following December. His lawyers reported nearly eight hundred essays by the time of that trial. In early 2010, more than six hundred Charter 08 signatories endorsed a separate declaration accepting shared responsibility with him, demonstrating continuing public solidarity.

terms.definition: A 2008 manifesto, co-authored by Liu Xiaobo, advocating fundamental rights and democratic reform in China.
The provision of China’s constitution cited by the committee for guarantees including freedom of speech, press, assembly and association.
A separate 2010 declaration by Charter 08 signatories supporting Liu after his conviction; its signers were not the charter’s entire signatory count.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental isolation of graphene using adhesive tape
sections.body: Repeatedly peeling graphite with adhesive tape produced progressively thinner flakes. The challenge was then to locate the rare single layers among thicker fragments. Geim, Novoselov and their colleagues placed the flakes on oxidised silicon. The underlying silicon-dioxide layer made sufficiently thin flakes visible through their optical contrast under a microscope; its thickness was crucial. This combination of preparation and identification made it practical to find individual graphene sheets for further experiments. The result was an atomically thin carbon lattice that could exist and be studied at room temperature.

sections.heading: Experimental isolation and characterization of graphene
sections.body: Finding a thin flake was only the beginning. The researchers used microscopy to establish that some samples were one atomic layer thick, shaped them by etching and attached electrodes for electrical measurements. This turned graphene from a candidate material into an experimental system. Its charge carriers behave in ways analogous to massless particles, producing unusual electronic phenomena. Later studies by several groups investigated an unusual quantum Hall effect and Klein tunnelling. The Nobel presentation highlighted how access to a real, measurable sheet allowed predictions about two-dimensional electronic behaviour to be tested.

sections.heading: Applications proposed when the prize was awarded
sections.body: The 2010 announcement highlighted possibilities arising from graphene's combination of properties. Its transparency and electrical conductivity suggested uses in touch screens, lighting panels and solar cells. Mixing graphene into plastics could improve electrical conduction, heat resistance and mechanical strength, suggesting lightweight composite materials. The committee also discussed prospects for faster transistors. These were research and development directions described at the time of the award. The Nobel-recognised achievement was making graphene available for experiments that could establish its properties and explore such possibilities.

terms.definition: A crystal whose structure extends over two directions while its thickness is limited to a single or very small number of atomic layers.
A conducting contact through which electrical signals or current can enter or leave a sample during an experiment.
A material formed by combining constituents to obtain useful properties, such as a plastic reinforced with graphene.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Experimental verification of fivefold symmetry in aluminum manganese
sections.body: On 8 April 1982, Shechtman examined an aluminium–manganese alloy with an electron microscope and observed a diffraction pattern with tenfold arrangements of bright spots. He tested whether the pattern could come from intergrown ordinary crystals, but found no evidence for that explanation. Rotating the specimen provided further information about its fivefold symmetry. These were checks on a surprising observation before it became a new structural interpretation. The finding met strong resistance because periodic crystals cannot possess that rotational symmetry. Shechtman's continued investigation ultimately helped establish ordered structures outside the conventional periodic classification.

sections.heading: Revision of symmetry and crystallinity concepts
sections.body: Shechtman's result challenged the assumption that every crystal must be periodic. It did not make fivefold symmetry compatible with an ordinary repeating crystal lattice. Instead, the observed structure had order without a periodically repeated unit. That distinction separated two ideas previously treated as inseparable: an arrangement can follow definite rules without repeating by translation through space. Quasicrystals therefore broadened the meaning of crystallinity and connected experimental materials science with mathematical descriptions of nonperiodic order. The 2011 presentation emphasised how a carefully checked observation could force revision of an established classification.

sections.heading: Mathematical patterns in atomic structures
sections.body: Mathematical patterns helped researchers understand order without periodic repetition. The Nobel announcement used geometric mosaics as a visual analogy and noted relationships to the golden ratio in distances within Shechtman's quasicrystals. Following the discovery, other quasicrystalline materials were produced in laboratories. Naturally occurring examples were also identified in mineral samples associated with a Russian river. Separately, a Swedish company found reinforcing quasicrystals in a type of steel. The announcement described experiments on possible uses in frying pans and diesel engines as work under investigation in 2011. These examples extended the discovery from a classification problem to questions about materials and their properties.

terms.definition: Symmetry in which a structure looks unchanged after rotation through one fifth of a complete turn about an axis.
Solids with long-range structural order but without the periodically repeating atomic arrangement of conventional crystals.
A ratio in which a whole is to its larger part as the larger part is to the smaller part.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Building a model for changes in policy rules
sections.body: Sargent's approach to systematic policy changes involves three stages. Researchers first specify a structural model containing relationships such as how households balance saving and consumption. They then solve it while accounting for expectations, including how people anticipate future inflation under the policy rule. Finally, historical data are used to estimate parameters assumed to remain stable when policy changes. The resulting model can be used to compare alternative rules, including policies with little historical precedent. Its usefulness depends on the relationships and expectations built into it. This differs from treating an observed correlation between policy and economic activity as a direct measure of causation.

sections.heading: Distinguishing causality in macroeconomic historical data
sections.body: Sims used vector autoregression to study how economies respond over time to unexpected changes. An impulse-response analysis traces an estimated response following a shock. The 2011 presentation illustrated this with an interest-rate cut: production and employment increased gradually, with the largest effect after roughly two years, while inflation responded later. These timings described the example presented, rather than a fixed law for every economy. The central challenge is that policy both influences economic conditions and reacts to them. Statistical models and the assumptions used to identify a shock help researchers separate those directions of influence.

sections.heading: Why expectations complicate cause and effect
sections.body: A policy decision can change behaviour before all of its effects appear in economic data. Expectations about future wages, interest rates or taxation influence saving and investment, while policymakers react to their own forecasts of private-sector behaviour. This two-way relationship makes observed movements difficult to interpret. Sargent's work examined how people adjust when policy rules change systematically; Sims's work helped analyse unexpected disturbances and their subsequent effects. The distinction between an anticipated policy and a surprise is therefore part of the causal question. The same recorded change can have different implications depending on what participants expected and why policymakers acted.

terms.definition: Unexpected occurrences in the economy, such as sudden declines in household consumption or unforeseen changes in the price of oil.
A time-series model relating several variables to their own past values and the past values of the others.
Beliefs about future economic policy that can influence decisions made by households and firms today.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Metaphorical visions and movement within poetic structures
sections.body: The poet's work utilizes brilliant metaphors to create illuminations within everyday life, often integrating images of vulnerability or stability. In the poem "Carillon," a figure in a Bruges hotel acts as an anchor against a great unknown shadow. His writing demonstrates a dual movement where internal states are projected onto external settings, such as a market square reflecting personal terrors and expectations. This technique employs sensuous precision to connect widespread phenomena into a single present. Through works like "Schubertiana," he captures precise movements, such as swallows returning to specific nests, mirroring how musical chords can signal an entire life. His poetic universe moves toward a central point, expanding from Swedish geography to include global locations like New York and Shanghai.

sections.heading: Influences and professional background of the Swedish poet
sections.body: Tranströmer's literary development was shaped by his studies in psychology, religious history, and literary history at Stockholm University College. His career as a psychologist at the Labor Market Institute and other facilities allowed him to integrate factual observation with the metaphorical reality of dreams into his verse. Early interests in entomology and geography, fostered at a pilot station on Runmarö, also informed his work, such as the collection Östersjöar. His poetry utilizes musicality and precise metaphors to explore existence, often addressing social motifs or themes of death in collections like Sorgegondolen. While his later writing became more concentrated following a 1990 stroke, he continued to utilize short forms like haiku to maintain a focus on concentrated expression and the connection between nature and the cosmos.

terms.definition: Moments of heightened perception in which an everyday scene reveals unexpected connections or meaning; the presentation uses the term for Tranströmer's poetic visions.
A quality found in Tranströmer's early poetry characterized by original metaphors and a connection between the natural world and existence.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Connecting tissue detection to T-cell responses
sections.body: Steinman isolated dendritic cells from mouse spleen and investigated why they were particularly effective at stimulating T cells. Later work showed that these cells occur in many tissues. After encountering microbial material, they can become activated and migrate to lymph nodes, where they help initiate lymphocyte responses. Signals from Toll-like receptors influence this activity, connecting innate recognition with adaptive immunity. Dendritic cells can also restrain T-cell activity. This regulation helps balance defence against infection with avoidance of harmful responses to the body’s own components. It is a control system that can fail, rather than a guarantee that immune responses never damage healthy tissue.

sections.heading: Related defence pathways in flies and mice
sections.body: Hoffmann’s fruit-fly experiments showed that the Toll pathway was essential to an effective defence against fungal infection. Beutler approached recognition from another direction: why mice differed in their response to bacterial lipopolysaccharide. Comparing strains identified a gene encoding a receptor related to Toll. Its signalling activates antibacterial defences, but excessive activation can contribute to life-threatening shock. Together the findings linked innate defence across insects and mammals. The receptor’s normal role in recognising microbial material and its involvement in dangerous inflammation belong to the same signalling system; encountering its target does not invariably produce septic shock.

sections.heading: Testing a new cell’s ability to activate T cells
sections.body: After identifying dendritic cells in 1973, Steinman tested their function in cell cultures. Adding them produced strong T-cell responses to substances the cells encountered. Subsequent experiments established their importance despite initial scepticism. Work by Steinman and other researchers then investigated how activation was controlled. Signals associated with innate responses could influence whether dendritic cells stimulated T cells. This connected the initial detection of microbial danger with a more specialised response and helped explain how inappropriate activation might contribute to inflammatory disease. The 2011 announcement linked that knowledge with vaccine development and attempts to stimulate immunity against tumours, while distinguishing the underlying discoveries from their developing applications.

terms.definition: An immune cell specialised in helping activate and regulate T cells, linking microbial detection with adaptive responses.
Rapid immune defences that recognise characteristic features of microbes and danger signals, operating alongside and influencing adaptive immunity.
Defence mediated by T and B lymphocytes that recognises particular targets and can develop memory of previous encounters.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Different routes to women's participation in peace
sections.body: The 2011 presentation compared grassroots mobilisation, journalism and national leadership. Gbowee brought more than 2,000 women together across Liberia, including public protests near Monrovia's fish market, and helped develop the Women in Peacebuilding Network. Karman founded Women Journalists Without Chains, organised peaceful sit-ins and information campaigns, and trained other women to participate. She became a leader of demonstrations in Sana's Change Square in 2011. Sirleaf's background included directing the UNDP's Africa bureau and serving on an Organization of African Unity investigation into Rwanda's genocide. The committee connected these different forms of action with women's equal participation in shaping peace.

sections.heading: Interfaith organising and pressure at peace talks
sections.body: Gbowee trained as a social worker and trauma counsellor, including work with former child soldiers. She became a founding member and Liberia coordinator of WIPNET, then helped bring Christian and Muslim women together in the Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace. Public protests pressed Charles Taylor to meet the women and agree to formal talks. Later, at stalled negotiations in Accra, Gbowee and nearly 200 women blocked the meeting hall's exits to pressure the negotiators to reach an agreement. These were distinct stages of the campaign. In 2006 she co-founded the Women Peace and Security Network Africa.

sections.heading: Sirleaf's route to elected leadership
sections.body: Before becoming Liberia's president, Sirleaf directed the UN Development Programme's Regional Bureau for Africa. She finished second in Liberia's 1997 presidential election and later campaigned for Charles Taylor's removal. During the transition to new elections, she chaired the Governance Reform Commission. She resigned in March 2004 to accept the Unity Party's nomination as its leader. In November 2005 she defeated George Weah with 59.4 percent of the vote and took office in 2006. Her historic distinction was becoming Africa's first democratically elected woman president, rather than the first woman ever to lead an African country.

terms.definition: A UN Security Council resolution adopted in 2000 addressing women's protection in conflict and their equal participation in peace processes.

terms.term: Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace
terms.definition: The interfaith movement that united Christian and Muslim women in public protest and pressure for an end to Liberia's war.
A body in Liberia's transitional government, chaired by Sirleaf before the 2005 elections, concerned with improving public governance.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Finding and calibrating brief stellar explosions
sections.body: Distant supernovae are useful only if they can be found and measured before fading. The teams needed rapid telescope access and coordinated follow-up observations, rather than waiting through normal scheduling cycles. They also had to separate the supernova's light from its host galaxy and account for dust. Type Ia explosions are not perfectly identical: the way brightness changes over time helps calibrate their luminosity against nearby examples. After these checks, the distant sample was still fainter than expected for a decelerating universe. The result indicated accelerating expansion while leaving its physical cause unresolved.

sections.heading: Comparing brightness distances with redshift
sections.body: Redshift tells astronomers how much cosmic expansion has stretched light, but turning it into a distance requires a model of the universe. Supernova brightness offered an independent comparison. By recognising the appropriate class of explosion and calibrating its luminosity, the teams estimated distance from apparent brightness. Digital searches repeatedly compared sky images to find candidates for these measurements. The supernovae were dimmer, and therefore more distant, than expected from a decelerating expansion history. Comparing the two kinds of information supported acceleration; it did not amount to measuring a star's motion directly or discovering what dark energy is made of.

sections.heading: Independent teams and improved observing tools
sections.body: Perlmutter's Supernova Cosmology Project began in 1988. Schmidt's High-z Supernova Search Team began in late 1994, with Riess playing a central role. More capable telescopes, computers and CCD imaging sensors made it possible to find and study distant explosions systematically. The teams examined type Ia supernovae, extremely bright events involving compact, evolved stars. The 2011 announcement reported that their combined distant samples exceeded fifty events. Finding the same unexpected faintness through independent projects increased confidence that the accelerating-expansion result was real. The achievement depended on sustained team observations and analysis, alongside the leadership recognised by the prize.

terms.definition: The name given to an unknown component used in cosmological models to account for accelerated expansion; the supernova observations did not establish its physical nature.
A shift of observed light toward longer wavelengths; cosmic expansion stretches the light travelling from distant galaxies.
A thermonuclear explosion involving a white dwarf star, used as a distance indicator after its intrinsic brightness is calibrated.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mapping the G-protein-coupled receptor family
sections.body: Lefkowitz's group used radioactively labelled substances, including beta blockers, to investigate and isolate adrenergic receptors. Cloning the beta-adrenergic receptor revealed a striking architectural similarity to rhodopsin: both cross the membrane seven times in helical segments and communicate with G proteins. This suggested a much larger receptor family. Determining a structure remained difficult because membrane proteins are hard to crystallise and receptors change shape as they signal. Kobilka's group eventually obtained a receptor–G-protein complex, reported in 2011. Its structure showed how the activated receptor accommodates the G protein on the cell's inner side.

sections.heading: Molecular mechanisms of G-protein-coupled receptor signaling
sections.body: The same broad receptor architecture serves very different forms of communication. Some family members respond to hormones such as adrenaline, others help detect odours or participate in vision. Their outward-facing parts recognise particular signals, while changes across the membrane communicate with machinery inside the cell. Lefkowitz and Kobilka developed methods for investigating these scarce proteins, establishing their structures, signalling behaviour and regulation. The 2012 presentation emphasised the combination of shared design and specialised function: related receptors allow cells to interpret many different aspects of their surroundings and produce appropriate internal responses.

sections.heading: Genetic cloning and structural studies of adrenergic receptors
sections.body: Kobilka made a genomic library from hamster lung DNA. Screening at Duke and Merck yielded a clone containing the complete beta-2 adrenergic receptor coding sequence, unexpectedly without introns. Related searches then identified other adrenergic receptors and an initially unidentified receptor later recognised as belonging to the serotonin family. Kobilka combined segments from alpha and beta adrenergic receptors to test which regions influence ligand binding and G-protein coupling. Later, with Greg Barsh, his group disrupted individual receptor genes in mice to investigate their cardiovascular and behavioural roles. These approaches connected gene sequences with receptor function before complete structural images were available.

terms.definition: A large family of cell surface sensors that use a shared mechanism to transmit external signals to internal G-proteins.
The process by which a cell converts a detected signal into changes in its internal activity.
Engineered receptors combining segments from different receptor proteins, allowing researchers to test the functions of particular regions.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Application of Gale-Shapley algorithm in medical markets
sections.body: Roth's 1984 analysis found that the National Resident Matching Program used a method closely related to Gale–Shapley matching. Studies of British medical markets later supported the importance of stability: systems producing stable matches tended to endure, while others broke down. The American system still faced problems, including the needs of couples seeking positions together and an advantage for hospitals as the proposing side. Roth and Elliott Peranson developed a revised, applicant-proposing algorithm accommodating couples. The NRMP adopted it in 1997. This was a separate reform from the 2003 redesign of New York school admissions.

sections.heading: Coordinating kidney exchanges
sections.body: A person willing to donate a kidney may be incompatible with the intended recipient. Exchange arrangements can connect that pair with others, allowing the donor to help a compatible patient while the original recipient receives a kidney from elsewhere. Chains can link many such donations and may begin with a donor who has no intended recipient. The Nobel presentation described a 2011 chain spanning the United States. It connected Roth's practical work with earlier theory about exchanges among people who already possess objects. Kidney exchange and two-sided school admissions draw on related matching ideas but require different arrangements and constraints.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of Stable Allocations and Market Design
sections.body: In the basic two-sided matching model, the Gale–Shapley algorithm produces a stable allocation. The design can systematically favour one side, so selecting a procedure also affects who benefits. Participants may have incentives to misrepresent preferences, making strategic behaviour another design concern. Roth combined empirical comparisons and laboratory experiments to investigate why particular matching institutions succeeded. Practical reforms adapted matching theory to settings such as doctor recruitment, school admissions and kidney exchange, each with its own constraints. The contribution was a way to connect mathematical properties of allocation rules with the needs and behaviour of real participants.

terms.definition: An allocation in which no acceptable pair of participants would both prefer to match with each other rather than keep their assignments.
An arrangement coordinating donations so that patients can receive compatible kidneys even when their intended donors cannot donate directly to them.
The development of rules and institutions for allocating opportunities or resources, taking account of participants' preferences, incentives and practical constraints.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary techniques and themes in Mo Yan's narratives
sections.body: The Nobel presentation reads Mo Yan's exaggeration, ridicule and folk imagery as ways of exposing deprivation, political hypocrisy and distorted official history. North-eastern Gaomi becomes a setting where ordinary life and the supernatural coexist. In The Republic of Wine, cannibalism provides a grotesque image of appetite and excess; the speech also interprets its treatment of boys and girls as a satire on family policy. Big Breasts and Wide Hips gives prominence to women's experience while moving through the Great Leap Forward, famine and the emergence of a new capitalism. Its absurd experiments in cross-breeding mock political pseudo-science and commercial fantasy. These critical readings show how fantastic events can carry arguments about historical suffering, greed and the persistence of human vitality.

sections.heading: Literary development and academic influences
sections.body: Mo Yan recalls beginning stories during his military service, sometimes retreating to a tool shed to write. Early submissions, including the play Divorce and the short piece Mama's Story, were rejected. In 1984 he entered the Literature Department of the PLA Arts Academy, where systematic study and translated works by Faulkner and García Márquez encouraged him to turn towards his native region. Childhood memories and people from his hometown supplied the material for his fictional Northeast Gaomi Township. He describes the 1985 publication of The Transparent Carrot as a turning point in his recognition as a writer. From 1988, a course run by the Lu Xun Literary Academy together with Beijing Normal University provided another period of study, during which he wrote The Republic of Wine.

terms.definition: A narrative style blending folk traditions, myths, and historical events with fantastic elements to critique social and political realities.
The place and social environment in which a story unfolds, often shaping its characters, events and themes.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Narrowing twenty-four candidates to four factors
sections.body: Yamanaka's team selected 24 genes associated with embryonic stem-cell pluripotency. Introducing individual candidates did not produce the desired change. Introducing the set together generated cells resembling embryonic stem cells, after which the researchers systematically reduced the combination. They found that four genes were sufficient for the reprogramming approach reported in 2006. The genes encode transcription factors that influence the activity of other genes. Later work developed ways to supply reprogramming instructions without permanently inserting DNA into the cell's genome. These developments addressed limitations of the original viral-delivery method, which could disrupt genes and contribute to tumour formation.

sections.heading: What nuclear transfer revealed about cell identity
sections.body: Gurdon placed a nucleus from a specialised tadpole intestinal cell into a frog egg whose own nucleus had been inactivated. Development after transfer showed that the donor nucleus retained instructions needed to generate other cell types. Specialisation therefore did not necessarily mean irreversible loss of the relevant genetic information. Yamanaka later achieved reprogramming by altering gene activity in intact cells. These were different experimental routes to the same broad question: how is a cell's identity maintained, and under what circumstances can it change? The resulting methods gave researchers tools for studying development and producing cells useful for investigating disease.

sections.heading: Using reprogrammed cells to investigate disease
sections.body: Yamanaka and colleagues tested combinations of genes in mouse fibroblasts, finding that four together could generate induced pluripotent stem cells. The work was reported in 2006. Related methods subsequently allowed human cells to be reprogrammed. Researchers could then direct such cells towards specialised forms, including nerve cells, and investigate how disease-associated changes affect their development or function. This provided a route from a patient's accessible cells to experimental models of less accessible tissues. The Nobel announcement emphasised opportunities for understanding disease and developing diagnostics and therapies, alongside the new understanding that differentiated cell states can be changed under suitable conditions.

terms.definition: Cells capable of developing into the different specialised cell types of the body.
Placing a donor cell's nucleus into an egg whose own nucleus has been removed or inactivated.
Cells experimentally reprogrammed from a specialised state into a pluripotent state capable of producing different body-cell types.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Binding cooperation grew from shared economic interests
sections.body: The presentation traces integration to the European Coal and Steel Community, established in 1951. Bringing strategically important production into shared arrangements was intended to reduce the likelihood of another war between France and Germany. Later enlargement linked economic participation with democratic government and common commitments. The United Kingdom, Ireland and Denmark joined in 1973, followed in the 1980s by Greece, Spain and Portugal. The committee viewed shared institutions, legal commitments and economic support as mutually reinforcing. Making war materially impossible was an ambition of the founding project, rather than a literal guarantee supplied by membership.

sections.heading: The committee’s assessment of enlargement in 2012
sections.body: The announcement credited membership conditions with helping consolidate democracy in southern Europe and later widening cooperation after the Cold War. It also pointed to Balkan developments then under way: Croatia’s expected accession, negotiations with Montenegro and Serbia’s candidate status. Its positive assessment of Turkey concerned the influence of a membership prospect during the preceding decade. These were judgments made in 2012, not descriptions of every country’s subsequent trajectory. The committee acknowledged economic hardship and unrest while choosing to recognize the union’s longer contribution to reconciliation and democratic institutions.

terms.definition: Bringing national economies into shared arrangements for trade, production or regulation, creating continuing interests and institutions across borders.
Requirements a state must satisfy to join an organization, used in this account to connect European integration with democratic standards.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Keeping a photon long enough to investigate it
sections.body: Haroche’s cavity used superconducting mirrors cooled close to absolute zero to retain microwave light for unusually long periods. Specially prepared Rydberg atoms passed through one at a time. Their interaction with the field changed the phase of the atoms’ quantum state, which could be measured after they left. This provided information about the photons while leaving them in the cavity. Wineland approached the complementary problem by trapping ions with electric fields and using laser light to control them. Both experiments required isolation and carefully controlled interactions, rather than complete separation from every measuring device.

sections.heading: Transferring and observing delicate quantum states
sections.body: Wineland used laser pulses to place an ion in a superposition of internal energy states and transfer that superposition to its motion. Haroche used excited atoms to investigate light stored between mirrors. These approaches made individual quantum systems accessible to controlled experiments. Preserving a particle is not the same as leaving every property of its state unchanged: the interaction must be designed around what is to be measured or manipulated. The presentation situates this work in quantum optics, where experiments investigate the fundamental relationship between matter and light.

sections.heading: Experimental tools for clocks and quantum information
sections.body: The 2012 announcement connected the methods with two promising applications. Precisely controlled ions supported clocks with much greater potential precision than the caesium standards then in use. Manipulating fragile quantum states also provided steps toward quantum information processing. These prospects followed from the ability to prepare, control and read individual systems reliably. The announcement’s expectations about future computers and time standards belong to the award’s historical setting; they do not mean that general-purpose quantum computers or a replacement international time standard had already been delivered in 2012.

terms.definition: Highly excited atoms used as sensitive probes of the microwave field in Haroche’s cavity experiments.
The study of light and its interactions with matter using quantum theory, including experiments with individual atoms or photons.
Preparing and changing a system’s quantum state through carefully managed interactions, while limiting unwanted disturbance from its surroundings.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Concentrating calculation where chemistry changes
sections.body: Multiscale modeling allocates computational effort unevenly. Electrons and nuclei directly involved in a reaction receive a quantum-mechanical treatment, while less critical surroundings can use simpler classical descriptions. Levitt and Warshel also explored reducing the number of separately represented atoms, and more distant surroundings can be approximated as a continuous medium. Their 1976 enzyme-reaction model was an important step toward this approach. The benefit is a tractable approximation of a large system, not unlimited simulation capacity or exact answers for every molecule. Selecting which region needs detailed treatment remains an essential modeling decision.

sections.heading: Approximations that make models informative
sections.body: The presentation speech emphasizes the choice of equations and approximations as much as the availability of computers. A calculation can be prohibitively demanding if every detail receives the same treatment. By combining physical descriptions suited to different parts of a chemical system, the laureates made more ambitious questions computationally accessible. Models can explore why a reaction occurs, what hinders it and how an enzyme or catalyst might be improved. Their value lies in connecting a proposed mechanism with testable behavior, with conclusions depending on the assumptions and resolution of the calculation.

sections.heading: Combining quantum and classical descriptions
sections.body: The announcement uses a drug interacting with a protein to illustrate the approach. A region directly involved in the interaction may be treated with quantum calculations, while much of the larger protein uses a less costly classical description. This balances local chemical detail with the influence of the surrounding structure. Related methods support investigation of processes such as catalysis and photosynthesis. The achievement was a practical framework for connecting levels of description; useful predictions still depend on choosing suitable models and comparing their results with experimental evidence.

terms.definition: An approximation representing surrounding material through its average electrical response rather than tracking every constituent atom explicitly.
A mathematical representation of a system used to investigate its behavior under stated physical assumptions and approximations.
Combining descriptions with different levels of detail within one calculation, so important local processes can be studied in their broader surroundings.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Testing a model rather than accepting a plausible explanation
sections.body: Changing risk and discount rates might help explain why asset prices fluctuate more than dividends. To evaluate that explanation, Hansen used his Generalized Method of Moments to test the standard consumption-based asset-pricing model against historical data. The basic model failed those tests. This result did not reject every possible rational account of markets; it identified limitations in a particular formulation and prompted new models and evidence. Shiller’s findings about longer-run patterns likewise concerned statistical tendencies, rather than a timetable reliably forecasting the price of an individual asset.

sections.heading: Different time horizons revealed different patterns
sections.body: Fama’s event studies examined how prices responded to new public information. Rapid adjustment made daily or weekly movements difficult to predict from already available news. Shiller instead compared prices with dividends over longer periods and found average patterns over several years. Such predictability did not imply a risk-free trading rule or certainty in every episode. Hansen’s statistical methods supplied tools for evaluating whether proposed economic models could account for the data. The contributions fit together as measurement, empirical challenge and model testing, despite differing interpretations of market behavior.

sections.heading: Competing explanations for persistent price patterns
sections.body: One explanation of longer-horizon return patterns emphasizes changing risk: investors may demand higher expected compensation during unusually uncertain periods. Another examines behavioral biases and limits on trading against mispricing. Borrowing constraints, for example, can prevent an investor from taking a position large enough to eliminate an apparent pricing error. The announcement presents these as research approaches that together inform understanding of asset prices. Their coexistence is part of the prize’s significance: the evidence stimulated a continuing debate rather than settling on one universal explanation of every price movement.

terms.definition: An approach linking asset values and expected returns to investors’ consumption decisions, preferences and exposure to risk.
A statistical method estimating and testing model parameters by comparing relationships implied by the model with corresponding patterns in observed data.
Research examining how psychological influences and market constraints affect financial decisions and asset prices.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary techniques and thematic depth in Ontario settings
sections.body: Munro utilizes a minimalist, transparent style characterized by precision and the absence of superfluous phrasing. Her narratives often unfold within the flat agricultural landscapes of south-western Ontario, presenting a tranquil exterior that masks a complex inner world. These stories function as emotional chamber plays, focusing on silences, unexpressed pain, and the lives of those on the sidelines. Through an elliptical technique, she explores how characters experience epiphanies regarding things they failed to understand in the moment. Her work examines the intersections of gender, class, and sexuality, often portraying the devastating nature of dreams or romantic love. By moving deftly between different time periods, a single brief text can summarize decades of a life, capturing extraordinary depth within a small page count.

sections.heading: Development of Munro's literary career and editorial support
sections.body: Robert Weaver of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation bought The Strangers in 1951, the first of fourteen Munro stories he would broadcast. He became an important editor, adviser and advocate. Lives of Girls and Women, published in 1971 as a novel composed of interconnected stories, widened her reputation. Her award biography also links her return to Huron County in 1975 with greater directness and complexity in depicting local life. Later, agent Virginia Barber and editors Ann Close and Douglas Gibson helped develop successive collections. New Yorker editors also worked on stories, although some magazine revisions were reversed for book publication.

terms.definition: A narrative method that leaves events or connections unstated, inviting the reader to infer them from selected details and shifts in time.
Related narratives linked by characters, setting or themes; Munro's Lives of Girls and Women brought such stories together as a novel.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Three complementary ways to understand cellular delivery
sections.body: Schekman found yeast mutants in which vesicles accumulated, then identified genes needed for different transport steps. Rothman investigated proteins that allow a vesicle to join a target membrane. Südhof examined the rapid release of neurotransmitters, identifying machinery that responds to calcium signals. These contributions addressed different questions: which components are required, how membranes fuse, and when release occurs. The presentation connects this coordinated delivery system with processes such as nerve communication and insulin secretion. Accurate timing matters alongside the destination, because a message released at the wrong moment can fail to perform its normal function.

sections.heading: An ancient mechanism adapted for rapid signaling
sections.body: Some genes identified in yeast encoded proteins corresponding to those Rothman studied in mammalian cells. That connection showed that important elements of vesicle transport were shared across very different organisms. In nerve cells, the same broad delivery problem requires exceptionally precise timing. Südhof identified proteins and interactions responding to an incoming calcium signal so that prepared vesicles release neurotransmitters rapidly. The announcement therefore links a general cellular transport system with a specialized signaling function, rather than treating every vesicle as carrying the same cargo or operating on the same schedule.

sections.heading: A failed replication exposed a different transport step
sections.body: Rothman recalls that he and Erik Fries initially struggled to reproduce their published cell-free transport experiment. Investigating the discrepancy revealed that their preparation had reconstructed transport within the Golgi apparatus, a process they had not initially recognized. The episode illustrates why identifying exactly what an assay measures matters as much as getting a positive result. His earlier training in membrane biochemistry supplied part of the foundation for this work. In his account, revising the interpretation of an experiment turned an apparent setback into evidence about a specific stage of the secretory pathway.

terms.definition: Joining of two membrane surfaces, allowing a vesicle’s contents to enter another compartment or be released outside a cell.
A small membrane-enclosed compartment that can carry material within a cell or deliver it for release outside the cell.
Recreating a biological process using components outside intact cells, allowing researchers to identify and test the machinery required.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A treaty aimed at eliminating a weapon category
sections.body: The Chemical Weapons Convention entered into force in 1997, and the OPCW was created to oversee its implementation. States joining the agreement undertook detailed obligations, including declarations of chemical weapons and production facilities. The 2013 presentation emphasised that the objective was elimination, rather than merely limiting arsenals. It contrasted this commitment with the unequal status of nuclear powers: the chemical-weapons treaty did not reserve possession rights for selected members. The committee also urged states outside the agreement to join. Its account celebrated a process of verified disarmament while recognising that important tasks remained. The aspiration to remove other weapons of mass destruction was part of the committee's wider argument, not the OPCW's mandate to supervise every kind of weapon.

sections.heading: Verification and unfinished work in 2013
sections.body: At the October 2013 announcement, the committee reported 189 states as parties to the Chemical Weapons Convention. It described inspections and verification of destruction as means of turning the treaty's prohibitions into practice. Earlier bans had addressed use; the convention also prohibited production and stockpiling. The announcement identified unfinished obligations: some states remained outside the agreement, while the United States and Russia had missed the April 2012 destruction deadline. Chemical attacks in Syria reinforced the urgency of the work. These figures and shortcomings describe the situation at the award, rather than current membership or today's stockpile status. The committee presented the prize as support for completing elimination, not a declaration that chemical warfare had already disappeared.

terms.definition: Reducing or eliminating weapons; in the OPCW's case, the convention aims at complete elimination of chemical arsenals.
The treaty that entered into force in 1997, prohibiting chemical weapons and requiring their destruction under international verification.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A field that changes how symmetry appears
sections.body: Quantum field theory describes particles as excitations of fields. Electroweak theory needed to accommodate massive W and Z force carriers while retaining a massless photon. The mechanism developed by Englert and Brout, independently of Higgs, showed how a field could have a physical state that hides a symmetry of the equations. The resulting theory permits massive particles without discarding its underlying structure. The Nobel background compared this to a phase transition, using freezing as an analogy. Particles' different interactions with the field determine their masses, while the photon remains massless.

sections.heading: From a proposed mechanism to a workable theory
sections.body: The 1964 papers showed how a theory analogous to electromagnetism could have a massive force carrier without leaving an unwanted additional massless particle. This was a mechanism that helped make later electroweak unification possible, rather than a complete Standard Model already constructed in those papers. A further question was whether such theories allowed consistent calculations. The presentation connected their acceptance with 't Hooft's subsequent work, recognised in the 1999 prize. This sequence links the mass-generation mechanism with the mathematical tools needed to test a theory against experiments. The Standard Model describes electromagnetic, weak and strong interactions, but does not include gravity.

sections.heading: The discovery at CERN and remaining questions
sections.body: On 4 July 2012, the ATLAS and CMS experiments announced a new particle at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Its properties supported identification as a Higgs boson. The 2013 announcement described two collaborations of around 3,000 scientists each finding the signal among enormous numbers of collisions. This supplied evidence for the proposed field and mass-generation mechanism. It did not complete every aspect of particle physics. The announcement highlighted observed neutrino masses, absent from the original minimal Standard Model, and dark matter as problems requiring further understanding. The theoretical prize therefore recognised a major confirmed component of a broader, still incomplete framework.

terms.definition: A situation in which a system's physical state does not display all the symmetries present in the equations describing it.
An interaction effective over a limited distance; the mechanism explained how massive force carriers could arise in a consistent field theory.
A particle corresponding to an excitation of the Higgs field, providing an observable way to investigate that field's properties.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Separating molecular signals instead of collecting them all at once
sections.body: Conventional fluorescence images blur together signals from nearby molecules. The awarded methods create ways to distinguish those contributions. Hell used stimulated emission to suppress fluorescence around a small region. The single-molecule route depended on detecting and controlling individual emitters so their positions could be determined separately. Moerner’s 1989 detection of absorption by one molecule was an early milestone, while Betzig developed approaches that combined many localized signals into an image. These methods overcame a limit of conventional image formation; they did not repeal diffraction or make every biological structure observable without practical limits.

sections.heading: Two routes to resolving closely spaced molecules
sections.body: In STED microscopy, one beam excites fluorescent markers and another suppresses their ordinary fluorescence around a small central region. Scanning builds an image with finer detail. Single-molecule localization takes a different approach: activate a sparse subset of markers, estimate their positions, switch them off and repeat with others. Combining the positions yields a detailed image. The key distinction is between controlling where fluorescence occurs and separating emissions in time. Neither method simply makes the conventional blurry image sharper by magnifying it more.

sections.heading: Imaging living processes with less unnecessary illumination
sections.body: Betzig’s biography describes a related challenge: observing living cells without damaging them through excessive light exposure. Inspired by light-sheet imaging, his team used a scanned Bessel beam to illuminate a thinner region. Later work on patterned optical fields led to lattice light-sheet microscopes, with several postdoctoral collaborators contributing essential methods and instruments. Restricting illumination to the region being observed improved three-dimensional studies of living systems and extended single-molecule approaches to thicker samples. This was a broader imaging program alongside the single-molecule localization work central to the prize.

terms.definition: Imaging methods that distinguish details more closely spaced than conventional optical microscopy can resolve, using additional control or information.
The conventional optical limit on separating nearby features, set by wavelength and light collection; it does not mean smaller objects can never be detected.
Imaging that illuminates a thin plane of a specimen at a time, reducing unnecessary exposure elsewhere while recording three-dimensional structures.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Regulation when firms know more than regulators
sections.body: A regulator typically cannot directly observe everything about a firm’s costs, effort or service quality. This gives the regulated company an informational advantage. Tirole, often working with Jean-Jacques Laffont, developed models of how incentives and contracts could address that problem. Game theory also helped analyze industries in which a few firms react strategically to one another. The resulting approach replaced the search for one simple rule with questions about available information, credible commitments and how decisions change over time. These details determine whether a proposed regulatory arrangement encourages efficiency or protects existing advantages.

sections.heading: Treating the regulator as part of the problem
sections.body: The presentation speech stresses that regulatory design must consider both company behavior and the incentives of public authorities. Firms respond to opportunities for profit, to what they know and to which commitments can be enforced. Regulators also make choices within constraints and may need rules governing their own conduct. Tirole used game theory to examine these interactions. The implications differ across industries, including banks, telecommunications and digital platforms. The contribution was an analytical framework for evaluating rules, not the direct authorship of every law later applied to those industries.

sections.heading: Why the same rule can have different effects
sections.body: The announcement gives examples of regulatory trade-offs. A price cap may encourage a firm to lower costs while also allowing high profits. Cooperation over prices can damage competition, whereas sharing access through a patent pool may have benefits. A merger between a producer and a supplier can encourage some innovations but can also disadvantage rivals. Tirole’s analysis asks which conditions make each outcome likely. The lesson is to examine incentives and market structure before applying a broad rule, rather than declaring every merger or form of cooperation either beneficial or harmful.

terms.definition: A situation in which different parties possess different relevant information, such as a firm knowing its costs better than its regulator.
The study of decisions whose outcomes depend on the choices of other participants, including how information and credible commitments affect behavior.
A firm’s ability to influence prices or other market conditions rather than simply accept terms set by competition.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Investigating an inherited past through fragments
sections.body: The presentation speech traces a change from the sharp rhythms of Modiano’s early novels toward the quieter prose associated with Villa Triste and Dora Bruder. Addresses, old telephone numbers and fragmentary documents become ways of approaching lives that are difficult to recover. The Academy interprets his early attention to occupied France as challenging reassuring public stories about the period. This is a literary and historical assessment, not a claim that he personally remembered events before his birth. His work repeatedly brings incomplete evidence into contact with questions of family, identity and responsibility.

sections.heading: A newspaper notice became a sustained investigation
sections.body: Modiano recalls finding a missing-person notice for Dora Bruder in an old issue of Paris-Soir while reading newspapers in 1988. Years of investigation followed before he wrote the book dedicated to her. His biography also describes work outside his usual novels: collaborating with Louis Malle on the screenplay of Lacombe Lucien, writing with his wife Dominique, and working with illustrator Jean-Jacques Sempé on Catherine Certitude. These examples show both the persistence of his historical inquiries and the range of forms through which he developed them.

terms.definition: Using surviving traces, narrative and imagination to approach a past that cannot be recovered completely from available evidence.
A written framework for a film’s scenes, action and dialogue, such as Modiano’s collaboration with Louis Malle on Lacombe Lucien.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: A pattern in activity, not a grid of physical cells
sections.body: O’Keefe found hippocampal neurons that became active at particular places as a rat explored. The Mosers later found entorhinal neurons that fired at several locations arranged in a repeating hexagonal pattern. The grid describes positions in the animal’s environment where a neuron fires; it does not describe the physical arrangement of neurons in the brain. Activity across many such cells provides information useful for tracking position and movement. Their connections with place cells helped explain how a distributed neural circuit could represent space.

sections.heading: Combining location with direction and boundaries
sections.body: Place and grid cells operate alongside other neurons that respond to head direction or environmental borders. Their combined activity links current location with the geometry of the surroundings and the direction of movement. The announcement also describes evidence for related spatial representations in humans from imaging and recordings during neurosurgery. It connects this research with questions about disorientation in Alzheimer’s disease, because affected brain regions include the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex. That connection provides a research direction for understanding symptoms, rather than a treatment established by the prize-winning experiments.

sections.heading: How spatial representations change between environments
sections.body: Moser’s account describes remapping: hippocampal populations can adopt substantially different firing patterns when an animal enters another environment or when a task changes. Such observations suggested a way to investigate how separate experiences are represented. The research program also identified cells combining spatial and directional activity, and border cells that responded near walls or edges. These findings expanded the study beyond a single kind of spatial neuron. Position, orientation and boundaries could be examined as interacting signals within a broader navigation system.

terms.definition: A neuron whose activity recurs at locations forming an approximately hexagonal pattern as an animal moves through an environment.
A hippocampal neuron that becomes especially active when an animal occupies a particular region of its surroundings.
A change in a population’s spatial firing pattern when the environment or relevant task conditions change.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Linking freedom from exploitation with access to education
sections.body: The presentation describes Satyarthi’s work as extending beyond rescue to rehabilitation and schooling. His international campaign brought child-rights groups and labor organizations together in the 1998 Global March Against Child Labour, contributing to the adoption of an ILO convention the following year. Yousafzai’s public advocacy began through accounts of life under Taliban pressure and defense of girls’ schooling. The committee connected these distinct approaches through a shared aim: children should have the security and opportunity to learn, rather than lose their education through coercion, exploitation or violence.

sections.heading: Why the committee connected children’s rights with peace
sections.body: The announcement argues that peaceful development depends on respecting young people’s rights. It recognizes Satyarthi’s nonviolent campaigns against exploitation and Yousafzai’s advocacy for girls’ education under dangerous conditions. The joint award also highlights the capacity of young people to act for themselves, rather than treating them only as recipients of adult protection. Its reasoning connects education, freedom from forced labor and the prevention of recurring violence. These are the committee’s grounds for the peace award, not a claim that either laureate had already eliminated the problems they confronted.

sections.heading: Organizing at international and village levels
sections.body: Satyarthi’s biography describes a coalition combining child-rights organizations, teachers’ unions and trade unions. Alongside international campaigning, it outlines a village-based approach in India and Nepal intended to keep children out of work and in school. Children’s parliaments give young people a way to raise concerns with local decision-making bodies. The account also connects consumer action with the carpet industry through GoodWeave. These are complementary methods: influencing international rules, changing local participation and using purchasing decisions to challenge exploitation in production.

terms.definition: An international campaign and coalition mobilizing support for ending child exploitation and securing children’s access to education.
A formal agreement between states establishing commitments on a subject, such as protections against the worst forms of child labor.
A representative forum through which children in the village program express concerns and participate in decisions affecting them.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Making the required semiconductor layers work
sections.body: Gallium nitride offered suitable properties for blue light, but growing useful crystals and producing a functioning p-type layer proved difficult. Akasaki and Amano developed one route, while Nakamura independently found a heat-treatment method for activating p-type material. Improvements using alloys with indium or aluminium helped create more efficient structures. In an LED, applied voltage drives electrons and positively charged holes into an active region, where their recombination can produce light. The research therefore combined crystal growth, control of electrical properties and device design.

sections.heading: Why blue light completed a practical lighting system
sections.body: Red and green LEDs were available well before efficient blue devices. Blue was needed to assemble practical white-light sources, but promising materials repeatedly failed to yield the necessary crystal and electrical quality. The presentation highlights the persistence of the Nagoya and Nichia research programs in overcoming those difficulties. Unlike an incandescent filament, an LED converts electrical energy into light through a semiconductor device, avoiding the need to heat a filament until it glows. Efficient blue emission therefore had consequences beyond adding another indicator color: it enabled a new approach to general lighting.

sections.heading: A research program spanning universities and industry
sections.body: Akasaki’s career record places the blue-LED work within a long semiconductor research program. He worked in industrial laboratories before becoming a professor at Nagoya in 1981. From 1987 to 1990 he led a development project on gallium-nitride blue LEDs. A later project, from 1993 to 1999, addressed short-wavelength semiconductor laser diodes. His subsequent Meijo University roles continued that research leadership. The chronology distinguishes the LED development program from related laser work and shows the institutional continuity behind advances that are often summarized as a single invention.

terms.definition: Semiconductor material in which mobile positive holes, representing missing electrons, are the majority charge carriers.
A compound semiconductor made from gallium and nitrogen, central to the development of efficient blue LEDs.
A semiconductor device that produces laser light, distinct from an LED; Akasaki’s later development project focused on short wavelengths.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Reconstructing the removal of ultraviolet damage
sections.body: Sancar investigated bacterial strains carrying mutations in genes called uvrA, uvrB and uvrC. Their sensitivity to ultraviolet light helped identify components of a repair system that works without illumination. He reconstructed how proteins recognize damage, cut out an affected stretch of DNA and enable restoration of the sequence. This nucleotide-excision pathway differs from photolyase, which directly repairs certain UV lesions using light. Research in human cells revealed more complex machinery performing a chemically related excision process. Comparing the systems made a hidden maintenance activity accessible to biochemical experiments.

sections.heading: Different errors require different repair routes
sections.body: Lindahl showed that DNA undergoes spontaneous chemical changes often enough to require continual maintenance. His work characterized base excision repair, which starts by removing a damaged base. Modrich investigated mismatches left when DNA is copied, while Sancar studied removal of damage such as ultraviolet lesions. These pathways address different kinds of problems rather than serving as interchangeable backups. Their discovery changed the picture of the genome from a chemically stable archive to information preserved through active surveillance and repair. Errors that escape or overwhelm these processes can have biological consequences.

sections.heading: What repair defects reveal about disease
sections.body: The announcement links the repair mechanisms with inherited vulnerabilities. Defects in nucleotide excision repair can make people exceptionally sensitive to sunlight and increase skin-cancer risk. Inherited defects in mismatch repair can predispose families to particular cancers, including colorectal cancer. These connections show why accurate copying alone is insufficient: cells also need systems that detect and correct problems. Understanding those systems has informed cancer research and treatment development, but identifying a pathway is distinct from establishing a successful therapy for every condition associated with it.

terms.definition: A repair pathway that removes a short stretch of DNA containing a lesion and replaces it using the undamaged strand as a guide.
A DNA repair pathway that begins by removing an altered base and then restores the affected region.
Correction of improperly paired DNA bases and related errors left after replication, improving the fidelity of copied genetic information.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Resolving contradictions in consumption and income data
sections.body: The Deaton paradox concerns a particular application of permanent-income reasoning to persistent aggregate income movements. If an unexpected income rise signals further increases, a representative consumer should raise consumption strongly in anticipation. Yet aggregate consumption was smoother than that prediction. Deaton showed why individual data mattered: personal incomes do not move like the economy-wide average, because increases for some people coincide with decreases for others. Modelling individual responses before adding them together, and allowing for borrowing constraints, brought predictions closer to observed patterns. The work also examined how differences in consumption widen within a generation as its members age, informing analysis of protection against income shocks.

sections.heading: Measuring poverty through expenditure analysis
sections.body: Deaton used household evidence to investigate living standards that aggregate accounts could obscure. Consumption data can reveal what people eat, their housing and their access to services, especially where income is difficult to measure. The approach also recognises that poorer and richer households buy different combinations of goods, so one average spending pattern cannot represent everyone. The 2015 presentation reported a declining global proportion of people in severe material poverty, while noting discrepancies between household evidence and measured production growth. Those were historical findings described at the award, illustrating why careful measurement matters when evaluating economic progress.

sections.heading: A demand model that can test consumer theory
sections.body: Deaton and John Muellbauer introduced the Almost Ideal Demand System in 1980. It models how households divide spending among goods as prices and overall expenditure change. Its flexibility makes it possible to estimate demand while testing restrictions implied by consumer theory. In their original application to British data, some of those restrictions were rejected, revealing limitations that required further investigation. The model was therefore a tool for testing and improving explanations of behaviour as well as estimating demand. Such analysis helps evaluate policies like consumption taxes, whose effects differ across households because their spending patterns differ.

terms.definition: The finding that aggregate consumption is smoother than predicted by a representative-consumer model using particular persistent income dynamics.
Extensive data collection tools designed and analyzed to track consumption, nutrition, and sanitary conditions to measure human welfare.
A model of how spending on different goods responds to prices and total expenditure, used to estimate demand and test consumer theory.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Listening beyond official accounts of history
sections.body: The five-book Voices of Utopia sequence examines Soviet experiences through individual testimony. For War's Unwomanly Face, Alexievich interviewed hundreds of women who had served in the Red Army. Their recollections include improvised hair curlers made from pinecones and the stigma some faced after returning home. Such details complicate heroic accounts that foreground male soldiers. Voices from Chernobyl likewise records the intimate consequences of a catastrophe through the people affected by it. The award presentation emphasises her questioning and listening: experiences of fear, suffering and endurance become the substance of literature rather than background to a grand historical narrative.

sections.heading: Documentary methods and historical themes in Alexievich's prose
sections.body: Alexievich developed a distinctive form of literary non-fiction from personal accounts. For The Boys in Zinc, she spent four years interviewing veterans and mothers affected by the Soviet-Afghan war and also visited Afghanistan. The book challenged the official portrayal of the conflict and provoked attacks in military and Communist newspapers. Her 1993 book Enchanted with Death examines people whose attachment to Soviet ideals shaped suicidal crises following the state's collapse. Across her work, she investigates how major political events enter private life. The linked biography characterises these accounts as a history of several generations' beliefs, hopes and disillusionment.

terms.definition: A five-book literary suite by Alexievich describing twentieth-century catastrophes through the mental history of Soviet citizens.
Writing based on real events and testimony that uses literary structure and style; Alexievich developed her own approach within this broader field.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Natural sources became starting points for experimental screening
sections.body: Ōmura selected and cultured soil bacteria, and Campbell’s team tested their products against parasitic worms in animals. An especially active culture led to avermectin and then its chemically modified derivative ivermectin. Tu followed a separate route, investigating traditional descriptions of sweet wormwood and changing extraction conditions after earlier results proved inconsistent. Avoiding excessive heat helped preserve an active component, later identified as artemisinin. In both programs, a natural source supplied a lead; controlled extraction, screening and further development established particular substances as useful medicines.

sections.heading: Practical methods behind antiparasitic research
sections.body: Campbell describes how collaboration between chemists and parasitologists supported drug discovery at Merck. Testing compounds for activity was a productive strategy even when researchers did not yet know the ideal biochemical target. He also developed methods for freezing and preserving certain parasitic worms for years. Keeping strains available in this way reduced the need to maintain them through repeated infections in large animals. Such laboratory infrastructure supported reliable comparisons and continuing research alongside the better-known discovery of a successful drug.

sections.heading: From a soil culture to veterinary and human use
sections.body: Ōmura’s account traces the producing microorganism to a soil sample collected near a golf course in Shizuoka, Japan. Testing in Campbell’s laboratory revealed strong activity against a worm infection in mice. Avermectin emerged from the culture, and chemical modification produced ivermectin. Veterinary development preceded its major use against certain human filarial infections. The biography describes the subsequent role of organized distribution programs in reaching affected populations. This history separates discovery, drug development and public-health delivery, each necessary to turn biological activity into widespread benefit.

terms.definition: A group of soil bacteria that produce many biologically active substances and supplied the original source of avermectin.
Preserving living material at very low temperatures so it can later be recovered for use, as in Campbell’s work maintaining nematode strains.
A drug acting against parasitic worms; activity against those organisms does not imply effectiveness against unrelated diseases.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The Quartet's mediation and constitutional impact
sections.body: Following the 2011 Revolution, Tunisia faced instability from political assassinations, terrorist killings of soldiers, and widespread demonstrations. To address this crisis, Hassine Abassi of the UGTT initiated a joint proposal involving four distinct organizations. This collective effort functioned as a mediator to prevent civil war and promote democratic development. The process led to the adoption of a new constitution on 26 January 2014, which established a system guaranteeing fundamental rights regardless of religious belief or gender. Following a roadmap that saw the Troika government replaced by a caretaker administration, the Quartet's work enabled parliamentary and presidential elections in late 2014. This transition allowed for the lawful replacement of both the interim president and the technocratic government with elected successors.

sections.heading: The Quartet's account of the transition
sections.body: In their Nobel lecture, the Quartet traced the crisis to the uprising that began in December 2010 and the difficult transition following it. They described an initial commission that helped prepare elections for a Constituent Assembly in October 2011, followed by renewed polarisation and opposition deputies' withdrawal from participation. The four organisations then sponsored dialogue among political parties to rebuild agreement. Their account linked this work with an interim government of independent specialists, adoption of a constitution, establishment of electoral arrangements and eventual parliamentary and presidential elections. They credited other political actors and civil society as well as their own mediation. This was a retrospective account of that transition, not a guarantee of Tunisia's later democratic development.

terms.definition: Organisations outside government through which people pursue shared interests and public causes, including the Quartet's labour, business, legal and human-rights bodies.
The Quartet-sponsored effort to bring competing Tunisian political groups into negotiations over completing the democratic transition.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
National Dialogue Quartet: mediation, the road map and unfinished challenges — Nobel lecture, 10 December 2015 (PDF)

sections.heading: Comparing neutrinos that traveled different distances
sections.body: Super-Kamiokande studied neutrinos produced in the atmosphere using a large underground detector. Muon-neutrino events were less common for particles arriving through the Earth than for those coming from overhead. The longer travel distance supplied evidence of transformation; the original result did not simply photograph tau-neutrinos appearing. SNO studied solar neutrinos through measurements sensitive to different interactions, showing that the shortfall in electron neutrinos was consistent with a changed mixture of types. Underground operation reduced cosmic-ray backgrounds, helping both experiments extract rare neutrino signals.

sections.heading: Why changing flavor implies differences in mass
