sections.body: Electron, muon and tau describe neutrino flavors: the categories identified through their interactions. A flavor state is a combination of states with definite masses. Those components evolve differently as the neutrino travels, changing the probabilities of the flavors that a detector can observe. Oscillation measurements therefore reveal differences between squared masses; they do not determine every neutrino’s absolute mass. This more precise quantum description explains why the experiments ruled out the earlier picture in which all neutrinos were massless.

sections.heading: Resolving a deficit without losing the particles
sections.body: Earlier solar measurements detected fewer electron neutrinos than calculations predicted. The Canadian experiment showed that accounting for the other flavors restored the expected overall flux, while atmospheric observations in Japan independently supported transformation. Together the results required an extension of the massless-neutrino version of the Standard Model. They established a missing ingredient rather than discarding the many successful predictions of particle physics. The announcement also emphasizes the cosmological importance of neutrinos: their enormous abundance makes even very small masses relevant to understanding the universe.

terms.definition: A change in the probability of detecting a neutrino in a particular flavor as its quantum state evolves during propagation.
The electron, muon or tau category of a neutrino, identified by its weak interactions and distinct from a state of definite mass.
The rate at which neutrinos pass through a given area, measured with attention to which flavors and interactions a detector can register.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Neutrino oscillations — scientific background for the 2015 prize

sections.heading: Advancements in molecular motor speed and mechanical applications
sections.body: Feringa's group progressively improved molecular motors, with the Nobel background describing a design reaching twelve million revolutions per second by 2014. In 2011 the group also demonstrated a molecular nanocar with four motor units that could move across a surface. Another experiment placed motors in a liquid crystal and used their collective effect to rotate a glass cylinder 28 micrometres long. The field also included a rotaxane-based molecular assembly system reported in 2013 that joined amino acids. These are distinct demonstrations of controlled molecular motion, not components of a single device. They show how energy supplied to molecular structures can produce organised movement or chemical work.

sections.heading: Mechanisms for controlling molecular motion and assembly
sections.body: The development of molecular machinery relied on creating specific mechanical bonds to enable movement. Sauvage utilized these bonds to link rings into catenanes that move freely without separating. Stoddart advanced this by designing rotaxanes, where a ring moves between fixed positions along an axle. These structures can be manipulated via external input to function as actuators, pumps, or even molecular muscles. Additionally, Feringa used isomerisable bonds and molecular asymmetry to drive unidirectional rotation, eventually creating a four-wheel drive nanocar that travels across surfaces.

sections.heading: Energy input turns movable molecules into working devices
sections.body: Movable components are only part of a molecular machine: their motion must be controlled and supplied with energy. The 2016 announcement highlighted Stoddart's rotaxane-based lift and muscle, along with Feringa's motor, as demonstrations of this principle. Interlocked components retain covalent bonds within their own structures; the mechanical link between components allows relative movement without their simply separating. Energy input can then drive selected changes rather than leaving the system at equilibrium. The committee presented possible uses in materials, sensing and energy storage as directions for development. The prize recognised the design and synthesis of working molecular mechanisms, while practical applications at larger scales remained an open research challenge.

terms.definition: A state with no net chemical change, even though forward and reverse processes may continue; sustained molecular work requires an energy supply that drives the system away from equilibrium.
Connections used in the synthesis of molecules that allow components to move relative to each other without being separated.
An interlocked structure with a molecular ring threaded over an axle and retained by bulky end groups, allowing controlled movement along the axle.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of contract design and decision rights
sections.body: Holmström's informativeness principle, independently developed by Steven Shavell in 1979, asks which performance measures should influence pay. In the model, useful information is information that helps distinguish an agent's actions from factors outside their control. A manager's own share price, for example, may be more informative when compared with other firms facing similar conditions. This helps balance incentives against the risk imposed on the employee. Hart's incomplete-contract approach addresses a different difficulty: some future decisions cannot be fully specified in advance. Allocating control rights then affects later bargaining and the incentive to invest. Both approaches show why contract design depends on what can be observed and enforced.

sections.heading: Economic theories regarding contract design and decision rights
sections.body: Bengt Holmström investigated how economic rewards like variable salaries influence behavior, noting they can increase goal orientation while potentially encouraging excessive risk-taking. His research also addresses adjusting agreements for long-term cooperation and managing situations where only team performance is observable. Complementing this, Oliver Hart developed theories on incomplete contracts to determine how decision-making rights should be allocated when future circumstances are unpredictable. His framework offers tools to analyze property rights, corporate mergers, bankruptcy law design, and the management of public or private welfare services.

sections.heading: When rewards distort effort across tasks and teams
sections.body: Holmström extended incentive analysis beyond a single worker paid for one measurable outcome. His later work considered promotion prospects, jobs containing several tasks and teams whose members can benefit from others' effort. These settings reveal why stronger performance pay is not automatically better: rewarding what is measurable can alter how effort is distributed, while collective output may conceal individual contributions. Hart's analysis of control rights provides another tool where detailed promises cannot be written or enforced. Together the frameworks inform questions about company ownership, debt and equity, and public or private provision of services. Their conclusions depend on the incentives and information in the model being examined.

terms.definition: The principle that incentive pay should use performance information that helps identify the agent's actions, taking account of risk and other available signals.
Agreements that cannot describe every conceivable future circumstance, requiring specific rules for allocating decision-making rights when uncertainty arises.
A framework in which one party delegates a task to another whose actions or information may be imperfectly observed, creating an incentive-design problem.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Transforming American popular music through poetic innovation
sections.body: The Swedish Academy described Dylan's art as a transformation of American popular music from within its existing traditions. He absorbed protest song, country, blues, gospel and early rock through recordings and radio, then tested what he heard on his own instruments. His writing combined everyday speech, jokes, prayers and inherited musical forms in unexpected ways. The presentation argued that this mixture gave commercially recorded songs a renewed poetic intensity, allowing an elevated style to address contemporary events. It also challenged a hierarchy that automatically places printed literary genres above popular song. These are the committee's critical judgments about Dylan's achievement, grounded in the relationship between musical inheritance, language and performance.

sections.heading: Evolution of Dylan's lyrical and prose publications
sections.body: Following his 1962 debut, Dylan released several influential albums including Bringing It All Back Home and Highway 61 Revisited in 1965. His discography continued with Blonde On Blonde in 1966 and Blood On The Tracks in 1975, later including Oh Mercy, Time Out of Mind, and Modern Times. Beyond musical compositions, he explored experimental prose poetry through the 1971 collection Tarantula. His lyrical writings have appeared in various editions since 1973, originally titled Writings and Drawings before being renamed Lyrics. Additionally, his 2004 autobiography, Chronicles, recounts his early New York experiences. These diverse works demonstrate a versatile career spanning music, painting, acting, and scriptwriting, while addressing themes like religion, politics, and social conditions.

terms.definition: The literary estimation regarding the relative greatness or importance of different types of writing, ranging from high to low.
A postwar American literary movement associated with writers who challenged conventional social and literary forms; its authors were among Dylan's influences.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Molecular mechanisms and regulation of cellular degradation
sections.body: Ohsumi used baker's yeast to investigate a cellular process whose molecular machinery had been difficult to identify. Experiments made autophagy visible and enabled genetic screens for cells in which it failed. By identifying the affected genes and examining their products, his group uncovered biochemical steps needed to build and operate the recycling machinery. Related mechanisms are widely conserved in organisms with nucleated cells, including humans, making yeast a valuable experimental model. Autophagy helps cells adjust to nutrient shortage and maintain their internal environment. The 2016 presentation also described links between impaired regulation and diseases including diabetes, cancer, infections and neurological disorders. Those connections made the machinery important for further biomedical research; they did not make autophagy a single explanation for every such disease.

sections.heading: Experimental identification of autophagy genes using yeast models
sections.body: Phase-contrast microscopy let Ohsumi observe structures accumulating inside yeast vacuoles. Further imaging showed enclosed cytoplasmic material, including ribosomes and organelles, supporting the identification of autophagy in yeast. Genetic experiments then turned observation into a way to find the machinery. Cells with an apg1 defect lost viability rapidly during nitrogen starvation. Screening for similar survival and morphological defects yielded roughly a hundred mutant strains in fourteen complementation groups. The affected functions proved necessary for autophagosome formation. Later studies identified eighteen genes required under the nitrogen-starvation conditions examined. Parallel work by Michael Thumm's and Dan Klionsky's groups helped connect related pathways and gene sets. These experiments established a tractable model for studying cellular recycling, including both bulk degradation and more selective removal of material.

terms.definition: A process meaning self-eating, where cells break down their own contents to maintain function and adapt to environmental changes.
A light-microscopy method that converts differences in optical phase into visible contrast, helping reveal transparent structures in living cells.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of the Colombian Peace Process
sections.body: The 2016 ceremony highlighted several features of the Colombian negotiations: sustained talks with FARC, participation by victims and efforts to involve critics. Cuba and Norway assisted the process internationally. The committee compared the prolonged dialogue to a continuing peace congress; this was a description of its function, not the name of a separate institution. It emphasised the proposed protection of victims' rights and dignity alongside truth and accountability. The presentation also welcomed FARC leader Rodrigo Londoño's public expression of regret. These measures were presented as foundations for reconciliation, with implementation and the country's wider social problems still requiring sustained work.

sections.heading: Efforts toward national dialogue and disarmament
sections.body: At the October 2016 announcement, the original agreement had just been narrowly rejected in a referendum. The committee welcomed Santos's invitation to supporters and opponents to join a broader national dialogue. It stressed the difficult balance between reconciliation and justice, rather than claiming that the agreement had already resolved those questions. Victims' representatives had participated in the talks, giving accounts of atrocities and confronting responsibility across the conflict. The committee hoped that the groundwork would support verifiable FARC disarmament and lasting peace. These statements describe the uncertainty at the time the prize was announced, before the revised agreement later that year.

sections.heading: Economic and political strategies of Juan Manuel Santos
sections.body: Before the presidency, Santos held economic and security portfolios. As Colombia's first trade minister in the early 1990s, he negotiated trade agreements and developed links with Asian countries. He founded the Good Government Foundation to promote public-governance practices and a Third Way approach influenced by Anthony Giddens. He later served as finance minister during an economic crisis and as defence minister from 2006 to 2009, before becoming president in 2010. His biography presents these experiences as part of his political development towards negotiations. They provide background to the peace initiative, while claims about the conduct of the armed forces require separate assessment.

terms.definition: A process of rebuilding relationships after conflict, which may involve acknowledging harm, establishing truth, accountability and renewed political cooperation.
A broad-based communicative process involving all parties to advance peace and address the challenges of national reconciliation.
A political approach seeking to combine a market economy with government action intended to secure social goals such as equality and public services.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Topological mechanisms in two-dimensional and atomic systems
sections.body: The laureates applied topology to different problems rather than one shared model. Kosterlitz and Thouless studied transitions in effectively two-dimensional systems in the early 1970s. In later work, Thouless and collaborators related the integer quantum Hall effect to a topological property. Haldane investigated antiferromagnetic spin chains, predicting a distinction between integer-spin and half-integer-spin chains: the former have an excitation gap in the model, while the latter do not. This concerns the spin carried at each site, not whether a chain contains an even or odd number of atoms. The spin-1 chain also became an important example of a phase with distinctive boundary behaviour.

sections.heading: Expanding the classification of matter phases
sections.body: The laureates demonstrated that Lev Landau's previous classification of matter phases was incomplete. By applying topological concepts, they identified additional topological phases characterized by specific values for different topological invariants. Their work explained observed transitions between phases that earlier theories suggested should not be possible. These theoretical discoveries involved predicting new phenomena that were subsequently observed through experiments and measurements. This mathematical approach provides a robust way to describe the properties of objects and the mechanisms behind phase transitions in matter.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of topological phase transitions
sections.body: Kosterlitz and Thouless showed how thin systems can undergo transitions outside the conventional picture of ordinary long-range order. Their early-1970s work explained low-temperature behaviour and a mechanism by which it changes as temperature rises. In the 1980s, Thouless connected the precisely quantised conductance observed in thin electron systems with topology. Haldane used related mathematical ideas to analyse magnetic chains. The contributions extended the ways physicists classify phases and transitions. The 2016 announcement pointed towards possible applications in materials and electronics, while the prize itself recognised theoretical discoveries rather than a particular commercial device.

terms.definition: States of matter distinguished by robust global features beyond the local symmetry descriptions used for many familiar phases.
A property unchanged by continuous deformations of the relevant mathematical object; the number of holes is a simple example.
The mathematical study of properties preserved under continuous deformation, providing tools for classifying robust features of physical states.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences: Scientific background on topological phases and transitions, 2016

sections.heading: Combining many weak views into a useful structure
sections.body: Frank developed computational methods to identify similar molecular views in noisy electron-microscope images and combine them. Grouping and averaging views improved the signal, while their different orientations supported three-dimensional reconstruction. Dubochet’s rapid-freezing method addressed a separate difficulty by preserving samples in noncrystalline water. Bringing these approaches together made biological structures increasingly accessible: Frank’s 1991 ribosome reconstruction from vitrified material was an important intermediate result, still far below the later atomic-scale detail. The history shows cumulative improvements in preparation and analysis rather than a single jump to perfect images.

sections.heading: Preservation, radiation damage and reconstruction
sections.body: Biological specimens posed several difficulties for electron microscopy. Water evaporated in the vacuum, and an intense electron beam could damage the molecules. Dubochet developed rapid freezing that preserved water as a noncrystalline solid. Henderson demonstrated that carefully acquired electron data could yield detailed protein structures, while Frank developed ways to recover three-dimensional information from faint projections. These contributions addressed complementary obstacles; they should not be read as a simple sequence in which each researcher merely applied the preceding researcher’s finished method.

sections.heading: Resolution improved through the whole imaging process
sections.body: The 2017 announcement describes a long progression from early demonstrations to increasingly detailed reconstructions. Sample preparation, image processing and microscope components all improved. By the time of the prize, cryo-electron microscopy was producing structures relevant to subjects such as antibiotic resistance and the surface of the Zika virus. These structures are reconstructed from many measurements, not ordinary photographs of a molecule seen by eye. Their biological value lies in revealing arrangements that help researchers investigate function, interactions and potential drug targets.

terms.definition: Solidification into a glass-like, noncrystalline state, used to preserve biological samples without disruptive water-ice crystals.
Changes to a specimen caused by the imaging beam, which can destroy the structural information researchers are trying to measure.
A model of spatial structure inferred by combining measurements or projections from multiple orientations.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: How separate mental budgets shape choices
sections.body: Mental accounting describes how people divide money into categories and judge decisions within each category. A household may protect a holiday or savings account while borrowing at high cost for another expense. Such rules can support planning but can also obscure the effect on total finances. Reference points matter too: an identical cash saving can seem more worthwhile on a cheap purchase than on an expensive one because its percentage differs. Thaler also studied how presenting investment outcomes over different time horizons changes experimental participants' choices. These examples show why the framing of a financial decision can matter alongside its monetary consequences.

sections.heading: Foundations of behavioral economics research
sections.body: Beginning his research career in the late 1970s, Thaler identified anomalies where individuals deviated from rational economic theory. He used cognitive psychology to develop models including the planner–doer framework, which examines conflict between long-term plans and immediate impulses. His theory of mental accounting studies how simplified decision rules shape financial choices. Research on fairness showed that consumers' reactions can discourage firms from increasing prices during a demand surge; holding prices down can then contribute to shortages. His work also influenced pension-programme design, using behavioural insights to help people act on plans to save.

sections.heading: Ownership and fairness change economic choices
sections.body: The endowment effect describes a tendency to value an item more highly once it is owned. Thaler showed how aversion to losses can help explain that difference. His fairness research also examined why consumers react differently to price increases caused by higher costs and increases responding to stronger demand. Such reactions can constrain firms' choices. With colleagues, he developed the dictator game as an experimental way to investigate attitudes towards fairness. Together, these studies brought motives and reference points into analysis that a narrow account of prices and material self-interest could overlook.

terms.definition: A theory describing the specific ways that people organize, formulate, and evaluate their various financial decisions.
A framework used to analyze how the tension between planning and impulsive selves influences human self-control and savings behavior.
The tendency for ownership to increase the value a person places on an item compared with the value assigned before owning it.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary techniques and thematic explorations in Ishiguro's prose
sections.body: Ishiguro uses controlled, exact prose to depict social conventions and their tensions. His narratives blend elements of detective stories, science fiction and myth; in When We Were Orphans, even a magnifying glass becomes a telling detail. The Academy's presentation places his work alongside writers concerned with consciousness, including Kafka, Proust and Woolf. It reads his varied stories as investigations of the relationship between present and past. Remembering is bound up with self-protection: characters and communities confront what they acknowledge, conceal or forget. The apparent restraint of the writing therefore coexists with difficult questions about personal responsibility and violent history.

sections.heading: Literary development and early professional milestones
sections.body: At the University of Kent, where he studied English literature and philosophy, Ishiguro encountered Kafka and Proust. During his later year at the University of East Anglia, he began publishing short stories. Three were accepted for Faber Introductions 7, published in 1981, leading editor Robert McCrum to offer a contract for his novel in progress. Ishiguro also wrote television scripts: A Profile of Arthur J Mason, broadcast in 1984, featured an English butler and anticipated that interest in The Remains of the Day. His 1986 novel An Artist of the Floating World received a Booker shortlisting and the Whitbread Book of the Year Award.

terms.definition: Combining conventions from different kinds of writing, such as detective fiction, science fiction and myth, within a narrative.
A book published by Faber and Faber containing short stories by new writers, including three works by Ishiguro.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Molecular components of the biological clock
sections.body: The period gene encodes PER, a protein whose changing abundance forms part of a feedback loop. Hall and Rosbash proposed that accumulated PER inhibits activity of its own gene; as protein levels fall, production can resume. Young's group identified additional genes, timeless and doubletime, whose products help control PER's behaviour and the timing of the cycle. The interacting proteins, rather than the genes physically joining PER, provide the molecular mechanism. Delays and regulation within this feedback system help generate an approximately twenty-four-hour rhythm. The clock enables organisms to anticipate regular environmental changes rather than merely responding to light at the moment it appears.

sections.heading: Genetic components of the Drosophila circadian clock
sections.body: Genetic screens extended the fruit-fly clock model beyond period. Young's timeless gene encodes a protein that works with PER, while doubletime encodes an enzyme affecting the timing of PER accumulation and turnover. Researchers also identified Clock and cycle: their protein products associate as transcription factors that activate period and timeless. Mutations affecting these components can disrupt rhythmic behaviour. The work combined observation of mutant flies with molecular analysis of the corresponding genes and proteins. This made it possible to connect a behavioural phenotype, such as loss of a daily rhythm, with particular steps in the molecular feedback system.

sections.heading: Michael Rosbash's academic development and mentorship
sections.body: Rosbash credits early mentor Norman Davidson with encouraging serious engagement in research and demonstrating the satisfaction of laboratory work. He later studied eukaryotic gene expression in Sheldon Penman's laboratory at MIT. His autobiography describes productive research alongside the political tensions of the Vietnam-war era. When disagreement arose over the time he devoted to political activity, he sought advice from David Baltimore. Baltimore supported Penman's expectation of sustained laboratory effort, influencing Rosbash's decision to stay. The account shows how mentorship and decisions about research commitments shaped his training before the later collaboration on biological clocks.

terms.definition: Internally generated rhythms with a period of roughly twenty-four hours that can be synchronised with environmental cycles such as day and night.
A protein that helps control the production of RNA from genes, for example by binding DNA and influencing transcription.
The use of genetic information to produce RNA and proteins in cells with a nucleus, including the processes that regulate their production.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: The humanitarian case for a nuclear ban
sections.body: ICAN argued that the unacceptable suffering caused by nuclear weapons should be the starting point for prohibition, as it had been for bans on other weapon categories. The 2017 presentation linked this argument with frustration over limited progress on the disarmament commitments in the Non-Proliferation Treaty. Austria's Humanitarian Pledge, initiated in December 2014, offered governments a way to commit themselves to pursuing prohibition and elimination. ICAN mobilised support for that pledge, which the committee reported had attracted 127 states by the award year. The campaign sought to turn such commitments into a treaty framework, while insisting that the difficulty of disarmament did not remove states' responsibility to pursue it.

sections.heading: Adopting a treaty and the work still ahead
sections.body: The committee's announcement described ICAN as a coalition of organisations from around a hundred countries and a leading civil-society participant in the prohibition campaign. On 7 July 2017, 122 UN member states voted to adopt the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. Adoption was a milestone, but the treaty still required 50 ratifications before entering into force for participating states. The committee explicitly recognised that a legal ban would not by itself dismantle a weapon, and that nuclear-armed states and their closest allies had not supported the treaty. It therefore called for further negotiations involving those states. This distinction between establishing a legal standard and achieving physical disarmament was central to the award's reasoning.

terms.definition: Austria's voluntary initiative inviting states to work toward stigmatising, prohibiting and eliminating nuclear weapons because of their humanitarian consequences.

terms.term: Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons
terms.definition: The nuclear-ban treaty adopted in 2017, establishing obligations for states that become parties rather than automatically disarming every nuclear-armed country.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of the laser interferometer detector
sections.body: To overcome background noise, researchers moved away from tuning fork designs toward a laser-based interferometer. While Rainer Weiss analyzed potential disturbances at MIT, Kip Thorne worked alongside Ronald Drever, who built early prototypes in Glasgow before joining Thorne at Caltech. This trio pioneered the instrument's development. The resulting LIGO project eventually captured signals from two black holes colliding 1.3 billion lightyears away. These waves, traveling at the speed of light, originated from a massive collision occurring over a thousand million years ago.

sections.heading: Mechanism of the LIGO laser-interferometer detectors
sections.body: LIGO compares laser light travelling along two perpendicular arms, each four kilometres long. Mirrors return the beams so that they interfere, making extremely small changes in relative arm length detectable. A passing gravitational wave can produce a characteristic differential stretching and squeezing. The observatory's two widely separated sites, about three thousand kilometres apart, help distinguish a common astronomical signal from local disturbances such as ground vibration. Agreement between the sites is one part of the evidence, alongside detailed analysis of detector noise and the signal's form. This arrangement turned interference, a familiar property of waves, into a means of measuring minute changes associated with spacetime disturbances.

sections.heading: LIGO leadership and technical infrastructure development
sections.body: When Barish took leadership of LIGO in 1994, he revised the proposal to strengthen technical teams, site staffing and infrastructure. The plan invested in developing technologies including solid-state lasers, digital controls and computer simulations of the interferometers. Later, Advanced LIGO introduced substantially improved isolation from ground motion alongside other upgrades. In Barish's account, commissioning reached a sensitivity more than three times better than Initial LIGO before the first observations in September 2015. The black-hole merger detected that month demonstrated the value of the long development programme. This early performance should be distinguished from the instrument's ultimate design sensitivity.

terms.definition: Ripples in spacetime generated by changing mass distributions, including orbiting or merging compact objects, that propagate away from their source.
A device using split laser light and mirrors to measure incredibly small changes in distance between two perpendicular paths.
Techniques that reduce transmission of ground motion to sensitive components, using mechanical isolation and, in advanced systems, active control.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Advancements in enzyme engineering and phage display
sections.body: Arnold's enzyme-engineering work showed how repeated variation and selection could develop useful catalysts. Some evolved enzymes enabled reactions not known in nature; others reduced unwanted by-products or avoided metals used in conventional processes. Her group also investigated conversion of sugars to isobutanol, a possible feedstock for fuels and materials. The 2018 background presented these as examples of how protein engineering could improve manufacturing. In a separate line of work, phage display connected displayed proteins with the genetic information needed to reproduce them. Winter applied this principle to antibody development. The resulting methods supported therapeutic research and drug production, without making every engineered protein automatically safe, effective or environmentally preferable.

sections.heading: Mechanisms for protein engineering and antibody development
sections.body: Smith's phage-display method links a protein's binding behaviour with the genetic information that encodes it. Protein variants are displayed on bacteriophages, while the corresponding DNA is carried by the phage. Researchers can expose a large collection to a target and retain phages whose displayed proteins bind it. Because the selected phages contain the encoding DNA, useful variants can be copied and examined further. Winter adapted this strategy to antibody fragments, retaining the regions responsible for recognising targets. Selection could then yield antibodies with desired binding properties for diagnostic and therapeutic development. The link between a displayed molecule and its genetic recipe made the selection process experimentally powerful.

sections.heading: Applications of directed evolution and phage display
sections.body: The 2018 announcement connected protein evolution with practical uses in chemical manufacture and medicine. Evolved enzymes had become tools for making pharmaceuticals and investigating renewable fuels. Phage display had helped develop adalimumab, first approved in 2002. By the time of the prize, its uses included rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease; these indications were not all necessarily part of the original approval. Other antibody programmes targeted toxins, autoimmune disease and cancer. The examples illustrated the range of applications enabled by selecting proteins for useful properties, while each medicine still required its own development and evaluation.

terms.definition: Repeated cycles of generating protein variants and selecting or screening for a desired property, using successful variants as the starting point for further improvement.
Displaying proteins or peptides on bacteriophages while retaining their encoding DNA, allowing selection of binding properties and recovery of the corresponding genes.
An antibody preparation based on one selected antibody sequence or clone, designed to recognise a particular molecular target.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of Integrated Assessment Models
sections.body: Nordhaus's integrated assessment models link economic activity with emissions, carbon movement, climate change and economic damage. Their carbon-cycle component tracks carbon between reservoirs such as the atmosphere and oceans; other components describe warming and its economic consequences. The 2018 background contrasted a regional RICE version containing eight economic regions with DICE, a simplified global version using one. These are model configurations described at that time, not fixed features of every later version. Researchers can vary assumptions and policies, such as carbon pricing, to compare paths for emissions, output and welfare. The results are conditional scenarios whose usefulness depends on the relationships and uncertainties represented.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of endogenous growth and integrated climate modeling
sections.body: Romer brought the creation of ideas inside a growth model rather than treating technological progress as an unexplained outside force. An idea can be used by many people simultaneously, but producing it can require costly effort. Incentives and institutions therefore influence investment in innovation. Patent protection is one way of offering returns to creators, with design choices affecting the balance between incentives and the spread of knowledge. Nordhaus addressed a different external effect: economic activity produces emissions that alter the climate and feed back into economic welfare. His integrated models combined relationships from economics and natural science to compare policy choices. Both contributions made important interactions part of the analysis of long-term growth.

sections.heading: Development of integrated climate and economic models
sections.body: Nordhaus first linked an energy model with equations for carbon emissions and movement among carbon reservoirs. Later, DICE used an economic-growth framework combined with emissions, carbon-cycle, climate and damage relationships and a variable representing emissions control. The purpose was a closed feedback system in which economic decisions affect the climate and climate effects alter welfare. Solving the model produces a shadow value for an additional emission under the assumptions used. That value can inform a carbon price intended to reflect social costs; it is a model result rather than an existing tax or a uniquely certain price. The framework permits systematic comparison of mitigation choices and their consequences.

terms.definition: Consequences for others that were not accounted for by individual polluters or innovators within the global market.
A framework focusing on how economic motivation and the creation of new ideas by entrepreneurs drive sustained global growth.
A dynamic integrated model of climate and the economy used to analyze the costs and benefits of climate change mitigation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary themes and historical perspectives in Tokarczuk's prose
sections.body: The Academy described Tokarczuk's prose as moving across social and cultural boundaries, combining everyday detail with fable, myth and historical inquiry. Its presentation focused especially on The Books of Jacob, which follows the eighteenth-century religious world surrounding Jacob Frank. The novel builds its panorama through settings ranging from monasteries and country houses to Jewish homes, attending to clothes, food, gardens and domestic life. The committee emphasised her ability to make neglected people visible, including women and servants often absent from conventional histories. Dictionaries, documents and stories become material for imaginative reconstruction. In this reading, movement between perspectives is central to her art: individual lives are placed within wider patterns of belief, power and historical change.

sections.heading: Development of the constellation novel technique
sections.body: Tokarczuk connects the origins of Flights with intensive travel around the turn of the century, especially journeys undertaken alone. Culture shock, language barriers and homesickness became part of her education as a writer. She called the resulting book a constellation novel, bringing separate narratives into relation while exploring what she sees as a deeply rooted human impulse to move. Her historical work used a different research process: The Books of Jacob required years of reading documents and visiting places associated with its characters. She describes gathering details, coincidences and unusual observations even when she is not writing. Cinema also informs her thinking about narrative. These practices combine investigation with the imaginative arrangement of material.

terms.definition: A literary technique used in Tokarczuk's prose to traverse socially and culturally fabricated borders through shifting perspectives.
Tokarczuk's term for a novel built from distinct, connected narrative pieces whose relationships create a larger pattern.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Development of checkpoint inhibition therapy
sections.body: Allison's experiments asked whether blocking an inhibitory signal on T cells could strengthen their response against tumours. Antibodies against the checkpoint protein CTLA-4 produced tumour rejection in mouse experiments, encouraging development for patients. Clinical work later showed that some people with advanced melanoma experienced substantial and lasting responses. Honjo's discovery of PD-1 opened a different checkpoint target. The ceremony highlighted how the two approaches could sometimes work particularly well in combination. These results established that manipulating immune regulation could treat cancer, moving an idea from basic immunology through animal experiments into clinical investigation. The response depended on the tumour and patient rather than occurring uniformly.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of immune system regulation and inhibition
sections.body: T cells are controlled by activating and inhibitory signals. Allison investigated CTLA-4 blockade as a way to enhance antitumour responses, while Honjo's work identified PD-1 and established a different inhibitory mechanism. The 2018 announcement described positive clinical results from targeting these checkpoints, including combinations tested in melanoma. It also stressed the need to understand their actions and reduce side effects. Immune brakes help protect healthy tissues, so releasing them can create unwanted immune activity as well as antitumour effects. The therapeutic principle is selective interference with inhibitory pathways, not indiscriminate stimulation of every immune function.

sections.heading: Mechanism of anti-CTLA-4 antibody in tumor reduction
sections.body: Allison's account describes mouse experiments in which tumours initially grew, then regressed in animals receiving anti-CTLA-4 antibodies. He argued that enhancing T-cell responses could complement approaches aimed directly at tumour-cell mutations. The biography also recounts meeting a patient whose metastatic melanoma had disappeared after an experimental treatment, illustrating the personal impact of a clinical response. Yet it explicitly records that other patients and tumour types did not respond. Subsequent work with clinical collaborators examined immune cells in blood and tumour samples, including CD4 T cells expressing the costimulatory protein ICOS. Linking patient samples with laboratory experiments aimed to explain both response and resistance, rather than assuming that releasing one checkpoint would cure every cancer.

terms.definition: A therapeutic approach that works by releasing the brakes on the immune system to trigger attacks against cancer cells.
An inhibitory receptor on immune cells, including T cells, whose signalling can limit their activity; blocking this pathway can enhance antitumour responses.
Antibodies that block CTLA-4-mediated inhibitory signalling, potentially strengthening T-cell activity against tumours while also risking unwanted immune effects.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Addressing sexual violence as a military strategy
sections.body: The use of systematic rape in warfare functions as a method to degrade victims and destabilize entire communities. At Panzi Hospital, medical interventions include repairing severe physical injuries caused by brutal assaults alongside providing trauma treatment and reintegration programs for women. This approach addresses the loss of family and social support following attacks. Simultaneously, efforts focus on breaking the stigma of shame and silence to ensure war crimes are recognized, demanding that perpetrators face prosecution rather than enjoying impunity.

sections.heading: Combatting sexual violence as a military strategy
sections.body: The award linked two responses to wartime sexual violence. Mukwege and the Panzi team provided treatment and support to survivors in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Murad used testimony and advocacy to draw attention to Islamic State's crimes against the Yazidi community, including abduction and sexual enslavement. The committee connected greater visibility with demands for accountability. It cited UN Security Council Resolution 1820 and the Rome Statute as parts of the international framework addressing such crimes. These efforts joined medical recovery, survivor participation and legal responsibility, while confronting the stigma that often prevents crimes from being reported.

sections.heading: Holistic healing model at Panzi Hospital
sections.body: Panzi's approach combined treatment of physical injuries with psychological, legal and socioeconomic support. A survivor might need surgery, help coping with trauma, assistance seeking justice and support rebuilding a livelihood. The model treated these needs as connected rather than reducing recovery to a single clinical procedure. Mukwege's Nobel biography reports that the team had treated more than fifty thousand survivors by the time of that account. The hospital, founded in 1999 for gynaecological and obstetric care, developed specialised expertise as increasing numbers of patients arrived with injuries from sexual violence. Its experience helped connect local medical work with international advocacy for survivors and accountability.

terms.term: Sexual violence as a weapon of war
terms.definition: A military strategy involving systematic rape and gross sexual violence intended to injure, degrade, and demoralize specific populations or communities.
A 2008 resolution demanding an end to conflict-related sexual violence and recognising that rape and other sexual violence can constitute war crimes, crimes against humanity or acts of genocide.
A recovery method that integrates psychological support, legal assistance, and socio-economic aid into existing medical clinical care.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Mechanisms of light manipulation and pulse amplification
sections.body: Ashkin combined forces from laser light with strong focusing to create a stable trap for small particles. The intensity pattern draws suitable particles towards the focus, while the full force balance holds them in place. Optical tweezers later enabled measurements of molecular machinery, including kinesin moving along microtubules. Strickland and Mourou addressed a separate limitation: a short pulse can damage the material used to amplify it. Their chirped pulse amplification method spreads the pulse in time, amplifies it at lower peak intensity, then compresses it. The resulting ultrashort pulses can probe rapid molecular events and process materials precisely. These inventions support delicate manipulation and intense interactions with matter.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of radiation pressure and chirped pulse amplification
sections.body: Arthur Ashkin utilized radiation pressure, the force light exerts on matter, to move microscopic particles. By focusing a laser beam through a lens, he created tools capable of grasping living cells to study molecular motors. To overcome limitations where intense light destroys amplifying materials, Mourou and Strickland developed chirped pulse amplification. This technique stretches a laser pulse in time to lower intensity for amplification before compressing it back to its original duration. This advancement allows for extremely high-intensity pulses used in precise eye surgery.

sections.heading: From trapping particles to investigating living systems
sections.body: Ashkin's 1987 demonstration that living bacteria could be held without damage helped open optical trapping to biology. Researchers could manipulate microscopic objects with a focused beam and study components of the machinery of life. The technique depends on choosing appropriate optical conditions; the result was a controlled experimental tool for delicate samples. The other half of the award recognised Strickland and Mourou's 1985 work on chirped pulse amplification, which became a foundation for high-intensity laser systems. The announcement cited corrective eye surgery among its uses. The shared prize therefore connected two different forms of light control: holding tiny objects and delivering very intense, short pulses.

terms.definition: A method that stretches a laser pulse in time, amplifies it at reduced peak intensity, then compresses it to obtain a powerful short pulse.
Pressure exerted when light transfers momentum to matter; intense, controlled beams can exert measurable forces on microscopic objects.
A tool using forces from a tightly focused light beam to trap and manipulate microscopic particles or suitable biological objects.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Storing lithium within electrode materials
sections.body: Early rechargeable lithium-metal designs faced a serious problem: repeated charging could produce needle-like deposits that caused short circuits. Yoshino replaced the metallic-lithium electrode with a carbon host capable of taking up lithium ions. The ions could be inserted and removed while much of the host structure remained intact. This is intercalation, a reversible chemical process; describing it as no reaction at all would be misleading. Moving between suitable host materials made repeated charging much more practical, while improvements in materials and device design remained important for performance and safety.

sections.heading: Different materials solved different parts of the battery problem
sections.body: Whittingham demonstrated that a titanium-containing electrode could take up and release lithium ions, producing a cell with roughly two volts. Goodenough’s search for alternative electrode materials, notably oxides, enabled higher voltages. Yoshino’s carbon-based electrode then replaced reactive lithium metal and worked with an oxide counterpart. These contributions changed both sides of the device and their compatibility. The presentation treats the modern lithium-ion battery as the outcome of linked materials discoveries, rather than a single new chemical substance that alone supplied all the required properties.

sections.heading: A layered sequence of improvements
sections.body: The 2019 announcement traces three milestones: Whittingham’s titanium-disulfide electrode, Goodenough’s lithium-containing cobalt oxide in 1980, and Yoshino’s petroleum-coke electrode in 1985. The oxide offered greater voltage, while the carbon host avoided reliance on a reactive lithium-metal electrode. Together they supplied a practical rechargeable architecture in which lithium ions move between electrode materials. The host structures accommodate those changes comparatively well; this is not a promise that electrodes remain perfectly unchanged or that a battery can be recharged indefinitely.

terms.definition: Insertion of a guest species into a host material without a major rearrangement of the host structure, often reversibly.
The electrical potential difference between a cell’s electrodes, reflecting the energy available per unit of transferred charge.
A material whose structure accommodates lithium ions as a battery is charged or discharged.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Field experiments for evaluating poverty alleviation interventions
sections.body: School experiments in Kenya compared interventions such as extra textbooks and meals. Average learning did not improve in the studies described, although textbooks benefited the strongest pupils. Later tutoring experiments in Mumbai and Vadodara targeted children falling behind the curriculum and found benefits from teaching adapted to their needs. Another study examined expanded access to microcredit in Hyderabad. It found modest increases in investment in existing businesses but no detected average consumption benefit at the measured follow-ups of 18 and 36 months. These results illustrate how an intervention can affect one outcome without producing the broader improvements initially hoped for.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and causes of global poverty
sections.body: The experimental approach combines economic hypotheses with interventions tested in everyday settings. Theory suggests possible explanations, while randomised comparisons help assess their importance. For education, the 2019 presentation highlighted studies pointing to teaching practices, teachers' knowledge and attendance as important constraints in the settings examined. Simply adding resources was therefore not always sufficient. Similar reasoning was applied to questions such as why farmers delayed adopting potentially useful technologies. The purpose is to distinguish between competing explanations and test a response suited to the problem, while recognising that results depend on the intervention and setting.

sections.heading: From a focused experiment to a larger programme
sections.body: The laureates broke broad questions about poverty into specific problems that could be investigated experimentally. School interventions in western Kenya were early examples; later research examined health, education and other areas in additional countries. The 2019 announcement reported that findings from remedial-tutoring studies had helped support programmes reaching more than five million Indian children. It also cited subsidies for preventive healthcare as an application of experimental evidence. These examples distinguish testing an intervention from the later work of expanding it. Evidence can inform a larger programme, while implementation and conditions still matter to its results.

terms.definition: The question of whether experimental results from one specific context can be applied or generalized to other different settings.
Experiments that randomly allocate participants or groups to intervention and comparison conditions to help estimate causal effects.
Assessment of a programme's effects using evidence about outcomes and, where possible, what would have happened without it.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary focus on peripheries and linguistic discovery
sections.body: Handke utilizes a meticulous gaze to document the edges of existence, often focusing on backwaters rather than metropolises. In his work My Year in the No-Man’s-Bay, he provides scrupulous details of his residence southwest of Paris, capturing elements like wild bees and beaver rats. His prose seeks to present the world freshly through a hyperactive sense for the particular. This approach is evident in Repetition, where a narrator observes a waiter launching dishes into a stream, and in The Fruit Thief, which follows a trek through Picardy. By rejecting contemporary conformity, his writing investigates the medium of language itself, using restrained descriptions to explore themes ranging from personal origins to encounters with the stateless.

sections.heading: Experimental techniques and literary influences
sections.body: Handke's debut novel Die Hornissen experiments with a character recalling fragments of another novel that the reader cannot know directly. His early play Publikumsbeschimpfung turns attention towards the audience, having actors insult people simply for attending. The Academy's notes identify the French Nouveau Roman as an influence on this experimental approach. They also describe Langsame Heimkehr as an important development in his attention to landscape. Across prose, drama, notebooks and translations of Greek tragedy, Handke seeks forms for closely observed experiences. Cinema and painting are further influences on his attention to the material world.

terms.definition: A literary focus that avoids metropolises to instead depict backwaters and the edges of human existence.
French for New Novel: the literary movement identified by the Academy as a major influence on Handke's early experimental prose.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Peter Handke — Swedish Academy bio-bibliographical notes

sections.heading: Oxygen sensing and cellular adaptation mechanisms
sections.body: Semenza identified an oxygen-responsive DNA element and the gene-regulating complex HIF. Ratcliffe's work showed that oxygen-responsive control extends beyond cells producing erythropoietin and linked HIF removal to VHL. Kaelin connected the VHL tumour-suppressor gene with inappropriate activation of oxygen-response genes in cancer cells. The Kaelin and Ratcliffe groups then showed how oxygen-dependent hydroxylation of HIF's alpha subunit enables recognition by VHL and subsequent degradation. When oxygen is scarce, this modification is reduced, allowing the alpha subunit to accumulate and HIF to activate adaptive genes. The mechanism couples oxygen availability to protein stability and gene expression.

sections.heading: Kaelin's investigation into VHL disease and tumor vascularity
sections.body: During medical training, Kaelin studied tumour blood flow with Randy Jirtle and read about the highly vascular tumours associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease. He became interested in the connection between blood-vessel growth, red-cell production and oxygen availability. Those observations helped suggest that the disease's underlying gene might participate in oxygen sensing. After reading the 1993 report identifying the VHL tumour-suppressor gene, he made it a focus of his laboratory. He expected the work to illuminate kidney-cancer development and angiogenesis, with the possibility of revealing oxygen regulation. The route into the problem therefore began with cancer biology and clinical features, rather than a direct search for the HIF degradation mechanism.

sections.heading: Discovery of a widespread mammalian oxygen sensing system
sections.body: Ratcliffe's group initially investigated oxygen-sensitive control of the erythropoietin gene. Hepatoma cells provided a useful experimental system when kidney cells proved difficult to study. He planned expression-cloning experiments to transfer the missing oxygen-sensing machinery into COS7 cells, assuming that cells not producing erythropoietin would lack it. Control experiments overturned that assumption: regulatory DNA from the erythropoietin locus already responded to oxygen levels in COS7 cells. The machinery was therefore not restricted to erythropoietin-producing cells. This redirected the investigation towards a more widespread oxygen-response system and other target genes, including genes involved in glycolysis. A control designed to validate one experiment instead revealed the broader biological question.

terms.definition: Hypoxia-inducible factor: a transcription-factor complex whose oxygen-regulated alpha subunit helps control gene activity during adaptation to low oxygen.
An inherited tumour-predisposition syndrome associated with alterations in the VHL gene, increasing the risk of particular tumours such as kidney cancer and haemangioblastomas.
Identifying a gene by introducing candidate DNA into cells and screening for the activity produced when that DNA is expressed.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Nobel Assembly: 2019 Medicine announcement explaining HIF hydroxylation and VHL recognition

sections.heading: The wider regional work recognised in 2019
sections.body: The award presentation described Abiy's activities beyond Ethiopia's agreement with Eritrea. It credited him with helping to normalise relations between Djibouti and Eritrea and with seeking to mediate the maritime dispute between Kenya and Somalia. These were presented as efforts to improve relations across the region, with some outcomes still uncertain. The speech also highlighted changes in Ethiopia's political leadership: women held half the ministerial posts, and women served as president, Supreme Court chief justice and Minister of Peace. These were developments the committee emphasised at the time of the 2019 award; the speech is a contemporary assessment of that period.

sections.heading: An award intended to encourage unfinished change
sections.body: The 2019 announcement praised measures taken in Abiy's first hundred days, including ending the state of emergency, granting amnesty to political prisoners, reducing censorship and legalising opposition groups. It also acknowledged escalating ethnic conflict and unresolved challenges. The committee explicitly anticipated criticism that the award was premature. Its stated reasoning was that recognition could encourage the peace and reform efforts while they were still developing. This matters when interpreting the prize: the announcement expressed hopes about future stability and cooperation, as well as recognising actions already taken. It did not describe Ethiopia's internal conflicts as settled.

sections.heading: Accepting the border decision
sections.body: The biography identifies a particular diplomatic obstacle behind the award. An international commission ruled on the Ethiopian–Eritrean border in 2002, but Ethiopia did not accept the decision. Abiy became prime minister in April 2018 and accepted the ruling after years of deadlock. He and Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki subsequently signed a peace agreement. The biography also notes that Ethiopia's internal political situation remained difficult in 2019, with conflict between communities and uncertainty about promised elections. Its account thus combines the resolution of a specific obstacle between neighbouring states with an unfinished domestic political transition.

terms.definition: Helping parties to a dispute seek an agreement, as in the regional diplomatic efforts described by the committee at the award.
A measure pardoning offences or removing penalties for a group; the announcement highlighted its application to thousands of political prisoners.
A process in which an appointed body decides a dispute; the biography centres on the commission's decision concerning the Ethiopian–Eritrean border.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Geometry, matter and the cosmological model
sections.body: The 2019 background described a cosmological model consistent with a spatially flat universe on large scales. In that model, ordinary matter accounted for about 5 per cent of the total energy density, dark matter for 26 per cent and dark energy for 69 per cent. These are model-based estimates, not a direct inventory of fully understood substances. Peebles helped revive the cosmological constant as a way to describe the energy associated with empty space. The framework connected background-radiation measurements with the universe's expansion and structure, while leaving the physical nature of dark matter and dark energy unresolved.

sections.heading: Finding a planet through its star's motion
sections.body: Mayor and Queloz used a spectrograph to detect small periodic shifts in a star's light. A planet and its star move around their shared centre of mass, so the star's motion towards and away from the observer changes the measured wavelengths. This offered an indirect way to detect a planet that was difficult to observe beside its bright host. The signal from 51 Pegasi revealed a giant planet completing an orbit in a little over four days. The discovery depended on measuring the host star's motion, not on imaging the planet itself.

sections.heading: An expanding variety of planetary systems
sections.body: The 1995 discovery of 51 Pegasi b established a planet around a star similar to the Sun. By the time of the 2019 award announcement, more than 4,000 exoplanets had been found, revealing a much wider variety of planetary sizes and orbits than the Solar System alone suggested. These observations challenged ideas about how planetary systems form and evolve. The announcement treated future searches as a way to investigate that diversity and the possibility of life elsewhere. The discovery of a planet itself did not demonstrate that life was present.

terms.definition: A universe whose large-scale spatial geometry has no curvature; the description concerns geometry, not a two-dimensional shape.
A shift in observed frequency or wavelength caused by relative motion between source and observer; stellar wavelength shifts can reveal orbital motion.
A planet outside the Solar System; 51 Pegasi b was the first discovered orbiting a star similar to the Sun.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Making a simpler, programmable guide
sections.body: The researchers combined two RNA components, tracrRNA and CRISPR RNA, into one guide molecule. They then changed the guide sequence to direct Cas9 towards selected positions in a DNA target. The experiment showed that the cutting machinery could be retargeted by changing its RNA instruction. This was a biochemical demonstration of programmability, distinct from the later work needed to edit particular organisms. The simplified guide made the system easier to use and helped turn knowledge of a bacterial defence mechanism into a broadly useful experimental tool.

sections.heading: Reconstructing the bacterial cutting machinery
sections.body: Charpentier's work on Streptococcus pyogenes identified tracrRNA as part of its defence against invading genetic material. Working together, Charpentier and Doudna reconstructed the DNA-cutting system in a test tube. This made it possible to investigate the components directly and then simplify the machinery. Their experiments established that its targeting could be programmed for selected DNA sequences. Cutting DNA was the crucial experimental advance described in the presentation; obtaining a particular desired genetic change in a cell also involves what happens after that cut.

sections.heading: Different CRISPR systems posed different questions
sections.body: Doudna's account traces work on several CRISPR-associated proteins before the collaboration on Cas9. One project investigated Cas6f, an enzyme that processes a long precursor RNA into shorter guide RNAs in a different CRISPR system. That RNA-processing activity should not be confused with Cas9's cutting of target DNA. After meeting Charpentier in 2011, Doudna joined the investigation of a type II system using Cas9. The history illustrates how studies of related but distinct bacterial defence systems supplied knowledge that helped researchers understand and redesign the RNA-guided machinery.

terms.definition: An engineered RNA combining the functions of tracrRNA and CRISPR RNA to help direct Cas9 to a selected DNA sequence.
An RNA component of the studied bacterial CRISPR-Cas9 system that works with CRISPR RNA; the engineered single guide combines their functions.
A short RNA carrying a sequence that can guide recognition of matching foreign genetic material in a CRISPR defence system.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Learning from the fact that you won
sections.body: For an asset with an uncertain common value, winning can itself be unwelcome information: the other bidders may have had lower estimates. Wilson analysed how a rational bidder should allow for that possibility rather than bid as though their own estimate were certain. Milgrom investigated how auction formats affect the information available during bidding. In an ascending auction, observing when competitors withdraw can help remaining bidders revise their estimates. These results explain how caution and information influence bids under particular models; they do not imply that every auction winner necessarily overpays.

sections.heading: Designing rules around the resource being allocated
sections.body: The presentation connected auction theory with practical allocation problems, including radio spectrum, electricity and emissions allowances. The relevant objectives can differ: raising revenue, allocating resources effectively or preserving incentives for future investment. Wilson's common-value models and Milgrom's work combining common and private values helped explain how rules affect bids and outcomes. Their spectrum-auction work responded to shortcomings in earlier allocation methods based on lotteries or administrative decisions. It illustrated how a theoretical understanding of incentives could inform a specific institutional design, rather than supply one auction format suitable for every purpose.

sections.heading: From equilibrium analysis to practical auction design
sections.body: Milgrom's biography describes an early phase of research with Robert Weber on bidding strategies, information and seller revenue. A later phase began when US authorities authorised auctions of spectrum rights. His subsequent work examined strategic bidding, connections between auction and matching algorithms, and ways of expressing bids in different formats. He also worked with collaborators on an advertising-auction format intended to reduce the winner's curse. The account shows repeated interaction between theoretical analysis and the details of particular markets, with designs developed and revised for different allocation problems.

terms.definition: The risk of winning because of an overly optimistic estimate and paying more than the asset is actually worth.
An underlying value shared by bidders, although they may have different information and estimates of it before an auction.
The rules for expressing offers in an auction, which determine what preferences or combinations a bidder can communicate.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Personal experience through other voices
sections.body: The Nobel presentation described Glück's use of autobiographical material without treating each poem as a straightforward confession. Mythological figures such as Persephone, Dido and Eurydice supply voices through which private experiences can acquire wider meanings. Faithful and Virtuous Night uses an elderly painter's perspective, while Ararat turns spoken language towards difficult family relationships. These are the presenter's interpretations of how form and voice work together. The speech also emphasised contradiction and renewal, presenting Glück's clarity as compatible with ambiguity rather than as the removal of every unresolved feeling.

sections.heading: Changing a voice through sentence structure
sections.body: Glück's autobiography describes setting herself specific formal tasks after periods when writing seemed impossible. One was to build poems from a single sentence, or from complex sentences whose clauses extended across several lines. Later, she deliberately introduced contractions and questions, finding that they brought a more recognisable everyday voice into her work. She also recalled disagreement with Stanley Kunitz about Ararat, a book that removed figurative language. Her account presents stylistic change as a process of experiments, resistance and renewed effort, with grammar and sentence shape central to the sound of a poem.

terms.definition: The voice or identity speaking in a poem, which may be distinct from the author; Glück often writes through imagined or mythological figures.
Sentence structure that delays completion of a thought, sometimes across several poetic lines, sustaining the reader's expectation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: From an unexplained illness to evidence of a cause
sections.body: Alter studied blood donors and patients with hepatitis that existing tests could not explain. In 1978 he demonstrated that the disease could be transmitted, supporting the search for another infectious agent. Houghton and colleagues then used molecular screening to identify the unknown virus despite the technical limits of the period. Rice investigated how the virus reproduced and constructed a viral genome that could produce infection and liver disease. These were complementary steps: showing transmission, identifying viral material, and establishing that the identified virus could itself cause the illness.

sections.heading: An unexpected route into hepatitis research
sections.body: As a blood-bank fellow, Alter tested whether transfusion recipients had antibodies reacting with proteins in donor serum. He placed samples in separate wells in agar so their components could diffuse toward one another. One reaction produced a line with an unexpected staining pattern. The material detected became known as the Australia antigen; Blumberg subsequently established its relationship to the surface of hepatitis B virus. This earlier finding concerned hepatitis B, not the hepatitis C virus recognized by the 2020 prize. Alter describes it as the chance encounter that drew him into hepatitis research.

sections.heading: The molecular search and its practical consequences
sections.body: After joining Chiron in 1982, Houghton turned his laboratory toward the cause of non-A, non-B hepatitis. Years of unsuccessful approaches preceded the 1989 publication identifying the hepatitis C genome with Qui-Lim Choo, George Kuo and Dan Bradley. Subsequent work produced diagnostic and blood-screening tests and helped identify viral enzymes that could serve as drug targets. His biography therefore connects the discovery to two different practical advances: detecting infection before contaminated blood reached a recipient, and finding vulnerable steps in the virus’s life cycle for treatment research.

terms.definition: The capacity of an infectious agent or disease to pass between hosts.
A laboratory method in which antigens and antibodies diffuse through a gel and can form visible lines where they react.
The historical name for hepatitis cases that could not be attributed to the recognized hepatitis A or B viruses.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Hunger can be both a consequence and a weapon of conflict
sections.body: The committee connected food assistance with peace through several mechanisms. War can interrupt production, distribution and access to food, while hunger can intensify distress and conflict. Starvation can also be deliberately imposed as a method of warfare. The presentation argued that the World Food Programme's work addressed these dangers by helping people obtain food in affected areas. This was a case for the contribution of humanitarian assistance to peaceful conditions, not a claim that distributing food alone could resolve every cause of conflict or guarantee that aid would reach everyone.

sections.heading: Connecting humanitarian work with international action
sections.body: The award announcement credited the WFP with participating in the diplomatic process leading to UN Security Council Resolution 2417 in May 2018. The resolution addressed links between armed conflict and hunger, condemned starvation as a method of warfare and emphasised access to food assistance. The committee also highlighted projects combining food-security work with efforts to support peace. These activities formed part of the broader aim of eliminating hunger. The announcement presented international cooperation and access for aid as continuing requirements, rather than describing the resolution as having ended the use of starvation.

terms.definition: A lack of reliable access to sufficient suitable food, a condition that conflict can worsen and that humanitarian assistance seeks to reduce.
A 2018 UN Security Council resolution addressing conflict-related hunger, starvation as a method of warfare and access to humanitarian food assistance.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Collapse without requiring a perfectly symmetrical star
sections.body: Earlier mathematical descriptions left open whether black holes depended on unrealistically exact symmetry. Penrose developed new methods to study gravitational collapse more generally, with a result published in 1965. Under the theorem's conditions, classical general relativity leads to a breakdown of a complete spacetime description. This gave black-hole physics a firmer theoretical foundation while also exposing a limit of the theory. The result left open what a theory extending beyond classical relativity would say about the interior.

sections.heading: Weighing an invisible object through stellar orbits
sections.body: Genzel's and Ghez's teams observed stars near the centre of the Milky Way using infrared light, which could pass through obscuring dust more effectively than visible light. The stars' rapid orbital motions revealed a large concentration of mass in a small region. Calculations gave a mass of about four million Suns. Within the gravitational framework used to interpret the observations, the results provided strong evidence for a supermassive black hole. These were measurements of surrounding stars, distinct from Penrose's mathematical argument about collapse and from direct observation of the black hole's interior.

sections.heading: Precision built through instruments and repeated observations
sections.body: The Galactic-centre discovery required long-term measurements as well as powerful telescopes. Both teams improved techniques for compensating for the distortion introduced by Earth's atmosphere and developed specialised instruments. Repeated observations from the early 1990s onwards mapped stellar motion with increasing precision. Agreement between the independently led programmes strengthened the evidence for the compact central mass. The announcement emphasised this sustained observational effort: an orbit becomes informative through measurements over time, and the quality of those measurements depends on controlling the effects that blur the image.
