terms.definition: A limit at which the classical spacetime description becomes incomplete; it signals a problem for general relativity's account rather than a demonstrated end to every law of physics.
Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than visible light, used to observe stars through dust towards the Galactic centre.
Changes imposed on incoming light by Earth's atmosphere that blur astronomical images; compensating for them improves the precision of stellar measurements.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Turning isolated examples into a general strategy
sections.body: Small organic molecules had catalyzed particular reactions before 2000, but the approach had not developed into a broad research program. List showed that proline could promote an asymmetric carbon-bond-forming reaction. MacMillan independently designed nitrogen-containing catalysts for reactions including the Diels–Alder reaction, favoring one mirror-image product. Naming and generalizing organocatalysis encouraged researchers to look for many more such catalysts. The significance was a productive design principle and expansion of useful reactions, rather than the first observation that any small organic molecule could affect a reaction rate.

sections.heading: Controlling which mirror-image product forms
sections.body: Many organic products can exist in two mirror-image forms, and their biological effects may differ. List’s proline work showed that a small molecule could perform a selective catalytic role associated with much larger enzymes. MacMillan’s designed catalyst activated a starting material in a way useful for the Diels–Alder reaction without relying on a metal center. In each case, the catalyst favored a particular spatial outcome. Asymmetric catalysis means preferential production of one form; the degree of selectivity depends on the reaction and conditions rather than guaranteeing a perfectly pure product every time.

sections.heading: Designing activity into a small carbon-based framework
sections.body: The announcement describes organic catalysts as carbon-based structures carrying chemical groups that perform the active role. Such groups commonly contain nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur or phosphorus. Changing the framework and active groups gives chemists ways to influence which starting materials react and how products form. This helps explain why the approach expanded into many different transformations after 2000. Some catalysts offer practical advantages in cost, handling or reduced reliance on metals, while the environmental performance of a complete synthesis still depends on its reagents, solvents and processing requirements.

terms.definition: Catalysis using small organic molecules whose chemical groups help reactions proceed, including reactions that favor a particular molecular handedness.
Molecules that are mirror images but cannot be superimposed, analogous to left and right hands.
A particular arrangement of atoms within a molecule that gives it characteristic chemical behavior.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Finding a credible comparison in an uncontrolled world
sections.body: Natural experiments exploit circumstances in which groups face different conditions for reasons useful to a causal comparison. Card and Alan Krueger, for example, studied a minimum-wage change in New Jersey using neighboring Pennsylvania as a comparison. The value of the design depends on why the groups differ and whether other changes could explain the outcome. A policy change alone is therefore not automatically a convincing experiment. Angrist and Imbens supplied methods for interpreting cases where the opportunity or requirement to participate changes, but individuals still respond differently.

sections.heading: A policy may change behavior for only some people
sections.body: Extending compulsory schooling does not make every student stay longer. Some would have continued anyway, while others alter their education because of the rule. This difference complicates interpretation: comparing outcomes must account for whose behavior the intervention changes. Angrist and Imbens established a framework for identifying well-defined causal effects under stated conditions. The presentation uses this example to show why an estimate needs a clear meaning and population, rather than being treated automatically as the effect that everyone would experience from an additional year of education.

sections.heading: What the unobserved alternative would have looked like
sections.body: Questions about wages, immigration or education require a comparison with an alternative that did not occur for the same person at the same time. Card’s studies used real-world changes to construct useful comparisons and challenged claims that some labor-market effects were inevitable. The announcement highlights findings such as minimum-wage increases not necessarily reducing employment and school resources affecting later outcomes. Angrist and Imbens clarified the interpretation of related designs. The combined contribution strengthened both the evidence available and the reasoning needed to say which causal conclusions it supports.

terms.definition: A real-world situation providing plausibly comparable groups exposed to different conditions, used to investigate causation under explicit assumptions.
The difference an intervention makes to an outcome for a specified person or group, relative to what would have happened without it.
The outcome that would have occurred under an alternative condition, such as a person’s earnings without the education change being studied.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Literary themes and narrative structures in Gurnah's novels
sections.body: Gurnah’s novels, including Paradise, Afterlives, Desertion, and Pilgrims Way, utilize specific narrative strategies to depict characters navigating hostile societies. His protagonists often employ irony, withdrawal, silence, and lies to manage the sorrow of ruptured connections to their pasts. These stories draw upon oral narrative patterns and mythologies, merging them with the modern novel's focus on individual fates. The writing explores how individuals resist disguised forms of slavery and endure the shock of encountering new worlds. Through these works, Gurnah examines the genesis of writers, showing how storytelling serves as a tool for understanding history or creating protective alternatives. Ultimately, his prose captures the complex, contradictory nature of modern individuals who must sustain their dreams despite the challenges of displacement.

sections.heading: Literary themes and narrative techniques in Gurnah's novels
sections.body: Gurnah writes in English about displacement and the construction of identity. In Dottie, a Black woman growing up in 1950s England turns to books and stories while struggling with the silence surrounding her family history. Paradise draws on research in East Africa and reworks the Quranic story of Joseph within a narrative of colonialism, coming of age and disappointed love. In Admiring Silence and By the Sea, first-person narrators use concealment to protect themselves from prejudice and from collisions between past and present. The Academy's notes stress the costs of this strategy, including self-deception. Names, withheld stories and changes of perspective become part of how the novels explore belonging.

terms.definition: Stories and storytelling practices passed on through spoken performance; Gurnah draws on them alongside written literary traditions.
A refugee's strategy used in Gurnah's novels to protect identity from racism and avoid collisions between past and present.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Abdulrazak Gurnah — Swedish Academy bio-bibliographical notes

sections.heading: Temperature, touch and the position of the body
sections.body: The presentation linked molecular sensors to several everyday experiences. Julius's identification of the capsaicin receptor connected the burning sensation of chilli peppers with a channel activated by heat. Further work on temperature-sensitive channels extended the explanation to other thermal sensations. Patapoutian's discoveries addressed physical force, helping explain touch and awareness of limb position. These are related but distinct sensory problems: the heat receptor alone does not account for coolness, pressure or body position. Identifying particular proteins made it possible to investigate how different physical inputs begin cellular signals.

sections.heading: Searching by function rather than by a guessed candidate
sections.body: Julius's group initially tested plausible receptors for responses to capsaicin, without success. Michael Caterina then led an expression-cloning approach that searched for the genetic instruction capable of conferring that response. With Makoto Tominaga and others, the group showed that the identified channel, TRPV1, also responded to heat. Julius's account credits these collaborators and explains the advantage of a function-based search. Related work by David McKemy and Werner Neuhausser used menthol to identify a cold-responsive channel, TRPM8, extending the chemical-to-temperature connection.

sections.heading: Removing and adding a candidate sensor
sections.body: Patapoutian's team tested whether a candidate protein was responsible for mechanically activated currents. Removing PIEZO1 from Neuro2A cells reduced their response to pressure, while introducing it into embryonic kidney cells conferred a response to mechanical force. These complementary experiments strengthened the causal link in the tested cells. A search for related genes then identified PIEZO2. Subsequent mouse experiments connected that channel with light-touch sensation, including responses to vibration and an object attached to the back. The work moved from a cellular current to a role in sensory behaviour.

terms.definition: The sense of the position and movement of one's body and limbs, allowing coordinated movement without relying only on sight.
Identifying a gene by introducing genetic material into cells and testing for the function it produces, such as a response to capsaicin.
A mechanically activated ion-channel protein identified through experiments that removed it from responsive cells and introduced it into other cells.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Why the committee connected journalism with peace
sections.body: The committee argued that independent reporting can expose abuses, challenge propaganda and make leaders answerable to the public. It linked this with the conditions for democratic participation and peaceful relations. The speech also recognised that media can contribute to violence, citing hate broadcasts during the Rwandan genocide. Its case therefore concerned an independent, evidence-based press, rather than an assumption that every use of mass communication promotes peace. Protecting journalists was presented as part of protecting the public's ability to learn about and scrutinise the exercise of power.

sections.heading: Reporting under pressure in two different countries
sections.body: The 2021 announcement described Rappler's investigations of violence and abuses in the Philippines, alongside its scrutiny of online disinformation and harassment. In Russia, Novaya Gazeta had reported on corruption, electoral fraud, police violence and military operations. By the award, six of its journalists had been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya. The committee credited Muratov with maintaining the newspaper's independence and defending reporting conducted to professional standards despite those attacks. These descriptions record the grounds for the 2021 award; they should not be read as an undated account of either organisation's subsequent circumstances.

terms.definition: The argument that democracies rarely fight wars against one another; the committee connected this idea with freedom of expression and public information.
The ability to choose and publish reporting without control by the powerful interests being investigated, a principle highlighted in the award's account of both news organisations.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Finding order without tracking every component
sections.body: The presentation connected the three laureates through problems too complicated to solve by following every constituent individually. Manabe combined important physical processes in computational climate models. Hasselmann explained how rapidly varying weather could contribute to slower climate changes, drawing an analogy with random molecular impacts producing observable motion. Parisi developed a mathematical description of disordered systems with many competing arrangements, including spin glasses. Their methods addressed different systems, but each showed how statistical or mathematical structure can support useful predictions despite complexity at the level of individual components.

sections.heading: Adding atmospheric and oceanic processes to climate models
sections.body: Manabe and Wetherald's 1967 single-column model combined radiation, convection and water-vapour feedback. It predicted that increased carbon dioxide would warm the surface and lower atmosphere while cooling the stratosphere. In 1969, Manabe and Bryan published simulations coupling atmospheric and ocean circulation. Later work used coupled models to investigate how climate changes over time as greenhouse-gas concentrations change. The group also examined past climate shifts, including how freshwater entering the North Atlantic could contribute to abrupt change. These were distinct stages in developing models with more interacting physical processes.

terms.definition: An arrangement that can persist for a long time even though a lower-energy state is possible, important in describing many disordered systems.
A simulation linking ocean and atmospheric circulation so that their interactions can be included in calculations of climate.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Reliable connections between molecular building blocks
sections.body: Click chemistry emphasised reactions with a strong tendency to form the desired connection while limiting competing reactions. The copper-catalysed reaction between an azide and an alkyne became a widely used example. Attaching these groups to other molecules allowed researchers to join many different building blocks and create libraries for screening. For work in living systems, strained alkynes offered a related route that could react with azides without copper. The strain belongs to a particular molecular arrangement; simply putting a group in any ring does not make it a suitable biological linking reaction.

sections.heading: A reaction must work alongside cellular chemistry
sections.body: The copper-catalysed azide–alkyne reaction creates a triazole connection, providing a robust way to link molecular components. Bertozzi's biological problem imposed an additional requirement: a useful labelling reaction had to operate among the many molecules in a living system without disrupting their normal chemistry. Her bioorthogonal approach made it possible to follow glycans and investigate their roles. The presentation treated this compatibility as a specific chemical design challenge. A reaction's efficiency in an ordinary laboratory vessel does not by itself establish that it is suitable inside cells.

sections.heading: Tools for tracking molecules and developing materials
sections.body: The award announcement described applications ranging from pharmaceutical research and DNA mapping to the construction of useful materials. In biology, reactions developed to label glycans allowed researchers to follow molecules that had been difficult to observe in living systems. The 2022 account also noted clinical trials investigating cancer-drug targeting using bioorthogonal approaches. That was a report of research and testing at the time of the prize, not a claim that all such treatments had been approved or shown effective. The wider contribution was a set of versatile chemical tools.

terms.definition: An approach favouring efficient, reliable reactions for joining molecular building blocks, rather than designing a different difficult connection for every target.
Chemistry designed to operate within a biological system while avoiding interference with its native molecules and reactions under the conditions used.
A sugar structure, often attached to a molecule at the cell surface; tracking glycans was an important motivation for Bertozzi's work.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: What is lost when a bank fails
sections.body: Bernanke examined the Great Depression using historical evidence and statistical analysis. His work argued that bank failures did more than accompany the downturn: they damaged the system that connected savings with productive borrowing and helped make the depression deeper and longer. Banks accumulate information about borrowers and learn how to evaluate loans. When an institution fails, those relationships and that knowledge cannot always be recreated quickly elsewhere. This mechanism complements the separate Diamond–Dybvig explanation of why banks' useful provision of liquidity also makes them vulnerable to runs.

sections.heading: A historical illustration of fragile banking
sections.body: The presentation opened with Stockholms Banco, which began operating in 1657 and made payments easier than carrying heavy copper currency. In 1660, a decision to issue lighter copper plates encouraged depositors to retrieve older plates with a higher metal value. The resulting rush illustrated the tension between readily withdrawable deposits and funds committed to lending. The speech used this historical episode to introduce the laureates' later analytical questions: why useful financial arrangements can become fragile, and why disruption of banking can have consequences far beyond the bank itself.

sections.heading: Monitoring borrowers and protecting access to deposits
sections.body: Diamond's research examined banks as intermediaries that assess borrowers and monitor the use of loans on behalf of many savers. Diamond and Dybvig's work addressed a different but related problem: depositors want ready access to money that banks have lent for longer periods. Fear of failure can make many depositors withdraw at once. Deposit insurance and emergency lending can help counter that destabilising incentive. The announcement presented these findings as foundations for understanding bank regulation and crisis responses, rather than a guarantee that every lending decision or intervention will succeed.

terms.definition: Information and experience about borrowers and lending relationships, built up over time and difficult to replace immediately when a bank fails.
A rush by many depositors to withdraw their funds, which can overwhelm a bank whose resources are committed to longer-term lending.
An authority, usually a central bank, able to provide emergency liquidity to banks when ordinary sources of funding are unavailable.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Connecting an individual life with social history
sections.body: The presentation traced Ernaux's movement from narratives labelled as novels towards explicitly autobiographical writing. Cleaned Out, published in 1974, reconstructed a young woman's experience of class constraints through a fictional character. Later work placed personal memory more directly within social and historical conditions. The Years developed this approach across six decades of French life, using third-person narration rather than a conventional first-person life story. The committee's account emphasised how Ernaux made an individual perspective part of a wider record of changing habits, expectations and inequalities.

sections.heading: Writing alongside teaching and domestic work
sections.body: Ernaux's autobiography describes writing Cleaned Out privately during afternoons without classes and sending the manuscript to publishers. Teaching, children and household responsibilities left limited time for subsequent books. She connected that double burden with A Frozen Woman and described a later departure from the novelistic form in A Man's Place. Teaching also gave her financial independence from book sales. Her account therefore locates the writing within the practical conditions of work, family life and income, as well as within decisions about literary form.

terms.definition: A form that connects an individual's remembered life with the experiences and historical changes of a wider society.
Writing based on the author's own life; Ernaux's account emphasises how those experiences are shaped by social circumstances and responsibilities.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Making ancient genomes accessible to comparison
sections.body: Recovering ancient genetic material required both laboratory methods and large-scale analysis. The presentation highlighted Pääbo's use of high-throughput sequencing and an international collaboration to analyse the Neanderthal genome. The resulting comparisons made it possible to investigate relationships and interbreeding directly through DNA, rather than rely only on differences in bones or tools. Sequencing a small Denisovan finger bone also revealed a previously unrecognised hominin group. These genomes supplied evidence about ancestry and inherited variants, including some with effects on present-day physiology, while leaving many questions about human evolution open.

sections.heading: Nuclear and mitochondrial DNA tell different parts of the story
sections.body: An early Denisovan genome had about 1.9-fold sequencing coverage. Its nuclear DNA placed Denisovans and Neanderthals as related sister groups, while mitochondrial DNA showed a more deeply divergent history. The technical background reported an average sequence divergence between Neanderthals and Denisovans of about 640,000 years; that estimate should not be treated as a precise date when two populations separated. Further Denisovan samples revealed additional variation, suggesting a long presence in the region. The comparison illustrates why a genome's different components and samples from different individuals must be interpreted together.

terms.definition: The study of ancient genomes, using recovered DNA to investigate the history and relationships of past organisms and populations.
The average number of times a genomic position is represented in sequencing reads; 1.9-fold coverage means an average of about 1.9 observations per position.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Building a record for assistance and accountability
sections.body: The Center for Civil Liberties' Euromaidan SOS initiative provided legal assistance and documented abuses during the protests in Ukraine. It also developed maps to help track enforced disappearances. After Russia's annexation of Crimea and the outbreak of conflict in Donbas, monitoring teams gathered information about detention and other violations, sharing it with partner organisations. The 2022 presentation described an expanded effort to document war crimes after the full-scale invasion. Collecting and preserving such material was intended to support future legal proceedings; documentation itself is distinct from a court's determination of individual criminal responsibility.

sections.heading: Preserving evidence of past and continuing repression
sections.body: Memorial connected research into Soviet-era persecution with documentation of later human-rights violations. Its archives recorded victims of Stalinist repression, while other work gathered information about political prisoners and abuses in contemporary Russia. The 2022 announcement presented this combination as a way of confronting past crimes and resisting their repetition. It also recognised the Center for Civil Liberties' documentation in Ukraine and Bialiatski's rights work in Belarus. The committee's emphasis was on independent civic action under pressure, including imprisonment and forced dissolution, rather than endorsement of the governments of the three countries.

terms.definition: An initiative providing legal assistance and documenting rights violations associated with the Ukrainian protests and their aftermath.
Organisations and associations through which people act collectively outside government; the award highlighted independent human-rights work within this wider sphere.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Turning a foundational dispute into experiments
sections.body: In 1972, John Clauser and Stuart Freedman performed a pioneering test of Bell's inequality on a limited budget. Their measured correlations exceeded the relevant bound and agreed with quantum predictions. The experiment made a dispute about how nature works accessible to laboratory tests, although experimental shortcomings left questions about alternative explanations. Alain Aspect and colleagues subsequently strengthened the tests. Anton Zeilinger's group combined increasingly demanding experiments with demonstrations of ways to use entanglement. The award presentation describes this progression from foundational questions to quantum information science.

sections.heading: Changing settings while photons travel
sections.body: A key difficulty in testing entanglement was excluding ways that a local explanation might reproduce the measured correlations. Aspect changed measurement settings after the photon pair had left its source, addressing an important experimental loophole. These tests strengthened the evidence against local hidden-variable explanations; they did not exclude every conceivable hidden-variable theory. Zeilinger and colleagues then used entangled states in demonstrations including quantum teleportation. That procedure transfers a quantum state between systems through entanglement together with ordinary communication. It does not send a controllable message faster than light.

terms.definition: A bound on measurement correlations predicted by theories with local hidden properties; suitable quantum experiments can exceed that bound.
A shared quantum state that cannot be described as a statistical mixture of separate quantum states for its particles.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Making particles with reproducible quantum properties
sections.body: Yekimov demonstrated size-dependent quantum effects in copper chloride particles inside glass in 1981. Brus subsequently showed such effects in particles suspended in liquid. Producing consistent particles remained difficult. In 1993 Bawendi’s group developed a process in which tiny crystals began forming together; controlled temperature changes then governed their growth, while the surrounding solvent helped produce even surfaces. Obtaining particles with well-controlled sizes and few imperfections made their optical behavior more predictable. A reproducible preparation method helped turn an intriguing physical effect into a material that other laboratories could study and use.

sections.heading: Why manufacturing quality mattered
sections.body: The presentation speech links the three contributions through a practical difficulty: producing useful quantities of particles with consistent properties. Yekimov worked with crystals inside glass; Brus made particles free in a solution. Bawendi’s later synthesis provided much greater control over crystal quality and could be adapted for more elaborate structures and industrial production. This sequence brought chemistry and physics together. The particles were interesting because quantum effects changed their behavior, but reliable chemical preparation was essential before those effects could support dependable devices and biological research.

sections.heading: Uses established by the time of the award
sections.body: The 2023 announcement described quantum dots in television and computer displays, in some LED lighting, and in techniques for marking biological tissue. Their usefulness comes partly from controlling optical properties through particle size rather than changing composition alone. The announcement also discussed research prospects such as flexible electronics, solar cells, tiny sensors and quantum communication. Those prospects should be distinguished from applications already described as in use at the award date: the prize recognized the discovery and development of a material platform, not the completion of every proposed device.

terms.definition: Extremely small particles in which quantum confinement makes properties such as light absorption and emission depend on particle size.
The design and use of structures at nanometer scales, where their small dimensions can give them distinctive properties.
Changes in how a material absorbs or emits light that arise when the dimensions of its particles change.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Why expanding demand did not immediately remove barriers
sections.body: Goldin’s historical reconstruction showed that women’s paid work did not simply increase whenever the economy grew. Industrialization initially reduced some opportunities for married women, while later growth of service work and education increased demand for their labor. Institutional restrictions could still block participation. Marriage bars, for example, excluded married women from some teaching and office jobs, and became particularly prominent around the Depression. The historical pattern therefore combines changing production with rules and expectations about marriage, rather than treating women’s employment as an automatic response to available jobs.

sections.heading: Recovering work that official records missed
sections.body: The presentation speech highlights Goldin’s archival evidence that women performed many occupations without being recorded as workers in historical censuses. Recovering those activities changes the starting point for a history of employment. It also describes factors affecting later choices: household technologies changed time use, while access to contraception improved the ability to plan education, careers and families. Such changes worked alongside institutions and expectations, often across generations. The speech presents this long perspective as a reason not to assume that the passage of time alone will produce equal opportunities or earnings.

sections.heading: Historical measurement required more than reading published totals
sections.body: Goldin explains that older censuses asked about gainful occupations rather than using modern labor-force definitions. A woman doing intermittent paid work might not report an occupation. Work in family businesses, boardinghouses, farms or piece-rate production at home could also disappear from published categories. Reconstructing these activities required returning to underlying records and reconsidering what counted as market work. Her later research on education and inequality similarly connected historical data with questions about earnings, including work with Lawrence Katz. The methodological contribution was making comparisons meaningful before drawing conclusions from them.

terms.definition: A rule restricting employment because a woman married or was already married, historically used in some professions and workplaces.
The share of a defined population working or actively seeking work; historical measurements require care because definitions and recording practices changed.
Economic activity missed or poorly classified by historical records, including work performed within homes and family enterprises.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Language carries what characters struggle to express
sections.body: The presentation speech emphasizes the tension between ordinary words and experiences that resist expression. In Closed Guitar, a mother’s separation from her baby shapes an increasingly anxious narrative. In Septology, the painter Asle’s thoughts flow through extended prose, linking everyday experience with prayer and uncertainty. Fosse’s drama explores related difficulties through pauses and silence rather than continuous explanation. The Academy reads these forms as ways of making hesitation and unspoken feeling present to readers or audiences. The effect depends on rhythm and duration as much as on what the characters explicitly say.

sections.heading: Minimal language with sustained emotional pressure
sections.body: The Academy’s notes connect Fosse’s early novels with the spare methods of his later drama. Familiar situations become charged with uncertainty through repetition, interrupted speech and the reluctance or inability to act. His plays can strip away names or conventional plot developments while retaining intense relationships between people. His larger prose works, including Septology, extend the use of rhythm and recurring thoughts in another form. The notes also stress the breadth of a career written in Nynorsk, encompassing poetry, essays, children’s books and translations as well as the better-known plays and novels.

terms.definition: A meaningful pause or absence of speech in a play, allowing tension and emotion to emerge without direct verbal explanation.
A deliberately pared-down artistic approach that draws attention to small changes, repetition or silence rather than elaborate explanation.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Jon Fosse — Swedish Academy bio-bibliographical notes

sections.heading: Testing how cells respond to laboratory-made RNA
sections.body: Karikó and Weissman wanted to use mRNA as a carrier of instructions for medical applications, but early experiments faced unwanted inflammatory responses. Their 2005 study compared how cells reacted to different forms of RNA. Incorporating chemical modifications resembling those in naturally occurring RNA greatly reduced inflammatory activation in the tested cells. This addressed a major obstacle to the approach. It helped establish the scientific foundation for later mRNA vaccines, alongside further advances in delivery and vaccine design. The result concerned the response to the introduced RNA; vaccination still depends on generating immunity to the protein it encodes.

sections.heading: Why modified RNA can produce more protein
sections.body: Karikó, Weissman and colleagues investigated links between RNA sensing and protein production. Their experiments showed that certain modified RNA bases reduced inflammatory activation in dendritic cells. Subsequent work found that pseudouridine-containing mRNA produced more protein, including after delivery into mouse spleens. Mechanistic studies showed reduced activation of protein kinase R, an antiviral protein that can inhibit translation through the initiation factor eIF2α. Modified RNA also reduced recognition by the OAS system and breakdown by RNase L. These findings identified several obstacles to using laboratory-made mRNA. The results came from defined experimental conditions; they do not mean modified mRNA prevents every immune or inflammatory response.

terms.definition: Chemical building blocks joined in RNA chains, whose sequence carries instructions that cells can translate into proteins.
Chemical alterations to RNA building blocks; some can reduce unwanted immune activation and improve production of the encoded protein.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Prison solidarity and the defence of equality
sections.body: The 2023 award presentation described Mohammadi's opposition to compulsory covering garments and restrictions on women's sport, dancing and freedom of movement. It also highlighted how she sustained collective activity in prison through education, singing, dancing and protest. She organised opposition to sexual violence and torture experienced by women prisoners and supported the Woman–Life–Freedom protests from confinement. Her long campaign against executions formed another part of this work. The committee connected these activities with universal equality and with the principle that rights belong to everyone, regardless of the political system under which they live.

sections.heading: Advocacy against death penalty and prison violence
sections.body: After her release on bail, Mohammadi intensified campaigning against executions. The 2023 prize announcement linked that activism to her rearrest in 2015. Back in prison, she opposed torture and sexual violence against political prisoners, particularly women. During the 2022 protests, she organised solidarity among fellow inmates at Evin prison. Authorities restricted calls and visits, but she managed to send out an article published by the New York Times on the first anniversary of Mahsa Jina Amini's death. Its message expressed her belief that collective resistance could grow despite imprisonment. These were activities documented at the time of the award.

terms.definition: A declaration setting out universal human-rights principles, including equal dignity and rights to life, liberty and personal security.
A slogan meaning Woman – Life – Freedom used by demonstrators to express dedication to equality and human rights.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Combining harmonics into extremely short pulses
sections.body: A strong laser field can pull an electron away from an atom and then drive it back. On recombination, energy gained from the field can be released as higher-frequency light. These harmonics provide wavelengths shorter than those of the original laser. Combining a suitable range of harmonics with controlled relative timing makes very short light pulses possible. The experiments developed ways to generate trains of attosecond pulses and, separately, isolated pulses. The electron's return is to the ion from which it escaped; this process does not involve inserting an electron into the atomic nucleus.

sections.heading: Measuring electronic change on its own timescale
sections.body: Attosecond pulses allow experiments to resolve changes in electron distributions that were previously too rapid to follow directly. The presentation connected this capability with questions about charge motion in molecules and materials, including processes relevant to catalysis, electronics and energy devices. Generating short pulses was only part of the challenge: researchers also needed methods to measure their duration and establish what the experiments were observing. The broader applications describe directions for research and control of electronic processes, rather than a claim that the original experiments delivered finished medical or industrial technologies.

sections.heading: Recovering a hidden oscillation in the measurements
sections.body: Agostini recalled an initially disappointing experiment involving doctoral researchers Pierre-Mary Paul and Elena Toma, working with him and Harm Muller. The expected regular oscillations appeared as random data. The team eventually identified fluctuations in laser intensity and corrected the analysis by normalising to the total counts. The recovered oscillations allowed measurement of the relative harmonic phases and demonstrated an attosecond pulse train, reported in 2001. This account distinguishes the prize-winning measurement from separate earlier plasma and X-ray experiments, showing how understanding experimental fluctuations was essential to the result.

terms.definition: Frequency components at integer multiples of a fundamental frequency, produced here through the interaction between intense laser light and atoms.
Research using timescales of billionths of a billionth of a second to investigate rapid electronic processes in atoms, molecules and materials.
The position of one wave's oscillation cycle compared with another's; measuring harmonic phases helps establish how the combined light forms a pulse.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Designing a sequence and testing the resulting protein
sections.body: Computational protein design begins with a desired molecular structure and asks which amino-acid sequence could produce it. Baker's 2003 work demonstrated that a new structure could be designed, made and checked experimentally. The presentation described later work extending the approach to proteins intended for roles such as sensing, switching, inhibiting viruses and assembling materials. Computation supplies candidates, while experiment establishes whether the produced molecules have the intended structure and behaviour. The achievement therefore joined theoretical design with physical validation, opening a route to proteins beyond those already observed in nature.

sections.heading: Structure predictions as starting points for research
sections.body: The 2024 announcement described the scale reached after AlphaFold2's 2020 breakthrough: predictions had been produced for roughly 200 million identified protein sequences. This greatly expanded access to structural models for investigating biological questions. Examples included research into antibiotic resistance and enzymes able to break down plastics. A predicted model represents a proposed three-dimensional arrangement; it is not an experimental image of every molecule or every state the protein can adopt. Its value lies in giving researchers a structural starting point for further analysis and testing.

terms.definition: The use of calculations to choose amino-acid sequences intended to adopt desired structures or perform functions, followed by experimental evaluation.
A representation of the three-dimensional arrangement of a protein; a computational prediction proposes such an arrangement from information including its amino-acid sequence.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Colonial institutions and unequal access to power
sections.body: The laureates studied how different colonial arrangements shaped later economic development. In their account, some systems concentrated resources and political authority in a narrow elite; others gave European settlers stronger incentives to invest and broader political rights. The latter were not modern democracies, and describing their institutions as inclusive does not imply equal treatment of indigenous populations. The accompanying theory examines conflicts over resources, popular mobilization and the credibility of rulers’ promises. Together these approaches connect economic opportunities to the distribution of political power, rather than treating prosperity as a simple consequence of geography.

sections.heading: Evidence about causes, and models of change
sections.body: A central empirical problem is distinguishing whether institutions produce prosperity or prosperous societies develop different institutions. The laureates used historical variation associated with colonial rule to investigate the direction of causation. Their theoretical models address a further puzzle: why arrangements that restrict wider prosperity can persist. Elites may promise reform during a crisis but have little incentive to honor that promise once the threat passes. Transferring political power can make future reform more credible. The presentation speech uses Sweden’s suffrage reforms to illustrate this logic, rather than as proof that every transition follows the same route.

sections.heading: Why institutions that restrict prosperity can endure
sections.body: The announcement emphasizes a tension between benefits to society over time and immediate advantages for those who hold power. More broadly inclusive institutions may improve long-run opportunities, while existing rulers benefit from restricting participation. If those rulers retain control, promises of future reform may lack credibility. This helps explain why harmful arrangements can persist even when change would produce wider gains. The research also connects colonial institutional differences with later reversals in relative prosperity. It supplies an explanation for important historical patterns, not a claim that institutions are the only cause of every country’s economic outcomes.

terms.definition: Rules and organizations that channel benefits toward a narrow group while limiting opportunities or influence for much of the population.
A situation in which a promise is difficult to trust because the person making it may later have an incentive to break it.
The tendency of political or economic rules to endure, including when groups with power benefit from keeping them.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Color, memory and the presence of the dead
sections.body: The presentation speech reads Han Kang’s recurring colors as carrying conflicting associations: white can suggest both sheltering snow and mourning, while red links life with injury. In We Do Not Part, a snowstorm accompanies the narrator’s movement through memories and encounters with the dead. The speech emphasizes how such shifts dissolve boundaries between past and present, dream and ordinary experience. These are descriptions of a literary method, not literal claims about supernatural events. Remembering violence demands painful attention from the living, and the persistence of that demand is central to the Academy’s interpretation of her work.

sections.heading: Narrative form as a way of confronting violence
sections.body: The Academy’s notes describe different forms through which Han Kang explores vulnerability. Your Cold Hands incorporates a missing sculptor’s manuscript, using casts of bodies to examine the tension between outward appearance and concealed experience. Human Acts turns to the 1980 Gwangju massacre, bringing victims and their continuing presence into the narrative. The White Book builds an elegiac meditation around white objects and the memory of a child who died. These formal choices make bodies, absence and memory part of how a story is told, as well as subjects that it discusses.

terms.definition: The use of images, objects or colors to suggest meanings beyond their literal appearance, sometimes carrying several conflicting associations.
Writing that bears testimony to suffering or historical violence; the Academy uses the term to situate Human Acts.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation
Han Kang — Swedish Academy bio-bibliographical notes

sections.heading: An additional layer of control over genes
sections.body: Cells regulate genes at several stages. Transcription factors help control whether DNA is copied into RNA, while microRNAs act on RNA messages after they have been made. Binding to a target message can reduce the amount of protein produced or promote loss of the message itself. Research beginning with a tiny worm revealed a mechanism later found widely in animals and plants, and in some viruses. The 2024 speech describes roughly a thousand human microRNA genes participating in development and adult cell function. The discovery therefore concerned regulation of existing genetic instructions, not the creation of a different genetic code.

sections.heading: From a developmental mutation to an RNA mechanism
sections.body: Ambros and Ruvkun investigated worms whose developmental timing was disrupted. The lin-4 gene produced a short, non-protein-coding RNA, while regulatory regions of the lin-14 message contained sequences that could pair with it. Comparing these findings revealed how one gene’s RNA product could control another gene’s protein output. Later work uncovered how cells manufacture microRNAs. In the canonical pathway, a longer RNA folds into a hairpin and is cut into a shorter precursor by a complex containing Drosha; further processing produces the mature regulator. The complete processing pathway was established through subsequent research, not all in the original 1993 discovery.

terms.definition: A short RNA molecule that helps regulate gene activity by interacting with target messenger RNA.
Control of gene output after an RNA copy has been made, including changes to message stability or its translation into protein.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Keeping the consequences of nuclear war visible
sections.body: The award speech argues that survivors’ testimony helps sustain a moral barrier against using nuclear weapons. Personal accounts give concrete meaning to consequences that strategic language can obscure: injury, loss and suffering extending far beyond an explosion. Nihon Hidankyo has carried those experiences into education and public advocacy over decades. The committee also warned in 2024 that this barrier remained vulnerable amid arsenal modernization and weakened arms-control arrangements. The prize recognized a continuing effort to influence public judgment and political choices, rather than evidence that nuclear danger had ended.

sections.heading: Turning testimony into organized advocacy
sections.body: Nihon Hidankyo combines individual accounts with sustained collective activity. The 2024 announcement describes thousands of witness testimonies, public appeals and resolutions, together with regular delegations to the United Nations and peace conferences. These methods carry survivors’ experiences beyond Japan and connect remembrance with demands for disarmament. The organization grew from survivor associations and groups affected by Pacific nuclear testing in 1956. Its work also includes defending survivors’ social and economic interests, linking the treatment of people already harmed with efforts to prevent future nuclear devastation.

terms.definition: A widely shared norm treating the use of nuclear weapons as unacceptable; it depends on social and political support, not physical impossibility.
Survivors of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, whose experiences underpin Nihon Hidankyo’s advocacy.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Using statistical physics to learn patterns
sections.body: Hopfield related a network’s changing node values to an energy function, borrowing ideas from interacting magnetic systems. Hinton’s Boltzmann machine extended this approach by treating network states probabilistically. Visible nodes represent observed data, while hidden nodes allow the network to represent relationships that are not supplied directly. Training adjusts connections so that patterns resembling the examples become more probable. Here energy is a mathematical quantity used to organize the model’s behavior; the computer is not literally cooling a magnetic material. This made tools from statistical physics useful for learning structure in data.

sections.heading: Memories as stable states of a network
sections.body: In Hopfield’s model, many connected nodes influence one another through weighted connections. Their updates can be described as movement toward lower values of an energy function. Stored patterns are represented by stable configurations, analogous to valleys in a landscape. Starting from an incomplete or altered pattern can lead the system toward a stored one. The presentation speech uses this relationship between collective dynamics and memory to explain the physics connection. Hinton’s subsequent work added probabilistic learning and pattern generation, helping broaden the uses of neural networks beyond retrieving a fixed set of memories.

sections.heading: From recalling examples to learning their structure
sections.body: The announcement distinguishes two related capabilities. A Hopfield network stores patterns through its connections and updates an incoming pattern toward a stable configuration. A Boltzmann machine instead learns statistical relationships from examples and can generate patterns with similar characteristics. Both rely on many simple components interacting, drawing inspiration from physical systems as well as biological neurons. Their importance lies in foundational methods for information processing and learning. The award does not imply that these early networks are identical to every modern AI system or that their nodes reproduce the full behavior of real brain cells.

terms.definition: A probabilistic neural network that learns relationships among variables by adjusting an energy-based distribution over possible network states.
A way of representing how a model’s energy function varies across possible configurations, with valleys corresponding to locally stable states.
Retrieval of a stored pattern from a related cue, such as an incomplete or distorted version of the pattern.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: From fragile frameworks to useful porous materials
sections.body: Early frameworks could admit and exchange guest substances but often fell apart. In 1995, Yaghi reported two-dimensional networks based on copper or cobalt. The cobalt material could withstand heating to 350°C when its spaces were fully occupied by guest molecules. MOF-5, introduced in 1999, marked another advance in framework design. Later variants offered substantial methane-storage capacity. Researchers have since developed many thousands of MOFs and investigated uses including water harvesting, pollutant removal, carbon dioxide capture and ethylene trapping to slow fruit ripening. These examples illustrate the range of possible functions; they do not establish that every proposed application is already widely deployed.

sections.heading: Building cavities through molecular assembly
sections.body: The award presentation compares MOF construction to adding the material around a hole, then explains the actual chemistry: metal-based nodes are linked by organic molecules. Robson assembled copper ions and four-armed organic components into a diamond-like framework with spacious cavities. Kitagawa demonstrated frameworks that could take up and release gases, and developed flexible structures whose cavities could change. Yaghi showed how stronger interactions between building blocks improved stability and helped establish systematic construction of families sharing a basic geometry. The building-block approach lets chemists vary structures and properties without starting from an unrelated design each time.

terms.definition: An extended, ordered structure assembled from metal-based components and organic molecules, potentially enclosing cavities that can hold other molecules.
Chemistry of metal centres and the molecules or ions bound to them; in MOFs, such connections assemble the framework.

sections.heading: Why invention needs both knowledge and practical skill
sections.body: Mokyr’s historical account connects scientific understanding with the skills needed to turn ideas into working products. He emphasizes Britain’s artisans and engineers as part of the explanation for sustained technological advance. Aghion and Howitt approached the problem through a mathematical model: firms invest in improvements, and successful innovations can displace earlier market leaders. Together these perspectives show why growth involves more than accumulating isolated inventions. Knowledge must support further advances, practical skills must make those advances usable, and economic incentives must encourage continued investment despite the disruption it brings.

sections.heading: Growth models as tools for examining policy
sections.body: Aghion and Howitt’s models explain how repeated displacement of existing firms can coexist with long-run growth under specified conditions. The presentation speech describes later uses of this framework to study innovation incentives and workers’ transitions. It also highlights the direction of innovation: new ideas often build on existing technologies, so an economy may remain on a path such as reliance on fossil fuels. Policy can influence those incentives and directions. These are conclusions from models and their extensions, not a guarantee that disruption always produces steady growth or that any particular intervention will succeed.

sections.heading: Why resistance to change matters
sections.body: The award announcement stresses that technological progress can threaten established interests. An improved product may benefit buyers while reducing the value of an incumbent firm’s technology or position. Mokyr’s historical research and Aghion and Howitt’s modeling approach both address conditions under which innovation can continue despite these conflicts. Openness to new knowledge matters, as does the ability to manage opposition from groups that expect to lose. The resulting account treats sustained growth as something requiring supportive conditions, rather than an automatic outcome once a society has made its first scientific discoveries.

terms.definition: The process through which successful innovations displace older products, methods or firms while creating new economic opportunities.
The way earlier choices and accumulated capabilities can influence which later developments become easier or more likely.
A business already established in a market, whose position may be challenged by new competitors or technologies.

sources.title: Historical award presentation — the committee’s explanation

sections.heading: Order, terror and the unsettling force of narrative
sections.body: The presentation speech describes Krasznahorkai’s fiction through the fragile boundary between order and violence. In Satantango, the inhabitants of a declining collective farm confront figures whose promises cannot be trusted. In The Melancholy of Resistance, a traveling spectacle becomes entangled with destructive forces in a small town. Herscht 07769 places compassion, violence and Bach’s music in a contemporary German setting. The Academy connects these works to a Central European tradition of grotesque comedy and existential unease. It also emphasizes the tension between their disturbing subjects and the momentum of their long, flowing sentences.

sections.heading: Different forms for journeys, art and displacement
sections.body: The Academy’s notes trace a range wider than apocalyptic fiction alone. Baron Wenckheim’s Homecoming follows a ruined baron returning to Hungary, drawing comedy and unease from his journey and reception. Travels in China and Japan informed more contemplative works. Seiobo There Below contains seventeen stories concerned with beauty and artistic creation, often approaching art through observers or craftspeople rather than centering the artist. Its numbered sequence follows the Fibonacci pattern. Spadework for a Palace offers another change of scale and setting, turning to Manhattan and the influence of Herman Melville. Together these examples show varied structures within a distinctive prose style.

terms.definition: A literary approach that explores bewildering or irrational situations and the difficulty of finding stable meaning, often through unsettling humor.
A form of episodic narrative organized around a wandering protagonist’s adventures, often exposing social pretensions through comic encounters.

sections.heading: Connecting a genetic defect with regulatory T cells
sections.body: Sakaguchi's mouse experiments showed that a subset of CD4-bearing T cells could restrain immune attacks. Brunkow and Ramsdell approached the problem genetically, investigating the severe illness of scurfy mice and a related human disorder, IPEX. In 2001, their work linked these conditions to mutations in Foxp3 in mice and its human counterpart FOXP3. That finding did not yet establish the whole cellular mechanism. In 2003, Sakaguchi and other researchers connected the gene to the development of regulatory T cells. The cellular and genetic discoveries thus converged on an active system that suppresses damaging immune responses and helps restore restraint after infection.

sections.heading: Genetic and cellular mechanisms of peripheral immune tolerance
sections.body: The discovery process involved investigating specific biological models to understand how the immune system avoids attacking host tissues. Shimon Sakaguchi studied newborn mice that developed severe autoimmunity following thymus removal three days after birth, eventually identifying a subset of cells marked by CD4 and CD25. Concurrently, Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell examined the "scurfy" mouse, which exhibited widespread inflammation and flaky skin. By analyzing this X-linked trait within a small twenty-gene region, they sequenced genes to identify FOXP3 as the critical component. Subsequent research in 2003 demonstrated that these regulatory T cells rely on the FOXP3 gene for their essential identity and function, providing a unified explanation for how immune responses are restrained.

terms.definition: Mechanisms that keep mature immune cells from attacking the body's own tissues; regulatory T cells provide one important component.
A specific mouse model characterized by widespread inflammation and flaky skin, used to investigate genes linked to autoimmunity.

sections.heading: Documenting votes as a form of political action
sections.body: The 2025 presentation describes the Venezuelan opposition’s use of organized documentation to challenge the official account of the 2024 election. Volunteers collected local tallies, which opposition leaders published as evidence of victory. The committee places this alongside changing tactics over many years, including participation, boycotts, dialogue and public mobilization. Its interpretation emphasizes nonviolent civic action under repression and the effort to secure representative government. The account explains the rationale for the award at that moment; it does not establish that a democratic transition had already been completed.

sections.heading: A blocked candidacy and a wider volunteer effort
sections.body: The award announcement recounts that Machado was barred from standing in 2024 and supported Edmundo González Urrutia instead. Volunteers from across political divisions trained to observe voting and document polling-station totals despite threats. The committee credited this collective effort with making the opposition’s evidence available internationally, while describing the authorities’ refusal to accept the outcome. It connected Machado’s role with a longer record of advocacy for judicial independence, human rights and political representation. The recognition concerned both leadership and the organized work of many citizens.

terms.definition: Collecting and preserving records of voting and counting so reported results can be examined and compared with the underlying evidence.
A person monitoring aspects of voting or counting and recording what occurs; observation can supply evidence without guaranteeing a fair process.

sections.heading: Measuring escape from a quantum state of a circuit
sections.body: The Berkeley experiments used a superconducting circuit containing a Josephson junction. Its collective state could remain trapped with current flowing but no voltage, then escape through quantum tunnelling and produce a measurable voltage. Repeating the experiment many times allowed the researchers to determine escape statistics rather than relying on a single event. Microwave excitation supplied a second test: absorption at particular frequencies revealed discrete energy levels. The measured tunnelling involved a collective circuit variable, extending quantum behavior beyond isolated particles and distinguishing the result from ordinary electron passage through a thin barrier.

sections.heading: Cold and filtering made the quantum behavior observable
sections.body: Cooling the circuit to roughly one hundredth of a degree above absolute zero reduced thermal disturbances that could mask its quantum behavior. The researchers also needed carefully designed filtering: room-temperature microwave noise had to be suppressed while controlled signals could still reach the experiment. This combination allowed measurements of tunnelling and discrete energy absorption in an engineered system containing enormous numbers of electrons. The achievement was not simply that the material became superconducting, but that the collective circuit could be isolated and controlled well enough to display these additional quantum effects.

terms.definition: A weak connection between superconductors, often made with a thin insulating layer, that supports quantum-coherent electrical behavior.
Unwanted fluctuations associated with thermal energy, which can disturb a sensitive circuit and obscure the quantum behavior under study.

sections.heading: Why autocatalysis alone does not amplify handedness
sections.body: Kagan's 1986 epoxidation work showed that a partially enantioenriched catalyst could yield a product with a larger enantiomeric excess. This measures the imbalance between molecular mirror images, rather than general chemical purity. Soai's 1990 reaction combined autocatalysis with selectivity: a chiral product catalysed further production of itself. Yet an initial catalyst with 86% enantiomeric excess gave product at only 35%. The 1995 result added the crucial amplification step. Self-production and preference for one mirror image therefore did not, by themselves, guarantee increasing handedness. Later work by Donna Blackmond analysed reaction rates and changes in enantiomeric excess during conversion, showing how non-linear behaviour could help investigate which catalytic species were active.

sections.heading: Amplifying a tiny imbalance through repeated reactions
sections.body: Soai's 2019 review describes a later amplification experiment using a substituted pyrimidyl alkanol as both product and catalyst. Starting with about 0.00005% enantiomeric excess, three successive reaction cycles raised the excess above 99.5% while increasing the amount of alkanol roughly 630,000-fold. These percentages describe the imbalance between enantiomers, not overall chemical purity. No additional chiral auxiliary was needed beyond the initial tiny imbalance. The review also compares proposed mechanisms: kinetic measurements and NMR examined dimers and larger catalyst aggregates, while X-ray studies found tetrameric or oligomeric crystal structures. Those observations informed competing models rather than establishing one mechanism for every version of the reaction. The laboratory result demonstrates amplification, without identifying the actual historical origin of biological handedness.

terms.definition: Departures from a proportional relationship between a catalyst's enantiomeric composition and that of its product; the effect can amplify or diminish the product's handedness.
A reaction in which a chiral product catalyses further production of that product, preferentially with the same molecular handedness.

sections.heading: Foundations for interest rate policy and consumption analysis
sections.body: Economic stabilization relies on understanding how individual decisions drive aggregate demand. Hall investigated consumption determinants, noting that because private spending is the largest component of aggregate demand, its drivers are essential for policy. Since consumption is forward-looking, it depends on expectations regarding future income and economic policy. Woodford contributed a New Keynesian framework featuring price-setting frictions, where prices do not change instantly. This mechanism allows monetary policy to exert significant real effects. Through various papers, Woodford established a foundation for interest rate-based policies used by most central banks today. Alongside Rotemberg, he demonstrated that these models could be estimated using economic data. This advancement enabled policymakers to build large econometric models to quantify the potential impacts of different policy measures.

sections.heading: Stochastic implications of the life cycle-permanent income hypothesis
sections.body: Hall's 1978 paper examined consumption under the life-cycle–permanent-income framework. Under its benchmark assumptions, marginal utility follows a random walk with trend, with consumption itself approximately following a similar pattern under additional conditions. The implication is about predictability: information already available should be incorporated into current decisions. Hall tested this using postwar American data. Real disposable income did not add predictive power for consumption in the tests reported, but a stock-price index did. That departure from the simplest benchmark was consistent with some consumption adjusting after a delay. The policy argument was similarly conditional: anticipated changes affecting lifetime resources may already influence spending before implementation, while genuinely new information can prompt a fresh adjustment. It was not a claim that every household's expenditure is literally random or unaffected by predictable income changes.

terms.definition: A framework featuring price and wage-setting frictions, implying that prices do not change every instant, allowing monetary policy effects.
A framework in which current consumption depends on expected long-term resources and choices about spending across a lifetime.

sections.heading: Translational methods and visual influences in writing
sections.body: In an interview conducted in 2013, Carson traced her approach to writing back to childhood drawing and painting. The surviving fragments of ancient poetry and the visual forms of Greek letters fitted that early interest. She also described word history as a starting point for research. One drawing project began with the Oxford English Dictionary entry for 'void': a usage example mentioning beans prompted her to draw beans from her garden. She then looked up another word from the sentence, selected a new example and continued the sequence. The project connected reading, objects, pictures and language through deliberately chosen rules. Her account helps explain why the visual arrangement of a page can be part of the writing itself.

sections.heading: Linguistic roots and creative cross-pollination
sections.body: In her 2004 Paris Review interview, Carson described moving among three desks devoted to academic work, writing and art. Switching projects allowed the activities to influence one another. She also explained how she connects writers or texts by sensing a resemblance in the shape of their ideas. Her account of discovering Greek through a high-school teacher and Sappho presented reading as an encounter with unfamiliar depths of language. Ancient fragments appealed partly because they carry traces of copying, damage, recovery and interpretation across centuries. Drawing, she said, felt more personally exposing than writing. These observations describe her working experience at the time of that conversation and illuminate the interaction between scholarship, visual form and literary invention.

terms.definition: The study of a word's origins and how its form and meaning have developed over time.
Carson's metaphor for structural or conceptual resemblances that suggest connections between different writers or texts.

sections.heading: Evolution of light-driven neuronal control methods
sections.body: Optical control of neurons had several predecessors. Early experiments used lasers and dyes but encountered damage from light exposure. Miesenböck and colleagues' chARGe system combined three proteins from a fly visual pathway to make cultured mammalian neurons respond to illumination through intracellular signalling. Another approach paired an ATP-sensitive receptor with light-releasable ATP to influence fly behaviour. These implementations involved multiple components and supplementary molecules, and their responses were slower than the later channelrhodopsin approach. The history explains the appeal of a compact light-sensitive channel that could directly alter membrane currents: it simplified an experimental task that earlier systems had shown was possible.

sections.heading: Functional expression of Channelrhodopsin-2 in diverse animal cells
sections.body: The 2003 study expressed channelrhodopsin-2 in frog egg cells and mammalian cells to test what the algal protein did. Illumination rapidly increased the membrane's permeability to positively charged ions, including ions carrying one or two charges. The resulting current could shift the cell's voltage. Continued illumination produced a smaller sustained response after the initial peak, showing that channel behaviour changes during exposure. Recovery and closing also depended on electrical and chemical conditions. Although the protein has seven membrane-spanning helices, its action is directly channel-like rather than a sequence of G-protein signalling reactions. These measurements established a useful connection between light and membrane electrical activity.

sections.heading: Millisecond-scale control of mammalian neuronal activity
sections.body: In the 2005 study, the team used a lentiviral delivery method to express channelrhodopsin-2 in cultured mammalian neurons. Brief light pulses could then trigger precisely timed electrical spikes and alter synaptic transmission. Changing pulse duration or intensity helped accommodate differences in expression between cells; weakly expressing neurons could respond without reaching the threshold for a spike. The researchers also checked membrane electrical properties and dye uptake as indicators of cell health. Under the tested conditions, expression and illumination did not increase detected damage relative to controls. These were experiments on prepared cells, establishing a tool for neural research.

terms.definition: A molecular tool that converts illumination into a change in cellular activity, such as an electrical current across a membrane.
Channelrhodopsin-2, an algal membrane protein that opens an ion-conducting pathway in response to light.
A shift in membrane voltage towards a less negative cell interior, which can help trigger an action potential if sufficient.

sections.heading: Legal interpretations from the Akayesu genocide judgment
sections.body: On 2 September 1998, the ICTR's Trial Chamber I found Jean-Paul Akayesu guilty on nine counts and acquitted him on six. The decision was unanimous among judges Laïty Kama, Lennart Aspegren and Navanethem Pillay. Convictions included genocide, direct and public incitement to genocide, and crimes against humanity. The chamber examined how rape and sexual violence contributed to the destruction of the Tutsi group, recognising that such acts can constitute genocide when the required intent is established. It also treated coercion as broader than physical force, including threats and intimidation. The ruling therefore connected findings about particular acts with the legal conditions for international crimes. It was a judgment of the chamber, involving all three judges.

sections.heading: Precedents established by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda
sections.body: Pillay began serving as an ICTR judge in 1995 following election by the United Nations General Assembly. Her work included the Kambanda case, in which Rwanda's former prime minister pleaded guilty to genocide and crimes against humanity and received a life sentence. She also participated in Akayesu, whose judgment addressed genocide and sexual violence. These cases contributed to the tribunal's developing jurisprudence. Pillay became ICTR president in May 1999 and was re-elected in 2001. In 2003 she was elected to the International Criminal Court, where she served until becoming UN High Commissioner for Human Rights in 2008. The chronology shows different judicial and institutional roles within a longer career in international law.

terms.definition: The specific intent to destroy a protected group, wholly or partly, required for an act to constitute genocide.
Legal principles and interpretations developed through courts' decisions and reasoning.

sections.heading: Neutrino detection through Antarctic glacial ice
sections.body: IceCube's completed array contains 5,160 optical sensors on 86 strings, distributed through a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice. The sensors detect light from charged particles produced in neutrino interactions. They do not photograph the neutrinos themselves. Most recorded activity comes from other sources: cosmic rays striking the atmosphere produce penetrating particles and atmospheric neutrinos. Researchers therefore select events and compare their combined properties with expected backgrounds. An astrophysical signal can emerge statistically even when the origin of an individual event remains uncertain. Neutrinos' lack of electric charge is valuable for astronomy because magnetic fields do not deflect their paths, although tracing a source also depends on reconstructing the detected event's direction.

sections.heading: Detection mechanisms and neutrino energy reconstruction
sections.body: Different event selections exploit different strengths of IceCube. For starting-event analyses, an outer part of the instrumented ice acts as a veto around a large inner region, helping reject particles that enter from outside. Other analyses use long tracks from muons created by neutrino interactions beyond the instrumented volume. Such tracks enlarge the effective detection volume and provide good directional information. The technical background quotes an angular resolution of about 0.3 degrees at 100 TeV for this channel. Muon-energy estimates are less precise because energy loss fluctuates along the track. Researchers infer a population's neutrino-energy distribution from the recorded energy deposits and detector response. Combining these approaches helped establish a diffuse astrophysical neutrino signal.

terms.definition: Energetic particles travelling through space, commonly protons or other atomic nuclei, whose interactions in Earth's atmosphere create secondary particles.
A selected event whose detectable neutrino interaction begins within the detector's inner analysis volume, rather than entering from outside.
